Contents of the texts

The table of contents of each of the 77 books and articles on museums this site is built from, with an overview of every chapter (1041 overviews). Open a book for a short overview of the whole work, a note on how far East and Southeast Asia are discussed in it, and its contents; open a chapter to read its overview and, where it has one, what it says about those regions. Chapter overviews were written by machine from a full reading of each chapter; the book overviews and Asia notes were written from those chapter overviews and from the passages of each text that name the region. None of it has been checked by a person.

Chapters on East and Southeast Asia (132: 64 chiefly, 68 in part)
  • The politics of nostalgia: museum representations of Lafcadio Hearn in Japan in Askew, The Politics of Nostalgia chiefly
    The whole article concerns Japan. It reads the three Hearn museums in Matsue, Kumamoto and Yaizu against the Yushukan museum at Yasukuni Shrine and the postwar nostalgia for a traditional Japan. It also covers Hearn's ambivalence about the common people of Kumamoto and his 1904 remarks on the Shokonsha war dead, which the displays leave out.
  • Four: The Chinese Question in Cuno, Who Owns Antiquity? chiefly
    China is the chapter's main subject. Cuno covers the Mogao caves at Dunhuang in Gansu, where Stein, Pelliot and Warner acquired manuscripts, paintings and a Tang sculpture now at Harvard, and the Dunhuang Academy director Fan Jinshi, who hosted him. Cuno follows the Chinese export, excavation and sale laws of 1930, 1950, 1982, 1987 and 1992, and the Poly Art Museum's 2000 purchase of the Yuanmingyuan bronze heads. Cuno also discusses Xinjiang, Turpan and Kashgar, the Uighur population and the Han settlement of the region, the Three Gorges Dam salvage, and the German expeditions to Turfan.
  • Antiquities and the Importance—and Limitations—of Archaeological Contexts James C. Y. Watt in Cuno (ed.), Whose Culture? chiefly
    Chiefly about China. Watt uses Liangzhu jade congs from the Lower Yangzi, jades from the tomb of Lady Hao (Fu Hao) at Anyang, a Shang ritual wine vessel, a Western Zhou ding, the bell chimes of the Marquis of Zeng in Hubei, a gold ornament from a Jin-period tomb near Suzhou that he traces to steppe and Xiongnu transmission, and the horse and groom from the tomb of Li Xian. Watt also discusses Neolithic jades from the National Palace Museum, Taipei, shown at the Metropolitan in 1996, and a Southern Song ceramic copy of a ts'ung jade.
  • Introduction in Denton, Exhibiting the Past chiefly
    The whole book concerns China. The introduction covers the National Museum of China's 2011 Road to Revival exhibit, the Nantong Museum founded in 1906, the Palace Museum in Beijing and its Taipei counterpart, and museum-building bursts since 1958. It also surveys museums in South Korea (the Seoul War Memorial), Taiwan and Japan, where displays range from whitewashing the war to documenting war crimes.
  • Chapter 1. National Origins and Local Identity: Museums of Premodern History in Denton, Exhibiting the Past chiefly
    The chapter is about China's premodern museums: the Ancient China hall of 2011, the Museum of Chinese History (opened to the public in 1926 and rehoused on Tiananmen Square in 1961), the Military Museum's premodern exhibit added in 1988, and local museums for the Liangzhu, Hongshan, Sanxingdui and Ba and Shu cultures. It also treats the Koguryo/Gaojuli dispute with Korea over an ancient kingdom, and the Nanyue kingdom of Guangzhou, which reached northern Vietnam.
  • Chapter 2. Exhibiting the Revolution: The Museum of the Chinese Revolution in Denton, Exhibiting the Past chiefly
    The whole chapter concerns China, so its content is central here. It covers the 1929 West Lake Exposition in Hangzhou, where a Nationalist Revolutionary Memorial Hall stood beside commercial halls, and the Beijing Museum of the Chinese Revolution from its 1961 opening to the 2011 Road to Revival exhibit. It also notes the Jinchaji street exhibitions, the 1948 Northeast Martyrs Memorial Hall in Harbin, and the 1990s special exhibits on Rewi Alley and George Hatem.
  • Chapter 3. Commodification and Nostalgia: Revolutionary History in the Era of the Market Economy in Denton, Exhibiting the Past chiefly
    The whole chapter concerns China. It covers the Red Crag sites in Chongqing, where a Zhou Enlai-centered display and a re-created Home of Democracy sit beside a conventional Southern Bureau exhibit, and the SACO controversy is downplayed; the Opium War and Naval Battle museums at Humen in Guangdong; the Nanjing Presidential Palace, which presents KMT rule and Republican industry positively; and the Shanghai Municipal History Museum, whose models of old Shanghai recall a commercial past. It also covers the First CCP Congress site in Shanghai's Xintiandi district.
  • Chapter 4. Martyrdom and Memory: Monuments, Memorials, and Museums for Dead Heroes in Denton, Exhibiting the Past chiefly
    Most of the chapter concerns China. It studies the Longhua Martyrs Memorial Park in Shanghai, with its glass-pyramid hall, individual martyr displays and restored Nationalist execution ground, and the Yuhuatai park in Nanjing, with its Jiang Zemin inscription and closing display of modern Nanjing. It also covers the Yue Fei shrine on West Lake in Hangzhou, the Huanghuagang memorial to the 1911 martyrs in Guangzhou, the martyr monuments at the Huangpu Military Academy, and the Longhua website's virtual flowers.
  • Chapter 5. Martial Glory and the Power of the State: Military Museums in Denton, Exhibiting the Past chiefly
    The chapter argues that the Beijing Military Museum uses ancient Chinese warfare, from Sunzi to Qing paintings of Qianlong's victories, to justify strong state power. It covers the Korean War exhibit, which presents China as a peace-loving nation that entered the war reluctantly against American aggression, and the Huangpu Military Academy near Guangzhou. It contrasts the Yushukan Museum at Yasukuni Shrine, which presents a sanitized Asia-Pacific War, with Japan's peace museums in Hiroshima, Nagasaki and Osaka.
  • Chapter 6. Heroic Resistance and Victims of Atrocity: Negotiating the Memory of Japanese Imperialism in Denton, Exhibiting the Past chiefly
    The whole chapter concerns China and Japan. It examines three Chinese museums of the occupation: the War of Resistance Memorial Hall in Wanping near Beijing, with its atrocity dioramas, tunnel-warfare display and 2005 Great Victory exhibit that adds Nationalist and Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau resistance; the Nanjing Massacre Memorial Hall, with Qi Kang's bleak design and 2007 expansion; and the Unit 731 Crimes Evidence Exhibition Hall at its original site in Pingfang, Heilongjiang, with its ruins and documentary film. It notes that the Nanjing mother-and-child statue echoes Japanese memorials at Hiroshima and Yasukuni.
  • Chapter 7. Heroic Models and Exemplary Leaders: Memorial Halls in Denton, Exhibiting the Past chiefly
    The whole chapter concerns China. It covers the Lei Feng Memorial Hall in Fushun, Liaoning, and the Lei Feng birthplace memorial in Wangcheng, Hunan; the Zhou Enlai Memorial Hall in Huai'an, Jiangsu, and the earlier Tianjin memorial to Zhou and Deng Yingchao; the Deng Xiaoping Memorial Hall in Guang'an, Sichuan; and the Chen Yun memorial in a village outside Shanghai. It also notes the Pingdingshan Massacre memorial and the Fushun War Prisoners Detention Center, which place Japanese atrocities and prisoners in the Fushun story.
  • Chapter 8. Literary Politics and Cultural Heritage: Modern Literature Museums in Denton, Exhibiting the Past chiefly
    The chapter is about the PRC throughout: the Lu Xun memorial halls in Shaoxing, Beijing, Shanghai, Xiamen and Guangzhou, the 2005 Wang Xiaobo exhibit in Beijing, the Lu Village theme park near Shaoxing, and the Modern Literature Museum in Beijing. It also notes premodern sites such as the Wenxuan Lou in Yangzhou and the Orchid Pavilion at Shaoxing, and says that Mao-era memorials excluded liberal writers.
  • Chapter 9. Ethnic Minorities and the Construction of National Identity: Ethnographic Museums in Denton, Exhibiting the Past chiefly
    The chapter concerns the PRC throughout: minority museums in Yunnan, Guangxi, Heilongjiang, Xinjiang, Tibet, Inner Mongolia, Guizhou and Beijing, and the Splendid China park in Shenzhen, which has replicas of Mongol and Tibetan sites. It discusses Yi, Miao, Dai, Mosuo and Tibetan representations, and mentions Vietnamese and Korean groups and the Taiwan aboriginal rights movement only in passing.
  • Chapter 10. Revolutionary Memory and National Landscape: Red Tourism in Denton, Exhibiting the Past chiefly
    The whole chapter concerns the PRC. Its case studies are Jinggangshan in Jiangxi, the Hunan memorial sites at Shaoshan and Huaminglou, and Xibaipo in Hebei, with brief mention of Yan'an, Anyuan, Chongqing's Red Crag and Shajiabang in Jiangsu. Foreign delegations were also taken to Shaoshan and Yan'an in the Maoist period, and the 2009 documentary New Socialist Climax, filmed at Jinggangshan, shows Chinese visitors with mixed attitudes to the sites.
  • Chapter 11. Museums of the Future: Municipal Urban Planning Exhibition Halls in Denton, Exhibiting the Past chiefly
    Every hall discussed is in mainland China, with Beijing's hall and Dalian's Modern Museum mentioned in passing. The chapter says the Shanghai hall presents Shanghai as a model of development for developing nations around Asia, and notes delegations from Ho Chi Minh City and a 2001 visit by the North Korean leader. A Hong Kong retrocession countdown clock between Beijing's Museum of History and Museum of the Chinese Revolution, and Taipei's Exploration Center as a contrast, are also discussed.
  • Conclusion in Denton, Exhibiting the Past chiefly
    The conclusion concerns museums and memory in the PRC throughout, so it is about East Asia from start to finish. It recalls the National Museum of China's Road to Revival exhibit and the urban planning halls, and says that municipal and provincial museums can present the modern past differently from the national museum.
  • 13 Dancing pot and pregnant jar? On ceramics, metaphors and creative labels Wing Yan Vivian Ting in Dudley (ed.), Museum Materialities chiefly
    Chinese ceramics are the whole subject: a Ding bowl from Dingzhou (Hebei), dated to the tenth to twelfth centuries, shown without a label, a Ming blue-and-white bottle, a Yuan blue-and-white wine jar, a Song celadon bowl with peony decoration and a Southern Song black tea ware, all in the museum's Chinese collection. Ting cites Chinese connoisseurs' terms such as 'moon white' and 'phoenix tail shaped' vases, and the whipped-tea practice behind a black tea bowl. The participants are not Asian; they were literacy and ESOL students from Africa and Eastern Europe.
  • The Re-Crafting of Design: Towards an Ethnographic Perspective in Chinese Exhibition Design Lisheng Zhang and David Francis in Guy, Williams & Wintle (eds.), Histories of Exhibition Design in the Museum chiefly
    China is the whole setting. The chapter discusses the Dong craftswomen of Dali village in Guizhou province and their textile cooperative, and the Chinese National Museum of Ethnology in Beijing, which has no permanent building and tours its exhibitions. It contrasts Chinese ethnographic museums, which present the peoples of China itself, with European ones that display non-Europeans, and it describes the 'Museum Boom' of the mid-2000s and state policy on intangible cultural heritage.
  • Ethnonational Identity and Mannequins in History Museums in Korea and Japan Kyunghee Pyun in Guy, Williams & Wintle (eds.), Histories of Exhibition Design in the Museum chiefly
    Korea and Japan are the whole subject. Pyun sets Osaka's ethnically uniform dioramas against the multi-ethnic families and migrants in both countries, and reads the Korean wedding diorama as a deliberate statement of Korean uniqueness. At the War Memorial of Korea, Korean officers have faces and the Korean Empire section is based on paintings and photographs of officers of the 1900s, while realistic mannequins of Vietnamese soldiers from North and South are now shown. The Gwangju National Museum's VR installation shows Chinese merchants at Ningbo and the 1975 Sinan shipwreck cargo of Song and Yuan porcelain bound for Hakata.
  • Classifying China: Shifting Interpretations of Buddhist Bronzes in Liverpool Museum, 1867–1997 Louise Tythacott in Hill (ed.), Museums and Biographies chiefly
    Almost all of the chapter concerns China: the five Putuo Island deity figures, the Chinese bronzes and other Asian objects at Liverpool Museum, and how Chinese objects were divided between ethnography, decorative art and antiquities in Britain and France. It notes that Gatty in 1882 placed the 'highly cultivated' Asian races outside ethnology, that Manchester Museum's 1958 Asia galleries separated 'Civilizations' (China, Japan, Siam, Burma) from 'Tribes', and that Oriental Ceramic Society collectors shaped British taste in Chinese art from the 1920s. It also notes that the Musée du Quai Branly shows only Southeast Asian textiles and puppets, with the art kept at the Musée Guimet.
  • From Landlord Manor to Red Memorabilia: Reincarnations of a Chinese Museum Town in Ho & Li, From Landlord Manor to Red Memorabilia chiefly
    Anren, in Sichuan, is the chief subject. The Landlord Manor Museum, opened in 1959 in Liu Wencai's seized home, taught class hatred through land deeds, shackles, a water dungeon and a dragon bed, and it later housed the Rent Collection Courtyard sculptures made in 1965. The chapter also covers the private Jianchuan Museum Cluster, with millions of Cultural Revolution artifacts, and the disputed history of Liu Wencai.
  • The Early China Trade John Ayers in Impey & MacGregor (eds.), The Origins of Museums chiefly
    Chinese porcelain, silks, paintings, carvings and Yixing teapots form the whole subject. Ayers covers Chinese goods in Venice, Florence, Dresden and Innsbruck, and the trade routed through Malacca, a Southeast Asian port where Chinese merchants met the Portuguese. Ayers notes that Chinese, Japanese and Southeast Asian objects were confused under 'Indian' in inventories, and that some Ambras lacquer was assigned to factories in the Ryukyu Islands.
  • Japan: Trade and Collecting in Seventeenth-Century Europe Oliver Impey in Impey & MacGregor (eds.), The Origins of Museums chiefly
    Japan is the whole subject: Namban-style and export lacquer (coffers, cabinets, scriptors, screens), Arita porcelain (blue-and-white, Imari and Kakiemon) and Japanese paper. Impey covers the trade through Portuguese, Chinese, Dutch and English middlemen at Nagasaki, Hirado and Deshima, and the Japanese converts who came to Europe in 1584 with lacquer and screens. Southeast Asia appears in an order of 1680 by the Siam office for Constant Phaulkon, who ruled Siam, for lacquered dishes to be given to the French court. Chinese merchants and their lacquer furniture also feature, since they undercut Japanese work after the 1680s.
  • Chapter 4: The Poetics of Exhibition in Japanese Culture: Masao Yamaguchi Masao Yamaguchi in Karp & Lavine (eds.), Exhibiting Cultures chiefly
    Japan is the chapter's whole subject. Yamaguchi draws on the tokonoma alcove, osira-sama figurines dressed by itako shamans in northeastern Japan, yamabushi-kagura performers, kabuki costume, Noh shaman-priests, furyu processions and the Matara cake offering at Motsu temple in Hiraizumi. Yamaguchi also reads the mid-nineteenth-century Japanese adoption of Western technology as an act of mitate, in which Western things were transplanted into Japan.
  • Chapter 11. Political change and the national museum in Taiwan Chi-Jung Chu in Knell et al. (eds.), National Museums chiefly
    Japan's Director-General's Museum in Taipei, founded in 1908, held collections of Taiwan's indigenous peoples and objects from South East Asia and southern China, which Chu links to Japan's colonial ambitions. The KMT's National Palace Museum, built in 1962 with US aid, showcased imperial Chinese art and sent treasures abroad, including to Japan's Expo '70 in Osaka and to Seoul in 1973. Chu notes that its exhibitions were used to teach Taiwanese people to be Chinese. Under the DPP, its director Tu Cheng-shen mounted Taiwan-focused exhibitions from 2002 and removed the Chiang and Sun statues in 2004.
  • Chapter 17. Re-thinking Korean cultural identities at the National Museum of Korea Sunghee Choi in Knell et al. (eds.), National Museums chiefly
    Korea is the chapter's whole subject: the National Museum of Korea's fine art and archaeology galleries, a Joseon documentary screen of court ceremonies, and the colonial-era idea of Korean art as 'sorrow', which the Japanese critic Yanagi Muneyoshi developed around Joseon white porcelain. Choi also compares Korean documentary painting with Chinese and Japanese neo-Confucian art, and argues that Korean identity was shaped under Japanese colonial rule.
  • Chapter 18. The aesthetics and narratives of national museums in China Marzia Varutti in Knell et al. (eds.), National Museums chiefly
    The whole chapter concerns China: the Shanghai Museum's aesthetic display, Beijing's National History Museum, Military Museum and Capital Museum, the China Millennium Monument's 2004 'Imperial Treasures' show, and the Sanxingdui Museum's presentation of the ancient Shu civilisation of Sichuan. It traces the Nantong Museum of 1905, the Palace Museum of 1925 and revolutionary displays under Mao, and notes that Western museums often file Chinese material under 'Asian Art' or 'Far-East Asian Antiquities'.
  • Chapter 21. Recounting history: Constructing a national narrative in the Hong Kong Museum of History Emily Stokes-Rees in Knell et al. (eds.), National Museums chiefly
    Hong Kong is the whole subject: the chapter analyses the Hong Kong Museum of History's The Hong Kong Story, which presents the territory's past as a rise from fishing village to metropolis, and sets it against the 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration and the 1997 return to China. It quotes a Hong Kong visitor calling the exhibition 'dumbing down', and the director of the Hong Kong Heritage Museum, Yim Shui-yen, on the public's need for an 'official history'. The mainland 'motherland' is the foil against which the narrative defines a distinct Hong Kong people.
  • Chapter 22. Kaesŏng Koryŏ Museum: The place of one Korean nation? Ruth Scheidhauer in Knell et al. (eds.), National Museums chiefly
    The chapter is entirely about Korea, with North and South Korea as its two states. It traces the Imperial Household Museum (opened 1909) and the Chosŏn General Government Museum (1915), the colonial-era museums that shaped Korean collecting, and the Kaesŏng Provincial Museum's collections, which were moved to Seoul and then to Pusan during the Korean War. It also reports the reactions of South Korean tourists to North Korean guides and displays on the Kaesŏng tours of 2005 to 2008, which they found backward yet romantic.
  • Chapter 23. The national museum as palimpsest: Postcolonial politics and the National Museum of Korea Jung Joon Lee in Knell et al. (eds.), National Museums chiefly
    Korea is the subject throughout. Lee traces the National Museum of Korea from the Yi royal family museum of 1908 and the Joseon Governor-General's Museum of 1915, through wartime removal to Busan, to the Japanese colonial building that Seoul demolished in 1995. Lee shows how colonial power is written into that building, whose architect Ichiro Nomura also designed the Governor-General's building in Taiwan. The chapter also cites a 2008 'Amity' exhibition of Thai contemporary art, staged by the Korean National Museum of Contemporary Art in Bangkok as cultural diplomacy.
  • Chapter 24. Exhibiting China in London Amy Jane Barnes in Knell et al. (eds.), National Museums chiefly
    China is the whole subject. Barnes traces how Opium War coverage, and Nathan Dunn's Celebrated Chinese Collection of the 1840s, presented Chinese things as exotic and degraded, including a human exhibit with bound feet and an opium-smoking display. Barnes examines the Chinese court at the 1851 Great Exhibition, drawn mostly from British holdings and largely export ware, and the South Kensington Museum's Asian galleries, which separated Chinese art from Western art. Barnes also discusses looted objects, including the Qianlong lacquered throne at the Victoria and Albert Museum, taken from the Nan Yuan hunting park in 1901.
  • CHAPTER 5: Intangible Heritage and Embodiment: Japan’s Influence on Global Heritage Discourse Natsuko Akagawa in Logan, Nic Craith & Kockel (eds.), A Companion to Heritage Studies chiefly
    Japan is the chapter's central case. Akagawa traces how craft skill, the mingei folk-craft movement and the concept of mukei (non-form) became symbols of Japanese identity from the Meiji period and the Paris (1867) and Vienna (1873) exhibitions, and how the 1950 Cultural Properties Law and its living national treasures shaped the intangible heritage model that UNESCO adopted. Akagawa also notes that Japanese archaeologists identified monuments in colonial Korea, from which South Korea's postwar system later grew, and that Japan funded UNESCO's intangible heritage programme.
  • CHAPTER 16: World Heritage and National Hegemony: The Discursive Formation of Chinese Political Authority Haiming Yan in Logan, Nic Craith & Kockel (eds.), A Companion to Heritage Studies chiefly
    China is the chapter's whole subject: the state's World Heritage rhetoric about the Great Wall (shown at the Great Wall Museum, Badaling), the Grand Canal, the Chengde Mountain Resort temples, the Potala Palace in Tibet, and the Fujian Tulou. It also treats the Old Town of Kashgar in Xinjiang, excluded from the Silk Road nomination and demolished in 2009. South Korea's 2004 nomination of Ganjeung Danojie, which Chinese public opinion treated as theft of a Chinese festival, is discussed briefly.
  • CHAPTER 28: Heritage in the “Asian Century”: Responding to Geopolitical Change Zeynep Aygen and William Logan in Logan, Nic Craith & Kockel (eds.), A Companion to Heritage Studies chiefly
    Japan and China are the chapter's main cases. Japanese experts such as Nobuo Ito pressed for the 1999 ICOMOS timber principles and the 1994 Nara Document, which let each nation set conservation approaches suited to its own culture, and Japan's diplomacy helped shift UNESCO towards intangible heritage. China adapted Western charters into its 2000 China Principles and now holds 47 World Heritage sites. The chapter also covers colonial heritage in Hanoi, George Town, Malacca and Yangon, heritage funding in the Philippines and Nepal, the Preah Vihear dispute between Cambodia and Thailand, and minority heritage in Tibet, Xinjiang and northern Thailand.
  • CHAPTER 31: Cross-Cultural Encounters and “Difficult Heritage” on the Thai–Burma Railway: An Ethics of Cosmopolitanism rather than Practices of Exclusion Andrea Witcomb in Logan, Nic Craith & Kockel (eds.), A Companion to Heritage Studies chiefly
    Witcomb's whole chapter concerns Kanchanaburi in Thailand and the Thai-Burma railway. Witcomb describes the JEATH Museum, set up in a Buddhist temple in 1977, whose photographs and objects donated by local Thai families and former prisoners record friendly exchanges, and the Weary Dunlop Peace Park, built by Kanit Wanachote on his own property. Witcomb notes that the railway is absent from Thai heritage lists, which favour royal and Buddhist sites, and that local authorities renamed the bridge to draw tourists after the film Bridge on the River Kwai.
  • CHAPTER 33: “Putting Broken Pieces Back Together”: Reconciliation, Justice, and Heritage in Post-Conflict Situations Patrick Daly and Benjamin Chan in Logan, Nic Craith & Kockel (eds.), A Companion to Heritage Studies chiefly
    Cambodia and Japan are the two case studies, so the chapter is chiefly about Southeast and East Asia. Daly and Chan describe the Tuol Sleng Genocide Museum in Phnom Penh, where photographs of Khmer Rouge cadres sit among images of their victims, and question how far official heritage is shaped by current leaders who were themselves involved in the Khmer Rouge. For Japan they discuss the Yasukuni shrine and Yushukan Museum, the Hiroshima Peace Memorial and the Nagasaki Atomic Bomb Museum, arguing that the narrative of Japanese victimhood was partly shaped by American occupation policy.
  • Preface in Lu, Museums in China chiefly
    Most of the preface concerns China. Lu sets the book in mainland China and Hong Kong and sketches three phases of Chinese museum history: early museums founded before 1949 by foreign elites, missionaries, Chinese governments or scholars; state-controlled museums from 1949 to the 1980s, when Marxism and Maoism were the only framework; and, from the 1980s, a rise in number and diversity, including ecomuseums and private museums. A 2010 Hong Kong incident opens the preface.
  • China between 1840 and 1949 in Lu, Museums in China chiefly
    Chapter 1 is chiefly about China, 1840 to 1949: the opium trade, the Opium Wars, the Taiping and other rebellions, the Sino-Japanese wars, the 1911 revolution, Yuan Shikai and the Nationalist and Communist parties. It names Chinese intellectuals such as Kang Youwei, Liang Qichao, Yan Fu and Zhang Jian, who founded a private museum in Nantong in 1905, and Western scholars working in China, including Andersson, Hedin, Karlgren and Weidenreich, whose work underpinned early museums.
  • Missionaries and early museums in Lu, Museums in China chiefly
    China is the whole subject: the Zikawei (Heude) Museum in Shanghai, the Chefoo, Tsingchoufu and Guangzhiyuan museums in Shandong, and the Hoang Ho Pai Ho Museum in Tianjin, with their natural history specimens, antiquities and visitors such as Hu Shih. Heude's collecting trips are also said to have reached Cambodia, the Philippines, Indonesia, Vietnam, Thailand and Japan between 1892 and 1902, a list the chapter does not develop.
  • Social elites and early museums in Lu, Museums in China chiefly
    Both museums are in China and the chapter is about China itself. The Shanghai Museum was a Western-run collection in the foreign concession, built around Chinese natural history specimens, antiquities, art and coins, and by the 1930s it drew mainly Chinese school pupils and students; its displays included Peking Man fossils and Shang bronzes, and its director Sowerby is described as sympathetic to China. The Nantong Museum in Jiangsu held local nature and culture, Buddhist scripts and objects such as a whale skeleton, and Zhang's proposals for a national museum in Beijing followed a Japanese imperial model.
  • Museums in modern state formation in Lu, Museums in China chiefly
    Almost all of the chapter concerns China. It covers the Qing imperial collection in Beijing, including objects from the Chengde and Shenyang palaces, paintings, bronzes, ceramics, jade and fake works, and the Palace Museum's exhibitions of Qing paintings, snuff bottles and Chinese opera. It names Aurel Stein, Paul Pelliot and Langdon Warner, who took thousands of Chinese antiquities to museums in France, Germany, Japan, Russia, the UK and the USA, and it describes the 1914 export ban. The collection later moved to Shanghai, Nanjing and Chongqing and, from 1965, to Taipei.
  • Museums under the communist state in Lu, Museums in China chiefly
    Much of the chapter concerns China, with a Taiwan thread. The Shanghai Museum mounted 1950s exhibitions 'Taiwan Must Be Liberated' and one on the Gaoshan people of Taiwan, and the Palace Museum toured a 1955 show against American attempts to steal antiquities in Taiwan. A 1976 Shanghai ceramics exhibition argued that Chinese civilisation was indigenous and that South China Sea islands had been occupied by Chinese since antiquity. The 1973-78 overseas tour of Cultural Revolution archaeological finds visited Japan, the Philippines and Hong Kong among other places, drawing over 6.5 million visitors.
  • Ecomuseums, ethnicity and the management of intangible cultural heritage in Lu, Museums in China chiefly
    The chapter is about China's southwest. It describes the Guizhou ecomuseums, a Miao village ecomuseum and two Dong village ecomuseums (Dang and Tei), founded from 1995 under a Sino-Norwegian project, and the private Tei Ecomuseum set up in 2005 by a Hong Kong businessman. Lu also compares the economies of Guangdong, Shanghai, Guizhou and Gansu, and notes discrimination against Zhuang people in Guangxi, Naxi people in Lijiang and the Mosuo of Yunnan, with a brief comparison to Tibet and Xinjiang.
  • Museums, tourism and local cultural changes in Lu, Museums in China chiefly
    The whole chapter concerns one site in Gansu, north-western China, where the Tsa grottoes are a Buddhist cave complex on the Silk Road. It covers the site's history under the Nationalists, the admission fees from the 1980s, the Bathing Buddha Festival, and three villages (Wei, Qu and Tang) whose economies moved from farming to camel-riding, home-stays and land resumption. It also notes that Buddhism reached Xinjiang and Gansu along the Silk Road, and that foreign explorers took Buddhist art abroad in the early twentieth century.
  • Museums in a changing China in Lu, Museums in China chiefly
    The whole chapter concerns mainland China, so its East Asian material is central. Lu covers the Dunhuang grottoes, whose conservation has been supported by the Getty Institute and the Japanese government since the 1980s, and the Jianchuan Museum Cluster's displays on the Sino-Japanese war, and notes that Chinese museums have organized more than 500 overseas exhibitions since the 1980s.
  • The Forbidden City Goes Abroad: Qing History and the Foreign Exhibitions of the Palace Museum, 1974-2004 in Naquin, The Forbidden City Goes Abroad chiefly
    Most of the shows went to East Asia: seven to Japan, four to Hong Kong, shows in Macao and Taiwan, and a 1992 exhibition in Seoul. The essay describes the 1974 Tokyo show at the Mitsukoshi stores and the 1981 Hong Kong Treasures of Imperial Palace show as the start of the formula, and it treats Taipei's National Palace Museum as the Beijing museum's rival, with the 2003 Kaohsiung and Taipei shows as an unusual visit to Taiwan. The Shenyang Palace Museum's 1989 Singapore show is the only Southeast Asian case.
  • 17 Towards social inclusion in Taiwan: Museums, equality and indigenous groups Marzia Varutti in Sandell & Nightingale (eds.), Museums, Equality and Social Justice chiefly
    Almost the whole chapter concerns Taiwan: museums commemorating the 2-28 Incident in Taipei and the white terror on Green Island, the 921 Earthquake Museum in Wufeng, and the National Museum of Taiwan History in Tainan, which presents Taiwanese history as multicultural. It details the indigenous collections of the National Taiwan Museum and the Shung Ye Museum, the Japanese colonial ethnology that gathered them, and the Big Museum Leads Small Museum programme with Amis and Atayal communities. It also notes exhibitions on migrant workers and Hakka museums.
  • Introduction in Tseng, The Imperial Museums of Meiji Japan chiefly
    The whole Introduction concerns Japan, so East Asia is its subject. It describes the Imperial Museums at Tokyo (Ueno Park), Kyoto and Nara and the Hyokeikan in Tokyo, along with Okakura Kakuzo's 1888 plan for a triad of museums in which the Tokyo museum would specialize in Tokugawa art and the artifacts of Asia. It also uses Japan's Hodden pavilion at the 1893 Chicago World's Columbian Exposition as a parallel national display. No other East or Southeast Asian place is discussed.
  • Encounters and Translations: The Origins of Hakubutsukan and Bijutsu in Tseng, The Imperial Museums of Meiji Japan chiefly
    Japan is the chapter's subject. Fukuzawa, Kume and Sano are Japanese officials and writers, and the chapter follows the Tokugawa envoys' missions of 1860 and 1862 and the Meiji government's 1873 display at the Vienna exposition, where Japan showed its products and a national pavilion. Sano's 1875 proposal envisions a composite museum for Ueno Park in Tokyo. No Chinese, Korean or Southeast Asian collections are discussed.
  • The Museum in Ueno Park: Styling the Nation in Tseng, The Imperial Museums of Meiji Japan chiefly
    Japan is the whole subject of the chapter. It covers the 1877 Art Gallery at the First National Industrial Exhibition in Ueno Park, built by the Japanese builder Hayashi Tadahiro, and the Japanese woodblock prints of the 1877 and 1881 exhibitions. The Japanese statesmen who fought over the Ueno site, Conder's Japanese students, and Baron Hamao Arata, who praised the building's Eastern taste at a 1920 ceremony, all appear. The Saracenic forms are read as an unstable sign for a generalized East, and the Jaipur building is used only as a comparison.
  • The Age of the Imperial Museum in Tseng, The Imperial Museums of Meiji Japan chiefly
    The chapter is mainly about Japan: the temple and shrine treasures of Kyoto and Nara, the Tokyo School of Fine Arts, the journal Kokka, and Okakura and Fenollosa's buying trips in the Kyoto and Nara regions. Fenollosa's outline proposes that Japan survey and collect art in China, Korea and Mongolia, as German and French museums did for Greece and Egypt. He also judged the Chinese ceramics and wood carvings at Philadelphia in 1876 and criticized Japanese and Chinese export ware as a sign of decline.
  • The Imperial Kyoto Museum: Locating the Past within the Present in Tseng, The Imperial Museums of Meiji Japan chiefly
    Japan is the whole subject. Tseng presents the Imperial Kyoto Museum as a Meiji state project that made Kyoto the historical and sacred counterpart to Tokyo, and he compares it with the Japanese national pavilion (Hōōden) at the 1893 Chicago fair, whose period interiors contrast with the Kyoto galleries that classified objects by medium and type. Its architect Katayama Tokuma drew on European and American models, and the chapter notes the Taiwan Government-General Museum (1915), built by Japan as an imperial institution in its colony.
  • The Imperial Nara Museum: Administering History and Religion in Tseng, The Imperial Museums of Meiji Japan chiefly
    Japan's Nara region is the whole subject: icons from Hōryūji, the Shōsōin and Nara temples are followed from Edo-period unveilings and airings into the Imperial Nara Museum. Tseng covers the early-Meiji separation of Shinto from Buddhism and the attacks on temples, the 1875 Nara Exhibition, and the Hōryūji treasures sent to Ueno Park in Tokyo, which he presents as a transfer of Buddhist art to a secular national collection. Fenollosa's proposal for a museum in Nara and the regulations paying temples for their loans are examined in detail.
  • The Hyokeikan Art Museum: Debating the Permanent Place of Art in Tseng, The Imperial Museums of Meiji Japan chiefly
    Japanese art is the subject, set against the Western standards of Japan's Meiji diplomacy. Japanese works were admitted to the Palace of Fine Arts at the 1893 Chicago fair as an exception, and the 1908 committee planned to show Chinese, Korean and Indian art beside Japanese painting and sculpture. Tseng notes that Japan had recently defeated China and was soon to defeat Russia, and he cites Natsume Sōseki's novel The Wayfarer, in which a son first admires Japanese painting in the Hyokeikan.
  • Conclusion in Tseng, The Imperial Museums of Meiji Japan chiefly
    Japan is the subject here. Tseng answers Valéry and Malraux, who said that China and the Far East lacked the museum, by pointing to late-Edo temple airings and painting gatherings as earlier public display, and to the Imperial Museums' role in educating foreign tourists as well as Japanese visitors about the nation's art lineage.
  • Keeping It Real: The Exhibition of Artifact Replicas in National Museums of Korea in Veldkamp, Keeping It Real chiefly
    Korea is the whole subject. The article looks at the National Museum of Korea's replica of the Paekche gilt-bronze incense burner, which is labelled as a replica while the original is in Buyeo, and at the reconstructed tomb of King Muryŏng at the Kongju National Museum. It discusses the Cultural Heritage Administration's programme of certified replicas and the dispute over lending the Pensive Bodhisattva to the Metropolitan Museum, and it notes a Korean celadon incense-burner replica held by the National Museum of Ethnology in Leiden.
  • 18. The Route to Peking in Yallop, Magpies, Squirrels and Thieves chiefly
    Bushell, a doctor at the British Legation in Peking from 1868, collected Chinese objects from palaces, private houses and the markets near the Wu Men gate, and in 1872 visited Shangdu, the Yuan summer capital in Inner Mongolia, with Thomas Grosvenor. From 1874 he sent consignments of Chinese bronzes, mirrors and weapons to South Kensington, and by 1880 he was building a collection with the museum in mind.
  • 19. The Promise of the East in Yallop, Magpies, Squirrels and Thieves chiefly
    The chapter surveys East Asian collecting from the 1860s to the 1880s: Japan's opening after sakoku and the Japonisme vogue for netsuke and tsuba, royal gifts of Japanese arms to South Kensington, and Franks's purchase of over 3,000 Japanese paintings for the British Museum in 1881. China comes through Bushell's Peking collecting, his bronzes, Ming porcelain and plain Chinese bangles, and the 1872 South Kensington catalogue's description of the Chinese as an 'effeminate race'. Franks and Bushell, Yallop shows, tried to replace that contempt with an understanding of the objects.
  • 20. Collecting Without Boundaries in Yallop, Magpies, Squirrels and Thieves chiefly
    Almost all of the chapter concerns China. Bushell spent thirty years in Peking, studying and buying Chinese bronzes, ceramics, ivory, jade and lacquer, and the imperial architecture of the Ming Tombs and the Summer Palace. Yallop describes the 1860 burning of the Summer Palace by British and French troops and the looting that followed, which scattered relics across more than 2,000 museums. Bushell's catalogue of Walters's porcelain, Oriental Ceramic Art (1896), and his jade purchases for Bishop, both made in Peking, are also described, as is his sale of Chinese bronzes to South Kensington Museum.
  • Introduction in Yoshida, From Cultures of War to Cultures of Peace chiefly
    Yoshida's focus is Japan, with museums in the People's Republic of China and the Republic of Korea as a second concern. Yoshida discusses the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum and the Nagasaki Atomic Bomb Museum, both opened in 1955, and the Battleship Mikasa museum, whose renovation in the Cold War was supported by American fleet admiral Chester Nimitz. Yoshida notes that six museums in China and South Korea use large photographs and wax figures to show Japanese atrocities, and that Japanese disputes over memory shape how they do so.
  • The Rise and Fall of War Museums in Imperial Japan in Yoshida, From Cultures of War to Cultures of Peace chiefly
    Japanese museums are the subject, with Taiwan and Korea as colonial sites. The Imperial Museum in Ueno and imperial museums in Nara and Kyoto collected the treasures of the empire, and a Memorial Museum of the Battle of Port Arthur opened in 1906. A zoo and botanical garden were built in Keijo (Seoul) in 1909 to facilitate imperial worship, and Yoshida notes that the handbook of the Museum of the Governor-General of Taiwan stressed peace and humanitarianism, although the imperial government had abandoned its cooperation policy by the mid-1930s and invaded northern Indochina in 1940.
  • Expansion of Peace Museums: Acknowledging Japanese Aggression in Yoshida, From Cultures of War to Cultures of Peace chiefly
    Most of the chapter concerns Japan's aggression in China, Korea, Taiwan and Southeast Asia. Okuno Island's director Murakami tells visitors of the more than 80,000 Chinese killed or wounded by Japanese chemical weapons, and the Kyoto museum displays atrocities in Taiwan, Korea, Manchuria, China and Southeast Asia. The Korea Museum in Tokyo covers Prince Shotoku's Korean tutors, the 1923 killing of Koreans after the Kanto earthquake, and the Hainan Island labor camps, along with a Taiwanese woman's memoir of a sex station. The Women's Active Museum traces sex stations in China and Burma and the testimonies of Korean women such as Pak Yongsim.
  • Peace Museums in China and South Korea in Yoshida, From Cultures of War to Cultures of Peace chiefly
    Yoshida discusses China and South Korea at length, and treats their museums as nationalist. The Nanjing Massacre Memorial Museum, opened in 1985 and rebuilt in 2007, honours Japanese such as Honda Katsuichi and in 2010 hosted the cartoonists' exhibition 'My August 15'. Beijing's Memorial Museum of the Chinese People's War of Resistance against Japan and Shenyang's September 18 Historical Museum are described as patriotic education bases. South Korea's Independence Hall of Korea (1987) and Seodaemun Prison History Hall (1998) present Korean martyrs against Japanese colonial rule, and the latter's torture experience rooms, staged for visitors, are described; the chapter says Korean governments' postwar abuses are not shown there.
  • Conclusion: Patriotism vs. Peace in Yoshida, From Cultures of War to Cultures of Peace chiefly
    Japan, China and South Korea are compared throughout. Yoshida contrasts Japanese museums such as the Kyoto museum, which covers victims of Japanese aggression and of the wartime state, with museums in China and South Korea that display vivid images of Japanese atrocities, legitimise just wars and foster 'innocent-us' nationalism. Yoshida wants those Chinese and South Korean museums to show citizens working with Japanese for reconciliation. Nosaka Sanzo, who founded an anti-war alliance in Yan'an, and the journalist Honda Katsuichi are cited as Japanese who challenged their own government.
  • CHAPTER 4: Acquisition: collecting networks and the museum in Alberti, Nature and Culture in part
    The main East Asian case is the Japanese ethnographic and art collection of Robert Wylie Lloyd, a London printer and art collector. Herbert Graham Cannon, introduced to Lloyd by Walter Hincks, persuaded him to leave his Japanese art to the Museum as well, a posthumous gift, and the Japanese material was then shown in a gallery on the top floor of the northern extension. The chapter also notes that a Burmese Buddha returned to Manchester in the 1969 exchange with Salford Museum.
  • 1 The Colonies in Paris in Aldrich, Vestiges of the Colonial Empire in France in part
    Indochina is the chief Asian theme. The Maison de l'Indochine student residence (1930), built on the initiative of a committee headed by an Indochina industrialist, opened amid protests over the repression of the Yen Bay rebellion, and a Maison du Cambodge followed in 1957. The 1931 fair's Salle d'Asie and Janniot's bas-relief of Indochinese peasants present the region as productive and exotic, and the Nogent pavilion and Place des Combattants en Indochine commemorate its colonial soldiers. Bao-Daï's exile apartment on the Rue Fresnel and a statue of Garnier, who died trying to conquer Tonkin, add further links.
  • 2 The Colonies in the Provinces in Aldrich, Vestiges of the Colonial Empire in France in part
    Lyon's Asian links are central: Jesuit missionaries in the Far East, silk merchants who obtained concessions in China and Japan and backed expansion into Indochina, and Emile Guimet, whose Asian art museum opened in Lyon in 1879 and moved to Paris in 1885. Lyon's natural history museum keeps a reconstructed Chinese room, a Vietnamese naga, a Thai Buddha and Cambodian sculpture, and the Institut Franco-Chinois trained 473 Chinese students before 1946. Fréjus's Hong-Hien Pagoda, built in 1917 for Indochinese soldiers, is described, and Marseille's street names include Annam, Haiphong, Hanoi and Tonkin. Bordeaux's museums display Asian tea chests, jade and porcelain.
  • 3 Colonial War Memorials in Aldrich, Vestiges of the Colonial Empire in France in part
    Indochina is central. The Jardin Tropical's Vietnamese dinh, shipped from Cochinchina for the 1906 Marseille fair, became a Temple du Souvenir Indochinois in 1920, burned in 1984 and was replaced by a new memorial in 1992. Cambodian and Laotian soldiers have their own monument there, and Indochinese dead are buried in Toulouse and Nogent-sur-Marne. The Fréjus Indochina memorial, beside a 1917 pagoda, is criticised for a text that presents French rule as benevolent and omits Vietnamese nationalism, forced labour and torture; Ho Chi Minh is never named.
  • 4 Of Men and Monuments in Aldrich, Vestiges of the Colonial Empire in France in part
    Asia runs through the Paris and provincial statues: Garnier's monument in Paris has Indochinese women at its base, a Cambodian-style monument in Grenoble honours Doudart de Lagrée, who died exploring the Mekong, and Pavie, who brought Laos under French control, is commemorated in Dinan. Loti's house in Rochefort has a Chinese room furnished with booty from the siege of Beijing, and Lyautey's Thorey has Indochinese rooms. Notre-Dame des Missions has a painting of the martyrdom of Théophane Vénard in Indochina, and the Rue du Bac seminary keeps relics of Vietnamese martyrs.
  • 5 The Colonies in Museums in Aldrich, Vestiges of the Colonial Empire in France in part
    Indochina recurs most: the Fréjus Troupes de Marine museum has a corner on Hanoi and Auguste Pavie, a Viet Minh banner and a Dien Bien Phu poster, plus a Korean authorities' monument to a Korean War doctor and a banner from the Boxer Rebellion expedition in China. The Val-de-Grâce shows the Pasteur institutes in Hanoi and Saigon, and the Alençon museum holds about five hundred objects collected in Cambodia by Adhémar Leclère. Kahn's Archives de la Planète include footage of Vietnamese trade and rice cultivation, and La Rochelle's Musée d'Orbigny-Bernon has Chinese furniture, lacquer and porcelain.
  • 6 The Colonial Legacy of Non-Western Art in French Museums in Aldrich, Vestiges of the Colonial Empire in France in part
    Indochina is the chief Asian strand: Khmer works from Angkor, collected by Delaporte and Aymonier, went to the Trocadero, and the EFEO sold Indochinese sculptures abroad, six of them to the Metropolitan Museum in 1936, a practice that Siem Reap residents protested in 1949. Eugenie's 'Chinese museum' at Fontainebleau held loot from the 1860 sack of the Beijing summer palace and gifts from the King of Siam. Guimet's museum, founded on his 1876 journey through Japan, China and Indochina, has strong Vietnamese and Cambodian sections, and Labit's Toulouse house held Chinese opium pipes and an Indochinese table.
  • 7 Temporary Exhibitions: Changing Perspectives in Aldrich, Vestiges of the Colonial Empire in France in part
    Asian material is confined to a few exhibitions. Léon Busy's 1920s photographs of Cambodia and Angkor Wat, and his Tonkin views including the Pont Doumer in Hanoi, were shown at the Kahn museum in 1992 and 1994. The 1997 'Paris-Hanoi-Saigon' show covered the Ecole des Beaux-Arts in Hanoi and the blending of French and Vietnamese techniques in silk painting and lacquer. Aldrich also notes Marcel Leguay, a painter who lived in Laos and designed Indochinese stamps, shown at the Musée de la Poste in 2002, and the Croisière Jaune's route across central Asia to Saigon in a 2002-2003 Paris display.
  • 6 Trade and Travel in Arnold, Cabinets for the Curious in part
    Chinese material is discussed across a section of several pages. Hans Sloane's account in the Philosophical Transactions for 1698 described a China cabinet sent home by Mr Buckley, chief surgeon at Fort St George, containing instruments, fruits and ear-pickers used in China, and a series of further articles followed. The Royal Society also held a Chinese statera inscribed with Chinese and European measures, and Petty's list of trades included Chinese varnishes and Chinese ink. A 1699 article urged English craftsmen to imitate Chinese workmanship.
  • CHAPTER 1 Flesh-eating Beetles and the Secret Art of Taxidermy in Asma, Stuffed Animals and Pickled Heads in part
    Wallace's years in the East Indies run through this chapter. Asma holds a bird of paradise that Wallace caught and tagged, a specimen from New Guinea, and notes that Aru Islanders had removed the legs of skins sold to European traders. Asma recounts Wallace's tropical fever in Borneo and his argument that a deep channel between Bali and Lombok divided the Australian and Southeast Asian fauna. These are episodes in Wallace's collecting and theory, not studies of the regions themselves.
  • The Philadelphia Commercial Museum: A Museum to Conquer the World in Conn, Museums and American Intellectual Life, 1876-1926 in part
    The Philippines is the main Asian thread. Wilson's 1904 St. Louis exhibit, with over 1,200 Filipinos shown on a 'reservation', brought a large Philippine collection back to Philadelphia, which the chapter calls 'a great museum of itself' with ethnology, industry and natural products. Chinese and Japanese delegates attended the 1899 congress, where applying the Chinese Exclusion Act to the Philippines was debated, and a journalist called Manila the 'Oriental Capital' for the Chinese market.
  • Preface in Cuno, Who Owns Antiquity? in part
    Chinese bronzes carry much of the preface. Cuno follows Chen Mengjia, who co-wrote a 1946 catalogue of the Art Institute of Chicago's bronzes and whose American study was published in 1960 without his participation. Cuno also follows Li Xueqin, head of an advisory committee for the Poly Art Museum, which buys back Chinese antiquities of undocumented origin. The Chicago fangding and a Western Zhou ding are presented as examples of encyclopedic collecting.
  • Introduction: The Crux of the Matter in Cuno, Who Owns Antiquity? in part
    China is the introduction's main Asian case. Cuno calls China's 2005 request for US import restrictions on objects from the Paleolithic to the Qing dynasty broad and unexplained, given a booming domestic Chinese market, and reads it as an attempt to keep what the state claims as cultural property. Cuno notes that Chinese citizens and corporations may buy back antiquities 'for China' in ways the state denies to foreign buyers, and that Italy and China hold stockpiles of antiquities that are not accessible to the public.
  • One: Political Matters in Cuno, Who Owns Antiquity? in part
    China is the chapter's main Asian case. Cuno describes the 2005 Chinese request for US import restrictions on objects from the Paleolithic to the Qing dynasty as covering nearly two million years of production, and reads it as a bid to retain what China claims as its cultural property. Cuno says China lost much of its heritage to foreigners in the early twentieth century and again when the nationalist government moved material to Taiwan. Cuno also argues that the request will not work, since China has a booming domestic trade in the same materials.
  • Two: More Political Matters in Cuno, Who Owns Antiquity? in part
    Asia appears through the Cirebon wreck off north Java, a 2000 find of a cargo from the Sumatran Sriwijaya kingdom that included Chinese Yue and Northern white wares and objects with Arabic inscriptions. Cuno notes that the Indonesian government planned to auction most of it, and that China, Japan and the United States had not ratified UNESCO's 2001 underwater heritage convention. Cuno also notes that China took part in the 1995 UNIDROIT negotiations, and that China, Japan and the United States had not signed the 2005 diversity convention.
  • Afterword to the Paperback Edition in Cuno, Who Owns Antiquity? in part
    Most of the afterword's East Asian material concerns China. Cuno says the Bush administration accepted a modified Chinese request for import restrictions on January 14, 2009, covering material from the Paleolithic to the Tang dynasty, and calls the decision political. Cuno traces the 2000 purchase of the Yuanmingyuan Zodiac heads by the Poly Museum, a Christie's auction in Paris of two heads owned by Yves Saint Laurent and Pierre Bergé, and the 2008 violence and the demolition of old Kashgar in Xinjiang.
  • Introduction James Cuno in Cuno (ed.), Whose Culture? in part
    The chapter's East Asian material is substantial. Two Chinese bronzes at the Art Institute, a Shang fangding and a Western Zhou Shi Wang Ding, are used to show how bronze working and courtly ritual flourished in China and in Benin. Cuno also traces Japanese influence on the English designer E. W. Godwin's sideboard, Japanese art shown at British exhibitions in 1861 and 1862, Whistler's Asian ceramics, Frank Lloyd Wright's 1908 exhibition of Japanese prints, and the Mingei movement led by Yanagi Sōetsu.
  • The Nation and the Object John Henry Merryman in Cuno (ed.), Whose Culture? in part
    Case 3 imagines a German museum offered a stone Buddha head, bought from a Singapore dealer on an Asian voyage with no known source. Merryman argues that if the Chinese Ministry of Culture showed the head belonged to a statue standing headless in a Xi'an museum, there would be a strong object-oriented case for reuniting head and body, even without a Chinese claim. Singapore and China appear only in this hypothetical; other Asian relics are mentioned only in a list.
  • 10 Engaging the material world: object knowledge and Australian Journeys Kirsten Wehner and Martha Sear in Dudley (ed.), Museum Materialities in part
    The chapter's Southeast Asian material is limited to two objects in the Australian Journeys gallery. The dàn tre, a bamboo instrument made by Minh Tam Nguyen, who migrated from Vietnam in 1982, is used to show how a visitor's position, as audience or as player, invites different imaginative engagements with his experience of being Vietnamese in Australia. Trepang fishermen from Makassar, now in Indonesia, appear through the cauldrons they used on northern Australian beaches, with a sensory station offering the smell of dried sea cucumber.
  • Searching for Paradigms in Findlen, Possessing Nature in part
    Kircher, unable to travel to China, made himself the leading expert on it by collecting others' reports, and he added Chinese to the languages he studied. The Roman College museum held Chinese scrolls beside Egyptian hieroglyphs and fragments of other scripts, and one of his catoptric machines multiplied an elephant said to be collected from all Asia and Africa.
  • Pilgrimages of Science in Findlen, Possessing Nature in part
    Kircher's knowledge of China came largely through other Jesuits. Martino Martini and Michael Boym sent him the atlas and flora that he drew on for China Illustrated (1667), and Boym returned to Rome in 1664 with manuscripts and specimens for the Roman College. Kircher, frustrated in his bid to become a missionary to China, depended on these witnesses to lend credibility to an account of a land he had never seen.
  • Peace is Never Neutral Per B. Rekdal in Fromm, Rekdal & Golding (eds.), Museums and Truth in part
    Rekdal opens with the 2009 ICME conference at the National Folk Museum of Korea in Seoul, where a conciliation process between the two Koreas makes reconciliation a live question. The museum's 2008 annual report records a cooperation agreement with a Russian museum and fieldwork in China, and its Children's Museum reopened with a fairy tale of a divided family reunited. These are cited as signs that peace work already belonged to the museum, but they are not analysed in depth.
  • Concepts of Remembrance and Commemoration Bärbel Kerkhoff-Hader in Fromm, Rekdal & Golding (eds.), Museums and Truth in part
    Kerkhoff-Hader's last example, 'A transaxial link to Korea', covers Berlin billboards and photo collages from 2007-2009 that commented on the division of Korea, by artists from South Korea, China and Germany. A 2009 exhibition of female Korean artists at the Women's Museum in Bonn was organized with the Korean Embassy. Both are presented as parallels to Germany's division rather than as studies of Korea in their own right.
  • The Arnold Arboretum: What it is and Does Charles Sprague Sargent in Genoways & Andrei (eds.), Museum Origins in part
    Sargent says that seeds sent in 1882 from Peking by Dr Bretschneider, physician to the Russian Embassy, led to plant exploration in China and then to Wilson's expeditions to central and western China, first sponsored by a London nurseryman and later by the Arboretum itself. Sargent credits Wilson's collecting with making the Arboretum the best place to study the woody plants of eastern Asia, and notes that its herbarium is rich in material from China and Japan.
  • 6. New disciplines: archaeology, anthropology and women in museums in Hill, Women and Museums, 1850-1914 in part
    Missionary collectors from China and Burma recur. Annie Royle Taylor, working in and around China and Tibet, sold objects to museums in Edinburgh and Glasgow to fund her mission, and Livne argues that her servant Pontso assembled some of them. Mr and Mrs Davidson, missionaries in China, sold a large ethnographic collection to the Horniman Museum in 1895, though Levell argues that Mary Davidson shaped it, a contribution recorded only under her husband's name. Charlotte Wheeler Cuffe sent Ridgeway photographs of ethnographic types in Burma for the Cambridge museum.
  • 5 Reading the Objects in Hill, Culture and Class in English Public Museums, 1850-1914 in part
    The Jacson and Foster collections given to the Harris Museum in 1894 include Chinese, Japanese and Algerian curiosities, Japanese swords, and needlework and pottery from India, China and Japan, which Hill reads as objects that placed their donors in a relation of power over those peoples. Other Preston gifts include Japanese jewellery given in 1911, and Liverpool received a systematic collection of Chinese industrial manufactures in 1892.
  • 3. The Public Museum in Hopkins, The Museum: From Its Origins to the 21st Century in part
    Tokyo National Museum is the chapter's main Asian case. Hopkins traces it from the Yushima Seido Exposition of 1872, which was sent to the Vienna World's Fair, to the Ueno Park complex whose Honkan, designed by the British architect Josiah Conder, opened in 1882, and links it to Japan's growing projection of itself abroad. Hopkins also notes that a museum of Korean culture was founded in 1909 under the Japanese-controlled Korean emperor, and that it became one of the founding collections of the National Museum of Korea after 1945.
  • 4. The Modern Museum in Hopkins, The Museum: From Its Origins to the 21st Century in part
    Japan is the main Asian case. Hopkins describes the Museum of Modern Art in Kamakura (1951), built by Junzo Sakakura with walls of local Oya stone beside Tsurugaoka Hachimangu Shrine, and the National Museum of Western Art in Ueno, designed by Le Corbusier from 1955 to house the Kojiro Matsukata collection of Western paintings and Japanese woodblock prints, seized in France after the war and handed back under the 1951 San Francisco treaty. Tange's Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum is cited as a symbol of reconciliation. Korea appears briefly, with Tae-Soo Kim's National Museum of Contemporary Art in Gwacheon (1986), which draws on temple architecture.
  • 5. The Global Museum in Hopkins, The Museum: From Its Origins to the 21st Century in part
    China gets the longest treatment: Hopkins traces its museum boom from the National Museum of China (2003) and the 2010 Shanghai Expo, which produced the Power Station of Art and the China Art Palace, to the Ordos Museum, the Qujing History Museum, the Nanjing Sifang Art Museum and Wang Shu's Ningbo History Museum, built from the ruins of demolished villages. Japan appears in the 1980s and 1990s building boom, with Tadao Ando's Benesse House on Naoshima and the Edo-Tokyo Museum among the examples. Taiwan and South Korea are mentioned briefly through Ando's commissions there, and Western outposts in Shenzhen and Shanghai are noted.
  • Early Dutch Cabinets of Curiosities Th. H. Lunsingh Scheurleer in Impey & MacGregor (eds.), The Origins of Museums in part
    Lunsingh Scheurleer says the Asian material in Dutch collections was mainly Chinese and Japanese porcelain and lacquerwork. He describes the Princes of Orange at The Hague, whose De Oude Hof held large Chinese porcelain collections set on wall shelves, as recorded in an inventory of 1632, and the black-and-gold Japanese lacquer balusters ordered in Japan for the Huis ten Bosch. He notes a Chinese vase and a Japanese helmet and armour in Jacob van Campen's painting of the Treasures of East and West, and that Japanese lacquer became popular after the Dutch were granted the only European trading post in Japan.
  • Natural Philosophers and Princely Collectors: Worm, Paludanus, and the Gottorp and Copenhagen Collections H. D. Schepelern in Impey & MacGregor (eds.), The Origins of Museums in part
    Schepelern shows that Paludanus's manuscript inventory of 1617-18 contains a majority of objects from the Far East, meaning China, Japan and especially India, whereas the printed list of 1604 was drawn mainly from Europe and the Near East. Schepelern attributes the change to Paludanus's collaboration with Jan Huygens van Linschoten, who had lived in Goa and settled in Enkhuizen, and to the Asian objects that Linschoten brought back. Schepelern also notes that seventeen oriental objects that probably came from Paludanus's collection survive in the National Museum in Copenhagen.
  • Alive or Dead: Zoological Collections in the Seventeenth Century Wilma George in Impey & MacGregor (eds.), The Origins of Museums in part
    The East Indies is a substantial source in this chapter. Birds of paradise were caught in New Guinea and sold to sailors calling at the Moluccas, and Schouten bartered for two in 1616; cassowaries came from the same area. A babyrousa skull from Celebes was often on show, Petiver labelled some butterflies as from Java, and Dampier's men bought cockatoos on Buru. Dutch East India Company ships carried live animals to Amsterdam, and Dutch captains returned from the East Indies with birds.
  • Conchology before Linnaeus Henry E. Coomans in Impey & MacGregor (eds.), The Origins of Museums in part
    Amboina (Ambon) is central to the chapter's Asian material. Rumphius, employed there by the Dutch East India Company from 1656, wrote on its shells, observed tropical species in the field, recorded local uses of shells for food, tools and shell trumpets, and sold shells to Cosimo de' Medici, some of which survive in Pisa. The introduction also notes that the Chinese long ago made Buddha figures from mother-of-pearl.
  • Exotica from Islam Julian Raby in Impey & MacGregor (eds.), The Origins of Museums in part
    Asian material is mainly porcelain. Hard-paste porcelain was the monopoly of the Far East, and cabinet owners such as Ferdinand of Austria and Philip II acquired blue-and-white pieces, some via Turkey or Lisbon. A Chinese writer of 1387 is quoted on damascened steel, and Holland received large cargoes of Chinese and later Japanese porcelain in the seventeenth century, which displaced Iznik ware. Persian pottery imitating Chinese blue-and-white was sold in Holland as Chinese.
  • Chapter 15: Why Museums Make Me Sad: James A. Boon James A. Boon in Karp & Lavine (eds.), Exhibiting Cultures in part
    Boon's one substantial Asian case is Bali, which he treats as part of the Dutch East Indies. Boon notes that Raffles declared Bali an archaeological remnant of pre-Islamic Java around 1817, that Balinese rajas in the 1920s hired Walter Spies to enhance their international reputation, and that Hindu-Balinese make museumy emblems of Dutch, British, Muslim and tourist outsiders and of one another. Javanese temple dancers appear only in a list of Brighton Aquarium attractions.
  • Chapter 19: Festivals and Diplomacy: Ted M. G. Tanen in Karp & Lavine (eds.), Exhibiting Cultures in part
    Tanen's Asian material is the planned Festival of Indonesia for 1990-91, organized by the private Yayasan Nusantara Jaya, which includes a training program for museologists hosted by American museums, alongside tourism and business goals. Japan appears as a country with ongoing cultural presentations in the United States, and Thailand and Vietnam only in a list of little-known countries.
  • Chapter 20: Objects of Ethnography: Barbara Kirshenblatt-Gimblett Barbara Kirshenblatt-Gimblett in Karp & Lavine (eds.), Exhibiting Cultures in part
    Kirshenblatt-Gimblett discusses Nathan Dunn's Chinese collection, shown at Peale's Museum in 1838 and then in London, with life-size clay figures of mandarins, shopkeepers and servants, and the wax scenes of Chinese daily life at the Oriental and Turkish Museum in 1850s London. Bali recurs as a case of tourist production: Balinese performances developed for the 1930s Paris exposition were brought back to be shown to visitors on the island, and cremations there have grown larger because tourists pay to attend. Chinese and Japanese people appear mainly in lists of displayed peoples.
  • Making Histories of Religion Mark O'Neill in Kavanagh (ed.), Making Histories in Museums in part
    Taiwan receives the most attention: the chapter notes that traditional religious belief has continued to grow there despite rapid economic growth since 1949, and it describes the proposed World Religions Museum at the Ling-chiu Shan Wu-Sheng Monastery, whose stated purpose is respect, acceptance and universal compassion. Marburg's museum has displays on non-Buddhist religions in China and Japan and on Buddhism in south-east Asia, China, Japan and Tibet, and Otto's Far Eastern Buddha figures are cited as an example of the sensual appeal of religious portraiture.
  • Six— Confusing Pleasures in Kirshenblatt-Gimblett, Destination Culture in part
    The festival's Pacific Rim programme was largely Asian: Children of Bali, court performers from the Yogyakarta palace in Java, Javanese shadow puppets, Chinese Kun opera, Korean shamans from Chindo Island, Cambodian court dance, and Japanese and Thai performers among the invited artists, with Cambodian and Korean immigrant communities cited as part of the city. The chapter notes that Brecht's encounter with Mei Lanfang's Chinese opera in 1935 and Artaud's glimpse of Balinese theatre in Paris shaped avant-garde taste for these forms.
  • National Museums And The National Imagination Simon Knell in Knell et al. (eds.), National Museums in part
    Korea and Taiwan are the main cases. Choi's study of the National Museum of Korea shows national identity performed through art motifs, a positioning Choi comes to see as a legacy of Japanese imposition, and South Korea has sponsored celadon galleries in European and American museums to build its international identity. Taiwan's national museums came to display things 'Taiwanese rather than Chinese' as democracy grew, and the Taiwan Museum of Art shows Ku Ping-Hsing's paintings. Varutti is cited on China's museums, which affirm a single great civilization by forgetting difficult histories. The Edo-Tokyo Museum is described as a musealised city, with Japanese prints used as reconstruction evidence.
  • CHAPTER 3: From Folklore to Intangible Heritage Kristin Kuutma in Logan, Nic Craith & Kockel (eds.), A Companion to Heritage Studies in part
    Kuutma gives Japan and China a section each. In Japan, folklore studies began in the late nineteenth century with Kunio Yanagita and developed into nativist ethnology that supported ethnic nationalism and the inter-war idyll of rural villages; municipalities hired folklorists to plan museum projects. In China, scholars began organised folklore study in the early twentieth century on European and Japanese models, collecting songs from many minorities, and after 1949 stories and folksongs were reworked to fit Communist Party politics.
  • CHAPTER 13: Heritagescaping and the Aesthetics of Refuge: Challenges to Urban Sustainability Tim Winter in Logan, Nic Craith & Kockel (eds.), A Companion to Heritage Studies in part
    Winter's section on Asia notes that Beijing's hutong were demolished for the 2008 Olympics, and that old factories were turned into the District 798 art precinct in Beijing and Moganshan Road in Shanghai. Winter cites the loss of colonial and wartime heritage in Hong Kong, Phnom Penh and Hanoi, and small World Heritage towns remade by tourism at Pingyao in China and Melaka in Malaysia. Refuge settlements such as Luang Prabang, Vieng Xai in Laos, Intramuros in the Philippines and Bogor in Indonesia frame his reading of Galle.
  • CHAPTER 22: The Economic Feasibility of Heritage Preservation Ron vanOers in Logan, Nic Craith & Kockel (eds.), A Companion to Heritage Studies in part
    Van Oers describes Preah Khan at Angkor in Cambodia, where American Express and the World Monuments Fund funded a restoration that trained local craftsmen and raised tourism revenue, and Manila, where the Far Eastern University Campus Conservation Program in the Philippines began in 1989 and grew into a neighbourhood revitalization movement. He also notes pilot Historic Urban Landscape projects under way in China and elsewhere in Asia, and draws on a 36-case study of partnerships in Asian and European heritage cities.
  • CHAPTER 32: Heritage and Cosmopolitanism in Logan, Nic Craith & Kockel (eds.), A Companion to Heritage Studies in part
    Meskell draws on two Asian cases. Denis Byrne's work on local restoration of Thai stupas and on the excavation and ownership of amulets shows popular religious practice being decoupled from foreign-led heritage management, and Meskell proposes that heritage scholars learn from it. Margaret Swain's account of heritage tourism in China argues that Confucian ideas of tianxia and shijie offer a non-Western cosmopolitanism, which the state uses alongside Western-derived UNESCO discourse.
  • CHAPTER 34: Achieving Dialogue through Transnational World Heritage Nomination: The Case of the Silk Roads Ona Vileikis in Logan, Nic Craith & Kockel (eds.), A Companion to Heritage Studies in part
    The Silk Roads nomination runs through China, so the chapter gives East Asia real attention, though its case study is mainly Central Asia. Vileikis describes the Gansu Corridor, with the oasis city of Dunhuang and the Mogao Caves, a World Heritage property since 1987, and Chinese sites such as Xi'an, Kizil and Luoyang. The Chang'an-Tianshan corridor, shared with Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, was the first corridor inscribed, in 2014.
  • Visiting the empire at the provincial museum, 1900–50 Claire Wintle in Longair & McAleer (eds.), Curating Empire in part
    Asian material appears mainly outside the museum walls. The museum held a Japanese pottery collection that visitors kept separate from the 'cannibal man-catchers', and one tour singled out poisoned darts from the Malay Peninsula. At the Brighton Dome's 1920 'Chinese Fair', in aid of the Royal Sussex County Hospital, a Chinese minister opened the event and personal costume collections from people with close ties to China were lent as an introduction to the region. Local bazaars also staged Japanese and Chinese figures, such as a 'winsome geisha', played by residents.
  • Museums as contested sites of remembrance: the Enola Gay affair • Vera Zolberg Vera L. Zolberg in Macdonald & Fyfe (eds.), Theorizing Museums in part
    Japan is one of the two parties to the dispute. Zolberg reconstructs how Japanese officials and the Embassy responded to the exhibit and to a US postal stamp showing the bombing, which was redesigned after Japanese protests. Zolberg discusses Japanese immigrants in the United States and their wartime internment, and notes that Japanese opinion is not uniform, citing the writer Kenzaburo Oe's criticism of his countrymen for not accepting responsibility for the war.
  • Canada: the Royal Ontario Museum, Toronto and the Royal British Columbia Museum, Victoria in MacKenzie, Museums and Empire in part
    The ROM's Chinese collection, among the richest in any museum, was built largely by the missionary bishop William Charles White and the Tientsin fur merchant George Crofts, through shipments gathered from railway-cut tombs, including three Yuan dynasty wall paintings from a derelict monastery. The chapter presents this as looting amid warlord instability, and contrasts it with the sinologist James Mellon Menzies, who refused to let oracle bones from the Huan River near Zhangde leave China. It also notes Japanese prints from Walker and a Korean collection assembled from private sources.
  • Museums in Asia in MacKenzie, Museums and Empire in part
    Singapore is the chapter's main Southeast Asian case: its Raffles Library and Museum, traced from Raffles's and Farquhar's natural history collecting, grew Malay silverware, Chinese porcelain and natural history paintings commissioned from Chinese artists, and drew Chinese New Year crowds of over 10,000 in 1908. The Perak, Selangor and Sarawak museums in the Malay peninsula and Borneo are also described, with Chinese, Malay and Tamil visitors far more numerous than Europeans. Far Eastern ceramics appear in Bombay's Prince of Wales Museum.
  • Conclusion in MacKenzie, Museums and Empire in part
    Singapore returns as the example of a colonial museum turned national: its ethnographic and Asian collections were moved from the National Museum on Stamford Road to the Museum of Asian Civilisations in Empress Place, opened in 2003 as a pan-Asian display. The chapter notes that when large numbers of Chinese, Indian and Malay visitors used South-East Asian museums as an extension of their religious festivals, the museums became places where identity was found. Singapore's museum history is cited as an example of how a colonial museum mutated into a national one.
  • Admiration and Fear. The Reports of Marius Vachon on Museums of Industrial Arts in Europe Lieske Tibbe in Meyer & Savoy (eds.), The Museum Is Open in part
    Vachon praised the Orientalisches Museum in Vienna, housed in the Exchange Building from the 1873 World Fair, as an ideal museum: its collections ranged from Turkey, Persia and India to Japan and China, and each object was labelled with price, means of production and sales channels, linked to an Austrian-Asiatic trade agency. He wanted France to create a similar agency, drawing on the unused Chinese collection at Fontainebleau, the Cernuschi collection and the new colonies. He also bought Japanese swords at the 1889 World's Fair for his museum in Saint-Etienne.
  • The Library Departments, 1856-1909 in Miller, That Noble Cabinet in part
    Douglas, who had served in the China consular service and had charge of the Chinese and Japanese books from 1865, catalogued them in 1877 and became first Keeper of the Department of Oriental Printed Books and Manuscripts in 1892. Giles later became its Chinese expert. Colvin's Prints and Drawings bought four private collections of Japanese woodcuts between 1902 and 1909 and the Wegener collection of Chinese paintings in 1910, and in 1912 a Sub-Department of Oriental Prints and Drawings was set up under Binyon, an authority on China and Japan, which became the basis of the later Oriental Antiquities department.
  • Two World Wars and After in Miller, That Noble Cabinet in part
    Miller describes the Eumorfopoulos Chinese collection, bought in 1934 for £100,000 jointly with the Victoria and Albert Museum, which ran from ritual bronze vessels of about 1122 BC through Han jades and Song ceramics to late Qing work. Miller also records the Stein manuscripts from a cave in the Gobi, on the edge of Eastern Turkestan, which Lionel Giles catalogued, the Backhouse collection of Chinese books, and a Chinese terrestrial globe of 1623 acquired in 1961. The 1929 Royal Commission's call for a Far Eastern department is noted.
  • 1 The heart of the matter: Integrating equality and diversity into the policy and practice of museums and galleries Eithne Nightingale and Chandan Mahal in Sandell & Nightingale (eds.), Museums, Equality and Social Justice in part
    Cedric Yeh's work at the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History (NMAH) is the main Asia case: he found Asian Pacific American objects catalogued as 'machinery' or 'fabrics', and the first object displayed was a porcelain figure of a white man pushing a Chinese labourer out of a nest, referring to the 1882 Exclusion Act. The chapter also notes the V&A's long work with South Asian and Chinese communities through its Asia department, a Chinese New Year festival and a Chinese Watercolours exhibition, and the Chinese Museum in New York.
  • 9 A question of faith: The museum as a spiritual or secular space John Reeve in Sandell & Nightingale (eds.), Museums, Equality and Social Justice in part
    Reeve draws on Karen Chin's account of the Asian Civilisations Museum in Singapore, which he calls the first museum in the region to present religions holistically, describing its pilgrimage displays, the way students respond to its galleries, and its aim to show religion as an ecosystem of ideas linked by trade. Reeve also discusses the British Museum's 2010-11 exhibition Images and Sacred Texts: Buddhism across Asia, which he judges object-centred and without context. Reeve notes that Burmese priests blessed the Burmese Buddha in the British Museum's Asian gallery, and that the main Asia gallery has almost no material after 1900.
  • 15 Creativity, learning and cultural rights David Anderson in Sandell & Nightingale (eds.), Museums, Equality and Social Justice in part
    Tibet is the chapter's main Asian case. The 2005 exhibition Tibet: Treasures from the Roof of the World, curated by Tibet's Bureau of Cultural Relics and staff of three Lhasa institutions, was shown at the Bowers Museum, the Houston Museum of Natural Science and the Rubin Museum of Art, and critics accused the venues of complicity in the occupation of Tibet. The Dalai Lama welcomed the show as evidence that Tibetan art had survived. The chapter also opens with the 2011 arrest of the Chinese artist Ai Weiwei, but only as an example of a narrow view of cultural rights.
  • Titian and Franklin (1827-1845) in Sellers, Mr. Peale's Museum in part
    Nathan Dunn, a Quaker merchant who had spent about thirteen years trading in Canton, brought a large Chinese collection to the Museum: life-size clay figures of mandarins, shopkeepers, priests and servants in costume, with furniture, tools, boats and a pagoda, which James Silk Buckingham and the diarist Sydney Fisher both admired. In 1841 Dunn took the collection to London, where it earned over $50,000 a year. The chapter also notes William Wood's purchases in China and the East Indies for the Museum, and butterflies from China and Japan, and an Argus pheasant from Malacca.
  • Selling Nations: International Exhibitions and Cultural Diplomacy Brian Wallis in Sherman & Rogoff (eds.), Museum Culture in part
    Wallis gives a substantial case study to the Festival of Indonesia (1990-92), whose exhibitions focused on classical sculpture and court arts and ignored Muslims, who make up 90 percent of the population, until an ethnographic show was added.
