Wallis describes oil-company sponsorship, Ford Foundation lectures on East Timor and deforestation, and a wall label praising 'Indonesian grace' beside a Vishnu. Five Thousand Years of Korean Art, and Thailand and Vietnam as future festival candidates, appear only in passing.
  • 3. Art Education in Museums in Silina, Soviet Museums Between the Two World Wars in part
    The chapter's main East Asian case is the 1928 exhibition of Japanese children's books and drawings, organised by VOKS, the Commission and Meksin's museum commission at the Historical Museum in Moscow. Silina describes it as a journey through Japan for a critical Soviet tourist, with a Tokyo railway station room, panels on rickshaw labour, separate schooling for boys and girls, and militarism in folk tales, all presented in class terms. Silina notes the German and Japanese children's exhibitions of 1928 in passing.
  • Chapter 4 Solve et coagula in Silverman, The Social Work of Museums in part
    Two East and Southeast Asian museums get a paragraph each. The Women's Active Museum on War and Peace in Tokyo, proposed by Yayori Matsui, works to make the Japanese government accept responsibility for the 'comfort women' system, using traveling exhibits and seminars. The Vietnam Women's Museum in Hanoi, a gender museum and research centre, makes documentary films and field trips to assess gender equity and raise awareness. The Asia Eros Museum of Seoul and the China Sex Museum are named in passing as sex-education venues.
  • Chapter 6 Birds in flight in Silverman, The Social Work of Museums in part
    Asia enters through the Cambodia Landmine Museum and Relief Facility, begun by the former child soldier Aki Ra, which pairs displays of rockets and defused mines with residential care for more than twenty landmine-amputee children. Japan appears in the Hirano-cho Ecomuseum in Osaka Prefecture, run by local residents, and in the Osaka Museum of Housing and Living, cited among reminiscence collections. The Culion Museum of the Philippines, devoted to leprosy and its discriminatory segregation laws, and the Kyoto Museum for World Peace, quoted on the meaning of peace, are briefly mentioned.
  • 5. The Battle of South Kensington in Yallop, Magpies, Squirrels and Thieves in part
    At the British Museum Augustus Franks, a collector as well as curator, bought Japanese porcelain instead of classical pottery and bequeathed some 1,500 netsuke, Japanese miniature sculptures, to the museum. Yallop also notes that he invested in Chinese bronzes, and that in 1885 he swapped a painted Japanese figure from the collection for a finer wooden one of his own.
  • 15. Rossetti’s Peacock in Yallop, Magpies, Squirrels and Thieves in part
    Blue-and-white is the chapter's main Asian thread. Yallop traces Chinese blue-and-white from the Yuan period (1271-1368) and the K'ang-hsi wares of the late seventeenth century, shipped by the Dutch East India Company, to the Chinese export services ordered with European coats of arms. Marks's supply came largely from seventeenth-century Chinese blue-and-white still on Dutch farmhouse dressers in the 1860s, which he bought up before prices rose and direct import from China became cheaper. Yallop also notes that Marks was interested in Chinese art from childhood and wanted to travel to the Far East, though his father refused.
  • 16. A Notorious Squabble in Yallop, Magpies, Squirrels and Thieves in part
    Blue-and-white from China and the Far East runs through the chapter: Marks assembled Sir Henry Thompson's collection from contacts in Paris, Holland and the Far East, and it was shown in 1878 with a supper served on blue-and-white dishes. Marks also supplied the Chinese blue-and-white that Frederick Leyland displayed on the shelves of the dining room now known as the Peacock Room. The chapter's Asian material concerns display and sale rather than the objects' makers or origins.
  • The Rise of Multi-layered Pacifism and Early Peace Museums in Postwar Japan in Yoshida, From Cultures of War to Cultures of Peace in part
    Most of the Asian content concerns China and Korea as victims. The Maruki panels toured China in 1956, where a one-legged woman in Beijing told the artists the panels helped her understand Japanese suffering. The chapter describes the 1953 return of 551 Chinese laborers' remains from Hanaoka in Akita to Tianjin, and the Fushun and Taiyuan confessions of atrocities in China. Korean victims of the atomic bomb and the Crows panel on Korean survivors are also discussed.
  • Bringing Peace to War Dead in Yoshida, From Cultures of War to Cultures of Peace in part
    The chapter says little about Asia except through absence. Chiran's displays include eleven pilots born on the Korean peninsula, and Tachiarai's exhibits include Korean pilots, yet no trace appears of the Korean laborers who expanded the air base. The Yamato Museum omits the Korean and Chinese workers who built Kure's underground tunnels, and the Tokyo center's symposia address Japan's bombing of Chongqing. A Chinese student visiting Himeyuri urged the museum to show Japanese aggression in China and Korea.
  • The Revival of War Museums in Postwar Japan in Yoshida, From Cultures of War to Cultures of Peace in part
    Its Asian content concerns how the Yushukan and SDF museums treat Japan's conduct abroad. The Zero panel cites a 1940 battle over Chongqing, and the locomotive display omits the roughly quarter-million forced laborers who built the Thai-Burma railroad, around 40,000 of whom died. The Yushukan honors Taiwanese and Korean colonial soldiers but no foreigner beyond Pal. The Kakishoshukan's panels omit the 20th Infantry Regiment's role in the 1937 Nanjing killings, documented in a corporal's diary, and the Kanoya museum leaves out some 500 Korean laborers who fortified the air base.
  • History Wars: Responding to Pressures from Different Interest Groups in Yoshida, From Cultures of War to Cultures of Peace in part
    Most of the disputes concern how Asia is shown. Nagasaki's display of the Nanjing Massacre and Japanese chemical and biological warfare in China was altered under LDP pressure. Peace Osaka's China and Korea corners, covering the Three-All Operation, Unit 731 and the March First Movement of 1919, drew attacks, and Saitama's references to Korean forced labor at Yoshimi were criticized as too thin. The three national Tokyo museums show only Japanese suffering, and a Japanese repatriate's childhood in Pyongyang is their sole link to Korea.
Alberti, Samuel J. M. M. (2009). Nature and Culture: Objects, Disciplines and the Manchester Museum. Manchester: Manchester University Press.Asia: occasional8 chapter overviews

Overview

Nature and Culture is a history of the Manchester Museum from its opening at Owens College in 1890 through the twentieth century. It uses the single institution as a prism for how a museum builds disciplines, how objects gain and lose meanings in the collection, and how visitors engaged with them. Alberti argues that the museum's disciplinary order, with natural history at its centre and a separate humanities wing added later, was contingent and shaped by buildings, specimens and personalities as much as by academic change. The book is organised in two halves: a Victorian prologue and the disciplinary topography of the collections, then the lives of objects through acquisition, practice and visiting, followed by a conclusion. It draws on manuscripts, minutes, guidebooks and oral testimony.

East and Southeast Asia in this work occasional

East and Southeast Asia are a minor strand. The most substantial case is the Japanese ethnographic and art collection of Robert Wylie Lloyd, a London printer and art collector, discussed in chapter 4 (Acquisition) as a gift. Herbert Graham Cannon, introduced to Lloyd by Walter Hincks, persuaded him to leave his Japanese art to the Museum as well, as a posthumous gift. Cannon's interest in Japanese artefacts is noted in chapter 2 (Nature), and chapter 3 (Culture) records that the Lloyd material was installed in 1960 in place of general archaeology, which ended the evolutionary sequence on that floor of the 1927 building.

A Burmese Buddha is the only Southeast Asian object that recurs. It was among the curiosities auctioned in 1868 under Darbishire's commission, bought by Salford Museum, and returned to Manchester in the 1969 exchange of local anthropology for Salford's exotica that David Owen arranged. The Society's 'large Burmese idol' in the curiosity room of the 1835 building (chapter 1, Prologue) belongs to the same early history.

Otherwise the region is absent or passing. Chapter 6 (Visitors) names the loss of 200 Japanese objects in 1960 and says nothing else about East or Southeast Asia. Chapter 3 mentions the Asian stage of Dawkins's evolutionary route, from Australasia to the Americas and then Asia. The book does not discuss Chinese, Korean or Southeast Asian collections as such, Asian visitors, curators or scholars, colonial collecting in Asia, or the heritage policy of Asian states.

Introduction: museum historiographiesp. 1

Alberti introduces Nature and Culture, a history of the Manchester Museum from its opening at Owens College in 1890, and uses the single institution as a methodological prism. Alberti places the book in two traditions: single-institution histories that began with David Murray's 1904 Museums: Their History and Their Use, and the early-1990s museum studies of Hooper-Greenhill, Pearce and Bennett, which cast museums as political instruments that make meaning. Alberti argues that twentieth-century museums are under-studied and that the Manchester Museum, comparable with the Hunterian, the Pitt Rivers and the Horniman, is a representative case. Alberti proposes three approaches: the disciplinary topography of the collections, the lives of objects from acquisition through storage and display, and the visitors who engaged with them. The introduction shows how William Boyd Dawkins replaced the Natural History Society's curiosities with a continuous sequence from palaeontology to zoology. It closes by framing the book as a study of the distinctions museums draw between things and of the people who gave those things their values.

Manchester Museum
1CHAPTER 1: Prologue: the Manchester Natural History Societyp. 10

Alberti traces the prehistory of the Manchester Museum through the fate of John Leigh Philips's private cabinet, which was sold after his death in 1814 and bought by a group of Manchester merchants who founded the Manchester Natural History Society (MNHS) in 1821. The chapter follows the Society's struggle for space, from rented rooms on King Street to its own building on Peter Street in 1835, and shows how a mixed collection of minerals, birds, mummies and curiosities took shape under honorary curators and paid staff. Alberti's evidence comes from Society minutes, admission records and the quarrels between curators and council members, including the feud between taxidermist Timothy Harrop and the young curator William Williamson. Visitor access, from proprietors and honorary members to working-class admissions and fears of Chartist unrest, is used to show who the museum was for. The chapter ends with the Society's collapse, the transfer of its collections to Owens College in 1873, and the appointment of William Boyd Dawkins on Thomas Huxley's advice, which set up the scientific museum that the rest of the book examines.

Manchester Natural History Society museum, Peter StreetManchester Museum
2CHAPTER 2: Nature: scientific disciplines in the museump. 31

Alberti follows the Manchester Museum's natural history collections through the twentieth century, asking how Dawkins's single sequence from minerals to botany gave way to separate disciplinary domains. The chapter is organised around three moments: the opening of the museum in 1887-1890, when Dawkins arranged the galleries from geology through zoology to botany; the extensions of 1912-13 and 1927, when zoology, entomology and economic geology gained ground and the natural and cultural collections were physically divided; and the years after 1950, when the science departments moved across Oxford Road and the museum turned towards a general public. Alberti draws on minutes, guidebooks, staff lists and interviews to show how donors such as James Cosmo Melvill and curators such as Hoyle, Tattersall and Carpenter reshaped the hierarchy of disciplines. Alberti also traces the exclusion of women from curatorial posts after 1950 and the loss of the tea-room links between museum and university staff. The chapter concludes that disciplinary order in museums is contingent, shaped by buildings, specimens and personalities as much as by ideas.

East and Southeast Asia Cannon, the zoology professor who chaired the Museum Committee, is cited as having an interest in Japanese artefacts and was given honorary care of the museum's Japanese collections, but the chapter says nothing more about them.

Manchester MuseumBritish Museum (Natural History)
3CHAPTER 3: Culture: artefacts and disciplinary formationp. 64

This chapter traces how the humanities collections at the Manchester Museum separated from its natural history displays between 1890 and 1990. It begins with William Boyd Dawkins's original plan, in which artefacts sat in one evolutionary sequence running from geology through prehistoric archaeology and ethnology to zoology, and shows how the Haworth loan of Flinders Petrie's Egyptian excavations, Margaret Murray's 1908 unwrapping of Khnum-Nakht and Jesse Haworth's gifts forced the creation of a separate cultural wing in the 1912-13 and 1927 buildings. Alberti then follows the successive keepers, Tattersall, Sayce, Willett, Forde-Johnston, Prag and Rosalie David, who redefined ethnology first as geography and then as a field allied with archaeology and art, until Egyptology became independent in 1990. The evidence comes from floor plans, display arrangements, staff appointments and the classical vase collection built up by T. B. L. Webster. Alberti argues that disciplines were built into the fabric of the building, and that the permanent galleries lagged behind academic change. The chapter concludes that the humanities moved from a province within the natural sciences to an independent federation.

East and Southeast Asia Mostly absent. The chapter mentions a Burmese Buddha that Dawkins had sold from the Natural History Society collections and that came back to Manchester in a 1969 exchange with Salford Museum. It also notes the Japanese gallery on the second floor of the 1927 building, opened in 1960 to show the Japanese material given by Robert Wylie Lloyd, which replaced general archaeology there.

Manchester MuseumPitt Rivers Museum
4CHAPTER 4: Acquisition: collecting networks and the museump. 91Asia: in part

This chapter examines how objects reached the Manchester Museum and by which routes, organised by mode of acquisition: gift, purchase, fieldwork, exchange and loan. Alberti argues that the institution itself acted as a collector, and that its growth depended on a network of donors, dealers, colonial agents, university staff and exchange partners. Early gifts came from Cosmo Melvill's herbarium, Charles Bailey, Leopold Grindon and the Rochdale businessman Charles Heape, whose colonial material shaped the early ethnology displays. Cases examined in detail include the Churchill coin bequest, which ended in the Court of Chancery, Henry Dresser's bird skins and eggs, the elephant Maharajah bought after his death from Belle Vue Zoo, and the Castlefield rescue excavations of the 1970s. Donors were repaid with committee seats, honorary posts and named collections, which Alberti reads as a vital contract between amateurs and professionals. The chapter concludes that objects arrived carrying traces of everyone who gathered, sold or dug them, and that each change of hands reshaped their meanings.

East and Southeast Asia The main East Asian case is the Japanese ethnographic and art collection of Robert Wylie Lloyd, a London printer and art collector. Herbert Graham Cannon, introduced to Lloyd by Walter Hincks, persuaded him to leave his Japanese art to the Museum as well, a posthumous gift, and the Japanese material was then shown in a gallery on the top floor of the northern extension. The chapter also notes that a Burmese Buddha returned to Manchester in the 1969 exchange with Salford Museum.

Manchester MuseumBelle Vue ZooWellcome Historical Medical MuseumSalford Museum
5CHAPTER 5: Practice: technique and the lives of objects in the collectionp. 123

This chapter looks behind the galleries at the everyday practices that kept objects usable: preparation and conservation, registration and cataloguing, storage and display. Alberti argues that these practices were craft-based, learned tacitly and carried out by largely unrecognised staff such as taxidermists, porters, technicians and charwomen, and that they shaped disciplines as much as theory did. Most examples come from the early decades: the sperm whale skeleton bought from Ward's Natural Science Establishment in Rochester, New York, and articulated by the Stockport taxidermist Harry Brazenor; the maceration and spirit preservation of vertebrates; and the accession ledgers and card catalogues devised by William Evans Hoyle. The chapter then follows the professionalisation of conservation, from Harry Spencer's on-the-job training to the department created in the 1970s under Frank Goodyear, and the Computer Cataloguing Unit that operated from 1979. Storage, lighting, case colour and labelling are discussed as shaping how stored and displayed objects were read. The chapter concludes that an object's biography did not end on arrival and that the museum was a dynamic, mutable entity.

Manchester Museum
6CHAPTER 6: Visitors: audiences and objectsp. 153

This chapter turns from those who worked at the Manchester Museum to those who visited it, estimating about ten million visits in its first century and asking how visitors were attracted, guided and controlled. Alberti argues that visitors were active participants whose responses often diverged from curatorial intentions. It covers the Sunday afternoon opening of 1895, which brought crowds and later complaints about unruly behaviour, and the uniformed porters who policed the galleries. It traces the printed guides, lectures and temporary exhibitions, notably the moon rock of 1969, the 'O! Osiris, Live Forever' Egyptology display of 1979 and the Lindow Man exhibition of 1987. The schools service and the tension between the University and the city, which both funded the Museum, are examined in turn. Oral-history testimony shows visitors awed by the sperm whale and the mummies and by the hushed, churchlike building. The chapter concludes that curators and visitors constructed the visit together, and that a handful of objects affected visitors far more than the rest of the collection.

East and Southeast Asia Only a passing reference. The chapter records that 200 Japanese objects were lost from the collection in 1960, one of the few losses it names, and says nothing else about East or Southeast Asia, whether as collections, visitors or curators.

Manchester MuseumBritish Museum
7CHAPTER 7: Conclusion: the museum in the twentieth centuryp. 189

This closing chapter steps back from the case studies to assess the Manchester Museum across the twentieth century. Alberti argues that objects were not the main actors: people acting on them shaped disciplines, values and meanings, so the book is a history of the museum rather than a set of object biographies. The chapter reflects on its sources, which are manuscripts, publications and oral testimony, and on the staff and visitors that earlier histories have neglected. It places the Manchester case alongside work on museums and empire and on the civic role of provincial collections. The humanities in the Museum, it says, were an unusual development, catalysed by the Egyptian collection and its architecture, while zoology overtook geology and botany stayed subordinate. The closing pages sketch the histories still unwritten, from twentieth-century biographies to the Cold War, and note that the book stops before the 1990s, when Tristram Besterman's arrival as director and a large capital project transformed the Museum. The final paragraph argues that natural history specimens, like human artefacts, belong to the material culture of science.

Aldrich, Robert (2005). Vestiges of the Colonial Empire in France: Monuments, Museums and Colonial Memories. Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan.Asia: substantial10 chapter overviews

Overview

Aldrich's study traces the colonial empire in metropolitan France as it stood around 2000: monuments, street names, statues, museums and temporary exhibitions. Its main argument is that the French remembered and forgot the empire selectively, and that its material traces pass through three phases: a display of empire from about 1890 to the 1940s, a concealment from the 1960s to the 1980s, and a renewed boom since the 1990s. The book has an introduction, seven chapters (Paris, the provinces, war memorials, commemorated men, museums, non-Western art, temporary exhibitions) and a conclusion on the planned Marseille Mémorial National de l'Outre-Mer. It excludes the overseas departments and territories and the former colonies.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

East and Southeast Asia form a substantial strand that appears in all seven chapters, though only as one theme among several. It is concentrated on Indochina (Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos). Chapter 1 (Paris) covers the Maison de l'Indochine (1930), the Maison du Cambodge (1957), the Salle d'Asie of the 1931 fair and the Nogent pavilion. Chapter 2 (provinces) covers Lyon's Jesuits, silk merchants and the Guimet museum, the Institut Franco-Chinois and Fréjus's Hong-Hien Pagoda (1917). Chapters 3 and 4 (war memorials; men and monuments) are central to the Jardin Tropical's Vietnamese dinh, the Fréjus Indochina memorial, the Garnier and Pavie statues, and Loti's Chinese room furnished with booty from Beijing.

The richest material is in chapters 5 to 7. Chapter 5 covers the Fréjus Troupes de Marine museum (Hanoi, Pavie, a Viet Minh banner), the Alençon collection of about 500 Cambodian objects gathered by Adhémar Leclère, and the Pasteur institutes in Hanoi and Saigon. Chapter 6 is the fullest account: Angkor sculptures collected by Delaporte and Aymonier, EFEO sales (six Khmer works to the Metropolitan Museum in 1936) and the Siem Reap protest of 1949, Empress Eugénie's Chinese museum at Fontainebleau with loot from the 1860 sack of the Beijing summer palace, the Cernuschi, d'Ennery and Labit collections, and the Musée Guimet's Asian holdings and its 2001 reopening. Chapter 7 mentions Léon Busy's photographs of Cambodia and Tonkin, the 1997 'Paris-Hanoi-Saigon' show and Leguay's Indochinese stamps. The conclusion mentions Asia only in passing.

Not covered: Asian states' own museum and heritage policy, Vietnamese and Cambodian voices beyond the Siem Reap petition and Vietnamese visitors at Fréjus, and Indonesia, Burma and Malaysia except as sections of the Guimet display. Korea appears only through a Korean War monument in Paris and a Korean authorities' monument in Fréjus. Japan and China figure as sources of collections rather than as subjects of French colonial display.

PrefacePDF p. 9

The preface sets out the book's scope: traces of the overseas empire in metropolitan France, and what these 'sites of memory' reveal about French attitudes to the colonial past. Because monuments and museums change, Aldrich describes them as they stood around 2000 and warns that the book is no reliable guide. It explains the terms 'colonialism', 'natives' and 'primitive', kept to preserve period usage, and says the study rests on visits and published catalogues rather than a full inventory.

Introduction: Sites of Colonial Memoryp. 1

Aldrich opens with Paris landmarks such as the Arc de Triomphe and the Bastille to show that monuments carry competing versions of the past, then argues that colonial traces in France are more widespread than they appear. Drawing on Halbwachs, Renan and Nora, the introduction treats monuments and museums as places where memory is built, displayed, forgotten or recalled. Selective memory is its central theme: the French celebrated the emancipation of slaves while forgetting slavery, and the Algerian War was buried under a wall of silence until General Aussaresses's 2000 confession. The introduction sets out three phases: display of empire from about 1890 to the 1940s, concealment from the 1960s to the 1980s, and a renewed boom since the 1990s. It ends with an unbuilt Paris colonial monument proposed in 1909 and 1913 and the 2004 naming of the Place Maurice Audin.

East and Southeast Asia Asian material recurs only briefly. Chinoiserie, the late-eighteenth- and nineteenth-century vogue for the Far East, is linked to French incursions in China in the 1840s and in Southeast Asia in the 1860s. The introduction notes the 1983 Fréjus monument to the Indochinese War, the lack of any monument to Ho Chi Minh, the Vietnamese 'boat people' of 1975 and the Musée Guimet, the national museum of Asian art.

Musée des ColoniesMusée de l'Homme
11 The Colonies in Parisp. 21Asia: in part

Aldrich's first chapter walks through Paris to read the colonial traces in its streets, shops, buildings and institutions. It begins with the mixed population of Barbès and Belleville and with the names of shops and restaurants, then turns to the Egyptian monuments that followed Napoleon's 1798 campaign, arguing that exoticism and colonialism were hard to separate in Paris architecture. The main evidence is the street map: some 275 of about 5,400 streets make explicit colonial references, and their placement follows only a vague logic. The fullest case studies are the Ministry of Colonies, the Ecole Coloniale, whose murals were partly hidden in the 1970s, and the Porte Dorée museum, built for the 1931 Exposition Coloniale, with its Janniot bas-relief. The chapter closes with recent renamings of streets for Chevalier de Saint-Georges and Mohammed V and concludes that Paris's colonial memory remains one-sided and largely unmarked.

East and Southeast Asia Indochina is the chief Asian theme. The Maison de l'Indochine student residence (1930), built on the initiative of a committee headed by an Indochina industrialist, opened amid protests over the repression of the Yen Bay rebellion, and a Maison du Cambodge followed in 1957. The 1931 fair's Salle d'Asie and Janniot's bas-relief of Indochinese peasants present the region as productive and exotic, and the Nogent pavilion and Place des Combattants en Indochine commemorate its colonial soldiers. Bao-Daï's exile apartment on the Rue Fresnel and a statue of Garnier, who died trying to conquer Tonkin, add further links.

Musée Colonial (Palais de la Porte Dorée)Musée de l'ArméeMuséum national d'histoire naturelleMusée de l'Homme
22 The Colonies in the Provincesp. 76Asia: in part

This chapter surveys how the French empire was present outside Paris, in provincial cities, towns and regions. Aldrich argues that each province built its own link with the colonies, through garrisons, trading houses, missionary societies and local men who had served overseas. The traces are scattered: short-lived exhibitions and 'villages noirs', exotic gardens and houses in Moorish or Chinese styles, street names, and war memorials. Three regions are then examined in detail. The Atlantic ports, among them Rouen, Le Havre and Nantes, grew rich on the slave trade, and Nantes receives the fullest treatment, through its slow public reckoning with slavery and the 1992 exhibition Les Anneaux de la Mémoire. Lyon is shown through its missionary orders, silk merchants and colonial museums, and the Midi through Marseille, Fréjus and the pied-noir town of Carnoux. The chapter ends at Champagney, a Vosges village whose 1789 cahier called for the emancipation of slaves and which now hosts the Maison de la Négritude. Aldrich concludes that provincial France still carries a colonial legacy.

East and Southeast Asia Lyon's Asian links are central: Jesuit missionaries in the Far East, silk merchants who obtained concessions in China and Japan and backed expansion into Indochina, and Emile Guimet, whose Asian art museum opened in Lyon in 1879 and moved to Paris in 1885. Lyon's natural history museum keeps a reconstructed Chinese room, a Vietnamese naga, a Thai Buddha and Cambodian sculpture, and the Institut Franco-Chinois trained 473 Chinese students before 1946. Fréjus's Hong-Hien Pagoda, built in 1917 for Indochinese soldiers, is described, and Marseille's street names include Annam, Haiphong, Hanoi and Tonkin. Bordeaux's museums display Asian tea chests, jade and porcelain.

Maison du Missionnaire (Vichy)Musée Guimet (Lyon)Musée Africain (Société des Missions Africaines, Lyon)Colonial museum of the Lyon Chamber of CommerceMusée d'Aquitaine (Bordeaux)Muséum d'histoire naturelle (Lyon)Maison de la Négritude et des Droits de l'Homme (Champagney)Les Anneaux de la Mémoire (Nantes exhibition)
33 Colonial War Memorialsp. 105Asia: in part

This chapter asks how colonial soldiers and colonial wars appear on French war memorials, the monuments aux morts. Aldrich argues that conquest was rarely memorialised, because French opinion was divided about empire and did not grant colonial enemies the status of armies. First World War monuments did commemorate colonial troops, but in a European idiom, and many inscriptions merged colonial and metropolitan dead. After 1962 many monuments from Algeria were 'repatriated' to France and re-erected in garrison towns and in places where pieds-noirs settled. Aldrich then follows memorials to the Second World War and to the Indochinese and Algerian wars. Two sites receive the most attention: the Vietnamese dinh and Buddhist temple in the Jardin Tropical in Paris, and the Indochinese memorial at Fréjus, which he judges to present a one-sided view of the war and of colonialism. The Algerian memorials, from provincial stelae to the 2002 Quai Branly column of scrolling names, show contested memories and a state only slowly coming to terms with the colonial past. The chapter concludes that French monuments remain ambivalent about the colonial epoch.

East and Southeast Asia Indochina is central. The Jardin Tropical's Vietnamese dinh, shipped from Cochinchina for the 1906 Marseille fair, became a Temple du Souvenir Indochinois in 1920, burned in 1984 and was replaced by a new memorial in 1992. Cambodian and Laotian soldiers have their own monument there, and Indochinese dead are buried in Toulouse and Nogent-sur-Marne. The Fréjus Indochina memorial, beside a 1917 pagoda, is criticised for a text that presents French rule as benevolent and omits Vietnamese nationalism, forced labour and torture; Ho Chi Minh is never named.

Jardin Tropical (Paris)Mémorial des Guerres en Indochine (Fréjus)Musée des Troupes de Marine (Fréjus)Quai Branly Algerian War memorial (Paris)Mémorial de la France combattante, Mont-Valérien (Paris)Monument aux Héros de l'Orient (Marseille)
44 Of Men and Monumentsp. 157Asia: in part

This chapter looks at how colonial figures are commemorated in France, in statues, plaques, graves, the Panthéon and museum houses. Aldrich argues that the empire's heroes were honoured as 'great men', mainly soldiers, explorers and missionaries, so the monumental record is narrow, with few settlers, traders or ordinary people. Aldrich surveys Paris statues, many of which, such as those of Ferry, de Gaulle and Camus, omit their colonial careers, and then provincial statues of native sons such as La Pérouse, Dupleix and Pavie, together with dozens of monuments 'repatriated' from Algeria after 1962. Missionaries and martyrs are commemorated in churches such as Notre-Dame des Missions and at the Rue du Bac seminary. Three houses turned museums, those of Loti, Lyautey and Schweitzer, are presented as shrines that offer a largely uncritical view of empire. The chapter closes with the Panthéon, where Schoelcher, Eboué, Grégoire and, through plaques, Toussaint Louverture and Delgrès were honoured in ways that Aldrich reads as a belated reinterpretation of colonial history. He concludes that statues and monuments give a limited, hierarchical view of the empire.

East and Southeast Asia Asia runs through the Paris and provincial statues: Garnier's monument in Paris has Indochinese women at its base, a Cambodian-style monument in Grenoble honours Doudart de Lagrée, who died exploring the Mekong, and Pavie, who brought Laos under French control, is commemorated in Dinan. Loti's house in Rochefort has a Chinese room furnished with booty from the siege of Beijing, and Lyautey's Thorey has Indochinese rooms. Notre-Dame des Missions has a painting of the martyrdom of Théophane Vénard in Indochina, and the Rue du Bac seminary keeps relics of Vietnamese martyrs.

Maison de Pierre Loti (Rochefort)Château de Thorey, Lyautey house museumSchweitzer house museum (Gunsbach)Fort de Joux, Toussaint Louverture exhibitionNotre-Dame des Missions (Épinay-sur-Seine)Salle des Martyrs, Société des Missions Étrangères (Paris)Maison de la Négritude (Champagney)
55 The Colonies in Museumsp. 196Asia: in part

Aldrich surveys how French museums keep the empire on display, from colonial museums and provincial collections to fine arts galleries and military museums. Aldrich opens with Marseille's colonial museum of 1935, built to present the port as a colonial gateway, then finds traces in unexpected places such as the Musee Albert Kahn. Orientalist painting, the colonial art of the 1930s revived at the Musee des Annees Trente in Boulogne-Billancourt, and avant-garde borrowings from Africa and Oceania come next. Two museums in Lorient and La Rochelle, which hold East India and New World collections, are judged more critical than most, though still traditional in style. Military museums at Fréjus, Aubagne and the Invalides are celebratory and unrevised, shrines to memory rather than history. The closing sections turn to anti-colonial art, such as the Grand Tableau Antifasciste, whose journey from Milan to Strasbourg shows how reluctant museums have been to display works that revive painful memories of the Algerian War.

East and Southeast Asia Indochina recurs most: the Fréjus Troupes de Marine museum has a corner on Hanoi and Auguste Pavie, a Viet Minh banner and a Dien Bien Phu poster, plus a Korean authorities' monument to a Korean War doctor and a banner from the Boxer Rebellion expedition in China. The Val-de-Grâce shows the Pasteur institutes in Hanoi and Saigon, and the Alençon museum holds about five hundred objects collected in Cambodia by Adhémar Leclère. Kahn's Archives de la Planète include footage of Vietnamese trade and rice cultivation, and La Rochelle's Musée d'Orbigny-Bernon has Chinese furniture, lacquer and porcelain.

Marseille colonial museumMusée des Années TrenteMusée des Troupes de MarineMusée de la Légion EtrangèreMusée de l'ArméeMusée de la Compagnie des IndesMusée du Nouveau MondeMusée Albert Kahn
66 The Colonial Legacy of Non-Western Art in French Museumsp. 245Asia: in part

Aldrich asks how French museums display the non-Western art gathered in the colonial era, and whether the institutions holding it can shed their colonial origins. Aldrich traces collecting from ancien regime cabinets of curiosities through the Louvre's ethnographic galleries and the Trocadero museum of 1878 to the Musee de l'Homme of 1938. The Trocadero's African and Oceanic displays are set against the Musee Colonial, which showed the 'after' of empire, while the Musee de l'Homme's functionalist displays are compared with the aesthetic style of the Musee Dapper. The chapter's centre is the plan for the Quai Branly museum, which merged the Musee de l'Homme and the MAAO and was driven by presidential ambition and opposed by staff. Aldrich then examines restitution, the illicit trade and the Baartman remains, and the Musee Guimet and Institut du Monde Arabe. Aldrich concludes that museums must trace each object's route into the collection as well as its source society, so that its colonial history is not erased by modern display.

East and Southeast Asia Indochina is the chief Asian strand: Khmer works from Angkor, collected by Delaporte and Aymonier, went to the Trocadero, and the EFEO sold Indochinese sculptures abroad, six of them to the Metropolitan Museum in 1936, a practice that Siem Reap residents protested in 1949. Eugenie's 'Chinese museum' at Fontainebleau held loot from the 1860 sack of the Beijing summer palace and gifts from the King of Siam. Guimet's museum, founded on his 1876 journey through Japan, China and Indochina, has strong Vietnamese and Cambodian sections, and Labit's Toulouse house held Chinese opium pipes and an Indochinese table.

Musée de l'HommeTrocadéro ethnographic museumMusée ColonialMusée des Arts Africains et Océaniens (MAAO)Quai Branly museumMusée DapperMusée GuimetInstitut du Monde Arabe
77 Temporary Exhibitions: Changing Perspectivesp. 291Asia: in part

This chapter surveys the temporary exhibitions French museums have mounted on colonial subjects since the 1980s, when colonies returned to museum programmes after decades of silence. Aldrich opens with 'L'Orient des Provençaux', the 1982 series of seventeen shows in Marseille whose Orientalist art and trade histories largely avoided colonial domination, and with the 1992 Invalides exhibition on the Algerian War, the first major show on the conflict. Aldrich then works through the Musée Albert-Kahn's photographic displays, the Boulogne-Billancourt colonial art show, and exhibitions on slavery, sport, colonial soldiers, colonial medicine, the penal colony at Guyane and the 2003 'Année de l'Algérie'. Each is read for its framing, its choice of objects and whether it celebrates or questions empire. Aldrich concludes that the 1990s shows were more critical than earlier displays, though most still avoid both praise and condemnation, and that short-lived exhibitions can revise memory as well as record it.

East and Southeast Asia Asian material is confined to a few exhibitions. Léon Busy's 1920s photographs of Cambodia and Angkor Wat, and his Tonkin views including the Pont Doumer in Hanoi, were shown at the Kahn museum in 1992 and 1994. The 1997 'Paris-Hanoi-Saigon' show covered the Ecole des Beaux-Arts in Hanoi and the blending of French and Vietnamese techniques in silk painting and lacquer. Aldrich also notes Marcel Leguay, a painter who lived in Laos and designed Indochinese stamps, shown at the Musée de la Poste in 2002, and the Croisière Jaune's route across central Asia to Saigon in a 2002-2003 Paris display.

Musée Albert-KahnMusée de l'HommeMusée des Arts d'Afrique et d'OcéanieMusée des Beaux-Arts de MarseilleMusée de l'ArméeHistorial de la Grande GuerreMusée des Arts et Traditions PopulairesInstitut du Monde Arabe
Conclusion: The Future of the Colonial Pastp. 328

Aldrich's conclusion asks what becomes of a colonial past that France has never housed in a museum of its own. It traces the 1990s debate over a national institution on empire, which stalled over questions of name, purpose and sponsorship, until the Marseille city government announced its own project and national authorities joined it as the Mémorial National de l'Outre-Mer, led by historian Jean-Jacques Jordi. He describes the planned building on the Parc Chanot site of the 1906 and 1922 colonial fairs, with themed sections such as 'light', 'peace and violence' and 'the land and the dead' for Algeria. He then places the Mémorial among new museums and monuments, and among the political uses that successive governments made of exhibitions and commemorations. The chapter closes by noting that colonial sites still carry conflicting memories held by pieds-noirs, Antillean descendants of slaves, harkis and Vietnamese visitors, so the question of how France presents its empire remains open.

East and Southeast Asia Asia appears in the conclusion only in passing: the planned Mémorial's Indochina section covers science, arts and culture and Dien Bien Phu, the 1983 Fréjus memorial to the Indochina war is noted, and Vietnamese visitors to Fréjus are said to remember differently. The revamped Musée Guimet is cited as a new home for Asian art.

Arnold, Ken (2006). Cabinets for the Curious: Looking Back at Early English Museums. Aldershot: Ashgate.Asia: occasional13 chapter overviews

Overview

Cabinets for the Curious (2006) is a cultural and intellectual history of seventeenth-century English museums, from Walter Cope's rooms and the Tradescant collection to the Ashmolean and the Royal Society's Repository. Ken Arnold, an exhibition maker, reads these collections as the workshops of a distinct museum-science that produced knowledge from individual objects rather than general laws. He argues that collectors used three strategies to get knowledge from things, which he calls narrative, functional and taxonomic. Chapters 3, 4, 6, 7, 9 and 10 trace these through local natural history, coins, travel, medicinal chemistry and classification, while chapters 5, 8 and 11 follow each strategy into the present. The main claim is that taxonomy displaced the curious object in the eighteenth century, a loss the author links to today's experience-led museums.

East and Southeast Asia in this work occasional

East Asia is present but marginal, and it is concentrated in one chapter. Chapter 6, 'Trade and Travel', has a section of several pages on Chinese material: Hans Sloane's 1698 account of a China cabinet sent home by Mr Buckley, chief surgeon at Fort St George; the Royal Society's Chinese statera; Petty's list of trades, which includes Chinese varnishes and Chinese ink; and a 1699 article urging English craftsmen to imitate Chinese workmanship. The same chapter notes Japan only in an anonymous list of 'Indian and Japanese Curiosities' and in the vague labelling of objects as 'Indian' or 'Japanese'. These are Asian objects in English cabinets, acquired through trade and travel and used to test the collectors' categories rather than as subjects in their own right.

Elsewhere East Asia appears in passing. Chapter 2 mentions Chinese boxes in Walter Cope's rooms, which Arnold calls exceptional for England. Chapter 9 uses Chinese characters as a model of an international script for language reform. The notes to chapters 5 and 11 cite Craig Clunas's work on the Chinese imperial collection in Britain, and a chapter 6 note cites Acosta's 'barbarian' categories, which set the Chinese and Japanese above peoples without letters. The chapter 11 notes also describe the Exploratorium's 'Memory' show, which includes Japanese photographs of Nagasaki, but that is an American display, not an Asian museum.

Southeast Asia is essentially absent: no Siam, Indonesia, Philippines or Vietnam appear. Colonial and overseas loot is discussed generically, and Arnold notes that Sloane's 'Miscelanies' include about 350 'ethnographic' items, excluding pieces from 'Oriental cultures'. The book discusses no Asian museums, Asian visitors or curators, and no state heritage policy, restitution or war memory in Asia. The book's concern is with English museums in the 1600s and 1700s.

Half Title
Title Page
Copyright Page
Table of Contents
General Preface to the Series
Preface

The preface states the book's purpose. Arnold examines seventeenth-century English cabinets of curiosities, but cares less about how collections were assembled than about what people did with objects afterwards. Drawing on his work as an exhibition maker, he argues that the early museum's idea of an isolated space for objects still shapes museums. The book is both a cultural history of early English museums and a framework for today's questions about objects.

Acknowledgements
11 Introduction: Museum-Science

This introduction sets out the book's central claim: that seventeenth-century English museums were sites of a distinct 'museum-science', which produced knowledge from individual objects rather than general laws. Arnold argues that historians of science have neglected collectors and fact-gatherers, and he challenges Kuhn's split between mathematical and experimental traditions. Drawing on Eamon, Ginzburg and Trigger, he describes an 'epistemology of the hunt' that worked from the single example. The book alternates synchronic chapters on historical practice with diachronic ones that follow narrative, functional and taxonomic strategies to today. Arnold answers Crimp and Mullaney, who deny that early cabinets resemble modern museums, by stressing both continuity and difference. Arnold ends by calling the eighteenth-century shift to taxonomy a 'dumbing-up' that lost the curious object, and by linking it to today's 'dumbing-down' through experience-led museums, with the aim of a usable history.

22 Museums Arrive in England

Arnold asks how museums arrived in England, where a visiting German in 1599 found nothing comparable to continental cabinets beyond one private apartment, that of Walter Cope. The chapter traces the European forerunners of the cabinet of curiosities, from Italian and Prague collections built as displays of princely power to the continental travel that drew aristocrats such as the Earl of Arundel into collecting. It then follows the habit down the social scale to middling figures such as John Tradescant, whose collection became known as the Ark, and shows how the Civil War turned museums towards Baconian, fact-based inquiry. Arnold argues that the move from private rooms to institutional buildings, chiefly the Ashmolean in Oxford and the Royal Society's repository, gave museums a public threshold and a research purpose. Institutional collections were, however, no safer than private ones, since neglect often squandered them. The chapter ends by presenting museums as workshops for producing public knowledge, a claim the rest of the book tests through natural history, coins and travel.

Ashmolean MuseumRoyal Society repositoryTradescant's Ark
Part I: The Narrative Tradition
33 Robert Plot’s Philosophical Histories

Plot's county natural histories of Oxfordshire (1677) and Staffordshire (1686) are the subject of this chapter, which argues that he wrote local surveys in which museum objects served as evidence for almost every claim. Arnold places Plot within the chorographical tradition running from Lambarde and Camden to Stow, and within John Childrey's Baconian Britannia Baconica, whose first-hand method Plot extended. The surveys cover fossils, coins, minerals and above all freaks and monsters, which Plot preferred to ordinary specimens. The main case is Plot's work as the Ashmolean's first keeper: moving the Tradescant collection to Oxford, presiding over the museum's 1683 opening, and directing the Oxford Philosophical Society, which met under the museum's roof and tested magnets, electricity and marbles. Arnold shows how Plot's accounts mix fact, anecdote and speculation, and ends with his coin of Prasutagus, which the chapter takes as the model of a narrative museum science.

Ashmolean MuseumRoyal Society repository
44 Learned Treasures

Chapter four turns from natural history to coins and medals, which Arnold argues were the most vocal of museum objects for seventeenth-century English antiquaries. It opens with the 1685 Colton's-Field find in Gloucestershire, a broadsheet tale of underground houses and a clockwork figure, and uses it to show how common such finds were. The chapter then examines how coins were bought, traded and arranged. Gentlemen such as the Earl of Pembroke collected them within a code of polite learning, while institutions such as the Ashmolean and the Bodleian gave numismatics the scholarly support that individual collectors could not. The second half follows antiquaries such as Camden, Speed and Cotton, who used coin images to illustrate history and read inscriptions as texts, and later figures such as Hearne and Woodward, who studied find-spots and metal as archaeological evidence. The chapter concludes that numismatics combined the reading of legends with the handling of the object itself, a narrative form of museum science.

Ashmolean MuseumBodleian LibraryRoyal Society repository
55 Telling Stories in Museums

Arnold argues that objects in seventeenth-century museums were valued as the starting point of stories, and that this narrative mode still shapes history and biography museums. The chapter opens with the anecdotal catalogues of Plot and John Bargrave, in which one object leads into digression, and with Hans Sloane's bone spoon, whose cure story is inscribed on its surface. It turns to medieval and Maori examples of objects bound to their histories, then to modern museums that rely on the authenticity of place: Down House, the Jenner Museum, the Alexander Fleming laboratory and Freud's Hampstead house. Souvenirs and personal memory supply the emotional charge, and Arnold draws on Baudrillard, Pearce and Susan Stewart to suggest that museums resemble graveyards, where objects are removed from circulation and given a half-life. The chapter ends by urging exhibitions, labels and visitor comment that let viewers add their own meanings to objects.

Down HouseJenner MuseumAlexander Fleming MuseumFreud MuseumSloane's museumSmithsonian Institution
Part Ii: The Functional Tradition
66 Trade and TravelAsia: in part

Arnold argues that museums were the densest way for English people to make sense of the lands that travel and trade were opening up, and that their foreign objects were studied for commercial use as much as for knowledge. The chapter begins with travel and the Royal Society's questionnaires for travellers, and with collectors such as Bargrave and John Tradescant the elder, whose cabinets were gathered on journeys abroad. It then shows how merchants, captains and colonists supplied Tradescant's Ark, the Royal Society's repository, Sloane's collection and the Ashmolean, and how a trade in curiosities grew up. Foreign objects were read through a utilitarian model asking how they were made, from what, and for what use. This produced early ethnography, but also limits: unfamiliar things were fitted into existing categories, and the most informative accounts came from objects least like anything known. The chapter ends by tracing this material inquiry towards physical anthropology, a path it presents as slow and uneven.

East and Southeast Asia Chinese material is discussed across a section of several pages. Hans Sloane's account in the Philosophical Transactions for 1698 described a China cabinet sent home by Mr Buckley, chief surgeon at Fort St George, containing instruments, fruits and ear-pickers used in China, and a series of further articles followed. The Royal Society also held a Chinese statera inscribed with Chinese and European measures, and Petty's list of trades included Chinese varnishes and Chinese ink. A 1699 article urged English craftsmen to imitate Chinese workmanship.

Tradescant's ArkRoyal Society repositorySloane's collectionAshmolean Museum
77 Medicinal Chemistry

This chapter argues that seventeenth-century English museums took their character from the medical trade. Arnold begins with the materia medica prized by collectors, such as unicorn horn, mummies and human skulls, and with the arrival of New World drugs and Paracelsian chemical remedies that increased demand for them. Apothecaries and physicians, including Petiver, Sloane, Woodward and Mead, kept or stocked many collections, and the College of Physicians, the Society of Apothecaries, the Royal Society and Oxford all founded physic gardens, laboratories or museums. The central case is the Ashmolean, where Ashmole imposed a strong medical character. Arnold then examines 'medicinal chemistry', showing how museum men tasted, smelt, burned and dissolved their specimens to learn their virtues, and how sympathy and signature doctrines gave way to mechanical and utilitarian explanations. The chapter closes with the medical use of museum objects becoming a matter of practical testing, a shift it carries into the exotic artefacts of the next chapter.

Ashmolean MuseumRoyal Society RepositorySociety of ApothecariesHarverian Museum
88 Using Museums

This chapter argues that the functional approach to objects which shaped seventeenth-century medical and exotic collecting persisted in museums and still defines their purpose. Arnold opens with the eighteenth-century joke about useless virtuosi and with Baudrillard and Pomian, who claim that museum objects lose their use, and rejects their view of museum value as sealed off. Most of the chapter traces the functional legacy in anthropology, from Pitt Rivers's tool displays of the museum age to Boas, who gave up object-centred display for meaning in context. Medical museums, from teaching cabinets and anatomical wax models to the recent turn to medical humanities, are treated next, followed by decorative-arts museums such as South Kensington, built to teach makers technique and later turned toward connoisseurship. The final section argues that museums have lost their educational role to science centres and heritage sites such as the Exploratorium, which replace authentic objects with experience. Arnold concludes that objects can still be made useful, by using them to teach and to provoke, if museum education is treated as more than a separate department.

Pitt Rivers MuseumSouth Kensington Museum (Victoria and Albert Museum)Museum of MankindExploratoriumScience Museum
Part Iii: The Taxonomic Tradition
99 The Reform of Learning

Arnold argues that the seventeenth-century drive to reform education and language, from Comenius's object lessons to Wilkins's philosophical language, put real things at the centre of English museums. Arnold begins with Swift's satire of a language of objects, then shows how Comenius, Hoole and Dury wanted schoolrooms and purpose-built schoolhouses organised around specimens, and how Willis and Hooke used the art of memory to treat collections as mental repositories. Wilkins's Essay of 1668 was the most ambitious attempt to build a language whose words matched the natural order, and the Royal Society's Repository was meant to supply its tables. The scheme failed on its own terms, but Hooke, Grew and Aubrey carried its ordering ambition into museum catalogues, and Ray found the artificial system constraining yet still useful. The chapter concludes that this systematic classification of nature, which came to dominate museums in the late seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, is the subject of the next chapter.

Royal Society RepositoryRobert Hubert's cabinet
1010 Classifying God’s Work

Arnold argues that taxonomy, the ordering of objects by shared and distinguishing features, became the dominant purpose of English museums in the late seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries, and that natural theology gave it moral legitimacy. Earlier collections were ordered for convenience or display, and numismatists ordered coins as a ritual, but after about 1650 keepers and naturalists began to strip objects of their stories and uses in favour of their relations to one another. The main case is the Royal Society's Repository, which was disordered, decayed and incomplete yet remained the model house of classification. Petiver, Woodward, Lister and Lhwyd are examined as taxonomists who turned their collections into catalogues and field tools. The chapter ends with re-ordering and the British Museum, whose 1759 plan by Gowin Knight arranged fossils, plants and animals from simplest to most complex, and whose display cabinets show that order had become a matter of visual calm and presentation.

Royal Society RepositoryAshmolean MuseumBritish MuseumWoodward's fossil cabinets
1111 Ordering Museums

Arnold argues that taxonomy, which had grown out of educational and linguistic reform into the organising principle of museums, was by the nineteenth century used to divide knowledge into separate disciplines and to define what counted as proper knowledge. Arnold traces how the logic of classification shaped museum architecture, catalogues, display furniture and connoisseurship, and how the Vienna picture gallery and the Great Exhibition sorted objects by school, industry or country. The argument then turns to the breakup of universal museums, as the British Museum lost its natural history to South Kensington and the Science Museum became separate in 1909. The final sections contrast this mild boredom of order with recent museums that rehang and question their own taxonomies, use temporary exhibitions as experiments, and invite outsiders to co-curate. Arnold concludes that the seventeenth-century habit of trying out objects, now revived in thematic exhibitions, offers a way to restore the cabinet of curiosity in its best sense.

British MuseumVictoria and Albert Museum (South Kensington)Great Exhibition of 1851Milwaukee Public MuseumKaiserlich-Königliche Bildergalerie, Vienna
1212 Conclusion: The Wonder of Museums

Arnold's conclusion argues that the narrative, functional and taxonomic ways of getting knowledge from objects, which seventeenth-century English museum makers developed, still structure museum work but have hardened into separate disciplinary styles. Arnold illustrates this with the camera, which a design museum treats by its look, a science museum by its mechanism and an art museum by its images, so that no single display shows how it worked and what its photographs did. The remedy he proposes is the concept of wonder, which he separates from the Romantic sublime and ties to a disciplined curiosity that makes visitors ask questions and then exhausts their words. Museums, on this view, are where private passion can become public knowledge, and digital reproduction makes the authenticity of objects more important, not less. He ends with the Neuchatel ethnographic museum, the one-picture gallery at Penza and the San Diego Zoo's Hippo Beach as examples of this wonder, and with an optimistic view of the seventeenth-century museum scientists as the book's heroes.

Askew, Rie Kido (2007). “The Politics of Nostalgia: Museum Representations of Lafcadio Hearn in Japan”. museum and society, 5.3 (November 2007): 131-147.Asia: central1 chapter overview

Overview

Askew examines three Japanese museums devoted to the writer Lafcadio Hearn, in Matsue, Kumamoto and Yaizu, and asks what their displays remember and what they forget. Askew argues that all three present Hearn as a cultural nationalist and folklorist who loved 'Old Japan', a nostalgic construction that sets a traditional past against a modernizing present. Askew compares them with the Yushukan at Yasukuni Shrine, which defends wartime Japan openly, and concludes that the nostalgia reflects a postwar sense of loss that the museums could address by facing the war.

East and Southeast Asia in this work central

The whole article is about Japan, so its Asian content is central. Askew describes the Lafcadio Hearn Memorial Museum in Matsue, rebuilt in a traditional style in 1984, the Old Residence of Koizumi Yakumo in Kumamoto, restored in 1995, and the Yaizu Hearn Museum, opened on 27 June 2007. Askew compares these with the Yushukan museum at Yasukuni Shrine in Tokyo, which justifies the Second World War as a struggle against Western domination.

Hearn's own remarks are central to the argument: his dislike of the common people of Kumamoto, his praise in Japan: An Attempt at Interpretation (1904) of self-sacrifice for the Emperor and the Shokonsha, and his view of Japan's modernization. The article draws on the postwar slogan datsu-A nyu-O (Leave Asia and Join the West) and on Nishida Kitaro's philosophy of overcoming modernity.

No other East or Southeast Asian country is discussed, and the article does not treat Asian collections in Western museums, colonial collecting, or the museum policy of any state other than Japan.

The politics of nostalgia: museum representations of Lafcadio Hearn in Japanp. 131Asia: chiefly

This journal article examines three Japanese museums devoted to the writer Lafcadio Hearn (Koizumi Yakumo), in Matsue, Kumamoto and Yaizu, and asks what their displays remember and what they forget. Askew argues that all three present Hearn as a cultural nationalist and sensitive folklorist who loved 'Old Japan', a construction that sets a traditional past against a modernizing, Westernized present. The article describes each museum in turn: the Matsue museum and its reconstructed samurai street, the Kumamoto house museum, which omits Hearn's dislike of the city's common people, and the newly opened Yaizu museum, which presents Hearn as a critic of materialism. It then compares these with the Yushukan at Yasukuni Shrine, which defends wartime Japan openly, and shows that Hearn's own praise of self-sacrifice for the Emperor is left out. The argument is that the museums' nostalgia reflects a postwar sense of loss, and that they could move beyond it by confronting the war and the problem of modernization.

East and Southeast Asia The whole article concerns Japan. It reads the three Hearn museums in Matsue, Kumamoto and Yaizu against the Yushukan museum at Yasukuni Shrine and the postwar nostalgia for a traditional Japan. It also covers Hearn's ambivalence about the common people of Kumamoto and his 1904 remarks on the Shokonsha war dead, which the displays leave out.

Asma, Stephen T. (2001). Stuffed Animals and Pickled Heads: The Culture and Evolution of Natural History Museums. New York: Oxford University Press.Asia: slight8 chapter overviews

Overview

Asma's book traces how natural history museums came to show nature, through the preservation, collecting, classification and display of specimens in London, Paris, Chicago and New York. Its argument is that a museum's presentation frame, the arrangement of specimens and the feelings they produce, carries ideas about nature that visitors rarely notice. Chapters 1 and 2 cover taxidermy, wet preparation and the eighteenth-century cabinets of Hunter, Peter the Great and Peale; chapters 3 and 4 follow taxonomy from Renaissance cabinets through Linnaeus, Buffon, Lamarck and Cuvier; chapters 5 and 6 compare how the Paris, New York, London and Chicago museums display evolution and its religious consequences; chapter 7 examines dioramas, drawings and the spectacle of edutainment. The book is organised as a sequence of museum visits interleaved with history, and it is not an exhaustive survey.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia figure only in passing. The museums studied are all in Europe and North America, and the book does not treat museums, collections or collectors in Asia. The fullest passage is in Chapter 1 (Flesh-eating Beetles and the Secret Art of Taxidermy), where Asma recounts Alfred Russel Wallace's years in the East Indies: the bird of paradise Wallace caught and tagged, the Aru Islanders who had removed the legs of skins sold to European traders, Wallace's fever in Borneo, and his argument that a deep channel between Bali and Lombok separated the Australian and Southeast Asian fauna. These episodes serve Wallace's collecting and theory, not a study of the regions. Chapter 5 (Exhibiting Evolution) returns to the Bali and Lombok argument and to the migration of Aboriginal Australians through Southeast Asia, used to show why folk racial categories mislead.

Elsewhere the references are brief. In Chapter 3 (Taxonomic Intoxication, Part I) Fremiet's 1898 marble of an orangutan strangling a Bornean man, in the Galerie d'anatomie comparée, is read as an 'ominous entry sculpture', and Borges's invented Chinese encyclopedia appears as an example of arbitrary classification. Aldrovandi's Siamese chickens appear among his freak cases in the same chapter. Chapter 4 mentions Hunter's conjoined-twin fetus, described as Siamese twins, and Linnaeus's variety 'asiaticus'. Chapter 6 (Evolution and the Roulette Wheel) quotes a visitor's letter praising the Field Museum's display on the wartime treatment of Japanese Americans; the letter concerns the United States, not Japan.

Nothing is said about museums in Asia, Asian states' heritage or museum policy, Asian objects in Western collections, colonial collecting in Asia, restitution claims, or Asian visitors and scholars. The Borneo and Indonesian material appears as sources of Wallace's specimens and theory. The index lists only the Aru Islands and the Japanese exhibit, both already noted.

Introduction

Asma opens with the Irish Giant's skeleton in London's Hunterian Museum and John Hunter's boiling of the body. Asma sets out the book's concern: natural history museums display ideas as well as specimens, and their presentation frame goes unnoticed. Its museums are in London, Paris, Chicago and New York. The book is not meant to be an exhaustive survey of modern museums.

Hunterian MuseumNatural History MuseumField MuseumAmerican Museum of Natural HistoryGrande Galerie de l'evolution
1CHAPTER 1 Flesh-eating Beetles and the Secret Art of TaxidermyAsia: in part

Asma opens with the Inuit skeleton of Qisuk at the American Museum of Natural History and Peter the Great's preserved curiosities, then asks how specimens are prepared and why people collect and display dead animals. Asma moves to the back rooms of Chicago's Field Museum, where he interviews taxidermists and the ornithologist John Bates, watches skin preparation, and sees dermestid beetles clean skeletons. Bates's genetic work on Amazonian birds and the McCormick Place bird-kill records show how specimens yield scientific data. Asma tests Freud's and Baudrillard's theories of collecting against these practices. The second half distinguishes kinds of spectacle (the odd, the wonderful, the grotesque) and examines edutainment through the Field's suitcase dioramas. He traces display from Hornaday's habitat groups to Albert Parr's 1943 warning against museums as exotica merchants. Asma concludes that spectacle can lead to reflection or to more spectacle, and that the frozen state of taxidermy makes it both revealing and unsettling.

East and Southeast Asia Wallace's years in the East Indies run through this chapter. Asma holds a bird of paradise that Wallace caught and tagged, a specimen from New Guinea, and notes that Aru Islanders had removed the legs of skins sold to European traders. Asma recounts Wallace's tropical fever in Borneo and his argument that a deep channel between Bali and Lombok divided the Australian and Southeast Asian fauna. These are episodes in Wallace's collecting and theory, not studies of the regions themselves.

American Museum of Natural HistoryField MuseumPeter the Great's museumNatural History Museum, LondonNational Museum (Smithsonian)
2CHAPTER 2 Peter the Great’s Mysterious Jars: How to Pickle a Human Head and Other Great Achievements of the Scientific Revolution

Chapter 2 follows how human and animal specimens were preserved, from funeral embalming and the legal supply of corpses for dissection to the wet preparations that filled eighteenth-century museums. Asma starts at John Hunter's collection in the Hunterian Museum of the Royal College of Surgeons in London, where jars show a digested stomach, grafted teeth and tumors. Asma reviews the body-snatching trade and the British Anatomy Act of 1832, then compares mummies, wax models, Charles Willson Peale's Philadelphia museum and La Specola in Florence. Robert Boyle's 1660s method of preserving specimens in spirit of wine is the basis of the wet technique, which Hunter perfected with sealed jars. The core argument is that Hunter arranged his specimens by physiological function, not by aesthetic or moral categories, which marks the change from the curiosity cabinet to scientific display. The chapter ends with a boy's reaction to a two-headed fetus and a look ahead to taxonomy, since the arrangement itself carries the meaning of a collection.

Hunterian MuseumPeale's MuseumLa Specola
3CHAPTER 3 Taxonomic Intoxication, Part I: Visualizing the Invisible

Chapter 3 argues that a museum communicates through how it groups its objects, and that the groupings change with theories of nature. Asma works from two Paris collections: the Musée de la chasse et de la nature, a hunting club's museum in a former mansion, and Cuvier's Galerie d'anatomie comparée at the Jardin des plantes, with its skeletal 'stampede'. Asma traces classification from the law of noncontradiction through Ripa's Iconologia, where images carried fixed meanings, to the spiritual cabinets of Aldrovandi and Gesner. A key case is Dürer's rhinoceros, copied across Europe for centuries despite its invented second horn. Asma then turns to the seventeenth-century search for a natural system, with Ray's attempt to find essential characters, Locke's doubts about essences, and Ray's turn to adaptation as evidence of design. Asma closes with Pluche's view that the engine room of nature should stay closed to the public, an early form of the edutainment question.

East and Southeast Asia Asia appears only in passing. Asma describes Emmanuel Fremiet's 1898 marble of an orangutan strangling a Bornean man in the Galerie d'anatomie comparée, which he reads as an ominous entry sculpture rather than a record of the region. Asma also cites Borges's invented Chinese encyclopedia, with its absurd animal categories, as an example of how classification can seem arbitrary. Neither region is studied for its own sake.

Galerie d'anatomie comparéeMusée de la chasse et de la natureMuseum of Comparative Anatomy, HarvardField Museum
4CHAPTER 4 Taxonomic Intoxication, Part II. In Search of the Engine Room

Chapter 4 traces how naturalists moved from describing surfaces to explaining causes, and how that shift changed the arrangement of specimens in Paris and London. Asma begins with Linnaeus's binomial names and Aristotelian method, then the 1784 purchase of his collection by James Edward Smith, which founded the Linnean Society. Asma sets Buffon's view that nature is continuous and that classes are human conventions against Linnaeus's system, and reviews Lamarck's transformism and his invertebrate cabinet. The core comparison is between Cuvier's Galerie, where specimens are kept within vertebrate embranchements and fossils are housed apart from living forms, and Hunter's London cabinets, which group organs across species by function. Asma suggests that Hunter's arrangement carried the continuity that may have helped prepare Darwin's thinking, while Cuvier's held to a physiological order that excluded transformation. The chapter ends at the Grande Galerie de l'évolution, where Asma concludes that Darwin's Origin of Species in 1859 made homology and adaptation parts of one historical account.

Galerie d'anatomie comparéeHunterian MuseumLinnean SocietyGrande Galerie de l'évolution
5CHAPTER 5 Exhibiting Evolution: Diversity, Order, and the Construction of Nature

Asma compares how evolution is displayed in three museums: the Grande Galerie de l'évolution in Paris, the American Museum of Natural History in New York and the Natural History Museum in London, with the Field Museum in Chicago as a brief point of comparison. Before turning to the exhibits, he reviews Darwin's mechanism of variation, overproduction and natural selection, and argues that it is good science, using the evolution of human skin colour and vitamin D as the main example. The Paris gallery is organised around biodiversity and an immersive spectacle of life, with a moralised ecology floor and a display of mutation genetics that gives selection little room. The New York halls arrange specimens as cladograms, and Asma uses the debate between cladists, pheneticists and evolutionary taxonomists to explain the logic of that layout. London centres its displays on Darwin and natural selection. Asma then ties these emphases to national traditions, French internalism and empiricism in particular, and closes by arguing that classifications are relative to research goals yet still reflect real genealogy, so that museums construct nature rather than simply reveal it.

Grande Galerie de l'évolutionAmerican Museum of Natural HistoryNatural History Museum, LondonField MuseumMusée de l'hommeHunterian Museum
6CHAPTER 6 Evolution and the Roulette Wheel: A Chance Cosmos Rattles Some Bones

Asma uses the Field Museum's 'Life over Time' exhibit, especially its gambling 'Wheels of Adaptation' and craps table, to ask what metaphysics a natural history museum conveys. Asma starts from an angry visitor's letter calling chance-based evolution immoral, and from the talk-back boards where other visitors replied. Asma surveys religious responses to Darwinism, from young-earth creationism at a creationist museum near San Diego to 'installment creationism' and deism, and finds in them a shared demand for order and a rejection of reductionism. Asma then examines Gould's 'nonoverlapping magisteria' and the Pope's acceptance of evolution, arguing that facts and values cannot be cleanly separated. An interview with the exhibit developer Eric Gyllenhaal covers how the exhibit was built and how visitors were tested. Asma concludes that the chance-based message fits the evidence better than design, but that disputes over belief turn on what a belief does in a person's life and actions.

Field MuseumInstitute for Creation Research museumNatural History Museum, LondonGrande Galerie de l'évolutionBrookfield Zoo
7CHAPTER 7 Drama in Diorama: The Confederation of Art and Science

Asma argues that natural history museums work through feeling and association as well as text, so their dioramas, drawings and displays shape how visitors think. Asma opens with Akeley's taxidermy at the Field, the Hunters' muscle-man statue, and Jan Van Rymsdyk's anatomical drawings, whose Museum Britannicum he sets against John Hunter's systematic collecting. Asma then shows how images have decided disputes over human ancestry, notably the reconstructions of Dart's australopithecine and the Zinjanthropus portrait. Drawing on Locke, Hume and associationism, he calls exhibits 'intuition pumps' and discusses humour and self-mocking displays. The chapter ends with the sponsorship of the Field's T. rex 'Sue' by McDonald's, and a warning that museums must keep their autonomy from corporations and from popular surveys.

Barrett, Jennifer (2011). Museums and the Public Sphere. Chichester: Wiley-Blackwell.Asia: slight7 chapter overviews

Overview

Jennifer Barrett's Museums and the Public Sphere (2011) asks what 'public' means when museums invoke it to justify their claims on resources, and argues that museum studies has seldom examined the term critically. Its central argument is that museums are a cultural public sphere, part of the public sphere but limited by their ties to the state and to society, and that 'public' cannot be replaced by 'community', 'audience' or 'visitors' without risking appropriation. Chapters cover the Habermasian public sphere, the historical formation of the museum as a public institution, the museum as public space, visitor studies, and the curator as public intellectual. The scope is mainly the museums of Europe, North America and Australia, with Habermas's theory and Anglophone museum studies as its frame.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia receive slight attention. No chapter is devoted to the region, and Southeast Asia is not discussed at all. In Chapter 3 (The Museum as Public Space) there are two passing references. Barrett quotes Malraux on Chinese painting, which was owned and unfurled for private contemplation rather than exhibited, to show how alien public display is to such objects. Barrett also notes that Taiwan, as a newly industrialising country, developed its museums only recently (citing Chang, 2006).

In the Conclusion (Chapter 7), the 'Museum Futures' section expects more museums in China and the Arabian oil states. It cites M+ (Museum Plus), the complex planned on reclaimed land in West Kowloon, Hong Kong, as an example of newly powerful states displaying power through museums, and notes that earlier plans for branches of universal survey museums were dropped after public pressure in favour of a locally driven process. Barrett also expects repatriation claims by European, British and American universal survey museums to be contested against state-backed museums in the People's Republic of China. Tokyo National Museum appears only in the caption to a Thomas Struth photograph of museum visitors, which is listed among the images and reproduced in the Conclusion.

Not covered: Japanese, Korean and Southeast Asian collecting, colonial display, and Asian visitors, curators or scholars. The book's case material is British, French, American and Australian. Hong Kong appears in the acknowledgments only as a place where the author has taught museum studies.
