Contents

Theoretical approach of this work
List of Imagesp. vii
Introductionp. 1

Barrett opens by asking what 'public' means when museums invoke it to justify their claims on resources, and she argues that museum studies rarely examines the term critically. The introduction traces the 'new museology' of the late twentieth century, which answered funding cuts and charges of elitism by stressing visitors, thematic display and community consultation, and it reads that shift through Bourdieu's research on how class shaped museum visiting. Barrett then distinguishes public, private, civil society and public space, drawing on Habermas, Keane, Sennett and Fraser, and argues that museums are themselves sites of public address that the literature has overlooked. A summary of the five chapters follows: the public sphere, the historical development of the museum, the museum as public space, visitor studies, and the curator as public intellectual. Barrett concludes that museums are a form of public space and part of the public sphere, but they fall short of unrealistic expectations because of their ties to the state and society, and she proposes that 'community', 'public' and 'public sphere' be understood more precisely.

1The Public Spherep. 15

Barrett examines the term 'public' through Jürgen Habermas's The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere, which she notes is the work most often cited when museum studies invokes the public. Barrett argues that Habermas defines the bourgeois public sphere through literary discourse, coffee houses, salons and the print media, and gives little attention to the spaces and visual culture where publics appear. The chapter reconstructs his account of a sphere between state and private life, then sets out the critiques of Nancy Fraser, Seyla Benhabib, Thomas McCarthy, Mary Ryan, Joan Landes and Geoff Eley, who argue that his demands for reason and decorum exclude women, workers and rival counter-publics. Barrett reads Habermas's remarks on art and aesthetic modernity, and uses Boilly's paintings of Paris cafés, David's Oath of the Horatii and Boullée's Newton cenotaph to argue that spatial and visual discourse is part of public life. The chapter ends by asking whether a museum can be genuinely public, open to all and democratic.

2Historical Discourses of the Museump. 45

Barrett traces how the museum came to be understood as public, moving from princely and merchant cabinets of curiosities to the institutions of the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Barrett argues that the opening of the Louvre in 1793 and the British Museum's origins in Sloane's collection mark a break with royal display, but that early public museums still addressed subjects rather than citizens. Drawing on Bennett and Hooper-Greenhill, she shows how nineteenth-century museums displayed imperial wealth to metropolitan crowds, how reformers such as Henry Cole wanted to draw the working classes away from the public house, and how Stanley Jevons doubted that turnstile counts measured any civilising effect. The chapter then follows the twentieth-century move to specialised and children's museums, using the Brooklyn Children's Museum and the universal survey ideal of the National Gallery in Washington, before turning to blockbuster exhibitions and the commercial pressures they bring. Barrett concludes that museums have been part of the public sphere from the start, but that their relation to the public has always been complex and open to debate.

LouvreBritish MuseumBrooklyn Children's MuseumNational Gallery (Washington, DC)
3The Museum as Public Spacep. 81

Barrett asks what makes a museum a public space, noting that the literature on public space concentrates on parks, squares and protest sites and rarely mentions museums. Barrett revisits the Athenian agora, whose citizenship excluded women, slaves and foreigners, and sets Mitchell's distinction between an abstract public sphere and material public space against Arendt and Zukin. Museums, she argues, act as spaces of memory and public address, as in the National Museum of Australia or the Lower East Side Tenement Museum, and she examines contested sites such as the British Museum with the Parthenon Sculptures and the Smithsonian's Enola Gay dispute. Drawing on Foucault's account of disciplinary space and heterotopias, she argues that the museum displays state power and also hosts publics that form within it. Malraux's 'museum without walls' and Hooper-Greenhill's 'post-museum', with its 'contact zones', are then set against the realities of online collections and community partnerships. Barrett warns that replacing 'public' with 'community' risks appropriation, and concludes that museums need reciprocity to avoid it.

East and Southeast Asia Asia gets only a short passage. Barrett quotes Malraux on Chinese painting, which was owned and unfurled for private contemplation rather than exhibited, to show how alien public display is to such objects. Barrett also notes that Taiwan, as a newly industrialising country, developed its museums only recently (Chang, 2006). Southeast Asia is not discussed.

British MuseumLouvreGuggenheim Museum BilbaoNational Museum of American History (Smithsonian)Musée du quai BranlyTe Papa Tongarewa
4Audience, Community, and Publicp. 118

Barrett asks why museums equate 'the public' with audience and how they define the people they serve. Australian multiculturalism policy serves as her example: each new category of inequity exposes the limits of the word 'public'. Bourdieu and Darbel's 1960s survey of European visitors, which found that class decided who felt at home, anchors the chapter, and Barrett weighs the critiques of Zolberg, Prior and Bennett. She then reviews visitor research, including segmentation, barrier analysis and visitor counts, and argues that its quantitative metrics reduce complexity and, under funding pressure, treat visitors as customers. Against this she sets 'embracing complexity' and case-study methods. Her central claim is that 'community' is no more democratic than 'public', since it too can be romanticised, and that alternative publics, such as Indigenous keeping places, are better understood through Fraser's counter-publics and Nancy's community without essence. The chapter concludes that museums remain open in rhetoric while cultural capital still determines who feels at home.

5The Museum as Public Intellectualp. 143

Barrett examines the museum professional and the museum as public intellectual, asking whether curators, long blamed for standing between museum and public, can still play that role. Barrett traces how the new museology and visitor studies displaced curators in favour of educators and managers, and how museum studies curricula followed. Three disciplines are then compared. Art curators are described mainly as project managers; social history is illustrated by the early years of the National Museum of Australia, where government policy and funding shaped the collection; and anthropology is treated through Shelton's critique of the visual white-cube displays at the Musée du Quai Branly and the former Museum of Mankind, set against the collaborative work of the National Museum of the American Indian and the Macleay Museums with indigenous communities. Drawing on Kreps's idea of appropriate museology, Barrett argues that curators are not inherently barriers and that their intellectual role needs more emphasis, not less. The chapter concludes that museums remain important spaces for the performance of the public sphere.

National Museum of AustraliaMacleay MuseumsMusée du Quai BranlyMuseum of MankindNational Museum of the American Indian
Conclusionp. 164

Barrett's conclusion draws the book together around its central claim that museums are a cultural public sphere, and that 'public' cannot be replaced by community, audience or visitors without risking appropriation. Barrett summarises each chapter, from the Habermasian public sphere and the historical formation of the museum as a public space, through the limits of visitor studies and the reconfigured curator, to the argument that aesthetics and visuality are themselves political forms of public address. Thomas Struth's photographs of viewers in museums are used to show that the museum has long been a place of public display. The final section, 'Museum Futures', anticipates more museums in the newly rich Arabian oil states and in China, contested repatriation claims, and the limits of social media as a remedy for museums' weak understanding of audiences. Barrett concludes that museums remain in a period of transition and that democracy, like the museum, is a process rather than a fixed thing, so museums will never be truly democratic without rethinking the basis of both.

East and Southeast Asia Barrett's Museum Futures section cites M+ (Museum Plus), the complex planned on reclaimed land in West Kowloon, Hong Kong, as an example of newly powerful states displaying power through museums; earlier plans for branches of universal survey museums were dropped after public pressure in favour of a locally driven process. Barrett also expects repatriation claims by European and American universal survey museums to be contested against powerful state-backed museums in the People's Republic of China. Tokyo National Museum appears only in the caption to a Thomas Struth photograph.

Bennett, Tony (1995). The Birth of the Museum: History, Theory, Politics. London: Routledge.Asia: slight10 chapter overviews

Overview

Bennett asks what the public museum is for and how it came into being. Bennett argues that it was formed in the nineteenth century as an instrument of liberal government, a means of regulating a population through culture and self-regulation rather than force. The museum is placed beside the fair and the international exhibition, which shared its techniques of display and its concern with conduct, and their relations are examined as parts of an 'exhibitionary complex'. Part I develops the theory through the museum's formation, its exhibitionary forms and its political rationality. Part II examines access, representation, the national past and art display in Britain and Australia. Part III treats museums, fairs and exhibitions as technologies of progress, with case studies of Expo '88 in Brisbane and Blackpool Pleasure Beach.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia receive slight attention, almost always as passing comparison. The most extended Asian material is in Chapter 8 on Expo '88, where Bennett notes that national pavilions were sorted into blocs by display technology: Japan, with Europe, North America and Australia, used advanced video and computer displays, while China, with Russia, still showed artefacts as in a nineteenth-century museum. He reads the Pacific Lagoon set between the American and Japanese pavilions, and a Fujitsu pavilion, as ranking devices rather than accounts of the countries themselves. Chapter 9 on Blackpool Pleasure Beach has two passing mentions: the River Caves, billed as exotic scenes from every culture in the world, and a replica of the temples of Angkor Wat in Cambodia, which the park's managing director said gave visitors the only chance to see them after the Khmer Rouge took over. Bennett reads this exoticism as tamed otherness, subordinated to the park's theme of modernity.

Chapter 2 gives nineteenth-century world exhibitions a more structural role. Bennett quotes the practice of grouping national pavilions by race, in which 'Oriental' was one of the favoured categories, and notes that Oriental civilisations were placed at an intermediate level, as once developed but degenerate, or as achievements judged inferior to Europe. The 1889 Paris exposition's colonial city, with Asian and African peoples in simulated 'native' villages, shows anthropology extended into the entertainment zones. Other references are slight: a Chinese lady's boot in Greenwood's list of disorderly provincial cabinets in the Introduction, Asian communities among the groups added to Australia's national history in Chapter 5, and Java in the War Memorial's entry court, which places Australia in an Empire-centred world.

No museum in East or Southeast Asia is studied, and the book does not address Asian collections in Western museums, colonial collecting in Asia, or restitution. Its Asian material concerns how exhibitions ranked and staged peoples, not how Asian states built their own museums. The Japanese heritage legislation appears only in a note.

Introductionp. 1

Bennett opens with Foucault's contrast between the museum and the fair, as places of accumulating time and of fleeting festival time, and argues that the two were defined against each other in the nineteenth century. Bennett shows the opposition breaking down: amusement parks and the Chicago Midway borrowed museum methods, and museums adopted fair crowd control. Using Greenwood's complaints about provincial museums, Murray's history of anatomical collections, and the National Museum of Victoria's wish to show small and ugly creatures, he traces how museums set themselves against the disorder of older collections. The book's three parts are previewed: the museum as a governmental technology for shaping visitors, the politics of representation and access, and the museum's role in technologies of progress. The introduction ends with Bennett's account of growing up with Lancashire fairs before he came to museums, which he presents as the motive for studying their similarities.

National Museum of VictoriaChicago Columbian Exhibition MidwayDresden anatomical collection
Part I History and theoryp. 15
11 The Formation of the Museump. 17

Bennett's first chapter argues that the public museum took shape in the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries as an instrument of government, a means of civilising the population through culture rather than force. Bennett traces this through Buckingham's model town, the rational recreation movement, Henry Cole's advocacy, and earlier police theory. Bennett then takes three issues in turn: how museums were opened to a mixed public and turned into exemplary spaces, with a gendered role for women and parallels to department stores; how display moved from curiosity cabinets and royal galleries, through the Louvre and the South Kensington programme, to evolutionary and representative arrangements; and how visitors were regulated through routes, watchers and self-policing, compared with the Tower of London and cathedrals. The chapter closes by arguing that museums and fairs came to share techniques for regulating their visitors.

LouvreSouth Kensington MuseumBethnal Green MuseumSir John Soane's MuseumTower of London armouries
22 The Exhibitionary Complexp. 59

Bennett's second chapter argues that in the nineteenth century art museums, history and natural history museums, panoramas, international exhibitions, arcades and department stores formed a single 'exhibitionary complex'. Setting it against Foucault's carceral system, he argues that these institutions opened objects and bodies to public view where prisons withdrew them. He traces this through the Great Exhibition of 1851, the Mechanics' Institute exhibitions, and the British Museum's long fear of the crowd, which gave way to the South Kensington Museum in 1857. He then shows how the fair zones of expositions, such as Chicago's Midway, were brought under official control, and how historical and evolutionary displays, including anthropological arrangements that placed non-white peoples at the origins of progress, built a representation of the world for a self-regulating public. The chapter ends by setting the museum's lessons of power against the penitentiary's punishments.

British MuseumSouth Kensington MuseumCrystal Palace (Great Exhibition of 1851)Pitt-Rivers MuseumMusee d'Ethnographie de Paris
33 The Political Rationality of the Museump. 89

Bennett's third chapter asks what political rationality the public museum embodies, using Foucault's account of the prison as a model. Bennett argues that demands for public access and for representational adequacy arise from a mismatch between the museum's democratic rhetoric and its actual work of reforming manners. Bennett then traces the museum's birth: collections that had been private and exclusive were opened to the public and arranged as evolutionary series presenting a universal order of things and peoples. Against Crimp's view that museums enclose like prisons, he argues that the two developed in opposite directions. Rules, emulation and galleries that let visitors watch one another regulated behaviour and set respectable visitors apart from the fairground crowd. The chapter ends by urging that museum politics focus on who takes part in showing, citing Australian Aboriginal control of displays, and on active use rather than passive instruction.

Pitt Rivers MuseumAltes MuseumMadame Tussaud's Chamber of HorrorsRipley's Believe It Or Not Museums
Part II Policies and politicsp. 107
44 Museums and 'the People'p. 109

Bennett asks whether the post-war turn in British museums towards the everyday lives and customs of non-elite groups has really given 'the people' a voice. Bennett argues that the open-air museum tradition, from Skansen onwards, tends to make working people a 'picturesque element', idealised and sentimentalised in ways that serve the dominant culture. Bennett’s main case is Beamish, the North of England Open Air Museum in County Durham, whose tape-slide introduction gives the region's history in the voice of a southern, authoritative narrator, and whose colliery, pit cottages and co-operative store present a people without politics, cut off from unions and suffrage campaigns and frozen at one moment of transition. Hyde Park Barracks in Sydney and the People's Palace in Glasgow come off better, because they tie everyday life to political traditions. Bennett concludes that how objects are displayed matters as much as which objects are shown, and that visitors should read such museums as lessons in ruling-class rhetoric rather than in regional history.

Beamish (North of England Open Air Museum)Hyde Park BarracksPeople's PalaceSkansenGreenfield VillageVictoria and Albert MuseumAustralian War Memorial
55 Out of Which Past?p. 128

Bennett argues that the meaning of a museum or historic site lies in the textual frame that presents it, not in its fidelity to the past. Opening with Borges's Pierre Menard, he shows that any preserved object becomes 'past' only through the present that organises it. He then traces how Australia built a national past after 1933, when a survey found almost no museum interest in post-settlement history. The Australian War Memorial made the digger its vehicle, and the Whitlam-era inquiries, the National Estate register and the planned Museum of Australia extended the nation back to 1788 by anchoring it in Aboriginal culture and explorers' voyages. The penal past, shown at Hyde Park Barracks and Port Arthur, and the tourist open-air museums Sovereign Hill, Timbertown and Old Sydney Town are, for Bennett, depoliticised and nostalgic, selling a rural past that disowns the economics behind it. He ends by urging a public past that cuts into national narratives rather than endorsing them.

Australian War MemorialHyde Park BarracksPort ArthurSovereign HillTimbertownOld Sydney TownMuseum of Australia (planned)
66 Art and Theory: The Politics of the Invisiblep. 163

Bennett argues that art museums sort their visitors into those who can and cannot see, because their displays point to an invisible realm of 'art' that only the trained recognise. Drawing on Bourdieu's account of the 'pure gaze' and on Bourdieu and Darbel's survey, he notes that working-class visitors welcome guidebooks and labels, while the cultivated classes resist them because such aids expose the learned basis of their privilege. Using Pomian's idea of semiophores, Bennett shows that all collecting institutions make an invisible order visible, and traces how Lenoir's Musée des monuments français and the chronological hang of London's National Gallery displayed the nation's progress, while late nineteenth-century provincial museums, with dense Baroque hangs and sparse labels, reinforced class distinction. Modernist display then made art itself the invisible. Bennett ends with feminist and ethnographic critiques that try to expose other invisibles, and argues that such interventions must teach the competences they assume, through schooling and didactics.

Musée des monuments françaisNational Gallery (London)LouvreBritish Museum
Part III Technologies of progressp. 175
77 Museums and Progress: Narrative, Ideology, Performancep. 177

Bennett argues that nineteenth-century museums were 'backtellers': narrative machines that arranged objects into evolutionary sequences and required visitors to walk those sequences as a route. Drawing on Huxley's account of Zadig's method and on Cuvier's reconstructions of extinct life, he shows how geology, palaeontology and archaeology made new pasts visible in museums, and how the visit became a bodily performance of progress. His examples include Parr's natural history plan, Pitt Rivers's anthropological rotunda and the typological displays at Bethnal Green, which Pitt Rivers designed as an automated pedagogy for working-class visitors. Bennett sets these against the flaneur's stroll and the colonial villages of world fairs. Bennett then argues that evolutionary narratives were tied to reformist social thought, so that only some visitors, notably white European men, could recognise themselves in them, while women and colonised peoples were placed behind. Anatomical displays at the Musee de l'Homme and Galton's measuring laboratory at South Kensington show this most clearly.

Bethnal Green MuseumSouth Kensington MuseumMusee de l'HommeMusee CarnavaletJardin des Plantes museum (Paris)
88 The Shaping of Things to Come: Expo '88p. 209

Bennett reads Expo '88 in Brisbane as an event that served its host city more than the nation, and as a training in modern conduct rather than a set of texts to read. Bennett argues that expositions keep time with the international rhythm of progress rather than the calendar of the nation, and that the Expo's theme of leisure in the age of technology and its motto addressed Queenslanders, who made repeat visits. Tracing the form back to the 1851 Great Exhibition, he shows how objects were displayed as stages in evolutionary series, and how Foucault's 'evolutive time' of discipline underlies the task of self-modernisation the Expo set its visitors. National pavilions and corporate displays, such as IBM's and Technoplaza, fused the time of the nation with that of modernity. Bennett also shows how fairs and amusement parks were absorbed into the civilising project of museums and parks, so that the orderly queues and strollers became a rehearsal of urban civility. Bennett concludes that the Expo prepared Brisbane for new consumption habits at the neighbouring Myer Centre.

East and Southeast Asia Bennett notes that Expo '88 sorted national pavilions into blocs by display technology: Japan sits with Europe, North America and Australia in using advanced video and computer displays, while China, with Russia, is placed among those still showing artefacts as in a nineteenth-century museum. Bennett also records that the Pacific Lagoon was set between the American and Japanese pavilions, and cites a Fujitsu pavilion as an example of corporate display, reading these as ranking devices rather than accounts of the countries themselves.

Expo '88 (Brisbane World Expo)Queensland Cultural CentreSouth Kensington MuseumNational Museum of VictoriaGreat Exhibition of 1851 (Crystal Palace)
99 A Thousand and One Troubles: Blackpool Pleasure Beachp. 229

Bennett treats Blackpool Pleasure Beach as a 'regime of pleasure' that dresses itself in the signs of modernity, progress and the future. Bennett traces its origins from a gypsy encampment and the mechanical rides of Blackpool's South Shore, through its 1895 purchase by two local entrepreneurs and the 1907-10 campaign that banned clairvoyance and quack medicine and evicted the gypsy families in the name of respectability. Blackpool's fragmented land tenure, he argues, let commercial interests cater for working-class visitors, and the Golden Mile grew up outside the park's walls. The 1930s remodelling by the modernist architect Joseph Emberton, and later borrowings from world fairs, complete the picture. Bennett then classifies the rides and shows how they address the body, inverting its normal relations with machinery in thrill rides, the Fun House and self-drive cars. Bennett rejects a reading of the park as Bakhtinian carnival, since its dominant order stays intact, and ends by stressing that visiting groups negotiate its pleasures on their own terms.

East and Southeast Asia Bennett notes the River Caves, billed as 'exotic scenes from every culture in the world', and quotes the Pleasure Beach's managing director on a replica of the temples of Angkor Wat in Cambodia, which he said offered visitors the only chance to see them after the Khmer Rouge took over. Bennett treats such exoticism as an assimilated, tamed otherness, subordinated to the park's theme of modernity.

Bilsel, Can (2012). Antiquity on Display: Regimes of the Authentic in Berlin’s Pergamon Museum. Oxford: Oxford University Press.Asia: slight7 chapter overviews

Overview

Bilsel's study of the Pergamon Museum on Berlin's Museum Island is a critical biography of its rooms rather than a full institutional history. It asks how and when the authentic came to matter in museum display: how the Great Altar of Pergamon, the Miletus Market Gate and the Babylonian Ishtar Gate were rebuilt from fragments excavated for the Prussian state between 1878 and 1918, and why the reconstructions were later treated as ancient monuments. The main argument is that the museum's architectural frame became the exhibit, and that modern practices of archaeology, museology and preservation turned monuments into objects of a 'regime of the authentic'. The book runs chronologically from Schinkel's and Stüler's early buildings through the Pergamon and Babylon displays, Bode's style rooms and the Berlin Museum War of the 1920s, to an epilogue on authenticity.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East Asia is a secondary theme, concentrated in chapter 3, 'A Museum for the Empire: The Problem of Style', and in the Museum War passages of chapter 5, 'Architecture in the Museum: Monuments for a Mass Spectacle'. In chapter 3 Bilsel shows Wilhelm von Bode founding an East Asian Art department in 1906, alongside Near Eastern (1899) and Islamic (1904) departments. From about 1880 Chinese and Islamic artefacts were placed in Berlin's ethnological collections, and Richard Schöne's wish to keep ethnology out of the art museum is part of the dispute over that classification. A note records that Bode commissioned an Asian Art Museum from the architect Paul Bruno, outside the Museum Island, to house ancient Chinese and Japanese art together with Islamic art; it was abandoned under the Weimar Republic when Theodor Wiegand's 'museum of ancient architecture' took the limited funds. In Bilsel's reading Bode's German Museum stands beside the East Asian and Islamic museums as part of a cross-cultural idea of art, in which a Chinese bronze could embody authentic art as much as German work.

In chapter 5 the same project returns in Karl Scheffler's Berliner Museumskrieg (1921), which Bilsel reads as a defence of Bode's programme. Scheffler insists that masterpieces of the courtly traditions of East Asia and the Middle East must be separated from the ethnological objects of 'primitive' peoples, and Bilsel notes that Wiegand defeated the Asian museum plan. Southeast Asia is almost absent: the only mention is that the Dutch East Indies sent a colonial delegation to the 1931 Athens Conference on monuments, in the epilogue. The book does not treat colonial collecting from East or Southeast Asia, Asian visitors or scholars, or restitution claims, and the Asian material it does discuss is held in Berlin rather than in Asia. Its colonial concern is the Ottoman Empire, Mesopotamia and the Mediterranean, which fall outside this question.

Introductionp. 1

Bilsel opens with the Pergamon Room in Berlin's Pergamon Museum, where a reconstructed west facade of the Great Altar of Pergamon and its Gigantomachy frieze make visitors feel they are inside an ancient building, though the room is a modern interior. Bilsel analyzes the pairing of original frieze with plaster copies, and the Miletus and Babylon gates, to argue that the museum reverses the usual relation between artwork and frame so that architecture becomes the exhibit. Bilsel’s method is historical: he traces these displays back through German excavations in the Ottoman Empire after 1871, the imperial ambitions of the Kaiserreich, and the Prussian museum reforms, and he rejects both post-Orientalist critique and reception history as frameworks. The Introduction closes by previewing the five chapters and the epilogue on the regimes of the authentic, and presents the book as a critical biography of the museum's spaces rather than a complete history.

Pergamon Museum
1No Place Like Greece: Berlin's Museum Island and the Architectures of Historyp. 29

Bilsel examines how Berlin's Museum Island was built and how its early museums framed antiquity for Prussian audiences. Bilsel starts with Schinkel's painting A View of Greece in its Prime (1824-25), which he reads as a theatrical decor that projects an ideal Greek community onto the modern museum, and he shows how its quotations from the Parthenon and the Ionic order draw on British publications. Bilsel then follows the Napoleonic removal of antiquities from Rome and the British purchase of the Parthenon marbles, which turned antiquities into contested national property. The bulk of the chapter analyzes Schinkel's Altes Museum, with its Ionic facade and rotunda, the aesthetic arrangements favored by Humboldt and Waagen, Schinkel's unbuilt palace on the Acropolis, and Stuler's Neues Museum, whose staircase imagery follows Hegelian and Schellingian models of history. Bilsel concludes that the Neues Museum builds history as a tower culminating in a Christian monarchy, a project that later gave way to a view of history as a tree.

Altes MuseumNeues MuseumBritish MuseumLouvre
2Reconstructing Pergamon: Antique Fragments, Modern Visionsp. 89

Bilsel follows the Great Altar of Pergamon from Carl Humann's excavation at Bergama to its reconstruction in Berlin, asking how far its Hellenistic sculpture belongs to the Greek classical tradition. Bilsel retells the 1879 discovery of the Zeus group as a quasi-mythic moment that later served a national story of German pioneering, and shows how the frieze's painterly forms prompted rival theories of style, from Conze and von Brunn to the 'Hellenistic baroque' label of Salis. Bilsel then turns to Hildebrand's Problem of Form, which he uses to test how relief should be framed. The display history runs through the 1886 Pergamon Panorama, Pontremoli's French restorations, and Wolff's first Pergamon Museum of 1901, which housed the frieze inside a neoclassical shell and was demolished in 1908. Bilsel concludes that the museum's successive frames turned the altar into a realist double that dissolves the boundary between pictorial and architectural space, failing Hildebrand's criteria of high art.

Pergamon MuseumAltes Museum
3A Museum for the Empire: The Problem of Stylep. 125

This chapter traces how the Pergamon Museum on Berlin's Museum Island was designed, through the collaboration of the curator Wilhelm von Bode and the architect Alfred Messel. Bilsel shows how the German academic split between classical philology and Orientalistik was blurred by new excavations at Pergamon, Miletus and Babylon, and how Bode's plans for Near Eastern, Antiquity and German museums challenged those categories. Bilsel draws on the museum competitions of 1875 to 1884, Orth's urban master plan and Messel's 1907 designs, analysing the drawings and the style rooms they proposed. The chapter also examines Bode's support for Julius Langbehn's nationalist book Rembrandt als Erzieher, his dispute with the director Richard Schöne over moving ethnology out of the art museum, and his idea of a German Museum. It concludes that Messel's scheme mapped a geography of cultures rather than a linear history, and that Bode's style rooms set the museum's architecture against the works it housed.

East and Southeast Asia East Asia gets only a little attention. Bode founded an East Asian Art department in 1906, and when the Royal Museums first took in non-Western objects in the 1880s, Chinese and Islamic artefacts were placed in the ethnological collection, which Schöne wanted kept apart from the art museum. A note also records that Bode commissioned an Asian Art Museum from Paul Bruno, outside the Museum Island, to house ancient Chinese and Japanese art, a project that was later abandoned.

Pergamon MuseumKaiser Friedrich MuseumMuseum of Ethnology (Völkerkunde Museum), BerlinSouth Kensington Museum
4Reconstructing Babylon: The Return of the Archaicp. 159

This chapter examines how the Ishtar Gate and Processional Way of Babylon were reconstructed for the Near Eastern Art Museum, which opened in the Pergamon complex in 1930. Bilsel starts with the German Orient Society's excavations from 1899, which were driven by Friedrich Delitzsch's claim that the Old Testament derived from Babylonian sources, and by the Kaiser's support for him. Bilsel then turns to Koldewey and Andrae, who had no established method for Babylonian architecture and who reassembled glazed brick fragments guided by Romantic ideas of organic form and by Goethe's theory of colour. Place's and Thomas's Assyrian reconstructions, and Andrae's stage design for the Sardanapal play, serve as comparisons. The chapter also covers the hostile press response of 1930, Andrae's writings on ornament as a degraded symbol, and the fact that many lions were built from modern bricks mixed with ancient ones. It concludes that the Babylon room is a modern assemblage that displaces any original rather than a faithful copy.

Near Eastern Art Museum, BerlinPergamon MuseumIstanbul Archaeology MuseumBaghdad Museum
5Architecture in the Museum: Monuments for a Mass Spectaclep. 189

This chapter follows the completion of the Pergamon Museum after Messel's death in 1909, when Ludwig Hoffmann, Wilhelm Wille and then the archaeologist Theodor Wiegand reshaped the building. Bilsel shows that Hoffmann simplified and neoclassicised Messel's interiors, that Wille's proposal to restore the Great Altar to its full plan was rejected, and that Wiegand prevailed with a display meant to recapture the theatrical experience of the ancients. The chapter examines the Berlin 'Museum War' of the 1920s, in which Karl Scheffler and Paul Schmidt attacked the reconstructions as plaster fakes and kitsch, and it describes the full-scale mock-ups and photographs used during construction. Bilsel argues that Wiegand's Market Gate of Miletus was a composite pastiche built from utilitarian fragments, and that the museum's mass popularity, including its appeal to the Nazi regime, rested on a cult of authenticity. The chapter ends by calling the Pergamon display a reproduction without an original.

East and Southeast Asia East Asia appears only in passing. Bode's planned Asian Art Museum at Dahlem was dropped in the 1920s when Wiegand's 'museum of ancient architecture' took the limited funds of the Weimar Republic. Scheffler, writing in 1921, insists that masterpieces of the courtly traditions of East Asia and the Middle East must be separated from the ethnological objects of 'primitive' peoples.

Pergamon MuseumBerlin Antiquity Collection
Epilogue: Regimes of the Authenticp. 215

The epilogue asks what makes an ancient monument authentic, and who decides. Bilsel traces the word from the classical 'authority' of Millin and Quatremère de Quincy, through Viollet-le-Duc's typological restoration and Riegl's 1903 cult of age value, to the bureaucratic practices that followed. Bilsel reads the 1931 Athens Conference and the French system of classement as the point at which monuments became unique, territorial and historical, and he examines how Balanos reassembled the Acropolis. The Pergamon Museum serves as a comparison, and Bilsel also discusses the Pergamon Room after its 1945 bombing and Struth's and Wrba's photographs of visitors. The chapter concludes that authenticity was produced by modern frames such as the museum and the photograph, rather than discovered in the monument, and that the crowds in the Pergamon Room now dissolve the architectural illusion.

Black, Barbara J. (2000). On Exhibit: Victorians and Their Museums. Charlottesville: University Press of Virginia.Asia: slight9 chapter overviews

Overview

On Exhibit: Victorians and Their Museums (2000) argues that the nineteenth century gave birth to the modern museum, tied to imperialism, mass education and fear of the mob, and that the museum's logic of gathering and ordering spread into homes, novels, poems and boys' fiction. The scope is London, from Soane's house-museum (1837) to Freud's study (1938), with the Great Exhibition and the South Kensington Museum as the main institutions. After an introduction and a chapter on London's museum spectacles, the chapters are literary case studies (FitzGerald's Rubaiyat, Soane's house, novels of the museum as meeting place, poems about acquisition, boys' adventure fiction, fiction of the museum in decline), closing with a coda on Freud's study. Its sources are chiefly novels, poems and advice manuals, read as museum texts.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia figure only in passing, and no chapter is concentrated on them. Southeast Asia does not appear in the text at all. The Introduction quotes Henry Cole and Monkure Conway on the value of collections for trade with India and the East and on England's appreciation of 'the Oriental world', and Chapter I (The Museum Crowd) mentions a Chinese foot distorted by binding, set against the foot of the Venus de Medici in Thomas Laurie's display of the human body.

The fullest passages are in Chapter II (Fugitive Articulation, on Edward FitzGerald). Its interest is FitzGerald's taste rather than China: he bought in the new Chinese Department of the Baker Street Bazaar in 1862 and wrote of wanting 'samples of China, Greece, Italy, etc., all mixed' in his room. Chapter III (Acquired Taste) lists the 42 Chinese ceramics in Soane's house-museum, quotes the importer Phillips and Company's trade in the faience and art manufactures of Japan, China and India, and cites Eastlake's Japanese fan as a lesson in design. Chapter VI (An Empire's Great Expectations) mentions Manchuria only as the place to which the father in Nesbit's The Story of the Amulet is sent on imperial business. The Coda (In Freud's Study) notes Freud's Asian artefacts among his antiquities, and H. D.'s reference to his 'Greek, Egyptian, and Chinese treasures'. Kim's Tibetan objects and the Lahore Museum belong to India, which is outside this question.

What is not covered is striking: Asian museums, Asian states' heritage policy, Asian visitors and curators, colonial collecting in Asia, and restitution claims are all absent. The Asian material is the goods of the British home and the Western collector's shelf, bought through bazaars, shops and department stores.

Acknowledgmentsp. vii
Introductionp. 1

Black opens his study of Victorian museums by arguing that the nineteenth century was an age of builders, and that the civic museum was its greatest constructive project. Black takes three texts as starting points: the official catalogue of the Great Exhibition of 1851, Robert Kerr's The English Gentleman's House, and Doré and Jerrold's London: A Pilgrimage (1872), whose list of London's museums he quotes at length. Black reads these as expressions of a museum culture in which the museum became a model for homes, novels, collections and science, and he cites Taine's view that museums showed a well-run, controlled society. Black sets out his scope: London's museums from Sir John Soane's house-museum (1837) to Freud's study (1938), with the Natural History Museum and South Kensington as the main institutions. Black’s central claim is that the nineteenth century gave birth to the modern museum, tied to imperialism, mass education and fear of the mob, with the Great Exhibition as its prototype. The introduction ends with a jumble of voices calling the museum a whorehouse, a mausoleum and a secular cathedral, which he presents as the source of its ambiguity.

Great Exhibition of 1851South Kensington MuseumBritish MuseumNatural History MuseumSir John Soane's Museum
IThe Museum Crowd: Fragments Shored against Their Ruinp. 21

Black opens his study of Victorian museum culture with a set of London spectacles: the Iguanodon dinner of 1853 held inside a dinosaur reconstruction at Sydenham, the Whale-bone Lounge at Charing Cross, and James Wyld's seventy-foot globe in Leicester Square. Black reads all three as versions of the museum, which, like them, builds wholes from fragments and places the viewer at the centre of a world made knowable. The chapter then turns to the South Kensington Museum, whose discarded parts were rebuilt as the Bethnal Green branch in East London, and to Thomas Laurie's display of the human body. Drawing on Foucault's heterotopia and on Baudrillard, Nietzsche, Valéry and Adorno, Black presents the museum as both a mausoleum and an instrument of national belonging. It ends by insisting that the museum's paradoxes of inclusion and exclusion, optimism and despair, call for both skepticism and enthusiasm.

Crystal PalaceNatural History MuseumWyld's Great GlobeSouth Kensington MuseumBethnal Green Museum
IIFugitive Articulation of an All-Obliterated Tongue: Edward FitzGerald's Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam and the Politics of Collectingp. 48

Black's chapter reads Edward FitzGerald's translation of the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam as a product of Victorian collecting. It opens by setting aside the standard explanations for the poem's popularity, its late-Victorian decadence and resignation, and argues that they miss the collector's appetite that FitzGerald shared with his age. Black draws on FitzGerald's letters, which record his purchases, his visits to galleries and the Crystal Palace, and his crowded house at Little Grange, to show a man who wanted exotic things at home. The chapter then examines how FitzGerald cut, condensed and reshaped Khayyam's quatrains into a narrative with a single theme, removing the bawdy and the boy-love and turning the verses into an English garden. It traces the poem's publication history, the Fitz-Omar craze and the Omar Khayyam Clubs, and ends by reading the translation as a domesticated, dispossessed text, an unhomely text that remains fugitive.

East and Southeast Asia FitzGerald's collecting took in Chinese goods as well as Persian: he bought a heap of things in the new Chinese Department of the Baker Street Bazaar in 1862, praised Oriental things for their quaint shapes and scents, and wrote of wanting samples of China, Greece and Italy mixed in his little room. These passages concern his taste for the exotic at home rather than China itself.

IIIAcquired Taste: The Museum Enterprise Comes Homep. 67

Black follows the museum out of the gallery and into the home. It opens with John Soane's house-museum at Lincoln's Inn Fields, which Soane secured as a national trust through Parliament in 1833, and reads his catalogues as the work of a self-made collector who used his objects to build an identity and a civic purpose. Advice manuals by Haweis, Eastlake, Cook and Loftie then urge middle-class families to form private museums, and the chapter shows how such collecting was also expected to improve working-class homes. Its main argument is carried by three novels: Brontë's Jane Eyre, where Thornfield's collected colonial past must fall; Gosse's Father and Son, a boy's claustrophobic childhood among his father's specimens; and Dickens's Our Mutual Friend, where Mr. Venus's shop of articulated skeletons turns collecting into a restorative force. The chapter ends by returning to Soane, whose wasps' nest image shows that collection is driven by anxiety about loss.

Sir John Soane's Museum
IVA Gallery of Readings: Rendezvous in the Museump. 100

Black argues that the Victorian museum was above all a place to meet. The chapter traces how Soane's house-museum admitted the public after his death and how Henry Cole's South Kensington Museum, with its evening hours, gas lighting, refreshment halls and cheap guidebooks, drew hundreds of thousands of visitors a year, while the British Museum resisted. Officials treated the crowd as a problem of decorum, and the museum taught visitors how to behave and how to look. Black then reads four novels as galleries of rendezvous: in Villette, Lucy Snowe's revisionary criticism of a Cleopatra painting resists the museum; in Middlemarch, Dorothea's visit to the Vatican shows her unease with the collected past; in Maurice, a blackmail meeting in the British Museum becomes a break from class and Hellenism; and in James's The American, the Louvre is the stage for social ambition. Museums and novels alike order a profusion of things, and both are concerned with who belongs.

Sir John Soane's MuseumSouth Kensington MuseumBritish MuseumVatican MuseumLouvreNatural History Museum
V"The Works on the Wall Must Take Their Chance": A Poetics of Acquisitionp. 127

Black examines poems about museums and argues that the museum changed what poetry could do with art. It opens with Tennyson's The Palace of Art, read as an allegory for the birth of the public museum, in which the aristocrat's house is unlocked for the people, and traces how Hazlitt's writing on the Louvre and the National Gallery registered that transfer of art into public hands. Black then defines the museum poem against ut pictura poesis and pictorialism: a poem that places art among other objects in a crowded, commercial and political setting. Keats's sonnets on the Elgin Marbles, Hardy's In the British Museum and Christmas in the Elgin Room, and Browning's A Likeness are read as poems about acquisition. Rossetti's The Burden of Nineveh, set at the British Museum, is the chapter's climax: a British collection holds a god taken from Nineveh and turns the bull into a relic of London. The chapter closes with the twentieth-century museum poem, from Auden to Ashbery.

British MuseumLouvreNational Gallery
VIAn Empire's Great Expectations: Museums in Imperialist Boy Fictionp. 148

Black reads museums as a central device of late-Victorian boys' adventure fiction, arguing that these stories taught young readers to see collecting as a patriotic duty. The chapter opens with real explorers such as Belzoni, Layard and Speke, whose travels became museum collections and best-selling narratives, and turns to Indiana Jones's insistence that a cross belongs in a museum, which Black treats as the modern survival of the same fantasy. Kipling's Kim is read at length: the Lahore Museum, or Wonder House, is a government front where a lama and a boy are watched, catalogued and recruited, a utopia of surveillance and benevolent rule. Nesbit's The Story of the Amulet, which opens near the British Museum, is read as a more ambivalent work in which the museum's collectibles fight back. The chapter ends with accounts of why people collect, from Jameson to Baudrillard, and with the claim that the museum's fantasy still shapes modern dreams.

Lahore MuseumBritish MuseumSouth Kensington MuseumCrystal PalaceNatural History Museum
VIIA Gallery of Readings: The Museum in Declinep. 167

Black turns to the museum in ruin, arguing that late-Victorian and Edwardian novels treat it as a diagnosis of a society that has lived too long and too well. The chapter opens with Morris's News from Nowhere, where the British Museum has become a home for an old antiquarian and the National Gallery is a curiosity few understand. It then reads Galsworthy's The Man of Property, in which Soames Forsyte turns his house and his collecting into a prison for his wife, and Wells's The Time Machine, where the Palace of Green Porcelain is a derelict museum that the Morlocks plunder and the Eloi neglect. Wells's The Croquet Player is read as a museal gothic in which a human skull in a museum forces the narrator to face the brute within. The chapter ends with Morris's Old Hammond, whose museum work keeps historical memory alive, and with the claim that these fictions of loss place the museum at the centre of a crisis about inheritance.

British MuseumNational GalleryPalace of Green Porcelain
Coda: In Freud's Studyp. 186

This coda returns to Sigmund Freud's study at 20 Maresfield Gardens in London, a public museum since 1986, to test the book's arguments about museum culture on a single collection-filled room. Black reads the dense arrangement of antiquities as an emblem of Freud's wish to reassemble fragments into wholes, and traces how his collection was moved from Vienna in 1938 amid fears of Nazi appropriation. Freud's archaeological analogies, from Schliemann to the excavated Rome of Civilization and Its Discontents, and his 1915 image of prewar Europe as a museum are set beside this. The main evidence is H. D.'s Tribute to Freud, which shows the collection structuring power between analyst and patient. Black also faults the 1989 traveling exhibition, which isolated sixty-seven objects in vitrines and lost that context. The chapter ends by linking the study to earlier chapters, arguing that museums are monuments to imperial and commercial power and memorials to loss.

Freud Museum, LondonSigmund Freud Antiquities (1989 traveling exhibition)

Çelik, Zeynep (2016). About Antiquities: Politics of Archaeology in the Ottoman Empire. Austin: University of Texas Press.Asia: slight8 chapter overviews

Overview

Zeynep Çelik’s About Antiquities (2016) traces the history of archaeology in the Ottoman Empire from the 1880s to 1914, centred on the Imperial Museum in Istanbul and, for comparison, the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. Its argument is that antiquities became entangled with empire, rivalry, national identity and money, and that the archaeologists’ records must be read against the grain to recover the workers and local people. Six chapters move from the two museums’ missions, through European reception of the Sidon sarcophagi and the museum’s visitors, to Ottoman periodicals, the excavation labour force and the dual settlements at Palmyra, Sardis and Nippur. The epilogue links these nineteenth-century politics to present restitution disputes, above all Turkey’s claims.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia are barely present. The book’s subject is Ottoman archaeology and the Imperial Museum in Istanbul, set beside the Metropolitan in New York, with the Middle East and Anatolia at its centre. Its one sustained Asian thread is the Metropolitan’s collections: in chapter 3 the museum’s publication programme is compared with Istanbul’s, and the catalogue of the Morgan Collection of Chinese Porcelains (1907 and 1913) is named beside its catalogues of European arms and Cypriot antiquities (lines 3014-3016).

Other references are passing. Chapter 3 notes the Metropolitan’s catalogue of Oriental rugs (1910), described only as a guide to their dates, regions and patterns. Chapter 5 cites an 1825 children’s book that lists the Great Wall of China among the wonders of the world (line 5565). In the epilogue, China and Cambodia are named among the “source” countries that demand the return of antiquities from Western museums (lines 6472-6473), and China appears with the Greek, Iraqi, Peruvian and Turkish states as a “modern national state” that has politicised its antiquities (line 6509).

No Japanese, Korean, Philippine, Indonesian, Vietnamese or other Southeast Asian museum, collection, collector, official or visitor is discussed, and the book does not treat the museum-building or heritage policy of any Asian state. The Orientalist vocabulary it analyses concerns the Ottoman and Middle Eastern world, which lies outside the question.

Theoretical approach of this work
Acknowledgmentsp. ix
Author's Note on Names, Dates, and Measurementsp. xi
Introductionp. 1

Çelik's Introduction sets out the book's scope: a history of archaeology in the Ottoman Empire from the 1880s to 1914, centred on the Imperial Museum in Istanbul and, for comparison, the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. It argues that antiquities became entangled with empire, rivalry, national identity and money, and that the history of the discipline admits many versions. The book builds on Scramble for the Past, which Çelik co-edited, and extends Çelik's earlier study of French and Ottoman architecture; the chapter then reviews recent work on Western archaeologists, Ottoman officials and labor. It previews the six chapters: the two museums' agendas, the reception of the Sidon sarcophagi, the Istanbul museum's public, periodical coverage, excavation labor and residential landscapes at Palmyra. It closes by admitting gaps in the sources, notably the lack of visitor numbers, Ottoman supervisors' reports and women's accounts, and concludes that workers' voices can be recovered only by reading archaeologists' records against the grain.

Imperial Museum, IstanbulMetropolitan Museum of Art
oneBeginnings: The Nineteenth-Century Museump. 13

Chapter 1 compares the Imperial Museum in Istanbul with the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, two institutions that were newcomers on the margins of established European museums. It opens with a 1912 rumor that the Ottoman state would sell the Istanbul collection to J. P. Morgan, and shows the rumor was baseless: the 1906 antiquities law had strengthened the museum, which kept expanding under Osman Hamdi. The chapter then contrasts the two missions: the Metropolitan as a private, democratic institution on public land in Central Park, the Imperial Museum as a state project tied to antiquities legislation and to Osman Hamdi's personal control. Çelik draws on New York Times and Ottoman press coverage of the Sidon sarcophagi and on the buildings' growth. Later sections set the Louvre, the British Museum and the Berlin museums beside the two, then trace the Istanbul museum's walled site in the Topkapı gardens, its tram access and the new Gülhane park. Çelik concludes that the museum was a secluded elite institution that made no visible contribution to the city's image.

Imperial Museum, IstanbulMetropolitan Museum of ArtLouvreBritish MuseumBerlin Museum Island
twoScholarship and the Imperial Museump. 43

Chapter 2 examines how Western scholars reacted to the Imperial Museum and how its best-known objects, the Sidon sarcophagi, entered debates on Greek art. The first part sets out the hostility of Reinach, Bent and others to the Ottoman antiquities laws of 1874 and 1884, alongside defenders such as Max Müller who accepted local museums. The second part follows the sarcophagi, excavated by Osman Hamdi and shown from 1891, through arguments over polychromy and over whether the Alexander sarcophagus was pure Greek or already decadent. Çelik then turns to the Ottoman press, from Servet-i Fünun to a photomontage in Malumat, and to Mehmed Vahid's full study of the sarcophagi in Turkish. A section on Strzygowski shows how Palmyra and Baalbek were cast as Oriental decline. The last section describes exchanges of casts, objects and excavation permits linking the Istanbul museum with the University of Pennsylvania and other institutions. Çelik concludes that knowledge was produced collaboratively, though the terms were set by Ottoman ownership.

Imperial Museum, IstanbulUniversity of Pennsylvania MuseumBritish MuseumLouvre
threeThe Imperial Museum and Its Visitorsp. 65

Chapter 3 asks who visited the Imperial Museum in Istanbul and how the museum tried to reach them, comparing it throughout with the Metropolitan in New York. It opens with three novels by Zola, Wharton and Kemal Tahir, which use the Louvre, the Metropolitan and the Istanbul museum as settings for characters seeking refuge. It then turns to foreign visitors as seen in travel accounts, photograph albums, public lectures and guidebooks by Murray, Baedeker and Macmillan, which lead tourists to the Sidon sarcophagi and the Çinili Köşk. Catalogues by Goold, Joubin, Mendel and Halil Edhem show the museum's publishing ambitions, which Çelik sets against the Metropolitan's far larger output. The last sections consider the local public: few residents visited before 1914, school groups became the main local users, and the Turkish catalogues and visiting rules responded to them. Çelik concludes that the Imperial Museum addressed foreign scholars first and grew into education only slowly, whereas the Metropolitan was founded with public education and Sunday opening as priorities.

Imperial Museum, IstanbulMetropolitan Museum of ArtLouvre
fourThe Ottoman Reading Public and Antiquitiesp. 95

Chapter 4 reads the late Ottoman periodicals, above all Servet-i Fünun and Şehbal, to show how they presented antiquities to readers. Articles gave thin historical background but vivid descriptions of Palmyra, Baalbek, Gerasa, Miletus and Sardis, often with reconstruction drawings and travel tips that invited readers to visit. Reports on foreign finds and European museums follow, notably Ahmed İhsan's travelogue on the Louvre and the British Museum, which offers little judgment. Halil Edhem and Mukbil Kemal then document the neglect and looting of Ottoman and Islamic monuments in Konya, Gebze and Aleppo, and praise the Museum of Pious Foundations as a remedy. The final section compares Byron's Sardanapalus with Abdülhak Hamid's play, showing how both drew on Layard's Nineveh and on theatrical sets. Çelik concludes that the Ottoman public was taught to value antiquity as part of modernity, although the play's readers were few.

Imperial Museum, IstanbulBritish MuseumLouvreMuseum of Pious Foundations, IstanbulAltes Museum, Berlin
fiveThe Landscape of Laborp. 135

Chapter 5 turns to the workers who dug the sites, a labor force that Çelik says histories of archaeology have largely left out. Using excavation records from Cesnola, Layard, Wood, Peters, Hilprecht, Osman Hamdi and Butler, it tracks numbers, wages, gang structures and, occasionally, the names of foremen. The chapter then shows how the Ottoman laws placed foreign teams under the watch of officials, kaymakams and gendarmes, shifting the hierarchy on site. Çelik examines the rails, carts and tools used at Sardis and Babylon, and then the Orientalist language in which Layard, Rassam, Peters and Hilprecht describe local people, dress and women. The concluding section reads these records against the grain, showing that workers left at harvest time, that crowds joined the Sidon excavations, and that local women collected beads from graves. Çelik concludes that the workers effectively set the length of the season, and that historians must take the risk of reading these records against the grain to recover their perspective.

Imperial Museum, IstanbulMetropolitan Museum of ArtBritish Museum
sixDual Settlementsp. 175

Çelik examines the settlements that grew up around archaeological excavations in the late Ottoman lands, and the duality between the expeditions' own quarters and the workers' villages. The chapter argues that this separation repeated the pattern of colonial cities. It works through three sites. At Palmyra, travelers and photographers recorded a village living among the ruins, whose residents treated the antiquities as part of their everyday economy. At Sardis, the American team built a comfortable compound and a field house, in a proto-regionalist style from local materials, that dominated the valley below. At Nippur, the University of Pennsylvania expedition built a fortified Castle and, beside it, a workers' village that Haynes and Meyer documented in photographs, sketches, diaries and notes on music. Çelik concludes by asking how the villagers saw the foreigners, questions the sources cannot answer.

University of Pennsylvania Museum
Epilogue: Enduring Dilemmasp. 215

Çelik closes the book by setting recent restitution disputes against the debates of the nineteenth century. On one side are encyclopedic museums that claim to serve 'all of us'; on the other are 'source' countries whose nationalist museums demand the return of objects. Çelik argues that Western museums were built on imperial and national politics from the start, so the claim that repatriation harms the public conceals the practical question of objects obtained illegally. Turkey is the main case: the chapter reviews the return of the Lydian Hoard from the Metropolitan Museum, the contested objects at the Getty and Cleveland, and the Weary Herakles statue, which Boston returned and which then drew large crowds in Antalya. Two short vignettes, from Tunisia and Anatolia, show ordinary visitors valuing local heritage. The chapter ends by asking whether wider perspectives can unsettle the question 'Who owns antiquity?' A postscript on ISIS looting in Iraq follows.

Conn, Steven (1998). Museums and American Intellectual Life, 1876–1926. Chicago: University of Chicago Press.Asia: substantial7 chapter overviews

Overview

Steven Conn's study of American museums from 1876 to 1926 argues that the museums of the late nineteenth century rested on an “object-based epistemology”: the belief that objects, systematically arranged in glass cases, could tell their own stories to untrained viewers. His main argument is that after 1876 universities took over the production of knowledge, so that by the 1920s this belief had lost its authority and museums turned to popular display. The book covers natural history museums, anthropology at Penn and the Field Museum, the Philadelphia Commercial Museum, the history museums of Henry Mercer and Henry Ford, and the art museums of Philadelphia and New York. It is organised as an introduction, five case-study chapters, and a closing chapter on the 1926 Sesquicentennial and the present.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

East and Southeast Asia are a minor part of the book. The one substantial Asian strand is in chapter four, on the Philadelphia Commercial Museum, where the Philippines is the main thread. William Powell Wilson organised the Philippine display for the 1904 St. Louis fair, which included over 1,200 Filipinos shown on a “reservation”, and the museum afterwards held a large Philippine collection that Wilson called “a great museum of itself”. The chapter also covers Chinese and Japanese delegates at the 1897 and 1899 International Commercial Congresses, the debate over applying the Chinese Exclusion Act to the Philippines, Manila as an “Oriental Capital” for the Chinese market, the museum's trade guide to Siam, and commercial museums in Japan modelled on Philadelphia.

Otherwise the Asian material is passing. In chapter three the University of Pennsylvania Museum's downstairs galleries (1899) held Buddhist objects and “ethnological objects of asiatic origin” beside Borneo material, within an evolutionary hierarchy that put the Near East upstairs. Boas's outline for the Field Museum listed China among the civilisations of Asia, and Gordon's 1912 plan named China and Japan among the cultures Penn should collect. In chapter five Mercer commissioned Rudolf Hommel to collect Chinese tools in 1921, published as China at Work (1937). In chapter six Coleman Sellers's 1879 complaint about a case mixing Spanish, Chinese and Japanese ivory is quoted, and the 1904 “Oriental” ceramics gallery is mentioned in brief. Chapter seven notes a Chinese Village at the 1926 fair.

Korea, Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaya and Burma do not appear. The Pennsylvania Museum's Main Street (1928) ran from “the austere beginnings in India and China down to the last flowering of the delicate art of Japan”, which Conn quotes without developing.

Contents

Theoretical approach of this work
Acknowledgmentsp. vii
ONEMuseums and the Late Victorian Worldp. 3

Conn opens with a visit in 1894 by the Smithsonian ethnologist Frank Cushing to the new anthropological museum at the University of Pennsylvania, where he 'read stories in pottery' for a reporter. This anecdote introduces what Conn calls an object-based epistemology, the late-nineteenth-century belief that objects arranged in systematic galleries of glass cases could tell their own stories to untrained viewers. He argues that the period's museums expressed a Victorian rage for order, in contrast to the antebellum sideshows of P. T. Barnum, and he challenges Foucauldian critics who read museums only as instruments of power or monuments to wealthy patrons. Conn contends that universities took over the production of knowledge after 1876, so that by the 1920s object-based display had largely disappeared. The chapter then previews the book's five central chapters on natural history, anthropology, the Philadelphia Commercial Museum, history museums and art museums, together with a sixth chapter on the 1926 Sesquicentennial.

University of Pennsylvania MuseumPhiladelphia Commercial MuseumAcademy of Natural Sciences, PhiladelphiaField MuseumAmerican Museum of Natural HistoryMercer MuseumPeale's MuseumPhiladelphia Museum of Art
TWO“Naked Eye Science”: Museums and Natural Historyp. 32

Conn argues that nineteenth-century American natural history museums rested on an object-based epistemology: the belief that careful observation and classification of specimens revealed God's design, and that displays could teach the public the same. Conn traces this from Charles Willson Peale's museum in Philadelphia, through the Academy of Natural Sciences, which opened its public museum in 1826, to the post-Civil War buildings of the Academy, the American Museum of Natural History, the Smithsonian and Harvard's Museum of Comparative Zoology. The hadrosaurus mounted at the Academy in 1867 serves as the case of museum popularity, and the paleontology of Leidy, Cope and Marsh shows how fossils fed the Darwinian debate. Conn follows Cope's attempt to reconcile evolution with theology and the Academy's rivalry with the University of Pennsylvania, which pushed museums toward laboratory science and specialization. Conn concludes that museums, by the early twentieth century, had ceded research to universities and turned to popular display, and that dioramas and lectures stressed entertainment over new science.

Academy of Natural SciencesAmerican Museum of Natural HistoryPeale's MuseumMuseum of Comparative ZoologySmithsonian National Museum
THREEBetween Science and Art: Museums and the Development of Anthropologyp. 75

Conn examines how anthropology took shape in American museums in the late nineteenth century and why it then moved into universities. Conn starts with George Brown Goode's 1888 call for a museum of 'Kulturgeschichte' between science and art, and with the 1893 Columbian Exposition, whose anthropological collections seeded the Field Museum in Chicago. There Franz Boas, who oversaw the installation, criticized the collections' heavy weighting toward the Americas. The central case is the University of Pennsylvania Museum, opened in 1899, whose upstairs galleries of ancient art were set apart from downstairs ethnology, and whose director from 1910, George Byron Gordon, kept an evolutionary schema of progress from savagery to civilization. Conn sets Boas's 1907 essay rejecting object-based systematics against Gordon's continued faith in museums, and shows Boas's victory: by 1920 about half of professional anthropologists worked in university departments. Conn concludes that by the 1920s museums had turned anthropology into popular display, such as the 1933 Field Museum bronze busts, while the serious work had left them.

East and Southeast Asia The University Museum's downstairs galleries in 1899 held Buddhist objects, 'ethnological objects of asiatic origin' and material from Borneo, which Conn reads as part of the hierarchy of cultures. Boas's outline for the Field Museum placed China and countries influenced by China among the civilizations of Asia. Gordon's 1912 plan for Penn named China and Japan among the cultures the museum should collect.

University Museum (Pennsylvania)Field MuseumPeabody Museum (Harvard)American Museum of Natural HistoryNational Museum (Smithsonian)
FOURThe Philadelphia Commercial Museum: A Museum to Conquer the Worldp. 115Asia: in part

Conn tells how William Powell Wilson, a botanist who left the University of Pennsylvania, turned material from the 1893 Chicago fair into the Philadelphia Commercial Museum, a museum built to help American businesses win foreign markets. Conn argues that the museum offered an 'epistemology of imperialism': its exhibits, arranged by region and by product, and its Bureau of Information together let American firms gain the knowledge that European colonies gave their merchants, without colonial rule. The chapter follows the 1897 and 1899 international commercial congresses held there, where delegates praised American commerce as a peaceful alternative to European conquest, and the 1904 St. Louis fair, where Wilson organized the Philippine display, including Filipinos shown on a 'reservation'. Its Madagascar exhibit, which set indigenous textiles beside the European cloth that had replaced them, becomes for Conn a case of a market process with the cultural disruption left out. Conn concludes that after the First World War federal agencies and university economists took over the Bureau's work, and that after Wilson died in 1927 the museum turned toward trade-show and convention use.

East and Southeast Asia The Philippines is the main Asian thread. Wilson's 1904 St. Louis exhibit, with over 1,200 Filipinos shown on a 'reservation', brought a large Philippine collection back to Philadelphia, which the chapter calls 'a great museum of itself' with ethnology, industry and natural products. Chinese and Japanese delegates attended the 1899 congress, where applying the Chinese Exclusion Act to the Philippines was debated, and a journalist called Manila the 'Oriental Capital' for the Chinese market.

Philadelphia Commercial MuseumLouisiana Purchase Exposition (St. Louis)World's Columbian Exposition (Chicago)Imperial Institute (London)French Colonial Museum (Paris)
FIVEObjects and American History: The Museums of Henry Mercer and Henry Fordp. 151

Conn compares two museums built on the claim that ordinary objects tell American history better than texts: Henry Mercer's Mercer Museum in Doylestown, Pennsylvania, and Henry Ford's Henry Ford Museum and Greenfield Village in Dearborn, Michigan. Conn traces how Mercer, an amateur archaeologist who searched for early human remains in America, turned in 1897 to the 'penny lots' of farm sales and began collecting colonial tools, arguing that history should be written from objects and that tools shaped the nation. Ford, who admired Mercer's museum and visited it in 1923, took the same view on a far larger scale, buying buildings and objects for Greenfield Village, which opened in 1932. Conn shows that both men used evolutionary and labor-centered frameworks that resembled the older natural history and anthropology museums, and that both were disconnected from the professional historians of their day. Conn concludes that the two men's history was neither purely nostalgic nor modern, but held past and present together in a way that neither could fully resolve, and he ends with Henry Adams's failure to find any pattern in history.

East and Southeast Asia Mercer's collecting reached China through a commission he gave Rudolf Hommel in 1921 to collect tools there, which Hommel published in 1937 as China at Work, a study of Chinese tools arranged with the same care as Mercer's museum. In his 'History in Implements' lecture Mercer asked how it is that this chinaman has one like it, to suggest that the same tools link peoples across the world.

Mercer Museum (Bucks County Historical Society)Henry Ford MuseumGreenfield VillageUniversity Museum (Pennsylvania)Colonial Williamsburg
SIXFrom South Kensington to the Louvre: Art Museums and the Creation of Fine Artp. 192

Conn traces how the American art museum came to be defined, comparing New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art, which modelled itself on the Louvre, with the Pennsylvania Museum in Philadelphia, which followed London's South Kensington complex. The Metropolitan's founders kept industrial objects out of fine art and closed their technical schools in 1894. The Philadelphia museum began as a centre for industrial design, arranging ceramics and textiles by material and process, but it turned toward painting after the Wilstach Collection went on display in 1893, and the struggle over a new building on the Benjamin Franklin Parkway ended with its opening in 1928. Conn uses attendance figures, press reactions to the Met's Sunday opening and overalls ban, and curators' letters to show who visited. Conn then reads Fiske Kimball's period rooms and 'Main Street' chronology as a shift from science to history. The chapter concludes that art museums won the cultural hierarchy because their objects keep the aura Walter Benjamin associated with ritual, and that paintings are valued above other museum objects.

East and Southeast Asia Sellers's 1879 complaint about a Pennsylvania Museum case mixing Spanish, Chinese and Japanese ivory carvings is quoted, and in 1904 the museum grouped its 'Oriental' ceramics in one gallery. These are brief references that Conn does not develop.

Metropolitan Museum of ArtPennsylvania Museum (later Philadelphia Museum of Art)South Kensington MuseumMuseum of Fine Arts, BostonLouvre
SEVEN1926: Of Fairs, Museums, and Historyp. 233

Conn uses the Sesquicentennial, Philadelphia's 1926 world's fair, as a starting point: a fiasco marked by corruption and unfinished buildings, whose most popular exhibit, the reconstructed High Street, celebrated a genteel colonial past. Conn reads the fair's failure as a sign that object-based knowledge had lost its authority, and traces the same shift at the Academy of Natural Sciences, in the Philadelphia Museum of Art's period rooms, and in the Franklin Institute's push-button museum of 1934, where original objects became a condiment. A lunch that may never have happened, at which Philadelphia's directors divided the field, shows the museums fixing their boundaries just as knowledge moved on. The second half turns to the present: Lucite cases that recast anthropological objects as fine art, museums as engines of post-industrial cities, and the closure of the Commercial Museum, which Conn treats as the death of a category of knowledge. The Requiem closes on the claim that museums still matter because objects work magically, even though they no longer explain the world.
