Coombes, Annie E. (1994). Reinventing Africa: Museums, Material Culture and Popular Imagination in Late Victorian and Edwardian England. New Haven: Yale University Press.Asia: slight12 chapter overviews

Overview

Coombes examines how Africa was presented to the British public between 1890 and 1913 through ethnographic collections in museums and through large commercial, philanthropic and missionary exhibitions. Coombes’s argument is that Africa was an ideological space, savage, exotic and productive at once, and that museum displays and exhibitions turned material culture and African people into evidence for a racial hierarchy with a scientific air, shaped by the professional interests of anthropologists and by the state's reluctance to recognise anthropology. The chapters cover the Benin 'bronzes' and the 1897 expedition, critics of empire, the Stanley and African Exhibition of 1890, the Earl's Court and Olympia spectacles, three museums (Liverpool, Pitt Rivers, Horniman), missionary exhibitions and the Franco-British Exhibition of 1908, before an epilogue on hybridity and restitution.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia are marginal. The book is about Africa, and Asian material appears only in passing. In chapter 6 (Temples of Empire) the Horniman Museum's 1890 visitor guide lists an African and Japanese room, a Chinese banner, Chinese and Japanese ivory carvings and a Buddhist shrine and deities from China. Coombes cites these to show how curio displays mixed regions without classification, not to discuss Chinese or Japanese culture. In chapter 7 (Containing the Continent) the Liverpool scheme of 1896 places China, Japan, Burma and the Malay Archipelago under the 'Mongolian' race, and Keane's scheme, which the curators followed, calls the Mongol family thrifty but morally low, 'very well represented by the modern Chinaman'.

Elsewhere Asia enters as comparison or rival. Chapter 4 notes Japan among the contributors to London and provincial trade exhibitions. Chapter 5 (The Spectacle of Empire 2) lists a 'doll-like Japanese' group among the national types in the 'Women of all Nations' spectacle at Earl's Court. Chapter 8 (missionary exhibitions) describes the London Missionary Society's 'Orient in London' of 1908, but its material concerns Africa and India. Chapter 9 (the Franco-British Exhibition of 1908) has an Indo-China pavilion in the French section and a passage on Japan as a commercial rival, and uses the Indian and Ceylonese 'villages' (South Asia, outside this question) as a yardstick for African craft.

Not covered: Southeast Asian collections, museums in Asia, Asian collectors and visitors, and restitution claims from Asian states. Asia is a comparative category in racial classification and the spectacle of nations, not a subject of study.

JapanChinaBurmaMalay ArchipelagoIndo-China

Contents

Theoretical approach of this work
Acknowledgementsp. vi
Introductionp. 1

Coombes opens with a 1989 photograph of an armoured vehicle parked at the British Museum entrance and a science feature on AIDS in Nairobi, arguing that both show how cultural authority, racial purity and anxiety about contamination are linked. The book analyses how Africa was presented to the British public between 1890 and 1913 through ethnographic collections in museums and large exhibitions that mixed scientific claims with entertainment. Coombes rejects the picture of a monolithic imperial propaganda and argues that Africa was an ideological space, savage, exotic and productive at once, whose images shifted with political needs. The introduction separates 'popular' from academic 'scientific' knowledge, and argues that museum displays reflected the professional politics of the Anthropological Institute and the state's reluctance to recognise anthropology more than the latest theory. Drawing on Gramsci's idea of hegemony as negotiation, and on Foucault, Coombes frames the colonial encounter as a dynamic exchange between coloniser and colonised. The introduction ends by suggesting that these exhibitions explain why colonial material remains contested today.

British Museum
1Material Culture at the Crossroads of Knowledge: The Case of the Benin ‘Bronzes’p. 7

Coombes examines how the 1897 British punitive expedition against Benin City, and the looting of its royal objects, were written up in the press and in the memoirs of the officers involved. The chapter argues that the same accounts both admired the bronzes and ivories and described Benin society as degenerate and savage, and it asks how such contradictory beliefs could be sustained. Coombes works through the trade disputes behind the expedition, the killing of the Acting Consul-General Phillips's party, and the illustrated press's images of Benin women and the city. The evidence then moves to Boisragon's and Bacon's books, and to the Liverpool, Horniman and Pitt Rivers collections, where curators and journalists treated the bronzes as art but debated whether Africans could have made them. The chapter concludes that the contradiction was not a blind spot but a product of colonial knowledge, in which the bronzes were praised as relics of a past civilisation while contemporary Edo craft was denied.

British MuseumLiverpool Mayer MuseumPitt Rivers MuseumHorniman Free Museum
2Voices in the Wilderness: Critics of Empirep. 29

Coombes turns from the officials and illustrators to the critics of the Benin expedition, asking how British and West African voices challenged the image of Benin as a degenerate society. The chapter opens with James Pinnock's 1897 lecture on the Benin River trade, which praised African capacity for civilisation while blaming the slave trade on Liverpool merchants, and shows how the Sierra Leone Weekly News and Lagos Weekly Record turned such remarks against colonial policy. It then follows the criticism of the exile of Jaja and Nana, carried by The New Age and by the Aborigine Protection Society and Anti-Slavery Society, and the trial of Oba Ovonramwen in 1897. The main evidence is the letters and editorials of Moses Da Rocha, A.E. Fletcher and John Payne Jackson, along with the writings of Blaize, Crowther and Blyden. Coombes argues that West African writers used the bronzes to claim an ancient history for Benin, and that the degeneracy idea was partly a British response to these nationalist arguments. The chapter ends by showing that both sides of the debate used the same vocabulary of race and degeneration.

3Aesthetic Pleasure and Institutional Powerp. 43

Coombes examines how the degenerationist theory of ornament, developed by anthropologists such as Henry Balfour, Alfred Haddon and Pitt Rivers, shaped the way Benin bronzes were studied and displayed in Britain after 1897. The chapter traces the debate among Ling Roth, Read and Dalton, Pitt Rivers and others over whether the bronzes were Portuguese, Egyptian or African in origin, and shows how each position reflected institutional and professional interests. It sets this against the wider evolutionary account of decoration, pitting Balfour's successive-copying experiments and Haddon's environmental analysis against Semper's functionalism and George Birdwood's defence of individual genius at the Royal Society of Arts. The second half turns to the British Museum, where the 1897 plaque exhibition, the auction of tusks and the acquisitions of the Berlin Museum fur Volkerkunde fed a press campaign over national heritage. Coombes concludes that the African attribution advanced the ethnographic department's bid for autonomy, and that treating Benin as an anomaly kept the degenerate label in place even as its art was admired.

British MuseumMuseum fur Volkerkunde, BerlinPitt Rivers MuseumBethnal Green Museum
4The Spectacle of Empire 1: Expansionism and Philanthropy at the Stanley and African Exhibitionp. 63

Coombes uses the Stanley and African Exhibition of 1890, held in London's Victoria Gallery, to show how an exhibition could present Africa as both particular and homogeneous. The chapter places the show within the growth of commercial and colonial exhibitions after 1851, and within the mix of trade, missionary, geographical and anti-slavery interests that sponsored it. It reads the exhibition's maps, portrait gallery, mock explorer's camp and trophy-style display of objects by named collectors, alongside The Times reviews, the catalogue and William Steains's sketchbooks. The chapter then examines the slavery display, the two Swazi boys Gootoo and Inyokwana, and the gorilla placed beside a group of African racial types, to show how the visitor was cast as explorer and as philanthropist. Coombes also follows the controversy over Stanley's dealings with the slave trader Tippu Tip and the legal case over the boys, which the Anti-Slavery Society used to restore its reputation. The chapter concludes that the exhibition's claim to scientific objectivity rested on an imperial narrative of progress and rescue, and that this narrative shaped the public image of Africa.

Stanley and African ExhibitionHorniman MuseumBritish Museum
5The Spectacle of Empire 2: Exhibitionary Narrativesp. 85

Coombes moves from the static displays of the exhibitions to the living performers, asking how the British presented Africans as authentic spectacle between 1890 and 1913. The chapter examines the rhetoric of authenticity in the publicity for the French Exhibition at Earl's Court, the Ashanti troupes, the Olympia drama 'Briton, Boer and Black' and Barnum and Bailey's Great Show, drawing on their guidebooks, programmes and press reviews. It shows how the exhibitions borrowed devices from colonial romance and from ethnographic writing, so that the performers were both entertainment and specimens, described in terms of physique, animal behaviour, dancing and motherhood. The best-documented case is 'Savage South Africa', where a dispute over the Zulu performers, a press panic over miscegenation, a legal action by Fillis, and campaigns by the Aborigines Protection Society over the performers' contracts led to the closure of the Zulu Kraal to women in 1899. The chapter concludes that the enduring stereotypes served imperial and gendered purposes, and that the performers themselves sometimes resisted, through court action and organised protest.

British Museum
6Temples of Empire: The Museum and its Publicsp. 109

Coombes asks what kind of public ethnographic museums in Britain set out to address between 1902 and 1913, and how their displays of colonised peoples fitted the state's educational and imperial aims. The chapter sets museum curators beside the exhibitions and the Museums Association, showing how the 1902 Education Act and social imperialism encouraged museums to present themselves as neutral places of popular education. Its main case studies are the Horniman Museum, whose early displays of curios, slave-trade objects and Zulu and Dahomeyan material are read through a Victorian philanthropic ideal, and the Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford, whose typological arrangement set out an evolutionary progression from primitive to civilised forms. Coombes uses the Horniman's visitor guide, Balfour's unpublished guide proposal, Pitt Rivers's lectures and the Oxford funding disputes to show how classification served social control and imperial purposes. The chapter also shows how anthropometry and eugenics shaped the use of photographs and skulls in displays. It concludes that the popularisation of anthropology gave the derogatory images of Africa a credibility drawn from supposedly scientific knowledge.

East and Southeast Asia Asian material appears only in the Horniman's 1890 visitor guide, which lists an African and Japanese room, a Chinese banner, Chinese and Japanese ivory carvings in glass cases, and a Buddhist shrine and deities from China in the annexe. Coombes cites these to show how curio-style displays mixed regions without classification, not to discuss Chinese or Japanese culture.

Horniman MuseumPitt Rivers MuseumBritish MuseumBethnal Green Museum
7Containing the Continent: Ethnographies on Displayp. 129

Coombes examines how three British ethnographic collections, the Liverpool Mayer Museum, the Pitt Rivers Museum at Oxford and the Horniman Museum in London, represented Africa between 1890 and 1913. It asks what kind of knowledge museum ethnography produced under the 'new museum idea' and how far it was shaped by Darwinian evolutionism. The evidence comes from accessions records, annual reports and correspondence. At Liverpool, the shipping director Alfred Jones and the engineer Arnold Ridyard supplied most of the West African material, and Ridyard's letters with colonial officials and missionaries show how donors described objects. The Torday and Joyce partnership shows how amateur collectors answered anthropological questionnaires for London experts. Each museum organised its displays by race, typology or evolutionary series, with photographs and lectures reinforcing the point. Coombes concludes that until about 1913 all three presented Africa through a European hierarchy of race and civilisation.

East and Southeast Asia Liverpool's 1896 scheme grouped its ethnographic collections by race, placing China, Japan, Burma and the Malay Archipelago under the 'Mongolian' heading, and the 1901 plan put the Mongolian race on the topmost floor. Keane's racial scheme, which the curators followed, describes the 'Mongol family' as thrifty but morally low, 'very well represented by the modern Chinaman'. These are classification points rather than discussion of East or Southeast Asian objects.

Liverpool Mayer MuseumPitt Rivers MuseumHorniman MuseumBritish Museum
8‘For God and For England’: Missionary Contributions to an Image of Africap. 161

Coombes asks how evangelical missionary societies shaped a popular British image of Africa between 1890 and 1914. Missionary exhibitions drew large crowds to the Royal Agricultural Hall in Islington, with the London Missionary Society's 'Orient in London' of 1908 and the Church Missionary Society's 'Africa and the East' of 1909 as the main examples. Coombes examines the steward manuals, the curio boxes lent by congregations and the African village of Nigerian artisans, arguing that these presented the African as a skilled craftsman and a malleable child rather than only a savage. The chapter also looks at the missionary museums and at the correspondence of donors such as William Allen, whose gifts to the Pitt Rivers Museum came with detailed accounts of their use. Missionaries are shown as close to anthropology yet tied to colonial rule. Coombes concludes that they were collaborators in imperial authority who also helped create an educated African elite that threatened it.

London Missionary Society MuseumChurch Missionary Society MuseumWesleyan Missionary Society MuseumPitt Rivers MuseumBritish MuseumOrient in London exhibition (1908)Africa and the East exhibition (1909)
9National Unity and Racial and Ethnic Identities: The Franco-British Exhibition of 1908p. 187

Coombes studies the Franco-British Exhibition of 1908 at White City in London, where a myth of national unity was built on racial and ethnic difference. The exhibition served social imperialism, which sought working-class support for empire at a time of anxiety over physical deterioration after the Boer War. The chapter describes employer-sponsored excursions, the colonial pavilions and the 'villages' in which Senegalese, Ceylonese and Irish people were displayed, and the trophy display of Benin material from Southern Nigeria. It contrasts the romantic presentation of French Algeria and Tunisia with the modernising British exhibits. The Irish 'Village of Ballymaclinton' is read as a harmonised Celtic heritage that defused militant nationalism. Haddon's anthropometric and evolutionary displays gave the racial hierarchy a scientific air. Coombes concludes that African and Irish critics exposed the contradictions of this imperial unity.

Franco-British Exhibition, White City (1908)
Conclusionp. 214

The conclusion draws the museums, missionary societies and exhibitions together. Their support came from industrialists, colonial servants, learned societies and missionaries, and they reached a mass public under an imperial vision. Anthropology's popularisation gave racial hierarchy a scientific air. The conclusion then points to Edwardian challenges to that vision, from African elites, the labour movement, suffragettes and Irish politics, and argues that the racial purity claimed for Englishness was never secure.

Epilogue: Inventing the ‘Post-Colonial’p. 217

The epilogue asks what becomes of ethnographic objects now that museums describe them as hybrid and post-colonial. Coombes argues that celebrating hybridity can disguise the unequal power that produced such objects, and that the museum's own visibility reaffirms the meaning it claims to question. The 1985 'Hidden Peoples of the Amazon' exhibition at the Museum of Mankind was picketed by Survival International and Indian rights representatives, who said it showed no sign of indigenous resistance. The 1988 Calgary exhibition 'The Spirit Sings', funded by Shell Oil, drew a boycott from the Lubicon Lake Cree. Benin bronzes, refused for the 1977 Lagos festival yet displayed prominently on the British Museum's main staircase, show how restitution demands expose the tensions between national sovereignty and multiculturalism. Coombes concludes that a post-colonial future requires a fuller account of the cultural object's imperial past.

Cuno, James (ed.) (2009). Whose Culture? The Promise of Museums and the Debate over Antiquities. Princeton: Princeton University Press.Asia: substantial10 chapter overviews

Overview

Whose Culture? The Promise of Museums and the Debate over Antiquities (2009), edited by James Cuno, is a collection of essays by museum directors, archaeologists, a philosopher, legal scholars and an art historian on whether museums should acquire and display antiquities whose find-spots are unknown or undocumented. The editor's introduction defends the encyclopedic museum against archaeologists who say such objects are meaningless and against nationalist governments that claim antiquities as national property. The essays are grouped in three parts: the value of museums, the value of antiquities, and museums, antiquities and cultural property. The scope is mainly Mediterranean, Near Eastern, Chinese, African and Indigenous antiquities, and the institutions are mostly Western museums, especially in Britain and the United States.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

East Asia is concentrated in one chapter. James C. Y. Watt’s chapter 4 is chiefly about China: Liangzhu jade congs from the Lower Yangzi, jades from the tomb of Lady Hao (Fu Hao) at Anyang, a Shang ritual wine vessel, a Western Zhou ding, the bell chimes of the Marquis of Zeng in Hubei, a gold ornament from a Jin-period tomb near Suzhou, and the horse and groom from the tomb of Li Xian. Neolithic jades from the National Palace Museum in Taipei, shown at the Metropolitan in 1996, are also discussed. Watt uses these cases to test whether archaeological context matters, and concludes that antiquities should be valued as works of art and as links to earlier creativity.

Cuno’s introduction gives East Asia a substantial passage. A Shang fangding and a Western Zhou Shi Wang Ding at the Art Institute of Chicago are set beside Benin objects to show courtly ritual. The introduction also traces Japanese influence in Britain and America: E. W. Godwin’s sideboard, Japanese art shown at the 1861 Bristol and 1862 London exhibitions, Whistler’s Asian ceramics, Frank Lloyd Wright’s 1908 exhibition of more than 650 Japanese prints, and the Mingei movement led by Yanagi Sōetsu in Japan. These are offered as evidence that culture is hybrid, not national. Japan figures as a source of influence on Western and Japanese design.

Elsewhere East Asia is brief. Merryman’s Case 3 is hypothetical: a stone Buddha head bought from a Singapore dealer, whose body stands headless in a museum in Xi’an. Singapore appears only as the place of purchase, and Japanese museums only as hypothetical buyers. MacGregor says the British Museum’s founders wanted Chinese and Japanese objects studied beside Greek and Roman ones, and he describes a Beijing exhibition of about 200 objects from outside China. Montebello notes Yuan and Ming porcelains in Istanbul’s Topkapi Palace. Southeast Asia is otherwise absent: there is no discussion of Southeast Asian museums, colonial collecting or restitution there. Afghanistan and the Bamiyan Buddhas belong to Central Asia and are outside this question.

IntroductionJames Cunop. 1Asia: in part

Cuno's introduction to the edited volume Whose Culture? sets out the dispute between nationalist governments, archaeologists and museums over antiquities whose find spots are unknown, and argues that museums should acquire them. Cuno summarizes the archaeologists' view that only context gives meaning and replies that an object has many contexts, not only its last one. Two cases make the point: the Laocoon, found by accident in Rome in 1506 and central to European taste, and the Rosetta Stone in the British Museum, whose value lies in its decipherment rather than its findspot. Cuno shows how learned journals would refuse to publish such objects, and he takes issue with Colin Renfrew's Loot, Legitimacy, and Ownership. Six objects in the Art Institute of Chicago then show what neighboring galleries can reveal. The introduction previews the contributions in three parts and concludes that the public trusts museums to build collections responsibly, and that the dispute must be resolved.

East and Southeast Asia The chapter's East Asian material is substantial. Two Chinese bronzes at the Art Institute, a Shang fangding and a Western Zhou Shi Wang Ding, are used to show how bronze working and courtly ritual flourished in China and in Benin. Cuno also traces Japanese influence on the English designer E. W. Godwin's sideboard, Japanese art shown at British exhibitions in 1861 and 1862, Whistler's Asian ceramics, Frank Lloyd Wright's 1908 exhibition of Japanese prints, and the Mingei movement led by Yanagi Sōetsu.

Art Institute of ChicagoBritish Museum
PART ONE The Value of Museumsp. 37
To Shape the Citizens of “That Great City, the World”Neil MacGregorp. 39

MacGregor, director of the British Museum, argues that the encyclopedic museum rests on the Enlightenment idea that gathering objects from across the world produces truths and a new kind of citizen, the citizen of the world. MacGregor traces this to Hans Sloane's gift, which was conditional on the collection staying together, open and free, and to the idea of trusteeship, which holds objects for all humanity, present and future. MacGregor shows objects acting as evidence, such as the Piranesi Vase, which is mostly eighteenth-century work, and Dr Woodward's shield, made in Renaissance France. Much of the chapter describes recent loans and exhibitions: a Sudanese lyre and a Roman bronze head of Augustus shown during the Darfur debate in London, a Mozambican throne of weapons toured across Britain, a show of objects from outside China in Beijing, the Benin plaques, and Hazina, an exhibition chosen by curators in Nairobi. MacGregor concludes that the museum's obligation is to lend its collections widely so that they provoke thought about a world that is one.

East and Southeast Asia East Asian material is limited to two points. MacGregor says the British Museum's founders wanted Chinese and Japanese objects studied alongside Greek and Roman ones, for example to learn how the Japanese think about God. MacGregor also describes a Beijing exhibition of about 200 objects from outside China lent to the Capital Museum, which he calls remarkable because China has great museums but no encyclopedic one.

British MuseumCapital Museum (Beijing)National Museum of Kenya
“And What Do You Propose Should Be Done with Those Objects?”Philippe de Montebellop. 55

Montebello, then director of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, defends the acquisition of antiquities, provenanced and unprovenanced, against archaeologists who say that objects without context are meaningless. Montebello opens with an 1870 definition of the encyclopedic museum as cosmopolitan and argues that long-term loans and exchanges can widen access without breaking up collections. Montebello cites the Naram-sin stele, taken from Susa to the Louvre, and the Metropolitan's returns to Turkey and Italy, including the Euphronios krater, for which Italy offered excavated finds in exchange. Montebello describes the Nimrud ivories, shared with Baghdad through partage, and a future arrangement for long-term loans of finds from joint excavations. Montebello then defends unprovenanced objects, such as Urkesh lion figures bought in 1948, whose inscriptions led excavators to Tell Mozan. Restrictions, he argues, have only pushed the market underground. He ends by asking what should be done with such objects, and says that refusing to acquire them is a loss to scholars, the public and history.

East and Southeast Asia Montebello notes that the Topkapi Palace in Istanbul, one of the earliest encyclopedic collections, held a great group of Yuan and Ming porcelains from China, formed by Mehmet II in the second half of the fifteenth century. Montebello also says that objects of the Han Empire can be seen within a short walk of Augustan works in the British Museum and the Metropolitan.

Metropolitan Museum of ArtLouvreTopkapi Palace Museum (Istanbul)
Whose Culture Is It?Kwame Anthony Appiahp. 71

Appiah examines the doctrine of 'cultural patrimony', the claim that cultural objects belong to the group that produced them and that removing them is a wrong. Appiah opens with the looting of the Asante palace in 1874, Baden-Powell's collecting there in 1896, the illicit digging of Djenne-jeno terra-cottas in Mali, and thefts from Nigerian museums. Appiah then tests the doctrine where it strains: Nok sculptures whose makers' descendants are unknown, Picasso's borrowings from Congolese carving, and a Nigerian artist's work bought by a private owner. Disputes with the Getty and Metropolitan Museum over Italian antiquities show how national export rules stretch the notion of origin. The 1999-2001 Kabul episode, in which UNESCO blocked a Swiss plan to shelter endangered artifacts, serves as a cautionary case. Appiah defends a cosmopolitan view in which collections hold objects in trust for humanity, and he accepts repatriation mainly where objects were stolen from known owners. Appiah ends by arguing that connection to art through shared human capacity matters as much as connection through identity.

British MuseumGetty MuseumMetropolitan Museum of ArtNational Museum in KabulAban (Asante palace museum), Kumasi
PART TWO The Value of Antiquitiesp. 87
Antiquities and the Importance—and Limitations—of Archaeological ContextsJames C. Y. Wattp. 89Asia: chiefly

Watt, of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, challenges the claim that objects lose all meaning without their excavation context. Using Chinese material, he argues that context matters most for prehistoric objects and matters less as periods become better documented by written sources. He takes a Neolithic jade cong from the Liangzhu culture as his example: burial context reveals the society but not why the object was made or what it meant. Other cases follow: jades in the tomb of Lady Hao of the Shang, a Shang ritual wine vessel decorated with split animal masks, a Western Zhou ding, the bell chimes of the Marquis of Zeng, and a Tang horse from the tomb of Li Xian, where the tomb adds little to what the horses already show. His second proposition is that once enough tombs of a period have been excavated, further digging becomes superfluous. He concludes that antiquities should be valued directly as works of art and as a link to earlier creativity, not reduced to scientific data.

East and Southeast Asia Chiefly about China. Watt uses Liangzhu jade congs from the Lower Yangzi, jades from the tomb of Lady Hao (Fu Hao) at Anyang, a Shang ritual wine vessel, a Western Zhou ding, the bell chimes of the Marquis of Zeng in Hubei, a gold ornament from a Jin-period tomb near Suzhou that he traces to steppe and Xiongnu transmission, and the horse and groom from the tomb of Li Xian. Watt also discusses Neolithic jades from the National Palace Museum, Taipei, shown at the Metropolitan in 1996, and a Southern Song ceramic copy of a ts'ung jade.

Metropolitan Museum of ArtNational Palace Museum, TaipeiHubei Provincial MuseumNational Museum of China, Beijing
Archaeologists, Collectors, and MuseumsSir John Boardmanp. 107

Boardman, an Oxford archaeologist and former Ashmolean assistant keeper, answers Colin Renfrew's Loot, Legitimacy, and Ownership and the anti-collecting legislation it inspired. Boardman argues that rules treating antiquities without documented pedigree as tainted damage scholarship. Such rules, he says, push finders to melt objects down, keep unprovenanced material from scholars and museums, and censor research that uses it. His examples include a clay snake vase he bought for Oxford for about 14 pounds, casual finds on Greek fields and building rubble in Chios, and the Gundestrup cauldron, whose Danish bog find tells little about its date. Many fields, including numismatics and the study of cuneiform tablets, rest on collections rather than excavation. Boardman also argues that the Euphronios krater's importance lies in the object itself, not in the tomb it came from. Boardman closes with six listed results of current policy and calls for regulating the trade rather than banning it.

Ashmolean MuseumMetropolitan Museum of Art
Censoring Knowledge: The Case for the Publication of Unprovenanced Cuneiform TabletsDavid I. Owenp. 125

Owen, a Cornell Assyriologist, argues that unprovenanced cuneiform tablets must be published, since many will otherwise be lost. Owen traces how looted tablets from Iraq began appearing on eBay and in shops after the Gulf wars, and how archaeological societies and journals responded by banning them. Owen counts fewer than five hundred genuine tablets recorded online since 2003, against the hundreds of thousands alleged by archaeologists. Owen shows that unprovenanced texts have reconstructed archival groups and enlarged knowledge of Ur III economy and history. Owen also argues that publication does not raise the value of a tablet already in a private collection. Owen turns to archaeologists' own unpublished excavations, citing Hasanlu and Umm al-Hafriyat, and to cases in which journals rejected unprovenanced mathematical texts. Owen ends by calling for such material to be recorded and published, while pursuing a separate campaign against looting.

Iraq Museum, BaghdadOriental Institute, Chicago
PART THREE Museums, Antiquities, and Cultural Propertyp. 143
Exhibiting Indigenous Heritage in the Age of Cultural PropertyMichael F. Brownp. 145

Brown, of Williams College, examines how indigenous claims to cultural property affect museums that display non-Western material. Brown argues that indigenous groups now seek control over intangible heritage such as songs, languages and religious knowledge, a shift that the notion of cultural property has widened. Brown traces how NAGPRA, the 1990 American repatriation law, encouraged such claims, and how museums now consult communities and sometimes share stewardship. The main case is the Musee du quai Branly in Paris, opened in 2006 and criticized for its colonial associations and for separating indigenous art from European art. Brown then examines the National Museum of the American Indian in Washington, whose celebratory exhibits drew complaints about shallow content. Brown also considers community-run museums such as the Mashantucket Pequot Museum. Brown concludes that community curation cannot settle questions of representation, and that museums should draw on their expertise and on shared humanity.

National Museum of the American IndianMusée du quai BranlyMashantucket Pequot Museum and Research Center
Heritage and National TreasuresDerek Gillmanp. 165

Gillman, of the Barnes Foundation, asks whether the language of heritage and national treasure gives nations or peoples moral claims to important works. Gillman takes three cases. The Taliban's destruction of the Bamiyan Buddhas in 2001 led UNESCO to call it a crime against the common heritage of humanity, but who owns such heritage remains open, since the Taliban did not regard the Buddhas as theirs. The Parthenon sculptures in the British Museum, which Greece has sought back since 1983, raise the question of whether a people can be wounded as a person can, and he weighs Moustakas's argument for group property rights against the problem of legal title. The Lansdowne portrait of George Washington, saved for the National Portrait Gallery in 2001 by a foundation-backed appeal, shows how national-treasure rhetoric works in America too. Gillman concludes by asking whether moral claims to such symbols are justified, and at what cost to the encyclopedic museum.

British MuseumNational Portrait Gallery, Smithsonian, WashingtonNational Museum in KabulAfghanistan-Museum in Exile, Bubendorf
The Nation and the ObjectJohn Henry Merrymanp. 183Asia: in part

Merryman, a Stanford law professor, argues that cultural property debates are dominated by 'cultural nationalism', the view that objects belong in the nation where they were found. Merryman sets against it an 'object-oriented' policy that ranks preservation, truth, and access. Merryman explains the basic legal position, under which one nation does not enforce another's export controls, and the strategy of declaring antiquities state property, which courts have often rejected, as in Peru v. Johnson. The 1970 UNESCO Convention limits theft to documented museum objects. His main test is the Cleveland Poussin, bought from a French collector without a French export permit; he argues the painting is no less a Poussin in Cleveland. He then works through five cases, including a looted Maya stela and a Kom sculpture, and concludes that return is justified mainly where a living culture still uses the object in ritual. He ends by welcoming the object-oriented principles in the UNIDROIT draft and criticizing European Community rules that enforce national export controls.

East and Southeast Asia Case 3 imagines a German museum offered a stone Buddha head, bought from a Singapore dealer on an Asian voyage with no known source. Merryman argues that if the Chinese Ministry of Culture showed the head belonged to a statue standing headless in a Xi'an museum, there would be a strong object-oriented case for reuniting head and body, even without a Chinese claim. Singapore and China appear only in this hypothetical; other Asian relics are mentioned only in a list.

Cuno, James (2008). Who Owns Antiquity? Museums and the Battle over Our Ancient Heritage. Princeton: Princeton University Press.Asia: substantial9 chapter overviews

Overview

James Cuno's book asks who may own ancient objects and argues against nation-state cultural property laws that treat antiquities as national patrimony. Its central case is the dispute over unprovenanced antiquities between American and European museums on one side and archaeologists and source nations on the other. Cuno contends that archaeologists back nationalist retentionist laws, that these laws serve national identity rather than site protection, and that encyclopedic museums offer a cosmopolitan alternative. The book runs from a preface and introduction through five chapters (Political Matters, More Political Matters, The Turkish Question, The Chinese Question, Identity Matters), an epilogue and a paperback afterword. Its cases span Greece, Italy, Egypt, Turkey, Iraq, China and Nigeria, and they are seen from the position of a US art museum director.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

East Asia matters most, and China carries it. Chapter four, "The Chinese Question" (lines 3022-3893), is the main treatment of the region: it opens at the Mogao caves at Dunhuang, where Stein, Pelliot and Warner acquired manuscripts, paintings and a Tang stucco bodhisattva now at Harvard, and it covers the Dunhuang Academy director Fan Jinshi, Chinese export and excavation laws of 1930 to 1992, the Poly Art Museum's 2000 purchase of Yuanmingyuan bronze heads, and Xinjiang and Kashgar. China recurs in the preface (Chen Mengjia's catalogue of Art Institute bronzes; Li Xueqin and the Poly advisory committee), the introduction and chapter one (the 2005 Chinese request for US import restrictions), and the afterword (the January 2009 decision and the Summer Palace zodiac heads). Taiwan appears as the place to which the Nationalists moved the Imperial collection.

Southeast Asia is nearly absent. Chapter two (lines 1931-1962) discusses the Cirebon wreck off Java, a cargo from the Sumatran Sriwijaya kingdom that the Indonesian government planned to auction, and notes that China, Japan and the United States had not ratified UNESCO's 2001 underwater heritage convention. Cambodia appears only in a list of countries whose US import requests were granted (line 1854).

Japan appears once, in chapter five (lines 4101-4108), as a contrast to Italy: its law ranks objects into National Treasures and Important Cultural Properties and leaves 95 percent of ranked objects open to export. South Korea appears only as a comparison in Sen's critique of Huntington (lines 4321-4334). Not covered: colonial collecting in Southeast Asia, and the museums and heritage policy of Japan and Korea.

PrefacePDF p. 8Asia: in part

Cuno's preface uses four episodes to frame the book's argument: the Elgin Marbles, the Rosetta Stone, Chinese bronzes in Chicago and Beijing, and six Art Institute of Chicago objects from China, Benin, Sicily and Egypt. Each shows that disputes over unprovenanced antiquities are less about looting than about nation-states claiming ancient heritage. Cuno defends encyclopedic museums as places for understanding across cultures and urges the debate to move beyond whether museums should acquire undocumented objects.

East and Southeast Asia Chinese bronzes carry much of the preface. Cuno follows Chen Mengjia, who co-wrote a 1946 catalogue of the Art Institute of Chicago's bronzes and whose American study was published in 1960 without his participation. Cuno also follows Li Xueqin, head of an advisory committee for the Poly Art Museum, which buys back Chinese antiquities of undocumented origin. The Chicago fangding and a Western Zhou ding are presented as examples of encyclopedic collecting.

British MuseumArt Institute of ChicagoPoly Art Museum
Introduction: The Crux of the MatterPDF p. 31Asia: in part

Cuno's introduction sets out the dispute between U.S. art museums and archaeologists over unprovenanced antiquities, meaning objects without documented ownership and export history. Cuno argues that the dispute is a diversion: archaeologists back source-nation laws that declare antiquities national property, so the real question is nationalist politics. Cuno traces the 2001 Schultz conviction, which treated Egyptian patrimony law as enforceable in an American court, and rejects ethical and archaeological-context arguments against acquisition. Drawing on Merryman's triad of preservation, knowledge and access, he argues for shared stewardship, and he previews chapters on Turkey, China and nationalism. The chapter ends by calling antiquity our common heritage and the real battle one over false claims of ownership.

East and Southeast Asia China is the introduction's main Asian case. Cuno calls China's 2005 request for US import restrictions on objects from the Paleolithic to the Qing dynasty broad and unexplained, given a booming domestic Chinese market, and reads it as an attempt to keep what the state claims as cultural property. Cuno notes that Chinese citizens and corporations may buy back antiquities 'for China' in ways the state denies to foreign buyers, and that Italy and China hold stockpiles of antiquities that are not accessible to the public.

Metropolitan Museum of ArtBritish MuseumMuseum of Fine Arts, Boston
One: Political MattersPDF p. 44Asia: in part

Cuno opens with his own experience: after being asked at a 1990 job interview whether he would acquire illegally exported antiquities, he describes buying a collection of Greek vase fragments for Harvard's art museums in 1995 and the criticism that followed. Cuno then turns from whether acquisition is legal to the history of the laws behind it, examining the 1954 Hague Convention and UNESCO's 1970 convention, the US Cultural Property Implementation Act of 1983, and early museum policies such as the University of Pennsylvania's Pennsylvania Declaration. Cuno covers prosecutions under the National Stolen Property Act, including the Hollinshead and McClain cases involving Pre-Columbian objects. Cuno argues that retentionist laws serve national identity and that US import restrictions are decided by foreign policy considerations. The chapter ends by noting that conventions and legislation have not stopped looting.

East and Southeast Asia China is the chapter's main Asian case. Cuno describes the 2005 Chinese request for US import restrictions on objects from the Paleolithic to the Qing dynasty as covering nearly two million years of production, and reads it as a bid to retain what China claims as its cultural property. Cuno says China lost much of its heritage to foreigners in the early twentieth century and again when the nationalist government moved material to Taiwan. Cuno also argues that the request will not work, since China has a booming domestic trade in the same materials.

Harvard University Art MuseumsUniversity of Pennsylvania Museum of Archaeology and AnthropologyMetropolitan Museum of ArtBritish Museum
Two: More Political MattersPDF p. 59Asia: in part

Cuno continues with the politics of international conventions, arguing that UNESCO's 1972, 2001, 2003 and 2005 conventions, and the 1995 UNIDROIT convention, each extend claims to heritage while placing its governance in narrower national hands. Cuno cites the Cirebon shipwreck off Java, where Indonesia chose to auction most of a cargo of Chinese wares rather than keep it together, and the Indigenous heritage report of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights. Cuno then shows how archaeology in Iraq served nationalist regimes, from British-era partage and Gertrude Bell's 1924 law to Saddam Hussein's Babylon projects, and ends with the looting of the Iraq Museum in 2003 and its later control. Cuno concludes that the question of acquisition cannot be settled apart from politics.

East and Southeast Asia Asia appears through the Cirebon wreck off north Java, a 2000 find of a cargo from the Sumatran Sriwijaya kingdom that included Chinese Yue and Northern white wares and objects with Arabic inscriptions. Cuno notes that the Indonesian government planned to auction most of it, and that China, Japan and the United States had not ratified UNESCO's 2001 underwater heritage convention. Cuno also notes that China took part in the 1995 UNIDROIT negotiations, and that China, Japan and the United States had not signed the 2005 diversity convention.

Iraq Museum, BaghdadOriental Institute of the University of Chicago
Three: The Turkish QuestionPDF p. 74

Cuno's chapter on Turkey asks how the republic's cultural property law reflects its nation building. Cuno sketches Istanbul's history from the Byzantine capital through the Ottoman court's dealings with Venice, France and England, then the census figures showing the city's Greek, Jewish and Armenian populations shrinking to almost nothing. Ataturk's secularizing reforms, the abolition of the caliphate in 1924, the choice of Ankara and the invented Anatolian identity are set against the rise of Islamist politics under Erbakan and Erdogan. The main case is the Istanbul Archaeological Museum, founded in 1846 and shaped by Osman Hamdi Bey, and the sequence of Ottoman and republican antiquities decrees from 1869 to 1983, which moved antiquities from private ownership to exclusive state property. Cuno argues that archaeology in Turkey serves a Turkish past while Kurdish, Greek and other heritage is neglected, and that Turkey's claim to the Sidon sarcophagi rests on sovereignty rather than on the past belonging to all. Cuno concludes that national museums and archaeology enforce identity control.

Istanbul Archaeological MuseumMuseum of Anatolian Civilizations (Ankara)Topkapi Palace Museum
Four: The Chinese QuestionPDF p. 88Asia: chiefly

Cuno's chapter on China begins at Dunhuang and the Mogao caves, where Aurel Stein and Paul Pelliot removed manuscripts and paintings early in the twentieth century and Langdon Warner took a Tang stucco sculpture for Harvard in 1924. Cuno describes his own visits and the seminar in which students debated whether the sculpture should stay at Harvard. From this he argues that national culture is a political construction and that China's cultural property laws, from the 1930 export ban through the 1982 and 1992 laws, serve a retentionist nationalist agenda. He sets against them the Poly Art Museum, which bought back looted Yuanmingyuan bronze heads and other Chinese antiquities, its parent group being a former arms dealer tied to the PLA. A long detour to Xinjiang and its Uighur population, and to the travels of Xuanzang and the German expeditions, argues that the Chinese state decides what counts as Chinese culture. Cuno concludes that Chinese culture has always been formed by exchange, and that the question of what counts as Chinese has no easy answer.

East and Southeast Asia China is the chapter's main subject. Cuno covers the Mogao caves at Dunhuang in Gansu, where Stein, Pelliot and Warner acquired manuscripts, paintings and a Tang sculpture now at Harvard, and the Dunhuang Academy director Fan Jinshi, who hosted him. Cuno follows the Chinese export, excavation and sale laws of 1930, 1950, 1982, 1987 and 1992, and the Poly Art Museum's 2000 purchase of the Yuanmingyuan bronze heads. Cuno also discusses Xinjiang, Turpan and Kashgar, the Uighur population and the Han settlement of the region, the Three Gorges Dam salvage, and the German expeditions to Turfan.

Poly Art Museum (Beijing)Mogao caves (Dunhuang Academy)Harvard Art Museums (Arthur M. Sackler Museum)Berlin Museum of Indian Art (Turfan collection)
Five: Identity MattersPDF p. 110

Chapter five, 'Identity Matters', is the book's most theoretical chapter. Cuno opens with Edward Said's and Amin Maalouf's accounts of multiple identities, then argues that nationality is one identity among many, one that the state forces people to choose. Cuno contests the claim of nationalist retentionist cultural property laws that antiquities belong to a nation because they came from its territory, using Italy's request to the United States, the Nok sculptures of Nigeria, and the failure of such laws to stop looting. Nationalism, drawing on Gellner, Anderson and Hobsbawm, is presented as an elite and relatively recent construction, and Amartya Sen's childhood experience in Dhaka and his critique of cultural explanations of development are used to argue for plural identities. The chapter then defends encyclopedic museums, tracing the British Museum to Enlightenment encyclopedias and cosmopolitanism, and closes with the Art Institute of Chicago as a museum serving a diverse city. It concludes that museums should argue against nationalist laws and show the hybridity of culture in their displays.

East and Southeast Asia Japan appears as the contrast to Italy: its cultural property law ranks objects into National Treasures, Important Cultural Properties and Registered Tangible Cultural Properties, and leaves about 95 percent of ranked objects open to export. South Korea appears in Sen's critique of Huntington, which compares it with Ghana in the 1960s. China is named only as one of three nations whose laws Cuno criticises.

British MuseumArt Institute of Chicago
EpiloguePDF p. 127

The epilogue returns to the book's question, Who Owns Antiquity?, and answers that antiquity belongs to all humankind rather than to modern states. Cuno tests the alternative of international trusteeship through UNESCO, reviewing its 1970 Convention, the United States' withdrawal in 1984 and return in 2003, and the Intergovernmental Committee for restitution, and finds the organization limited by its member states. Cuno turns to archaeologists, who depend on nation-states for access, and proposes partage, the sharing of finds, together with Merryman's triad of preservation, knowledge and access as better principles. The argument then turns to globalization, which Cuno illustrates with his first visit to the Louvre in 1970 and with the history of communications since then, and with Thomas Friedman's and Nayan Chanda's accounts of interconnection. It ends by claiming that a common culture, ancient and interconnected, belongs to everyone and should be preserved and shared.

Louvre
Afterword to the Paperback EditionPDF p. 138Asia: in part

Cuno's afterword, written for the 2009 paperback, updates the book's case and answers its critics. It reports the outcome of China's 2005 request to the United States, which the Bush administration accepted in modified form in January 2009, and the sale of the Summer Palace zodiac bronzes, which Cuno presents as political acts of Chinese nationalism. He then turns to Xinjiang, where the Han share of the population has risen and the old city of Kashgar is being demolished, and to the 2008 violence there. He also revisits the United States' withdrawal from UNESCO in 1984 and return in 2003, both presented as matters of national self-interest. Cuno answers the charges of imperialism and colonialism by arguing that encyclopedic museums are products of the Enlightenment and that their collections were largely acquired legally on the terms of their time. Cuno defends a cosmopolitan view drawing on Diogenes, Hume, Nussbaum and Edward Said, and argues for long-term loans and exchange in place of ownership. Cuno concludes that the legal regime should be softened, since national culture is always hybrid.

East and Southeast Asia Most of the afterword's East Asian material concerns China. Cuno says the Bush administration accepted a modified Chinese request for import restrictions on January 14, 2009, covering material from the Paleolithic to the Tang dynasty, and calls the decision political. Cuno traces the 2000 purchase of the Yuanmingyuan Zodiac heads by the Poly Museum, a Christie's auction in Paris of two heads owned by Yves Saint Laurent and Pierre Bergé, and the 2008 violence and the demolition of old Kashgar in Xinjiang.

Cvetkovski, Roland; Hofmeister, Alexis (eds.) (2014). An Empire of Others: Creating Ethnographic Knowledge in Imperial Russia and the USSR. Budapest: Central European University Press.Asia: slight10 chapter overviews

Overview

An edited volume (2014) on how ethnographic knowledge was made in imperial Russia and the USSR. Its editors, Roland Cvetkovski and Alexis Hofmeister, argue that ethnography was not a neutral cultural technique but a knowledge culture formed in particular milieus, and that its categories were built into state policy from the 1897 census onwards. The eleven chapters, grouped as Paradigms, Representations and Peoples, cover physical anthropology, Marxism and ethnogenesis, the 1910 Russian Ethnographic Museum, children in museum and school folklore, Ukrainian folklore, Ingush and Chechen ethnography, the Crimean Karaites and Siberia. Most cases fall in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries and the Stalin years, and are set in the Russian Empire, Siberia, Central Asia and the Caucasus.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia are marginal here. No chapter is about either region, and the chapter notes mark none of them as a main or part treatment of East Asia. The clearest material lies on the Siberian and Far Eastern frontier, in Sergey Glebov's chapter 'Siberian Ruptures' (lines 12075-13437, listed in the contents only under Part III). It covers the Sibiriakov expedition of 1894-96, led by Klements, who left Irkutsk for an expedition in Mongolia, the Ussuri region, and the figure of Dersu Uzala, and it describes Siberia as bordering on China and Mongolia (line 12128).

Cvetkovski's chapter on the 1910 trial exhibition of the Russian Ethnographic Museum (lines 9027-10852) is the other concentration. The fourth hall showed the 'non-Russian tribes' of the Kalmyk, Buryat, Mongolian, Chinese and even Japanese peoples (lines 10535-10538), and Chinese items from the Ussuri region were in the third hall (line 10534). Objects were registered by collection in the 'Stockholm system', so that a purchased Chinese collection of A.V. Vereshchagin and a Buddhist collection of E.E. Ukhtomskii were kept as separate groups (lines 10391-10434). Mogilner's chapter on physical anthropology (lines 3501-5297) lists 'Mongolo-Manchuria tribes' among the Mongoloids in Alektorov's 1906 survey (line 3600), and in Smirnov's 1901 plan for a St Petersburg museum the Mongols, Kalmyks, Buryats, Chinese and Manchu fall under the 'yellow race' (lines 5019-5023).

Hofmeister's chapter (lines 1098-2234) mentions Northeast Asia only through Kotzebue's voyages (line 1887) and compares Russia with China as states that have not faced their colonial pasts (line 1244). Southeast Asia does not appear at all. Central Asia (Abashin on Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, lines 6288-7382) is outside this question and is noted only as a contrast.

Contents

Theoretical approach of this work
Table of ContentsPDF p. 5
Introduction: On the Making of Ethnographic Knowledge in RussiaRoland Cvetkovskip. 1

Cvetkovski introduces an edited volume on how ethnographic knowledge was made in Russia, arguing against Konrad Köstlin's view that ethnography can serve as a neutral cultural technique separate from politics. In imperial and Soviet Russia, ethnic categories were built into state policy, from the 1897 census listing 130 nationalities to Bolshevik efforts at a 'conquest of difference'. Cvetkovski proposes a knowledge history that treats ethnography as fluid and plural, produced in particular milieus such as the Rumiantsev circle, the Imperial Russian Geographical Society and physical anthropology. The contributions cover photography, maps, museums and children as subjects of ethnography, along with the Caucasus, Karaite Jews in Crimea, Siberia and Ukraine. The introduction closes by arguing that a historian of knowledge must also reflect on their own knowledge culture.

Russian Museum, ethnographic sectionState Museum of Ethnography
Imperial Case Studies: Russian and British Ethnographic TheoryAlexis Hofmeisterp. 23

Hofmeister compares how ethnographic knowledge was gathered and theorized in two imperial settings, Britain and Russia. Hofmeister argues that a maritime empire with a global civilizing mission needed a universal theory of ethnic difference, whereas the land-based tsarist empire, facing many local situations, never developed one. The chapter first traces the German-speaking origins of the terms Völkerkunde, ethnography and anthropology, through August Ludwig Schlözer and the Göttingen circle. It then turns to Britain, where the Ethnological Society, the Anthropological Society and the Royal Anthropological Institute, together with the Notes and Queries questionnaire, shaped a discipline led by marginal figures such as Prichard, Tylor and Haddon, and later Malinowski and Radcliffe-Brown. For Russia it examines the Second Kamchatka Expedition, the ethnographic section of the Russian Geographical Society and exiled ethnographers such as Sieroszewski and Shternberg. The conclusion is that Russian ethnography offered detailed but unsystematic description of a diversity-in-(imperial)-unity, while British anthropology ranked peoples on a ladder of civilization.

Museum of Anthropology and Ethnography, St PetersburgPitt Rivers Museum
Part I. Paradigmsp. 51
Beyond, against, and with Ethnography: Physical Anthropology as a Science of Russian ModernityMarina Mogilnerp. 81

Mogilner argues that Russian physical anthropology, usually dismissed as marginal, shaped how the empire classified its peoples, and that it developed in tension with ethnography rather than apart from it. Mogilner follows the disputes from the 1860s to the 1910s across three centres: the Moscow Imperial Society of Lovers of Natural Sciences, Anthropology and Ethnography, the St Petersburg circle around Petri, Koropchevskii and Volkov (Vovk), and the Kazan school. Mogilner’s cases include Anuchin's 1899 racial study of Pushkin, the 1892-96 Multan trial of Votiaks, where the ethnographer Smirnov and the anthropologist Khomiakov drew opposing conclusions, and the Kiev anthropological society that imperial officials refused because they feared ethnography's nationalist uses. Mogilner also examines a planned St Petersburg ethnographic museum arranged by racial category. Moscow's liberal 'mixed physical type' lost its purpose as the empire collapsed, and after 1917 anthropologists survived by offering the Bolsheviks productive-force and population studies. The chapter concludes that Soviet physical anthropology never became a critical reflection on race.

Russian Museum, St Petersburg (planned ethnographic section)
Ethnography, Marxism, and Soviet IdeologySergei Alymovp. 121

Alymov revisits the introduction of Marxism into Soviet ethnography, usually described as the discipline's fall in 1928-1932, and follows Francine Hirsch in reading it as the invention of a Soviet ethnography. Alymov traces two routes by which Marxism entered the field, the sociological history of societal forms taught in the communist universities and Nikolai Marr's Japhetic theory, and then the campaign led by Aptekar' against bourgeois ethnology. Alymov’s central case is Pavel Kushner, whose Gornaia Kirgiziia (1929), a study of the Kyrgyz manap, was attacked by economists for failing to find classes, and whose career was damaged by the dispute. Alymov then follows the 1930s monographs of Potapov on the Altai and Dolgikh on the Ket, which applied the formation scheme to survivals of clan life, and Tokarev's work on Yakut and Oirot society. Alymov argues that the formation paradigm weakened from the 1940s, when ethnographers turned to pre-colonial history and to the positive socialist present, and that Bromley's later definition of ethnos ended the Marxist framework.

Ethnogenesis and Historiography: Historical Narratives for Central Asia in the 1940s and 1950sSergey Abashinp. 145

Abashin examines how the two volumes of the History of the Peoples of Uzbekistan, published in 1947 and 1950, shaped Soviet ethnography in Central Asia. Rather than treating ethnography as a tool of power, he describes it as an autonomous zone in which institutions, careers and disputes continually redefine what counts as ethnography. The chapter follows three scholars involved in the project. Semenov, whose 1925 article on Aryan monuments in Tajikistan was denounced in 1949 as pan-Iranian, later moved to Tajikistan. Iakubovskii, whose 1941 pamphlet on Uzbek ethnogenesis offered a compromise between Turkic and Iranian roots. Tolstov, director of the Institute of Ethnography, whose Marrist account of mixed origins shaped the revised History of the Uzbek SSR (1955-56). Abashin shows how the notion of narod became central to these arguments about titular nations. Abashin concludes that the Marrist ethnogenesis Tolstov championed won through institutional struggle, and that ethnography as a discipline was formed in these very debates.

Part II. Representationsp. 171
Empire Complex: Arrangements in the Russian Ethnographic Museum, 1910Roland Cvetkovskip. 211

Cvetkovski asks how the Russian Ethnographic Museum in St Petersburg, founded in 1902 and opened to the public only in 1923, tried to turn its ethnographic objects into a picture of the Russian Empire. The chapter argues that the museum's founders assumed objects could carry imperial knowledge by themselves, and that this assumption failed. Cvetkovski traces the 1901 committee debates, in which Slavophile and geographical models of classification were argued out and a cultural-geographical arrangement centred on the Great Russians was adopted. The second case is collecting: expeditions, purchases from local collectors, and the 'Stockholm system' of storage, which grouped objects by collection rather than by region. The third is the 1910 trial exhibition in six halls, which the contemporary reviewer V.V. Bogdanov criticised for fragmentary everyday scenes and faceless mannequins. The chapter concludes that the museum did not mirror the imperial self but represented the Other, and that the objects produced a kind of equality among peoples rather than a clear imperial message.

Russian Ethnographic MuseumKunstkamera (Academy of Sciences Museum of Anthropology and Ethnography)Rumiantsev MuseumPitt Rivers MuseumMuseum fur Volkerkunde Berlin
Learning about the Nation: Ethnographic Representations of Children, Representations of Ethnography for ChildrenCatriona Kellyp. 253

Kelly examines how Russian ethnography, and especially ethnographic museums, has represented children, who were central to the discipline's idea of the narod yet largely invisible within it. The chapter argues that children were treated as objects of adult shaping rather than as subjects with experience of their own, and that their representation followed the changing needs of state education. Kelly traces folklore collecting and child-oriented studies from the 1880s, the school essays and questionnaires of the 1900s and 1920s, and the Stalinist turn to folklore after the 1936 decree against pedology. The longest case is the State Museum of Ethnography in Leningrad, whose schools commission, excursions and 'narrative' tours, such as 'The Fate of Little Maison', set a Soviet present against a tsarist past. Kelly concludes that the picture of unchanging rural folk life, taught to children through museums and school folklore, proved more durable than the adult-centred ethnography that produced it.

State Museum of Ethnography (Leningrad)Russian Ethnographic MuseumKunstkamera
Part III. Peoplesp. 281
Concepts of Ukrainian Folklore and the Transition from Imperial Russia to Stalin’s Soviet EmpireAngela Rustemeyerp. 311

Rustemeyer examines Ukrainian folklore studies in the transition from late imperial Russia to Stalinism, asking how ethnographers working on Ukrainians handled ideas of time, space and class. The chapter argues that folklore was never ideologically neutral: it could build national identity under the tsars and, in the 1920s, be made to naturalize Marxist class categories. Rustemeyer first criticizes the Soviet and Ukrainian national histories of the discipline, which personalize the field into heroes and opponents. Two case studies follow. The first is the chumak, the Ukrainian salt trader, whose songs were filed as 'wage earners' songs' and read as evidence of exploitation in a monetary economy. The second is the miracle legends of 1920s Right and Left Bank Ukraine, which the journal Etnohrafichnyi visnyk treated as signs of crisis and subversion. The journal was closed as Soviet nationalities policy moved towards Soviet patriotism. Rustemeyer concludes that Soviet ethnography helped turn folklore into a tool of political diagnosis, and points to interwar Polish ethnography as a parallel case.

No Love Affair: Ingush and Chechen Imperial EthnographiesChristian Dettmeringp. 341

Dettmering asks how ethnographic knowledge of the Chechens and Ingush shaped Russian policy in the North Caucasus, and whether it changed the outcome. The chapter argues that ethnography served army needs: it was commissioned to find customary law, elders and clans that could be set against Islamic law and Muslim leaders. Dettmering traces the commanders' accounts of Chechen and Ingush raids, the attempts to co-opt elders and princes, and the resettlement of clans after the Shali affair and the deportations of the 1860s. A long section follows on language policy, in which Uslar's Cyrillic alphabets were meant to weaken Islam, and which lapsed under a new viceroy. Ethnographers also merged the Ingush into the Chechen people in the 1870s, a decision the administration then applied to the Ingush as well. Dettmering concludes that ethnography impeded rather than improved policy towards the Vainakh peoples.

National Inventions: The Imperial Emancipation of the Karaites from JewishnessMikhail Kizilovp. 369

Kizilov examines how the Crimean Karaites, a community of Jewish origin, came to define themselves as a non-Jewish people in the nineteenth century. Kizilov starts with the Crimea's transformation after the Russian annexation of 1783, when Christian and Muslim populations left and colonists arrived, and with the Karaite petitions that won exemptions from double taxation and military service, since officials valued the community as a tool against the Talmudic Jews. The turning point was the 1839 inquiry by Governor-General Vorontsov, which demanded historical proof of their privileges. The central case is Abraham Firkovich, whose expedition took manuscripts from a Krymchak synagogue geniza and then forged colophons and tombstone dates at Chufut-Kale and Mangup, including the spurious grave of Isaac Sangari. Kizilov follows the Khazar and Kypchak theories that Szapszal and later Karaite scholars built on these foundations, and argues that the community's de-Judaization was a constructed national ideology. Kizilov ends by drawing lessons for historians of ethnic identity.

Damousi, Joy; Tout-Smith, Deborah; Ziino, Bart (eds.) (2020). Museums, History and the Intimate Experience of the Great War: Love and Sorrow. London: Routledge.Asia: slight12 chapter overviews

Overview

An edited volume of eleven essays by historians and museum curators on Australia and the First World War, published in 2020 alongside Museums Victoria’s Love and Sorrow exhibition (shown 2014–2018). The editors argue that the war was fought in the senses and emotions as well as on the battlefield, and that its intimate, family-centred experience has been hidden from public view. Chapters cover the soundscapes of the war, the generals Pompey Elliott and John Monash, the home front, facial wounds, family caregiving, difficult family histories, the emotional turn in military history, the historiography of trauma, the exhibition’s curation and visitor response, and online learning. The book has four parts: battlefront and home front, bearing wounds, historians’ own emotions, and the museum.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia are barely present. The editors’ introduction does not mention them, and most chapters do not either. The only sustained passing references come in chapter 7, Peter Stanley’s “‘Gonzo’ Historians and the Emotional turn in Australian Military History”. Stanley describes the Australian War Memorial’s 1945: War & Peace display of paybook photographs of Australians who died on the Sandakan death marches in Borneo, set beside artefacts from the Sandakan prisoner-of-war camp, which drew visitors to tears. He also notes that the Memorial’s World War II gallery displayed the possessions of Jan Ruff-O’Herne, who had survived months of sexual abuse in a Japanese brothel, and he names Hank Nelson and Tim Bowden’s POW: Australians Under Nippon as one of the phenomena that made emotion academically acceptable.

Japan appears once more, in chapter 6. Alistair Thomson notes that Hector Thomson’s sons, David and Colin, served with the occupation force in Japan after the war, and that in that period Hector sold his failing farm. Otherwise the Asian references are incidental.

No chapter discusses Asian museums, collections, heritage policy, visitors, curators or scholars, or restitution. The objects and families of Love and Sorrow, as described, are Australian, British and German. Southeast Asian and East Asian experiences of the war and its museums are outside the book’s scope.

JapanBorneo (Sandakan)
