Introduction: War, Emotion and the MuseumJoy Damousi, Deborah Tout-Smith and Bart Ziinop. 1

The introduction frames this collection of essays on Australia and the First World War. It argues that the war was fought in the emotions and the senses as well as on the battlefield, and that the intimate experience of soldiers and civilians has long been hidden from public view. The book takes its occasion from Love and Sorrow, the Museums Victoria exhibition shown from 2014 to 2018, which set out to challenge triumphant stories of nationhood and military prowess by showing the physical and family costs of war. The editors place family relations at the centre of the war's emotional history and draw on scholarship on emotion since the 1990s. They explain the four parts of the book, which cover the emotions of the battlefield and home front, the bearing of wounds, historians' own emotions in writing the war, and the museum itself. Essays on Pompey Elliott, John Monash, facial wounds and family carers fill those parts. The introduction closes by arguing that the intimate war survives in private mementoes and that its emotional weight must still be shown long after the fighting ended.

Museums Victoria
Part I: Emotions in Conflict: On the Battlefield and at Homep. 7
11 Emotions and Memory in the Soundscapes of World War IJoy Damousip. 9

Damousi asks how sound shaped the experience and memory of the First World War for soldiers and civilians. The chapter opens with the physician John Springthorpe, whose wartime writing called the battlefield 'Hell Sound', and with the cotton wool used to muffle shellfire in casualty clearing stations. It then works through three cases. On the battlefield, the Somme bombardment and the Messines mines were recalled by memoirists such as Aubrey Wade as a shaking of the ground. Birdsong, recorded in ornithological reports, could comfort, anger or amuse soldiers. The London Zeppelin raids of 1915 form the third case, where the noise of the raids and the warnings given by pheasants and owls shaped civilian fear and memory. Damousi also traces deafness as a form of shell shock, noting that it was treated as less debilitating than blindness, so that support and employment for deafened veterans attracted little attention. The conclusion turns to the silence after the Armistice, which for some bereaved families opened decades of private grief. Sound, the chapter argues, is central to a cultural history of the war's emotions.

22 Pompey Elliott, Australia’s Emotional GeneralRoss McMullinp. 28

McMullin follows Harold 'Pompey' Elliott, commander of the 15th Brigade, through letters and diaries that show how emotional volatility ran alongside Elliott's reputation as Australia's most famous fighting general. Letters to Kate Elliott, written during five years apart, are candid about the men lost at Gallipoli, Lone Pine and Fromelles, where one night cost 5533 Australian casualties, and about the mud and sickness of the 1916-17 winter. The chapter traces a cycle of exhilaration in battle followed by collapse, including grief after the death of Elliott's brother George at Polygon Wood and bitterness at being passed over for promotion after Villers-Bretonneux. It then turns to the suicide in 1931, which McMullin links to a head injury from a riding accident, post-traumatic stress, the Depression and worry over returned soldiers. The chapter ends with a quotation from Elliott on the sights and sounds of war and with the argument that Elliott deserved better remembrance than was given.

33 For the Duration: Surviving World War I: at HomeBart Ziinop. 48

Ziino examines how Australians at home endured the war, using letters that passed between John Monash in France and his family and friends in Melbourne. The chapter argues that anxiety and grief were central to the home front, and that love tied the two fronts together under an open-ended war. Drawing on letters from Monash's wife, daughter, cousins and business associates, Ziino traces how the strain of waiting grew from the Gallipoli landing through the Somme and the conscription votes, which divided families and produced accusations of shirking. Gallipoli letters show pride mixed with fear, while casualty lists and censored or delayed mail made the war feel closer. From late 1917 requests to Monash to remove sons and brothers from the front became more frequent, and were framed in terms of ill health and loss. The chapter ends with the Armistice, which brought relief and gratitude, and argues that the strain of the home front left traces on those who had stayed behind.

Part II: Bearing the Wounds of Warp. 65
44 A Familiar Face: Wartime Facial Wounds and William KearseyKerry Nealep. 67

Neale uses the case of William Kearsey, an Australian wounded in the face at the Third Battle of Ypres in 1917, to write about disfigurement and veterans' lives. The chapter describes the Queen's Hospital at Sidcup, opened in 1917 under Harold Gillies, where surgeons treated thousands of facial wounds, and where Tonks and Lindsay painted the patients. It turns to the reactions of nurses, orderlies and journalists, who found the men repellent or overwhelming, and to the view that disfigurement drew revulsion where other disabilities drew sympathy. Neale weighs the tragic case of Henry Nodrum, who died from nicotine poisoning in 1933, against Kearsey's resilience as a sheep farmer in New South Wales who married late and raised an adopted son. Neale also describes the family contact that led to Kearsey's story being told in Museums Victoria's Love and Sorrow exhibition. It ends by arguing that facially wounded veterans were long neglected in histories and that their experience helps in understanding the wounds of recent conflicts.

Museums Victoria
55 War Disability and the Centenary of Family CaregivingMarina Larssonp. 88

Larsson examines how the centenary of World War I led Australian museums to show war disability and family caregiving that the Anzac legend had obscured. Museums Victoria's Love and Sorrow exhibition is the leading example, presenting shell shock, limblessness and facial disfigurement alongside family mementoes. Larsson notes that the Australian War Memorial had judged a disability exhibition too confronting only two decades earlier, and that a modest facial wounds section later appeared in its revised gallery. The chapter then turns to the wives and mothers who nursed disabled veterans at home and kept households going on inadequate pensions, a labour hidden by the Repatriation Department's preference for photographs of men at work. About 90,000 men were receiving disability pensions by 1920, and the chapter argues that the care they needed was largely unpaid family labour. The chapter closes with the 2016 'Rosemary' statue at Ascot Vale, which commemorates women carers and makes their labour visible.

Museums VictoriaAustralian War Memorial
Part III: Emotions in Histories of World War Ip. 97
66 Searching for Hector Thomson: Telling Difficult Family War HistoriesAlistair Thomsonp. 99

Thomson uses the story of his grandfather Hector, a Gippsland farmer and Light Horse veteran, to show how hard family war histories are to write. Hector was described as 'in and out of mental hospital' in the author's draft of Anzac Memories, and at his father's insistence the phrase was softened, a change the chapter treats as undercutting the book's own argument about silenced histories. Family war stories, the chapter argues, are shaped by the Anzac legend, by wartime letters that reassured rather than informed, and by postmemory once veterans are gone. The main case study uses Repatriation files to trace Hector's malaria, a diagnosis of encephalitis lethargica, later mental illness, and Nell Thomson's campaign for a pension until her death in 1932. The files show that a claim often turned on whether a physical war cause was accepted. The chapter ends by urging family and public historians to question family myths and use the full archive.

77 “Gonzo” Historians and the Emotional turn in Australian Military HistoryPeter Stanleyp. 123

Stanley traces how emotion entered Australian military history and its museums, a shift he dates to the 1990s. Drawing on his years at the Australian War Memorial from 1980 to 2007, he describes the Sandakan paybook wall in the 1945: War & Peace exhibition, which moved visitors to tears, and the Memorial's 1995 Gallery Master Plan, which asked galleries to engage 'visitors' intellect, imagination and emotion'. He sets this beside the social history and 'New Military History' of the 1960s and 1970s, citing Keegan's The Face of Battle and Browning's Ordinary Men. His central example is Alistair Thomson's Anzac Memories, which Stanley calls 'gonzo' history, a term borrowed from Hunter S. Thompson for historians who write themselves into their stories. He then discusses Bruce Scates's pilgrimage books and the criticism by McKenna and Ward of 'sentimental nationalism'. Stanley concludes that historians have so far studied mainly grief and bereavement, that lighter emotions remain largely unexplored, and that whether emotional history makes better history is for the future to decide.

East and Southeast Asia Stanley mentions the region only in passing. The 1945: War & Peace exhibition displayed paybook photographs of Australians who died on the Sandakan death marches in Borneo, and the Memorial's World War II gallery showed the possessions of Jan Ruff-O'Herne, who had been held in a Japanese brothel. He cites Hank Nelson's POW: Australians Under Nippon as a text on prisoners of the Japanese.

Australian War MemorialMuseums Victoria
88 Distance, Intimacy and Identification : Reflections on Writing a History of TraumaTracey Loughranp. 136

Loughran, a historian of shell shock, reflects on how her own identification with the First World War shaped her work. Loughran opens with Doris Lessing's novel-memoir Alfred and Emily to frame 'familial histories', which she distinguishes from the popular boom in family research. Loughran surveys revisionist historians such as Brian Bond and Dan Todman, who distrust emotion and post-war fiction, and sets against them Ziino's and Thomson's arguments that family memory actively composes national myths. Loughran’s central case is her own teenage identification with Billy Prior, the working-class officer in Pat Barker's Regeneration, which she links to her own silence and self-harm. Loughran describes how her doctoral thesis on medical texts did not turn out as planned, and how the death of her younger brother while her book was at proof stage changed how she wrote it. The chapter concludes that trauma is found in silences that sources cannot hold, and that empathy must be balanced with empiricism. It ends by rejecting the 'emollient lie that time heals'.

Part IV: World War I: In The Museum: Love and Sorrow at Museums Victoriap. 151
99 After One Hundred Years: Exhibiting World War IDeborah Tout-Smithp. 153

Tout-Smith, the curator of Museums Victoria's World War I: Love and Sorrow exhibition, explains how the show was built around personal lives and emotional responses rather than military or political history. Its structure is eight personal stories followed through the war, a Glencorse Wood panorama and interactive that names soldiers from all sides, and a closing scene at a present-day Anzac Day service. Her main cases are the Kemp family, whose butcher Albert was killed in 1917 and never found; the Roberts family, whose undelivered baby bootie became the exhibition's most affecting object; John Hargreaves's diary, with its missing final pages; and the Demant brothers, whose German family's story runs through war and Kristallnacht. She argues that setting dissonant voices side by side unsettles victor-centred narratives. The chapter then reports visitor evaluation, including a survey in which 97 per cent of visitors said they were made to think about the war's impact on Australian society, and concludes that emotional engagement changes minds and that the meanings of the war will keep being remade.

Museums Victoria
1010 “Sticky” Objects, Faces and Voices in the Museum: Love and Sorrow’s Use of Affective Interpretation Strategies to Challenge Masculinist Commemorations of World War IAndrea Witcombp. 171

Witcomb argues that Museums Victoria's Love and Sorrow, though not a women's history exhibition, uses the family to challenge the masculinist Anzac legend. Witcomb reviews critics of the legend, who see its emotional language as producing sentimentality, and sets against them social historians such as Larsson and Luckins, whose work on families and women at home treats emotion as a resource for critique. Witcomb then identifies four interpretive strategies in the exhibition: following eight biographies through the emotions of love and sorrow, using faces and voices, anchoring these to 'sticky' objects in Ahmed's sense, and bringing a descendant on screen as witness. Drawing on Gibbs on mimetic communication and on Holocaust testimony theory, she explains how visitors become witnesses. Her three detailed cases are the Roberts family and Ruby's returned bootie, the Kemp family and the Glencorse Wood panorama, and Eliza Amery, whose grief after her son Alex's death in France ended in a suspected suicide. The chapter concludes that these strategies make a 'pedagogy of feeling' that offers critical history at its best.

Museums Victoria
1111 “The Stories Are Like Magnets”: Love and Sorrow and the Engagement of On-Line LearningBruce Scates and Margaret Harrisp. 190

Scates and Harris examine World War One: A History in 100 Stories, a free online course run through FutureLearn, which drew more than 50,000 enrolments over nine runs. They show how it was built alongside Museums Victoria's Love and Sorrow exhibition, sharing its opening panorama of Glencorse Wood, its objects such as Ruby Roberts's undelivered bootie, and its focus on individual lives. They describe the course's silent three-minute keynote presentations, which the Anzac Centenary advisory board contested. The board's wish to avoid the Frank Wilkinson story, of a soldier settler who murdered his family before killing himself, shows the pressures at work. From forum posts, the authors trace learners drawn in by family history and fictive kinship, disputes over the Aboriginal digger Alex McKinnon's medals, British objections to an Australian-made course, and Turkish responses to the Atatürk statue at Chunuk Bair. They argue that online learning creates emotional communities that neither teacher nor curator controls, and that the course's real achievement lay in the independent research it prompted.

Denton, Kirk A. (2014). Exhibiting the Past: Historical Memory and the Politics of Museums in Postsocialist China. Honolulu: University of Hawai‘i Press.Asia: central13 chapter overviews

Overview

Denton's book examines how museums in the People's Republic of China display the past from the Maoist era to the 2010s. Its main argument is that state museums remain tied to party politics, but that their narratives have been remodelled under market reform rather than abandoned: revolutionary history is commodified, nostalgia is used for the Republican and imperial past, and red tourism, martyrdom and Confucian values are brought in. The book reads visual language, architecture and location (a narratological method) across history, revolutionary, military, martyrs', literature and ethnographic museums, red-tourism sites and urban planning halls. The introduction traces museum building from the late nineteenth century to the 1990s boom, and the conclusion ends on the 'museums of the future'.

East and Southeast Asia in this work central

East Asia is the whole subject. Every chapter concerns museums and memorial sites in the People's Republic of China: the National Museum of China and its Road to Revival exhibit (introduction, chapters 1 and 2), the Museum of the Chinese Revolution (chapter 2), the Red Crag sites in Chongqing, the Humen naval museums and the Nanjing Presidential Palace (chapter 3), the Longhua and Yuhuatai martyrs' parks (chapter 4), the Beijing Military Museum (chapter 5), the Wanping, Nanjing and Unit 731 museums of the Japanese occupation (chapter 6), the Lu Xun memorial halls and the Modern Literature Museum (chapter 8), minority museums in Yunnan, Guizhou and Beijing (chapter 9), red-tourism sites at Jinggangshan, Shaoshan and Xibaipo (chapter 10), and the Shanghai, Suzhou and Chongqing planning halls (chapter 11).

Taiwan, Japan, South Korea and Hong Kong appear mainly as comparison or contrast. The introduction surveys the Seoul War Memorial and Japanese museums that range from whitewashing the war to documenting atrocities. The Koguryo dispute with Korea is treated in chapter 1, and the Korean War exhibit in the Beijing Military Museum is set against the Yushukan at Yasukuni and Japan's peace museums in chapter 5. The Palace Museum in Taipei and a Taiwan prehistory museum are noted in the introduction and chapter 1, and a Hong Kong retrocession countdown clock sits between Beijing museums in chapter 11.

Southeast Asia is slight. Nanyue, a Guangzhou kingdom that reached northern Vietnam, appears in chapter 1, Hanoi's Museum of the Vietnamese Revolution is named in chapter 2, and Vietnamese and Ho Chi Minh City delegations are mentioned in chapters 9 and 11. The book does not treat Asian objects in Western museums, colonial collecting, or restitution claims.

Introductionp. 1Asia: chiefly

Denton opens with the 2011 reopening of the National Museum of China in Beijing, whose modern-history exhibit Road to Revival presents the Chinese Communist Party as the driving force of national revival, and sets it beside an Enlightenment exhibit and luxury-brand shows that she reads as the 'multiple faces' of postsocialist China. Denton’s argument is that museums remain tightly tied to party-state politics, but that state narratives have changed under market reform, and she insists that the state should not be written out of accounts of popular memory. Denton traces the modern museum's links to nation-building and to Soviet models, and sketches three bursts of museum building, after 1958, after the Cultural Revolution and after 1989. The book's method is narratological, reading the visual language, architecture and location of museums, and the book covers history, military, ethnographic and literature museums, red tourism, and urban planning halls. She ends with the rise of private and city-branding museums in a leisure economy.

East and Southeast Asia The whole book concerns China. The introduction covers the National Museum of China's 2011 Road to Revival exhibit, the Nantong Museum founded in 1906, the Palace Museum in Beijing and its Taipei counterpart, and museum-building bursts since 1958. It also surveys museums in South Korea (the Seoul War Memorial), Taiwan and Japan, where displays range from whitewashing the war to documenting war crimes.

National Museum of ChinaPalace Museum (Beijing)Nantong MuseumMuseum of the Chinese RevolutionMilitary MuseumJianchuan Museum Cluster
1Chapter 1. National Origins and Local Identity: Museums of Premodern Historyp. 27Asia: chiefly

Denton asks how museums of premodern history built a national origin story for the People's Republic, and how that story has shifted since the 1980s. Denton follows the Museum of Chinese History (later part of the National Museum of China) through its exhibit changes: a 1950s Marxist sequence of primitive, slave and feudal society, a Cultural Revolution merger with the Museum of the Chinese Revolution, and a late-1990s dynastic arrangement that presents the imperial past as glory. Denton argues that archaeology, which supplies museum collections, has been used to claim territory, as in the dispute with Korea over Koguryo, and that the 2011 Ancient China hall stresses cultural continuity and a 'common spiritual homeland'. The chapter then turns to local culture museums, which since the 1980s have multiplied with claims to plural origins of Chinese civilization, for example at Liangzhu, Sanxingdui and Nanyue. Denton concludes that these local narratives can fit national ones, but also express nostalgia in response to globalization and to the decline of socialism.

East and Southeast Asia The chapter is about China's premodern museums: the Ancient China hall of 2011, the Museum of Chinese History (opened to the public in 1926 and rehoused on Tiananmen Square in 1961), the Military Museum's premodern exhibit added in 1988, and local museums for the Liangzhu, Hongshan, Sanxingdui and Ba and Shu cultures. It also treats the Koguryo/Gaojuli dispute with Korea over an ancient kingdom, and the Nanyue kingdom of Guangzhou, which reached northern Vietnam.

National Museum of ChinaMuseum of Chinese HistoryChinese Military MuseumSanxingdui MuseumLiangzhu Culture MuseumMuseum of the Western Han King of Nanyue
2Chapter 2. Exhibiting the Revolution: The Museum of the Chinese Revolutionp. 45Asia: chiefly

Denton traces how the Museum of the Chinese Revolution in Beijing has exhibited the revolution from the late Qing to the present. The chapter opens with the Nationalist commemoration of the 1911 revolution, using the Revolutionary Memorial Hall at the 1929 West Lake Exposition in Hangzhou to show that KMT and CCP commemoration share Leninist roots. The bulk of the chapter follows the Beijing museum from planning in the 1950s, when Central Committee meetings demanded a 'red line' of Mao's thought, through its closure during the Cultural Revolution, the post-Mao revisions of 1979 and 1990, and the 1996 Modern China exhibit, to the Road to Revival displays in the renovated National Museum of China in 2011. Denton draws on internal reports, Chang-tai Hung's history and the galleries themselves, from false walls to Mao quotations. Denton concludes that the displays changed in name and in their treatment of Mao, the KMT and the Republican era, while keeping the party at the center, and that Road to Revival passes over the Mao-era famines and the 1989 protests.

East and Southeast Asia The whole chapter concerns China, so its content is central here. It covers the 1929 West Lake Exposition in Hangzhou, where a Nationalist Revolutionary Memorial Hall stood beside commercial halls, and the Beijing Museum of the Chinese Revolution from its 1961 opening to the 2011 Road to Revival exhibit. It also notes the Jinchaji street exhibitions, the 1948 Northeast Martyrs Memorial Hall in Harbin, and the 1990s special exhibits on Rewi Alley and George Hatem.

Museum of the Chinese RevolutionNational Museum of ChinaRevolutionary Memorial Hall, West Lake Exposition, HangzhouMuseum of Chinese HistoryNortheast Martyrs Memorial Hall, Harbin
3Chapter 3. Commodification and Nostalgia: Revolutionary History in the Era of the Market Economyp. 75Asia: chiefly

Denton examines how revolutionary history museums in China have adapted to the market economy since the 1990s. The opening sets out the crisis identified by museum workers and state bodies, including weak funding and political appointees, and the red tourism and patriotic education campaigns that followed. The chapter then compares paired exhibits in which a popular display and an academic one compete on one site. At the Red Crag Revolutionary Memorial Hall in Chongqing, a Zhou Enlai-centered Red Crag Village display and a re-created Home of Democracy sit beside a conventional Southern Bureau exhibit, and the SACO controversy is downplayed. The Nanjing Presidential Palace presents the Republican era as the start of Chinese capitalism and largely drops class, while the Shanghai Municipal History Museum recreates old Shanghai in models and dioramas with no revolutionary narrative. Denton ends with the First CCP Congress site in Xintiandi, where party history is absorbed into nostalgia for old Shanghai.

East and Southeast Asia The whole chapter concerns China. It covers the Red Crag sites in Chongqing, where a Zhou Enlai-centered display and a re-created Home of Democracy sit beside a conventional Southern Bureau exhibit, and the SACO controversy is downplayed; the Opium War and Naval Battle museums at Humen in Guangdong; the Nanjing Presidential Palace, which presents KMT rule and Republican industry positively; and the Shanghai Municipal History Museum, whose models of old Shanghai recall a commercial past. It also covers the First CCP Congress site in Shanghai's Xintiandi district.

Red Crag Revolutionary Memorial Hall, ChongqingShanghai Municipal History MuseumNanjing Presidential PalaceFirst CCP Congress Meeting Hall, ShanghaiNaval Battle Museum, HumenOpium War Museum, Humen
4Chapter 4. Martyrdom and Memory: Monuments, Memorials, and Museums for Dead Heroesp. 95Asia: chiefly

Denton examines how the Chinese state uses martyrs in museums and memorial parks, arguing that martyrdom is a political construction that props up present legitimacy. The chapter begins with comparisons, setting Christian and Islamic martyrs and those of 9/11 beside Chinese examples, and then traces loyal martyrs such as Yue Fei and the late Qing and Republican cult of revolutionary martyrs, including the Huanghuagang memorial in Guangzhou. It shows how Mao-era martyrdom became a full cult through the Monument to the People's Heroes, the Martyrs Memorial Festival and state benefits for martyrs' families. The main case studies are the post-Mao Longhua Martyrs Memorial Park in Shanghai and the Yuhuatai Martyrs Memorial Park in Nanjing, read through their architecture, exhibits, Jiang Zemin's inscriptions and the Longhua website. Denton concludes that both parks frame sacrifice within modernization and red tourism, and that they keep alive a leftist memory the Shanghai history museum has erased.

East and Southeast Asia Most of the chapter concerns China. It studies the Longhua Martyrs Memorial Park in Shanghai, with its glass-pyramid hall, individual martyr displays and restored Nationalist execution ground, and the Yuhuatai park in Nanjing, with its Jiang Zemin inscription and closing display of modern Nanjing. It also covers the Yue Fei shrine on West Lake in Hangzhou, the Huanghuagang memorial to the 1911 martyrs in Guangzhou, the martyr monuments at the Huangpu Military Academy, and the Longhua website's virtual flowers.

Longhua Martyrs Memorial Park, ShanghaiYuhuatai Martyrs Memorial Park, NanjingHuanghuagang Memorial, GuangzhouYue Fei Shrine, HangzhouChangsha Martyrs Memorial Hall
5Chapter 5. Martial Glory and the Power of the State: Military Museumsp. 116Asia: chiefly

Denton asks what military museums do in the present, distinguishing those that glorify war from those that document its suffering, and then examines the Military Museum of the Chinese People's Revolution in Beijing. The chapter first surveys glorifying museums (the Yushukan at Yasukuni, American WWII museums, the War Memorial of Korea) against humanist ones (the Imperial War Museum, the Dresden Military History Museum). It then traces Chinese military culture from Qianlong's victory paintings through the Republican military academies to the militarized Mao era. The main case is the Beijing Military Museum, which opened in 1960 as one of the ten great structures, was revised after the Cultural Revolution, gained exhibits on ancient and early modern warfare in 1988, and added a contemporary PLA exhibit in 2010. Denton argues that the museum links imperial and Maoist military power to present state authority, and closes by noting its handling of Lin Biao and the army's role in 1989.

East and Southeast Asia The chapter argues that the Beijing Military Museum uses ancient Chinese warfare, from Sunzi to Qing paintings of Qianlong's victories, to justify strong state power. It covers the Korean War exhibit, which presents China as a peace-loving nation that entered the war reluctantly against American aggression, and the Huangpu Military Academy near Guangzhou. It contrasts the Yushukan Museum at Yasukuni Shrine, which presents a sanitized Asia-Pacific War, with Japan's peace museums in Hiroshima, Nagasaki and Osaka.

Military Museum of the Chinese People's Revolution, BeijingYushukan Museum, Yasukuni ShrineImperial War Museum, LondonWar Memorial of KoreaMilitary History Museum, Dresden
6Chapter 6. Heroic Resistance and Victims of Atrocity: Negotiating the Memory of Japanese Imperialismp. 133Asia: chiefly

Denton examines three museums in China that present the Japanese occupation, arguing that they combine two narratives: a heroic story of resistance that the Communist Party claims, and a newer story of victimhood that the state uses to build nationalist feeling. The chapter places this shift in the post-Mao rethinking of the war, the market economy, and the 'not forgetting national humiliation' campaigns of the 1990s, and it notes how atrocity displays borrow from Holocaust museums and from dark tourism. The War of Resistance Memorial Hall in Wanping, near the Marco Polo Bridge, is studied through its successive exhibitions, from an academic overview and atrocity dioramas to the 2005 Great Victory display, which Denton reads as a move toward confident nationalism. The Nanjing Massacre Memorial Hall is analyzed through Qi Kang's bleak design, its mother-and-child statues and the 2007 monumental expansion. The Unit 731 museum in Harbin is described for its authentic ruins and restrained displays. Denton concludes that these museums use horror to inscribe visitors in a shared national suffering.

East and Southeast Asia The whole chapter concerns China and Japan. It examines three Chinese museums of the occupation: the War of Resistance Memorial Hall in Wanping near Beijing, with its atrocity dioramas, tunnel-warfare display and 2005 Great Victory exhibit that adds Nationalist and Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau resistance; the Nanjing Massacre Memorial Hall, with Qi Kang's bleak design and 2007 expansion; and the Unit 731 Crimes Evidence Exhibition Hall at its original site in Pingfang, Heilongjiang, with its ruins and documentary film. It notes that the Nanjing mother-and-child statue echoes Japanese memorials at Hiroshima and Yasukuni.

Memorial Hall of the Chinese People's War of Resistance against Japan, WanpingMemorial to Victims of the Nanjing MassacreCrimes Evidence Exhibition Hall of Japanese Army Unit 731, Pingfang
7Chapter 7. Heroic Models and Exemplary Leaders: Memorial Hallsp. 153Asia: chiefly

Denton examines post-Mao memorial halls to heroic models and leaders, arguing that they revive a Confucian moralism to restore faith in the party after the Cultural Revolution and the 1989 protests. The chapter opens with Ha Jin's poem about a dead soldier who still asks after Mao, to show how the figure of the model has lost its meaning in the reform era. It then treats the cult of Lei Feng, from the Mao-era diary and campaign to the Lei Feng Memorial Hall in Fushun, Liaoning, where the displays stress Lei Feng's poverty, orphanhood and study, and an official article defends his place in the market economy. The Zhou Enlai Memorial Hall in Huai'an presents Zhou as a humanist figure, while the Deng Xiaoping Memorial Hall in Guang'an, Sichuan, uses a restrained design and personal memories, though it omits Deng's role in the Anti-Rightist campaign and in 1989. Denton concludes that the halls offer a humane face of party power and asks whether citizens still believe the myth.

East and Southeast Asia The whole chapter concerns China. It covers the Lei Feng Memorial Hall in Fushun, Liaoning, and the Lei Feng birthplace memorial in Wangcheng, Hunan; the Zhou Enlai Memorial Hall in Huai'an, Jiangsu, and the earlier Tianjin memorial to Zhou and Deng Yingchao; the Deng Xiaoping Memorial Hall in Guang'an, Sichuan; and the Chen Yun memorial in a village outside Shanghai. It also notes the Pingdingshan Massacre memorial and the Fushun War Prisoners Detention Center, which place Japanese atrocities and prisoners in the Fushun story.

Lei Feng Memorial Hall, FushunZhou Enlai Memorial Hall, Huai'anDeng Xiaoping Memorial Hall, Guang'anZhou Enlai-Deng Yingchao Memorial Hall, TianjinChen Yun Memorial Hall, near Shanghai
8Chapter 8. Literary Politics and Cultural Heritage: Modern Literature Museumsp. 177Asia: chiefly

Denton opens with a 1964 film scene set in a Lu Xun exhibition and a 2005 show on the writer Wang Xiaobo held in Beijing's Lu Xun Memorial Hall, and argues that state literature museums in the PRC help form a national canon of modern Chinese literature. The chapter traces how Lu Xun became the 'soul of the nation' through memorial halls founded in Shanghai, Beijing and Shaoxing in the 1950s, and how the Shaoxing hall and its redeveloped Old Home District now present him as a native son who serves local tourism. Lu Village, a theme park built on his stories and including a Madman Memorial Hall, is read as nostalgia that softens his critique. The second half examines the Beijing Museum of Modern Chinese Literature, which opened in 2001 from Ba Jin's archive proposal, and shows how its lobby murals, its seven 'great masters' and its chronology favour a May Fourth realist tradition and leave the Cultural Revolution blank. Denton concludes that these museums promote a socially engaged literary ideal while market nostalgia and official selection narrow what visitors see.

East and Southeast Asia The chapter is about the PRC throughout: the Lu Xun memorial halls in Shaoxing, Beijing, Shanghai, Xiamen and Guangzhou, the 2005 Wang Xiaobo exhibit in Beijing, the Lu Village theme park near Shaoxing, and the Modern Literature Museum in Beijing. It also notes premodern sites such as the Wenxuan Lou in Yangzhou and the Orchid Pavilion at Shaoxing, and says that Mao-era memorials excluded liberal writers.

Lu Xun Memorial Hall (Shaoxing)Lu Xun Memorial Hall (Beijing)Shanghai Lu Xun Memorial HallLu Village (Shaoxing)Modern Literature Museum (Beijing)Lu Xun Old Home District (Shaoxing)
9Chapter 9. Ethnic Minorities and the Construction of National Identity: Ethnographic Museumsp. 199Asia: chiefly

Denton asks how museums and theme parks in the PRC display the 'ethnic minorities' classified after 1949, mostly for Han visitors. Setting Western ethnographic museums beside the Soviet model that reached China in the 1950s, the chapter argues that minority cultures are shown as evidence of unity under a shared ideology and as a backward 'other' that Han-led modernization must uplift. It surveys state-funded museums such as the Yunnan Museum of Nationalities, the national ethnology museum that remains unbuilt, and the Beijing Nationalities Culture Palace, partly leased to merchants and used for political exhibits such as Tibet: Past and Present. The Chinese Nationalities Museum, a park of replica villages, makes the nation a miniature for Han tourists, and the Suojia Miao ecomuseum in Guizhou shows the limits of letting villagers represent themselves, since its staged performances feel forced. Denton concludes that even local and community displays are shaped by state priorities and tourism.

East and Southeast Asia The chapter concerns the PRC throughout: minority museums in Yunnan, Guangxi, Heilongjiang, Xinjiang, Tibet, Inner Mongolia, Guizhou and Beijing, and the Splendid China park in Shenzhen, which has replicas of Mongol and Tibetan sites. It discusses Yi, Miao, Dai, Mosuo and Tibetan representations, and mentions Vietnamese and Korean groups and the Taiwan aboriginal rights movement only in passing.

Yunnan Museum of Nationalities (Kunming)Chinese Nationalities Museum / Chinese Ethnic Culture Park (Beijing)Nationalities Culture Palace (Beijing)Suojia Miao Ecomuseum (Guizhou)Splendid China (Shenzhen)Mosuo Folk Culture Museum (Yunnan)
10Chapter 10. Revolutionary Memory and National Landscape: Red Tourismp. 214Asia: chiefly

Denton studies red tourism, the state-promoted visiting of revolutionary sites launched in 2004 as patriotic education and rural development. Denton argues that museums alone no longer make the revolution vivid for young people, and that red tourism fixes revolutionary memory onto the national landscape. Three sites are examined in turn: Jinggangshan, where Mao's poems are carved into the scenery and sung in rock versions of Cultural Revolution songs; the Hunan 'golden triangle' of memorial halls for Mao at Shaoshan, Liu Shaoqi at Huaminglou and Peng Dehuai, where Liu and Peng are Confucianized; and Xibaipo, where Hu Jintao's 2002 visit and his 'two duties' speech tie present leaders to the 1949 revolution. Group tours, wreaths, costumed photographs and commercial branding are described along the way. Denton concludes that red tourism turns the revolution into commodified nostalgia, which makes it hard to turn against the present.

East and Southeast Asia The whole chapter concerns the PRC. Its case studies are Jinggangshan in Jiangxi, the Hunan memorial sites at Shaoshan and Huaminglou, and Xibaipo in Hebei, with brief mention of Yan'an, Anyuan, Chongqing's Red Crag and Shajiabang in Jiangsu. Foreign delegations were also taken to Shaoshan and Yan'an in the Maoist period, and the 2009 documentary New Socialist Climax, filmed at Jinggangshan, shows Chinese visitors with mixed attitudes to the sites.

Jinggangshan Revolutionary MuseumJinggangshan Revolutionary Martyrs ParkMao Zedong Memorial Hall (Shaoshan)Mao Zedong Memorial Park (Shaoshan)Liu Shaoqi Memorial Hall (Huaminglou)Peng Dehuai Memorial HallXibaipo Memorial Hall
11Chapter 11. Museums of the Future: Municipal Urban Planning Exhibition Hallsp. 243Asia: chiefly

Denton argues that China's urban planning exhibition halls, which proliferated from the late 1990s, are 'museums of the future' that display utopian visions of cities rather than the past. Their models, light shows and digital videos invite visitors to identify with a modern, green, globally connected city, and the chapter ties these visions to state legitimacy and the market-era promise of modernization. Three halls are examined in detail: the Shanghai Urban Planning Exhibition Hall, with its vast city model, its branding as a global port city and its nostalgic 'Paris of the Orient' past; the Suzhou hall, which stresses literati heritage and historic preservation under a 'one bird, two wings' planning metaphor; and the Chongqing Urban Planning Center, an underground hall whose future city has no people. A section on the Nantong City Museum, where real estate showrooms adjoin the displays, shows commerce and state finance merging. Denton concludes that these halls elide Maoist history and the trauma of displaced residents.

East and Southeast Asia Every hall discussed is in mainland China, with Beijing's hall and Dalian's Modern Museum mentioned in passing. The chapter says the Shanghai hall presents Shanghai as a model of development for developing nations around Asia, and notes delegations from Ho Chi Minh City and a 2001 visit by the North Korean leader. A Hong Kong retrocession countdown clock between Beijing's Museum of History and Museum of the Chinese Revolution, and Taipei's Exploration Center as a contrast, are also discussed.

Shanghai Urban Planning Exhibition HallSuzhou Urban Planning Exhibition HallChongqing Urban Planning CenterNantong City MuseumShanghai Archives on the Bund
Conclusionp. 265Asia: chiefly

The conclusion argues that past, present and future are intertwined in Chinese exhibitionary culture, with museums using an idealized past to justify present policy, as Xi Jinping's 2012 'China Dream' speech and the Road to Revival exhibit at the National Museum of China show. Denton finds that memory is shaped by a state split between municipal and national agendas, and by new narratives ranging from nostalgia and red tourism to Confucian revival. Yet most visitors accept official narratives because their own lives are bound up with them, not because they are passive.

East and Southeast Asia The conclusion concerns museums and memory in the PRC throughout, so it is about East Asia from start to finish. It recalls the National Museum of China's Road to Revival exhibit and the urban planning halls, and says that municipal and provincial museums can present the modern past differently from the national museum.

Dudley, Sandra H. (ed.) (2010). Museum Materialities: Objects, Engagements, Interpretations. London: Routledge.Asia: substantial19 chapter overviews

Overview

Museum Materialities (2010), edited by Sandra H. Dudley, is a collection of essays on how museum objects are experienced through the senses, emotions and bodies of visitors, curators and artists. The editor's introduction argues that museum studies has treated objects as parts of an object-information package and has neglected their physical and sensory force, and that a materialist approach should return physical experience to the museum. The chapters cover Western museums and galleries, from the Tate Modern and the Churchill Museum to house museums, a Holocaust museum, a Horniman Museum education project and the Getty's performance art exhibition, with a Foreword by Pearce and an Afterword by Morphy. The book is organised in three parts, Objects, Engagements and Interpretations.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

East and Southeast Asia are present but thin across most of the volume. The Foreword (Pearce) and the Afterword (Morphy) each mention Korea, China or the Chinese ceramics chapter in a sentence or two. Edwards (chapter 2) cites the Tuol Sleng museum in Cambodia and the Pitt Rivers Museum's Tibet Album, a photograph collection taken by the British in Tibet, for their emotional and album-based design.

Chapter 10 (Wehner and Sear, on the National Museum of Australia's Australian Journeys gallery) discusses two Southeast Asian objects in an Australian museum: a dàn tre, a bamboo instrument made by Minh Tam Nguyen, who migrated from Vietnam in 1982, and cauldrons used by Trepang fishermen from Makassar, now in Indonesia. Chapter 13 (Ting, on Chinese ceramics) is the one substantial treatment: a Ding bowl from Dingzhou, a Yuan blue-and-white wine jar, a Song celadon bowl and a Southern Song black tea ware, all in the Chinese collection of Bristol City Museum, used in a community labelling project with African and Eastern European ESOL students. The chapter concerns British visitors' interpretation of Chinese objects rather than Chinese museums or collectors, and Chinese connoisseurs' terms appear only as examples.

Chapter 4 (Wingfield, on the Sultanganj Buddha in Birmingham) is South Asian; Burmese monks and a Burmese monastery appear only as part of the ceremony that is the chapter's opening. The volume has no chapter on museums in East or Southeast Asia, and it does not discuss Asian states' heritage policy, restitution claims, or Asian visitors, curators or scholars. Its Asian material is almost wholly in Western museums and is largely about Western responses to it.

ForewordSusan M. PearcePDF p. 15

Pearce introduces this collection by arguing that materiality is all we are and all we have, so that old divisions between mind and body, and nature and culture, no longer hold. Pearce contrasts the modernist museum, built on sight and evidence, with objects that carry feeling, memory and social meaning. Pearce previews the essays, from the Tate Modern Turbine Hall to the house museums of Woolf and Bell. Objects, she concludes, shift in meaning through the senses.

East and Southeast Asia Pearce notes in passing that visitors to museums in Korea leave flowers before images, and summarises Ting's chapter on a way of interpreting Chinese ceramics that departs from typological scholarship. Both are one-sentence mentions in a foreword that otherwise concerns Europe and Australia.

Tate Modern (Turbine Hall)Birmingham City MuseumHorniman MuseumChurchill MuseumMonk's HouseCharlestonNational Museum of Australia
11 Museum materialities: objects, sense and feelingSandra H. Dudleyp. 1

Dudley's introduction argues that museum studies has treated objects as carriers of information, so that the physical thing becomes one element in an object-information package and its sensory and emotional force is neglected. Drawing on the material turn in anthropology and on sensory studies, she proposes that the museum object is best understood as an engagement between a viewer's body and the thing's physical qualities. She develops the case through the museum's privileging of sight, its modernist display style and its rules against touch, setting this against older cabinets of curiosities. Her examples include the Victoria and Albert Museum's Touch Me exhibition, handling collections, museum work in therapy and digital touch screens, as well as Celia Fiennes's surprise at the weight of a cane in the Ashmolean. She concludes that the book's three parts (Objects, Engagements and Interpretations) are a joint attempt to return physical experience to museum studies, while recognizing that an object's meanings are also social and historical.

Victoria and Albert Museum (Touch Me exhibition)Ashmolean MuseumFisher Gallery, University of Southern California
Part 1 Objectsp. 19
22 Photographs and history: emotion and materialityElizabeth Edwardsp. 21

Edwards argues that photographs are multi-sensory objects whose emotional force depends on handling, speech and touch as much as on the image, and that museums have been slow to recognize this. Edwards draws on phenomenology, material culture studies and the anthropology of the senses, and prefers the idea of 'feeling-tones' to meaning alone. Edwards’s evidence includes family albums, Barthes's refusal to reproduce the photograph of his mother, and the massed victim photographs in Holocaust and genocide memorials. Edwards then turns to exhibitions that made the materiality of photographs central, among them Picturing Paradise at the Pitt Rivers Museum, Forget Me Not at the National Media Museum in Bradford and How We Are at Tate Britain, and finds that they still face the limits of display. The second half examines digital archives such as Flickr and local image banks, where photographs still move people but the archive is dispersed beyond the museum's control. Edwards concludes that photographs sit between visual document and emotional conduit, and that museums should treat their collections as sensory and emotional enablers rather than as a series of documents.

East and Southeast Asia Edwards mentions Cambodia briefly, noting that the Museum of Genocidal Crimes at Tuol Sleng uses massed photographs of victims to convey the scale of atrocity. Edwards’s digital examples include the Tibet Album, a Pitt Rivers Museum resource of some 6,000 photographs taken by the British in Tibet, which she cites for its album-based design. Picturing Paradise concerns Samoa and is not counted here.

Pitt Rivers MuseumNational Media Museum (Bradford)Tate BritainCambridge University Museum of Archaeology and AnthropologyImperial War Museum
33 Remembering the dead by affecting the living: the case of a miniature model of TreblinkaAndrea Witcombp. 39

Witcomb asks why a hand-made model of the Treblinka camp, built by the survivor Chaim Sztajer in his Melbourne living room and shown at the Jewish Holocaust Museum and Research Centre, moved her to grief when the professional Holocaust models elsewhere left her numb. Witcomb argues that objects can work through affect, a pre-rational bodily response drawn from Tomkins, Best and Deleuze, so that a museum can produce transformation rather than only recognition. Witcomb sets the model against the professional models at Auschwitz, the Imperial War Museum and the US Holocaust Memorial Museum, and against scholarship on memorials and testimony by Young, van Alphen and Hirsch. Witcomb’s analysis of the model's naive detail, its colour, its survivor-maker and its status as a miniature leads to a critique of Susan Stewart's account of miniatures and nostalgia. Witcomb concludes that the model asks viewers to imagine themselves as potential victims, and that such objects need interpretation that opens a gap for memory rather than closing it into a standard narrative.

Jewish Holocaust Museum and Research Centre (Melbourne)United States Holocaust Memorial MuseumImperial War Museum (London)Museum of Tolerance (Los Angeles)Auschwitz State Museum
44 Touching the Buddha: encounters with a charismatic objectChristopher Wingfieldp. 53

Wingfield examines the Sultanganj Buddha, a monumental Gupta-period copper figure that Birmingham Museum & Art Gallery has displayed since 1864 and that visitors repeatedly touch. Wingfield opens with a 2008 Buddha Day ceremony in which a monk sprinkled the crowd and the statue with water, and argues that the object is charismatic: its human face, lateral symmetry and polished surfaces draw people into physical, almost reverent contact. The chapter then traces the statue's biography through three recurring responses, idolatry, iconoclasm and co-option. These include the burial of the figure in the ground at Sultanganj, the local Hindu priests' wish to acquire it after its 1861 excavation by the railway engineer E.B. Harris, and the donor Samuel Thornton's gift to Birmingham in 1864 as a means of pressing for a public gallery. Later episodes include a councillor's 1998 suggestion that it be returned to India. Wingfield concludes that the Buddha's charisma rests on the skill of its makers, which he links to the South Asian practice of darsan.

Birmingham Museum & Art GalleryBritish Museum
55 Contemporary art: an immaterial practice?Helen Phebyp. 71

Pheby, a curator at Yorkshire Sculpture Park, asks what counts as an artist's material once art no longer has to be a painting or a carved object. Pheby surveys the history of materials from cave painting and early sculpture through pigments, the collapsible paint tube and the Impressionists, then turns to Duchamp's Fountain and to the New Generation sculptors of the 1960s, who put their work on the floor rather than on plinths. Pheby’s main case studies are James Turrell's light installations, including the Deer Shelter Skyspace that YSP opened in 2006, and Andy Goldsworthy's work made from materials found outdoors. Through Sol LeWitt, Lucy Lippard's account of 'dematerialisation', and performance and relational art, she shows that the idea, the experience or the act can replace the physical object as the work. The chapter concludes that the traditional categories of material, subject, concept and viewer no longer fit contemporary practice, and that contemporary art is best interpreted for audiences through its relevance to everyday life.

Yorkshire Sculpture Park
66 The eyes have it: eye movements and the debatable differences between original objects and reproductionsHelen Saunderson, Alice Cruickshank and Eugene McSorleyp. 89

Saunderson, Cruickshank and McSorley ask whether an original artwork is experienced differently from a reproduction, and test this with an eye-tracking experiment. Opening with the Parthenon marbles in the British Museum and the plaster casts in the new Acropolis Museum, they review philosophical debates about copies and the psychology of viewing. Their experiment at the University of Reading had 24 participants, half art experts and half novices, look at six semi-abstract paintings for 30 seconds each, as originals on canvas, as photographic prints and as monitor images, while an eye tracker recorded their gaze. No significant difference emerged between originals and reproductions or between experts and novices, although eye movements changed over time, with short fixations and large saccades early on and longer fixations later. The authors explain the null result through 'facsimile accommodation', in which viewers adjust for material differences, and argue that mobile eye trackers in galleries are needed, since laboratory settings resemble the white cube.

British MuseumAcropolis Museum
Part 2 Engagementsp. 99
77 Experiencing materiality in the museum: artefacts re-madeAlexander Stevensonp. 103

Stevenson, an artist, describes a project based on archaeological artefacts in the stores of Leicester's Jewry Wall Museum, which carry little documentation. Stevenson drew selected objects, re-made them as icons on stretched animal hide, and scraped the surfaces to show wear and extend broken fragments. Twelve people from outside the museum world, including a folklorist, an artist working with complexity theory and a secularist, were then interviewed while handling these objects and invited to interpret them freely. Their readings diverged widely, and repeated handling degraded the inks, so one three-horned bull was seen as a cow, a cat, a bear and a map fragment. Stevenson presents these outcomes as a 'rhizomatic' rather than 'dendritic' research structure, and charts ten transitions from artefact to final output. Stevenson concludes that letting people with no link to the objects reinterpret them creates new connections between artefacts and contemporary residents, though the value of these readings to knowledge of the originals is debatable. The project ended in an audio guide built from the transcripts.

Jewry Wall Museum
88 Virginia woolf ’s glasses: material encounters in the literary/artistic house museumNuala Hancockp. 114

Hancock examines the material encounter with the belongings of others in Charleston and Monk's House, the Bloomsbury house museums of Vanessa Bell and Virginia Woolf in Sussex. Drawing on her own phenomenological fieldwork in the Charleston archive, she takes three objects as case studies: a dressing table from the room where Julia Stephen died, a cupboard Bell painted in 1917, and a pair of Woolf's spectacles kept in an archive box. Handling the glasses, she traces Woolf's dependence on sight for her writing and her dread of being looked at, and argues that such relics bring visitors close to a life while making them complicit in intruding on private things. The painted cupboard is read as a self-portrait of Bell's tension between expression and domestic duty, and the dressing table as a charged site of bereavement. Hancock concludes that unprotected house museum objects implicate visitors in grief and the moment of dying, which challenges the image of Charleston as a place of bohemian ease.

CharlestonMonk's House
99 When ethnographies enter art galleriesLydia Nakashima Degarrodp. 128

Nakashima Degarrod examines how audiences responded to a set of ethnographic paintings, Following the Trails of Urban Miracle Seekers, shown in three galleries in 2004 and 2005. The paintings are based on her research into the animitas, the roadside shrines in Santiago, Chile, that honour souls of people who died violent, unjust deaths. She explains why she chose painting for an ethnography: words cannot convey emotional textures, the cult itself is transmitted visually, and images can reach a public beyond academic readers. Comparing the exhibits, she finds that audiences given lectures and texts showed understanding of the cult, while all audiences responded with personal, embodied knowledge. A retired soldier who had trained military personnel in Latin America described how the paintings recalled his own experience of civil war. Drawing on Doris Salcedo, Jill Bennett and Alfred Gell, she argues that images carry sensory knowledge that viewers receive without the artist's intention. The chapter concludes that many questions remain about how such art might work within ethnographic representation.

1010 Engaging the material world: object knowledge and Australian JourneysKirsten Wehner and Martha Searp. 143Asia: in part

Wehner and Sear describe how the National Museum of Australia developed Australian Journeys, a gallery on the transnational experiences of migrants, sojourners and travellers, with an object-centred method. They explain 'object biography', which traces each key object's making, use, circulation and meaning, and illustrate it with a gold-washing cradle from the Victorian goldfields, a snuff box given to Governor King in 1801 and a Latvian national dress made over twenty years. Arguing against exhibitions in which objects merely illustrate themes stated in text, they propose 'object knowledge', an embodied understanding of how things look, feel and weigh. Their design includes about forty exhibits built around a key object in four-sided glass cases, text kept outside the case, sensory stations and objects viewed from both sides. The authors conclude that such displays should open an inter-subjective space in which visitors imagine others' experience while recognising how their own differs.

East and Southeast Asia The chapter's Southeast Asian material is limited to two objects in the Australian Journeys gallery. The dàn tre, a bamboo instrument made by Minh Tam Nguyen, who migrated from Vietnam in 1982, is used to show how a visitor's position, as audience or as player, invites different imaginative engagements with his experience of being Vietnamese in Australia. Trepang fishermen from Makassar, now in Indonesia, appear through the cauldrons they used on northern Australian beaches, with a sensory station offering the smell of dried sea cucumber.

National Museum of AustraliaAustralian Journeys
1111 Watch your step: embodiment and encounter at Tate ModernHelen Rees Leahyp. 162

Rees Leahy examines how the bodies of visitors are shaped by Tate Modern, and how they resist. Since the eighteenth century, she argues, museum rules and spatial codes have taught visitors to walk, look and behave in set ways, and the modernist white cube reinforced a disembodied 'Eye'. She contrasts the gallery floors, where visitors walk and look, with the Turbine Hall, where sitting, lying and touching are allowed. Her main evidence is the series of Turbine Hall commissions from 2000, including Bourgeois's towers and Elliasson's The Weather Project, in which visitors lay on the floor to watch themselves in mirrors. Her central case is Salcedo's Shibboleth (2007), a crack in the floor meant to address racism and the history of modernity, which visitors instead stepped over, straddled and photographed. Rees Leahy argues that the Tate has turned this bodily play into a strategy for attracting young audiences, and that the museum reincorporates visitors' transgressive bodies into its audience development. The chapter ends by noting that a planned extension will keep the institution predicated on young, embodied consumers.

Tate Modern
1212 Reconsidering digital surrogates: toward a viewer-orientated model of the gallery experienceBradley L. Taylorp. 175

Taylor asks whether digital surrogates of museum objects can convey what a visitor feels before an original, and argues that digitisation has been built around the object rather than the viewer. Taylor reviews library and information science work that tested viewers only through reproductions, then four information-seeking theorists whose user-centred models put the seeker's feelings and setting first. The evidence comes from the Toledo Picture Study, in which over 80 subjects named the emotions evoked by twenty Western paintings shown as originals, slides, prints and digital images. Aggregate results showed no surrogation effect, but informal talk while subjects moved between galleries pointed to the physical space, the other senses (live piano music, a subject touching a canvas) and personal histories with museums. Taylor proposes a viewer-oriented model built on these factors. Taylor concedes that museums cannot easily re-catalogue their records, and suggests that demand for customised content may force them to put visitors at the centre.

Toledo Museum of ArtUniversity of Michigan Museum of Art
Part 3 Interpretationsp. 185
1313 Dancing pot and pregnant jar? On ceramics, metaphors and creative labelsWing Yan Vivian Tingp. 189Asia: chiefly

Ting asks how a Chinese ceramic can speak to visitors when, as at Bristol City Museum, it sits in an old-fashioned case without a label. Ting argues that technical, disciplinary interpretation leaves most visitors with only an aesthetic judgement, and proposes 'metaphorical association', adapted from Tilley's 'object as metaphor', which links an object's formal qualities to visitors' bodily and personal experience. Most of the chapter reports Creative Space, a 2006-7 outreach project with literacy and ESOL students at the Schiller Gallery. Participants compared biscuits with bisque and glazing, explored ceramics by touch while blindfolded, and listened to music while looking at bowls and jars before writing labels, which the museum installed. Ting cites the labels as evidence, including one that imagines a black tea bowl as a survivor of an 'explosion' and another that tells a Native American story about a Chinese tea ware. Ting concedes that such readings can distort formal qualities and confirm misunderstanding. Ting concludes that personal interpretations are as valid as official histories, and that when confusion arises visitors should be sent back to the object to listen to it.

East and Southeast Asia Chinese ceramics are the whole subject: a Ding bowl from Dingzhou (Hebei), dated to the tenth to twelfth centuries, shown without a label, a Ming blue-and-white bottle, a Yuan blue-and-white wine jar, a Song celadon bowl with peony decoration and a Southern Song black tea ware, all in the museum's Chinese collection. Ting cites Chinese connoisseurs' terms such as 'moon white' and 'phoenix tail shaped' vases, and the whipped-tea practice behind a black tea bowl. The participants are not Asian; they were literacy and ESOL students from Africa and Eastern Europe.

Bristol City Museum
1414 Myth, memory and the senses in the Churchill MuseumSheila Watsonp. 204

Watson asks how the sound and images in the opening section of the Churchill Museum, in the Cabinet War Rooms, shape visitors' sense of the past. Drawing on work on historical consciousness, sense memory and affect, she argues that museums produce 'historical sense' through emotional, embodied responses rather than the detached critique that academic history demands. Her case is a grey gallery where visitors stand before eight black-and-white photographs and hear extracts from Churchill's speeches from May to September 1940, the sound stopping when they step away. Much of the chapter examines the myth of 1940 that this display draws on, Britain standing alone and muddling through, and how Churchill's reputation grew largely after 1945 from recordings few had heard during the war. Watson also reads the official photographs, such as Churchill at Hartlepool, as carefully selected images. Watson concludes that the display conveys the confusion of 1940 and the sense of one leader's certainty, but that it also reinforces a national identity built on that myth.

Churchill MuseumCabinet War Rooms
1515 Dreams and wishes: the multi-sensory museum spaceViv Goldingp. 224

Golding asks how the senses and embodied knowledge can be used when teaching with anthropology collections, and reports a project at the Horniman Museum. The chapter opens with King's 'I have a dream' speech beside a racist insult the author suffered as a teenager, and it draws on Classen's work on the senses and Freire's critical pedagogy to challenge Western 'eye-minded' display. The fieldsite is African Worlds, the museum's permanent exhibition of sub-Saharan art, where a Shona headrest is the key object. The case study is 'Inspiration Africa!' (2001), in which a class of pupils on the autistic spectrum from Brent Knoll School handled gourds, headrests, stools and textiles, heard stories from a Ghanaian storyteller, and made screen-printed 'dream cushions'. Using teachers' observations and pupils' responses, Golding argues that touch, sound and storytelling helped these pupils communicate and voice fears. She concludes that multi-sensory programmes can advance intercultural understanding, provided museums allow time and a safe social space.

Horniman Museum
1616 Making meaning beyond displayChris Dorsettp. 241

Dorsett, an artist, asks what happens when an artist is invited to work with a museum's reserve collection, the objects kept out of sight. Dorsett introduces the 'agent of change' idea and sets an asymmetry between curators, who select and interpret, and artists, who value material presence and accumulation, which he calls 'stuff'. The main case is Andy Warhol's Raid the Icebox 1 (1969) at the Rhode Island School of Design, where Warhol displayed the storage shoes and the director, Daniel Robbins, came to see the collection differently. Dorsett then describes his own commission for Cheltenham Art Gallery and Museum's centenary in 1999: display cases holding barely visible storage objects, imagined community donations and a rumour about a tram linked to Brian Jones. Drawing on Hooper-Greenhill, Kristeva, Fish and Peirce, he argues that artists and curators work within incompatible semiotic frames, and that this tension is productive. He concludes that the iconic, personal responses artists bring can open museum meanings to re-meaning.

Cheltenham Art Gallery and MuseumRhode Island School of Design Museum of Art
1717 Authenticity and object relations in contemporary performance artKlare Scarboroughp. 260

Scarborough uses the 2007 Getty Research Institute exhibition Evidence of Movement to ask how viewers can reconstruct the 'truth' of ephemeral performance art from its documents. The exhibition grouped photographs, scores, prints, videos and relic-like objects under thematic headings, with no narrative and no descriptions of the actions, so visitors had to act as detectives. Scarborough argues that performance documentation was often staged and promoted by artists, citing the faked Schwarzkogler photographs, Tate Liverpool's 2003 exhibition Art, Lies and Videotape, and Yves Klein's Leap into the Void, a staged composite published as a simulated newspaper. Drawing on Auslander, Jones and Goffman, she argues that the authenticity of a document lies in its relationship to its audience rather than to a lost original, so that each viewing is shaped by the exhibition's space and by conversation with others. She ends by arguing that viewers perform the meaning-making alongside the artists.

Getty Research InstituteTate Liverpool
AfterwordHoward Morphyp. 275

Morphy, an anthropologist, reflects on the book's concern with the materiality of museum objects. Morphy traces how material culture was neglected for much of the twentieth century, through art history's focus on form, archaeology's typologies and a utilitarian view of objects, and how a new paradigm emerged that treats objects as integral to social life and as bearers of affect. Morphy cautions against the cliche of treating objects as persons, and argues that an object's power lies in the context of its making and use rather than in the object alone. Using Yolngu, Massim and Mende examples and several of the book's chapters, he proposes a 'disjunctive' space between the producing community, the curator and the audience, in which curators must step back from their own assumptions. He concludes that materiality is a potential rather than a given, and that the meaning of objects lies as much in the mind that produces form as in the form itself.

East and Southeast Asia Morphy notes that the excitement a Western reader feels at an original manuscript may not be shared in China, and he calls Ting's chapter on Chinese porcelain an interesting experiment in which students engage with the sensual qualities of the ceramics through musical association and food.

Duncan, Carol (1995). Civilizing Rituals: Inside Public Art Museums. London: Routledge.Asia: slight6 chapter overviews

Overview

Carol Duncan argues that public art museums are ritual structures. Their buildings, rooms and collections script a visit that conveys values about social, sexual and political identity, so they cannot be treated as neutral containers for masterpieces or as architectural statements. The first chapter sets out the idea, drawing on liminality and the marked-off script of the visit. Five case studies follow: the Louvre and the National Gallery in London; the municipal museums of New York and Chicago; donor memorials such as the Wallace, Frick and Getty collections; and modern art museums, with the Museum of Modern Art as the main case. The study is confined to Western democracies, mostly Anglo-American, and sets aside how museums represent other cultures.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia get little attention. The Louvre chapter notes that after the Second World War the museum moved its far eastern art to the Musée Guimet, and that an official judged this removal to have clarified the museum's western programme (lines 1231-1247). The introduction places a few far eastern courtly cultures among the producers of art, set against non-western producers of artifacts (line 338).

The most specific material is in chapter 3, on the municipal museums of New York and Chicago. At the Art Institute of Chicago, Samuel Nickerson insisted that his modern paintings and far eastern objects be shown together, and the Lucy Maud Buckingham rooms, opened in 1924, led from far eastern bronzes through an ancient Chinese doorway into a French medieval-style room (lines 1991-2001); Duncan cites both as breaches of the civic programme. At the Met, the Chinese and Japanese sections are described only as additions fitted around the European core (lines 2086-2090). The old Boston museum arranged world civilisation with Japan, China and India set against Greece, Rome and Egypt, an order the new East Wing has disrupted (lines 2238-2245).

Asia otherwise appears only in comparison or as a detail. A note to chapter 1 cites a study of Japanese exhibition poetics on secular ritual sites (line 4144), and the grounds of the Huntington include a Japanese garden among several (line 2487). Southeast Asia is not discussed at all, and no Asian state, collection or colonial episode is treated.

Preface And Acknowledgmentsp. ix
INTRODUCTIONp. 1

Duncan argues that art museums are ritual structures, in which the building, its spaces and its collections script a visit conveying values about social, sexual and political identity. It rejects treatments that see museums as neutral containers for masterpieces or as architectural statements, and previews five case-study chapters: the Louvre and National Gallery, American civic museums, private donor collections, and modern art wings. The study is limited to Western democracies, mainly Anglo-American, and sets aside how museums represent other cultures.

1The Art Museum As Ritualp. 7

Duncan sets out the organizing idea of the book: that public art museums work as ritual sites. The chapter first argues that the sharp modern division between religious ritual and secular museum culture is historically made, and that secular societies still stage many rituals. It then argues that museum space is marked off, set apart by monumental architecture and governed by rules of conduct, and that visitors perform a script laid out by the installations. The evidence is mostly testimony from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries: Goethe at the Dresden gallery, Hazlitt at the Louvre and the National Gallery, Gilman's Boston doctrine of aesthetic contemplation, and Kenneth Clark's view of museums as places of spiritual restoration, set beside a visitor-instruction sign at the Hirshhorn. Drawing on Van Gennep and Victor Turner, Duncan describes the art museum as a liminal space where visitors step out of ordinary time. The chapter ends by naming three constants, a marked-off zone, a visitor's script and a promised transformation, which the later chapters test against particular museums.

Dresden GalleryLouvre MuseumNational Gallery, London
2From The Princely Gallery To The Art Museum: The Louvre Museum And The National Gallery, Londonp. 21

Duncan treats the Louvre as the prototype of the public art museum. When the French revolutionary government opened the royal collection in 1793, the chapter argues, the old princely gallery was rehung by art-historical school and decorated with ceilings and staircases celebrating genius and the nation, turning it into a display of civic virtue and state legitimacy. The National Gallery in London had no royal collection to nationalize, and a landed oligarchy resisted a national gallery until the Angerstein purchase of 1824 supplied one. Radical reformers, drawing on the 1835-36 Select Committee, pressed for historical hanging and open access. The gallery became a fully civic ritual only in the third quarter of the nineteenth century, when political pressure forced the British state to recognize the value of a prestigious monument. Duncan concludes that both institutions staged the citizen's relation to the state, though through different political histories. The chapter ends by noting that the Louvre now also serves mass tourism.

East and Southeast Asia Duncan mentions East Asia only in passing: after the Second World War the Louvre moved its far eastern art to the Musee Guimet, and an official judged that removal to have clarified the museum's western program. Nothing further on East or Southeast Asia.

Louvre MuseumNational Gallery, London
3Public Spaces, Private Interests: Municipal Art Museums In New York And Chicagop. 48

Duncan examines the municipal art museums founded in New York, Chicago and Boston in the 1870s, chiefly through the Metropolitan Museum of Art. These institutions borrowed the European public museum to make American cities look civilized, but their elite trustees kept control of collections and management, and the chapter argues that the museums marked class boundaries while appearing public. The evidence includes the Met's entry fee and its closure on Sundays for its first twenty years, the Cesnola scandal, and the reforms under J. P. Morgan after 1904 that made art-historical arrangement official policy. Duncan then shows how donor rooms, such as the Bishop jade ballroom, the Buckingham rooms and the Linsky collection, reintroduced private memorial rituals and undermined the civic program. The chapter closes by arguing that the modern Met has largely given up the public ideal and now shapes the visit around dining, shopping and affluent consumers.

East and Southeast Asia In Chicago the Art Institute's restricted galleries included far eastern objects. Samuel Nickerson insisted that his modern paintings and far eastern objects be shown together, and the Lucy Maud Buckingham rooms led from far eastern bronzes through an ancient Chinese doorway into a French medieval-style room. Duncan cites these donor installations as breaches of the civic program. The Met's later Chinese and Japanese sections are noted only as additions around its European core.

Metropolitan Museum of ArtArt Institute of ChicagoMuseum of Fine Arts, Boston
4Something Eternal: The Donor Memorialp. 72

Duncan turns from municipal museums to donor memorials, collections kept intact under one donor's name and often housed in replicas of aristocratic residences. The examples include the Wallace Collection in London, the Frick and Huntington in the United States, the Getty at Malibu and the Gardner in Boston. Each casts the visitor as a guest or outsider admiring an absent owner rather than a citizen sharing a common culture. The chapter argues that many donor memorials blend art with the mausoleum: Dulwich Picture Gallery joins a gallery to a sarcophagus rotunda, the Huntington mausoleum sits in a grove away from the collections, and the Morgan Library treats its collection as a monument. Duncan reads the National Gallery in Washington, which Mellon declined to name after himself, as a memorial too, with the state's authority standing in for the donor. The chapter ends by considering restricted wings at the Met, such as the Lehman wing, as evidence that donors still seek something eternal in public museums.

Wallace CollectionFrick CollectionHuntington Library and Art GalleryJ. Paul Getty MuseumIsabella Stewart Gardner MuseumDulwich Picture GalleryMorgan LibraryNational Gallery of Art, Washington
5The Modern Art Museum: It'S A Man'S Worldp. 102

Duncan argues that modern art museums build a ritual around the story of modernism, in which artists progressively renounce representation and achieve moral and spiritual transcendence. The chapter takes the Museum of Modern Art in New York as its main case, tracing its narrative from Cezanne through Cubism and Surrealism to Abstract Expressionism, and notes that other museums repeat its plot. Duncan's central claim is that this story is male: the galleries are full of female bodies, mostly anonymous nudes and prostitutes, that frame the male artist's struggle. Picasso's Les Demoiselles d'Avignon and de Kooning's Woman I are read in detail as Gorgon-like threats, and a Penthouse advertisement photographed on a New York bus shelter serves as a comparison. Duncan also likens the museum's construction of an isolated, spiritual self to the consumerism of advertising. The chapter calls for a more revisionist museum and ends with the Art Institute of Chicago, whose reinstallation of twentieth-century art gives space to women and African-American artists.
