Findlen, Paula (1994). Possessing Nature: Museums, Collecting, and Scientific Culture in Early Modern Italy. Berkeley: University of California Press.Asia: occasional10 chapter overviews

Overview

Findlen's Possessing Nature (1994) is a history of the early modern museum as a site of natural history in Italy, from the sixteenth to the late seventeenth century, and of the naturalists who built and used collections, above all Ulisse Aldrovandi in Bologna and Athanasius Kircher in Rome. Its main argument is that collecting let naturalists modify inherited authority rather than overturn it: the museum 'saved appearances', and old and new, sacred and scientific, professional and amateur systems of knowledge coexisted there until Baroque marvels and new experimental philosophy undid the encyclopedic ideal. The book has three parts: the museum's intellectual and spatial setting, its use as a laboratory (experience, dissection, medicine), and the social economy of collectors, brokers and patrons. An epilogue carries the story into the eighteenth century and the new public museum.

East and Southeast Asia in this work occasional

East Asia enters the book almost only through Athanasius Kircher, the Jesuit mathematician at the Roman College, whose interest in China is noted in chapters 1, 2 and 4. Chapter 2 (Searching for Paradigms) is the main place: Kircher, 'unable to travel to China', added Chinese, Sanskrit and Aramaic to his languages, and the Roman College museum held Chinese scrolls beside Egyptian hieroglyphs and Etruscan tablets as material for reconstructing the original language of humans. One of his catoptric machines multiplied an elephant 'collected from all Asia and Africa'. Chapter 4 (Pilgrimages of Science) covers the Jesuits Martino Martini and Michael Boym, whose New Chinese Atlas (1654) and Chinese Flora (1656) Kircher used in China Illustrated (1667), and Boym's return to Rome in 1664 with manuscripts and specimens for the Roman College. Findlen notes that Kircher relied on such witnesses to lend credibility to an account of a land he had never seen.

Chapter 6 (Museums of Medicine) treats Asia as a source of drugs rather than a subject of study: Aldrovandi sent the Grand Duke an Indian plant identified as pseudocalamus, an approved substitute for a theriac ingredient, and the Mantua apothecaries Bertioli made balsamo orientale in 1594, which Alpino certified against Padua specimens. Jan Eck's complaint about physicians mixing Africa, Asia, Europe and the New World into their recipes is quoted as a sign of medical conservatism. Chapter 8 (Patrons, Brokers, and Strategies) quotes Kircher's dedication of the Egyptian Obelisks to Alexander VII, which asks the obelisk to speak to 'Europe, Asia, Africa, and America'. Chapter 5 and the chapters on Galileo and the Baroque collectors do not discuss Asia.

Southeast Asia is absent: no Siam, Philippines, Indonesia, Vietnam, Malaya or Borneo appears. Asia is a generic 'Orient' in the travel quotations of Rauwolf and in the Jesuit geography of the catoptric theatre, and the book's East Asia is China as Kircher knew it at second hand.

China

Theoretical approach of this work
Acknowledgmentsp. xi

Photo Creditsp. xvii
Introductionp. 1

Findlen's introduction sets out two linked histories: the rise of early modern museums that aimed to bring all of nature into one space, and the reshaping of natural history as a discipline. Italy is the case study, since collecting of antiquities and natural objects spread there first, and since the universities of Pisa, Padua and Bologna studied nature intensively. Findlen argues that naturalists such as Aldrovandi and Kircher used collecting to modify ancient authority rather than overturn it, so that the museum saved appearances. Findlen describes a social world in which princes, physicians, apothecaries and patricians shared collections as sites of patronage, civility and display. The introduction previews three parts on the museum's intellectual setting, its use as a laboratory and the sociology of collectors, and it recovers minor brokers and naturalists whose work is now forgotten. It concludes that old and new, sacred and scientific forms of knowledge coexisted in the museum.

Aldrovandi's museum, BolognaKircher's museum, Rome
Part ILocating the Museump. 13
1"A World of Wonders in One Closet Shut"p. 17

Findlen opens with the dragon captured near Bologna in 1572, which Ulisse Aldrovandi acquired, displayed and used as the subject of his Dracologia. Findlen shows how the portent circulated among patrons, friends and the new pope's court, and how Aldrovandi read the two-footed serpent as a natural wonder rather than a sign, which suited his papal cousin. The chapter then follows the museum after his death: the custodians who edited his manuscripts, and the merger with Ferdinando Cospi's collection in 1657, which shifted the museum from encyclopedic erudition toward Baroque marvels. Findlen turns to the apothecaries Calzolari and Imperato, whose catalogues moved from medicine to courtly wit, and to the Lincean academy, Kircher's Roman museum and Settala's Milan collection. It ends with Van Kessel's painting Europa and Kircher's catoptric theatre, which present the collector and his museum as objects of display, and concludes that wonder became a virtue in itself.

Aldrovandi museum, BolognaCospi museum, BolognaCalzolari museum, VeronaImperato museum, NaplesSettala museum, MilanRoman College museum (Kircher), RomeChigi museum, Rome
2Searching for Paradigmsp. 48Asia: in part

Findlen asks how early modern naturalists made their collections meaningful, and argues that they relied on inherited paradigms even as they claimed to break with them. Findlen starts with the word musaeum, which collectors stretched to cover studios, cabinets and encyclopedias alike. Aldrovandi in Bologna organized his holdings by Aristotelian and Plinian authority, using synoptic tables and an eighty-three-volume pandechion of excerpted books. The Accademia dei Lincei under Federico Cesi claimed to read the book of nature without authority, yet its Phytosophical Tables still followed Aristotelian method. Kircher in the Roman College blended Hermeticism, natural magic and Jesuit theology, reading the museum through hieroglyphs, magnets, the Ark and the Tower of Babel. Findlen concludes that by the late seventeenth century these frameworks gave way under the weight of new objects, leaving collectors with curiosity but no settled criteria for truth.

East and Southeast Asia Kircher, unable to travel to China, made himself the leading expert on it by collecting others' reports, and he added Chinese to the languages he studied. The Roman College museum held Chinese scrolls beside Egyptian hieroglyphs and fragments of other scripts, and one of his catoptric machines multiplied an elephant said to be collected from all Asia and Africa.

Roman College museumStudio AldrovandiCalzolari museumCospi museumSettala museum
3Sites of Knowledgep. 97

Findlen asks where collecting took place and argues that the museum was a social space as much as a scholarly one. Collections moved from the private studiolo into the galleria, a shift traced through Italian palaces, the Jesuit colleges that trained patrician sons, and the etiquette of letters of introduction. Aldrovandi's museum passed from his house to the Palazzo Pubblico in Bologna, where it shared rooms with the papal legate's quarters and became a civic showpiece. Kircher's Roman College museum acquired a gate and a speaking tube that at once limited and facilitated access. Aldrovandi's visitors' books record 1,579 visitors, mostly scholars, with women and servants left out. Findlen draws on travel accounts by Ray, Skippon, Burnet and Magalotti to show how introductions opened doors. Findlen ends with the Ashmolean Museum at Oxford, whose open admission shocked a German visitor and marks a different idea of the public museum.

Studio AldrovandiCospi museumRoman College museumImperato museumCalzolari museumUffizi galleryPisa botanical garden galleryAshmolean Museum
Part IILaboratories of Naturep. 151
4Pilgrimages of Sciencep. 155Asia: in part

Findlen argues that collecting began with travel, so that the museum was the end point of a voyage into nature. Findlen follows Aldrovandi, the apothecary Calzolari and Luigi Anguillara on their 1554 excursion up Monte Baldo near Verona, whose quarrels show how competing claims to expertise shaped the community of naturalists. The chapter then turns to the fishmarkets, apothecaries, falconers and enslaved people whose local names and observations entered learned treatises while their makers stayed anonymous. It ends with the Baroque volcano hunters: Kircher's ascents of Etna and Vesuvius in 1637 and 1638, and Bonanni's frontispiece of a shell collector guided by Neptune. Findlen concludes that the pilgrimage metaphor made nature a theatre, and that the museum tried to hold the drama of the voyage within its cabinets.

East and Southeast Asia Kircher's knowledge of China came largely through other Jesuits. Martino Martini and Michael Boym sent him the atlas and flora that he drew on for China Illustrated (1667), and Boym returned to Rome in 1664 with manuscripts and specimens for the Roman College. Kircher, frustrated in his bid to become a missionary to China, depended on these witnesses to lend credibility to an account of a land he had never seen.

Studio AldrovandiCalzolari museumRoman College museumMuseum WormianumGiganti studio
5Fare Esperienzap. 194

Findlen argues that by the mid-seventeenth century the museum had become a laboratory, a place where naturalists tested, displayed and argued about nature, and where the Aristotelian idea of experientia (experience gathered from particular things) gave way to experiment. Findlen opens with Redi's frontispieces, in which Minerva sits at an experimental table beside books and a microscope, and then follows the collecting of experience through Giganti, Aldrovandi, Calzolari, Imperato and Della Porta in Bologna, Verona and Naples. Dissection comes next, first in the studios of university professors and then in the courtly demonstrations of Redi and Steno in Florence, where anatomy became a social accomplishment. Spectacles of natural magic such as asbestos and the luminous lapis Bononiensis are examined as repeatable experiences that Linceans prized. The chapter closes with fossils: Imperato's collection helped Colonna, Steno and Scilla move towards an organic account of them, while Kircher kept to an inorganic one. Findlen concludes that experience gave naturalists a shared language even as they used it to contest intellectual authority, and that the museum sat at the centre of that contest.

Aldrovandi museumImperato museumCalzolari museumRoman College museumSettala museumBarberini museumDella Porta museumMercati Metallotheca
6Museums of Medicinep. 241

Findlen argues that in sixteenth-century Italy the study of medicinal simples (materia medica) was reformed inside the universities, and that museums and botanical gardens became the tools of that reform. Findlen traces the creation of university chairs in simples at Pisa, Ferrara, Padua and Bologna, the spread of botanical gardens, and the role of physicians and apothecaries in regulating pharmacy through the Colleges of Physicians and the Protomedicato. The central case is theriac, the composite antidote whose vipers and rare ingredients collectors hunted down. Calzolari's Verona theriac, defended against his former apprentice Scalcina, shows how public display and testimonials authenticated a medicine. Aldrovandi's dispute with the Bologna College of Physicians over the 1575 Jubilee theriac, carried to Rome and settled in his favour, shows what was at stake in controlling that authority. Findlen closes with Kircher's and Redi's later uses of the serpent's stone and of vipers, where the objects stayed the same but their meaning shifted from therapy towards philosophical proof.

Aldrovandi museumCalzolari museumImperato museumRoman College museumPisa botanical gardenPadua botanical gardenBologna botanical garden
Part IIIEconomies of Exchangep. 289
7Inventing the Collectorp. 293

Findlen asks how collectors in early modern Italy used their museums to fashion and display their identities. The evidence centres on four naturalist-collectors: Ulisse Aldrovandi in Bologna, Giambattista della Porta in Naples, Manfredo Settala in Milan and Athanasius Kircher in Rome. For them a museum was a self-portrait. Its objects, emblems, villa decorations and portraits presented the owner as a moral and intellectual exemplar, drawing on classical models and the humanist vocabulary of imitation, exempla and invention. Aldrovandi cast himself as Ulysses and as Aristotle, Della Porta as a magus and a 'door' to nature, Settala as a new Archimedes whose inventions outlived him, and Kircher as Aeneas and then Hermes. Chameleons, mirrors and the Narcissus myth recur as emblems of the shifting self. The chapter ends by setting these self-fashioning identities against Galileo, who rejected humanist learning in favour of a scientific self.

Aldrovandi's museum, BolognaMuseo Settala, MilanKircher's museum, Rome (Roman College)Della Porta's museum, NaplesStudiolo of Francesco I, Palazzo Vecchio, FlorenceAldrovandi's villa, San Antonio di Savena
8Patrons, Brokers, and Strategiesp. 346

Findlen examines how collectors in Italy and Rome built their careers through patronage, and how a museum served to attract princes, popes and their brokers. The evidence is mainly letters, gifts and dedications connected with Ulisse Aldrovandi, who pursued patrons from the Habsburgs and Philip II to the Medici, the papacy and the Barberini, and who saw his Ornithology in print only with the help of many backers. A smaller case is the apothecary Calzolari, whose Gonzaga medal and ring ennobled his museum. Athanasius Kircher emerges as the most skilled broker, turning the Habsburg eagle and a Roman College portrait gallery into political emblems. Brokers such as Pinelli, Mercuriale and Peiresc passed on letters, specimens and introductions through the republic of letters. Findlen argues that gifts, dedications and courtly rhetoric were central to natural history, and that most museums did not survive their founders. The chapter ends by noting that by the seventeenth century collecting was no novelty, which made it hard for any collector to offer a prince something unique.

Aldrovandi's museum, BolognaCalzolari's museumRoman College museum (Kircher)Cospi's museum, BolognaVatican metallotheca (Mercati)
Epilogue: The Old and the Newp. 393

The epilogue argues that the Renaissance and Baroque museum was undone in the eighteenth century, when Buffon, Linnaeus and Spallanzani claimed to refound natural history on method, order and classification. The evidence runs from the Swammerdam anecdote and the Hollis gift to the British Museum, to Maffei's lapidary museum in Verona, Florence's new cabinet of physics and natural history, and the Baconian aims of the Royal Society repository. Findlen shows how the collections of Aldrovandi and Kircher were broken up, absorbed into public institutions or left to decay, while Enlightenment writers dismissed their predecessors' credulity and erudition. Findlen argues that the new public museum sought utility and taxonomic order, and that it saw less rather than more. The chapter ends by setting Galileo beside Aldrovandi and Kircher: all three depended on patrons and brokers, so the scientific revolution was as much a matter of social and rhetorical position as of discovery.

Fromm, Annette B.; Golding, Viv; Rekdal, Per B. (eds.) (2014). Museums and Truth. Newcastle upon Tyne: Cambridge Scholars Publishing.Asia: slight13 chapter overviews

Overview

Museums and Truth (2014) is an edited collection of ten essays from the International Committee for Museums of Ethnography (ICME), drawn from its meetings in Korea, China and Germany. Its argument is that museums present history as simplified and authoritative, while truth is always partial and situated. The editors ask ethnographic and history museums to face injustice, post-conflict memory and their own role in contested narratives, rather than offer celebration or relativism. The chapters sit in four parts (truth and faith; difficult heritage and reconciliation; old realities in new settings; emerging postnormality) and take cases from Britain, Norway, Germany, Italy and Croatia, Switzerland, Luxembourg, Sweden and Guatemala.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East Asia appears mainly as the setting of the ICME meetings that produced the book (Seoul 2009, Shanghai 2010, and the Korea, China and Germany series named in the Preface), and in passing. Chapter 1 (Golding) notes an eighteenth-century Japanese ukiyo-e print of the blind men's tale by Hanabusa Itcho and a Thai wall relief, and does not develop them. Chapter 4 (McKinnon) names the Tuol Sleng Museum in Cambodia among models of memory museums, and chapter 7 (Rein) mentions a museum of religion in Taiwan and quotes Paine on Buddhism in South and Southeast Asian art.

The only sustained treatment is of Korea, in two chapters marked as part-coverage. Chapter 2 (Rekdal, 'Peace is Never Neutral') opens with the 2009 ICME conference at the National Folk Museum of Korea in Seoul, the conciliation process between the two Koreas, and the museum's 2008 annual report, which records a cooperation agreement with a Russian museum, fieldwork in China and a Children's Museum fairy tale of a divided family. Chapter 3 (Kerkhoff-Hader) ends with 'A transaxial link to Korea': 2007-2009 Berlin billboards and photo collages by artists from South Korea, China and Germany on the division of Korea, and a 2009 Bonn exhibition of Korean women artists, 'The Last Wall', organised with the Korean Embassy. Both are used as parallels to Germany's division, not studied in their own right.

No museum in East or Southeast Asia is studied, and no Asian collection in a Western museum is traced to its acquisition. Southeast Asia is essentially absent: the chapters by Sem, Jungblut and Schweizer, Garberg and Grinell do not mention it, and the colonial cases discussed are not Asian.

Theoretical approach of this work
Table Of ContentsPDF p. 5
AcknowledgementsPDF p. 7
FOREWORDAnnette B. FrommPDF p. 9

Fromm's foreword introduces essays from the International Committee for Museums of Ethnography. It notes that since 2000 museums have turned from what to collect toward public accountability and community-based programmes, and traces the committee's meetings from Copenhagen in 2000 to Shanghai in 2010. It credits Per Rekdal with proposing the working group behind the essays, which are meant as a platform for questions about the political and historical realities of societies.

PREFACEViv GoldingPDF p. 13

The preface introduces Museums and Truth as ten chapters drawn from ICME conferences on 'Challenging Museums' held in Korea, China and Germany between 2009 and 2011. It outlines the four parts: truth and faith, difficult heritage and reconciliation, old realities in new settings, and postnormal conditions. Its argument is that museums, which present themselves as authoritative, should face injustice and the limits of their own truths, since truth is always an approximation.

INTRODUCTIONPer B. RekdalPDF p. 19

Rekdal, one of three editors, explains that the editors wrote separate introductions instead of a single agreed one, and that museums often present history as simplified and authoritative. Rekdal reflects on how museums' claims to truth can be challenged, on injustice and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, on post-conflict memorials, and on the risks of inviting visitors to give their own opinions. The chapter closes by pointing towards postnormal diversity and the value of creative disagreement inside museums.

Part One: Truths, Faiths And Realitiesp. 1
Museums and Truths: The Elephant in the RoomViv Goldingp. 3

Golding uses the 'elephant in the room' as a metaphor for the topics museums avoid, and a Jain tale of blind men describing an elephant as a model of many-sided truth. Drawing on Orwell's 'Shooting an Elephant' and Animal Farm, Golding argues that the lines between truth and fiction, and history and story, are blurred, and that museums should work across them. Her main evidence is her own practice at the Horniman Museum in London, with storytelling and sensory activities, and a case study of three women in England responding to the English Defense League. Cultural translation is theorized through Gadamer, Asad and Wittgenstein. Concrete cases include the Museum of World Culture in Göteborg, Romuald Hazoumé's mask installation La Bouche du Roi, which the British Museum bought, Felix Gonzalez-Torres's sweets pieces at Williams College Museum of Art, and controversies over Chris Ofili's painting at the Brooklyn Museum and Sooreh Hera's work in The Hague. The conclusion is that engaging the body and emotions can widen visitors' horizons, but that relativism is not enough and museums must take firm stands against injustice.

East and Southeast Asia Golding notes that versions of the blind-men tale differ in detail: a Japanese Ukiyo-e woodblock print by Hanabusa Itcho (1652-1724) shows eight blind monks, and a Thai wall relief shows six blind boys. The chapter does not treat these works further.

Horniman MuseumMuseum of World Culture, GöteborgSmithsonian (Woolworth's lunch counter display)British MuseumWilliams College Museum of ArtBrooklyn MuseumGemeentemuseum, The Hague
Part Two: Museums And ‘Difficult’ Heritagep. 21
Peace is Never NeutralPer B. Rekdalp. 23Asia: in part

Rekdal, who had planned to speak about the future of ethnographic museums, takes up the 2009 ICME theme of museums' responsibility for peace and reconciliation, which he first found too optimistic. Rekdal argues that ethnographic museums have a particular responsibility here, and that their approach depends on circumstances such as a nation's age or whether it is divided by borders. Rekdal’s central claim, that peace is never neutral, rests on examples: a peace after war can be a victory for some and the start of new oppression for others, and reconciliation is often contested, as in Norway's debate over those who fought for Nazi Germany. Rekdal’s cases include museums in former colonies that build national unity while confronting colonial injustice, Sami museums that foster a cross-border identity, a Norwegian museum forced to cancel an exhibition after veterans protested, and his own museum's decision not to show a map of Albanian-speaking areas. The conclusion is that museums should show complexity and scholarly disagreement, because celebratory messages can be emotionally deep but intellectually shallow.

East and Southeast Asia Rekdal opens with the 2009 ICME conference at the National Folk Museum of Korea in Seoul, where a conciliation process between the two Koreas makes reconciliation a live question. The museum's 2008 annual report records a cooperation agreement with a Russian museum and fieldwork in China, and its Children's Museum reopened with a fairy tale of a divided family reunited. These are cited as signs that peace work already belonged to the museum, but they are not analysed in depth.

National Folk Museum of KoreaSwedish Army Museum
Concepts of Remembrance and CommemorationBärbel Kerkhoff-Haderp. 31Asia: in part

Kerkhoff-Hader asks how museums and memorials shape remembrance of Europe's twentieth-century upheavals, arguing that objects and authentic places anchor collective memory. The chapter sets out Europe's long history of shifting borders, the expulsion of Germans from the east after 1945 and the division of Germany until 1989, and notes the rapid growth of German museums since the 1970s. The five case studies are the Egerland Museum in Marktredwitz and the Silesian Museum in Görlitz, on expulsion; the Museum of the Two German States at Mödlareuth and the Berlin Wall Memorial, on the inner German border; and a 2007-2009 Korean-German art project in Berlin. The chapter praises the personal stories told through objects, but questions re-enactments and souvenir sales, asking whether they produce memory or commerce. The conclusion is that museums should show how the past is selected and forgotten.

East and Southeast Asia Kerkhoff-Hader's last example, 'A transaxial link to Korea', covers Berlin billboards and photo collages from 2007-2009 that commented on the division of Korea, by artists from South Korea, China and Germany. A 2009 exhibition of female Korean artists at the Women's Museum in Bonn was organized with the Korean Embassy. Both are presented as parallels to Germany's division rather than as studies of Korea in their own right.

Egerland Museum, MarktredwitzSilesian Museum, GörlitzMuseum of the Two German States, MödlareuthBerlin Wall MemorialWomen's Museum, Bonn
Proposing a Museum of Memory: Reparations and the Maya Achí Genocide in GuatemalaHeidi McKinnonp. 51

McKinnon argues that museums of memory have a distinct moral role in post-conflict societies, but that their creation depends on who controls the truth. The case is Guatemala, where the 1996 Peace Accords mandated a National Museum of Historical Memory that still did not exist. The chapter traces the Río Negro massacres of 1980-1982, linked to the Chixoy Dam and to army policies that displaced Maya Achí communities. Its central story is the Achí reparations campaign, which produced a 2010 accord calling for an Achí museum of memory, and McKinnon's own proposal for one, which joins historical memory to recovery of lost cultural practices. Comparisons with Chile's Museum of Memory and Human Rights and the contested Place of Memory in Peru show how state museums are shaped by changing governments. The conclusion is that Guatemala's projects depend on political will, and that the National Police archive is already legitimizing historical memory.

Rabinal Achí Community MuseumMuseum of Memory and Human Rights, SantiagoPlace of Memory, Tolerance and Social Inclusion, LimaHistorical Archive of the National Police, Guatemala CityNational Museum of Historical Memory (Guatemala, planned)
Towards Which Reconciliation? Museological Approaches in the Istrian RegionMario Buleticp. 87

Buletić compares two museum approaches to the Istrian exodus and the foibe killings, asking what reconciliation can mean for ethnographic museums. The chapter sketches the context of a borderland shared by Italy, Slovenia and Croatia, shaped by fascism, Yugoslav communism and the emigration of around 225,000 people, mostly Italians, between 1945 and 1971. The first case is the planned Istrian, Fiuman and Dalmatian Cultural Civic Museum in Trieste, whose central monolith representing a foiba is read as a one-sided memorial to exiles. The second is the exhibition Suitcases & Destinies at the Ethnographic Museum of Istria in Pazin, presented as a multi-voiced display built on the life histories of twelve emigrants. The chapter argues for dialogue and inclusion over black-and-white framings of conflict, and for oral history to recover silenced memories. The conclusion is that the Trieste project serves a post-fascist political agenda, while oral history can support a bottom-up reconciliation.

Ethnographic Museum of Istria, PazinIstrian, Fiuman and Dalmatian Cultural Civic Museum, Trieste (planned)
Black Holes of Memory: Defining a Norwegian Museum of Human RightsLeiv Semp. 101

Sem analyses the controversy over a planned exhibition at Falstad, a Nazi camp in Norway, which was to show the site's other histories: a youth correctional school, a post-war forced labour camp, and a school for children labelled 'weak in ability'. The plan provoked a two-year public debate, and the Falstad Centre dropped it, opening in 2006 an exhibition limited to wartime imprisonment and the UN Declaration of Human Rights. The debate is read through discourse theory, which identifies the discourses of occupation, the Holocaust and human rights. The evidence is forty-one of the most decisive contributions, mostly newspaper pieces and letters, examined for who speaks and with what authority. Veterans dominated, while former borstal boys and pupils of the special school had almost no voice, and one former pupil's intervention was ignored. The conclusion is that the wartime narrative silenced the other eras.

Falstad Memorial and Human Rights Centre
Part Three: Coping With Old Realities In New Settingsp. 123
Framing Religious World Views in Museum PresentationsAnette Reinp. 125

Rein asks how museums should frame religious objects, which carry personal and sacred meanings for their communities. The opening case is a Montréal taxi driver whose religious items on the dashboard led to fines and a court case, used to compare taxis and museums as secular public spaces that decide what is displayed and how. Distinguishing religious from sacred objects, the chapter argues that museum collecting removes objects from circulation in a way that echoes sacred taboos. It contrasts the 'art-party', which displays religious objects as aesthetic works, with the 'context-party', which tells the stories of their makers through relational dialogue. The evidence is two exhibitions: Glaubenssache at the Stapferhaus in Lenzburg, Switzerland, which made visitors declare themselves believers or non-believers, and Religious Energy at the Deutsches Hygiene-Museum in Dresden, which was more academic and descriptive. The conclusion is that museums must combine scholarly knowledge with personal voices in their educational mission.

Stapferhaus, LenzburgDeutsches Hygiene-Museum, Dresden
Murder and Manslaughter: An Exhibition about LifeMarie-Paule Jungblut and Simon Schweizerp. 147

Jungblut and Schweizer describe Murder and Manslaughter: An Exhibition about Life, shown at the Luxembourg City History Museum in 2009-2010 and then at the Bernisches Historisches Museum in Berne in 2011-2012. The chapter asks why a history museum would take on so controversial a subject, and how the exhibition works in two different places. It was built around fifteen questions, from 'What is my life worth?' to 'What should be done with murderers?', and it hid disturbing material in drawers and peep boxes rather than using shock. The evidence is visitor response: about 25,000 visitors in Luxembourg and 28,841 in Berne, a card vote on whether visitors would kill in self-defence or to eliminate a tyrant, and written comments. The vote results were very similar in both cities, apart from a higher share in Berne willing to end their own life with an incurable illness. The conclusion is that the participatory approach widened both museums' audiences and made them places of public debate.

Luxembourg City History MuseumBernisches Historisches Museum, Berne
Minda, the Girl in the Pharmacy: An Educational Program on Sexual AssaultAnn Siri Hegseth Garbergp. 155

Garberg describes a programme that the Sverresborg Trøndelag Folk Museum in Trondheim developed in 2008 around Minda, a fourteen-year-old girl found unconscious outside a city pharmacy in 1888. The case, and the riot and trial that followed, is set out as the press reported it. The chapter asks whether an open-air museum should address sexual assault at all, and argues that the historical milieu and the case's place in local intangible heritage justify it. The programme used museum theatre and ended with pupils voting guilty or innocent in discussions led by young actors. It also records staff objections and the advice of abuse support organisations. Evidence on learning is a thesis study in which half of the girls interviewed said they had learned something new. The conclusion is that museums must ask questions for which there is no exact truth, and rethink their role in society.

Sverresborg Trøndelag Folk Museum, Trondheim
Part Four: Emerging Postnormality In Museums?p. 167
Challenging Normality: Museums In/As Public SpaceKlas Grinellp. 169

Grinell asks whether museums can function as public spaces or should instead act as agents in the public sphere, and argues that the category 'museums' hides very different institutions with different roles. Working from Judith Butler's recent writing on embodied appearance and grievable life, and from Jennifer Barrett's terminological analysis of 'public', Grinell sets out a postnormal diagnosis drawn from Ziauddin Sardar, a pluriversal ethics drawn from Tariq Ramadan, and a phenomenological account of the limits of representation. The central argument is that public space arises only when bodies appear to one another, so museums with gates and admission fees cannot be public spaces in that sense; they are public institutions offering public services. The concrete material is Grinell's curatorial experience at the Museum of World Culture in Göteborg, notably the Jerusalem exhibition, which exposed an unclear museum role to public critique. The chapter ends by asking museums to admit opposing experiences while taking a firm stance against prejudice, and to treat ethnographic collections as resources from the perspective of those whose humanity was once questioned.

Museum of World Culture, GöteborgJane Addams Hull House Museum

Gardner, James (2020). The Louvre: The Many Lives of the World’s Most Famous Museum. New York: Atlantic Monthly Press.Asia: slight14 chapter overviews

Overview

Gardner's study traces the Louvre as a building, an institution and a royal and national symbol, from Philippe Auguste's medieval fortress of 1191 to the completion of I. M. Pei's glass pyramid. Its main argument is that the palace is the product of some twenty building campaigns over five centuries, although architects and patrons long presented it as a single design, and that the museum, which opened in 1793, is one layer in that history. The scope is Paris and the French crown, with the collections treated through their acquisition and display rather than as a survey of world art. The book runs in ten chronological chapters from the origins to the Grand Louvre of the 1980s and 1990s, framed by a preface, an introduction and an epilogue on the museum since then.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia are touched on only in passing. The book has no chapter on them, and none of the places or collections it mentions is developed.

In chapter 9 (The Louvre in Modern Times) Gardner notes that Georges Salles, director of the national museums and of the Louvre for most of the 1950s, was a specialist in Asian art, and that the Mona Lisa went to Tokyo in spring 1974, where more than one and a half million people saw it; on the flight back it was lent to Moscow. In chapter 10 (The Creation of the Contemporary Louvre) he gives I. M. Pei's background, born in Guangzhou in 1917 and raised in Hong Kong and Shanghai before studying in the United States from 1935, and says plainly that the book does not connect this to the Louvre commission. Chapter 1 mentions a priest buried in a church on the Louvre site who was a native of the Philippines, and chapter 6 notes that Vivant Denon, the museum's director under Napoleon, owned Chinese porcelain and Japanese bronzes in his private apartment, not in the museum.

The epilogue names the Louvre-Lens, designed by the Japanese firm SANAA, as a regional branch in France, and Louvre Abu Dhabi, which lies outside the region in question. The text does not describe the Louvre's own collections of Asian art.

Contents
Preface

Gardner's preface sets the method: the Louvre is traced at once as a building, an institution and a royal and national symbol, from a medieval fortress to Pei's glass pyramid. The main point is that the building is the product of some twenty campaigns over five centuries, although its architects and patrons long presented it as a single design. The preface also notes the Tuileries, burned in 1871, explains the European numbering of floors, and ends with thanks and a note that the book's illustrations can be found online.

Louvre
Introduction

Gardner argues that the Louvre is itself a work of art, as much as anything it contains. Its history runs from a medieval fortress on a site already called le Louvre, through a royal palace, to a museum only about two hundred years old. The introduction stresses the building's superhuman scale and promises to trace the dynastic and urban forces behind each phase. It closes on the collection's four hundred thousand objects, each with its own story of acquisition.

Louvre
11 The Origins of the Louvre

Gardner's first chapter argues that the Louvre's origins as a military outpost still shape the museum. Philippe Auguste built a fortress around 1190-1200 just beyond the western wall of Paris to guard the Seine against English raiders, and the site already bore the name le Louvre. Gardner draws on Adolphe Berty's nineteenth-century excavations and on the 1980s digs that uncovered the medieval foundations. Gardner then follows Charles V, who in the 1360s and 1370s turned the fortress into a palace with a spiral staircase, gardens, a famous library in the Falconry Tower, and a new city wall that brought the Louvre inside Paris. The chapter ends with the palace's decline under Charles VI and the English occupation of the 1430s, when the Louvre fell into disrepair, and it leads on to François I's decision to live there.

Louvre
22 The Louvre in the Renaissance

Gardner's second chapter follows the Louvre through the sixteenth century, when François I turned a medieval fortress into a royal residence. It argues that his acquisitions of Italian masterpieces, including the Mona Lisa and Michelangelo's Slaves, and his decision in 1528 to live in Paris, laid the foundations of both the palace and the collection. The chapter traces the demolition of the donjon, the closing of the river gate, and the commission given to Pierre Lescot in 1546, whose west wing, with Jean Goujon's sculpture and the Salle des Caryatides, it treats as the high point of French Renaissance classicism. Gardner then covers the Valois queen Catherine de Médicis, the Saint Bartholomew's Day Massacre of 1572 that centred on the palace, and Philibert Delorme's Tuileries Palace, which Catherine began west of the Louvre. The chapter ends with the Tuileries burned by the Communards in 1871, which left the view from the Pyramide to the Arc de Triomphe.

Louvre
33 The Louvre of the Early Bourbons

Gardner's third chapter covers the Louvre under Henri IV, Marie de Médicis and Louis XIII, from 1594 to the 1640s. Its main subjects are Henri's building programme, above all the Grande Galerie along the Seine with its artists' apartments and the first room for displaying art, and the Petite Galerie with its Galerie d'Apollon. Gardner reads the cipher carved on the façades as a record of Henri's love life, and describes his assassination in 1610 and the three weeks his effigy lay in state in the Salle des Caryatides. The chapter then turns to Marie de Médicis and her Rubens cycle, which was painted for the Luxembourg and not for the Louvre, and to Richelieu's patronage and Lemercier's work on the Cour Carrée and the Pavillon Sully. It closes with Nicolas Poussin, summoned to paint the Grande Galerie in 1640, who left Paris in 1642 after completing seven of its bays, leaving the gallery unfinished.

Louvre
44 The Louvre and the Sun King

Gardner's fourth chapter covers Louis XIV, from his birth in the Louvre in 1638 through the Fronde and his move to Versailles in 1682. It argues that Louis, more than any predecessor, used architecture and spectacle as public relations, and it treats the 1662 Carrousel and the Galerie d'Apollon as examples of that. Gardner traces Le Vau's interventions and Louis's purchases of paintings, including Caravaggio's Death of the Virgin, Louis's acquisition of the Jabach drawings, and the sculptures of Mazarin. The chapter's longest section covers the competition for the eastern façade, in which designs by Bernini, Pietro da Cortona and Carlo Rainaldi were rejected in favor of Claude Perrault's Colonnade, whose authorship remains disputed. It ends by contrasting the Louvre, which never overwhelms its visitor, with Versailles, to which Louis moved his court in 1682 with the Colonnade still unfinished.

Louvre
55 The Louvre Abandoned

Gardner's final chapter covers the century after Louis XIV left for Versailles in 1682, when the Louvre became a half-finished, partly derelict palace shared by nobles, artists and the académies. It argues that the Salon, held in the Salon Carré from 1737 and open to the public, was the first step towards a museum, and that the public debate it provoked made art a matter of public judgement. Gardner works through the Plan Turgot and the critics Voltaire and La Font de Saint-Yenne, who complained of the clutter in front of the Colonnade, and through Marigny's clearance of the site. Gardner then describes the lives of painters and sculptors in the Grande Galerie, the royal exhibition at the Luxembourg from 1750, and the purchases of d'Angiviller, which laid the basis for the collection. The chapter ends with d'Angiviller, the museum's chief promoter, going into exile in 1791, two years before the Louvre opened as a museum on 10 August 1793.

LouvreSalonPalais du Luxembourg exhibition
66 The Louvre and Napoleon

Chapter 6 follows the Louvre through Napoleon Bonaparte's rise, from the 1799 coup to his fall in 1815. Gardner uses Bonaparte's movements around the Tuileries and the Louvre as a framework, from the 1797 banquet in the Grande Galerie to the 1800 Christmas Eve bomb near the Carrousel. The chapter then returns to the Revolution in the same quarter, from the 1789 Salon and the 1791 royal flight to the 1792 attacks on the Tuileries. It describes the opening of the Musée Central des Arts in November 1793, its dim galleries and visitor rules, and its early directors Roland and David. The central case is the seizure of art from conquered Italy, Germany, the Low Countries and Spain under Denon, including the Apollo Belvedere, Veronese's Wedding Feast and the Venetian horses, and the 1797 triumph that paraded them through Paris. Denon's 1814 exhibition of 'primitive' Italian paintings, chosen for its difference, comes next, and the chapter ends with Percier and Fontaine's rue de Rivoli and the Arc du Carrousel.

LouvreMusée Central des Arts
77 The Louvre under the Restoration

Chapter 7 covers the Louvre from Napoleon's defeat in 1815 to the July Monarchy of 1830, when the Bourbon kings ran the museum as the Musée Royal. Its first theme is restitution: the allied armies reclaimed their art, and by November 1815 more than five thousand works had gone home, although exchanges let the Louvre keep a few major pieces. Gardner then turns to the Restoration's reorganization, including the removal of Napoleonic emblems, longer opening hours and purchases that brought medieval art into the museum. The Venus de Milo in 1821 and the Greek vases are set against the British Museum's Elgin Marbles, and the new Egyptian and Assyrian departments show the museum's wider range. The chapter ends with the Musée Charles X and the Galerie Campana, whose painted ceilings stage a contest between allegory and history, and with the unfinished Galerie d'Apollon series.

LouvreBritish MuseumMusée Charles XGalerie CampanaMusée ÉgyptienMusée Assyrien
88 The Nouveau Louvre of Napoleon III

Chapter 8 explains how Napoleon III finished the Louvre, joining it to the Tuileries between 1852 and 1857. Gardner covers the emperor's path to power, the architects Visconti and Lefuel, and the symmetrical plan of the Cour Napoléon. Gardner then describes the clearance of the old Quartier du Louvre, including the Impasse du Doyenné bohemia and the construction site recorded by Baldus. The interiors come next, notably Duban's Salon Carré and Galerie d'Apollon, the Appartement du Ministre and the Salle des États. The chapter also covers the collections: Jeanron's art-historical hanging, the purchases and donations of Campana, Sauvageot and La Caze, and the Winged Victory of Samothrace. It ends with Baudelaire's poem on the vanished Paris, and Gardner's argument that the Second Empire Louvre, first mocked, has become part of Paris itself.

LouvreMusée des SouverainsGalerie Campana
99 The Louvre in Modern Times

Chapter 9 follows the Louvre from the fall of the Second Empire in 1870 to Mitterrand's expansion in 1981, arguing that it became the world's leading art museum in this period. Gardner moves through three crises: the Prussian siege and the Commune, when the Tuileries burned and curator Barbet de Jouy saved the Louvre; the two world wars, when the collections were evacuated and the Mona Lisa moved; and the German Occupation, when Jacques Jaujard resisted German pressure to return the collections. Between them the chapter covers the display of the Winged Victory, the 1911 theft of the Mona Lisa, the admission charge, Henri Verne's reforms and temporary exhibitions, and Malraux's cleaning of the Cour Carrée and his cultural nationalism. It ends with postwar schemes for car parks and underground roads at the Louvre, most of them never built.

East and Southeast Asia Gardner mentions in passing that Georges Salles, director in the 1950s, was a specialist in Asian art, and that the Mona Lisa went to Tokyo in spring 1974, drawing more than one and a half million visitors. Neither point is developed.

LouvreMusée de l'OrangerieJeu de PaumeMusée des Arts Décoratifs
1010 The Creation of the Contemporary Louvre

Chapter 10 explains how the Louvre's present form came from the Grand Louvre project of 1981 to 1993, begun under President Mitterrand and designed by I. M. Pei. Gardner first argues that the museum had to change because tourist numbers were doubling, its nineteenth-century additions were never built for display, and its façades were decaying. The chapter then traces the decision, minister Jack Lang's 1981 report, the 1989 target and the choice of Pei over other architects. Most of it concerns the Pyramide and the underground Hall Napoléon, the reopening of the Aile Richelieu and Passage Richelieu, and the Carrousel du Louvre shopping centre, which Gardner presents as reconnecting the museum to Paris. Excavations of the medieval walls and the Chapel of Saint Louis, and the new landscaping of the Tuileries and place du Carrousel, complete the account. It concludes that a project greeted with hostility produced a museum that is now a happy place.

East and Southeast Asia The chapter gives I. M. Pei's background in passing: born in Guangzhou in 1917, raised in Hong Kong and Shanghai, and educated in the United States from 1935. It does not connect this to the Louvre commission or discuss any East or Southeast Asian collection.

LouvreNational Gallery (Washington, DC)Musée d'Orsay
Photo Insert

This picture section has no running text, only twelve captions. They cover a Jean Clouet portrait of François I, a Très Riches Heures miniature of the medieval Louvre, the Aile Lescot and Colonnade, Veronese's Wedding Feast at Cana, the Galerie d'Apollon and Appartement du Ministre, Ingres's Napoleon I, Baldus's photograph of the Nouveau Louvre, the Pavillon des Sessions, the Escalier Daru and the Hall Napoléon. Each caption gives a date, a maker and a short note.

Louvre
Epilogue

The Epilogue reviews the Louvre since the Grand Louvre opened, noting its growth into eight curatorial departments, the rise in attendance to over eight million a year, and a shortage of gallery space. Gardner observes that acquisitions have grown smaller relative to prices, that contemporary artists now work inside it, and that the Lens and Abu Dhabi branches have opened. It ends by suggesting the museum, though less central to a present-minded culture, remains unique.

Back Cover
Genoways, Hugh H.; Andrei, Mary Anne (eds.) (2008). Museum Origins: Readings in Early Museum History and Philosophy. Walnut Creek, CA: Left Coast Press.Asia: slight58 chapter overviews

Overview

An anthology of fifty-one historical writings on museums, from antiquity to 1925, edited by Hugh H. Genoways and Mary Anne Andrei as a teaching resource and a source for scholars. Its concern is the history and philosophy of museums: their origins in princely and university collecting, the aims of natural history, art and history museums, their educational role, exhibition design, and their relation to universities and living collections. Most authors are American, ten are English, and most selections date from 1850 to 1925, when natural history museums dominated the profession. The texts are truncated with ellipses and the book includes no how-to material. It is organised in seven sections (origins, philosophy, the new museum, education, exhibition, museums and universities, living collections), each with an editorial introduction.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia are barely present. No chapter discusses a museum, collection or visitor in Southeast Asia, and no Southeast Asian object or country is named. East Asia appears in passing in several readings: Hermann Hagen mentions Chinese relics among the curiosities of princely cabinets (chapter 7, The History of the Origin and Development of Museums); Mariana Van Rensselaer compares Japanese love of the sparse appeal to the eye with the taste of American museum-goers (chapter 15, The Art Museum and the Public); Laura Scales lists Japanese among the immigrant groups who use the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (chapter 32, The Museum's Part in the Making of Americans); and John George Wood criticises a Crystal Palace group that shows Asiatic tigers with a Moorish rider (chapter 36, The Dulness of Museums).

The one substantial passage is in chapter 47, The Arnold Arboretum: What it is and Does, by Charles Sprague Sargent. Seeds sent in 1882 from Peking by Dr Bretschneider of the Russian Embassy led to plant exploration in China, and then to the Wilson expeditions to central and western China, which made the Arboretum the best place to study the woody plants of eastern Asia. Its herbarium is described as rich in material from China and Japan. Ethnographic halls in chapter 37 (Dorsey on the American Museum of Natural History) refer to northeastern Asia only as a region of collecting.

What is not covered: colonial collecting, Asian states' museum policy, Asian museums, restitution, and Asian visitors or scholars, apart from immigrants in Boston. Cesnola's Cyprus and Babylonian material and the Near Eastern references fall outside this question.
