Contents

Theoretical approach of this work
PrefaceHugh H. Genoways and Mary Anne Andreip. 9

The editors explain that the book gathers fifty-one historical writings on museums, from antiquity to 1925, as a teaching resource and a source for scholars. They set it against Edward Alexander's studies of 'museum masters', aiming for a broader view of museums in society. Most authors are American, with ten from England, and most selections date from 1850 to 1925, when natural history museums dominated the profession. The texts are truncated, with ellipses marking cuts, and the book includes no how-to material.

About the Editorsp. 11
Section IMuseum Originsp. 13
Introduction to Section Ip. 13

This headnote introduces the section's seven readings on museum origins. It opens with two ancient texts, a description of the Museum of Alexandria and Varro's account of a Roman game park, and proceeds to Anthony Wood's account of Oxford's Ashmolean, the first public university museum in the English-speaking world. Further readings cover Peale's Philadelphia museum of 1794, the house museum at Mount Vernon, Godkin on New York and Hagen's history of Western European museums to 1875.

Museum of AlexandriaAshmolean MuseumMount Vernon
1GeographyStrabop. 15

An excerpt from Strabo's Geography (Book 17) describing the Museum of Alexandria, which the text calls the most famous museum of the ancient world. Strabo places it within the royal palaces, with a public walk, a seated exedra and a common mess-hall for scholars who held property in common. A priest, first appointed by the kings and later by Caesar, was in charge. The note before the excerpt observes that Strabo does not mention the Library, so it is unclear whether the two were separate buildings.

Museum of Alexandria
2Rerum Rusticarum Libri TresMarcus Terentius Varrop. 4

An excerpt from Varro's Res rustica (Book III), in which Appius and Axius discuss game parks. Appius explains that wild boars and roe deer are fed at set hours from a platform, and Axius recounts a dinner at Hortensius's villa near Laurentum, where deer and boars gathered at a trumpet call as Orpheus sang. Axius compares the spectacle to the hunts the aediles staged in the Circus Maximus. The passage is a conversation about farm management and spectacle.

3The Life and Times of Anthony Wood, Antiquary, of Oxford, 1632-1695, described by Himself, Collected from his Diaries and Other PapersAndrew Clarkp. 19

Wood's diary entry of 22 May 1683 describes the Ashmolean Museum at Oxford, built by the university to house Elias Ashmole's donated collection. He describes the stone building, its portal and inscription, then its ten rooms: a public museum, a School of Natural History where Robert Plot lectured on chemistry, a laboratory and a chemical library. He ends with gifts received, including an Egyptian mummy, and predicts that the collection will become one of the most famous in Europe.

Ashmolean Museum
4My Design in Forming this MuseumCharles Willson Pealep. 23

This is a 1792 broadside in which Charles Willson Peale sets out, for a group of prominent Philadelphians and members of the American Philosophical Society, his design for the museum he would open in 1794. He asks them to become its Visitors and Directors because his private collection has grown too large for him to manage alone and his means are too small to enlarge it. The argument follows Linnaeus's classes of natural history. Peale describes his portrait gallery of Revolutionary leaders, his plan to preserve the bodies of distinguished men, and his stuffed birds, including a bald eagle he has kept alive. Peale discusses how to mount large animals, fish and insects, and sets out plans for skeletons, fossils, minerals, plants and Native American artifacts. The cost of glass cases and rooms is the chief obstacle. Peale closes by thanking the Directors and saying that he is teaching his children his methods and intends to send one of them to South America to collect for the museum.

Peale's Philadelphia Museum
5The Mount Vernon AssociationSara Agnes Pryorp. 29

Sara Agnes Pryor, a founding member, tells the history of the Mount Vernon Ladies' Association, which bought George Washington's house and grounds and made it the first historic house museum in the United States. Her article is a first-hand memoir rather than a scholarly study. She describes the Richmond meeting of 1853 or 1854 at which Ann Pamela Cunningham began organising women across Virginia, the Association's first board, and the reluctance of Colonel John Augustine Washington, whose correspondence with the state's governors over the price of the estate is set out in detail. She also covers the fund-raising, which relied on newspaper appeals in the Richmond Enquirer and lectures by William L. Yancey and Edward Everett, and the handover of the house to the state of Virginia and to regents from each state. The article ends with a description of the house, tomb and river, and with a tribute to the women who still care for the site. Its interest lies in showing how women's patriotic organising created an early museum of national memory.

Mount Vernon
6A Word About MuseumsEdwin Lawrence Godkinp. 33

Godkin, associate editor of the New York Evening Post, writes an editorial in The Nation in 1865 after the fire that destroyed P. T. Barnum's American Museum in New York. He argues that the museum was a disorderly, unscientific place that pandered to crowds with freak shows, sensational drama and deceptions, and that its loss gives the city a chance to found a real American Museum on the model of the British Museum. Godkin describes the British Museum's national collections in detail and notes how scattered London's collections were. Godkin proposes that New York choose a department, such as natural history or antiquities, and that the New York Historical Society, which has been granted the old arsenal in Central Park, take the lead. Godkin warns that joint-stock companies and showmen cannot make a museum serve public education. The editorial ends with an appeal to wealthy citizens to fund a permanent museum for public instruction.

Barnum's American MuseumBritish MuseumNew York Historical Society
7The History of the Origin and Development of MuseumsH. A. Hagenp. 39

Hagen traces the early history of collections, mainly of natural history, from ancient temples and the collections attributed to Aristotle and Alexander to the nineteenth century. Hagen’s evidence comes from classical authors, medieval treasuries, and printed catalogues of Renaissance cabinets, including those of Kenntmann, Tradescant and the Jesuits at the Collegium Romanum. Hagen argues that the printing press, paper and alcohol as a preservative made collecting possible, that princes and merchants formed cabinets of curiosities, and that the Dutch cabinets of Swammerdam and Ruysch set the standard. Linnaeus's binomial nomenclature, his printed instructions for museums, and Cuvier's comparative anatomy at the Jardin des Plantes turned collections into scientific institutions. Hagen describes how museums became closed to the public in the early nineteenth century and then reopened. Hagen concludes that museums should be pitched at the level of ordinary visitors, as textbooks are pitched at their readers.

Jardin des PlantesAshmolean MuseumBritish MuseumJesuit collection at the Collegium Romanum
Section IIMuseum Philosophyp. 49
Introduction to Section IIp. 49

This short introduction to Section II, Museum Philosophy, asks why museums exist and what they do, and notes that administrators' answers have changed with the social issues of their day. It sorts the selected articles into three groups: general philosophy (Cesnola, Lucas, Rea), specialised regional museums (Bolton, Barbour, Thwaites, Farrington) and art museums (Van Rensselaer, Robinson). It ends with a list of additional readings on museum theory.

8An Address on the Practical Value of the American MuseumLuigi Palma di Cesnolap. 51

Cesnola, the first director of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, gave this address in 1887 at the opening of the George West Museum of Art and Archaeology in Round Lake, New York. Cesnola argues that a museum is a library of objects and a school of object-teaching, which instructs the casual visitor better than books can, and that it serves artists, craftsmen and scholars as well as the public. Cesnola’s evidence comes from his own experience in New York, where the Metropolitan's collections of Greek jewellery and pottery supplied craftsmen, and where Babylonian tablets and a clay barrel of Nebuchadnezzar gave new evidence for history and the Bible. Cesnola argues that museums are charitable institutions that should avoid debt and grow slowly, and that a museum is the people's vested fund. The address ends by praising the influence of American museums and by thanking the founders of this one for dedicating it to light and truth.

Metropolitan Museum of ArtGeorge West Museum of Art and ArchaeologyBritish Museum
9Purposes and Aims of Modern MuseumsFrederic A. Lucasp. 57

Lucas, director of the Brooklyn Museum, gave this address in 1907 to the Staten Island Association of Arts and Sciences as it prepared to become a general museum. Lucas asks why museums exist and whether the public gets a return on its money, and answers with the definitions of Gray and Goode, which make the purpose of a museum the preservation of objects for the increase of knowledge and the enlightenment of the people. Lucas’s case is local: since Henry Hudson sailed into New York Bay the forests, rocks and wildlife have largely vanished, so a museum must record what has gone. Lucas traces the shift from the old storehouse for students to the new museum that illustrates ideas, using a single bird in its habitat in place of rows of species. Museums must interest a casual public without losing seriousness, and they need trained staff. He ends by describing their civilising work in instilling order and a love of beauty, and by urging the audience to support their museum.

Brooklyn MuseumBritish MuseumStaten Island Association of Arts and Sciences
10The Functions of MuseumsPaul M. Reap. 61

Rea, director of the Charleston Museum in South Carolina, gave this lecture to the American Association of Museums in 1911, using his own institution, which he calls the oldest continuously operating museum in the United States, to illustrate his argument that museums exist for the people. Rea says a museum's scope depends on who supports it. Private owners set their own aims, schools and colleges should keep collections that serve teaching and transfer or develop those that do not, and municipal and national museums owe an obligation to the taxpayer. Museums should take an active part in civic life, serving as a clearing house for progress through industrial exhibits, bird and tree protection, and health campaigns. His case study is the Charleston Museum, which in the early 1900s moved from a neglected college collection with a small city grant to a city-maintained public institution, with a building, lectures, and joint work with the Park Board and the Advertising Club. He ends by arguing that a museum that serves its community will win the people's support.

Charleston Museum
11War MuseumsH. Boltonp. 65

Bolton, director of the Bristol Museum and Art Gallery, writes in 1918 for a conference of provincial museums on how to plan local war museums to remember the dead, the wounded and those affected by the First World War. Bolton argues that without a definite plan, collecting war material produces a heap of unrelated objects, and that a war museum must be a memorial as well as a realistic record. It should show the unity of purpose of the British Empire, the great stresses it met, the resources it mobilised, and the scale and character of the conflict, with a hall of names and local records of service. Bolton insists that such museums must not exalt war but show its national and personal losses, devastation and barbarism. Bolton closes by arguing that a war museum should instil pride, public duty and justice, and that it should be built as a deterrent to future war. The piece describes no particular collections.

12Museums and the PeopleErwin H. Barbourp. 69

Barbour, who directed the University of Nebraska State Museum, gave this paper to the Nebraska Academy of Sciences in 1912. Barbour argues that every state should maintain a museum, as it maintains libraries, because museums hold practical material such as injurious insects, pathological specimens, building stone and textile fibres, and because they teach people who have had no schooling. Barbour describes state museums as the institutions closest to local feeling, displaying each state's resources and history and so attracting settlers and investors. Barbour argues that museums have a wholesome moral effect, drawing young people from commonplace pursuits, and cites the school parties at the American Museum of Natural History and at the Nebraska museum as evidence. Barbour calls for museums to open on Sundays and holidays so that working people can study nature rather than books. Barbour concludes that the state owes museums the exhibition room needed for donated collections.

Nebraska State MuseumAmerican Museum of Natural History
13State and Local Historical SocietiesReuben Gold Thwaitesp. 73

Thwaites, long the executive of the State Historical Society of Wisconsin, reports in 1905 to the American Historical Association on how state and local societies should be organised and what they should do. Thwaites argues that a society depends on a strong personality as well as on its form, and compares privately endowed, state-supported and departmental arrangements without choosing one. Thwaites sets its scope as the archaeological, historical and genealogical material of its territory, and lists local sources from diaries and newspapers to pioneer interviews. Thwaites warns that relic museums must not become unmeaning collections of popular attractions. Thwaites urges societies to publish edited sources rather than genealogies, and to pursue public work such as field meetings, lectures and historic markers. The excerpt ends by arguing that a society must win popular support before it can expect public money.

14On the Ideal Relations of Public Libraries, Museums, and Art Gallery to the CityOliver C. Farringtonp. 79

Farrington, of the Field Museum, chaired the Chicago Library Club subcommittee that sets out the ideal relations between the city's public libraries, museums and art gallery and the people who support them. The report argues that these institutions should be governed together by one board, since museums illustrate what libraries describe. It weighs the board's size, pay, terms and appointment, and proposes that its powers grow from advice to direct service as public support grows.

15The Art Museum and the PublicMariana Alley Van Rensselaerp. 83

Van Rensselaer, an artist, architect and writer on art, argues in this 1917 essay that art museums should educate the public as well as serve experts, and that visitors must learn to see for themselves. Knowledge of art is not the same as sensitivity to beauty, she argues, so museums should help people educate their own eyes through arrangement, guided tours, study rooms, lectures and loan collections. She asks whether museums should show only fine art or also industrial and ethnographic objects, and cites the public's interest in Egyptian collections in favour of the wider view. She prefers grouping objects by period rather than by kind, as in the Metropolitan Museum's Egyptian rooms, and favours plentiful display over reserves. The essay ends by urging museums to be warm and welcoming, with pleasant rooms and music, so that looking becomes a lasting habit.

Metropolitan Museum of Art
16English Art Connoisseurship and CollectingSir J. C. Robinsonp. 91

Robinson, Surveyor of the Queen's Pictures from 1880 to 1901, writes in 1894 on the decline of art connoisseurship in England. Robinson contrasts a century ago, when collecting was confined to the aristocracy and a few bankers, with his own day, when merchants, financiers and manufacturers buy art and every town has a gallery and dealers. Robinson’s evidence is historical: the few visits to great country houses, the continental galleries of Paris, Rome and Florence, and early pioneers such as Horace Walpole and Sir Andrew Fountaine, who looked beyond classical art. Robinson then traces the history of collecting old master drawings, whose owners' marks make their succession traceable. Robinson attributes the decline of this field to public museums that withdrew the best specimens, to changing fashion, and to the sale of the Lawrence collection. Robinson concludes that English taste has grown less serious and that continental buyers are taking the nation's finest works.

British Museum
Section IIIThe New Museump. 97
Introduction to Section IIIp. 97

This editorial introduction to Section III, The New Museum, explains the new museum idea, which separated public exhibition galleries from research collections. It credits William Henry Flower with implementing the idea in the British Museum's South Kensington building and George Brown Goode with a parallel movement at the United States National Museum, and it notes that Sellers gives Charles Willson Peale priority. It says that the section's first articles concern the public side of the new museum, and that its last two are early writing on museum ethics.

British MuseumUnited States National Museum
17The Use and Abuse of MuseumsW. Stanley Jevonsp. 99

Jevons, the economist, reviews English museums in a condensed article of 1883. Jevons argues that the main use of a museum is public education, and that European museums are failing at it, mainly because they crowd galleries with systematic displays that give visitors no understanding. Jevons’s evidence comes from his own visits to the British Museum, the South Kensington Museum and its loan exhibitions, and the Crystal Palace, where a Pompeian house and an Alhambra court created a stronger unity of effect. Jevons contrasts the Thorwaldsen Museum in Copenhagen, which presents one sculptor's work in a single building, with the vast galleries of London. Jevons concludes that collections should be grouped into coherent wholes, that a few well-studied objects teach more than thousands glanced at, and that a private collection is the key to the public museum. The article ends by urging a professional association of curators and a board of trustees run like a college.

British MuseumSouth Kensington MuseumThorwaldsen MuseumCrystal Palace
18The Relationships and Responsibilities of MuseumsG. Brown Goodep. 111

Goode, an administrator at the Smithsonian Institution, presented this paper in 1895 to the Museums Association at Newcastle upon Tyne as a codified statement of museum principles. It answers Jevons's call for a general theory of administration with 215 theses in eleven chapters. Goode defines the museum, distinguishes it from the exposition, and contrasts the monument-filled cities of Italy with the museum proper. Goode argues that each museum should be preeminent in at least one specialty, and he proposes cooperation between museums, including transfers of specimens. Goode lists five necessities: stable support, a definite plan, collections, trained staff and suitable buildings. Goode insists that a finished museum is a dead museum, that the public museum is a necessity of civilisation, and that a nation's standing can be judged by its museums and how they are supported.

Smithsonian InstitutionRuskin's workingmen's museum near SheffieldSouth Kensington Museum
19Modern MuseumsWilliam Henry Flowerp. 125

Flower, of the natural history departments of the British Museum at South Kensington, addresses the Museums Association in 1893 on the ideal design of a natural history museum. Flower sets aside General Pitt-Rivers's circular plan as impractical and proposes a grid of intersecting lines that separates exhibition rooms, reserve collections and workrooms. Flower favours top lighting and a central hall, and for small museums advises a limited type collection with a local collection.

British Museum (Natural History)
20Museum Ideals of Purpose and MethodBenjamin Ives Gilmanp. 129

Gilman, secretary of the Boston Museum of Fine Arts, challenges George Brown Goode's dictum that an educational museum is a collection of instructive labels, each illustrated by a well-selected specimen. Gilman argues that art objects are unica, valued for their concrete individuality, so the formula fails for art museums. Science museums aim at abstract knowledge and are in essence schools, while art museums aim at concrete satisfaction and are in essence temples. The primary purpose of an art museum, he holds, is aesthetic, letting the beholder share the artist's vision. Education is a secondary use, through shaping ideals, supporting historical study and technical skill, and interpretive aids for visitors from other civilisations. He concludes that a fine art museum is an artistic institution with educational uses, not an educational institution with art as its teaching material.

Boston Museum of Fine Arts
21The New MuseumJohn Cotton Danap. 137

Dana, founder and director of the Newark Museum, sets out in 1917 his version of George Brown Goode's new museum. Dana argues that a museum should serve its community as a local institution of visual instruction, and he attacks the grand architecture, top-lit galleries and rows of costly cases that isolate museums from the people who most need them. Dana does not condemn collections outright, but says their immediate value is overrated and their cost out of proportion. Dana’s general theory is a list of eleven activities: entertaining casual visitors, teaching adults and school groups, lending objects, placing small branches in shops and schools, drawing on local collectors, showing local industry, publicity, and linking with the public library. Dana sees the collecting habit among young people as one of the most promising fields of all.

22The Museum ConscienceJoseph Grinnellp. 143

Grinnell, first director of the Museum of Vertebrate Zoology at the University of California, writes in 1921 on the duties of curators of scientific collections. Grinnell argues that a research museum exists to make facts available, so its specimens must be kept in order and labelled with accuracy, since label errors pass into the literature and are almost impossible to correct. Grinnell condemns the habit of general museums that claim to house scientific collections without systematic arrangement or careful labels, and he estimates that perhaps 90 per cent of the vertebrate collections he has seen in the larger museums are unsatisfactory. Simplicity matters as much as order, since a complicated system defeats the research student. He points out that many species are disappearing and that surviving specimens are the only evidence future scientists will have. He concludes that every museum urgently needs a curator with a museum conscience, who devises the best arrangement and corrects errors at once.

Museum of Vertebrate Zoology
23Museum EthicsL. Earle Rowep. 147

Rowe, director of the Rhode Island School of Design, presents in 1917 what is probably the earliest American discussion of museum ethics, eight years before the American Association of Museums adopted a code. Rowe argues that museum policy has been debated along scholarly and aesthetic lines, while the ethical questions of conduct between museums, dealers, collectors and staff have gone undiscussed. Rowe urges art museums to cooperate: to lend stored material to smaller institutions, to respect one another's local interests in acquisitions, and to share expert advice. On dealers, he advises cordial but businesslike dealing, and refusing gifts that seek to create obligation. He recommends frank dealing with collectors, no fees for advice, and no naming of prospective buyers to dealers. He concludes that the director, as the most influential officer, should take no fees or gifts and should avoid collecting, since strict ethics also make good policy.

Section IVMuseum Educationp. 153
Introduction to Section IVp. 153

This editorial introduction to Section IV, Museum Education, argues that museum professionals have written about educating the public for 150 to 200 years, long before the 1969 Belmont Report that many take as the start of the movement. It notes that half the articles are by women, who were often confined to public education rather than research. It previews the articles by Gallup, Rea, Morse, Starr, Baker, Whitmore, Scadding, Greenwood, Scales and Howe, and ends with a list of additional readings.

24The Children's Museum as an EducatorAnna Billings Gallupp. 155

Gallup, curator of the Brooklyn Children's Museum, describes in 1908 the origins and methods of what she calls the only museum of its kind in the world. Gallup argues that a children's museum should offer what school and home cannot, and that its success depends on understanding children's tastes, above all their need for action. Gallup’s evidence is the museum's history: it began in 1899 in two rooms of a Bedford Park house with a few insects, shells and birds, and grew to twelve exhibition rooms on zoology, geography, history and art. Gallup describes zoological rooms arranged by age, model groups of peoples such as the Eskimo, a children's library with trained librarians, and lectures and loan material for schools. Gallup cites boys who learned wireless telegraphy and defends the museum's physics classes against critics. Gallup ends by noting the need for a larger building and the prospect of similar museums elsewhere.

Brooklyn Children's Museum
25The Relation of the Museum to the SchoolsCarolyn M. Reap. 161

Carolyn Morse Rea, wife of the director of the Charleston Museum, writes in 1907 on how schools can use the museum. She argues that the museum is an almost unrecognised part of education, and that its public image as a stuffed animal house is the museums' own fault, since their exhibits were not designed to teach. Her example is a group of mounted beavers, which would teach only if set in natural surroundings with pictures, maps and clear labels. She proposes portable loan collections sent to schools with notes and bibliographies, supervised by a special instructor, together with a library that supplements school textbooks, classroom space and lecture courses for visiting classes. She also recommends a museum bulletin mailed to principals. Her underlying point is that most of a museum's work, its research, lies below the surface, and that teachers should understand this. The article is a practical plan for linking a museum to a city's schools.

Charleston Museum
26If Public Libraries, Why Not Public Museums?Edward S. Morsep. 165

Morse, director of the Peabody Academy of Science in Salem, writes in 1893 in reaction to the Massachusetts Public Library Act, urging similar legislation for town museums. Morse argues that a museum, like a library, is an educational institution, because a real object with a clear label conveys information faster than any description, and because it encourages collecting and the study of local natural history. Morse lists what a town museum should hold: local natural products, a general collection for comparison, anatomical series, illustrations of natural selection, and developmental series. Morse contrasts the Cluny Museum in Paris, a mass of beautiful medieval objects that exhausts the visitor, with the Pitt-Rivers collection at Oxford, which provokes inquiry. Morse’s model is the Peabody Academy, whose Essex County collections are linked by coloured labels to the public library. Morse ends by advising that gifts be merged with existing collections, that new accessions be shown for a year, and that useless material be discarded.

Peabody Academy of ScienceCluny MuseumOxford University Museum
27The Museum in Educational WorkFrederick Starrp. 171

Starr, a biologist and ethnologist, writes in 1892 on how museums should serve each level of education. Elementary schools should build their own cabinets, high schools need complete local series, colleges need balanced systematic collections, and universities need large study collections. He argues that a museum without a teacher behind it is dead, and that public museums should become educational centres linked to every school.

28The Museum, the Original Exponent of Visual EducationFrank C. Bakerp. 175

Baker, a natural history curator, writes in 1922 on why museums are not yet used as an efficient aid to visual education. Baker blames weak cooperation between schools and museums, and museums whose installations serve systematists rather than general teachers. Baker welcomes the modern group or diorama, which shows animals and peoples in natural settings, and argues that university collections should supplement courses, with developmental series in zoology and fossil sequences in geology.

29The Function of the Museum InstructorElizabeth M. Whitmorep. 179

Whitmore, assistant to the director of the Worcester Museum of Art, writes in 1916 on the art museum docent, the person who puts the collections within the public's reach. Whitmore sets out a dispute between those who would have the docent impart facts about an object and those who would develop appreciation of its qualities. Whitmore argues that the two aims are not exclusive, since the instructor must rouse emotion and the appreciator must provide background. Whitmore’s two scenarios, set among the Greek vases of an unnamed museum, show a docent first lecturing a school party on Greek daily life, then guiding an adult visitor to see a hydria in terms of its use and form. Whitmore concludes that the docent needs three kinds of knowledge: of the objects, of their history, and of the museum public. Both roles, she says, belong to the museum instructor, one as a supplement to schooling and the other as a host.

30Museums and Other Classified Collections as Instruments of Education in Natural ScienceHenry Scaddingp. 183

Scadding, president of the Canadian Institute, writes in 1871 after the Paris Exhibition of 1867. Scadding argues that visitors to great classified collections should go with a plan and a definite subject, so that a museum becomes a gallery of illustration and an instrument of self-education rather than a show. Scadding chooses natural science, with its mechanical philosophy, chemistry and physiology, as the subject that Canadian youths travelling in Europe should study in the great collections. Scadding thinks education should give every youth the elementary principles of contemporary knowledge, and that museums display the reign of law in nature. Scadding lists museums to visit in Boston, Philadelphia, Washington and Montreal, and suggests that the Canadian Institute's small collection might become a repository of Canadian archaeological and historical objects. Scadding ends by insisting that natural science should have a high place in schools, though not as the only subject.

University Museum, TorontoCanadian Institute museumBarnett's Museum, Niagara Falls
31The Place of Museums in EducationThomas Greenwoodp. 187

Greenwood writes in 1893 that museums should be recognised as part of the national education system, since a museum is a library of objects that awakens interest in common things. Greenwood hopes a working man's visit could turn him from drink to natural knowledge. Greenwood warns that huge collections distract visitors, producing what he calls museum drunkenness, and suggests folding screens for quiet study. Greenwood quotes Kingsley, Emerson and Forbes, and asks that curators be teachers as well as scholars.

32The Museum's Part in the Making of AmericansLaura W. L. Scalesp. 191

Scales, an instructor at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, writes in 1917 on the museum's part in turning immigrants into American citizens. Scales argues that immigrants come to museums because the objects link their old culture to the new country, and that a love of beauty is a shared inheritance. Scales’s examples are lectures in foreign languages, high school drawing classes, and children's stories on the long journey to America, which use museum objects as background. Scales argues that the museum should show newcomers that their skills and tastes can enrich their new country as well as their pockets. The article presents the museum as a civic institution rather than a repository of treasures.

Museum of Fine Arts, Boston
33The Museum's Educational CredoWinifred E. Howep. 195

Howe, editor for publications at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, reprints the museum's educational credo of 1918, a nine-point staff statement. Its argument rests on the museum's 1870 charter, its 1908 status as an educational institution and its New York location among immigrant communities. Every person, the credo holds, has a latent love of beauty that the museum should cultivate, through links to visitors' interests, school cooperation, publications and lending collections. It ends by calling this work a wartime service.

Metropolitan Museum of Art
Section VMuseum Exhibitionp. 199
Museum Exhibitionp. 199

This short introduction to the section on museum exhibition argues that between the mid-nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, as museums separated research and exhibit collections, public display was transformed. It introduces Wallace, Wood and Krefft, who favoured habitat groups and educational display, and the 1907 debate in Science between Dorsey and Boas over arranging ethnographic objects, which Ward supported with dioramas. A reading list closes it.

Australian MuseumField Museum of Natural HistoryAmerican Museum of Natural HistoryMilwaukee Public Museum
34Museum for the PeopleAlfred Russel Wallacep. 201

Wallace, co-discoverer of natural selection, sets out in this 1869 article his design for an ideal popular natural history museum. Wallace argues that museums fail the public because their specimens are badly chosen and mounted and their buildings are ill suited to close viewing. Each family or genus, he proposes, should occupy its own room as a well-mounted group showing males, females, young, prey, habitat and useful products, with seats for study. A students' department would hold the rest of the collections. Ethnological cases would trace tools, pottery and painting using models and casts, and Wallace follows Hooker in siting the museum in an open park. He ends by arguing that such a plan has never been applied systematically.

National Museum of Natural History (Wallace's proposed model)
35The Improvements Effected in Modern Museums of Europe and AustraliaGerard Krefft, with extensive quotes from John E. Grayp. 209

Krefft, of the Australian Museum, sets out his exhibition philosophy, drawing heavily on John Edward Gray, Keeper of Zoology at the British Museum. The article quotes Gray's proposals at length: each case should present one study theme with labels explaining its purpose, and large animals should be isolated and kept low, no higher than about five feet from the floor. Krefft then turns to practical matters, including portable iron and glass cases that resist insects, study collections of skins, bones and tooth slides kept apart from display, and fossils such as a large plesiosaur shown on slanting platforms. Krefft argues that Gray's proposals to the British Museum Trustees had already been largely carried out in Australia. The piece closes by faulting the Dublin Museum's horizontal table display, which wastes space and hides the animal.

British MuseumAustralian MuseumMelbourne MuseumDublin Museum
36The Dulness of MuseumsJohn George Woodp. 217

Wood, a popular British natural history writer, argues in this 1887 article that museums are dull for the general public because they display collections as static, systematic arrangements. Wood surveys coins, china, botany, geology, art galleries and zoological galleries, where animals stand motionless on boards, and claims that visitors are drawn only to creatures doing something, as at feeding time. Wood proposes three kinds of museum, for scientists, for beginners and for the general public, and notes that the new natural history departments at South Kensington serve only the second. Wood then sketches an ideal public zoology museum in which habitat groups show actual episodes in animals' lives, copied from photographs and travellers' accounts, with lecturers explaining them in words ten thousand listeners can understand. Wood criticises the Wurtemburg group at the Crystal Palace for placing a Moorish rider with Asian tigers and for arming women and other peoples with weapons, errors that teach falsehoods.

Natural History departments, South KensingtonCrystal Palace (Wurtemburg Gallery)British Museum
37The Anthropological Exhibits at the American Museum of Natural HistoryGeorge A. Dorseyp. 220

Dorsey, curator of anthropology at the Field Museum, criticises the American Museum of Natural History's reorganised ethnological halls in this 1907 Science article. Dorsey first praises the department's earlier installations, in which objects were ordered by type from 'primitive' to 'civilised' and most of the collection was on view, giving visitors a real sense of tribal cultures. Dorsey then argues that the museum has moved large collections into flimsy storage and replaced them with type exhibits. Working through the Peruvian, Eskimo and Plains halls, he shows that the Peruvian hall sorts objects by material rather than showing an agricultural, settled culture, and that the Eskimo hall treats the Eskimo as one culture and uses misleading scenes, such as a woman fishing through ice and an improperly lined house. He concludes that such displays suit a school or a small museum, and that a national institution should serve scientists.

American Museum of Natural History
38Some Principles of Museum AdministrationFranz Boasp. 231

Boas replies in this 1907 Science article to George Dorsey's criticism of the American Museum of Natural History's ethnological halls. Boas argues that museums serve three purposes, entertainment, instruction and research, and that the large museum is chiefly justified by preserving long series of material for science. Visitors come to be entertained and cannot follow systematic displays, so exhibits should present single ideas set against a plain background, and groups should be used sparingly because repetition weakens each one. He insists that popularising science must not simplify it, and that anthropological objects, which gain their meaning from social and religious life, cannot be arranged in a single scheme without distortion. Boas proposes separating public exhibits from study collections, citing suburban storage in Berlin, and concludes that systematic museums must be small while the large museum serves the advancement of science first.

American Museum of Natural HistoryUnited States National MuseumEthnographical Museum, Berlin
39Modern Exhibitional Tendencies of Museums of Natural History and Ethnology Designed for Public UseHenry L. Wardp. 241

Ward, director of the Milwaukee Public Museum, argues in this 1909 paper that a public museum must be educational rather than an undigested reflection of nature. Ward contrasts older museums, which charged fees, restricted visitors and displayed rows of similarly posed specimens with bare name labels, with his own museum, which has admitted the public free every day since 1905. Ward defends taxidermy groups that show animals in their habitats, argues that they have improved taxidermy and added to zoological and ecological knowledge, and notes that the group method has spread to geology and anthropology. Ward holds that labels must give common names, provenance and sex, written for untechnical readers. Ward ends by describing museums as entering a period of rapid development as part of popular education.

Milwaukee Public MuseumBritish Museum
Section VIMuseums and Universitiesp. 249
Museums and Universitiesp. 249

This short introduction to Section VI argues that universities and museums both see themselves as educational institutions but teach in very different ways. It previews the essays: Edward Forbes on the campus museum in science teaching, Peabody on a campus museum for social science, Edward Waldo Forbes on art museums as teaching tools, Dill on museum training in natural history museums, and Winchell's case that research should be the campus museum's main purpose. A reading list follows.

40On the Educational Uses of MuseumsEdward Forbesp. 251

Edward Forbes, lecturer in natural history at the Royal School of Mines, gives this 1853 opening address at the school's Museum of Practical Geology. He argues that museums cannot educate by themselves, but can instruct the educated and stir the ignorant: a labourer who walks through the British Museum learns that every object has meaning and that its arrangement reveals science. He claims that schools neglect training in observation, which museums can supply if competent teachers explain the collections. Forbes insists that curators must address the uninformed as well as scientists, and that national museums should be tied to public teaching, as college museums are. Forbes proposes exchanging duplicate specimens among institutions, with larger museums supplying smaller ones rather than money being given, and closes with a vision of every British town having a museum, library, parks and gallery for public education.

British MuseumMuseum of Practical Geology
41The Social Museum as an Instrument of University TeachingFrancis G. Peabodyp. 257

Peabody, who founded the 'social ethics' movement at Harvard, describes in this 1911 paper the Social Museum set up to support social science teaching. Peabody argues that science is learned by seeing and handling, so the social sciences need collections of documents and images just as zoology has museums. Peabody traces Harvard's sequence of collections from the Museum of Comparative Zoology in 1859 through the Semitic Museum of 1889 and the Germanic Museum of 1902 to the Social Museum begun in 1903. Peabody presents American social problems, from crowded cities and immigration to labour conflict, as demanding comparison with Germany, England and other countries. Peabody then describes the Social Museum's holdings, among them German insurance charts and reports, labour colonies, housing schemes and settlement exhibits, which give students material for inductive study.

Social Museum, HarvardGermanic Museum, HarvardSemitic Museum, HarvardMuseum of Comparative Zoology, Harvard
42The Relation of the Art Museum to a UniversityEdward W. Forbesp. 261

Edward W. Forbes, director of Harvard's Fogg Art Museum, argues in this 1911 address that a university art museum must serve students who study art in theory as well as those who make it. Art, unlike chemistry with its laboratories, cannot be brought into the classroom, so the museum must supply photographs, slides, casts and originals, and universities have seldom bought art, relying on gifts. He distinguishes the art school, for painters, from the university, for critics and general students, and insists that a critic should know how to paint. He describes the Fogg's equipment, about 43,000 photographs, 5,000 slides, a small library and original works, which he says stir enthusiasm that reproductions cannot. He defends temporary exhibitions, including a Degas show and modern etchings, while noting the limits of space and the difficulty of judging living artists. He concludes that the university museum should inspire students to create and to appreciate art.

Fogg Art Museum
43Training Museum WorkersHomer R. Dillp. 265

Dill, who ran the museum training course at the State University of Iowa, argues in this 1917 paper that college natural history museums can recover if they are run by trained men. Dill traces their decline to the division of natural science into specialist departments, which left no one to build the series of specimens that the old professor of natural history had gathered, and he cites replies from a survey of museums that many listed collections were inactive. Dill describes 'paper museums' that exist only in printed catalogues, and a city collection so neglected that its specimens were unrecognisable. Dill then sets out the Iowa course: a first year of drawing and modelling, a natural science major, practical mounting work in a zoological museum and museum theory, leading to a B.A. or B.S., together with a six-week summer course for those who cannot spare a year. Dill concludes that a good director matters more than anything else to a college museum.

44Museums and Their PurposeN. H. Winchellp. 269

Winchell, Minnesota's state geologist, gives this 1891 lecture to the Academy of Sciences of St Paul, tracing the word 'museum' from the Athenian temple of the Muses to modern usage. Winchell argues that the modern museum has three aims: entertainment, as in Barnum's Museum or the dime museum, where the visitor is passive; instruction, found in most colleges, which leaves visitors with unassimilated facts; and research, which he calls the true museum, whose purpose is to inspire the visitor to instruct others. Winchell traces the research idea to Bacon's New Atlantis, to the British Museum established in 1753 and to the Louvre after 1789. Winchell notes that great national collections such as the United States National Museum serve instruction and research at once. Winchell concludes that the work of research happens in laboratories and stores that the public never sees.

British MuseumBarnum's Museum, New YorkLouvreUnited States National Museum
Section VIIPhilosophy of Museums with Living Collectionsp. 275
Philosophy of Museums with Living Collectionsp. 275

This introduction to Section VII, on museums with living collections, argues that zoos, aquaria, botanical gardens and arboreta belong with museums. It credits Charles H. Townsend, first director of the New York Aquarium, with showing that aquaria and zoos share the aims of natural history museums. It previews the essays on botanical gardens and zoos and four case studies: the Missouri Botanical Garden, the Arnold Arboretum, the New York Zoological Park and the New York Aquarium.

New York AquariumMissouri Botanical GardenArnold ArboretumNew York Zoological Park
45Botanical GardensNathaniel Lord Brittonp. 277

Britton, first director of the New York Botanical Garden, sets out in this 1896 paper the mission of the modern botanical garden. Britton traces its origins to medieval monks' healing gardens and to eighteenth-century patrons who collected rare plants, and argues that four elements came to define it as gardens opened to the public: the economic, the aesthetic, the scientific and the philanthropic. For the economic element he proposes an Economic Garden and an Economic Museum arranged by product, such as drugs, fibres and woods, rather than by biological sequence. He insists that the scientific department must support this work and that a university link strengthens it. The aesthetic element calls for naturalistic planting in place of rectilinear beds, and the philanthropic element for orderly instruction and recreation, which he says a garden provides better than a park. He concludes that the four elements may carry different weight depending on local conditions.

New York Botanical Garden
46The Missouri Botanical GardenWilliam Treleasep. 283

Trelease, first director of the Missouri Botanical Garden, tells the early history of the garden that Henry Shaw turned from his private grounds into a public trust. Trelease describes Shaw's 1859 enabling act and will, which provided for a garden, a museum, a library and lectures, and the Botanical Museum and Library that came to hold a herbarium of some 60,000 specimens. Shaw's plans waited on the advice of Asa Gray until Engelmann's death prompted an endowed school of botany at Washington University, and the will set up an independent board of trustees and required the garden to stay ornamental. Trelease argues that a herbarium is indispensable because its type specimens fix the true characters of species. Trelease concludes that research is the garden's ultimate purpose, and that its staff has so far done only a little of it.

Missouri Botanical Garden
47The Arnold Arboretum: What it is and DoesCharles Sprague Sargentp. 289Asia: in part

Sargent, director of the Arnold Arboretum at Harvard, explains in this 1918 pamphlet what the arboretum is and does. Sargent traces its origin to a bequest of $100,000 from the New Bedford merchant James Arnold in 1868, which George Emerson and John Dixwell turned in 1872 into an agreement with Harvard for part of the Bussey Farm. The early history was one of neglect and political difficulty: the income could not be spent until the principal grew, and Frederick Law Olmsted's plan led to an 1882 contract by which the Boston Park Commission took the land and leased it back to the University for a thousand years, opened to the public. Sargent describes the living collection as a tree museum arranged in botanical sequence, with native oaks and a hemlock grove on Hemlock Hill, and says that the nurseries and herbarium send plants and information far beyond the United States. Sargent concludes that the arboretum serves research and education together.

East and Southeast Asia Sargent says that seeds sent in 1882 from Peking by Dr Bretschneider, physician to the Russian Embassy, led to plant exploration in China and then to Wilson's expeditions to central and western China, first sponsored by a London nurseryman and later by the Arboretum itself. Sargent credits Wilson's collecting with making the Arboretum the best place to study the woody plants of eastern Asia, and notes that its herbarium is rich in material from China and Japan.

Arnold Arboretum
48Zoological Gardens, a Critical EssayTheodore Linkp. 293

Link, an architect, argues in this 1883 essay that zoological gardens fail their own stated aim of studying animals' natural habits. Link describes lions and tigers pacing in iron-grated cells and bears kept in pits copied from the Jardin des Plantes, and he links the failure of captive breeding to unnatural housing, citing the black bear. Link calls for enclosures rather than cages, with landscaping that imitates each animal's home, and calls cages inexcusable in zoological gardens.

St. Louis zoological garden
49The Making of a Zoological-Park MasterpieceWilliam T. Hornadayp. 297

Hornaday, long-time director of the New York Zoological Park, explains in this 1925 essay the principles behind the park he built in the Bronx. Hornaday argues that a city can make a zoological park through a union of private society effort and municipal money, and lists the essentials: a free public site, permanence of control, freedom from politics, expert planning, merit-based staffing, society-supplied collections and taxpayer-funded upkeep. Hornaday contrasts this with European gardens, usually bought by societies, set in city centres and charging fees that keep out the poor. Hornaday then describes the park's 264 acres, open-air ranges, primate house, lion house with wire fronts, elephant house and bison herd, and ends with its 1924 attendance of 2,572,050 and its collection of 8,363 living specimens.

New York Zoological Park
50Administration of the Public AquariumCharles H. Townsendp. 303

Townsend, director of the New York Aquarium, argues in this 1917 paper that public aquaria are museums of natural history in function, since they educate and entertain. Townsend explains how aquaria differ from museums in cost: freshwater tanks are cheap to run, while marine exhibits need pumps and stored sea water. Townsend describes the difficulty of collecting live specimens, which cannot be left to fishermen, and the feeding and staffing of the New York Aquarium.

New York Aquarium

Greenhalgh, Michael (2019). Plundered Empire: Acquiring Antiquities from Ottoman Lands. Leiden: Brill.Asia: slight19 chapter overviews

Overview

Plundered Empire examines the Western travellers, diplomats and consuls who visited the Ottoman Empire from the Renaissance to the First World War, coveted its classical antiquities and carried them home. Its main argument is that the Empire was plundered by its own inhabitants long before Europeans arrived, and that Western acquisition, by stealth, gift, payment and force, stripped ruins across Asia Minor, the Aegean islands, Syria, Mesopotamia, Egypt, North Africa and Greece. The book concentrates on what happened in the field rather than on museum politics. It is organised in three sections: planning (shopping lists, consuls, identifying sites), acquisition (locals, digging, vandalism, regional surveys, Athens and mainland Greece) and consequences (shipping, museum rivalry, export laws and partage), closing with the argument that looting continued after 1918 and in Iraq after 2003.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East Asia and Southeast Asia are almost absent. In this book 'Asia' means Asia Minor, Syria, Mesopotamia and the other Ottoman provinces, and the chapters on those regions treat them at length. Chapter 9, Sites and Travellers in European and Asiatic Turkey, is the nearest to a regional study, but it concerns Ottoman Europe and Anatolia. No museum, collection, collector, visitor, curator or state from China, Japan, Korea, the Philippines, Indonesia, Indochina, Siam or Malaya appears.

China is named only in passing, four times. Travellers to the Ottoman lands went on, the book notes, to India, the East Indies or China (chapter 1, line 1081). Chinese porcelain imports are mentioned beside the Dresden and Meissen factories, which made copies of antique statues (line 6231). The British ambassador's appeal to spare Athens would be 'like sending a mission to the Emperor of China' (line 19016), and modern colossal statues are popular 'in the Far East' (line 22813). None of these is analysed.

Not covered: no East or Southeast Asian museum, state heritage policy or restitution claim is discussed. The Ottoman and Greek antiquities laws of the late nineteenth century (chapter 17) are the nearest the book comes to an Asian state's own heritage policy, and they concern the Empire, not East Asia. The preface also sets aside Mycenaean, Minoan and Phoenician work and the arts of Iraq. Asian visitors, scholars and curators are absent throughout.

Contents

Theoretical approach of this work
Prefacep. xi

Greenhalgh's preface defines the book as a study of Western travellers who visited the Ottoman Empire, coveted its classical antiquities and carried them home, from the reports that opened the way to archaeology to the shipping of marble blocks. It explains the three-part structure of planning, acquisition and consequences, why the account stops at the First World War, and why it concentrates on what happened in the field rather than on museum politics back home.

List of Maps and Illustrationsp. xvii
Mapsp. xxvii
Part 1Planning Shopping Lists, Ambassadors and Consuls, Sites and Scholarsp. 1
1Setting the Scenep. 3

Greenhalgh's first chapter sets the framework of the book: the rise and decline of the Ottoman Empire, which kept large stretches of the Mediterranean, Asia Minor, Syria, Mesopotamia and Egypt full of classical remains that were little dug and often broken or reused. Greenhalgh defines plunder, listing the natural and human agents that destroyed sites, and notes that Ottoman rulers themselves gave antiquities to Britain, Germany and France. Much of the chapter concerns travel conditions, including firmans, capitulations, pirates, disease and poor roads, and travel books were often unreliable and self-promoting. He then traces the move from antiquarianism to archaeology, contrasting medieval Venice and Pisa, which reused marble without seeking classical sculpture, with the Renaissance and later collectors. The chapter ends by arguing that the museums stocked with these objects rest on looting rather than ethical acquisition, and that later chapters trace the looting that success stories leave out.

British MuseumLouvre
2Armchair Collectors and Shopping Listsp. 29

Greenhalgh examines the shopping lists that scholars and officials drew up for collectors in the Ottoman lands, from Peiresc and Spon in the seventeenth century to Colbert's royal commissions and the Society of Dilettanti. English aristocrats such as the Earl of Arundel used agents like Sir Thomas Roe, while French royal envoys, among them Galland, Wansleben, Fourmont and Paul Lucas, were pressed from Paris and often damaged the sites they dug. Later sections cover stone, bronze, coins and lead, showing how locals melted coins and bronzes into kettles or prised metal from walls, while travellers bought cheaply and rarely recorded where objects came from. Greenhalgh also covers the funded expeditions of the Dilettanti, independent collectors and consuls at Smyrna, and the French state missions of the nineteenth century. The evidence comes from travel books, correspondence and official instructions. The chapter ends with the founding of foreign schools in Athens, which Greenhalgh argues would have changed the story had they come earlier.

British MuseumAshmolean MuseumSoane MuseumCabinet du Roi
3Ambassadors, Consuls and Firmansp. 65

Greenhalgh turns to the diplomats and consuls who made collecting possible. Firmans, the Sultan's passports, opened or closed sites, and their force depended on distance from Constantinople and on local bribes. Ambassadors Ponsonby, Stratford Canning and Henry Elliot obtained permissions for British digs at Xanthus, Halicarnassus and Ephesus, and Charles Newton, while a consul at Mytilene, excavated the Mausoleum site for the British Museum. Consuls, often underpaid, traded in antiquities, sold or gave away finds and bought land to dig, and some locals took the title to escape taxes and law. Greenhalgh describes rivalry between French and British consuls at Tarsus, the smuggling of Maspero as Budge reported it, and Henry Salt's consular trade in antiquities, which made him rich. Greenhalgh concludes that ambassadors could win export permission through diplomacy while consuls moved goods home through naval and merchant shipping, so that the final phase of looting depended on these networks.

British MuseumLouvreEgyptian Museum
4Identifying Sites and Antiquities in Ottoman Landsp. 86

Greenhalgh asks how the antiquities of the Ottoman Empire were first located and identified, since sites could not be plundered until someone knew where they were. The chapter argues that travellers, scholars and the maps they made turned ruins into named, findable places, and that this same knowledge served the collectors who followed. Early maps of Asia Minor were unreliable, so travellers depended on Pausanias and other ancient authors, on compass-and-pace itineraries and on inscriptions to name a ruin. Greenhalgh works through Leake, Hamilton, Texier, Tchihatchef and Davis as examples, then turns to encyclopaedias and to the Murray and Baedeker guidebooks. The bulk of the chapter surveys the collecting of inscriptions, manuscripts, marble spolia in cemeteries and mosques, and painted pottery, with cases from Athens, Tanagra, Konya, Algeria, Tunisia and Mount Athos. Throughout, local suspicion that foreigners were hunting hidden treasure recurs. The chapter closes by turning from identification to classifying the remains by style, and to the long dispute over whether so-called Etruscan vases were in fact Greek.

British MuseumLouvreImperial Museum, Constantinople
Part 2Discovering and Digging Antiquitiesp. 139
5Antiquities and the Localsp. 141

Greenhalgh asks how the people living among Ottoman ruins treated them, and how that treatment shaped what outsiders could find. Locals were rarely indifferent. They valued marble as building stock and as cannonball material, and later as something to sell, so foreign digging competed with local extraction from the start. Greenhalgh works through the Ottoman artillery forts on the Dardanelles and at Rhodes, whose marble shot was cut from ancient columns; through governors and agas who claimed finds or suppressed them to avoid being taxed on any treasure; and through Delphi, where villagers built houses from the ruins and bargained hard with the state over compensation. Mosques and cemeteries, where access was restricted, hid inscriptions in plain sight. Fear of treasure-hunting made foreign excavators suspect, and local workmen eventually learned to dig and sell for themselves. The chapter ends by blaming lime kilns and the export trade for the losses.

LouvreBritish MuseumImperial Museum, Constantinople
6Digging Opportunitiesp. 186

Greenhalgh asks where a would-be excavator in the Ottoman lands could realistically dig, since most sites were already stripped or built over. Ruin fields were numerous, and travellers used Roman roads and the Bible to narrow the search, but many lacked inscriptions to name them. The real limit, Greenhalgh argues, was cost and labour rather than knowledge: early digs were small and privately funded, while later government excavations employed hundreds of men. The chapter surveys ruin fields in Tunisia and Algeria, the Holy Land, and surface sites such as Mut, where streets could simply be mapped. It also traces the travellers' taste for mosaics, which were lifted whole or broken into souvenirs, and the damage done by gunpowder and quarrying at Athens. The chapter closes by arguing that training local workmen turned them into diggers and dealers, so that dig sites became selling opportunities.

LouvreBritish MuseumMetropolitan Museum of Art
7Vandalismp. 207

Greenhalgh's seventh chapter argues that Westerners, not Ottoman authorities, were the true vandals of the region's antiquities. Vandalism is defined broadly to include removal, so Napoleon's expedition, the British seizure of the Rosetta Stone from the French and Elgin's removal of Parthenon sculptures all count alongside casual damage. The chapter moves through Egypt, where tomb frescoes were cut out and mummies broken up for souvenirs, and Greece, where guidebooks such as Baedeker advised tourists on purchases while ignoring export bans. Hammers, paint and graffiti by travellers and naval officers damaged the Acropolis, Pompey's Pillar and the Philopappus Monument. Local destruction is judged more leniently, since much of it was re-use for barracks, forts and lime kilns. The chapter ends by noting that unprovenanced objects in Western museums represent a further loss. Its conclusion is that the Western claim to rescue antiquities was itself a form of destruction.

British MuseumMusée Charles XCambridge University Library
8Mediterranean Islandsp. 237

This chapter surveys the Mediterranean islands, placed before the mainland because travellers reached the East by sea and hopped between islands for antiquities, provisions or shelter from storms. Greenhalgh shows how islands with many ancient sites were stripped of marbles, inscriptions and statues from the late 17th to the mid-19th century. Each island gets a short entry, roughly alphabetical from Aegina to Thasos, drawn from travellers' accounts by Piacenza, Wheler, Spon, Clarke, Newton and others. Two cases recur at length: the Aegina sculptures from the Temple of Jupiter Panhellenius, which went to Munich rather than London, and the Venus de Milo on Melos, whose acquisition by the French diplomat Marcellus is recounted with its melodrama. Other entries show spoliation for lime kilns, building and church fabric, and the Greek export bans that led to a museum on Aegina by 1830. The conclusion holds that islands lost their antiquities quickly, and that most island pieces in Western museums cannot now be traced, since they were bought without provenance.

British MuseumLouvreGlyptothek, MunichLeiden MuseumMuseum on Aegina
9Sites and Travellers in European and Asiatic Turkeyp. 269

This chapter covers Ottoman Europe and Asia Minor, from Constantinople and its fortresses to temple towns, seaside sites and inland cities such as Aphrodisias, Sardis and Xanthus. Greenhalgh shows how Constantinople's mosques and fountains were built from marbles taken from older Greek and Byzantine buildings, and how Ottoman masons recut spolia for new work. Its longest sections treat temple towns such as Ephesus, Magnesia, Mylasa, Pergamum and Priene, and seaside sites such as Alexandria Troas, Bodrum and Cnidus. Bodrum's Mausoleum reliefs and the Pergamum Altar, sent to London and Berlin under firmans and bargains with officials, show how foreign excavators removed major monuments. Travellers saw sites quarried for lime, tombstones and new buildings, and Priene shows how a dig could hasten the loss by drawing in local looters. The conclusion holds that the closer a site lay to the West, the fewer monuments survived, and that inland sites lasted longer.

Pergamon Museum, BerlinBritish MuseumLouvreEphesus Museum, ViennaKunsthistorisches Museum, ViennaImperial Museum, Constantinople
10Syria and Mesopotamiap. 319

This chapter covers Ottoman Syria and Mesopotamia, which Western travellers reached for biblical and Crusader associations and as a route to British India. Greenhalgh surveys fortresses such as Acre and Athlit, where Crusader walls were built from older marble, and the temple complexes of Baalbek and Palmyra, quarried for centuries by locals. Beirut, Damascus, Jerusalem and Aleppo are treated as cities whose antiquities were largely gone or hard to dig, while Sidon's necropolis, dug by Renan's French mission and later by Hamdi Bey, shows the shift toward Ottoman retention. Most of the chapter then concerns Mesopotamia, where Botta at Khorsabad and Layard at Nimrud raced for reliefs bound for the Louvre and the British Museum under firmans whose terms changed mid-dig. The conclusion holds that European collections gained most of these riches until the Ottomans began refusing firmans for export toward the century's end.

LouvreBritish MuseumImperial Museum, Constantinople
11Egypt and North Africap. 343

This chapter covers Egypt and North Africa, where looting was easier than in the Ottoman lands because Egypt had one river and one main port, and Muhammad Ali let foreigners dig and export. Greenhalgh traces the French and British rivalry for antiquities, from the Description de l'Egypte to consular dealing, then turns to Cairo and Alexandria. Pompey's Pillar was proposed for Paris for decades and never moved, while obelisks from Alexandria and Luxor did reach London and Paris. The longer middle sections treat Cyrenaica, where Le Maire and Beechey dug Leptis Magna, Cyrene and Benghazi and shipped columns and statues, and Algeria and Tunisia, where colonial building turned Roman ruins into quarries and Carthage, Utica and El Djem were dug by consuls and dealers. The conclusion blames modernisation and colonial construction for more loss than scholarship, and notes that Cato's wish for Carthage's destruction was largely fulfilled by European looters.

British MuseumLouvreChapel of Saint Louis, Carthage (depot)
12Athens under the Ottomansp. 392

Greenhalgh's chapter follows the fate of Athens's monuments under Ottoman rule, from the first travellers' descriptions to the removal of the Parthenon sculptures. It has five sections: the monuments before Morosini's bombardment of 1687, the damage done by that attack and by Ottoman masons and gunners, the extraction of the Elgin Marbles under the 1801 firman, the decline of Athens from Elgin to independence, and an estimate of what Morosini and Elgin each left behind. The evidence comes almost entirely from travellers and consuls, among them Spon and Wheler, Chandler, Clarke, Hobhouse and Morritt, and from the French agents Fauvel and Choiseul-Gouffier, who made casts and collected fragments. The longest section surveys British and French arguments about Elgin, from Byron's charge of vandalism to Bramsen's defence, and shows how often those arguments were self-serving. Greenhalgh concludes that Morosini, Ottoman builders and gunners, and foreign collectors had already reduced the site before Elgin arrived, so his removals cannot be judged in isolation.

British MuseumMusée NapoléonVenice Archaeological Museum
13Athens under the Greeksp. 418

Greenhalgh's Chapter 13 covers Athens from independence in 1832 to the First World War, when the new Greek state made the ruined Ottoman town its capital and built a modern city over much of the ancient one. Greeks were keen to stop foreign export, but the chapter shows that the new town destroyed many antiquities: the streets were laid out with little regard for what lay beneath, and the Acropolis was stripped back to its Periclean monuments. The evidence comes from travellers, excavators and officials, among them Ross, Pittakys, Wordsworth, Burnouf and Mahaffy, and from the 1832 town plan, which marked old ruins but allowed building over them. The sections on King Otto's palace, on the Elgin debate and on the museums show a state that spent heavily on prestige buildings while lacking money for excavation, guards and a national museum. Greenhalgh concludes that modernism won out over archaeology, and that Greek policy, as much as foreign collecting, cost Athens its buried past.

Theseion museumAcropolis museumBritish MuseumSchliemann Museum
14Mainland Greecep. 462

Chapter 14 surveys the antiquities of mainland Greece outside Athens, region by region, from Epirus and Thessaly to the Peloponnese. Greenhalgh shows how monuments were used as building stone, burned for lime, sold to travellers and shipped out, and records the sites that were excavated, such as Megalopolis, Bassae, Aegina, Corinth, Eleusis, Olympia and Mycenae. Its central cases are Aegina, whose sculptures reached the British Museum after a pasha accepted money when he was about to lose his post, and Olympia, where the French Morea Expedition took metopes to the Louvre in 1829 before a Prussian dig began in 1874. The chapter draws on travellers such as Dodwell, Leake, Clarke, Burgess and Trant, and on the French Commission scientifique de Morée, whose director Bory de Saint-Vincent thought the expedition poorly run. Greenhalgh's conclusion is that spoliation was general, and that Mahaffy's proposal to leave monuments on their sites could not be realised without roads and funds.

British MuseumLouvreOlympia site museum
Part 3Transporting Antiquities, Competing Museums, Imperial Embargoesp. 499
15Shipping Antiquities Homep. 501

Chapter 15 examines the practical problems of moving antiquities from Ottoman and Egyptian sites to the sea and then to Europe. Greenhalgh shows that roads, wagons, cranes and sailors determined what could be taken: heavy pieces were left by the roadside, sawn down to reduce their weight, or carried by warship, as when the Royal Navy moved Bodrum and Ephesus material for Newton and Wood. The chapter draws on accounts by Clarke, Newton, Wood, Budge and Belzoni, and on French cases such as the Mylasa statues the Louvre lost for want of transport. A long section on colossal monoliths follows, notably Belzoni's head of Memnon and the Rameses II statue at Memphis. It ends with casts, which Choiseul-Gouffier, Elgin and the British Museum used both to study Greek sculpture and as diplomatic gifts. Greenhalgh concludes that the nineteenth-century transfer of antiquities to Berlin, London and Paris depended on transport technology and naval power, and that casts, though sent abroad, were never treated as substitutes for originals.

British MuseumLouvreSoane MuseumMetropolitan Museum of Art
16Museums and International Competitionp. 518

Greenhalgh's Chapter 16 turns from the source sites to the museums that drove the trade. Its argument is that national museums in Paris, London and Berlin, and the rivalry between them, created the demand that stripped the Ottoman Empire, Greece and Egypt. It opens with Greek decrees of the 1820s and 1830s and the gap between regulation and practice, using Mure and Leake on sites in Phocis and Boeotia, then moves to the rivalry between British and French embassies and governments. Mariette's career in Egypt, as curator and plunderer at once, and the trophy displays of the Louvre and British Museum follow. The longest argument is the defence of Elgin, in which Hamilton, Bramsen and Aberdeen claimed that the Marbles were safer in London, and Greenhalgh shows how often this rested on blaming the French and on selective evidence. The conclusion asks whether museums can survive without new, non-looted acquisitions, citing Mumford's view that museums were a defence against the past.

British MuseumLouvreEgyptian Museum, CairoApsley House (Wellington Museum)
17The Empire and Greece Strike Back against Governments and Travellersp. 538

Greenhalgh's final chapter follows how Ottoman and Greek governments tried to stop the export of antiquities, and how European diggers worked around the rules. It moves from the Ottoman regulation of 1884 to Salomon Reinach's attacks on Hamdi Bey and on European ambassadors who failed to protest, then to partage, the system under which excavators shared finds with the host state. Greenhalgh shows how the French at Myrina and the Germans at Pergamum profited from it, while British diggers at Ephesus used bribes and coins to keep their firmans. The Mschatta facade, given to Berlin after an Ottoman council decision, serves as a case of concession. Digging also stalled for lack of money, at Tarsus and at Olympia, where funding took twenty years. The chapter concludes that the laws ended spectacular looting but not evasion, and that the West held the money while the East held the sites.

British MuseumLouvreKaiser-Friedrich Museum, BerlinImperial Museum, Constantinople
The Rapacity of Verres!p. 556

This closing chapter returns to the looting of antiquities from the Ottoman lands and asks whether anything changed once the museum boom had passed. Greenhalgh argues that the plunder never ended: it continued under legal forms after 1918 and survives in the vague labels of today's national museums, where provenance is reduced to phrases such as 'said to come from'. Greenhalgh sets Quatremere de Quincy's early objection that museums cut objects off from their setting beside Willis's 1853 attack on Elgin, then tests the claim that museums rescue what would otherwise be lost against the Getty Kouros, the Getty Aphrodite and the looting after the 2003 invasion of Iraq, quoting Fisk and Stein. Greenhalgh rejects the arguments of recent books that defend keeping the marbles in Western museums, and quotes Renfrew's charge that the great museums set the ethos for private collectors. The chapter ends by saying that the Plundered Empire has been broken up, but its wooden horse and snakes are still there.

Guy, Kate; Williams, Hajra; Wintle, Claire (eds.) (2024). Histories of Exhibition Design in the Museum: Makers, Process, and Practice. London: Routledge.Asia: substantial16 chapter overviews

Overview

Histories of Exhibition Design in the Museum (2024), edited by Kate Guy, Hajra Williams and Claire Wintle, is a volume of fifteen essays on the people who made museum displays: designers, technicians, carpenters, label writers, curators and administrators, from the nineteenth century to the recent past. Its argument is that exhibitions have usually been studied as finished, static products, so the labour, process and collaboration behind them are lost. The introduction frames exhibition design as a creative process, stresses embodied and emotional labour, and asks for a decentred history. The case studies range over the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Switzerland, Argentina, China, Japan and Korea, and the chapters are grouped in four parts: exhibition makers, beyond the museum, the material culture of display, and exhibition afterlives.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

East Asia is a substantial theme in two chapters and a minor one elsewhere. Chapter 8, by Lisheng Zhang and David Francis, examines the Dali Project in Guizhou, in which the Beijing studio ATLAS Design worked with Dong craftswomen, and the exhibition Tradition@Present (2013) at the Chinese National Museum of Ethnology. It contrasts Chinese ethnographic museums, which present the peoples of China, with European ones that display non-Europeans, and it discusses the Museum Boom of the mid-2000s and intangible heritage policy. Chapter 10, by Kyunghee Pyun, is wholly on Japan and Korea: mannequins in the Osaka Museum of History, the National Folk Museum of Korea (its wedding diorama of 2006 and 2021), the War Memorial of Korea, where Vietnamese soldiers are now shown, and a VR shipwreck installation at the Gwangju National Museum, with Chinese merchants and Song and Yuan porcelain bound for Hakata.

Elsewhere the references are brief. Chapter 3 (Guy) notes that the British Museum's Keeper of Oriental Antiquities had mounted a show of Chinese art before Margaret Hall arrived. Chapter 4 (Charles, on Crossroads of Continents) covers Hokkaido and the Russian Far East, includes a Chinese-style Nanai coat, and records a Japan tour that was considered and not made. Chapter 12 lists Japan among countries sending material to nineteenth-century Paris economics exhibitions, and Chapter 13 (Kriebel) places Asian ceramics and large Japanese vases in Bode's 1883 Berlin display. Chapter 15 (Newby) mentions the Sainsbury Institute for the Study of Japanese Arts and Cultures.

Southeast Asia is almost absent. No museum, collection or visitor there is discussed; the only link is the Dutch-Indonesian designer Kho Liang Ie, named in Chapter 15 for his own biography. South Asia, through Cartwright Hall and Sikh art in Chapter 7, is the volume's main non-Western community case.

Introduction: Museum Exhibition Design HistoriesKate Guy, Hajra Williams, and Claire Wintlep. 1

Guy, Williams and Wintle introduce a volume on the history of museum exhibition design, arguing that exhibitions, central to museum income and public purpose, have been poorly documented because the designers, technicians and label writers who made them remain largely invisible. They review critical museum studies from Bennett's 'exhibitionary complex' to Staniszewski's study of the Museum of Modern Art, which tended to treat exhibitions as finished and static. The book, they say, will look behind the scenes at makers, labour and process across 250 years and institutions in a dozen countries. The introduction sets out three themes: design as a creative process, the impact of labour, emotion and embodiment, and the need to decentre design through identity, collaboration and hierarchy. It then previews four parts on exhibition makers, networks beyond the museum, the material culture of display, and afterlives. Its stated aim is a blueprint for students and designers who want to understand how past practice shapes present museums.

East and Southeast Asia The introduction summarises two chapters with East Asian content. Zhang and Francis analyse the partnership between Dong craftswomen from Guizhou and the design studio ATLAS Design on Tradition@Present, a 2013 exhibition at the Chinese National Museum of Ethnology, and Pyun examines mannequin design in contemporary Korean and Japanese museums.
