Part 1Part 1: Exhibition Makersp. 19
1Exhibition Work: Exploring Labour in the Federal Community Art Center ProjectSara Woodburyp. 21

Woodbury examines the labour behind the Federal Community Art Center Project, a New Deal programme of travelling exhibitions and community art centres run by the WPA's Federal Art Project between 1935 and 1941. The chapter first asks how the logistics of moving art shaped what was shown: trains, varied buildings and staff with uneven skills pushed the programme towards small, two-dimensional and standardised works, which helped reinforce a modernist canon of painting and prints. It then takes the Roswell Museum in New Mexico as a case study, using timesheets, letters and photographs to recover the work of carpenters such as Domingo Tejada, whose furniture gave the building its Spanish Colonial look, and of women and Hispano staff. Woodbury shows how marriage led Ruth Covey to resign, and how local sponsors questioned the competence of Rainey Woolsey, who was demoted and then dismissed. The chapter concludes that exhibition labour, too often ignored, shapes both content and appearance, and that archives weighted towards administrators need to be read against the grain.

Roswell Museum
Referencesp. 31
2Putting Joseph Towles’ Name in the Credit Line: Institutional Racism at the American Museum of Natural HistoryJacklyn Grace Laceyp. 33

Lacey recovers the role of Joseph A. Towles, an African American anthropologist whose work is usually subordinated to that of his partner, the white British anthropologist Colin Turnbull. The chapter centres on the Hall of Man in Africa at the American Museum of Natural History, which opened in 1968. Lacey shows that Towles planned the ground-breaking 'Slavery in the Americas' section, collected objects in Uganda, and worked with a Yoruba community in Spanish Harlem on an Orisha shrine, while Turnbull received sole credit as curator. The chapter documents the hostility Towles faced at the museum, including a racist letter from the archaeologist James Ford, pressure to revoke his volunteer credentials, and a criminal record used against him, and traces how these pressures and his later illnesses have been used to discredit his scholarship. The chapter closes by calling on museum practitioners to credit Towles and to address the institutional racism that continues at the museum, including the controversy over the Roosevelt equestrian statue, and by asking white practitioners to examine their own obligations.

American Museum of Natural HistoryHall of Man in Africa
Referencesp. 44
3‘Miss Hall and Her Busy, Energetic Design Group’: The Emergence of Professional In-House Design at the British MuseumKate Guyp. 47

Guy traces how the British Museum came to appoint its first in-house exhibition designer, Margaret Hall, in 1964, and how the Design Office she built grew out of that appointment. The chapter places the decision in the wider British shift, from the educational ambitions of the 1930s and the wartime and Festival of Britain exhibitions, to the rise of visitor-focused museums in the 1960s. Director Frank Francis's reforms and his trustees' interest in display provided the context. Guy describes Hall's lack of brief, the mixed reception from curators, some of them hostile, and the meagre £50 grant she was given. The chapter then follows her working with the technicians and with the graphic designer David Cordingly, hired in 1967, to produce Masterpieces of Glass (1968), whose minimalist, backlit cases gained the Design Office its reputation. Guy argues that the Museum of Mankind and Treasures of Tutankhamun, often credited with establishing the department, followed a foundation laid earlier. Guy concludes that the Design Office shaped a collaborative practice and drew on established display techniques rather than revolutionising museum design.

British MuseumMuseum of Mankind
Referencesp. 62
4An Immersive Journey – Crossroads of Continents: Cultures of Siberia & AlaskaBarbara Fahs Charlesp. 65

Charles, the designer, reflects on designing Crossroads of Continents: Cultures of Siberia & Alaska, a travelling exhibition that opened at the Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History in 1988 and presented eight Indigenous peoples of the North Pacific. The chapter recounts how the show grew from a 1973 meeting of anthropologists Fitzhugh and Arutiunov and from a 1987 agreement between the Smithsonian and the Soviet Academy of Sciences. Charles describes the competitive design process, the 'Big E' case built for costumes, and the texts, written in English for North America and in Russian for the USSR. The account of the shaman's burial from Ekven, the handling of fragile garments, and the making of custom mannequins with heads sculpted from turn-of-the-century life masks shows how design depends on conservators, curators and craftspeople. The final sections trace the tour, which ended in Ottawa in 1992 after the Soviet partners could no longer host it. Charles concludes that designing the show was one of the great joys of the career, despite the unfulfilled Soviet leg.

5A Latin American Model of Professional Training in Exhibition Design: Alliances, Outcomes, and ChallengesAmérico Castillap. 85

Castilla describes a collaborative exhibition design training model that he developed in Argentina from 1993, first through the Antorchas Foundation, which he managed until 2003, and later through the Fundación TyPA. The chapter opens with the state of regional museums in Latin America, which often hold important collections with few resources, and explains why the first workshops focused on ethnographic museums. Its case studies include The Lords of the Jaguar in Buenos Aires (1997), Our Grandparents, the Pioneers in San José (1999), The Earth: A History of Change at La Plata (2002), and an interpretation centre at the San Ignacio Jesuit mission (2007). Castilla notes the tensions these projects produced, including a local title vote and a municipal withdrawal of funding in Mar del Plata. The final sections describe community-centred projects in Santa Cruz and the online training of 2020. Castilla concludes that more than 500 museum workers have trained in the model and that Argentine museums had begun to display collections differently, though the case studies are not conclusive.

6Fashioning Beaton Portraits: 1928–1968 ExhibitionMarlène Van de Casteelep. 103

Van de Casteele reconstructs Beaton Portraits: 1928–1968, the photography show with which Roy Strong opened his directorship of the National Portrait Gallery in London in 1967. The chapter argues that the exhibition, built around the work of the fashion photographer Cecil Beaton and designed by the scenographer Richard Buckle, was a turning point: it treated fashion photography as a legitimate subject for a national museum and staged it as theatre, with a one-way trail divided into 'Acts', music, incense, perfume, a revolving postcard stand and a reconstructed studio. Its evidence comes from NPG archives, leaflets, display plans, visitor letters and press reviews, which record both praise and complaints that the effects distracted from the photographs. Van de Casteele places the show in a lineage running from Buckle's earlier Diaghilev and Shakespeare exhibitions to the V&A's Fashion: An Anthology (1971–72) and Diana Vreeland's displays in New York. She concludes that the exhibition blurred the boundaries between art, commerce and popular culture, and deserves recognition as a pioneering example of exhibition design.

National Portrait GalleryVictoria and Albert MuseumMetropolitan Museum of Art
Referencesp. 117
7Collaboration and Exhibition Making at Cartwright Hall: Strategies of PermanenceHajra Williamsp. 119

Williams examines collaboration at Cartwright Hall, the municipal gallery in Bradford, during the curatorship of Nima Poovaya-Smith from 1985 to the late 1990s. The chapter argues that community partnerships there, above all with the local South Asian population, were structured and substantial rather than informal, and that they changed what the museum collected and how it displayed. The evidence is a 2020 interview with Poovaya-Smith, set against the gallery's history, its loans from national collections, and the Warm and Rich and Fearless exhibition of Sikh art (1991), developed with Sikh organisations, whose contributors pressed for two objects to be relabelled. Williams sets this work against the funding crisis of local authority museums and national reports urging them to become entrepreneurial. Williams concludes that temporary exhibitions shaped by consultation led to the Transcultural Galleries (1997) and the Connect Galleries (2008), so that exhibitions altered permanent collecting and the physical building. Williams also reflects on her own role as an educator at the V&A, and on the power that institutions keep even in collaboration.

Cartwright HallVictoria and Albert Museum
Referencesp. 135
8The Re-Crafting of Design: Towards an Ethnographic Perspective in Chinese Exhibition DesignLisheng Zhang and David Francisp. 137Asia: chiefly

Zhang and Francis examine how exhibition designers in China work with the communities whose crafts they display. Their case is the Dali Project, in which the Beijing studio ATLAS Design has worked since 2010 with Dong craftswomen in Dali village, Guizhou, on textiles and a community centre, and then designed Tradition@Present (2013) for the Chinese National Museum of Ethnology. The chapter argues that long collaboration changed the designer's outlook, and that this 'ethnographic perspective' shaped the exhibition: a non-linear route, four modular themes, and an installation that follows the lunisolar calendar through a year of indigo dyeing. The evidence comes from the authors' participant observation in the Craft China project (2018–2020) and an interview with the ATLAS designer Jenny Chou. The authors set the case against China's Productive Protection policy, the mass museum building of the 2000s and the inward-looking tradition of Chinese ethnographic museums. They conclude that an ethnographic perspective must be present in exhibition design as well as curation, and that designers can act as social mediators between makers and museums.

East and Southeast Asia China is the whole setting. The chapter discusses the Dong craftswomen of Dali village in Guizhou province and their textile cooperative, and the Chinese National Museum of Ethnology in Beijing, which has no permanent building and tours its exhibitions. It contrasts Chinese ethnographic museums, which present the peoples of China itself, with European ones that display non-Europeans, and it describes the 'Museum Boom' of the mid-2000s and state policy on intangible cultural heritage.

Part 3Part 3: The Material Culture of Displayp. 153
9The Afterlives of Labels: Materiality and Labour in the Science and Technology Exhibition Label Archive of National Museums ScotlandKate Bowellp. 155

Bowell treats the exhibition labels of National Museums Scotland as historical sources. The museum printed over 20,000 science and technology labels in-house between 1864 and 1967, and kept them in eight ledger books, one of the most complete collections of its kind. Bowell argues that the labels are objects in their own right, and that their paper, inks, typefaces and changing length record the museum's shifting aims, from step-by-step instruction to textbook-style content and then to newspaper-style layouts. Bowell’s evidence is the marks left on the labels themselves: marginal notes that organise the archive, cross-references between editions, green ticks and red crosses showing whether an exhibit was on show, pencilled revisions, and pages cut or torn out. These traces show a labour of organising, tracking, changing and removing that official records seldom document. Bowell concludes that seeing labels as partial, personal objects, rather than as the neutral voice of an institution, opens new ways of studying museum history and interpretation.

National Museums Scotland
Referencesp. 167
10Ethnonational Identity and Mannequins in History Museums in Korea and JapanKyunghee Pyunp. 169Asia: chiefly

Pyun examines how mannequins in Korean and Japanese history and folk museums present one nation and one people, even as both countries acquire foreign residents, interracial families and migrant workers. Drawing on interviews and surveys with designers, conservators and curators, the chapter works through three cases. The Osaka Museum of History fills reconstructed Naniwa-kyō, Edo-period markets and a Meiji-to-postwar Great Osaka section with hairless, expressionless mannequins and no visible ethnic diversity. The National Folk Museum of Korea's wedding diorama, first made in 2006 and revised in 2021, follows the fashion mannequins of Heo Young and his 'Korean face'. At the War Memorial of Korea, Korean officers have faces while foreign soldiers are faceless body forms. Pyun also looks at a virtual reality shipwreck installation at the Gwangju National Museum, where she could hardly tell Japanese, Chinese and Korean characters apart. Pyun concludes that mannequins still perpetuate modernist ideas of a unified nation, though they are not static, and that digital media will shape their future without replacing them.

East and Southeast Asia Korea and Japan are the whole subject. Pyun sets Osaka's ethnically uniform dioramas against the multi-ethnic families and migrants in both countries, and reads the Korean wedding diorama as a deliberate statement of Korean uniqueness. At the War Memorial of Korea, Korean officers have faces and the Korean Empire section is based on paintings and photographs of officers of the 1900s, while realistic mannequins of Vietnamese soldiers from North and South are now shown. The Gwangju National Museum's VR installation shows Chinese merchants at Ningbo and the 1975 Sinan shipwreck cargo of Song and Yuan porcelain bound for Hakata.

Osaka Museum of HistoryNational Folk Museum of KoreaWar Memorial of KoreaGwangju National Museum
Referencesp. 184
11Exhibition Design and the Construction of Race, Gender, and Class in the First Ladies Hall of the United States National MuseumEmily Mazzolap. 186

Mazzola examines the First Ladies Hall of the United States National Museum in Washington, which displayed historical White House gowns from 1914 onwards. Mazzola’s focus is how the collectors Cassie Mason Myers Julian-James and Rose Gouverneur Hoes, working with the museum's sculptor William H. Egberts, designed mannequins that would not look like department-store figures or like the museum's ethnographic figures of Indigenous people. She argues that their solution, ivory plaster figures with faces copied from a neoclassical bust, materialised elite white Protestant womanhood as an idealised form. The evidence comes from the museum's archive: a 1915 report, a 1933 newspaper article, photographs of Egberts at work, and visitor complaints about placing the two Mrs Wilsons side by side. Mazzola sets this against the museum's older displays of Washington's uniform, Osceola's bust and habitat groups of Indigenous figures, which show how whiteness and indigeneity were already constructed through display. Mazzola concludes that the hall's rigidity and uniformity expressed a pronounced whiteness, and that the exhibition has been judged by the same standards of morality and taste as the women it honours.

United States National Museum
Referencesp. 201
12‘Above All Matter of Facts’: Material Knowledge, Exhibition Culture, and the Making of EconomicsSophie Cras and Claire-Lise Debluëp. 203

Cras and Debluë ask how economic knowledge has been put on display in museums and world fairs since the nineteenth century. They argue that, as the discipline grew more abstract, its exhibitions relied on a 're-materialisation' of ideas in objects, machines and bodily activity, often for ideological ends. The evidence is a sequence of displays: the Paris economics exhibitions of 1855 to 1900, including W.E.B. Du Bois's 'Exhibit of American Negroes'; the Swiss Social Museum in Zurich (founded 1917), whose animated diorama of the city's population invited visitors to turn a handle; Basel war-economy fairs of 1942–44; the Museum of American Finance in New York; and interactive economics museums such as the Cité de l'économie in Paris. The Zurich case shows how playful statistics could make social problems look like matters of individual responsibility rather than conflict. The authors conclude that what separates these displays is less the kind of institution than the authority their economic discourse claims and the room it leaves the visitor to debate.

Swiss Social MuseumCité de l'économie (Citéco)Musée socialMuseum of American FinanceMuseum of Science and Industry, Chicago

13‘Gesamtwirkung’: Researching Wilhelm von Bode’s Design for the Exhibition of Old Master Paintings (1883) as a Model for Future Museum PracticeSandra Kriebelp. 223

Kriebel reconstructs the 1883 Exhibition of Old Master Paintings, held at Berlin's Royal Academy of Arts to mark the silver wedding of Crown Prince Frederick and Princess Victoria. Its curator, Wilhelm von Bode, arranged Italian, Flemish, Dutch, French and Rococo works in atmospheric ensembles with furniture and tapestries, and Kriebel argues that this 'Inszenierung', or staging, aimed at an overall impression, the 'Gesamtwirkung' of the title. The exhibition is known from a catalogue and photographs by the Braun studio, which Kriebel combines with press reports, later shows Bode designed in the 1890s, and his own writings on lighting, to produce digital plans and wall reconstructions. These reveal changes Bode made after the catalogue went to print. The chapter argues that Bode's concept, presented in a memorandum under Princess Victoria's name, became the basis of the Kaiser-Friedrich-Museum, now the Bode Museum. Kriebel concludes that drawing and comparing past displays is a valuable method for studying the 'ephemeral museum'.

East and Southeast Asia The 1883 display included Asian ceramics from the royal palaces and large Japanese vases on stands beside the wall of Watteau's Shop Sign, which Kriebel places in her reconstruction of the arrangement. The chapter mentions these objects only as part of the layout and does not discuss them further.

Kaiser-Friedrich-Museum (Bode Museum)Berlin Royal Academy of ArtsBerlin Royal MuseumMuseum of Decorative Arts

14Visual Interventions: Exhibition Graphic Design as Critical PracticeJona Piehlp. 237

Piehl examines how graphic design can be used critically to reframe historic exhibitions with colonial origins. Museums that co-create new narratives, he notes, often still rely on plinths, vitrines and labels, so he treats exhibition graphics as a site of reflexive practice. The chapter proposes an initial typology of 'visual interventions', graphic additions that reframe a historic display while keeping it visible. The evidence is his own visits in February 2020 to the American Museum of Natural History, the Field Museum in Chicago and the Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History, where he documents the Bones Hall annotations, the Carl Cotton panels, a photographic cover over a vitrine, the 'Old New York' diorama and a museum reply to a visitor's protest. Piehl argues that such interventions make the different 'narrating times' of an institution visible, and so present exhibitions as ongoing processes. Piehl also warns that interventions may become a cosmetic fig leaf that leaves the display unchanged. Piehl concludes that graphic design is a useful tool where full redesign is impossible, though no substitute for it.

American Museum of Natural HistoryField MuseumSmithsonian National Museum of Natural History
Referencesp. 254
15The Living Area at the Sainsbury Centre: Looking Back to Look ForwardLisa Maddigan Newbyp. 255

Newby looks back at the Living Area of the Sainsbury Centre at the University of East Anglia, the open-plan gallery where Robert and Lisa Sainsbury's collection has been displayed since 1978. The chapter argues that the Sainsburys' personal aesthetic account, in which objects from around the world are shown as art rather than specimens, must be read against the debates that such displays had already provoked in London. The evidence comes from two exhibitions that included Sainsbury works: 40,000 Years of Modern Art at the Institute of Contemporary Arts in 1948, which compared 'primitive' and modern art and drew contrasting responses from Herbert Read, William Fagg and Edmund Leach; and Sacred Circles at the Hayward Gallery in 1976, which Susan Hiller criticised as stripping North American Indigenous objects of their history. Newby draws on catalogues, press views and reviews. Newby concludes that these histories reframe the Living Area as a personal project with a long and contested reception, and that its future can be explored by asking what its design overlooks.

Hall, Patricia; Seemann, Charlie (eds.) (1987). Folklife and Museums: Selected Readings. Nashville: American Association for State and Local History.Asia: slight15 chapter overviews

Overview

An edited anthology of fourteen essays on folklife (the traditional knowledge, crafts, performance and customary practice of ordinary communities) and museums, assembled by Patricia Hall and Charlie Seemann and published in 1987. Its contributors are folklorists, museum professionals, historians and anthropologists. Their main argument is that folk culture belongs in museum collecting, exhibition, live performance and interpretation, and that folklife research can make museum presentation more contextual and representative. The essays range over folk museums and living history farms, live demonstrators, art museums, history museums, anthropological displays, American Jewish life and historic houses, and are grouped by kind of institution and problem rather than by a single thesis.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia are almost absent. No chapter is about them, and none treats an Asian museum, Asian collection or Asian state's heritage policy. Asian material appears only in passing, in a handful of sentences across the book.

Japan and China come up as examples in incidental places. Louis Jones and Candace Matelic recall a Japanese actor's costume among the odd objects of a nineteenth-century county collection, valued for its links to well-to-do travellers rather than for what it showed (chapter 4, line 549). Willard Moore cites traditional Chinese knotting as a craft whose skill a visitor cannot judge without the concept of its process (chapter 7, line 2706). Charlie Seemann suggests Chinese dragon dancers at Chinese New Year as a festival programme for a museum serving a Chinese community (chapter 8, line 2894). Jay Anderson lists Japanese-made cars and a Japanese-made television in an inventory of a 1980s house (chapter 17, lines 7203, 7297).

Southeast Asian and Korean communities appear in Robert Baron's account of New York programmes. The DeWitt Historical Society of Tompkins County showed Southeast Asian embroidery within exhibitions on its ethnic communities (chapter 5, lines 1218-1220), and a planned 1987 New York street-games exhibition included a Korean game of chance (line 1266). These are American museums presenting Asian communities, not museums in Asia. The text does not discuss colonial collecting, restitution, war memory or Asian visitors. Its only other Asian-related references are to South Asia and the Himalayas, marked as contrast: India in Baron's 1985 Aditi exhibition (line 1144) and Himalayan weavers in Hernandez's essay (line 3209).

PrefacePatricia Hall and Charlie Seemannp. xv

Hall and Seemann, the editors, explain in this 1986 preface why they assembled an anthology on folklife and museums: museums had grown interested in folk culture since the 1950s, and folklorists were working in them. The essays are a third previously published, a third revised conference papers and a third new, drawn from folklife studies, museology, history and anthropology. The editors name their intended readers, from museum professionals to students, and thank the people and funders who made the book possible.

Folklife and Museums: How Far Have We Come since the 1950s?Louis C. Jones and Candace T. Matelicp. 1

Jones and Matelic, both of the Cooperstown Graduate Program in History Museum Studies, trace the partnership between folklife studies and museums across three decades, beginning with Jones's early-1950s articles calling for cooperation among historians, folklorists and museologists. They describe the elitist, 'dusty' history museums of the 1940s, run by village-attic societies that displayed associational relics, and the rise of social history at a few universities and of immigrant museums such as Vesterheim in Iowa. The chapter then charts the growth of open-air and folk museums, living history, hands-on programs and craft demonstrations, using the Farmers' Museum in Cooperstown and the Valentine Museum's race relations exhibition in Richmond as examples. The authors argue that much of this progress happened without folklife studies receiving credit. They conclude with a 'living color' analogy for richer interpretation and urge closer integration of folklife research into collecting and public programs.

Vesterheim (Norwegian-American Museum, Iowa)Farmers' Museum (Cooperstown)Valentine Museum (Richmond)National Museum of American History (Smithsonian)
Folklife and the American MuseumRobert Baronp. 12

Baron argues that folklife, the traditional knowledge, crafts and performance of ordinary communities, belongs at the center of museum work, and shows how curators can use folklorists' methods for exhibits, education programs and events. Baron traces the history from John Cotton Dana's Newark Museum exhibits of local artisans and immigrant 'homelands' demonstrations, through the folk art shows of the 1920s and 1930s, and criticizes the connoisseurship that treats folk objects as fine art. The core examples are performance projects: the 1978 Brooklyn Museum Haitian festival, which staged Vodoun ritual in a 'sacred space' built with careful replicas, Smithsonian festival presentations linked to galleries, and New York documentation projects such as the East Hampton baymen's exhibit. Baron ends by urging museums to build archives and long-term folklife programs, and warns living history sites against demonstrations that cannot be documented for their region and period.

Newark MuseumBrooklyn MuseumNational Museum of American HistoryMuseum of Modern ArtEast Hampton Historical Society
Folklife and the Rise of American Folk MuseumsHoward Wight Marshallp. 27

Marshall defines the 'folk museum' as an outdoor institution that uses folklife research and living history to show everyday regional life, and traces its origins to Artur Hazelius's Skansen in Sweden and the European open-air museums. Marshall surveys the American living historical farm movement that began in the 1950s, with Conner Prairie in Indiana, the Farmers' Museum at Cooperstown and Plimoth Plantation as early leaders, and lists examples with their periods and goals. Marshall argues that research must underpin these sites, because they represent the past rather than recover it, and that curators should avoid nostalgic 'Age of Homespun' myths and show conflict and cultural change. Marshall weighs first-person role-playing interpreters against their limits for teaching facts, and proposes a two-part regional model that combines an outdoor village and working farms with a static exhibit complex. The chapter concludes that folk museums can become folklife research centers and lively extensions of the classroom.

Skansen (Stockholm)Conner Prairie Pioneer Settlement (Indiana)Old World WisconsinPlimoth PlantationFarmers' Museum (Cooperstown)Westville (Georgia)
Connecting the Past with the Present: Reflections upon Interpretation in Folklife MuseumsWillard B. Moorep. 51

Moore argues that folklife museums should be interpretive programs rather than collections of buildings and artifacts, using objects to connect past, present and future. Interpretation, for him, is a metaphorical activity: the interpreter asks 'What else is it like?' so that visitors grasp an object through their own experience, as a quilting bee or a celebratory meal can be likened to a community's shared rules. His evidence is mostly from his own practice. At Conner Prairie Pioneer Settlement a teacher pulled children away from their hand-clapping games and toward the interpreters' play party. At the Minneapolis Museum of Art, Norwegian-American quilters demonstrating on site drew out memories of depression quilts and quilting-bee meals. A New York immigrant museum curator showed what East European newcomers actually wore, not stereotyped national costume. A South Dakota toymaker's sales depended on whether buyers saw the skill as their own, and a steam fitter's family revealed a trade continuum. Moore concludes that museums should include the present in their interpretation and train teachers who bring classes.

Conner Prairie Pioneer SettlementMinneapolis Museum of ArtImmigrant Museum of New York City
Presenting the Live Folk Artist in the MuseumCharlie Seemannp. 59

Seemann argues that live folk artists and demonstrators can strengthen a museum's exhibitions, events and education, because they offer face-to-face contact with people who have lived the traditions on display. Seemann lists occasions for bringing them in: alongside exhibits, at calendar festivals such as Christmas or Passover, at civic events such as Black Heritage Month, and through school outreach. Seemann’s two main concerns are authenticity and context. Museums too often choose easy performers, such as revivalists who learned quilting in a community college class, and institutional pressure for a smooth 'good show' can overstructure and bowdlerize a tradition. His practical advice covers finding artists through state folklorists, university programs and national bodies, putting elderly performers at ease, using a presenter to bridge cultural gaps such as a Basque bertsolari's improvised verse, and attending to sound systems and publicity.

Folk Art in the Fine Art MuseumJo Farb Hernandezp. 67

Hernandez argues that art museums should present folk art as part of their ordinary programming, since traditional material culture draws large audiences, builds community ties and widens visitors' aesthetic range. Hernandez contends that the line between folk and fine art blurs in practice, citing 'primitive' art from Africa and Oceania whose abstraction anticipated Western modernism, and she advises curators to drop the label 'folk'. Hernandez’s main case is the Mexican Indian dance masks exhibition her museum mounted in 1982, the largest of its kind outside Mexico. The masks were installed by dance complex rather than by region, with a folklorico performance, bilingual labels and a catalog. She describes Spanish-language publicity, school and college programs, teacher packets and corporate outreach at the Triton Museum in Silicon Valley. She cautions that curators need specialist training, since untrained presentation risks becoming a rehash of 'Grandma Moses lookalikes'.

Triton Museum of ArtMonterey Peninsula Museum of Art
Applying Theory to Practice: Folklife and Today's History MuseumsPatricia Hallp. 76

Hall argues that folklife belongs in history museums and that folkloristic concepts can improve their interpretation. Hall sets out four tools: folkloric truth, which museums can set beside historical fact; the collecting of twentieth-century handmade folk art, as in the Oakland Museum's hippie exhibit; the esoteric-exoteric distinction, illustrated by the Tennessee State Museum's exhibit on Southern and outsider views of the antebellum South; and the contextual approach, which studies the making and use of an object as well as the object. Hall discusses reenactment and revivalist performance, which can aid understanding if visitors are told when an activity is a revival, and the 'shrine' appeal of famous possessions, explained through Frazer's idea of contagious magic. The chapter ends on marketing: Adams and Boatright's forecast of a return to family and nostalgia suggests that folklife methods could help history museums secure their finances.

Oakland MuseumTennessee State MuseumHenry Ford Museum
A Sense of Another World: History Museums and Cultural ChangeJames Deetzp. 88

Deetz calls on history museums to interpret cultural change rather than continuity, treating the artifact as the basic building block of an exhibit. Deetz’s central example is the delft plate: a dinner plate can be read as a modern analogue, but in seventeenth-century New England trenchers were shared by 'trenchermates' and large delft chargers were displayed in the parlor for social show, so interpretation must reflect those differences. Deetz traces period rooms to Charles P. Wilcomb's colonial kitchens, first installed in 1895 at the Golden Gate Park Museum and later at the Oakland Museum. Deetz argues that rooms should show clutter and older objects as probate inventories do, that houses reveal changing privacy in their plans, and that full-scale re-creations such as Plimoth Plantation should avoid tidy gardens and 'borning rooms' that come from later sources. Deetz recommends first-person interpreters who do real work instead of repeated demonstrations, and concludes that a re-created community must be treated as a single exhibit.

Plimoth PlantationWinterthur MuseumOakland MuseumColonial WilliamsburgOld Sturbridge VillageConner PrairieSmithsonian Museum of History and TechnologyGolden Gate Park Museum
The Value in Things: Folklore and the Anthropological Museum ExhibitM. Jane Youngp. 99

Young argues that anthropological museum exhibits should show objects in their cultural context, drawing on the performance-centered approach of folklore theory, which studies process as well as product. Young traces the shift of museums from elite cabinets of curiosities to democratized educators, and warns that displaying objects on pedestals, such as Kwakiutl masks, Navajo sandpaintings, baskets and Zuni pottery, presents them as high art when they were made for ceremonies, daily water-carrying or communal use. Young’s examples come mostly from the Southwest, where her fieldwork at Zuni produced a traveling rock-art exhibit. Young proposes that exhibits show several interpretations of an event, including those of the people who made and used the objects, and that they present the losses as well as the gains from acculturation. Young notes that surviving artifacts are unrepresentative, since pottery outlasts textiles and museums keep unusual objects. Young’s conclusion is that museums should collect the present as well as the past, hiring fieldworkers to document contemporary folk material culture.

Folklore and Museum ArtifactsJohn Michael Vlachp. 108

Vlach argues that folk artifacts should have a central place in museums, because they support a more democratic and detailed history than one built on elite objects. Vlach traces the marginal standing of folklore in American academic life, contrasts European folk parks and open-air museums with the American situation, and holds that folk objects are historical yet still living, as Georgia potters make churns the way their nineteenth-century ancestors did. Vlach sets out three roles for folklorists in museums: shaping policy around popular themes, gathering and presenting information such as interviews with miners, and winning back audiences for urban museums through local fieldwork. Vlach’s case rests on the representativeness of folk objects: a Buncombe County potter's crocks reflect local food preferences in a way a single elite piece cannot. Vlach lists the public lessons folk artifacts can teach, such as hand technology and the career of a blacksmith, and concludes that artifacts can check the authenticity of written history when historians and folklorists work together.

National Museum of American History
The Delicate Tasks of the Folklife/History Museum: Balancing the GivensEdward L. Hawesp. 122

Hawes examines how a folklife and history museum can balance four 'contemporary givens' (its facilities, supporters' expectations, visitors' projections and its own identity) against the 'historical givens' of folk and popular culture. Hawes’s case is the Clayville Rural Life Center and Museum near Springfield, Illinois, a site with a pioneer-style tavern and a Stagecoach Stop name that a university foundation took over in 1973. Hawes describes research that overturned an earlier two-culture account of northerners and southerners, showing that time of settlement, not regional origin, shaped where people settled, and that the Broadwell family were litigious rural entrepreneurs rather than a self-sufficient pioneer household. The inn was reinterpreted around these findings, many objects were moved to storage, and the fifth-grade 'Mornings at Clayville' program was revised. He argues for combining folklife studies, social history and cultural geography, and for treating the museum as a model of the past and a 'museum in the making.' The chapter closes with his later view that the museum's identity has become confused.

Clayville Rural Life Center and Museum
American Jewish Life: Ethnographic Approaches to Collection, Presentation, and Interpretation in MuseumsBarbara Kirshenblatt-Gimblettp. 143

Kirshenblatt-Gimblett argues that museums presenting American Jewish life should adopt an ethnographic model rather than the history or art models that dominate. Kirshenblatt-Gimblett shows how exhibitions have framed the subject: the history model celebrates the Jewish contribution through great men and prominent families, while the art model, exemplified by the Jewish Museum and the Museum of American Folk Art's 'The Jewish Heritage in American Folk Art', selects objects by an aesthetic of naivete that she questions as a modern category defined by what the makers did not know. The ethnographic model studies ordinary people in living communities, uses categories internal to those communities and treats context as the frame of meaning, illustrated with photography and live presentations. She criticizes the American Museum of Natural History's Jews section for presenting Judaism as normative and outside time and place, and contrasts salvage collecting at the Israel Museum with the overabundance of common American material. She proposes project-based collecting, a division of labor among North American Jewish museums, and a set of questions for museums to answer about their holdings.

Jewish MuseumAmerican Museum of Natural HistoryIsrael MuseumMuseum of American Folk Art
Folklorists Working in Museums: An International PerspectiveYvonne Langep. 163

Lange argues that a museum needs trained folklorists, or staff trained in fieldwork, to make sound decisions about collecting and interpreting folk artifacts. Drawing on her directorship of the Museum of International Folk Art in Santa Fe, she describes the exhibition 'What Is Folk Art?', built around stereotypes such as 'folk art is always rural', which set visitors arguing over definitions. She does not think a folklorist should be director, since administration leaves no time for research. Inside the walls, a folklorist can show the social function of objects and draw out information from people who carry the traditions. Her outreach examples come from New Mexico: a natural-dye revival among Hispanic weavers, which the museum supported with its textile collections and grant help, and an embroidery project at Villanueva, where thirty-six women turned their oral traditions into tapestries now hung in the village church. A young staff member recorded interviews, though she admits a trained folklorist would have done better. She concludes that the American Folklife Center should train curators in fieldwork so that cultures are not misrepresented.

Museum of International Folk Art
Almost Gone: Historic Houses of Our Own TimeJay Andersonp. 170

Anderson argues that the homes of the mid-to-late twentieth century are a neglected part of American material culture and need deliberate documentation before they are lost. Anderson opens with a Finnish manor house whose guest house had been shut up since 1912, its newspaper still on the breakfast table, to show how an unaltered home carries cultural memory. Anderson then gives an ethnographic study of a family living in a brick ranch house, room by room: the living room with its television and dulcimer, the country kitchen, a teenager's bedroom and bathroom, and a garage. Anderson describes his own 1960s subdivision, where the mix of residents has shifted, and rejects the idea that the twentieth century is a 'tasteful interlude' that preservation can ignore. Anderson traces the Scandinavian precedent, Hazelius at Skansen and Olsen in Denmark, and the Swedish Homes Pool, which studied a family's household as a museum studies a farm. Anderson notes that critics dismiss modern houses as not historical, and concludes that a museum should buy a lived-in home, interview its occupants and seal it away for future curators.

Hicks, Dan (2020). The Brutish Museums: The Benin Bronzes, Colonial Violence and Cultural Restitution. London: Pluto Press.Asia: slight20 chapter overviews

Overview

Dan Hicks, curator of world archaeology at the Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford, writes about the British sacking of Benin City in February 1897 and the more than ten thousand royal and sacred objects looted from it. His main argument is that displaying this loot in anthropology museums prolongs colonial violence, so the museums should return, disperse or repurpose the objects and become sites of conscience. The scope is British militarist and corporate colonialism in West Africa from 1884 to 1914, the Royal Niger Company, and the present-day holdings of Benin loot worldwide. It runs through eighteen chapters, from the expedition and its press framing to the looting, the dispersal of objects and restitution, then an afterword and appendices listing collections.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia are barely present. The book's scope is West Africa and Britain, and no chapter is concentrated on Asia; the references are passing comparisons and one collection in a list. Chapter 6 (Corporate-Militarist Colonialism) cites the 1888 agreement with the Sultan of Brunei as a model of British protectorate status, under which the Sultan kept his rule until 1984. Chapter 5 (World War Zero) reproduces a list of Victorian wars that includes the first and third Chinese wars and the Burmese wars.

China appears most in Chapter 13 (Necrology). Admiral Rawson, commander of the naval forces at Benin, had witnessed the looting of Beijing and the Summer Palace in 1860, and Hicks notes that younger soldiers later joined the Boxer-era plunder of China, when a multinational force pillaged the Caves of a Thousand Buddhas. This is evidence of a continuing practice of Western looting, not a study of Chinese museums or collections. Chapter 11 (Iconoclasm) makes a brief comparison with the Great Wall of China, and Chapter 3 (Necrography) quotes Nick Thomas's use of the category 'high Oriental'.

Japan appears once, in the provisional list of collections in Appendix 5, which includes the National Museum of Ethnology in Osaka. Southeast Asia is not discussed beyond the Brunei comparison, and the book does not treat Asian museum-building, Asian visitors or curators, or restitution claims from Asia. The gap is not remarked on.

Preface

Hicks introduces the book as written from the Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford, where he is curator of world archaeology. Drawing on Lindqvist's call for workers to investigate their own workplaces, he proposes a 'Euro-pessimism' in which knowledge of African objects in anthropology museums cannot be separated from colonial violence. The book aims to catalyse acknowledgement of British colonialism in Benin and to begin restitution. It ends with a request for help correcting a provisional list of where the 1897 Benin loot is held today.

Pitt Rivers Museum
11. The Gun That Shoots Twice

Hicks opens with the Pitt Rivers Museum's triple vitrine of Benin objects, whose interpretation panel repeats the British story of an ambush and retaliation. The chapter argues that the museum is not a neutral container but a weapon in its own right, and that its display of loot from the sacking of Benin City in February 1897 extends that violence across time. Hicks uses Alan Boisragon's adventure narrative of the January 1897 ambush, the Daily Mail and Times coverage, and the 1899 British Museum catalogue to show how the story of retaliation was fixed in print and display. Photographs taken during the expedition, many circulated as if new, are read as devices that, like cameras and museum cases, measure out duration. Hicks treats the failure of colonial displays as a moment of visibility, and sets out the book's aims: to widen the story of the punitive expedition, expose the looting, and link the museum to militarist corporate colonialism. The chapter ends by proposing a theory of taking and a coming time of returns.

Pitt Rivers MuseumBritish Museum
22. A Theory of Taking

Hicks argues that anthropology built its theory of material culture on gifts and reciprocity, following Mauss's Essay on the Gift, yet the objects in its museums were taken rather than given, and the discipline has never written a theory of looting. Hicks sets this gap against Marx's account of primitive accumulation and Rosa Luxemburg's argument that capitalism needs non-capitalist pasts in the colonies, a role he says Africa was cast into as 'pre-capitalist'. The 'world culture' museum, he suggests, works as a temporal device that holds unfulfilled obligations in its cases. Using Ann Laura Stoler's notion of 'duress' and Mauss's remark that refusing to give is tantamount to war, Hicks asks what refusal to give back means. He points to African collections, especially from Nigeria, Egypt and Ethiopia, whose predicament he says has reached breaking point. The chapter ends by calling for a theory of taking that treats looting as central to extractive colonialism and attends to the death histories of objects as well as their life histories.

33. Necrography

Hicks names two ideas that he says have stopped museums confronting colonial violence: 'object biographies', as in the British Museum's defence of the Parthenon marbles, and 'entanglement', as in Alfred Gell's Art and Agency and Nick Thomas's Entangled Objects. Both treat accession as a creative act and blur the line between Western and non-Western, so that loss and killing drop out of view. Hicks shows how these ideas shaped the Pitt Rivers Museum's 'relational museum' project and erased Victorian violence and questions of restitution. Hicks draws on Foucault, Agamben and Mbembe, and on Kopytoff and Orlando Patterson, to argue that the slave trade's blurring of persons and things set the precedent for treating sacred royal objects as cargo. Hicks proposes a 'necrography', a forensic writing of death and loss, in place of entanglement, and ends by urging museums to move from representation towards what Arendt called a space of appearance.

Pitt Rivers MuseumBritish Museum
44. White Projection

Hicks argues that the British framing of the sacking of Benin City as retaliation for a 'massacre' is an instance of 'white projection', in which the attackers' violence is attributed to their victims. Hicks opens with Richard Kandt's 1897 remark that half the objects in a museum were stolen, and reconstructs the Victorian context of the Diamond Jubilee and the 1841 Niger Expedition. Hicks shows how the accounts by Bacon, Boisragon and Roth, and the Illustrated London News, filled the press with images of human sacrifice, and how curators, including William Fagg at the British Museum, repeated those accounts. Hicks sets against them historians since the 1960s, who saw the expedition as a policy to depose Oba Ovonramwen. Hicks traces how anti-slavery rhetoric and racial ideology supplied the pretext, and criticises Trevor-Roper's denial of African history. The chapter ends by framing its 'necrography' as an attempt to break the frame of a timeless colonial past.

British MuseumPitt Rivers Museum
55. World War Zero

Hicks reframes the sacking of Benin City as one episode in a sustained series of punitive expeditions, which he calls World War Zero, from the Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1914. Hicks starts with Callwell's definition of 'small wars' and a Western Gazette list of Victorian conflicts, to show that Britain was at war in every year of Victoria's reign. Medals of the East and West Africa Campaign, with their clasps for some thirty interventions, serve as material evidence of a continuous campaign that official accounts split into separate 'disturbances'. Hicks argues that the punitive expedition combined a claim of crisis with white fragility to justify brutality. Hicks traces the Royal Niger Company from George Goldie's trading ventures to its role after Berlin, when Britain gained custody of the Niger, and presents the corporation as the driver of a militarist colonialism. The chapter ends by pointing towards the corporate-militarist structures that the next chapter examines.

66. Corporate-Militarist Colonialism

Hicks sets the British attack within the structures of corporate and militarist colonialism. Hicks traces chartered trading companies from the Muscovy Company to the Royal Niger Company, granted a charter in 1886 with monopoly and sovereign rights on the Niger. The confused status of the Company and the Niger Coast Protectorate produced a 'dual mandate' with different standards of law. Trade in palm oil, palm kernels and rubber drove the policy, and a treaty of 1892 with the Oba became a pretext for force. Hicks documents the Brohemie expedition of 1894 against Chief Nana and the Brass expedition of 1895 against Nembe, with rocket and Maxim fire and burned towns. Hicks cites Kirk's inquiry into violence against Brass people and shows that official reports refused to count African dead. The campaigns of 1894 to 1896 formed one continuous operation, which he calls a self-styled War on Terror. The chapter also notes that the corporation was added as a fourth 'C' to commerce, Christianity and civilisation.

East and Southeast Asia The chapter cites the 1888 agreement with the Sultan of Brunei as a model of British protectorate status, under which the Sultan kept his rule under British protection until 1984.

77. War on Terror

Hicks reads the removal of powerful African rulers between 1892 and 1900 as regime change carried out in the name of humanitarianism. Hicks sets the Salisbury government's rhetoric of 'savage countries' beside the French sacking of Abomey and the Royal Navy's campaigns under Admiral Rawson in East Africa, Zanzibar and Asante. Such operations, he suggests, used time as a weapon, presenting African retaliation as long premeditated while British attacks were described as reactive. Turning to Benin, Hicks shows that the expedition had been prepared for months, through the Protectorate's surveys, Liverpool traders' lobbying and James Phillips's letter of November 1896 asking to depose the Oba. The 'Phillips massacre' is examined through the press, the delayed reply from Salisbury and Flora Shaw's Times article coining the name 'Nigeria', which he compares to the Jameson Raid. He suggests that the Phillips mission was designed to provoke the retaliation that justified war, and that museums have repeated the story uncritically.

Pitt Rivers Museum
88. The Benin-Niger-Soudan Expedition

Hicks argues that the Benin expedition must be understood together with the Royal Niger Company's simultaneous campaign against the emirates of Bida and Ilorin, which he calls the Benin-Niger-Soudan Expedition. Hicks shows how Goldie and Moor coordinated the two operations, and how Flora Shaw's Times coverage presented them as one event. Hicks describes the battles of Bida and Ilorin, where Maxim guns and field guns cut down cavalry and infantry and the cities were bombarded and burned, with casualties unrecorded. Critics such as Dilke and the Spectator condemned the mowing down of men, while Goldie defended the Company. Vandeleur's memoir, with its accounts of looted cloth, brass and manuscripts, shows the routine plunder that followed the violence. The chapter ends by setting the northern campaign against the Protectorate's sacking of Benin City, which comes next. Hicks notes that the Company's charter was revoked in 1900.

99. The Sacking of Benin City

Hicks describes the sacking of Benin City between 9 and 27 February 1897 as a naval operation led by Admiral Rawson, with three columns, about 1,400 troops, 2,500 carriers and 38 Maxim guns. Hicks sets the firepower of the attackers against the Bini defenders, who fought with flintlock muskets, cutlasses and a few old cannon. The flying columns burned towns along the river, and the palace and sacred sites in the city were blown up with gun cotton and burned. Hicks reads the destruction against the 1874 Brussels Declaration and the 1899 Hague Convention, which banned pillage and the bombardment of undefended towns. Hicks argues that the sack was indiscriminate and formed part of a wider chronopolitics in which time was used as a weapon of control. It describes the sack as an attack on human life, culture, belief and sovereignty. The chapter ends by setting out the next three chapters, on killing, destruction and looting.

1010. Democide

Hicks argues that the deaths in the Benin attack can never be counted, and that official reports' refusal to estimate African casualties was part of the violence. Hicks sets the eight British dead in the Protectorate's casualty list against the uncounted Bini and iJekri dead. Military manuals by Callwell and Heneker recommended volley firing into the bush and raking it with Maxim fire, which made casualties hard to see. Colonial administrators avoided counting populations in the 1890s, and the Commons never obtained figures on the numbers killed, so that men on the spot escaped accountability. Hicks compares the Benin deaths with the Matabele Wars, the Battle of Shangani and the Battle of Omdurman, and examines the 'rule of difference' in colonial violence. The chapter ends by arguing that the destruction of royal and sacred objects formed part of the same violence, and turns to looting in the next chapter.

1111. Iconoclasm

Hicks argues that the British sacking of Benin City was an attack on the built environment itself, aimed at obliterating a monumental urban landscape. Hicks describes the iya earthworks, which Graham Connah dated to the twelfth century, and notes how inflated claims about their size, from Patrick Darling to the Guinness Book of Records, passed into myth. Hicks then reconstructs the systematic destruction of February 1897 through Captain Egerton's to-do list, which included knocking down walls, blowing up the 'Ju-Ju houses' and burning the Queen Mother's house, and through Walker's diary. The stated purpose was to 'break the power of the fetish priests', and the ruins that remained were read as proof of decline. Hicks shows that these ruined royal houses were sacred mortuary monuments, since Read and Dalton described how a king's house was shut up after his death with his objects buried beneath the floor. The chapter ends by linking the erasure of the city to the looting that follows.

1212. Looting

Hicks argues that no fixed list of the Benin loot is possible, and proposes instead to 'count back' by tracing each object through the events that took it. Hicks puts the total at around 10,000 objects and distinguishes three categories: uncarved ivory, which was sold for Protectorate funds; some 900 to 1,000 brass plaques reported to the Admiralty; and the remaining brass, ivory and wood, shared out among officers. Hicks shows that the claim that sales paid pensions was euphemistic, and that objects were on display in London within six months. Hicks traces the sales through dealers such as William Downing Webster and the purchases of the British Museum and of Berlin's Museum fur Volkerkunde, which he says acquired collections in many ways superior to London's. Hicks argues that the market and the museums worked together, and that the nation state is the wrong target for critique, since corporate colonialism was the real agency. The chapter ends by calling for a necrography that reads loss in the collections.

British MuseumMuseum für Völkerkunde Berlin
1313. Necrology

Hicks argues that museum knowledge of the Benin loot is haphazard, and proposes 'necrology' for the knowledge made through death and loss. Hicks notes the uncertain holdings of British regional and university museums, from the McLean Museum at Greenock to the Pitt Rivers, and the many private collections that cannot be traced. The chapter then offers an A to Z of seventeen British officers and officials, from Allman and Bacon to Walker and Roupell, setting out what each is known to have looted and where those objects went through sales, gifts and dealers. Hicks follows the two Queen Idia pendants that Ralph Moor kept, one of which reached the British Museum and the other Rockefeller and later the Metropolitan Museum. Hicks notes that Walker's grandson returned two brass objects to Benin in 2014. Hicks argues that looting was passed on through naval and military custom, which the Boxer-era plunder of China continued. The chapter ends by rejecting the 2007 claim that military action brought Benin's art to wider attention.

East and Southeast Asia Hicks notes that Admiral Rawson had witnessed the looting of Beijing and the Summer Palace in 1860, and that younger soldiers later joined the western plunder of China during the Boxer Rebellion, when a multinational force pillaged the Caves of a Thousand Buddhas.

British MuseumPitt Rivers MuseumMetropolitan Museum of Art
1414. ‘The Museum of Weapons, etc.’

Hicks traces the two Pitt Rivers Museums, the founder's first collection at Oxford and his second collection at Farnham, both established in 1884. Hicks shows that the Farnham collection was formed mostly in the last three years of Pitt-Rivers's life, drawing on dealers such as William Downing Webster, who supplied about two-thirds of its 188 Benin objects. After the founder's death the Farnham collection was broken up and sold through the agency of his grandson George Pitt-Rivers and of Stella Lonsdale. Hicks describes how the Oxford museum came to hold at least 145 Benin objects, including the Egerton loan from the Dumas-Egerton Trust, and how both museums presented the material through typological theory and 'object lessons'. Hicks notes that the 1929 Handbook framed the Benin room in terms of 'savage' religion, and he ends by tracing dispersal and destruction, including the 1941 fire at Liverpool Museum. The chapter concludes that the two Pitt Rivers Museums became weapons in their own right.

Pitt Rivers Museum, OxfordPitt-Rivers Museum, FarnhamLiverpool Museum
1515. Chronopolitics

Hicks argues that the museum's work of turning objects into statues and fetishes is a form of chronopolitics, drawing on Mbembe's account of mummification alongside Fanon's 'immobile world of statues' and Césaire's 'chosification'. Hicks contrasts Johannes Fabian's denial of coevalness with a more material process, in which whole cultures were stripped of their technologies and their landscapes turned into ruins. The chapter traces Pitt-Rivers's typological museum, which began as a collection of arms, and Tylor's 'object lessons', which Ralph Moor also invoked to justify punishing Benin. Hicks shows how the Benin material was displayed as a coherent archaeological body, framed by horror fiction and by Mary Kingsley's claim of cultural incommensurability. Hicks describes scholars who attributed the bronzes to Portuguese, Egyptian or Atlantean origins, and the Tervuren 'human zoo' as part of the same racial display. The chapter ends by arguing that museums made Benin a lost world, extending the violence of 1897 across time.

Pitt Rivers MuseumBritish MuseumRoyal Africa Museum, Tervuren
1616. A Declaration of War

Hicks argues that the 2002 Declaration on the Importance and Value of Universal Museums, signed by eighteen directors of mainly Northern Hemisphere museums, defended collections against restitution, and that the 'universal museum' was a 21st-century invention rather than an old tradition. Hicks traces the Benin Bronzes looted in 1897 through decades of claims, including Akenzua II's 1936 request, the British Museum's transfers to Nigeria in the 1950s and 1972, and the 1977 refusal to lend the Queen Idia mask to FESTAC. Newspaper investigations of 2002 exposed these transfers. Hicks sets the Declaration beside the 1983 Lords debate on the British Museum Act, MacGregor's reorganisation of the museum, and Cuno's American defence of encyclopaedic collections, and widens the argument to the Iraq war and Blair's rhetoric of universal values. The chapter ends by reading the failure of the 2007-08 Benin Kings and Rituals exhibition to travel to Nigeria as evidence of the same stance.

British MuseumMuseum of MankindNational Museum, LagosBerlin State Museums
1717. A Negative Moment

Hicks argues that the Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford became a focal point in 2015, when Rhodes Must Fall Oxford, inspired by the Cape Town campaign against the Rhodes statue, challenged the museum's permanent displays of looted African material. Hicks treats these displays as a continuing act of violence, not a past event. Hicks sets this against the defences offered by other 'universal museums': MacGregor's Humboldt Forum rhetoric, Hunt's claim that decolonising means decontextualising, and US museums that treat recent acquisitions as settling title. The chapter then follows the money: the slave-compensation fortune that funded Pitt-Rivers's Benin purchases in 1897-99, and the Royal Niger Company's compensation after its 1899 charter revocation. It proposes a 'necrographic' method and a reckoning with the British 'small wars' of the 1890s. It concludes that anthropology museums should return every violently taken object and become sites of conscience.

Pitt Rivers MuseumBritish MuseumMuseum of Fine Arts, BostonHumboldt ForumLouvre Abu DhabiHorniman MuseumVictoria and Albert Museum
1818. Ten Thousand Unfinished Events

Hicks argues that restitution is a continuing process rather than a subtraction, and that museums should treat returns as acts of conscience. Hicks criticises the Victoria and Albert Museum and the British Museum for calling looted Maqdala and Benin objects 'contested' or 'difficult' heritage, and presents Macron's 2017 pledge and the Sarr-Savoy Report as a turning point. The chapter ends with the phrase 'Ten thousand unfinished events'.

British MuseumVictoria and Albert Museum
Afterword: A Decade of Returns

Hicks sets out practical steps for restitution after the book's arguments. Hicks describes 2018 protests at the Rhode Island School of Design and the Brooklyn Museum, and says the Pitt Rivers holds 422 looted objects under his purview. Hicks calls for museums to publish accession data and proposes a typology of seven kinds of taking, from violent looting to purchase. The afterword ends with a call to make the 2020s a decade of restitution.

Overview

Edited by Kate Hill, this 2012 volume gathers 21 chapters from a 2009 conference of the Museums and Galleries History Group on biography and museums. Its argument is that museums are arenas where relationships among people, things and institutions produce narratives, and that the usual life-stories of curators, donors, buildings and objects smooth out messier histories. The chapters fall into six sections: individual biography, problematising individuals, institutional biography, object biography, museums as biography and museums as autobiography. Cases range from Stockholm, Paris and London to Liverpool, Berlin, Edmonton, Denmark, Brazil and Northern Ireland.

East and Southeast Asia in this work occasional

The main concentration is chapter 12, Louise Tythacott’s ‘Classifying China’, on five Buddhist deity figures from Putuo Island, taken from a temple after the First Opium War and placed in Liverpool Museum in 1867. The chapter follows how their identity changed with each curator and classification: ethnology, a ‘Mongolian’ race category under Henry Ogg Forbes, Oriental art under Trevor Tomas in the 1930s, archaeology under Elaine Tankard and antiquity from 1966. It also treats the wider division of Chinese objects in British and French museums, including Manchester Museum’s 1958 ‘Asia: Civilizations’ gallery (China, Japan, Siam, Burma) and the Musée du Quai Branly, which shows only Southeast Asian textiles and puppets while the art stays at the Musée Guimet.

Elsewhere East and Southeast Asia appear only in passing. The editors’ introduction mentions the Putuo bronze in Tythacott’s chapter and nothing else from the region. In chapter 19, Belinda Nemec’s account of Pierre Loti’s house notes a Japanese pagoda and a Chinese room among the display rooms he began in 1877 from the trappings of his naval voyages, which she reads as an appropriation of exotic and colonised lands. The Pacific collection in chapter 14 and the Indian heads in chapter 15 lie outside the question.

Not covered: museums in East or Southeast Asia, Asian visitors, curators or scholars, Asian states’ heritage policy, and any restitution claim from those regions. The one restitution claim in the book, the Tupinambá claim in chapter 13, concerns Brazil.
