Theoretical approach of this work
List of Illustrationsp. vii
Introduction: Museums and Biographies – Telling Stories about People, Things and RelationshipsKate Hillp. 1

Hill's introduction sets out the aim of a volume on museums and biographies, arising from a 2009 conference of the Museums and Galleries History Group. Hill argues that biography and museums both tell stories about people, things and relationships, and that both inherit a nineteenth-century belief in the rational individual and in a knowable world separate from the knower. Hill reviews how museum history has been written as the life of an institution or of its charismatic curators, a 'smoothing out' that several contributors challenge. Hill then introduces the six sections, covering individual biography, problematic individuals, institutional biography, object biography, museums as biography and museums as autobiography, and shows how the chapters treat agency as shared among people, buildings and objects. Hill’s examples range from the Moderna Museet to the Museum of French Monuments. The introduction concludes that museums should be read as arenas where relationships produce narratives, and that their stories should do justice to the complicated histories of things, institutions and people.

East and Southeast Asia The introduction mentions one object from East Asia only: Louise Tythacott's chapter follows a Chinese Buddhist bronze through a museum, where the museum's classifications fixed its meaning. Nothing else about East or Southeast Asia appears.

Museum of French MonumentsModerna MuseetNational Gallery (London)Schinkel Museum
Individual Biography and Museum Historyp. 11
1A Show of Generosity: Donations and the Intimacy of Display in the 'Cabinet des médailles et antiques' in Paris from 1830 to 1930Felicity Bodensteinp. 13

Bodenstein examines donations to the Cabinet des médailles et antiques, the coin and antiquities department of the Bibliothèque nationale in Paris, from 1830 to 1930. Bodenstein first treats donation as a social fact with clear chronological limits: gifts were rare before 1830 and grew sharply from 1860 to 1914. Bodenstein then reads two donations as biographical events. The Duke of Luynes gave his entire collection in 1862 on condition that it be shown complete in its own room, a condition that shaped later reinstallations. Wilhelm Froehner, a German archaeologist dismissed from the Louvre in 1870, kept his collection hidden and bequeathed it in 1908 as a final assertion of self. Bodenstein argues that donors' demands gave the department an intimate, almost private character, with displays arranged around donor names and fin-de-siècle bibelot taste rather than systematic series. The chapter concludes that the network of benefactors defined the institution's identity as much as its curators' scholarship did, so that the lives of donors cannot be separated from the museum's history.

Cabinet des médailles et antiquesLouvre
2Introducing Mr Moderna Museet: Pontus Hultén and Sweden's Museum of Modern ArtStuart Burchp. 29

Burch examines Pontus Hultén, who led Moderna Museet in Stockholm and later the Centre Pompidou, and the bequest of some 700 works and a library that Hultén made to the Stockholm museum shortly before his death in 2006. The chapter opens with the Pontus Hultén Study Gallery, opened in 2008, where paintings slide across the ceiling on a touchscreen-operated conveyor. Burch reads Hultén through Bourdieu's Distinction, arguing that the gift turns a donor's taste into the museum's legitimacy. Burch traces Hultén's career from the 1961 exhibition Movement in Art, first shown at Amsterdam's Stedelijk under Willem Sandberg, through his posts in Los Angeles and Paris. Two episodes test the bequest: the catalogue The Pontus Hultén Collection, which places the donor's family photographs among the artists, and the Brillo box scandal, in which wooden boxes made after Warhol's death were sold as originals. The chapter concludes that the museum now mirrors its donor, and that the gallery works as a mechanism keeping Hultén present, turning a museum which moves a lot into a monument to one man.

Moderna MuseetStedelijk MuseumLos Angeles Museum of Contemporary ArtCentre PompidouModerna Museet Malmö
3Sydney Pavière and the Harris Museum and Art Gallery, PrestonLaura Grayp. 45

Gray asks how far one curator could shape a provincial museum, taking Sydney Pavière, art director of the Harris Museum and Art Gallery in Preston from 1926 to 1959, as her case. Gray sets his career beside those of other interwar curators who gave their collections strong identities. Pavière rearranged the galleries and bought controversially, most notably the Nude of 1927, which divided the Art Gallery Committee. He also built historical decorative arts collections, including the Devis room, the Houghton ceramics and a large Victorian dress collection, and used press coverage to reach both connoisseurs and Preston's cotton-trade workers. Gray compares his historical approach with Lawrence Haward's contemporary Industrial Art Collection in Manchester. Gray argues that the shift of power from council committees to professional curators gave Pavière his agency, but that his own press cuttings and letters have fixed his reputation and obscured his assistant and successor, Helena Gibbon. The chapter concludes that his 33-year tenure was the museum's most significant period, while warning against taking his self-portrait at face value.

Harris Museum and Art GalleryManchester Art GalleryFerens Art GalleryLady Lever Art Gallery
Problematising Individuals' Biographiesp. 59
4'His Best Successor': Lady Eastlake and the National GalleryJulie Sheldonp. 61

Sheldon examines the reputation of Lady Eastlake, widow of Sir Charles Eastlake, the first Director of the National Gallery, and asks whether she shaped his purchases. Historians from Holmes and Collins Baker in 1924 to Steegman, Ames and Conlin have credited her with his success, often relying on the posthumous Journals and Correspondence, which her nephew edited from letters to her mother. Sheldon tests these claims against the Gallery's archive and finds few instances of Lady Eastlake's influence on decisions. Sheldon shows that Lady Eastlake wrote letters on her husband's behalf, defended his reputation against critics and publishers, and offered a hedged opinion on whether to buy Piero della Francesca's Baptism. Sheldon’s own taste for early Italian painting developed partly through his guidance, and she worked as his research assistant, since his travel notebooks record her drawings. The chapter concludes that after Eastlake's death in 1865 she lobbied his successors and sought a nephew's appointment, so that her legacy is one of interference rather than the joint partnership historians have assumed.

National Gallery, London
5Women, Museums and the Problem of BiographyAnne Whitelawp. 75

Whitelaw uses the founding and running of the Art Gallery of Alberta in Edmonton to test whether biography is a useful way to write the history of a museum. The chapter's main case is Maud Bowman, the Edmonton Museum of Arts' founding president and first director, who organised exhibitions, art classes and loans from the National Gallery of Canada in Ottawa, and whose pay was resisted by the male board. Whitelaw then sets her against the Women's Society, a volunteer group formed in 1944 whose bake sales, gala balls and gift shop raised over a million dollars for acquisitions but left almost no individual trace in the records. Whitelaw reviews the feminist critique of biography, drawing on Kathleen McCarthy and Dianne Sachko Macleod's studies of American women collectors, and argues that a life-story built around leaders reproduces the exceptionalism that feminist historians have criticised. The chapter concludes that biography cannot account for the collective labour and institutional structures that keep museums running, and that such histories need to trace the institution's discourses as well as the individuals who work in it.

Art Gallery of AlbertaNational Gallery of Canada
6A Curatocracy: Who and What is a V&A Curator?Linda Sandinop. 87

Sandino uses oral life-history interviews with seven retired and serving V&A curators to ask what a curator is. The chapter starts from the 1989 reorganisation of the Victoria & Albert Museum, which separated scholarship from the care and management of the collections. Drawing on Paul Ricoeur's idea of narrative identity, Sandino argues that the curators' accounts combine continuity and change: the civil service ethos of public duty, and the requirement to sign the Official Secrets Act, persisted into the 1990s, while cataloguing the permanent collection was treated as the core of curatorial expertise. The chapter then examines the connoisseur's 'embodied eye', built by handling objects, comparing plastics and identifying fakes, and shows how that expertise has been reframed around historical understanding. Sandino concludes that the curator's identity is shaped by the institution's history and its civil service past, and that the V&A, as both a place and a repository of memory, sustains that identity.

Victoria & Albert Museum
Institutional Biographiesp. 101
7Significant Lives: Telling Stories of Museum ArchitectureSuzanne MacLeodp. 103

MacLeod argues that biography can give architectural history of museums a way past the usual focus on architects and smooth stories of stylistic progress. Its case study is the Walker Art Gallery in Liverpool, whose construction she traces through the 1870s: James Picton's plans for a publicly funded gallery collapsed under ratepayer opposition, and the brewer and mayor Andrew Barclay Walker then paid for the building and kept Picton's group out of the design. MacLeod also reads two fragments as traces of the people who used and contested the building: a 1948 photograph of newspaper scraps left on a gallery wall after the wartime Ministry of Food occupied it, and a caricature linked to the temperance reformer Ronald McDougall. Drawing on Janes and Bradburne's critiques of museum building, she concludes that such attention to lived bodily occupation can expose the messy, political processes behind museum architecture and help the profession rethink present-day capital projects.

Walker Art Gallery
8Schinkel's Museums: Collecting and Displaying Architecture in Berlin, 1844–1933Wallis Millerp. 119

Miller traces the Schinkel Museum in Berlin, which opened in 1844 in the Bauakademie rooms where Karl Friedrich Schinkel had worked, and which the National Gallery reopened in 1931 before it closed in 1933. Its history moves through a neglected collection in a technical university and a return to the National Gallery, and Miller argues that these shifts mirror changing views of Schinkel and of architecture. The chapter's main evidence is the museum's arrangement of Schinkel's portfolios, plaster casts and paintings, and of photographs of his drawings from 1858. These mixed archive and exhibition and challenged an art academy that valued authorship in objects and excluded buildings. In the 1920s the faculty of the Technische Hochschule lost the collection to Ludwig Justi, who placed it in the National Gallery, and the 1931 display presented Schinkel as an artist rather than an architect. Miller concludes that the architecture museum is a new type defined by its confrontations with authenticity and representation, and that Schinkel's museum shows why buildings resist conventional display.

Schinkel MuseumNational Gallery, BerlinArchitecture Museum of the Technische HochschuleAltes Museum
9Personifying the Museum: Incorporation and Biography in American Museum HistoryJeffrey Abtp. 133

Abt starts from Bayle St John's 1855 book on the Louvre, subtitled 'Biography of a Museum', and asks what it means to treat a museum as a person. Abt’s answer is that American museums were created as private non-profit corporations, a legal form that gives an institution one identity before the law. Abt traces the English and colonial history of corporate charters, from Blackstone and the Virginia and Plymouth companies to the state incorporation statutes of the 1830s and the Dartmouth College case, which held that an institution's character depends on how and why it was formed. Abt then shows how late nineteenth-century boards of businessmen, tax exemptions and the non-profit category shaped the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston, the Art Institute of Chicago and the Detroit Institute of Arts. Abt concludes that the corporate idea hides the differences among boards, staff, volunteers and audiences, and that museum histories written as life stories repeat this by celebrating milestones rather than internal disputes or local ties.

LouvreMetropolitan Museum of ArtMuseum of Fine Arts, BostonArt Institute of ChicagoDetroit Institute of Arts
10Making an Exhibition of OurselvesHelen Rees Leahyp. 145

Leahy examines the recent fashion for 'exhibitions of exhibitions', in which museums remount or reconstruct earlier shows, and asks what this reveals about institutional memory. Leahy’s cases include the Courtauld Gallery's 'Art on the Line' (2001), which rebuilt an early nineteenth-century Royal Academy hang in its original room, and Tate Britain's 'William Blake 1809', which left a blank wall where a lost painting had hung. Leahy shows that loans, surviving archives and risk-averse museums limited what could be reproduced, and that Tate Modern's 2009 reinstallation of Robert Morris's 1971 show lost its radical edge under modern safety rules. Using Baxandall's 'period eye' and Gide's mise en abyme, Leahy explains why some re-dos make viewers aware of how they look and others do not. She concludes that every gallery is a palimpsest of past shows, and that revisiting earlier exhibitions can expose the institution's own habits.

Courtauld GalleryTate BritainTate ModernManchester Art GalleryRoyal AcademyMuseum Boijmans van Beuningen
11Institutional Autobiography and the Architecture of the Art Museum: Restoration and Remembering at the National Gallery in the 1980sChristopher Whiteheadp. 157

Whitehead examines what the restoration of the Barry Rooms at London's National Gallery, carried out in 1984 to 1986, says about the museum's relationship to its own past. The rooms, designed by Edward Middleton Barry and completed in 1876, had been boxed in and repainted in the twentieth century in line with the modernist ideal of neutral, isolated displays. Whitehead sets the restoration against a wider revaluation of Victorian interiors, which began with the Victorian Society in 1958, and against critics such as Gervase Jackson-Stops and Gavin Stamp who attacked the gallery's modernist blankness. Whitehead shows that the project relied on paint-layer analysis and Barry's drawings to recover a scheme that Barry had wanted, and that it left out the Reynolds inscription the Trustees had objected to in 1876. Whitehead then tests the restoration against the Venice Charter and asks whose intentions, and which period, count as authentic. Whitehead concludes that conservation choices are historiographical and political, and that museums should say so openly and explain them to visitors.

National Gallery, LondonVictoria and Albert MuseumNational Gallery of Scotland
Object Biographiesp. 171
12Classifying China: Shifting Interpretations of Buddhist Bronzes in Liverpool Museum, 1867–1997Louise Tythacottp. 173Asia: chiefly

Tythacott follows five Buddhist bronze figures from Putuo Island in China, including a large Guanyin probably of the early fifteenth century, from their seizure after the First Opium War to their arrival at Liverpool Museum in 1867 and their decades in storage. Using Igor Kopytoff's idea of the cultural biography of things, she argues that the statues' identity changed with each curator: first as ethnology, then as specimens of the 'Mongolian' race under the director Henry Ogg Forbes, then as Oriental art under the modernist Trevor Tomas in the 1930s, and as archaeology under Elaine Tankard after the war. Their move into antiquities in 1966 and their metallurgical study by Eldon Worrall, who reassembled the dismembered Guanyin, follow. The chapter places these shifts within the wider classification of Chinese objects in British and French museums, where material culture was split between ethnography, decorative art and antiquities. Tythacott concludes that the bronzes' meaning depended on their guardians' interests, and that each curator's interpretation carried assumptions that the original temple setting, with its frontal and low viewing, did not share.

East and Southeast Asia Almost all of the chapter concerns China: the five Putuo Island deity figures, the Chinese bronzes and other Asian objects at Liverpool Museum, and how Chinese objects were divided between ethnography, decorative art and antiquities in Britain and France. It notes that Gatty in 1882 placed the 'highly cultivated' Asian races outside ethnology, that Manchester Museum's 1958 Asia galleries separated 'Civilizations' (China, Japan, Siam, Burma) from 'Tribes', and that Oriental Ceramic Society collectors shaped British taste in Chinese art from the 1920s. It also notes that the Musée du Quai Branly shows only Southeast Asian textiles and puppets, with the art kept at the Musée Guimet.

Liverpool MuseumWalker Art GalleryManchester MuseumBritish MuseumMusée du Quai Branly
13'Dressed like an Amazon': The Transatlantic Trajectory of a Red Feather CoatMariana Françozop. 187

Françozo follows a red feather cape, probably made by the Tupinambá of coastal Brazil in the first century of colonial contact, from its making to the National Museum of Denmark, where it is now displayed. The chapter begins with the cape's loan to the 2000 'Mostra do Redescobrimento' in São Paulo, where its display provoked a claim by Tupinambá Indians that it was part of their ancestral heritage; the claim never went to court. Françozo draws on Arjun Appadurai's idea of things in motion to reconstruct the cape's history: from ritual dress and a trade item to a gift from Tapuia allies to the Dutch governor Johan Maurits van Nassau-Siegen. Françozo then traces its place in Johan Maurits's kunstkammer in The Hague, a Hanneman portrait of Mary Stuart wearing a feather cape linked to the 1655 Ballet de la Carmesse, and its probable gift to the Danish king Frederik III around 1654. Françozo concludes that the cape's meaning was built through exchange and gift-giving, and that museums should show such trajectories so that visitors can consider colonial history and present claims to heritage.

National Museum of DenmarkMostra do Redescobrimento, São Paulo (2000)MauritshuisDutch National Portrait Gallery
14Individual, Collective and Institutional Biographies: The Beasley Collection of Pacific ArtefactsLucie Carreaup. 201

Carreau examines the Pacific collection formed by Harry Geoffrey Beasley, a brewery director whose private collection of over 10,000 objects, some 6,000 of them from the Pacific, was displayed as the Cranmore Ethnographical Museum in Chislehurst from 1928. Scholars have long dismissed such amateur collections as contaminated by their makers, and Carreau shows the limits of that view by reading the collection through overlapping biographies: those of the collector, the private museum, individual objects, and the collection after Beasley's death in 1939. The evidence includes his acquisition ledgers, his dealings with dealers, his Royal Anthropological Institute fellowship and his fish-hook monograph. The chapter also points to his interest in museography, his advertisements in the Museums Journal, and his deliberate collecting of contemporary objects, such as a fish hook carved from a Bakelite toothbrush handle. Finally the chapter follows the bombing of the museum in 1940 and the division of the collection among British and other public museums, which left it fragmented and hard to read. Carreau concludes that the collection is more contaminated than previously thought, and that these contaminations explain how collections moved into and out of museums.

Cranmore Ethnographical MuseumBritish MuseumPitt Rivers MuseumMuseum of Archaeology and Anthropology, CambridgeNational Museums of ScotlandWorld Museum, LiverpoolRed House Museum, Christchurch
15Sculptural Biographies in an Anthropological Collection: Mrs Milward's Indian 'Types'Mark J Elliottp. 215

Elliott examines the 100 plaster and bronze portrait heads of Indian 'types' that the English sculptor Marguerite Milward made during expeditions from 1935 to 1938 and gave to the Cambridge Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology in 1948. The heads were moved out of view and forgotten until a staff member found them in an old display case around 1985. Elliott argues that the sculptures are best read through several overlapping biographies: those of Milward herself, whose life in Paris, Sri Lanka and Shantiniketan led to her Indian project; those of the models, many of whom she met through colonial officials, missionaries and anthropologists; and those of the institutions and disciplines that received the heads. Elliott uses the case of Nihu Angami, a Naga interpreter who became a political figure, and the sittings with Suni and Koba, to show how differently the encounters went. Elliott concludes that the heads, once seen as anachronistic anthropometric specimens, can be re-presented as portraits, and that their polysemy makes them useful to a museum facing its colonial past.

Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology, CambridgeIndian Museum, Calcutta
Museums as Biographyp. 229
16Houses and Things: Literary House Museums as Collective BiographyAlison Boothp. 231

Booth examines literary house museums, the former homes of writers kept as museums, and argues that they work as collective biographies. The chapter opens with David Parker, curator of the Charles Dickens Museum in London, who envied the Carlyles' house for its surviving possessions and admitted that such museums are in the business of calling up ghosts. Booth treats the house museum as a narrative built from documentary evidence, setting and time, and compares it with biography and prosopography, the study of groups of people. The chapter traces the rise of these museums through travel memoirs, homes and haunts books, and the biographies that drew pilgrims to Haworth, where the Bronte Parsonage Museum opened in 1928. The case studies are the Carlyles' house in Chelsea, built up from portraits and memorial volumes, and Washington Irving's Sunnyside on the Hudson. Booth argues that visitors complete these narratives by animating rooms and objects, which gives the house an uncanny effect. Booth concludes that a literary house museum is a collective portrait assembled by curators, donors, pilgrims and visitors, and that its ghosts belong as much to the audience as to the author.

Charles Dickens Museum, LondonCarlyle's House, ChelseaSunnyside, Irving's houseBronte Parsonage MuseumEmily Dickinson Museum
17'Keepers of the Flame': Biography, Science and Personality in the MuseumSophie Forganp. 247

Forgan examines the personality museum, a museum built around a single famous scientist and his home, and asks how such sites tell scientific lives. The chapter takes three cases: Newton's birthplace at Woolsthorpe Manor in Lincolnshire, Darwin's Down House in Kent, and Freud's last home at 20 Maresfield Gardens in London. For each, the chapter traces how the house was saved and opened, which shows that survival depended on a few influential keepers of the fame rather than on architectural merit. Woolsthorpe was bought by the Royal Society in 1942 through contacts such as Sir Henry Dale and G M Trevelyan; Down House was rescued through Sir George Buckston Browne and Sir Arthur Keith, and later by English Heritage; the Freud Museum was created from Anna Freud's bequest. Forgan argues that these museums present a whole life through personal objects, stressing the scientist's industry and ceaseless thought while leaving out quarrels and weaknesses. Forgan concludes that personality museums act as mirrors, showing visitors both the scientist and their own changing values.

Woolsthorpe ManorDown HouseFreud Museum, LondonMarie Curie Museum, Paris
18National History as Biography: Alexandre Lenoir's Museum of French MonumentsAlexandra Starap. 265

Stara examines Alexandre Lenoir's Museum of French Monuments in Paris, which grew from a revolutionary depot in the former convent of the Petits-Augustins and ran as a public museum from 1795 to 1816. Rather than a chronological history of French art, Stara argues that Lenoir built the museum around the personalities commemorated by its monuments, so that the nation's past appeared as a series of individual lives. The chapter describes how Lenoir gathered tombs and fragments from churches and from sales of nationalised property, exchanged pieces he thought useless, and restored or invented missing parts in his fabriques. The catalogues, which went through several editions, supply anecdotes about kings, lovers and poets, and the chapter closes with visitors' responses, including those of Ann Plumptre and Jules Michelet, who read the faces of the statues as expressions of character. Stara concludes that the museum offered empathy and emotion rather than rational progress, so that visitors could identify France's personalities with the nation itself.

Museum of French MonumentsLouvre
Museums as Autobiographyp. 277
19Autobiographical MuseumsBelinda Nemecp. 279

Nemec defines the autobiographical museum as a museum whose main subject is the life or career of the person who founded it, and argues that this genre has received little scholarly attention. The chapter separates these museums from collectors' house museums, which reveal their owners only indirectly. Its central case is the Grainger Museum in Melbourne, which the composer Percy Grainger planned after his mother's suicide in 1922 and built in his lifetime to present his career. Nemec shows how Grainger's letters, memoirs and way of cataloguing correspondence by closeness to himself serve that aim, and contrasts the museum with the art-centred Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum. The chapter then surveys painters and writers such as Gustave Moreau, Pierre Loti and Gabriele d'Annunzio, whose houses or memorials turned their lives into theatrical displays, along with Christian C Sanderson's relic collection. Nemec concludes that the Grainger Museum is the only example the chapter finds that combines a lifelong collector, self-conscious autobiographical material and a dedicated permanent building.

East and Southeast Asia The chapter notes that Pierre Loti's house included a Japanese pagoda and a Chinese room among its thematic display rooms, begun in 1877 from the trappings of places he visited on naval voyages. It reads these rooms, beside Turkish and Arab rooms and a mosque, as an appropriation of exotic or colonised lands that linked Loti's personal and national stories.

Grainger Museum, University of MelbourneIsabella Stewart Gardner MuseumSir John Soane's MuseumMusee Gustave MoreauMaison Pierre LotiIl Vittoriale degli Italiani
20Who is History? The Use of Autobiographical Accounts in History MuseumsStef de Jongp. 295

De Jong examines the use of autobiographical videos and interviews, in which witnesses recount their own lives, as exhibits in history museums. The chapter opens with the Museum of Europe's 'It's our history!' exhibition, which presented 27 citizens, one from each member state, as representatives of European integration. De Jong traces how such recordings became museum material, from oral history projects and the Imperial War Museum's Sound Archive to the Eichmann trial and the Fortunoff Archive, and shows how the Bergen-Belsen and Neuengamme memorials now exhibit clips from their interviews. Drawing on the Assmanns' distinction between communicative and cultural memory, de Jong argues that curators turn witnesses' stories into carriers of cultural memory. Clips are paired with objects, such as a pair of gloves at Bergen-Belsen, so that each authenticates the other. De Jong concludes that giving ordinary people a voice goes with a devaluation of the individual life-story, which becomes a sample standing for a time, a community or an event, chosen by curators who did not witness it.

Museum of Europe, BrusselsImperial War MuseumBergen-Belsen MemorialNeuengamme Memorial
21Community Biographies: Character, Rationale and SignificanceElizabeth Crookep. 309

Crooke examines community history projects in which local groups research and write their own histories from oral testimony and photographs, and argues that these are a form of community autobiography. The most detailed case is the Shared History Society, a cross-community group formed in 2010 in north-east Northern Ireland, which produced an exhibition of almost 500 photographs that has toured sixteen venues. Crooke also describes the Northern Ireland Community Archive, an online photographic archive linked to Causeway Museums Service, and the Eastside Community Heritage project in London, whose oral histories include a school project on the Troubles shown at the Tower Museum in Derry. Crooke explains what motivates these groups, from recovering from trauma and asserting identity to preserving memories before they are lost, and draws on Halbwachs, Assmann and Kansteiner to distinguish autobiographical, historical and collective memory. The chapter notes that such histories are selective and often driven by one person. Crooke concludes that community biography is an applied process, a social agent that communicates the ideals of those who make it.

Tower Museum, DerryCauseway Museums Service
The Homunculus and the Pantograph, or Narcissus at the MetDonald Preziosip. 321

Preziosi closes the volume with a meditation rather than a summary of its contributions. The pantograph, an instrument that copies and enlarges a drawing and also conveys power to a moving vehicle, serves as an image of the relation between viewer and museum object. Drawing on the Magnificat, Preziosi suggests that the encounter is a mutual magnification, in which the visitor's spirit is enlarged by the artefact and the artefact by the viewer, and tests this with Preziosi's own encounter with Picasso's Guernica. The argument links this to Narcissus, the patron of the museum-goer, who must keep a measured distance from the image, and to the long Western dispute between iconophilia and iconoclasm. Preziosi briefly raises Sir John Soane's house, read as an early autobiographical fiction, and concludes that museums allow visitors to see fiction as fiction, and so to see the contingency of our world. The piece is dense and allusive, working as a provocation about the uncanny relation between person and object that runs through the volume.

Sir John Soane's Museum

Hill, Kate (ed.) (2021). Museums, Modernity and Conflict: Museums and Collections in and of War since the Nineteenth Century. London: Routledge.Asia: slight12 chapter overviews

Overview

An edited volume (2021) by Kate Hill on how war and museums shaped each other from the 1870s to the 1940s, closing with a chapter on Canada. Hill's introduction argues that modern museums took their form during modern warfare: imperial conquest and total war drove their development as much as secularisation did, and museums served the state, the war effort and personal memory. The eleven chapters fall into four parts: collecting and conflict (the London art market after 1870, Priam's Treasure, the Louvre's wartime evacuation); protection, propaganda and resistance in Spain, Britain, Germany and the occupied Netherlands; memorial and camp displays; and war museums, including the Imperial War Museum, the RAF Museum and the Canadian War Museum. The focus is Europe, and imperial collecting is largely set aside.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia hardly figure. The introduction says the volume focuses primarily on Europe and that its chapters do not generally engage with the history of imperial collecting, although the objects involved were often colonial loot. The one substantial passage is in chapter 1 (Stammers, on the London art market after 1870). Théodore Duret and Henri Cernuschi travelled to Japan in 1871, a visit that shaped the Asian collections of the Musée Cernuschi in Paris, and a Chinese enamel vase from the burnt Pompeian House was among the lots sold in London. The Prince's 1872 sale also included fashionable 'Oriental' and ethnographic items.

Elsewhere the references are incidental. Chapter 7 (Scheltinga) notes that the Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam housed a Museum of Asian Art in 1940; its curator H. F. E. Visser, the museum's only Jewish employee, was dismissed in November 1940 and fled to Switzerland. Chapter 6 (Müller-Kelwing) mentions the Japanese Palace in Dresden as the home of the Saxon state library from 1935, a building name only. Chapter 3 (Vannier) concerns the Louvre's Near Eastern and 'Oriental' antiquities, such as the Hammurabi code, which lie outside this question. Chapters 10 and 11 mention the Korean War only as a date: the IWM's collecting remit was extended to all wars after 1945, and Canada sent no war artists to Korea.

Not covered: Asian objects in Western wartime collections beyond these lines; museums in Asia; the Asian theatres of the Second World War; the heritage policy of Asian states; and Asian visitors, curators or scholars.

Introduction: museums and warKate Hillp. 1

Hill's introduction to this edited volume argues that war and museums have shaped each other since the Napoleonic era, and that the relationship is productive as well as destructive. Hill outlines four themes: how conflict moved collections, as with Napoleon's confiscations and the flow of French art to Britain after 1870; how bombardment and occupation threatened museums, with the Louvre's evacuation plans as an example; how museums were drawn into the war effort, through wartime exhibitions and propaganda under Nazi occupation; and how war museums, notably the Imperial War Museum, have struggled to narrate war, especially atrocity. Hill argues that 'total war' and nation-building made museums part of modernity itself. The volume covers Europe from the 1870s to the 1940s and largely sets aside imperial collecting, though the objects involved were often colonial loot. The introduction ends by noting that modern museums, which present themselves as promoting peace, were shaped by conflict.

LouvreImperial War Museum
PART I: Collecting and conflictp. 13
11. Salvage and speculation: collecting on the London art market after the Franco-Prussian War (1870–1871)Tom Stammersp. 15

Stammers traces how the Franco-Prussian War and the Paris Commune of 1870-71 moved art onto the London market. Drawing on Guerzoni's statistics, he shows that London's share of European sales rose to 41 per cent in 1871 as Paris auctions collapsed. He follows the consignment books at Christie's and the stock books at Agnew's, reconstructing the sales of the Marquis du Lau, the Louvre antiquities curator Héron de Villefosse, and Empress Eugénie's jewels, which raised £45,000 in 1872. He also covers Prince Napoléon's 1872 sale, where lots from the Palais-Royal and the Pompeian House were marketed with their fire damage as evidence of survival. Stammers argues that the war made collecting a political and patriotic act, as in Richard Wallace's purchases and Hamerton's attack on Communard vandalism. Stammers concludes that market movements, not the state, moved much of this art, and that conventional institutional histories have overlooked how war shaped museum collections.

East and Southeast Asia Stammers notes that Théodore Duret and Henri Cernuschi travelled to Japan in 1871, a visit that shaped the Asian collections of the Musée Cernuschi in Paris. A Chinese enamel vase from the Pompeian House, fused in the 1871 fire, was among the lots sold in London.

Wallace CollectionMetropolitan Museum of ArtNational Portrait Gallery
22. Treasure, triumph and trespass: the place of conflict in the collecting and display of 'Priam's Treasure'Zoe Mercer-Goldenp. 39

Mercer-Golden examines how four museums present 'Priam's Treasure', the Trojan gold that Schliemann dug at Hissarlik and that is now held in Istanbul, Berlin, Athens and Moscow. Mercer-Golden traces Schliemann's digging without a firman, his smuggling of finds to Athens, his gift of most of the Trojan finds to Berlin, and their removal by the Soviet army in 1945 and hidden Moscow holdings until 1996. Mercer-Golden’s method is forensic: close reading of each museum's plan, room arrangement, wall panels, object labels, handouts and audio guides. Mercer-Golden shows that each display builds its claim through a national narrative: Istanbul through a loss to a wily foreign archaeologist, Berlin through a generous gift and replicas, Athens through a patriotic Schliemann, and Moscow through war reparations. Mercer-Golden finds the displays defensive, often out of date, and centred on Homer and gold more than on the objects. Mercer-Golden’s conclusion urges the museums to tell the complicated, honest story that the Iliad itself tells about conflict and theft.

Istanbul Archaeological MuseumsNeues MuseumNational Archaeological Museum AthensPushkin State Museum of Fine Arts
PART II: Keeping going?p. 59
33. The evacuation and management of the Louvre Museum's Near Eastern Antiquities Department during the Second World WarZoé Vannierp. 61

Vannier asks how the Louvre kept its collections safe during the Second World War, taking the Near Eastern Antiquities Department as a case study and reconstructing events from its inventories, correspondence and committee minutes. Vannier traces the emergency plan drawn up in 1932 and revised until 1939, which relied on moving objects to the Chambord and Cheverny castles and the Valençay depot, and shows how the department's 359 boxes left Paris between August and October 1939. Under Vichy, the chapter examines the tacit alliance between Louvre director Jacques Jaujard and Franz Wolff-Metternich of the Kunstschutz, which blocked Otto Abetz's attempt to bring works back to Paris for possible shipment to Germany, and the 1940-41 exchange with Spain that included the Lady of Elche. It ends by arguing that protection depended less on the plan than on officials who shared the same heritage values, and it links this lesson to later civil conflicts.

Louvre MuseumCheverny castleChambord castleValençay depot
44. Implementing preventive strategies between World War I and II: the Catalan art museums and the Spanish Civil WarEva Marchp. 79

March examines how the Catalan government protected art museum collections in the first months of the Spanish Civil War, when churches and private collections were burned or confiscated. March describes the Generalitat's decrees that seized works, the Museu d'Art de Catalunya's role as a storehouse for requisitioned objects, and its director Joaquim Folch i Torres's decision in autumn 1936 to move the main works to Olot, a town near the Pyrenees, following the International Museums Office's 1936 guidelines on shelters and remote depots. The chapter then follows the works to Paris for the 'L'Art Catalan' exhibition of 1937 at the Jeu de Paume, which March reads as an assertion of national identity that made the rescue of heritage urgent. She sets the Catalan case beside the Prado's evacuation and the League of Nations transfer of Spanish works to Switzerland in 1939. The chapter concludes that Spain served as a test bench for wartime heritage protection, and that the IMO's 1939 advice to evacuate works from museums drew on that experience.

Museu d'Art de CatalunyaMusée du Jeu de PaumePrado MuseumMaisons-Laffitte château
PART III: Propaganda, morale and resistancep. 103
55. 'The present is pretty terrible, the future is unknown, the past is the only stable thing to which we can turn': Philip Ashcroft, Rufford Village Museum and the preservation of rural life and tradition during the Second World WarBridget Yatesp. 105

Yates traces the Rufford Village Museum, a small collection that the young produce merchant Philip Ashcroft began in July 1939 in a room of Rufford Old Hall, which the National Trust had acquired in 1936. Yates places it within the interwar movement for local rural museums, which tied collecting to ideas of English identity, and builds the chapter from Ashcroft's letters to Ernest Jarratt, the sub-committee chairman. The scheme began as a store, but it grew through wartime salvage drives, newspaper publicity, school visits and Ashcroft's own collecting, guided by H. J. Massingham's Country Relics and Jekyll and Jones's Old English Household Life. Yates argues that the war gave the museum its purpose, presenting rural objects as what Britain was fighting for, and that Ashcroft's personal control ended when the collection passed to the National Trust in 1946. Set beside wartime folk museums at Gloucester and Mary Arden's House, the case shows how wartime conditions shaped small museums, and the chapter closes by noting how post-war local history museums took a more shared and democratic form.

Rufford Village MuseumRufford Old HallGloucester Folk MuseumMary Arden's House
66. Museums without objects? The Staatliche Sammlungen für Kunst und Wissenschaft in Dresden during the Second World WarKarin Müller-Kelwingp. 129

Müller-Kelwing asks how Dresden's Staatliche Sammlungen kept functioning under the Nazis once most objects were packed away. Müller-Kelwing first looks at staffing, showing how political reliability replaced specialist knowledge after 1933, with about 45% of scholarly employees joining the NSDAP. Three careers are profiled: Hermann Voss, appointed to the Gemäldegalerie in 1943; Hans Kummerlöwe, a party member with no museum experience; and Fritz Fichtner, whose party and probable security-service ties advanced him. The chapter then traces the wartime closures, from the crating of the most valuable objects in 1939 to the relocation of holdings to more than 40 sites in Saxony in 1942 and the final closure after October 1944. Its core is three exhibitions staged without their objects: Edmund Kesting's photographs of the Grünes Gewölbe in 1943, a touring Veit Stoss show in 1944 that Müller-Kelwing reads as propaganda celebrating the removal of the Kraków altar, and a serial porcelain display. She concludes that wartime museum work served a 'home front' mission under ideological direction.

Staatliche Sammlungen für Kunst und Wissenschaft, DresdenGemäldegalerieGrünes GewölbePorzellansammlungHistorisches Museum
77. Exhibiting in wartime Nazification and resistance in Dutch art exhibitionsEvelien Scheltingap. 149

Scheltinga reconstructs the exhibition histories of two Dutch art museums under German occupation, 1940 to 1945: the Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam and the Van Abbemuseum in Eindhoven. With collections hidden in bunkers, galleries stood empty and were filled by artist societies and by bodies such as the Kultuurkamer and the Department of Propaganda and Arts. At the Stedelijk, she argues that the literature has centred on curator Willem Sandberg's resistance and overlooked the programme itself, which included the Jan Sluijters solo show, the fashion exhibition '150 jaar mode' and 'Stad en land', whose advisory board included NSB members. The Germans also forced the 'Kunstenaars zien den Arbeidsdienst' show on the museum. At the Van Abbemuseum, the installation of an NSB mayor and a new director, Louis Vrijdag, brought craft exhibitions and the kitsch show 'Wansmaak en gezonde kunst'. Scheltinga concludes that national socialist influence grew slowly, from small adjustments to open propaganda, and that postwar accounts of resistance and collaboration have drawn an overly black and white picture.

Stedelijk MuseumVan AbbemuseumKunsthuis Amsterdam
PART IV: Museums of war and conflictp. 169
88. Displaying Ravensbrück concentration camp memorial: from the 'antifascist fight' to 'history and memory of the women's concentration camp'Doreen Pastorp. 171

Pastor traces how the Ravensbrück concentration camp memorial, north of Berlin, was displayed under the GDR and after reunification, arguing that each exhibition reflected the state's account of the Nazi past. Pastor sketches the camp's history from 1938, including its female prisoners, the Sulfanomid experiments and the Uckermark youth section, then follows the GDR memorial from the 1948 wooden pillar through Will Lammert's statue The Burdened to the 1959 museum, whose displays cast the women as communist antifascist fighters. The 1980s redesign, the post-1990 clearance of Soviet army buildings to the 1945 landscape and the exhibitions opened from 1993 to 2013 come next, with the 2013 main exhibition presented as the first full treatment of female victims, asocial prisoners and sex slave labour. Pastor concludes that visitors must now navigate two memorial landscapes at once, the GDR's path from dark to light and the present focus on responsibility, while the Soviet base and the local community's experience have largely been erased.

Ravensbrück concentration camp memorialRavensbrück Lagermuseum (1959)
99. 'Flight without feathers is not easy': John Tanner and the development of the Royal Air Force MuseumPeter Elliottp. 191

Elliott traces the long, funding-bound birth of the Royal Air Force Museum, which opened at Hendon in 1972, and centres the story on its founding director John Tanner, previously librarian and museum organiser at RAF Cranwell. The chapter first asks what a military museum is for, arguing that a service museum fosters esprit de corps, commemorates the dead and helps recruitment, and compares the RAF's case with the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum and the National Maritime Museum. It then follows the RAF's repeated campaigns for its own museum, from a 1931 Air Council memorandum to the 1950s National Aeronautical Collection, and shows that Treasury and departmental reluctance to fund a new museum, rather than lack of public interest, blocked each attempt. The evidence comes largely from Treasury, Air Ministry and trustee files. The chapter ends by arguing that Tanner's hope of a national aviation museum failed on funding, scope and administration, though the aircraft collection he built became the museum's greatest attraction.

1010. 'We are a social history, not a military history museum': large objects and the 'peopling' of galleries in the Imperial War Museum, LondonKasia Tomasiewiczp. 213

Tomasiewicz examines two components of the Imperial War Museum in London, its large objects and its 'peopling' of galleries, and asks why staff describe the museum as 'a social history, not a military history museum'. The chapter first historicises the IWM, tracing its move to the former Bethlem asylum in 1936, and reads its development through Kjeldbaek's three generations of purpose: ethos, logos and pathos. It then examines the two 15-inch naval guns installed in the forecourt in 1968, using Scott's celebratory, sanitised and realistic modes of display, and the protests they provoked, including an arson attack on the dome. The second half turns to peopling, from silhouettes and wax figures in early displays to the Blitz Experience (1989) and the Holocaust Galleries (2000), which relied on invented narratives and edited oral testimony. Tomasiewicz concludes that the two approaches should be brought together, citing the D-Day Museum's projection of actors' scripts onto a landing craft as a model.

1111. War stories: the art and memorials collection at the Canadian War MuseumSarafina Pagnottap. 235

Pagnotta examines the Art and Memorials Collection at the Canadian War Museum, the official war art commissioned through the Canadian War Memorials Fund from 1916, and sets it beside a small group of soldier-made trench art in the museum's vault. The first part explains how Max Aitken, Lord Beaverbrook, turned to commissioned painting and sculpture after official photographs proved blurred and uninformative, and how the collection passed to the National Gallery and grew through Second World War and post-1945 programmes. The second part turns to trench art, defining it, describing the practice of souveniring and showing how shell cases and bullets became objects of private memory. Pagnotta's central case is Private Arthur Frederick Lee, whose matchbox, identity bracelet and watch fob came to the museum with postcards recording where and when each was made, details the chapter checks against his service file. The conclusion argues that official and private war art should be shown together.

Hill, Kate (2005). Culture and Class in English Public Museums, 1850–1914. Aldershot: Ashgate.Asia: occasional8 chapter overviews

Overview

Kate Hill's study of English municipal museums, the rate-supported institutions that councils founded and ran between 1850 and 1914, mainly in the north and midlands. It asks who created these museums, what objects and displays they used and how visitors responded. Against accounts that read museums as instruments of discipline and reform, Hill argues that their power was negotiated, inconsistent and often unplanned, and that they served local elites and middle-class identity more than any single programme of working-class improvement. The book is organised in eight chapters: an introduction on theory and method, the urban context, the history of public museums, the social makeup of museum governance, the objects collected, the layout and displays, the visitors, and a conclusion. Its main cases are Liverpool, Preston, Birmingham, Sheffield, Leicester and Hull.

East and Southeast Asia in this work occasional

East Asia appears only in chapters 4 and 5, and then as a source of objects and gifts, not as a subject in its own right. Hill names no museum, collection or collector in China or Japan and does not discuss the museum-building or heritage policy of any Asian state. The fullest discussion is in chapter 5, "Reading the Objects": the Jacson and Foster collections given to Preston's Harris Museum in 1894 include Chinese, Japanese and Algerian curiosities, Japanese swords, and needlework and pottery from China, Japan and India. Hill reads these as objects that placed their donors in "a relationship of power and exploitation" over the people of the countries of origin, and he reads the Foster gift as moving from souvenir to fetish to systematic group.

Other gifts recur. Liverpool received a systematic collection of Chinese industrial manufactures in 1892, and a Chinese army uniform was among the textiles in Professor Newberry's gift of 1914. Preston received antique Japanese jewellery in 1911 and oriental coins in 1896. Sheffield's curator solicited cutlery and tools from consuls in China, Japan and Turkey through the Foreign Secretary. In chapter 4 Hill estimates that Europe, Asia and the Americas each supplied about 15 per cent of Preston's accessions, and he notes that Liverpool's acquisitions from Asia became much less important in the 1890s and early 1900s. Hull's curator Tom Sheppard acquired much of the Anglo-Japanese Exhibition of 1910.

Chapter 6 has no Asian material. Liverpool's classification of man-made objects as Melanian, Mongolian or Caucasian includes a Mongolian category, but Hill names no peoples or countries for it. Southeast Asia is absent: there is no reference to Siam, the Philippines, Indonesia, Vietnam, Malaya or Borneo. Central Asian hunting trophies, given to Liverpool in 1902 and to Preston in 1909, are mentioned only as trophies of big game. Not covered: Asian visitors, curators or scholars, restitution claims, and any museum in Asia.

11 Introduction: Interpreting Museumsp. 1

Hill introduces his study of English municipal museums between 1850 and 1914, asking why so much hope and fear was pinned on these rate-supported institutions and how they acted on the towns that built them. Hill surveys recent work that treats museums as sites of power, as texts to be decoded, and as instruments of class formation and cultural distinction, drawing on Foucault, Bennett, Hooper-Greenhill, Pearce and Bourdieu. Hill finds two unresolved tensions, between theoretical and empirical approaches and between materialist and discursive readings, and argues that museum power was negotiated and inconsistent rather than imposed. The chapter then sketches the book's plan, covering urban context, funding, the social makeup of museum governance, objects, display and visitors. It also justifies the focus on England, especially the north and midlands, and on 1850 to 1914, the period of the municipal museum's greatest success. Hill concludes that these museums were a public story that towns, mainly their middle classes, told about themselves, and that not all of them told the same story.

Warrington MuseumMuseum of Fine Arts, Boston
22 Negotiating the New Urban Environmentp. 20

Hill's second chapter argues that municipal museums cannot be understood apart from the towns that created them. Hill sorts English towns into industrial, cotton, large commercial, port, resort and county types, showing how each had different sizes of middle class, different wealth and different patterns of segregation. Drawing on Blackburn, Oldham, Liverpool, Birmingham and Lincoln, he argues that middle-class fear of a working class seen as immoral and in need of improvement shaped urban policy. Voluntary societies, residential segregation and expanding local government were all ways of managing class tension and of negotiating authority. Councils took on powers over public health, utilities and civic ceremony, and town halls, processions and new public buildings presented them as legitimate, though these symbols could also be contested by working-class groups. Hill concludes that civic rituals and public institutions were shaped by conflict and negotiation rather than simple class control, and that municipal museums should be seen as part of the machinery through which that conflict was channelled.

33 The Public Museum in the Nineteenth Centuryp. 36

Hill traces the making of public museums in Britain, from exclusive eighteenth-century collections such as the Ashmolean and British Museum to the rate-supported municipal museums founded after the 1845 Act. Hill shows that the National Gallery, bought and housed in the 1820s and 1830s, was justified as a means of cementing social bonds, while parliamentary committees and Rational Recreation campaigners of the 1830s and 1840s saw culture as a tool for improving workers and design. The 1845 Act allowed towns to levy a small rate for museums, but in practice local councils were cautious, and many museums were built with the collections and money of learned societies and wealthy donors. Hill argues that middle-class elites used these museums to display their own authority and values, and that working-class visitors, though nominally welcome, were discouraged by limited opening hours, dress rules and a ban on children at some museums. The public museum, he concludes, helped the middle class reconcile the transcendent value of art and science with their own commercial wealth.

Ashmolean MuseumBritish MuseumNational GallerySouth Kensington MuseumLiverpool Royal InstitutionLiverpool MuseumHarris Museum, PrestonBirmingham Museum and Art Gallery
44 The Social Characteristics of Municipal Museumsp. 53

Hill asks who actually produced municipal museums, meaning council committee members, donors and staff, and argues that their composition shaped what each museum became. Hill compares Liverpool, where merchant families and later professionals ran the museum committee, with Preston, where cotton manufacturers and professionals sat on the Free Public Library Committee, and with Birmingham, where a group of Nonconformist councillors and editors pursued a civic gospel. In Leicester and Sheffield, learned societies such as the Literary and Philosophical Society handed over their collections and kept close ties with the council. Hill examines major donations, including Lord Derby's natural history collection and William Brown's money in Liverpool, the Tangye brothers' gift in Birmingham and the Mappin bequest in Sheffield, and shows how donors gave for prestige and to keep collections together. Hill also traces the shift of curators, from amateurs such as Howarth and Sheppard to more professional staff with university links by 1914, a shift that was patchy. Hill concludes that councillors, amateurs, donors and curators each sought status or authority through the museum, and that curators' conflicts with councils were the sharpest.

Liverpool MuseumHarris Museum, PrestonBirmingham Museum and Art GallerySheffield Museum (Mappin Art Gallery)Leicester MuseumHull Municipal Museum
55 Reading the Objectsp. 69Asia: in part

Hill asks what objects municipal museums held and why donors and curators chose them, using Susan Pearce's categories of souvenir, fetishistic, systematic and trophy collecting. Hill argues that the older collecting habits of the Renaissance and early Royal Society survived in municipal museums long after the systematic ideal was proclaimed. Natural history dominated until about 1890, and Liverpool stood out for building its collection around the other: ethnography from West Africa, often gathered through the engineer Arnold Ridyard, and trophy-like gifts from hunters and colonial officials. Preston's Harris Museum, by contrast, received donations that mainly expressed the prestige of local elites through souvenirs, casts and curiosities, with the Jacson and Foster collections of 1894 as the clearest case. Hill shows curators gradually tightening their criteria and rejecting curiosities, while women donors, more visible after 1900, gave fans, lace and embroidery that entered the museum on public terms. Hill concludes that municipal collections kept much of the character of the older cabinet, so the systematic model was never fully achieved at local level.

East and Southeast Asia The Jacson and Foster collections given to the Harris Museum in 1894 include Chinese, Japanese and Algerian curiosities, Japanese swords, and needlework and pottery from India, China and Japan, which Hill reads as objects that placed their donors in a relation of power over those peoples. Other Preston gifts include Japanese jewellery given in 1911, and Liverpool received a systematic collection of Chinese industrial manufactures in 1892.

Liverpool MuseumHarris Museum, PrestonBirmingham Museum and Art GallerySheffield MuseumLeicester MuseumHull Municipal Museum
66 Decoding the Displays and Layoutp. 90

Hill asks whether the physical layout and displays of nineteenth-century municipal museums worked as the disciplinary machines that Tony Bennett and others have described after Foucault. The chapter takes the building and its room plans first, analysing them with the room-and-route diagrams of Markus and Hillier and Hanson, and then the individual displays. Its evidence is a set of case studies: Liverpool, whose 1860 building and 1906 extension are compared through ground plans; Preston's Harris Museum, with its ring of rooms and monumental statues; Birmingham's art gallery, fitted into a Gas Committee building; Sheffield's Mappin Art Gallery and municipal museum; and Leicester. Hill finds that most plans were shaped by existing buildings, scarce budgets and donors' prestige, so that only Liverpool approached a coherent one-way route with an evolutionary narrative. Display techniques varied as widely, from the evolutionary invertebrate cases arranged by Higgins at Liverpool to Preston's decontextualised sculpture, which invited aesthetic awe. Hill concludes that municipal museums were unplanned spaces responding to local conditions rather than uniform disciplinary machines.

Liverpool MuseumHarris Museum and Art Gallery, PrestonBirmingham Museum and Art GalleryMappin Art Gallery, SheffieldSheffield MuseumLeicester MuseumMuseum of Practical Geology
77 Consuming the Museum: Museum Visitorsp. 125

Hill turns from the museum's intended uses to the visitors who actually used it, arguing that middle-class identity was made and defended inside the museum while working-class visitors refused the roles planned for them. Visitor numbers, Sunday opening disputes and letters to the Sheffield papers after the Mappin Art Gallery opened in 1887 form the main evidence, with material from Liverpool, Birmingham, Preston and Leicester. Students, scientific societies and the conversazione show privileged access and an elite social culture. The rough-versus-respectable division in commentators' descriptions is set against Thomas Wright and Peter Bailey on St Monday, which suggests that working-class visitors promenaded, ate and ignored pictures as they did at music halls and parks. Attendance fell after the 1880s and 1890s, and the chapter ends with Annie Coombes's account of the Horniman Museum, whose spectacle drew working-class visitors. Hill concludes that the museum's project of defining middle-class status largely succeeded, while its attempt to reform working-class behaviour largely failed.

Mappin Art Gallery, SheffieldSheffield Public MuseumHarris Museum and Art Gallery, PrestonLiverpool MuseumBirmingham Museum and Art GalleryLeicester MuseumHorniman Museum
88 Conclusionp. 143

The conclusion argues that municipal museums were significant arenas for forming social identities and hierarchies, but were never a single project of discipline, modernity or working-class reform. Hill shows how councillors, staff and donors claimed ownership of the buildings through busts, portraits and memorial plaques, and how they used space, attendants and policing to shape behaviour. Drawing on Bourdieu and DiMaggio, the chapter explains how objects and displays conferred cultural capital and naturalised hierarchies, with Liverpool's evolutionary and racial classifications as the clearest case and Preston's statues as an example of elite distinction. Liverpool, large and well resourced, is set against Hull, Leicester, Preston and the one-room Scunthorpe museum. Hill concludes that the museums were local, varied and not simply modern, and that by 1914 they had become safer and more exclusive places for the middle classes, which is why the nineteenth century was their heyday.

Hill, Kate (2016). Women and Museums, 1850–1914: Modernity and the Gendering of Knowledge. Manchester: Manchester University Press.Asia: occasional9 chapter overviews

Overview

Kate Hill's Women and Museums, 1850-1914 (2016) argues that women and English museums remade each other in these decades. Women worked inside museums as paid staff and volunteers, and also as donors, sellers, visitors, patrons, founders and fieldworkers' wives or missionaries. Their influence was cumulative and marginal, and it worked through networks rather than through leadership of national institutions. Hill treats the museum as a distributed institution shaped by dealers, donors, fieldworkers and visitors as well as curators. Seven chapters cover women inside museums, donations and the meaning of donated objects, visiting, patronage, archaeology and anthropology, and Ruskinian community museums. An introduction and a conclusion, which looks at the First World War and the interwar years, frame them. The evidence is mainly English, from accession registers, annual reports and personal papers.

East and Southeast Asia in this work occasional

East and Southeast Asia figure occasionally and only in passing. The attention is concentrated in two chapters, each with a short passage. In Chapter 2 (women as donors and vendors), Mr Vieweg's 1898 donation to the Horniman Museum of objects from China, India and Burma is read as perhaps suggesting a career in Asia, though his wife gave only a pipe. In Chapter 3 (donations, materiality and the museum object), Hill draws on Shaun Garner's account of Merton and Annie Russell-Cotes in Japan in the late nineteenth century. Annie's collecting was partly botanical and partly touristic, and a bank manager in Japan advanced them cash for curios. Merton later used his Japanese collection to claim expertise, became a founding member of the Japan Society, and presented himself as an explorer. Hill cites this as evidence of a gendered split between female souvenir collectors and male 'scientific' collectors.

Chapter 6 (archaeology, anthropology and women in museums) has the fullest Asian material, all about missionaries. Annie Royle Taylor, working in and around China and Tibet, sold objects to museums in Edinburgh and Glasgow to fund her mission, and Livne argues that her servant Pontso assembled some of them. Mr and Mrs Davidson, missionaries in China, sold a large ethnographic collection to the Horniman Museum in 1895, and Levell argues that Mary Davidson shaped it, a contribution recorded only under her husband's name. Charlotte Wheeler Cuffe sent Ridgeway photographs of ethnographic types in Burma for the Cambridge museum, gathered through missionary and colonial networks.

Not covered: Asian museums, Asian states' heritage policy, Asian visitors or curators, restitution, and Asian objects as a subject of display or colonial collecting in their own right. Asia appears only as a source of gifts, as a site of travel and mission work, and as a setting for collectors' biographies. India, which recurs in the General and Mrs MacNair donations, lies outside this question.

IntroductionPDF p. 15

Hill's introduction states the book's central claim: between 1850 and 1914, women and museums remade each other. Opening with Beatrix Potter's 1896 complaint about the British Museum, Hill argues that women both reoriented museums towards feminine concerns and sought entry to the male world of scholarship. She proposes the 'distributed museum', a network shaped by donors, dealers and visitors rather than by single curators, and previews the book's seven chapters, from women's work and donations to Ruskinian museology.

British MuseumNational Gallery
11. Inside the museum: including or excluding women?PDF p. 31

Hill asks how women worked inside English museums between about 1850 and 1914, and why so few became curators. Hill argues that museums were neither simply open nor closed to women: the professionalising Museums Association wanted to raise curators' status and feared that cheap, under-qualified women would undercut it, while women were welcomed for cleaning, cataloguing and popular education. The chapter's central case is Kate Hall, who ran the Whitechapel Museum from 1894 to 1909 and was probably the first paid woman curator in the country. Further evidence comes from Manchester Museum, which employed the most women, including Grace Wigglesworth, who moved from volunteer to paid keeper; from Kathleen Dearden, dismissed at Sheffield for not qualifying herself for scientific work; and from Nina Layard, who controlled her own donated collection at Ipswich. Hill concludes that women's roles were fluid, and that museums both excluded them and offered a niche in education and service.

Whitechapel MuseumManchester MuseumIpswich MuseumSheffield MuseumBritish Museum (Natural History)Bristol MuseumHorniman Museum
22. Outside the museum: women as donors and vendorsPDF p. 61

Hill turns to women who gave or sold objects to museums without working inside them, drawing on accession registers from a dozen museums between 1880 and 1914. Hill argues that donation carried family and domestic networks into the public museum: women gave with their husbands, passed on the collections of dead fathers, husbands and brothers, and often memorialised relatives through their gifts. Examples include Mrs Smith's fossils at the British Museum (Natural History), Anna Tylor's donations to the Pitt Rivers Museum, and widows such as Eliza Cruikshank and Elizabeth Edwards, who shaped their late husbands' reputations by placing work in several museums. Most women gave only once, and their sales were small, but a few, such as the dealers Eva Cutter and Mrs Brazenor, took over family businesses. Hill concludes that these donors and sellers claimed public value for the domestic without copying male professional routes.

East and Southeast Asia Mr Vieweg's 1898 donation to the Horniman Museum, objects from China, India and Burma, is read as suggesting a career spent in Asia, though his wife gave only a German pipe. Hill does not develop the point.

British MuseumPitt Rivers MuseumHorniman MuseumManchester MuseumBrighton Museum and Art GalleryLeicester MuseumBristol MuseumNorwich Castle Museum
33. Outside the museum: women’s donations, materiality and the museum objectPDF p. 90

Hill asks what objects women gave and sold to museums, and what meanings those objects carried into the museum. Working from accession registers and annual reports of nine museums (Ipswich, Whitby, Brighton, Bristol, Cheltenham, Warrington, Manchester, Birmingham and Sunderland), she first counts donation events by discipline. Natural history dominates, but manufactured objects make up about a third of women's gifts, more than the museums' priorities would predict. Because most donations have only a sentence or two of documentation, the chapter uses a collective object biography rather than the life story of single famous objects. It examines textiles and clothing, relics and souvenirs, and 'old things' such as bygones, with cases from Leicester, Norwich, Warrington and Bristol. Hill argues that objects kept in the home for about thirty years carried family memory and an aura of authenticity into the museum, which unsettled its classifications. The chapter concludes that women's donations helped move museums towards social history, memory and affect in the twentieth century.

East and Southeast Asia Hill notes Garner's account of Merton Russell-Cotes and his wife Annie, who collected in Asia and Australasia, especially Japan, in the late nineteenth century. Annie's collecting there was partly botanical and partly touristic, and a bank manager in Japan advanced them cash to buy curios. On returning to Britain, Merton used his Japanese collection to claim expertise in Japanese culture, helped found the Japan Society, and presented himself as an explorer. The chapter cites this as evidence of a gendered split between female souvenir collectors and male 'scientific' collectors.

Leicester MuseumNorwich MuseumWarrington MuseumBristol MuseumHorniman MuseumBirmingham Museum and Art GalleryManchester Art Gallery
44. Women visiting museumsPDF p. 117

Hill argues that visitors, and women visitors in particular, have been largely absent from museum histories, though they shaped what museums became. Hill starts from Duncan and Wallach's account of the museum visit as a scripted ritual and from Rees Leahy's study of museum bodies, which notes that women's bodies were remarked on far more than men's. The chapter then traces how women visitors were perceived after 1850: working-class women and nursing mothers were seen as a source of pollution, while middle-class women were later praised for their refining sensibility. Evidence of use includes conversazioni, student tickets and the lady copyists at the National Gallery. Through the diaries and letters of Susan Burney, Beatrix Potter, Matilda Betham-Edwards and others, Hill shows the pleasures women took in imaginative and self-educating visits. The chapter ends with the suffragette attacks of 1913-14 on paintings at the National Gallery and the National Portrait Gallery, arguing that women visitors were both disciplined and disruptive.

National GalleryNational Portrait GalleryBritish MuseumBritish Museum (Natural History)Horniman MuseumHarris Museum, PrestonBirmingham Museum and Art Gallery
55. Women as patrons: the limits of agency?PDF p. 141

Hill asks how far women could consciously shape museums as patrons, donors and founders, and finds that their power was tightly limited. Hill distinguishes three positions among major women patrons: a masculinised professional stance, a feminine domestic and relational approach, and an overtly feminist one, which most women mixed. Women critics such as Lady Eastlake, Harriet Grote and Anna Jameson wrote on the British Museum and the National Gallery, mostly blaming Parliament rather than curators. Lady Charlotte Schreiber's ceramics and fan and playing-card gifts to the South Kensington Museum and the British Museum are examined in detail, including the catalogues she produced with help from male experts. The Davies sisters' modern French paintings, which the Tate initially refused, went to Wales instead. Founders such as Josephine Bowes, Lady Wallace, Caroline Birley and Marianne North built museums in which domestic settings and women's taste were prominent. Hill concludes that women's influence was cumulative and marginal, and that all-male trustee boards kept them from the centre of national museums.

British MuseumSouth Kensington MuseumWallace CollectionBowes MuseumMarianne North Gallery, KewNational Museum of WalesNational GalleryTate Gallery
66. New disciplines: archaeology, anthropology and women in museumsPDF p. 170Asia: in part

Hill examines how women took part in the new disciplines of archaeology and anthropology in museums up to 1914, and argues that they mainly mediated between field and museum. Women gave and collected objects through family, amateur and missionary networks, and Hill treats several as 'accidental' anthropologists, such as Mary Edith Durham, who valued the freedom of fieldwork. In archaeology, Nina Layard excavated and gained control of a room at Ipswich Museum, while wives such as Hilda Petrie drew, catalogued and arranged finds in Egypt and Britain. The Egypt Exploration Fund, with its many women secretaries and fundraisers, sent Egyptian finds to provincial museums, most notably Bolton. Women reached the subject through London colleges and the women's colleges of Oxford and Cambridge, but found that fieldwork was valued above cataloguing, which was badly paid. Hill concludes that the division between fieldwork and museum work persisted and hardened after the First World War, and that women's contribution was largely hidden.

East and Southeast Asia Missionary collectors from China and Burma recur. Annie Royle Taylor, working in and around China and Tibet, sold objects to museums in Edinburgh and Glasgow to fund her mission, and Livne argues that her servant Pontso assembled some of them. Mr and Mrs Davidson, missionaries in China, sold a large ethnographic collection to the Horniman Museum in 1895, though Levell argues that Mary Davidson shaped it, a contribution recorded only under her husband's name. Charlotte Wheeler Cuffe sent Ridgeway photographs of ethnographic types in Burma for the Cambridge museum.

Pitt Rivers MuseumIpswich MuseumHorniman MuseumMuseum of Archaeology and Anthropology, CambridgeManchester MuseumBolton MuseumLiverpool MuseumEdinburgh Museum of Science and Art
77. Ruskin, women and museums: service and salvagePDF p. 197

Hill asks why women were so prominent in museums shaped by John Ruskin's ideas, which prized authentic craft, the domestic past and the moral education of working-class audiences. Hill argues that women, often outsiders to the professional museum world, used these ideas to reshape museums in feminine ways, making domestic craft and tradition a route to influence. The chapter traces Ruskin's own ambivalence about museums, from the Oxford University Museum to his St George's Museum at Walkley, Sheffield, where Emily Swan did much of the practical work. It then follows women at the Ancoats Museum in Manchester, where they ran classes, clubs and children's events, and at the Whitechapel and South London galleries. Haslemere's Peasant Handicrafts Museum and Gertrude Jekyll's Godalming collection show women trying to save vanishing rural craft. The conclusion argues that Ruskinian community museums kept women's influence alive after 1900, but only in small, marginal institutions.

St George's Museum, WalkleyAncoats Museum (Manchester Art Museum)Whitechapel Art GallerySouth London Art GalleryHaslemere Peasant Handicrafts MuseumWatts GalleryGodalming MuseumManchester Art Gallery
ConclusionPDF p. 231

This concluding chapter draws the book together and asks what the years 1850 to 1914 meant for women and museums. Hill argues that the First World War did not turn women into museum workers, since the men who enlisted were mostly young and junior and women already held assistant posts; the workforce feminised slowly, driven by low salaries. Hill disputes Ruth Hoberman's claim that interwar women sought a segregated feminine space, suggesting instead that acceptable forms of women's involvement became clearer after 1918. Women's amateur and philanthropic expertise, rooted in domestic skills with children, the poor and objects, remained central, while leading curatorial posts stayed male. The evidence includes donations to the Pitt Rivers Museum and the Museum of Childhood in Bethnal Green. The chapter ends by arguing that women's hidden but substantial work in the distributed museum helped rehabilitate the authentic souvenir and make modern identities, within clear limits.
