Ho, Denise Y.; Li, Jie (2016). “From Landlord Manor to Red Memorabilia: Reincarnations of a Chinese Museum Town”. Modern China.Asia: central1 chapter overview

Overview

Ho and Li trace the Landlord Manor Museum in Anren, a town in Sichuan, from its opening in 1959 in the seized home of the landlord Liu Wencai to the private Jianchuan Museum Cluster across the street. Their main argument is that Chinese museums have never been static mausoleums but living public spaces that repeatedly redefine the past. The article is organised as a sequence of roles the museum has played: a collection of spoils, a schoolroom, a temple, a stage, a courtroom and a marketplace. It draws on fieldwork in Anren, interviews, archives and printed sources.

East and Southeast Asia in this work central

Anren, in Sichuan, is the whole subject, so East Asia is central and Southeast Asia does not appear. The article follows the Landlord Manor Museum, opened in 1959 and renamed several times until it became the Liu Family Manor Museum, and the Jianchuan Museum Cluster, opened by the collector Fan Jianchuan across the street in 2005 and described as China's largest private museum complex. The 1965 Rent Collection Courtyard sculptures, the 1966 documentary, the Shanghai and Beijing replicas and Cai Guoqiang's 1999 Venice version are all discussed.

The Asian material is concentrated in 'The Museum as a Collection of Spoils' (lines 217-316), 'The Museum as Schoolroom' (363-534), 'The Museum as Temple' (536-661), 'The Museum as Stage' (663-852), 'The Museum as Courtroom' (855-1030) and 'The Museum as Marketplace' (1037-1303). The people involved are Chinese: the propaganda chief Ma Li, the sculptors, museum directors Wu Hongyuan, the Liu family (Liu Xiaofei, the grandson), the old cadres, the journalist Xiaoshu, and shopkeepers and visitors in Anren. Liu Wenhui, Liu Xiang and Jiang Qing appear in passing.

Colonial collecting, restitution and war memory outside China are not covered. The only other Asian reference is to Japan, through the Yasukuni Shrine Museum, which Fan Jianchuan studied as a model, and through Robson's remark that museums in Asia function in religious ways. The main comparisons are Western: the Louvre, Benjamin, Adorno and Bennett.

China

Contents

Theoretical approach of this work
From Landlord Manor to Red Memorabilia: Reincarnations of a Chinese Museum Townp. 1Asia: chiefly

Ho and Li trace the museum in Anren, a town in Sichuan, from its origin as the Landlord Manor Museum of 1959, which exhibited the seized property of the landlord Liu Wencai, to the present-day Jianchuan Museum Cluster across the street. The article argues that Chinese museums have never been static mausoleums but living spaces that continually redefine the past. The Landlord Manor served as a schoolroom, where objects like the oversized peck were used for class education, and as a temple, modelled on city god temples, with the Rent Collection Courtyard sculptures placed inside. Under the Cultural Revolution it became a stage for model theatre, and afterward a courtroom where Liu Wencai's grandson Liu Xiaofei disputes the museum's account. The final section looks at the market: souvenir card games and the private Jianchuan cluster, whose owner Fan Jianchuan collects Red Age artifacts with curatorial choices that test the limits set by censors. The conclusion holds that Anren has survived through malleability rather than material permanence.

East and Southeast Asia Anren, in Sichuan, is the chief subject. The Landlord Manor Museum, opened in 1959 in Liu Wencai's seized home, taught class hatred through land deeds, shackles, a water dungeon and a dragon bed, and it later housed the Rent Collection Courtyard sculptures made in 1965. The chapter also covers the private Jianchuan Museum Cluster, with millions of Cultural Revolution artifacts, and the disputed history of Liu Wencai.

Hooper-Greenhill, Eilean (1992). Museums and the Shaping of Knowledge. London: Routledge.Asia: slight8 chapter overviews

Overview

Hooper-Greenhill asks what counts as knowledge in museums and what a museum is, arguing that museum studies has projected present-day arrangements back onto the past. Drawing on Foucault’s ‘effective history’ and his Renaissance, classical and modern epistemes, she rereads four episodes: the Medici Palace in Florence as the supposed ‘first museum of Europe’, the cabinet of the world, the Royal Society’s Repository, and the revolutionary Louvre as a ‘disciplinary museum’. The closing chapter argues that museums have no essential identity and assesses the modern shift towards experience, participation and pleasure, which it treats as a new form of control. Scope is European, from fifteenth-century Italy to contemporary Britain and Canada.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia are almost absent. The book concerns Italian, German, French and British collections from the fifteenth century onwards, and no Asian collection, object or collector is discussed. The one substantive reference is in the closing chapter, ‘A useful past for the present’ (chapter 8, lines 8197–9244), where new museums in Japan are said to be built with channels for cables and optical fibres that carry collection, visitor and environmental data, citing Mizushima (1989) on the ‘intelligent’ museum (lines 8707–8718). Japan is mentioned nowhere else.

Asia appears only in passing elsewhere. In the same chapter, the Birmingham Gallery 33 project draws on holdings from ‘the Americas, Africa, Asia, and the Pacific’ (lines 8893–8906), with no Asian object named. In chapter 6, on the Royal Society’s Repository, the search for a universal language is linked to voyages that revealed ‘the languages of the Far East or West’ (line 6432). Foucault’s opening quotation of a ‘certain Chinese encyclopedia’ (line 407), taken from Borges, is an example of classification rather than a museum reference.

Not covered: Asian objects in European collections, colonial collecting or display in Asia, Asian museum-building and heritage policy, war and memory museums, and restitution. Colonial acquisition is treated only through the Caribbean (Sloane’s collecting, chapter 1) and through removals from conquered territories to the Louvre (chapter 7), so the silence on Asia is notable for a book that treats museums in general.

Japan

Theoretical approach of this work
Book CoverPDF p. 2
TitlePDF p. 4

List of platesPDF p. 9
What is a museum?p. 1

Hooper-Greenhill opens by arguing that museums have changed rapidly, and that their justification has shifted to education and knowledge, most visibly in corporate sponsorship of exhibitions. Museum studies has rarely questioned what counts as knowledge in a museum, how objects, visitors and curators are constructed, or what a museum is. Drawing on Foucault, she proposes an effective history that studies discontinuity and error rather than a smooth line from past to present. Her account of the Renaissance, classical and modern epistemes shows how cabinets, classificatory tables and organic classification each set the terms of knowledge. Her examples include Sloane and the British Museum, Tradescant and the Ashmolean, the Dresden Kunstkammer and Joseph Mayer's donation to Liverpool Museum. She argues that existing histories are safe, uncritical accounts that project the present back into the past. The chapter ends by asking how the museum's histories would change if written as effective history.

British MuseumAshmolean MuseumKunstkammer of the Elector Augustus, DresdenLiverpool Museum
The first museum of Europe?p. 23

Hooper-Greenhill tests the claim, made by Taylor and Alsop, that the Medici Palace in fifteenth-century Florence was the first museum of Europe. Hooper-Greenhill first narrates the house: Cosimo de' Medici's plain but richly decorated palace of the 1440s, whose rooms, described in a 1459 letter and a 1492 inventory, held paintings, sculpture, books, gems and a copper clockwork, and whose studiolo was used by Piero. The second part sets out the wider context of mid-fifteenth-century Italy: merchant wealth turned into display, a rediscovery of the classical past through collected antiquities, a moralised and animate universe governed by astrology, correspondences and talismans, and a new calculating gaze that valued paintings by skill and cost. These older forms of knowledge, magic included, were integral rather than superseded, so the palace cannot be read as a proto-modern museum. The collection was a means of making the Medici more powerful and knowledgeable than their fellow citizens, a point the next chapter pursues through the palace's specific elements.

Palazzo Medici (Riccardi), Florence
The palace of the princep. 47

This chapter is the longest case study of the Medici Palace, covering 1450 to 1500. Hooper-Greenhill argues that the palace fused medieval treasure-hoarding, which kept precious metal as bullion, with new classical collecting and a shift from public, religious patronage to private display. Inventories of 1456, 1465 and 1492 show that carved antique gems and coins were valued above the commissioned decoration, and that a unicorn horn, prized for its magic, was one of the most valuable items. The collecting is traced through humanists such as Niccoli and Bracciolini, whose open libraries trained visitors' gaze, and the chapter argues that objects were read through magical and astrological meanings, so Piero's contemplation of his jewels was a form of divination. It closes with the palace's dispersal after 1494 and the golden-age myth Vasari later built around the Medici, concluding that the 'first museum of Europe' served the family alone.

Palazzo Medici (Riccardi), Florence
The irrational cabinetp. 78

Hooper-Greenhill rereads the cabinets of curiosity that earlier histories dismiss as disordered, starting from Francis Bacon's 'universal nature made private'. By the late sixteenth century the cabinet of the world, she argues, was a deliberate attempt to picture all of creation through assembled objects, and its rationality rested on Foucault's Renaissance episteme and on the classical art of memory. The key case is Giulio Camillo's Memory Theatre, built for Francis I, whose seven planetary levels held images and boxes arranged as memory places. She surveys the forms these cabinets took: Italian palace-gardens, princely Kunstkammern in Germany and Austria, and small Kunstschränke made by merchants for princes. The Kunstkammer of Rudolf II in Prague, where Arcimboldo's paintings carried Habsburg emblems, is read as imperial propaganda, and English visitors such as John Evelyn are cast as viewers who had to decipher the prince's messages. The cabinets, she concludes, were rational within their own episteme, and the 'direct ancestors' of modern museums arose within a different frame of reference.

Kunstkammer of Rudolf II, PragueSchloss Ambras KunstkammerAmerbach collection, BaselKunstschrank of Gustavus Adolphus (Hainhofer)
The 'cabinet of the world'p. 105

Hooper-Greenhill's longest chapter follows the cabinet of the world from Florence to Prague, Munich, Ambras, Uppsala and the scholarly collections of Italy. Hooper-Greenhill argues that these cabinets were deliberate attempts to represent the entire world through material things, ordered by Renaissance resemblance and by the art of memory. The studiolo of Francesco I in Florence, a windowless and secret room, is a prototype, and the Kunstkammern of Albrecht V in Munich, Ferdinand II at Ambras and Rudolf II in Prague are examined through their cupboards, paintings and Jamnitzer's fountain, which carried imperial meaning. Small Kunstschränke made by the merchant Hainhofer for princes are read as cabinets of the world in miniature, and physicians' museums in Bologna, Naples and Verona are shown to be arranged by alternation and sympathy rather than by function. The chapter also treats palace-gardens as cabinets of the world. Hooper-Greenhill concludes that the cabinets were rational within their own episteme, and that histories which judge them by the modern category of 'art' misread them.

Studiolo of Francesco I, FlorenceKunstkammer of Rudolf II, PragueKunstkammer of Albrecht V, MunichSchloss Ambras KunstkammerAldrovandi museum, BolognaCalceolari museum, VeronaImperato museum, NaplesUppsala Kunstschrank (Hainhofer)
The Repository of the Royal Societyp. 133

Hooper-Greenhill treats the Repository of the Royal Society, founded in 1660, as the third case study of Foucault's classical episteme, arguing that seventeenth-century collections were ordered by identity and difference rather than by the hidden resemblances of the Renaissance. The chapter moves from Renaissance studioli and galleries, such as Francesco I de' Medici's studiolo and the Habsburg picture gallery in Prague, where paintings were grouped by visual form, to the Society's donation-based collection. It then examines the Society's aim of a complete, classified inventory of nature, tied to John Wilkins's universal language and to the tables drawn up by Hooke and Grew. The evidence comes from the Society's minutes, its catalogues and the gifts it received, including petrified foetuses, stones and rare exotics. The Repository failed, the chapter concludes, because it lacked endowment, a selection policy, specialist staff and workable technologies, and it became a store of curiosities. The closing section warns that modern curators who aim to 'fill the gaps' of a classificatory table repeat the same limitations.

Royal Society RepositoryStudiolo of Francesco I de' MediciHabsburg picture gallery in PragueBritish Museum
The disciplinary museump. 167

Hooper-Greenhill's fourth case study follows the French Revolution's transformation of royal and aristocratic collections into the public Louvre, opened in 1793 and renamed the Musee Napoleon in 1803. The chapter argues that the revolution produced a 'disciplinary museum': church, aristocratic and royal property was confiscated, war indemnities and removals from conquered territories were organised by commissions and expert agents, and objects were catalogued in depots before being displayed to educate citizens and celebrate the Republic. It traces new display practices, such as hanging paintings by national 'schools' to make a visual history of art, and the emergence of curators, guards and separate visitors' guides. Its evidence is drawn from commission reports, letters and catalogues. The chapter then turns to Britain, where the National Gallery and National Portrait Gallery were intended to improve the population through heroic national history. It ends by arguing that the museum divides the hidden work of producing knowledge from the surveilled public spaces where visitors are shaped.

Louvre (Musee Napoleon)Musee des Monuments FrancaisBrera, MilanNational Gallery, LondonNational Portrait Gallery, London
A useful past for the presentp. 191

Hooper-Greenhill's closing chapter draws the four earlier case studies together and asks what 'effective history' implies for museums today. Its central claim is that museums have no essential identity: an object's meaning shifts with the epistemic framework, technologies and power relations of each period, from the Medici palace and the cabinet of the world to the Royal Society's Repository and the revolutionary Louvre. The chapter then turns to the modern museum, tracing how the layout of the Natural History Museum, open storage in Canada, 'intelligent' buildings in Japan, shops and restaurants, and participatory exhibitions such as Birmingham's Gallery 33 and Edinburgh's 'The People's Story' have altered the relation between curator and visitor. Hooper-Greenhill accepts that opening museums to many voices is a gain, but argues that the language of experience and pleasure can disguise new forms of control. The chapter ends with questions about whether the modern age, and the modern museum with it, is coming to an end.

East and Southeast Asia The chapter mentions Japan once, in its discussion of the 'intelligent' museum: new museums in Japan are said to be built with channels for cables and optical fibres that carry collection, visitor and environmental data, citing Mizushima (1989). No Japanese collection or object is discussed.

Hopkins, Owen (2021). The Museum: From Its Origins to the 21st Century.Asia: substantial9 chapter overviews

Overview

Hopkins's The Museum (2021) is a general history of the museum, from princely and Renaissance cabinets through the Enlightenment, public, modern and global museums to the present. It is organised chronologically: an introduction, then Origins, The Enlightenment Museum, The Public Museum, The Modern Museum, The Global Museum and The Museum Now. Its argument is that museums are the bedrock on which understanding of civilisation rests, but that each phase of their history was shaped by power, empire and, increasingly, the symbolic architecture of the building. Its scope is mainly Europe and North America, with cases from the Gulf, China, Africa and Latin America, and it ends by calling for museums to be rethought on decolonial and inclusive terms.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

East Asia is a thread through three chapters, not a theme, and Southeast Asia is absent. The Public Museum (chapter 3) gives the main Asian case: the Tokyo National Museum, from the 1872 Yushima Seido Exposition, sent to the Vienna World's Fair, to the Ueno Park complex whose Honkan (Josiah Conder, 1882) is linked to Japan's projection of itself abroad. Hopkins also notes a Korean culture museum founded in 1909 under the Japanese-controlled Korean emperor, which became one of the founding collections of the National Museum of Korea after 1945.

The Modern Museum (chapter 4) treats postwar Japan: Junzo Sakakura's Museum of Modern Art, Kamakura (1951), and Le Corbusier's National Museum of Western Art in Ueno, built from 1955 for the Matsukata collection seized in France and returned under the 1951 San Francisco treaty. Tange's Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum is cited as reconciliation, and Tae-Soo Kim's National Museum of Contemporary Art, Gwacheon (1986), stands for Korea.

The Global Museum (chapter 5) gives China the longest treatment, but as a building boom, not as Asian collections: the National Museum of China (2003), the Shanghai Expo's Power Station of Art and China Art Palace, and city museums at Ordos, Qujing, Nanjing (Steven Holl) and Ningbo (Wang Shu). Japan's 1980s-90s boom (Ando's Benesse House, the Edo-Tokyo Museum) and Ando's work in Taiwan and South Korea appear briefly. Chinese museum building is linked to state prestige and to trade and investment in Africa. Chinese or Asian collections abroad, restitution claims and Asian visitors are not discussed.

Title
Contents
Preface

Hopkins's preface, written during the 2020-21 closures, notes the pandemic's damage to museum income and the acceleration of trends such as the decline of blockbuster exhibitions and the shift to digital. It then turns to the murder of George Floyd and the Black Lives Matter protests, arguing that museums, as arbiters of what society values, remembers and excludes, are complicit in systemic racism. The preface ends by asking what museums should do next, and answers that they should put diversity, representation and racial equality at the centre of their mission.

Introduction: The Age of Museums

Hopkins argues that museums are the bedrock on which understanding of civilisation rests, and that their appeal endures even when they are critiqued. Hopkins opens with Marcel Broodthaers's 1968 Musée d'Art Moderne, Département des Aigles, an installation of empty crates that exposed the storage, transport and installation hidden behind the museum's façade, as an example of institutional critique. Hopkins then compares museums with libraries, civic spaces and law courts, arguing that they are arbiters of knowledge who must balance access with scholarly rigour. Hopkins cites Douglas Crimp's 1980 essay and Rauschenberg's Centennial Certificate to argue that the museum's image as a timeless treasury has survived critique. Record visitor numbers and the museum boom are described, and the Parthenon and the Acropolis Museum show how building and collection are inseparable. The introduction ends by outlining the book's chronology, from princely and cabinet collections to Enlightenment, modern and global museums.

East and Southeast Asia China is the only Asian setting touched on. The introduction notes that China had 349 museums in 1978 and about 5,100 now, against the government's goal and the 35,000 museums in the USA, and it lists the National Museum of China on Tiananmen Square among the world's most visited museums.

Musée d'Art Moderne, Département des AiglesAcropolis MuseumBritish MuseumMetropolitan Museum of ArtLouvre
11. Origins

Hopkins traces the origins of the museum through Ole Worm's seventeenth-century cabinet in Copenhagen, which he treats as the closest precursor to a modern museum, and through the ancient Mouseion at Alexandria, which was a place of learning rather than display. Hopkins moves to the medieval treasuries and reliquaries, whose containers offered a model for uniting object and setting. Renaissance studioli, such as Piero de' Medici's in Florence, Federico da Montefeltro's at Urbino and Francesco I's in the Palazzo Vecchio, are described, along with the rarities collectors prized, such as armadillos, narwhal tusks and mandrakes. Rubens and Jan Brueghel's The Sense of Sight is used to show the cabinet as a microcosm of the known world. The chapter then turns to public display: the Capitoline sculptures given by Sixtus IV, the Laocoön at the Vatican, the Uffizi, and Tradescant's Ark, whose collection passed to Ashmole and became the Ashmolean in Oxford, the first modern museum.

Museum WormianumMouseion at AlexandriaCapitoline MuseumsUffizi GalleryTradescant's ArkAshmolean Museum
22. The Enlightenment Museum

This chapter traces the emergence of the Enlightenment museum in Europe from the mid-eighteenth century, beginning with the British Museum and its Enlightenment Gallery, the former King's Library. It examines Hans Sloane's collections, built partly on Jamaican plantations and slavery, and the shift from curiosity cabinets to classificatory display. Hopkins then moves to the Louvre, where Diderot's Encyclopedie and the Revolution turned a royal palace into the Musee Napoleon, stocked with works seized in Italy and the Rosetta Stone taken from Egypt. The Parthenon sculptures, removed by Elgin and sold to the British Museum, illustrate contested acquisition, and Byron's protest stands as a contemporary critique. Further cases include the Belvedere in Vienna, the Rijksmuseum, the Prado, the Hermitage under Catherine the Great, and the Altes Museum in Berlin, where Schinkel made architecture and collection one unity. Soane's house-museum in London ends the survey. Hopkins argues that the universal encyclopaedia of the Enlightenment museum rested on conquest and empire, and the chapter closes by leading to the public museum of the nineteenth century.

British MuseumLouvre (Musee Napoleon)Belvedere, ViennaRijksmuseumPradoHermitageAltes MuseumSir John Soane's Museum
33. The Public MuseumAsia: in part

This chapter traces how the museum became a public institution in the nineteenth century, in contrast to the Enlightenment museum of the previous chapter. It opens with the Frick Collection in New York, a house and art collection left to the public by the industrialist Henry Clay Frick, whose career raises the question of why public museums were so valued. The central case is the 1851 Great Exhibition in London, whose profits founded the South Kensington Museum, later the V&A, and the 'Albertopolis' precinct. Hopkins then surveys the National Gallery, the Smithsonian, and the New York Met and American Museum of Natural History, showing how each combined an educational mission with historicist architecture. Hopkins argues that public museums were instruments of moral improvement for the working classes, an idealism that sat uneasily with condescension and with fortunes built on exploitation. The chapter closes by introducing Modernism, whose new architectural languages the next chapter takes up.

East and Southeast Asia Tokyo National Museum is the chapter's main Asian case. Hopkins traces it from the Yushima Seido Exposition of 1872, which was sent to the Vienna World's Fair, to the Ueno Park complex whose Honkan, designed by the British architect Josiah Conder, opened in 1882, and links it to Japan's growing projection of itself abroad. Hopkins also notes that a museum of Korean culture was founded in 1909 under the Japanese-controlled Korean emperor, and that it became one of the founding collections of the National Museum of Korea after 1945.

Frick CollectionGreat Exhibition (Crystal Palace)South Kensington Museum (V&A)National Gallery, LondonSmithsonian InstitutionAmerican Museum of Natural HistoryMetropolitan Museum of ArtTokyo National Museum
44. The Modern MuseumAsia: in part

This chapter traces how Modernism reshaped the museum in the twentieth century, beginning with the Centre Georges Pompidou in Paris, whose open steel frame and piazza realized an adaptable building and a neutral white-cube gallery. Hopkins then goes back to Manet, whose A Bar at the Folies-Bergere he treats as an early Modernist work made in a sense for the museum, and to the founding of MoMA in New York in 1929, where Alfred Barr organized departments by medium. Exhibitions such as Machine Art show how museums embraced functional design, while the Nazi contrast between Degenerate Art and the Haus der Deutschen Kunst shows how museums became political. Post-war cases follow: Malraux's Museum Without Walls, MoMA's The Family of Man and its critics, Lina Bo Bardi's MASP in Sao Paulo, and the Guggenheim, Whitney and Kimbell, which Hopkins reads as buildings that symbolize their values. He concludes that Postmodernism, as in Stirling's Neue Staatsgalerie, put the museum back into history, and the next chapter turns to the global museum.

East and Southeast Asia Japan is the main Asian case. Hopkins describes the Museum of Modern Art in Kamakura (1951), built by Junzo Sakakura with walls of local Oya stone beside Tsurugaoka Hachimangu Shrine, and the National Museum of Western Art in Ueno, designed by Le Corbusier from 1955 to house the Kojiro Matsukata collection of Western paintings and Japanese woodblock prints, seized in France after the war and handed back under the 1951 San Francisco treaty. Tange's Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum is cited as a symbol of reconciliation. Korea appears briefly, with Tae-Soo Kim's National Museum of Contemporary Art in Gwacheon (1986), which draws on temple architecture.

Centre Georges PompidouMuseum of Modern Art, New YorkMuseum of Art of Sao Paulo (MASP)National Museum of Western Art, TokyoNeue Nationalgalerie, BerlinSolomon R. Guggenheim MuseumWhitney Museum of American ArtKimbell Art Museum
55. The Global MuseumAsia: in part

This chapter traces the rise of the 'global museum' from the 1990s, with Gehry's Guggenheim in Bilbao as its emblem: a sculptural building whose form overshadows its collection. Hopkins links it to the Postmodern Sainsbury Wing of the National Gallery, to culture-led regeneration at Tate Modern, whose Turbine Hall was carved out of a power station, and to starchitects such as Libeskind, Hadid and Chipperfield. Chipperfield's restoration of the Neues Museum in Berlin serves as the model of a building that makes sense of the past. The chapter then examines Gulf outposts such as the Louvre Abu Dhabi and China's museum boom, which Hopkins reads as bargaining chips for states and as culture-washing. Its final section takes up the 'post-national' museum, exemplified by Dakar's Museum of Black Civilizations and the National Museum of African American History and Culture in Washington, which complicates national narratives rather than telling one.

East and Southeast Asia China gets the longest treatment: Hopkins traces its museum boom from the National Museum of China (2003) and the 2010 Shanghai Expo, which produced the Power Station of Art and the China Art Palace, to the Ordos Museum, the Qujing History Museum, the Nanjing Sifang Art Museum and Wang Shu's Ningbo History Museum, built from the ruins of demolished villages. Japan appears in the 1980s and 1990s building boom, with Tadao Ando's Benesse House on Naoshima and the Edo-Tokyo Museum among the examples. Taiwan and South Korea are mentioned briefly through Ando's commissions there, and Western outposts in Shenzhen and Shanghai are noted.

Guggenheim Museum BilbaoSainsbury Wing, National GalleryTate ModernNeues Museum, BerlinLouvre Abu DhabiMusee des Civilisations Noires, DakarNational Museum of African American History and CultureWeltmuseum Wien
66. The Museum Now

This concluding chapter considers the challenges facing museums in the twenty-first century and how they might be reinvented. It opens with the looting of the Iraq Museum in Baghdad in 2003, which Hopkins uses to argue that museums hold a special status, so that attacks on them are attacks on shared civilization. It then turns to the digital revolution, including the difficulty of collecting apps and digital files, and to decolonization: the Benin Bronzes and Parthenon debates, the #MuseumsAreNotNeutral campaign, and Macron's call for restitution to Africa, set against the cautious position of the V&A's director Tristram Hunt. Workforce diversity and Te Papa's bicultural approach follow, with Avani Tanya's residency at the V&A and the Mobile Worlds exhibition in Hamburg as examples of museums opening collections to competing voices. Hopkins closes by arguing that collections, audiences and buildings must each be rethought, perhaps through virtual reality, because museums have always been about the future.

End Notes

The end notes for the whole book, keyed by chapter from the Introduction through Chapter Six, with a separate list for each. They give sources for quotations and facts, including Crimp's essays on museum ruins, Byron's Childe Harold, Le Corbusier's The Decorative Arts of Today, MoMA press releases, Ballard's review of the Bilbao Guggenheim and the Sarr and Savoy restitution report. Many references are web pages. The notes contain no argument; they are a trail to the sources.

Hudson, Kenneth (1975). A Social History of Museums: What the Visitors Thought. London: Macmillan.Asia: occasional6 chapter overviews

Overview

Kenneth Hudson's social history asks how museums came to serve a broad public, and argues that for most of their history visitors were admitted on the owners' terms, as a privilege rather than a right. It runs from eighteenth-century collections in Vienna, Dresden, London and Paris through American museums, the great world's fairs and the Victorian palace-museums, to twentieth-century visitor research. The text is an introduction and five chapters (privilege; right; educational purpose; arrangement and communication; the market research age), followed by plates of museums in nineteen countries, appendices reproducing visitor-survey reports and questionnaires, notes and an index. Its evidence is historical and anecdotal: letters, press comment, catalogues and survey reports, mainly from Europe and North America.

East and Southeast Asia in this work occasional

East and Southeast Asia are touched on only lightly. The book is about museums in Europe and North America, and Asia enters as objects in collections, as brief examples and in one plate. In the Introduction Japan appears once, in the Research Institute of Industrial Safety museum in Tokyo, which Hudson tests against the definition of a 'permanent' museum (lines 124-130). Chapters 1 and 2 (Entry as a privilege; Entry as a right) mention Asian material only in passing: a 'Tonquin bean' and Oriental figures at the Salem museum, Chinese shoes at Charleston, and a jackal and mongoose 'from China' at Peale's (lines 1363, 1459, 1522-1534).

Chapter 3 (Museums as educational instruments) has the longer passages. Victorian palace-museums were stocked with 'loot' from China and Japan (lines 2172-2175), and the chapter compares socialist museums in Poland, Russia and China with English Victorian museum rules: 'In this sense, the Socialists are Victorians' (lines 2627-2636). Chapter 4 (Arrangement and communication) has a note on open-air museums that says the first was in the Netherlands, built from houses from Indonesia brought from the Amsterdam International Colonial Exhibition of 1883 (note 25, lines 6316-6319). Chapter 5 (Museums in the market research age) sets the Russian and Chinese ends of the Communist spectrum against each other, where displays mix old and new for education (lines 4402-4407).

The one sustained treatment of China is plate 5, 'China, People's Republic' (lines 5015-5057): a Confucian temple at Ch'ufu, the museum at Loyang, and a village house in Kiangsi where Mao Tse-tung lived. The captions say Chinese museums preserve old buildings, mix tractors with jade carvings, and aim to leave visitors 'better citizens than it found them'. The text gives no Korean or Southeast Asian museum, no colonial collecting or display in Asia, no Asian visitors or curators, and no restitution claims.

Introduction: The changing idea of a museumPDF p. 7

Hudson opens his social history by asking what a museum is, using the International Council of Museums definition as a starting point and testing each of its terms: 'permanent', 'public interest' and 'for the pleasure and education of the public'. Hudson questions whether institutions with constantly changing displays, such as the Museum of Science and Industry in Chicago, count as museums at all, and proposes the term 'expo-museum' for them. The introduction then turns to curators' attitudes towards visitors, quoting Charles Gibbs-Smith's complaint that staff patronise, resent or despise the public. Hudson describes how European collections in Vienna, Dresden and London were run as favours for connoisseurs rather than rights for visitors, and cites Joseph II's free admission and the failed Luxembourg experiment in Paris. Hudson notes that nineteenth-century museums measured success by turnstile counts and that surveys of visitors barely existed, so the historian must rely on scattered comments. The chapter sets out the book's question of how museums came to serve a broad public.

East and Southeast Asia Japan appears once, in the Research Institute of Industrial Safety museum in Tokyo, which Hudson uses as a test case for whether a museum with changing displays can be called permanent. He grants it educational purpose, professional staff and efforts to make exhibits intelligible, but notes it has no fixed collections. No East or Southeast Asian collection is discussed further.

British MuseumZwinger gallery, DresdenImperial Gallery, ViennaScience Museum, LondonMuseum of Science and Industry, ChicagoResearch Institute of Industrial Safety museum, Tokyo
IEntry as a privilegep. 8

Hudson's second chapter argues that eighteenth- and early nineteenth-century museums admitted visitors as a privilege granted by autocratic directors rather than as a right. Hudson builds the case through the British Museum's 1759 Statutes, which required written applications and limited tickets, and through William Hutton's hurried 1784 visit, which left him feeling his time had been wasted. Hudson compares private collections such as the Earl of Arundel's house gallery, Sir Hans Sloane's cabinet and Charles Townley's gallery in Park Street, showing how connoisseurship produced exclusive taste. Two contrasting cases, Sir Ashton Lever's museum and Dr Richard Mead's gallery, illustrate how owners tried to keep out 'the common people', though Mead admitted students to copy his pictures. Hudson links the shift to a new middle-class patronage and to the reorganisation of the Belvedere in Vienna, where von Mecheln arranged pictures in rows to educate rather than to please. Hudson ends with Waagen's 1830s tour of British houses, admiring the arrangement at Panshanger and criticising pictures ruined by damp at Corsham.

British MuseumSir Ashton Lever's museum, Leicester HouseSloane collectionArundel House galleryTownley gallery, Park StreetMead's gallery, Great Ormond StreetBelvedere, Vienna
2Entry as a rightp. 31

Hudson turns to the United States, where public museums came earlier than private collections, and follows the Charleston Museum, Peale's Museum in Philadelphia and the East India Marine Society's museum at Salem. Each began as a gathering of natural curiosities and gifts and survived by becoming more public, through advertising, season tickets and donor recognition in the press. The chapter's central theme is the public reception of the great exhibitions. The Great Exhibition in London of 1851 and later world's fairs opened museums to very large crowds, and Hudson quotes a letter from 'A Mechanic' fearing a 'London mob' and a country groom complaining about train times. The agricultural shows of the Bath and West of England Society brought art and applied design to rural audiences, and the chapter sets out the principles of its Arts and Manufactures Department. It closes with the Marlborough House museum and the South Kensington buildings of 1857, where seats and refreshment rooms signalled that visitors were now treated as human beings rather than supplicants.

East and Southeast Asia The chapter's East and Southeast Asian material is incidental. Caroline Howard King remembers the Salem museum hall in the 1830s, with life-size figures of merchants in their own dress, sandalwood gifts, a Tonquin bean and a sense that the Spice Islands lay near. Chinese shoes at Charleston and a jackal and mongoose from China at Peale's appear only in lists of exhibits.

Charleston MuseumPeale's Museum, PhiladelphiaEast India Marine Society museum, SalemBritish MuseumNational GalleryVernon GallerySouth Kensington MuseumMarlborough House museum
3Museums as educational instrumentsp. 48

Hudson asks whether museums are meant to instruct visitors or to shape their responses, and how that changed over time. Hudson opens with a 1958 statement by Lothar Witteborg that a museum's primary function is to educate, and questions its assumptions through a Bristol nuclear exhibition whose young visitor responded only to the shapes of the reactors. The historical core contrasts founders who sought to shape feeling rather than teach facts, such as Ludwig I's Glyptothek in Munich, the Berlin Old Museum and Osthaus's Folkwang at Hagen, with Sir John Soane's London house museum, which left visitors free to form their own views. Patriotic and ethnographic purposes come next, with Siebold's Leiden museum and the Bonn museum of the Fatherland. The Peabody penguin and Gustav Klemm's Dresden bequest show how collections reached the public. Evening opening figures for South Kensington and Bethnal Green follow, then Socialist and Nazi museums tied to state doctrine. The chapter ends with a painting of a Royal Academy private view, where privileged guests saw the collections apart from the public.

Sir John Soane's MuseumGlyptothek, MunichOld Museum, BerlinFolkwang Museum, HagenPeabody Museum, SalemNatural History Museum, LondonSouth Kensington MuseumBethnal Green Museum
4Arrangement and communicationp. 74

Hudson argues that museums serve several publics, not one, and that a museum should pick a few main reasons for visiting and arrange its displays to serve them. Hudson draws on the Leiden ethnology director's aesthetic, romantic and intellectual motives and on studies of visitors' eye levels. The chapter traces nineteenth-century palace buildings and congested displays, citing a 1939 Dijon gallery where pictures hung floor to ceiling, and it presents the Rijksmuseum's Night Watch lighting tests of 1898 as a case where museum arrangement was reconsidered. A dispute over the National Gallery's cleaning of 1845 shows Victorians preferring grimy pictures to restored ones. Later sections cover lighting, multi-storey buildings, Boston's mass-audience policy, the Anacostia neighbourhood museum and the 1967 McLuhan and Parker seminar. The chapter ends with open-air museums, eco-museums and historic houses, which Hudson calls museums 'in which one feels safe', and with low staff pay and rare visitor surveys.

Rijksmuseum, AmsterdamNational Gallery, LondonMuseum of Science and Industry, ChicagoAnacostia Museum, WashingtonMuseum of Fine Arts, BostonBeamish open-air museumMuseum of the Royal College of Surgeons, LondonHayward Gallery
5Museums in the market research agep. 100

Hudson surveys attempts to study museum visitors, beginning with Cameron and Abbey's verdict that the research so far had yielded little. Hudson argues that visitor research was often badly done, and that curators still prefer overheard remarks to surveys. Early work measured how long people looked at pictures, from Robinson's 1928 figure of nine seconds, to label studies and the National Gallery of Art's interpretation leaflets. The Ulster Museum survey found visitors saw museum-going as 'a juvenile pastime', and Erwin's Belfast survey showed that non-visitors had heard of the museum mainly from friends and television. Bourdieu and Darbel's French survey found working-class visitors likening museums to churches, and the chapter also recounts the 1911 Albright Art Gallery nudes controversy. It ends with the MUSE neighbourhood museum in Brooklyn, Pott's call for museum hosts rather than guardians, and a 1973 London survey showing visitors overwhelmingly middle class.

Impey, Oliver; MacGregor, Arthur (eds.) (1985). The Origins of Museums: The Cabinet of Curiosities in Sixteenth- and Seventeenth-Century Europe. Oxford: Clarendon Press.Asia: substantial34 chapter overviews

Overview

An edited volume (1985) by Oliver Impey and Arthur MacGregor: an introduction and some thirty essays on the Kunst- and Wunderkammern of sixteenth- and seventeenth-century Europe, the cabinets of curiosities that preceded public museums. Its central argument is that these cabinets were not whimsical: their miscellany was part of a programme aiming at universality, and the contemporary terms (Kunstkammer, Wunderkammer, studiolo) were unstable. The essays revise or reject Julius von Schlosser's 1908 survey through case studies of particular collections and themes rather than an overview. The scope is European, with chapters on Italy, the Habsburg lands, Prague, Dresden, Munich, Berlin, Copenhagen, the Dutch Republic, Spain, Britain and Basle, and thematic chapters on natural history, shells, gardens, geology, instruments, antiquities, ethnography and exotic objects.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

Asia is a secondary theme, but it is not absent. Two chapters are devoted to it. John Ayers's 'The Early China Trade' (ch. 31) covers Chinese porcelain, silks, paintings and carvings in Venice, Florence, Dresden and Innsbruck, and the Portuguese trade through Malacca. Oliver Impey's 'Japan: Trade and Collecting in Seventeenth-Century Europe' (ch. 32) covers Namban and export lacquer, Arita porcelain and Japanese paper, the middlemen at Nagasaki, Hirado and Deshima, the Japanese embassy of 1584, and a 1680 Siam order of lacquered dishes for Constant Phaulkon. Both concern objects in European collections, not museums in Asia.

Asian material is a substantial strand in several other chapters. Schepelern (ch. 15) shows that Paludanus's inventory of 1617-18 holds more Far Eastern objects than the 1604 list, through Linschoten, who had lived in Goa. Lunsingh Scheurleer (ch. 14) describes Chinese porcelain and Japanese lacquer at The Hague and the Huis ten Bosch. George (ch. 21) covers East Indies animals: birds of paradise from New Guinea, a babyrousa skull from Celebes and cockatoos from Buru. Coomans (ch. 22) covers Rumphius's shells from Amboina, and Raby (ch. 30) treats porcelain as the main Asian material among Islamic exotica.

Elsewhere Asian items are passing references: Chinese porcelain at Ambras (ch. 8) and in the Settala collection (ch. 7), 'Indian' and 'Turkish' labels at Munich (ch. 14), VOC-supplied oriental arms in Berlin (ch. 17), Japanese swords at Rosenborg (ch. 20), a Japanese teapot at Leiden (ch. 25) and Chinese goods in Platter's account of Cope's cabinet (ch. 23). No passage I found discusses Korea, Vietnam, Cambodia, Burma or the Philippines, and no Asian visitors, curators, national museums or restitution claims appear.

ForewordDavid PiperPDF p. 5
PrefaceOliver Impey and Arthur MacGregorPDF p. 7
