IntroductionOliver Impey and Arthur MacGregorPDF p. 17

Impey and MacGregor introduce a set of essays on the Kunst- and Wunderkammern of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. They open with Francis Bacon's description of the learned gentleman's apparatus, including his 'goodly, huge cabinet', and use it to argue that the cabinet of curiosities was not a whimsical precursor of the museum but a serious programme aimed at universality. The mixture of natural and man-made objects, they say, was central to that programme: naturalists needed reference collections, collectors sought antiquities and exotic goods from new contacts, and everyday objects such as tools and costumes were gradually added. The introduction traces how objects moved between cabinets and changed status, with unicorn horn reclassified as narwhal and porcelain shifting from art to household use. It notes that contemporary terms such as Kunstkammer were unstable. The authors then say that the volume revises or rejects von Schlosser's 1908 survey, but with essays on particular themes rather than an encyclopaedic reach.

Electoral collection, DresdenCollection of Albrecht V, Munich
Science — Honour — Metaphor: Italian Cabinets of the Sixteenth and Seventeenth CenturiesGiuseppe OlmiPDF p. 21

Olmi compares the sixteenth- and seventeenth-century Italian collections of natural objects with the princely studioli and with the encyclopaedic cabinets of northern Europe. Olmi argues that the scientific museums of Calceolari in Verona, Aldrovandi in Bologna, Mercati in the Vatican and Imperato in Naples had a practical purpose: they were reference tools for physicians, pharmacists and naturalists, and their objects were arranged by function rather than symbolic programme. Olmi then shows how the naturalists' fondness for the rare and the exotic, and their display of fragments such as teeth and horns, drew on ancient authors such as Pliny and on Mannerist taste. In the seventeenth century, he contends, the Milanese and Bolognese collections of Settala, Cospi and Moscardo were more encyclopaedic and marvel-driven, advertised through printed catalogues, and they represent a retreat from the sixteenth-century naturalists. The chapter ends with Marsili and Maffei, whose specialised and didactic collections anticipated eighteenth-century museum practice.

Aldrovandi museum, BolognaCalceolari museum, VeronaMetallotheca of Michele Mercati, VaticanImperato museum, NaplesMedici studiolo, FlorenceSettala museum, MilanCospi museum, BolognaMoscardo museum, Verona
Museography and Ethnographical Collections in Bologna during the Sixteenth and Seventeenth CenturiesLaura Laurencich-Minellip. 19

Laurencich-Minelli compares two Bolognese collections of the sixteenth century: the museum of the naturalist Ulisse Aldrovandi, linked to the university, and that of Antonio Giganti, secretary to ecclesiastical patrons, whose inventory of 1586 survives with a plan. Both were encyclopaedic, but she argues that Giganti arranged his museum in a harmonious system of alternating and repeating symmetries that evoked art and nature together, whereas Aldrovandi stressed natural history and used ethnographic items to study how distant peoples worked raw materials. The two men shared objects: Aldrovandi drew on Giganti's holdings for his own catalogues, and some American and Mesoamerican pieces possibly passed to him after Giganti's retirement in 1597. In the seventeenth century the Aldrovandi collection went to the Bolognese Senate and was joined by the Cospi museum, whose published catalogues did not match the actual arrangement. Laurencich-Minelli concludes that the term Wunderkammer should be dropped from Italian museography in favour of studiolo, guardaroba and museo.

Giganti museum, BolognaAldrovandi museum, BolognaCospi museum, Bologna
Towards a History of Collecting in Milan in the Late Renaissance and Baroque PeriodsAntonio Aimi, Vincenzo de Michele, and Alessandro Morandottip. 29

Aimi, de Michele and Morandotti examine collecting in Milan under Spanish rule from the late sixteenth to the seventeenth century. They argue that local collecting was shaped by a decentralised political class rather than a court, so that picture galleries served patrician prestige, while antiquities sometimes acquired scholarly value. Their evidence comes from several collections: the antique casts of Leone Leoni, the holdings of Figino, the Visconti Borromeo collection displayed in a nymphaeum at the family villa, and the museum of Lodovico and Manfredo Settala. The Settala museum is the centre of the chapter. The authors list its groups of objects, from instruments and minerals to fossils, zoological remains and ethnographic items, and show how Manfredo Settala's technical and scientific work, together with three editions of printed catalogues, made the collection one of the city's leading cultural institutions. They argue against labelling it a Wunderkammer, since its illustrated codices show a classificatory and scientific approach, and conclude that it was a working resource rather than only a showcase of curiosity.

East and Southeast Asia The chapter's inventory of the Settala museum lists 'ethnographic objects: clothes, ornaments and weapons from America, Asia, Africa', and it notes that Manfredo Settala invented a ceramic paste giving 'the appearance of Chinese porcelain', on which Tschirnhaus later drew to start European porcelain. Asian objects are named only in this list, and the porcelain point is one item among Settala's technical activities.

Settala museum, MilanVisconti Borromeo collection (nymphaeum), MilanLeone Leoni's collection of antique casts, MilanArdemanio collection, Milan
The Collection of Archduke Ferdinand II at Schloss Ambras: its Purpose, Composition and EvolutionElisabeth Scheicherp. 37

Scheicher analyses the Kunstkammer of Archduke Ferdinand II at Schloss Ambras near Innsbruck, built in the Unterschloss from 1573. Scheicher’s main argument is that the objects were displayed by material, following Pliny, with cupboards painted in colours to suit their contents and the room lit from both sides, so that the display was aesthetic as well as practical, which she sees as the birth of the modern museum in central Europe. Scheicher then examines the 'universal Kunstkammer', sorting its contents into naturalia, carved corals and hand stones, artefacts, scientific instruments, mirabilia and coins, and she argues that Ferdinand had little interest in antiquity. Using the inventories of 1596 and 1621, she separates gifts, heirlooms and the Archduke's own acquisitions, and she compares the collection with the Munich Kunstkammer of his brother-in-law Duke Wilhelm V, which shared objects and artists. The chapter concludes that Ambras differed from Munich in its arrangement, which was the source of its individuality.

East and Southeast Asia Scheicher notes that cupboard no. 9 held 'a great mass of Chinese porcelain' beside pre-Columbian featherworks and three silk paintings, probably gifts from her cousin King Philip of Spain. The porcelain is a passing point in a list of exotica from North Africa, Asia and the New World, and she does not discuss Chinese or other Asian objects further.

Ambras Kunstkammer, Schloss Ambras, InnsbruckMedici studiolo, FlorenceMunich Kunstkammer of Duke Wilhelm VDresden Kunstkammer
The Habsburg Collections in Vienna during the Seventeenth CenturyRudolf Distelbergerp. 51

Distelberger examines the Habsburg collections in Vienna in the seventeenth century, a period the literature has tended to treat as one of consolidation rather than acquisition. The centrepiece is the Vienna treasury (Schatzkammer), which Emperor Matthias founded after Rudolf II's death with objects selected from the Prague Kunstkammer, and which Distelberger argues was designed to glorify the emperor and the House of Austria rather than to serve scientific ends. His evidence is four visitor reports, by Codebo (1659), Müller (1660), Edward Brown (1677) and an anonymous account of 1677, which he uses to reconstruct the treasury cupboard by cupboard: ivory, silver, gold, rock crystal by Dionysio Miseroni, the imperial crown and many works attributed to Dürer. He then turns to Archduke Leopold Wilhelm's picture gallery and Kunstkammer, a more specialized collection of paintings, bronzes and sculpture, and to its display in the Stallburg under Karl VI. The chapter concludes that these collections reflect the absolutism and Counter-Reformation politics of the age, while the Habsburgs' scientific interests were pursued elsewhere, at the court library.

Vienna Schatzkammer (Habsburg treasury)Leopold Wilhelm's Kunstkammer and picture gallery, ViennaPrague Kunstkammer of Rudolf II
The Collection of Rudolf II at Prague: Cabinet of Curiosities or Scientific Museum?Eliška Fučíkováp. 63

Fučíková uses the newly published inventory of Rudolf II's Kunstkammer (1607-11) to ask whether the Prague collection was a cabinet of curiosities or a scientific museum. Fučíková stresses the scale and range of the inventory, which lists naturalia and artificialia alongside paintings, and argues that it covers only the Kunstkammer proper, so that the whole collection was perhaps twice as large. Comparing it with the later inventories of 1619 and 1621, she reconstructs the building history of the Hradschin palace and the layout of the rooms: three vaulted front chambers with seventeen cupboards, a principal chamber with twenty numbered cupboards, and the galleries above. She reviews Neumann's view of the collection as an encyclopaedic 'Mannerist museum' and Kaufmann's emphasis on its diplomatic role, then argues that its arrangement was systematic yet hard for a modern reader to decode. Her closing point is that the collection served craftsmen and court artists as a working resource as well as a display, and that it was never destined for a wider public.

Kunstkammer of Rudolf II, Prague Castle
'His Majesty's Cabinet' and Peter I's KunstkammerOleg Neverovp. 71

Neverov traces the origins of Peter the Great's collection of rarities, 'His Majesty's Cabinet', from the treasures of earlier tsars to the public St Petersburg Kunstkammer that Peter founded in 1714. Neverov follows Peter's first journey abroad in 1697-8, when he visited apothecaries, anatomists and private cabinets in Amsterdam, Leiden, Utrecht, London and Dresden, and shows how that experience shaped a collection of exotic animals, anatomical specimens, arms and ethnographic objects. The chapter then describes the move to Vasilievsky Island, the Latin catalogue of 1741 and the fire of 1747, which destroyed much of the collection. Neverov reconstructs what was lost from watercolours, engravings and surviving plaquettes, and shows the systematic arrangement under the Academy of Sciences, from naturalia and anatomical curiosities to turned work, archaeological finds and coins. Neverov ends with the nineteenth-century dispersal of the collection to Tsarskoye Selo and the Hermitage, and with Catherine II's disregard for the universal museum, arguing that the drawings and catalogue still allow the whole to be reconstructed.

Kunstkammer of Peter I, St PetersburgHermitage Museum
The Basle Cabinets of Art and Curiosities in the Sixteenth and Seventeenth CenturiesHans Christoph Ackermannp. 81

Ackermann surveys the humanistic art and curiosity cabinets formed in Basle in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, arguing that they belong to a humanist tradition rooted in the circle of Erasmus. Ackermann follows the Amerbach collection from the legacy Erasmus left in 1536, through Bonifacius Amerbach, to his son Basilius, whose inventories record over 4,000 items, goldsmiths' models and drawings by Holbein and Urs Graf, and whose spending he traces year by year. After Basilius's death the cabinet was bought by the city in 1661, which Ackermann regards as the first public collection bought by a city rather than derived from a princely one. He then sketches other Basle collections: Felix Platter's cabinet of natural curiosities, instruments and North American objects, and the cabinet of the lawyer Remigius Faesch, which passed to the university in 1817 and was united with the Amerbach collection. The chapter concludes that the survival of both the collections and their inventories makes Basle an unusually well documented case.

Amerbach cabinet, BasleFaesch Museum, BasleHistorisches Museum, Basle
Elector Augustus' Kunstkammer: an Analysis of the Inventory of 1587Joachim Menzhausenp. 91

Menzhausen analyses the inventory of 1587 of the Kunstkammer that Elector Augustus of Saxony formed in Dresden, which lists about 9,600 entries. Its most striking feature is that roughly three-quarters of the objects are tools, grouped by the crafts and professions they served, with scientific instruments and clocks, books, turned ivories and only a small number of pictures and natural objects. Menzhausen places this composition in its setting: a Saxony rich in mines, manufacturing and water-powered industry, where the Elector was a skilled ivory-turner and where tools were lent to craftsmen for princely commissions. Menzhausen describes the seven rooms and the loose order by which objects declined in importance from the first room to the last, and presents the Kunstkammer as a working collection rather than a microcosm. Menzhausen then sets it against Gabriel Kaldemarck's report of 1587, which proposed removing the tools and instruments in favour of an Italian-style art collection. The chapter concludes that the Dresden Kunstkammer was the forerunner of the scientific-technical museum.

Dresden Kunstkammer of Elector Augustus
The Munich Kunstkammer, 1565-1807Lorenz Seeligp. 101

Seelig reconstructs the Munich Kunstkammer that Duke Albrecht V of Bavaria founded in the 1560s and housed in a purpose-built four-winged building beside the Antiquarium. Seelig distinguishes it from the inalienable household treasures and the court library, and shows that it was conceived, in Quiccheberg's terms, as a wide-ranging theatre of historical and geographical objects. Using Fickler's inventory of 1598 and Hainhofer's account of 1611, he reconstructs the rooms, the ash-grey tables and cupboards, the silverwork, the Bavarian town models and the non-European objects, which were recorded under the labels 'Indian' or 'Turkish'. He compares the collection with Dresden and Ambras, arguing that it aimed at sumptuous abundance rather than systematic order, and that its scientific holdings were small. The later sections follow its decline: Maximilian I's withdrawal of the finest works to his private Kammergalerie, the Swedish plunder of 1632, and its survival as a phantom collection. Seelig concludes that Albrecht V was its authoritative creator and that it never regained its former character.

East and Southeast Asia Seelig notes that the Munich inventory records non-European objects under the rubrics 'Indian' and 'Turkish', and that from the Far East came some porcelain and lacquered wooden bowls, which possibly stem from Japan. The inventory of 1598 lists about 195 porcelain items, but their origin is not given. Otherwise East Asia receives no discussion, and Chinese and Japanese objects appear only in these passing references.

Munich Kunstkammer (Albrecht V)Munich AntiquariumMunich SchatzkammerKammergalerie of Maximilian I, Munich
Philipp Hainhofer and Gustavus Adolphus' Kunstschrank in UppsalaHans-Olof Boströmp. 111

Boström follows the Augsburg merchant and diplomat Philipp Hainhofer, whose private Kunstkammer, begun in 1604, drew princely visitors, and whose main achievement was a series of multi-purpose cabinets (Kunstschränke) that gathered collections in miniature. Boström shows how Hainhofer's trade fed his collection and how the Pomeranian, Florentine and Brunswick cabinets were made and sold. The chapter centres on the cabinet made for Gustavus Adolphus between 1625 and 1631, which the Augsburg council gave the king in 1632 and which now stands in Uppsala University. Boström describes its naturalia and artificialia, its biblical and allegorical imagery and its intarsia view of Augsburg, and argues against the view that its tools were merely symbolic: many objects were meant to be used or to surprise, such as an automatic virginal, mirror anamorphoses and 'vexing' objects. Boström reads the cabinet as a microcosm in the spirit of Robert Fludd and as a theatre of memory, linked to the art-of-memory teacher Lambert Schenkel. The chapter concludes that the cabinet's iconography is so dense that its meaning will remain open to debate.

Hainhofer's Kunstkammer, AugsburgGustavus Adolphus's Kunstschrank, Uppsala UniversityKunstschrank in the Pitti Palace, FlorenceAmbras Kunstkammer
The Kunstkammer of the Hessian Landgraves in KasselFranz Adrian Dreierp. 137

Dreier traces the Kunstkammer of the Landgraves of Hesse-Kassel from a medieval treasury to the public Museum Fridericianum of 1779, and argues that Kassel is one of the few places where the making of a public museum can be studied through surviving objects and buildings as well as documents. Dreier begins with the eastern and Islamic objects of the treasury, such as the celadon bowl and Syrian enamelled glass, and then turns to Landgrave Wilhelm IV, an astronomer whose collecting ranged from instruments and Jost Bürgi's work to portraits and a short-lived Venetian glass house. Dreier follows the collections into the stable building under Moritz the Learned, using the inventory of 1612 and the travel account of Lupold von Wedel to establish where the Kunstkammer stood. Landgrave Carl's Kunsthaus of 1709, which grouped art and curiosities by subject, and its successor, which admitted visitors, form the central section. The chapter concludes with the Museum Fridericianum, built between 1769 and 1779 to hold its collections from the outset, and with the wax figures of the landgraves that survived as a last concession to the older cabinets.

East and Southeast Asia Dreier notes that the celadon bowl, the earliest Chinese pottery documented as arriving in Europe, may have been brought by Count Philipp of Katzenelnbogen from an eastern journey and passed to the House of Hesse. In the eighteenth-century Kunsthaus one room displayed Chinese porcelain, and the costumes there included Chinese specimens, according to Schminke's description of 1767.

Kassel Kunstkammer of the Hessian LandgravesKunsthaus of Landgrave Carl, KasselMuseum Fridericianum, Kassel
13The Brandenburg Kunstkammer in BerlinChristian Theuerkauffp. 149

Theuerkauff traces the Kunstkammer of the Electors of Brandenburg in Berlin from its first preserved inventory of 1603 to its move, in 1703, into rooms in the new Berlin Schloss. Theuerkauff follows the collections through the Thirty Years War, when many objects were lost, and their revival under Friedrich Wilhelm, who bought antiquities and built up the Antiquitätenstube. The main focus is the reign of Friedrich III, when the Kunstkammer grew through purchase, inheritance and gifts, and when the antiquary Lorenz Beger took charge of the antiquities and the rarities. Theuerkauff describes the succession of officials, the decree of 1689 that ordered objects to be concentrated in one place, the acquisitions of naturalia and the Bellori collection, and the disputes that led to the separation of the Cabinet of Antiquities and Medals from the Kunst- und Naturalienkammer. Theuerkauff reconstructs the contents from Beger's publications and later descriptions, including ivories by Leonhard Kern and Leygebe, enamel portraits and presents from rulers. The chapter concludes with the separation of the cabinets and the Kunstkammer's move, in 1703, to rooms in the new Schloss, whose exact location he admits remains unresolved.

East and Southeast Asia Theuerkauff notes that from 1671 the Berlin collections acquired oriental weapons, porcelain and Indian manuscripts, mostly from the Dutch East India Company. In 1674 the Elector thanked the Dutch for rare seaplants and 'indianisch' arms from Batavia and asked for more. Otherwise East Asia receives only these passing references.

Brandenburg Kunstkammer, Berlin SchlossCabinet of Antiquities and Medals, Berlin
14Early Dutch Cabinets of CuriositiesTh. H. Lunsingh Scheurleerp. 157Asia: in part

Lunsingh Scheurleer surveys cabinets of curiosities in the Dutch Republic in the late sixteenth and seventeenth centuries and argues that they shared an emblematic view of God's creation. He opens with Crispin de Passe's title-page to the 'Catena aurea Platonis', which he uses as a key to the Low Countries collections. He then takes the reader through the collectors: the shell enthusiasts such as van Borsselen and Jan Govertsen, the coin and medal collectors, Abraham Gorlaeus and his rings, and the Reynst brothers, whose antique sculptures and pictures were valued as models and as food for thought. Exotic material from Asia and South America comes next, with the Princes of Orange at The Hague and Johan Maurits of Nassau's Brazilian museum as examples. Finally he examines Frederik Ruysch's anatomical collection in Amsterdam, with its moralizing vanitas groups, and quotes Swammerdam's dedication to Thévenot to show how collectors saw their work as the revelation of divine wisdom. The chapter concludes that the impulse to collect was shared across social classes, and that Ruysch was an extreme but not an isolated case.

East and Southeast Asia Lunsingh Scheurleer says the Asian material in Dutch collections was mainly Chinese and Japanese porcelain and lacquerwork. He describes the Princes of Orange at The Hague, whose De Oude Hof held large Chinese porcelain collections set on wall shelves, as recorded in an inventory of 1632, and the black-and-gold Japanese lacquer balusters ordered in Japan for the Huis ten Bosch. He notes a Chinese vase and a Japanese helmet and armour in Jacob van Campen's painting of the Treasures of East and West, and that Japanese lacquer became popular after the Dutch were granted the only European trading post in Japan.

Reynst collection, AmsterdamRuysch collection, AmsterdamJohan Maurits's museum, Mauritsstad (Brazil)Mauritshuis, The HagueHuis ten Bosch, The Hague
15Natural Philosophers and Princely Collectors: Worm, Paludanus, and the Gottorp and Copenhagen CollectionsH. D. Schepelernp. 167Asia: in part

Schepelern examines two northern collectors of the early seventeenth century, the Copenhagen professor Olaus Worm and the Enkhuizen physician Bernhard Paludanus, and the princely collections that absorbed them. Schepelern opens with the wars that made universities and collections vulnerable, and with medicine and natural philosophy in Copenhagen. Worm's collection, formed from about 1620, is the main subject: Schepelern describes the Museum Wormianum of 1655, a folio history of natural and artificial objects in four books, which followed the arrangement of Imperato and Calceolari and identified the narwhal tusk as a marine rather than a unicorn's horn. Paludanus is set beside him through his manuscript inventory of 1617-18, which Schepelern compares with a printed list of 1604 to show how the collection came to hold more objects from China, Japan and India, probably through the traveller Linschoten. He then traces both collections into the Gottorp Kunstkammer and the royal Kunstkammer in Copenhagen, and argues against Schlosser that princes and philosophers collected on the same systematic principles.

East and Southeast Asia Schepelern shows that Paludanus's manuscript inventory of 1617-18 contains a majority of objects from the Far East, meaning China, Japan and especially India, whereas the printed list of 1604 was drawn mainly from Europe and the Near East. Schepelern attributes the change to Paludanus's collaboration with Jan Huygens van Linschoten, who had lived in Goa and settled in Enkhuizen, and to the Asian objects that Linschoten brought back. Schepelern also notes that seventeen oriental objects that probably came from Paludanus's collection survive in the National Museum in Copenhagen.

Museum Wormianum, CopenhagenPaludanus collection, EnkhuizenGottorp KunstkammerRoyal Kunstkammer, Copenhagen
16From the Royal Kunstkammer to the Modern Museums of CopenhagenBente Gundestrupp. 177

Gundestrup follows the Royal Danish Kunstkammer from its foundation by King Frederik III after 1648 to its dispersal in the 1820s and the modern museums of Copenhagen. Gundestrup begins with Frederik's education, his travels in Holland and France and his years as Archbishop of Bremen, which she presents as the setting for his interest in exotic and ethnographic objects, and with the earlier Drehezimmer and Rosenborg collections of his predecessors. Gundestrup then describes how the Kunstkammer, housed in the castle and from about 1680 in its own building, grew by gifts such as Johan Maurits of Nassau's paintings by Eckhout, by purchase, by the incorporation of Worm's museum in 1655 and, by conquest, through the Gottorp collection. The central section examines the inventories of 1674, 1689, 1737 and later, and the numbering systems that tracked the objects. The last part describes the reorganization under Adam Hauch after 1802 and the transfers of 1821 to 1825, which split the collection among new museums. She ends by hoping to identify 90 per cent of the original royal collection.

East and Southeast Asia Gundestrup notes that some Japanese swords, knives and tapestries were kept in a small cabinet at Rosenborg, as a visitor recorded in 1623, and that the Kunstkammer's great collections of Japanese lacquer and Chinese porcelain were in place by the end of the seventeenth century, probably acquired through the minister Peder Charisius in the Dutch ports. The inventory of 1674 lists an East India Cabinet of ethnographic specimens. Otherwise Asian material is mentioned only in passing.

Royal Kunstkammer, CopenhagenRosenborg Castle collectionRoyal Art Museum (Kongelige Kunstmuseum), CopenhagenNational Museum, Copenhagen
Appendix: A note on the Rosenborg Collection in CopenhagenMogens Bencardp. 177
17Some Notes on Spanish Baroque CollectorsRonald Lightbownp. 189

Lightbown uses Vicente Carducho's dialogues of 1633 and the letters and descriptions of the Aragonese collector Vicencio Juan de Lastanosa to describe Spanish collecting in the Baroque age. Spanish collections followed Italian models, he suggests, but were driven by a universal curiosity for the rare and the marvellous. Carducho's tour of the Madrid collections introduces owners who combined paintings with swords, rock crystal and scientific instruments, such as the Marquis of Leganés, who used his collection to teach mathematics and artillery, and Don Gerónimo de Villafuerte, who made clocks himself. The chapter then turns to Aragon, where the Conde de Guimerá, Ximénez de Urrea and Lastanosa formed an erudite circle around Zaragoza and Huesca, devoted to Iberian and Aragonese coins. Lastanosa's house and museum, documented in descriptions of 1639, 1647 and 1662, occupy most of the essay, showing how the collection was built by purchase, inheritance, commission and gifts, and how his publications and his hostility to alchemy shaped it. The essay concludes that Lastanosa's museum had a European reputation and is better documented than any other seventeenth-century museum.

Lastanosa's museum, HuescaRoyal collections, Madrid
18The Cabinet of Curiosities in Seventeenth-Century BritainArthur MacGregorp. 201

MacGregor asks how the cabinet of curiosities took shape in seventeenth-century Britain, and argues that British collections were more diffuse, more private and later to start than the ordered Continental cabinets, with no princely taste for rarities. MacGregor begins with Walter Cope, whose collection is the earliest English one with detailed accounts, and then follows John Tradescant the elder and younger, whose museum at Lambeth, The Ark, was open to visitors for a fee. The chapter reconstructs the Ark from its 1656 catalogue and from visitors' accounts, and shows how Elias Ashmole's gift of it to Oxford produced the Ashmolean. It then surveys smaller cabinets: Robert Hubert's show near St Paul's, the modest Canterbury collection of John Bargrave, Ralph Thoresby's coin-heavy cabinet in Leeds, Scottish collections, Woodward, Browne, Petiver and Charleton, ending with Sloane, whose collection formed the basis of the British Museum. By the early eighteenth century connoisseurs of painting and sculpture had replaced curiosity as the common currency of British collecting.

East and Southeast Asia Asian material is passing only. Platter's 1599 account of Cope's cabinet lists porcelain and other items from China and a Javanese costume among exhibits from many parts of the world. The chapter adds nothing further on either region.

The Ark (Tradescant museum, Lambeth)Ashmolean MuseumHubert's museum, LondonBargrave cabinet, CanterburyThoresby museum, LeedsSloane collection
19The Cabinet Institutionalized: the Royal Society's 'Repository' and its BackgroundMichael Hunterp. 217

Hunter examines institutional collections in England in the seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries, which he places between private cabinets and public museums because a corporate body could outlast its members. Hunter argues that most of them, including college and university collections, were as miscellaneous as private cabinets, and tests this against the Royal Society's 'Repository', the most important of them. The chapter first surveys the Bodleian's coins and oddities, the Oxford Anatomy School, the East India House rarities seen by Magalotti in 1669, and the College of Physicians' 'Museum', which was mostly a library and was lost in the Fire of London. It then follows the Society's purchase in 1666 of Robert Hubert's cabinet, its hopes for a systematic collection, and Nehemiah Grew's 1681 catalogue, which showed the collection still dominated by exotic and monstrous items. Problems of staff, record-keeping and funds are traced until the collection was offered to the British Museum in 1779. Hunter concludes that the move from private to public was far less straightforward than the founders had assumed.

Royal Society repositoryAshmolean MuseumBodleian LibraryOxford Anatomy SchoolEast India House collectionCollege of Physicians museumHubert's cabinet
20Some Cabinets of Curiosities in European Academic InstitutionsWilliam Schupbachp. 231

Schupbach offers an allusive sketch, not a survey, of seven cabinets in four countries that were attached to universities, religious houses and other learned bodies. Schupbach argues that such cabinets were neither simply marvel-seeking nor purely rational, and that wonder was a proper response for the learned as well as the uninstructed. Schupbach starts with the medical museums of Pisa and Leiden, where physic gardens and anatomy theatres sheltered collections, and where Paaw's skeletons with memento mori mottoes were later expanded by van Heurn, who wrote to request Egyptian mummies and other objects. Schupbach then takes the surgeons' guild cabinet at Delft, the abbey of Sainte-Genevieve in Paris, Kircher's museum at the Jesuit college in Rome, and the Naturalienkabinett of Francke's orphanage at Halle. Academies rarely sustained museums, and Leibniz's cabinets existed only on paper. The chapter sets the defenders of the cabinet, who valued the old, fragmentary and enigmatic, against its critics, and argues that the creators' actions outweigh the critics' judgments.

East and Southeast Asia Asian material is passing only. Leiden's anatomy-theatre inventory of 1620 lists a Japanese teapot and Chinese scrolls among its exhibits, and Kircher's Rome museum drew on exotica from the Far East. Halle's cabinet, built on donations from missionaries, received gifts from former pupils sent as missionaries to the Far East.

Leiden anatomy theatrePisa physic garden galleryDelft surgeons' guild cabinetSainte-Genevieve abbey cabinetKircher museum, RomeHalle Naturalienkabinett
21Alive or Dead: Zoological Collections in the Seventeenth CenturyWilma Georgep. 245Asia: in part

George asks what seventeenth-century cabinets and menageries contributed to the ordering of natural history. George analyses the printed catalogues of thirteen cabinets, among them Tradescant's, Hubert's, the Royal Society's, Petiver's, Worm's and Kircher's, and two menageries at Versailles and London, counting 1,657 identifiable dead specimens and 227 live ones by type of animal and place of origin. Armadillos, birds of paradise and cassowaries recur in many collections, most specimens came from Europe, then South America and Africa, and North America is scarcely represented. She shows that specimens reached collectors mainly through sailors, traders and ships' cargoes rather than through the collectors' own expeditions, and that the cabinets were usually arranged haphazardly. The chapter then argues that Aldrovandi's mammal classification was followed by some collectors, but that curiosity collectors contributed little to the systematic work of Ray and Willughby, who relied on living and fresh animals. Its conclusion is that the cabinets gave viewers a way of seeing and questioning nature, rather than a science in themselves.

East and Southeast Asia The East Indies is a substantial source in this chapter. Birds of paradise were caught in New Guinea and sold to sailors calling at the Moluccas, and Schouten bartered for two in 1616; cassowaries came from the same area. A babyrousa skull from Celebes was often on show, Petiver labelled some butterflies as from Java, and Dampier's men bought cockatoos on Buru. Dutch East India Company ships carried live animals to Amsterdam, and Dutch captains returned from the East Indies with birds.

Tradescant's Ark, LambethRoyal Society repositoryVersailles menagerieWorm's museum, CopenhagenKircher's museum, RomeHubert's cabinet
22Conchology before LinnaeusHenry E. Coomansp. 257Asia: in part

Coomans surveys conchology, the study of shells, before Linnaeus's Systema Naturae of 1758, covering shell collecting, the collectors, the books and the fate of the collections. Coomans argues that shell collecting began in the Renaissance as Europeans brought shells back from the East and West Indies, and that early collectors such as Erasmus, Gesner and the Tradescants gathered everything curious rather than shells alone. Coomans distinguishes collectors who prized perfection and rarity from scientific collectors who valued knowledge, and sorts collectors into scholars, physicians, apothecaries and noblemen. The chapter then turns to illustrated books, notably Lister's Historia Conchyliorum and Rumphius's account of shells from Amboina, which he treats as the first field-based work on tropical shells. He traces collections by Petiver, Seba, the French royal cabinet and Sloane, notes how few early originals survive, and describes the Dutch 'Lovers of Neptune's Cabinet' and eighteenth-century shell auctions. The chapter closes with shells pasted over grottoes and clocks, which he takes to mark the end of the cabinet of curiosity.

East and Southeast Asia Amboina (Ambon) is central to the chapter's Asian material. Rumphius, employed there by the Dutch East India Company from 1656, wrote on its shells, observed tropical species in the field, recorded local uses of shells for food, tools and shell trumpets, and sold shells to Cosimo de' Medici, some of which survive in Pisa. The introduction also notes that the Chinese long ago made Buddha figures from mother-of-pearl.

Ashmolean MuseumCabinet du Roi, ParisSeba collection, AmsterdamSloane collection
23'Curiosities to adorn Cabinets and Gardens'John Dixon Huntp. 267

Hunt traces the relationship between the cabinet of curiosities and the garden, arguing that in the Italian Renaissance and then in England the two were closely linked as places for displaying rarities, and that by the late seventeenth century they had separated. Hunt draws mainly on Evelyn's Italian diary, which treats gardens as cabinets of antiquities, shells, citrus trees and grottoes, and which calls Rome the world's sole cabinet. The botanical gardens at Pisa and Leiden, the hydraulic theatre of the Villa Aldobrandini and Thomas Bushell's Enstone grotto show how garden display used art to contest nature. The chapter then follows English examples: Arundel's sculpture garden beside the Thames, the Tradescants' garden at Lambeth, Howard's amphitheatre garden with its laboratory, and the botanical garden founded at Oxford. Hunt concludes that the garden and the museum each came to occupy its own territory, so that grottoes and garden cabinets became fossils of an earlier tradition.

Tradescant's Ark, LambethAshmolean MuseumArundel sculpture garden, LondonPisa botanical garden galleryLeiden Ambulacrum
24Early Collecting in the Field of GeologyHugh Torrensp. 281

Torrens traces geological collecting from the sixteenth to the early eighteenth century, arguing that collectors and museum-keepers built the basic methods of the field before the eighteenth century. Torrens starts with fossils valued as curiosities, charms and medicines, and then follows the classifications of Agricola and Gesner, and Kentmann's illustrated mineral cabinet at Torgau. Italian collectors, notably Mercati at the Vatican, Colonna and the Accademia dei Lincei, are presented as ahead of others in identifying true fossils, while Worm, Merret and the Tradescant catalogue show how northern museums arranged stones and minerals. The chapter then turns to England: Plot and Lhwyd at the Ashmolean, and Hooke, who argued for organic origins of fossils and urged the Royal Society to build a repository of them. Woodward is its central figure, since his instructions to collectors required numbered specimens and recorded depth and stratum, and his cabinets went to Cambridge. Torrens concludes that the bases of scientific collection, documentation and curation were in place by the end of the seventeenth century.

Ashmolean MuseumRoyal Society repositoryMuseum Tradescantianum (The Ark)Worm's museum, CopenhagenAldrovandi museum, BolognaWoodward's cabinets, Cambridge
25The Cabinet of Experimental PhilosophyGerard L'E. Turnerp. 295

Turner argues that the cabinet of experimental philosophy, a collection of instruments for experiment and teaching, had economic as well as intellectual roots, and that its origins lie earlier than its flowering in the later seventeenth century. Turner places it within a general account of collecting as self-advertisement, economic use and intellectual satisfaction, illustrated with Louis XIV, the Medici and the Kunstkammer. The core of the chapter is the problem of longitude, which drove the work of Tycho Brahe, Kepler, Flamsteed, Gilbert and Galileo, and the instrument trade that grew up at Louvain, Augsburg and London. He traces the instrument rooms of princes such as Wilhelm IV of Hesse, Rudolf II and Francesco I, the Accademia del Cimento, the Ashmolean and the Royal Observatories in Paris and Greenwich. Later collections include Teyler's Museum in Haarlem and the lecturing of Whiston. Turner concludes that the cabinet was an amalgam of laboratory and teaching apparatus, and that its eighteenth-century role in popularizing science rested on the same economic imperative that had driven its making.

Ashmolean MuseumTeyler's Museum, HaarlemReale Gabinetto di Fisica, FlorenceScience Museum, London (George III collection)Orrery collection, Christ Church
26Greek and Roman Antiquities in the Seventeenth CenturyMichael Vickersp. 309

Vickers argues that the seventeenth century changed attitudes to classical antiquity more radically than any earlier period, and he examines two traditions of collecting. Vickers starts with the Renaissance, when princes and popes used Roman antiquities to claim imperial and temporal authority, and when gems and sculpture were valued as convertible wealth, as with Cardinal Barbo's cameos and Lorenzo de' Medici's gems. Vickers contrasts this 'aristocratic' approach with the antiquarian tradition of local scholars, illustrated by Scott's Oldbuck and Sir Arthur Wardour, and by the Luxemburg Jesuit brothers Wiltheim and the Canterbury canon Casaubon, who studied Roman pottery and glass. The main case is Thomas Howard, Earl of Arundel, whose Roman statues, Greek sculpture and inscriptions from Smyrna were displayed at Arundel House and in its garden, and whose buying was shaped by his political ambitions. Vickers concludes that neglect of pottery reflects the values of precious metal, and that antiquaries' interest in pots tells us as much about modern assumptions as about the ancient past.

Arundel House collectionAmerbach cabinet, BaselMedici collection, FlorenceCharles I royal collectionAshmolean Museum
27North American Ethnography in the Collection of Sir Hans SloaneJ. C. H. Kingp. 319

King examines the North American ethnographic material in English cabinets of the seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries, and notes that no systematic study of it had been made. King identifies material in the Tradescant catalogue of 1656, the Royal Society's repository and Thoresby's Leeds cabinet, and then concentrates on the collection of Hans Sloane, whose Miscellanies list 2,111 items, of which some 210 seem to be North American. The chapter sorts these by origin, with Hudson Bay and Greenland, New England, the Carolinas and Virginia as the largest groups, and by type, from wampum, scalps and drums to snowshoes, bows, moccasins and flaked stone points. King's key point is documentation: Sloane's correspondence survives and records donors and dates for many items, which makes him one of the first scientific collectors of ethnographic material, although he never classified his collection. Donors included the botanist John Bartram, whose letters describe the field contexts of pipes and sherds. King concludes that the Sloane material is closer to the cabinets of the previous century than to the later museums, which displayed ethnography in whole rooms.

Sloane collection (British Museum)Tradescant's Ark, LambethRoyal Society repositoryThoresby museum, Leeds
28Mexico and South America in the European WunderkammerChristian Feestp. 327

Feest surveys the surviving and documented Mexican and South American objects in sixteenth- and seventeenth-century European Wunderkammern, to show what early collecting contributes to knowledge of extinct cultures, which selective principles governed collecting, and which objects need better documentation. Feest takes Mexican featherwork, mosaics and stone sculpture in turn, separating pre-Columbian pieces from colonial ones made for Christian devotion, and then turns to Taino artefacts from the West Indies and to Brazilian clubs, anchor axes, featherwork and hammocks. Much of the evidence comes from the Ambras collection, whose inventory of 1596 is the key early record for several Mexican pieces, and from Copenhagen, where the Gottorp and Worm collections hold many Brazilian objects, most probably from the activities of Johan Maurits of Nassau. Feest checks each object's history against catalogues and inventories and finds that most early losses happened before objects entered Kunstkammer collections. Feest concludes that the typology of Brazilian clubs and axes is poorly worked out, and that no identification should be accepted without firm documentation. The chapter ends by noting how few early collections include Andean, and especially Peruvian, material.

East and Southeast Asia Asia is passing only. Six Copenhagen bows listed in 1689 as Japanese or East Indian are discussed only to question whether they are really Brazilian, and an early colonial obsidian mirror in Vienna was once thought to be Chinese.

Ambras collection, Schloss AmbrasGottorp collection, CopenhagenWorm museum, CopenhagenBibliotheque Sainte-Genevieve, ParisCospi collection, Bologna
29African Material in Early CollectionsEzio Bassani and Malcolm McLeodp. 334

Bassani and McLeod argue that few African artefacts survive from before the nineteenth century, partly because of the roles objects played in African systems of thought, and that the best route to what survives is through the royal, noble and bourgeois collections that held even small numbers of African items. They begin with the earliest records, including Charles the Bold's purchase in 1470 and the Congo presentations to the King of Portugal in 1489, and set out three broad categories of object: things made for local use that Europeans found interesting, things valued for their materials, and things made in Africa to Western models. Their main subject is the Afro-Portuguese ivories made at Benin and in the Bulom or Sherbro areas, horns, spoons and salt-cellars, perhaps two hundred of which survive, many used as diplomatic gifts. They then follow the holdings through the Medici, Ambras, Settala, Cospi, Kircher, Weickmann, Danish royal, Gottorp and Sloane collections, showing how inventories and watercolours date them. They conclude that many African items reached European collections long before any record of them, so that their histories are often lost.

Medici collection, FlorenceAmbras collection, InnsbruckSettala collection, MilanCospi collection, BolognaMuseo Kircheriano, RomeWeickmann collection, Ulm
30Exotica from IslamJulian Rabyp. 345Asia: in part

Raby asks how objects from the Islamic world reached European cabinets of curiosities, and whether cabinets treated them differently from the Islamic textiles and metalwork in princely treasuries. Raby traces the medieval religious treasuries, which held silks, rock crystal and enamelled glass, and then the gifts exchanged with Safavid Persia, the Ottomans and the Barbary states, which princes received at the highest quality and mainly in textiles. Raby considers the rationale of the cabinet, arguing that virtuosi chose Islamic objects for materials or techniques unavailable in Europe, or for historical associations, which were often mistaken. Medicinal earths such as terra lemnia, Turkish daggers, captured Ottoman weapons and Iznik pottery are the main categories, and their scarcity is explained by the decline of Islamic arts in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Raby's central finding is that the cabinets held mostly contemporary Ottoman objects that illustrated Islam at war, and almost no textiles, which were treated as utilitarian. Raby concludes that the divide between Schatzkammer and Wunderkammer was above all a material one.

East and Southeast Asia Asian material is mainly porcelain. Hard-paste porcelain was the monopoly of the Far East, and cabinet owners such as Ferdinand of Austria and Philip II acquired blue-and-white pieces, some via Turkey or Lisbon. A Chinese writer of 1387 is quoted on damascened steel, and Holland received large cargoes of Chinese and later Japanese porcelain in the seventeenth century, which displaced Iznik ware. Persian pottery imitating Chinese blue-and-white was sold in Holland as Chinese.

Medici Guardaroba, FlorenceRudolf II Kunstkammer, PragueCospi collection, BolognaSettala collection, MilanTradescant's Ark, LambethRoyal Kunstkammer, Copenhagen
31The Early China TradeJohn Ayersp. 353Asia: chiefly

Ayers surveys the Chinese arts and artefacts that reached European collections before the eighteenth century, asking how they travelled and how they were understood. Sixteenth-century Europeans knew little of China, since foreigners were confined to southern ports, and inventories often labelled Chinese, Japanese and Southeast Asian goods alike as 'Indian'. He examines three early porcelains: a vase in the Treasury of San Marco in Venice, the Gaignieres-Fonthill ewer and a Longquan celadon dish once owned by the Medici, whose routes (through the Middle East, as diplomatic gifts or with missionaries) remain uncertain. The paper then follows the Portuguese trade from Malacca and Macao and the Italian and northern courts that bought porcelain, silks and paintings. Schloss Ambras at Innsbruck, with its 1596 inventory, supplies most of the detail, including rhinoceros-horn cups, ivory and soapstone figures and a Chinese landscape painting. Seventeenth-century Dutch trade brought Yixing teapots and Coromandel lacquer to Copenhagen. The paper ends at Charlottenburg, where porcelain covers whole walls, and suggests that the cabinet of curiosities was becoming decoration.

East and Southeast Asia Chinese porcelain, silks, paintings, carvings and Yixing teapots form the whole subject. Ayers covers Chinese goods in Venice, Florence, Dresden and Innsbruck, and the trade routed through Malacca, a Southeast Asian port where Chinese merchants met the Portuguese. Ayers notes that Chinese, Japanese and Southeast Asian objects were confused under 'Indian' in inventories, and that some Ambras lacquer was assigned to factories in the Ryukyu Islands.

Schloss Ambras, InnsbruckRoyal Danish Kunstkammer, CopenhagenDresden KunstkammerMedici collection, FlorenceMuseo degli Argenti, FlorenceTreasury of San Marco, VeniceCharlottenburg Palace, Berlin
32Japan: Trade and Collecting in Seventeenth-Century EuropeOliver Impeyp. 365Asia: chiefly

Impey traces the Japanese goods that reached European collections in the seventeenth century, chiefly lacquer, porcelain, screens and furniture, and asks which were trade goods and which were collectors' pieces. Impey divides the commerce into two periods, before the closure of Japan in 1639, when Portuguese and Chinese traders dominated, and after it, when the Dutch and Chinese shared the monopoly, and explains how goods passed through middlemen. Early Namban-style pieces came with the Jesuit embassy of 1584, and an inventoried cabinet at Ambras shows the lacquer that followed. Impey then follows the Dutch orders for lacquered coffers and cabinets, the arrival of Arita porcelain after 1650, and the inventories of Burghley House and Dresden. The chapter ends with the van Diemen box, now in the Victoria and Albert Museum, a special gift that passed through Pompadour to William Beckford. Impey concludes that such objects moved from trade into private collecting over the century.

East and Southeast Asia Japan is the whole subject: Namban-style and export lacquer (coffers, cabinets, scriptors, screens), Arita porcelain (blue-and-white, Imari and Kakiemon) and Japanese paper. Impey covers the trade through Portuguese, Chinese, Dutch and English middlemen at Nagasaki, Hirado and Deshima, and the Japanese converts who came to Europe in 1584 with lacquer and screens. Southeast Asia appears in an order of 1680 by the Siam office for Constant Phaulkon, who ruled Siam, for lacquered dishes to be given to the French court. Chinese merchants and their lacquer furniture also feature, since they undercut Japanese work after the 1680s.

Schloss Ambras, InnsbruckRoyal Danish Kunstkammer, CopenhagenDresden porcelain collection of Augustus the StrongBurghley House, StamfordVictoria and Albert MuseumGripsholm Castle
33Indian Art and Artefacts in Early European CollectingRobert Skeltonp. 375

Skelton asks which objects in early European collections really came from India or Ceylon, since inventories used 'Indian' far more widely. Skelton tests attributions by looking closely, so that a rock-crystal elephant in Vienna is ruled out because it does not look like an elephant, and he reattributes several pieces that earlier writers assigned to India. Most of the chapter follows objects that can be traced: Gujarati mother-of-pearl work such as a shield in the Bargello, katar daggers in Copenhagen and Oxford, and chintz and carpets commissioned by East India merchants. Furniture at Uppsala and ebony chairs once owned by Horace Walpole and William Beckford are judged doubtful or well documented. The longest section concerns Mughal and Deccan paintings that reached Rembrandt, Schellinks and the Richardson collection, some now at the Ashmolean. Skelton ends with the Pala Vishnu given to the Ashmolean in 1695, which Harle identified as an early and securely documented piece of Indian sculpture in the West. Skelton concludes that little of real importance from India reached Europe before the eighteenth century.

Janes, Robert R. (2009). Museums in a Troubled World: Renewal, Irrelevance or Collapse?. London: Routledge.Asia: slight9 chapter overviews

Overview

Robert R. Janes's 2009 book is a practitioner's polemic on whether museums can respond to a troubled world of energy, climate, population and biodiversity stress. Janes argues that museums have been captured by market values, by internal habits and by a fixation on collections, and that they have stopped asking why they exist. Janes’s remedy is for museums to become stewards of their communities and environments, moving from temple to forum and working as an ecology of interdependent organisations. The book has seven chapters after a foreword by Elaine Heumann Gurian and a prologue of fables and an account of the Willow Lake Dene: museums and irrelevance, a troubled world, internal self-inflicted challenges, the marketplace, resilient examples, the mindful museum, and stewards or spectators. Its scope is mainly Canadian and North American museums, with examples from Britain and Australia.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia receive only passing attention, and no chapter is devoted to either region. Chapter 2 (A troubled world) notes that 80 percent of China's 50,000 kilometres of major river systems no longer support fish, as a counterpoint to its economic growth; it lists business entertainment in Japan among global consumption figures; and it names Cambodia and East Timor among the genocides treated in the Imperial War Museum's 'Crimes against Humanity' exhibition. Chapter 4 (Debunking the marketplace) cites China's plan for 1,000 new museums by 2015 and the 60,000 square metre Capital Museum in Beijing as examples of vanity architecture, without discussing Chinese museums or their collections. Chapter 5 (Searching for resilience) describes the Morikami Museum and Japanese Gardens in Delray Beach, Florida, a Japanese-style garden and cultural centre in the United States, where a depression study was run, and it says nothing about Japan itself.

What is absent is as striking as what is present: there is no discussion of Asian objects in Western museums, colonial collecting, Asian states' museum or heritage policy, Asian visitors or curators, or restitution claims from the region. The restitution discussion, which centres on the Universal Museum Declaration and the Parthenon sculptures (chapter 3) and on Canadian First Nations (chapter 2), concerns no Asian collections.

ChinaJapanCambodiaEast Timor

Theoretical approach of this work
Book CoverPDF p. 2

ContentsPDF p. 8
FiguresPDF p. 10

ForewordElaine Heumann GurianPDF p. 14

Gurian introduces Janes's book as a personal and passionate polemic about museums' failure to change. Gurian summarizes his claim that museums have been captured by market values and internal agendas, and his hopes for mindfulness, shared leadership, ecological sustainability and collections as a record of material diversity. Gurian finds the book provocative rather than a how-to guide, and suggests it be read chapter by chapter in staff discussion groups.

Prologuep. 1

The Prologue combines a First Nations story of an animal council that decides whether to help humans, an account of the Willow Lake Dene, a hunting community in Canada's subarctic, and three fictional vignettes about museum staff. The Dene section shows the gap in collections: in The Athapaskans: Strangers of the North, only 57 of 268 specimens were wooden, and most of those were made in the twentieth century. The vignettes present a curator haunted by undocumented collections, an exhibit technician whose attempt to move a sacred rattle without its ethnologist shatters a glass case, and a chief executive pursuing a market plan without consulting staff, who is shot in his office. A closing parable of a ship whose admirals squabble over its parts until it runs out of food and fuel sets the book's theme. Janes uses these fables to show the uncertainties museums face and to set up his claim that they must rethink their purpose.

Royal Scottish MuseumNational Museum of Man
11 Museums and irrelevancep. 13

Janes argues that museums have drifted into captivity to market economics and their own internal agendas, and have stopped asking why they exist. Janes rests this on five assumptions: that people co-create their organizations, that museums could be the freest workplaces, that learning means questioning, that the future cannot be known, and that museums are irreplaceable places for reflecting on what it means to be human. Janes contrasts performers, who avoid failure, with learners, and says museums are inveterate performers. Janes criticizes elitism, since most museums serve the most educated and affluent, and the reliance on corporate sponsorship, illustrated by a 1994 conference in Grenoble. Janes also points to self-inflicted problems, including vanity architecture, fundraising priorities and peer pressure against reflection. The chapter closes by calling for an ecology of museums built on interdependence, choosing renewal over decline, with the future invented through courage.

22 A troubled worldp. 26

Janes argues that museums ignore the major stresses on the planet, including energy, climate, population and biodiversity loss, and the disappearance of indigenous cultures. Janes opens with the Copenhagen Consensus rankings and Homer-Dixon's five stresses, then recalls Duncan Cameron's 1971 call for museums to become forums as well as temples. A virtual survey of eight flagship Canadian museums finds that most omit the environment from their goals; only the Canadian Museum of Nature states an explicit commitment. Janes sets against this the Western Development Museum's footprint target, the Buffon Declaration of natural history institutions and the Encyclopaedia of Life. Drawing on his fieldwork among the Willow Lake Dene, he discusses language loss and examples such as Te Papa and the Sites of Conscience network. He diagnoses reductionism, dualism and neo-classical economics as causes of failed stewardship. The chapter closes by previewing the next chapter, on the internal habits that hold museums back.

East and Southeast Asia Janes notes in passing that 80 percent of China's 50,000 kilometres of major river systems no longer support fish because of pollution, as a counterpoint to the country's economic growth. Nothing else in the chapter concerns East or Southeast Asia.

Canadian Museum of CivilizationCanadian Museum of NatureRoyal Ontario MuseumRoyal BC MuseumWestern Development MuseumImperial War MuseumTe Papa TongarewaKelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum
33 It’s a jungle in here: Museums and their self-inflicted challengesp. 57

Janes diagnoses the internal habits that keep museums from engaging with the world's problems. Drawing on Will Phillips's three agendas, he argues that museums focus on content and neglect organization and change. He examines the fallacy of authoritative neutrality through the American Museum of Natural History's eugenics-tinged Hall of the Age of Man and the Museum of Modern Art's 1940 cancelled exhibition 'For Us, the Living'. He criticizes the lone director model, proposing a primus inter pares alternative, and draws on the hunting way of life to argue for self-organized teams. He then questions exhibitions, which he calls linear books, and collections, whose unchecked growth he links to elite self-interest and the Universal Museum Declaration. Grading and deaccessioning at the Glenbow Museum and shared stewardship at Te Papa are offered as remedies. The chapter closes by asking whether museums have become microcosms of unbridled consumption.

American Museum of Natural HistoryMuseum of Modern ArtGlenbow MuseumTe Papa Tongarewa
44 Debunking the marketplacep. 94

Janes argues that marketplace ideology and corporatism are pulling museums away from their purpose. Janes draws on his own career, from a publicly funded northern museum in Canada, to a science institute with a mixed funding model, to the Glenbow Museum in Calgary, where a 1992 deficit projection forced a turn to commercial ventures and earned revenue. Janes then names four symptoms of the market model: short-term thinking, money as the measure of worth, culture as consumption and business tribalism on boards. Janes’s evidence includes attendance-based performance measures, the Royal Ontario Museum's restaurant and fundraising plans, bond-financed building, the 'Bilbao Effect' at the Guggenheim Bilbao, and the failed Glenbow courtship with the oil company EnCana. Janes concludes that museums are complex mixed portfolios whose stewardship cannot be run on the bottom line, and that they should examine their values rather than adopt business methods wholesale. The chapter ends by asking whether museums will be stewards or spectators.

East and Southeast Asia China appears only as an example of the building boom: Janes cites its plan for 1,000 new museums by 2015 and the renovated Capital Museum in Beijing, which at 60,000 square metres he says is as large as the Louvre. He uses these figures to criticize vanity architecture rather than to discuss Chinese museums or their collections.

Glenbow MuseumRoyal Ontario MuseumGuggenheim Museum BilbaoPrince of Wales Northern Heritage CentreSmithsonian Institution
55 Searching for resiliencep. 121

Janes searches for museums that have resisted the marketplace and taken up social relevance, which he calls resilience. Janes’s examples include the Field Museum in Chicago, whose programs link biodiversity conservation with urban community research; a Morikami Museum garden study finding that walking in a Japanese-style garden relieved depression as well as art therapy did; Glasgow's Gallery of Modern Art, which built exhibitions and outreach around asylum seekers; the Quebec Economuseum network of craft workshops; the UK Museums Association's benevolent fund and sustainability paper; and the Murray-Darling Outreach Project of the National Museum of Australia, which left controversial community content online. Each case shows that resilience comes from loosening the links between growth, consumption and museum success, and from working across disciplines, hierarchies and boundaries. He concludes that size and money are not prerequisites, only leadership and the courage to act beyond the museum walls.

East and Southeast Asia Only the Morikami Museum and Japanese Gardens in Delray Beach, Florida, touches the region: a centre for Japanese arts and culture whose 16-acre Japanese-style garden, with its lake, cascades, gates and roofed contemplation pavilion, hosted the depression study. The chapter describes the garden's features but says nothing about Japan itself.

Field MuseumMorikami Museum and Japanese GardensGallery of Modern Art, GlasgowNational Museum of Australia
66 The mindful museump. 147

Janes applies the Buddhist idea of mindfulness, moment-to-moment awareness of what one is doing, to museums. Janes criticizes Adam Gopnik's use of the word for an object-centred museum, arguing that the preoccupation with collections is itself an obstacle. Janes describes the 'chatter' that fills museum life, including visitor pressures, governance, staff stress and negativity, which crowds out purpose. To break this habit he proposes thinking 'orthogonally', a rotation of consciousness that keeps conventional practice but questions its assumptions. Practical suggestions include study circles run without experts, strategic thinking that asks what not to do, scenario planning with 'what if' questions, ecosystem-style management that shares authority with citizens, and a reimagined role for curators. A governance case, in which a board chair's conduct was handled through a director's review committee, shows how a museum can protect its director. The chapter ends by imagining a mindful, post-museum organization whose mission asks why it exists rather than how it works.

Ontario Science CentreField MuseumGallery of Modern Art, Glasgow
77 Museums: Stewards or spectators?p. 169

Janes asks whether museums care about their wider relationships and their place in a troubled world. Janes recalls a 1976 Canadian conference that urged engagement with social and environmental issues, and an early American environmental handbook, both largely ignored. Janes sets out funding figures showing that Canada's four national museums in Ottawa receive about CA$205 million a year, against roughly CA$20 million for the country's other museums, and cites a UK government paper complaining that museums fail to communicate their value. Janes argues that museums remain trusted public institutions that can renew themselves, and offers six reasons: their autonomy, their role as seed banks of material knowledge, their diversity as a global network, their local rootedness, their capacity to bridge the sciences and humanities, and their duty to bear witness. The chapter ends by saying that museums must become community organisations of the highest order, since anything less means irrelevance and possible collapse.

Canadian national museums in OttawaCanadian Museum for Human RightsScience Museum, London
