Jasanoff, Maya (2005). Edge of Empire: Conquest and Collecting in the East, 1750–1850. London: Fourth Estate.Asia: slight11 chapter overviews

Overview

Edge of Empire studies how British and French imperial expansion in India and Egypt between 1750 and 1850 was lived and shaped through the people who collected objects there, from Robert Clive and the mixed court world of Lucknow to Napoleon's savants, the Seringapatam trophies of Tipu Sultan's defeat and the Anglo-French contest for Egyptian antiquities. Its main argument is that the British empire was contingent, collaborative and contested by indigenous powers and by France, not a triumphal or purely oppositional project. The book is organised chronologically in three parts (India, 1750-1799; Imperial Collision, 1798-1801; Egypt, 1801-1840) with an introduction and a conclusion that moves to the Somnath gates and the Marble Palace in Calcutta. Its scope is South Asia and Egypt, and the museum institutions it follows are the East India Company's Oriental Repository (later the India Museum), the British Museum, the Louvre and the Townley Gallery.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East Asia gets one paragraph and Southeast Asia gets passing mentions. The one substantial East Asian case is in chapter six, The Objects of Victory (lines 7146-7162): the 1860 sacking and burning of the Chinese emperor's Summer Palace by Britain's high commissioner after the second Opium War, which scattered its objects across Britain and France. Jasanoff sets this beside the Seringapatam collecting as a demonised enemy whose possessions Europeans eagerly collected. The conclusion (lines 11989-11990) lists the Opium Wars of 1839-1842 and 1859-1860 among the scattered imperial wars, and the notes cite James Hevia on the Summer Palace.

Southeast Asia appears in chapter one, Conquests (lines 372-373 and 1059-1064): the Dutch controlled the spice islands of modern Indonesia, and the 1623 Amboina attack on English traders at a Company post turned English traders away from the spice islands towards India. Java recurs only as a British campaign target in 1811 (lines 7803, 8331), and Singapore only as a garrison station for Indian sepoys by the century's end (line 12020). Burma and China are named as places where Company troops fought after Egypt (line 8017).

Chinese goods appear as objects in household inventories: de Boigne's lost trunk held eight Chinese metal spittoons (line 3742), in chapter three, Compromises. In chapter two, Crossings, chinoiserie is raised once, as a European style built in Gujarat (line 3088). Japan, Korea, Siam, Vietnam, Malaya and the Philippines (the last only in a footnote on Kipling, line 12801) are not discussed. The book has no Asian visitors, curators or scholars from East or Southeast Asia, and no restitution or heritage-policy material from those regions.

ChinaIndonesiaJavaSingaporeBurma

Contents

Theoretical approach of this work
A World of Empires, an Empire of the Worldp. 3

Jasanoff opens with the Marble Palace in Calcutta, a Palladian house full of European art owned by a Hindu family, to argue for a history of empire seen from its eastern edges. The book studies Britain's acquisition of territory in India and Egypt between 1750 and 1850 through the people who collected objects there. The evidence is the material trail they left: Mughal letters in an Alpine archive, a tiger-headed sword from Seringapatam in a Tuscan villa, and an inscription at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Britain was marginal to Mughal and Ottoman power and at war with France for decades, Jasanoff argues, so its empire was more contingent and collaborative than triumphalist accounts allow. The sections follow Robert Clive in Bengal, the court at Lucknow, the campaigns in Egypt and Seringapatam, and antiquities collecting in Egypt. The introduction closes by rejecting both imperial triumphalism and nationalist condemnation, and asks instead what empires did, to whom, and how.

Marble Palace, CalcuttaMetropolitan Museum of Art, New York
Part OneIndia, 1750-1799p. 15
Chapter OneConquestsp. 17

Conquests argues that the Seven Years War made Britain an empire that was both Atlantic and Asian, with India, not the thirteen colonies, becoming its centre of gravity. It opens with Wolfe's victory at Quebec in 1759 and its afterlife in Benjamin West's painting The Death of General Wolfe, which projects a patriotic clash of civilizations. Plassey in 1757 is treated as the more consequential battle: Robert Clive won Bengal through a conspiracy with Mir Jafar, and monsoon rain disabled the nawab's artillery. Going back to 1600, the chapter explains the East India Company's factories, its rivalries with the Dutch and French, and the Mughal decline that opened India to outsiders. Its second half follows Clive's fortune into land, parliamentary seats, and an art collection of Old Masters and Indian objects, all aimed at a British peerage. The parliamentary inquiry of 1772 and Clive's death in 1774 close the chapter, which concludes that Clive of India and Clive of Britain were one man.

East and Southeast Asia Southeast Asia appears only in passing. The Dutch controlled the spice islands of modern Indonesia, and the 1623 Amboina attack, in which Dutch soldiers killed English traders at a company post, drove English traders away from the spice islands towards India. The chapter does not treat either region further.

Robert Clive's private collection (Indian curiosities and Old Master paintings)
Chapter TwoCrossingsp. 45

Crossings uses the careers of Antoine Polier, Claude Martin and the nawab Asaf ud-Daula to argue that British India in the late eighteenth century was still a loose, mixed world rather than a settled British possession. It opens with Polier's 1768 panorama of Calcutta, a flattering view painted by a Swiss-born engineer shut out of Company promotion. The chapter then shows how many non-British Europeans served the Company and how much of the subcontinent remained under Mughal and princely rule. Its central section portrays Lucknow, the court city of Awadh, as a cosmopolitan centre where Europeans and Indians collected manuscripts, paintings and music and reinvented themselves. Elizabeth Plowden's diary, which records her receiving a Mughal title, shows how ordinary such crossings were. The chapter closes by setting Martin's European collection, catalogued in eighty pages, against Asaf's Aina Khana, a hall of English clocks and mirrors. Jasanoff concludes that Lucknow was both Indian and European at once, and asks how long that mixture could last.

Aina Khana (Mirror Hall) of Asaf ud-Daula's palace, LucknowClaude Martin's collection, LucknowAntoine Polier's manuscript collection
Chapter ThreeCompromisesp. 81

Compromises is the third chapter of Jasanoff's Edge of Empire. It follows three Europeans who built mixed Indian and European lives in Awadh and the Maratha dominions and then had to decide whether, and how, to leave India: Antoine Polier, Benoit de Boigne and Claude Martin. Polier went back to Lausanne and then to Provence, where bandits murdered him in 1795; his manuscripts survived through his cousin Marie de Polier. De Boigne, who had raised an army for Mahadji Scindia, reached England in 1797 with his Indian wife Nur and their children, lost his arms and objects when the Cromberg sank, and married again in London before retreating to Savoy. Martin stayed in Lucknow and built the house and tomb Constantia. Using wills, inventories and receipts, Jasanoff shows the mixed world being split into new categories of object, person and nation. The chapter ends with the founding of the East India Company's Oriental Repository, later the India Museum, in 1801.

India Museum
Part TwoImperial Collision, 1798-1801p. 115
Chapter FourInvading Egyptp. 117

Invading Egypt opens Part Two and argues that the Revolutionary-Napoleonic Wars, begun after Louis XVI's execution in 1793, were ideological, mass-mobilised and explicitly imperial in a way earlier Anglo-French wars were not. Jasanoff then traces the long build-up to the French invasion of Egypt: the Nathalia disaster of 1779, George Baldwin's campaign for a British conquest, and a dozen French plans drawn up by officers, consuls and merchants. Most of the chapter follows Napoleon's landing in 1798, the Battle of the Nile that stranded his army, and his attempts to win Egyptians through pro-Islamic proclamations, festivals and a fatwa on conversion. The Cairo revolt of October 1798 and its bloody suppression show the limits of that strategy. Jasanoff sets the savants' collecting in Egypt beside Wellesley's display of Mysorean trophies as two forms of imperial collecting. The chapter ends with Napoleon's letter to Tipu Sultan of January 1799, which set up the campaign in Mysore.

Chapter FiveSeizing Seringapatamp. 149

Seizing Seringapatam is a case study of Mysore under Tipu Sultan and its alliance with France. Jasanoff opens with the Jacobin Club founded among French residents of Seringapatam in 1797, then traces the Franco-Mysorean relationship from Haidar Ali's use of French officers and gunners, through the battle of Pollilur in 1780, to Tipu's embassy to Versailles in 1788. Louis XVI offered only festivals and porcelain, and Tipu's hopes of ten thousand French troops were repeatedly disappointed. Using Ripaud's visit, Napoleon's intercepted letter of 1799 and Richard Wellesley's war plans, the chapter argues that the Fourth Mysore War was shaped by the wider Anglo-French conflict and that Wellesley's evidence of French collusion was tailored to his war. It then recounts the storming of Seringapatam on 4 May 1799, Tipu's death and the prize agents' accounts of the plunder. The chapter closes with the British legend of the fall, carried by a panorama, plays and pamphlets, and with the first Company surveys of Mysore.

India MuseumLyceum
Chapter SixThe Objects of Victoryp. 177

The Objects of Victory, the last chapter of Part Two, follows the trophies and private collections made after the fall of Seringapatam. It starts with Tipu's Tiger, a mechanical wooden tiger devouring a British soldier, which was shown at India House from 1808 and which Jasanoff reads as propaganda presenting the East India Company as a conquering ruler. Other trophies, such as Tipu's gold throne, were auctioned or cut up by the prize agents and partly bought back by the Company, while officers and soldiers hunted relics including Tipu's body and his library. The chapter's central case is Henrietta Clive and her husband Edward, whose 1800 tour of South India and collections of Tipu relics, natural specimens and Indian bronzes show how aristocratic collecting helped them claim a place in India. It ends with the 1801 British invasion of Egypt and the Indian sepoys' encounter with the temple at Dendera.

East and Southeast Asia China is discussed in one paragraph: the 1860 sacking and burning of the Chinese emperor's Summer Palace by Britain's high commissioner after the second Opium War, which scattered its objects across Britain and France. Jasanoff sets this beside the Seringapatam collecting as a parallel case of a demonised enemy whose possessions were eagerly collected by Europeans.

India MuseumVictoria and Albert MuseumClive Museum, Powis CastleBritish Library
Part ThreeEgypt, 1801-1840p. 209
Chapter SevenRivalsp. 211

Rivals, the seventh chapter, follows the Anglo-French contest that replaced open war in Egypt after 1801. Jasanoff argues that the 1801 Treaty of Capitulation, which handed the savants' antiquities to Britain, including the Rosetta Stone, turned imperial rivalry into a competition for collections. The chapter sets the British Museum's Egyptian sculptures against the Louvre's Egyptian rooms, and shows how the Townley Gallery, the museum's first purpose-built wing, came to house the French spoils. Most of the chapter is biographical. It follows Bernardino Drovetti, a Piedmontese in French service who became the French vice-consul, collected in Upper Egypt from 1811, and won the favor of Muhammad Ali. It also follows Henry Salt, a failed portrait painter turned British consul, whose social ambitions and patronage network made him a collector. The chapter ends in 1815, as Salt sails for Egypt with a double mandate to pursue British politics and to buy antiquities, and Jasanoff notes that he soon found himself at war with Drovetti.

British MuseumLouvreTownley Gallery
Chapter EightRemovalsp. 241

Removals, the eighth chapter, follows Henry Salt and Giambattista Belzoni as they dug for and shipped Egyptian antiquities between 1816 and 1823, and as their rivalry turned into a quarrel. Jasanoff describes Belzoni's removal of the Young Memnon bust from the Ramesseum, his discoveries in the Valley of the Kings, and his clashes with agents working for Drovetti over sites and the Philae obelisk. The central episode is the dispute over who employed Belzoni: Salt, who saw himself as a gentleman collector, and Belzoni, who insisted he worked for Britain. The chapter then follows Salt's collection, offered to the British Museum with a price list that caused outrage and sold for about half its cost in 1823. Belzoni's popular Egyptian Hall exhibition and his final, fatal expedition toward Timbuktu, which ended in Benin in 1823, show the two men's different approaches to fame. The chapter closes with the names Salt and Belzoni left carved at the Ramesseum.

British MuseumEgyptian Hall, PiccadillyTownley GallerySir John Soane Museum
Chapter NineRecoveriesp. 275

Recoveries, the ninth chapter, covers the 1820s and 1830s, when Champollion's decipherment of hieroglyphs and the Greek War of Independence reshaped the Anglo-French rivalry over Egypt. Jasanoff argues that after Salt and Drovetti, collecting divided along national lines. The French state, through Champollion's Louvre gallery and the Franco-Tuscan mission, pursued antiquities with public money, while British expatriates such as Robert Hay, James Burton and John Gardner Wilkinson, who lived in tombs at Thebes, increasingly argued for preservation in place. The chapter follows the 1826 sale of Salt's second collection to France, the battle of Navarino in 1827, the removal of a Luxor obelisk to Paris in 1833, and a 1829 dispute over reliefs from the tomb of Seti I. It closes with Muhammad Ali's 1835 antiquities ordinance, which failed, and with the 1840 settlement that ended his ambitions and bound Egypt into European informal control.

Louvre (Musée Charles-X)Ezbekiyya Museum, CairoMetropolitan Museum of Art
Conclusion: Collecting an Empirep. 307

The conclusion moves from Egypt to India and draws the book's threads together. Jasanoff opens with Emily Eden's 1839 letter from Simla, a British enclave in the hills, and then narrates the 1842 retreat from Kabul, the worst British defeat in the East. Lord Ellenborough's answer, the seizure of the Somnath gates from Ghazni, is read as a trophy that concealed weakness, and the parliamentary row over the gates as a debate about how Britain should rule Hindus and Muslims. Turning to Calcutta, Jasanoff describes Rajendro Mullick's Marble Palace, a Western-style collection built to educate Indian visitors, and then Kipling's Kim, where a museum and a cannon embody imperial order. Jasanoff argues that empires were fluid and entangled, and that collecting left lasting legacies in Egypt and India. The chapter closes with the hope that embracing forms of collecting will outweigh the violence of collecting empires.

Marble Palace, CalcuttaRed Fort, AgraLahore Museum

Karp, Ivan; Lavine, Steven D. (eds.) (1991). Exhibiting Cultures: The Poetics and Politics of Museum Display. Washington: Smithsonian Institution Press.Asia: occasional23 chapter overviews

Overview

Exhibiting Cultures is an edited volume of essays and practitioner reflections on how museums display other cultures and what their exhibitions say about the people who make and view them. Its central argument, set out by the editors Lavine and Karp, is that every exhibition draws on the cultural assumptions of its makers, so exhibiting is a contested terrain, especially in multicultural America. The chapters fall into five parts: culture and representation (Alpers, Baxandall, Greenblatt, Yamaguchi, Goswamy); art museums, national identity and Hispanic art (Duncan, Livingston and Beardsley, Marzio, Ybarra-Frausto); museum practices (Crew and Sims, Gurian, Vogel, Houlihan, Clifford, Boon); festivals (Bauman and Sawin, Kurin, Hinsley, Tanen); and other cultures in museum perspective (Kirshenblatt-Gimblett, Munjeri, Hudson). The cases are mainly American and European, with Native American, African, Chicano and Hispanic material, and a few Asian examples.

East and Southeast Asia in this work occasional

East and Southeast Asia appear as a few case studies rather than as a theme. The fullest treatment is Chapter 4, Masao Yamaguchi's "The Poetics of Exhibition in Japanese Culture", which is wholly about Japan: the tokonoma alcove, osira-sama figurines dressed by shamans in northeastern Japan, kabuki and Noh costume, and the Matara cake offering at Motsu temple in Hiraizumi, set against the Paris Exposition of 1867 and the Western museum.

Two other chapters treat Bali, part of the Dutch East Indies, at length. Chapter 15 (Boon) notes that Raffles declared Bali an archaeological remnant of pre-Islamic Java around 1817, and that Balinese rajas hired Walter Spies in the 1920s to enhance their reputation. Chapter 20 (Kirshenblatt-Gimblett) covers Nathan Dunn's Chinese collection, shown at Peale's Museum in 1838 and then in London, with life-size clay figures of mandarins and shopkeepers, and Balinese performances developed for the 1930s Paris exposition and then shown back to tourists on the island.

Other references are brief. Duncan (Chapter 6) reads Imelda Marcos's Metropolitan Museum of Manila, assembled in 1975 for an IMF meeting, as reenacting Philippine dependence on the United States. Marzio (Chapter 8) mentions the Quest for Eternity show of Xian tomb sculpture in Houston. Baxandall (Chapter 2) cites the Chinese concept pi-i as a useful label, and Clifford (Chapter 14) notes that the UBC museum's visible storage holds Chinese, Japanese and Indonesian material. Tanen (Chapter 19) describes the planned 1990-91 Festival of Indonesia. Not covered: Asian museum-building and heritage policy, Asian visitors, curators and scholars, war memory, and restitution claims. The South Asian material (Goswamy, the Festival of India) lies outside this question.

JapanChinaIndonesiaPhilippines

Introduction: Museums and Multiculturalism: Steven D. Lavine and Ivan KarpSteven D. Lavine and Ivan Karp

Lavine and Karp argue that every museum exhibition reflects the cultural assumptions of its makers, so exhibiting is a contested terrain, especially in multicultural America. They illustrate this with the 1984 Te Maori exhibition at the Metropolitan Museum, the Hispanic Art in the United States show in Houston, and Duncan and Wallach's critique of universal survey museums. Museums, they conclude, need to give communities control over their own presentation, expand expertise on non-Western cultures, and experiment with designs that show multiple perspectives.

Metropolitan Museum of ArtMuseum of Fine Arts, Houston
Part I: Culture and Representation: Ivan Karp
1Chapter 1: The Museum as a Way of Seeing: Svetlana Alpers

Alpers argues that museums make objects into things to look at, a 'museum effect', a way of seeing. Her examples include Renaissance cabinets, a Dutch landscape exhibition that imposed categories the painters did not share, a Utrecht show that buried a historic event under documents, and the Musée d'Orsay, which she finds hard to see. She urges museums to attend to installation and let visitors look freely, and concludes that viewers see their own culture in other peoples' objects.

Musée d'OrsayCentral Museum, Utrecht
2Chapter 2: Exhibiting Intention: Some Preconditions of the Visual Display of Culturally Purposeful Objects: Michael BaxandallMichael Baxandall

Baxandall sees an exhibition as a field where three agents act: maker, exhibitor and viewer, the viewer working between object and label. Using a Kota mbulu-ngulu, he shows labels explain objects by cause, while viewers look for visual interest and intention. He recommends exhibiting objects made for looking, juxtaposing cultures, and offering cultural facts that make visitors work. Exhibitors cannot represent cultures, he concludes, so they should set up conditions for viewers to act.

East and Southeast Asia Baxandall cites the Chinese concept pi-i (literally 'brush-idea') as the most effective way he knows to explain Chinese painting to viewers, because its difficulty and cultural strangeness make visitors work at it. This is a single passing point in an argument about labels, which draws its main examples from Kota, Fang and Maori objects.

3Chapter 3: Resonance and Wonder: Stephen GreenblattStephen Greenblatt

Greenblatt sets two models of display against each other: resonance, the power of an object to evoke the cultural forces that produced it, and wonder, which stops the viewer in an enchanted act of looking. Greenblatt links resonance to the new historicism, his own scholarly practice, and to the marks of damage and use that museums often efface. Greenblatt’s main case is the State Jewish Museum in Prague, whose synagogues hold objects the Nazis confiscated and assembled, and which he calls the most purely resonant museum he has seen. Against it he sets the Museum of Modern Art, where wonder reigns. Tracing wonder from medieval marvel texts and Renaissance cabinets to Dürer's response to Mexican objects sent to Charles V, he argues that modern museums both evoke and evacuate the dream of possession. He ends by faulting the Musée d'Orsay for sacrificing visual wonder to resonance, and by arguing that the best exhibitions combine the two.

State Jewish Museum, PragueMuseum of Modern Art, New YorkMusée d'Orsay
4Chapter 4: The Poetics of Exhibition in Japanese Culture: Masao YamaguchiMasao YamaguchiAsia: chiefly

Yamaguchi argues that exhibition is a general human practice and that Japanese culture has its own distinctive way of doing it. Yamaguchi begins with fairground booths, shop windows and department stores, which show that display frames ordinary goods and gives them new meanings. Japanese display is then traced through mitate, the technique of linking an everyday object to a classical or mythological image, and through yama, a mediating space between humans and gods. Examples include the tokonoma alcove, the osira-sama figurines dressed by itako shamans, the clothing of kabuki actors and Noh performance. He sets this against the Paris Exposition of 1867, where everyday commodities were turned into art, and against the Western museum, which excluded the sounds and smells of daily life. Museums, in his account, turn time into space and act as social memory, a view he links to Lévi-Strauss on totemism and Yates on the art of memory. He ends by holding that Japanese display makes the invisible visible through objects, and that exhibitions acquire authenticity only when placed in a theatrical context.

East and Southeast Asia Japan is the chapter's whole subject. Yamaguchi draws on the tokonoma alcove, osira-sama figurines dressed by itako shamans in northeastern Japan, yamabushi-kagura performers, kabuki costume, Noh shaman-priests, furyu processions and the Matara cake offering at Motsu temple in Hiraizumi. Yamaguchi also reads the mid-nineteenth-century Japanese adoption of Western technology as an act of mitate, in which Western things were transplanted into Japan.

Paris Exposition of 1867
5Chapter 5: Another Past, Another Context: Exhibiting Indian Art Abroad: B. N. GoswamyB. N. Goswamy

Goswamy describes curating two 1986 exhibitions of Indian art, Rasa at the Grand Palais in Paris and Essence of Indian Art at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco. Instead of masterpieces or a chronology, he organized the works around rasa, the Indian theory of aesthetic delight, which he presents as the key to how Indian art was once experienced. The chapter explains the theory with care: the nine rasas, the bhavas that generate them, and the viewer, not the object, who tastes the rasa. It then weighs the approach's limits, since genre painting and Mughal or Deccani work sit awkwardly within it. The exhibition design comes next: sculpture and miniatures mixed within each section, no chronology, catalogue entries that point to the details creating mood, color-coded walls in San Francisco, and nine-sided tables that let viewers see a miniature series in turn. Goswamy concludes that visitors gained some insight into Indian art and a sense of the Indian mind, while accepting that the result was a strictly personal view.

Grand PalaisAsian Art Museum, San Francisco
Part 2: Art Museums, National Identity, and the Status of Minority Cultures: The Case of Hispanic Art in the United States: Steven D. Lavine
6Chapter 6: Art Museums and the Ritual of Citizenship: Carol DuncanCarol Duncan

Duncan argues that public art museums are ceremonial monuments that do political work, legitimizing the state and defining citizenship while presenting themselves as neutral. Duncan begins with the Revolutionary conversion of the Louvre into a national museum, then turns to governments that use Western-style museums abroad, such as the Metropolitan Museum of Manila. Duncan’s main case is the Louvre: the decree inscribed over the Apollo Gallery, the nineteenth-century ceilings that honor patrons and then 'Great Artists', and the Rotunda of Mars, where national schools form a sequence ending in France. Art history, she shows, turned princely treasures into a national spiritual heritage that anyone could be awed by. She then follows the Metropolitan Museum and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, where newer wings and primitive-art galleries have disrupted the older Civilization narrative. Her conclusion is that controlling a museum means controlling a community's identity, which is why museum practice is contested.

East and Southeast Asia Duncan's only Asian case is the Metropolitan Museum of Manila, which Imelda Marcos assembled in a matter of weeks in 1975 for the International Monetary Fund meeting in Manila. Duncan reads it as reenacting the Philippines' economic and military dependence on the United States, since it opened with loans from American museums and collectors and occupied a building that was effectively an American donation.

LouvreMetropolitan Museum of Art, New YorkMuseum of Fine Arts, BostonMetropolitan Museum of Manila
7Chapter 7: The Poetics and Politics of Hispanic Art: A New Perspective: Jane Livingston and John BeardsleyJane Livingston and John Beardsley

Livingston and Beardsley explain the making of Hispanic Art in the United States: Thirty Contemporary Painters and Sculptors, organized between 1984 and 1987 and first shown at the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston. They open by comparing an exhibition to a photograph, in which the curator's point of view shapes what is seen. They searched Hispanic communities from Los Angeles and San Francisco to New York and Puerto Rico, showed contemporary painting and sculpture rather than murals and posters, and showed each artist in depth. They balance stylistic range, from Ibsen Espada to Robert Graham, with recurring images such as the Madonna and the outlaw. Most of the chapter answers critics who argued that the show cut Hispanic art from its community roots and homogenized it under a term first used for government and marketing purposes. The authors defend 'Hispanic' as the least incorrect option and argue that the show's political force lay in its place in a mainstream museum. They end by hoping that criticism will not deter similar projects.

Museum of Fine Arts, Houston
8Chapter 8: Minorities and Fine-Arts Museums in the United States: Peter C. MarzioPeter C. Marzio

Marzio, director of the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, gives the museum director's view of Livingston and Beardsley's account of Hispanic Art in the United States. Marzio agrees that minority art belongs in mainstream programs and that apathy, not debate among curators, is the real enemy. The main subject is cost: the curators had to research contemporary Hispanic art from scratch, since there were no dealers, catalogues raisonnés or university slide libraries for it, and the project drew criticism from both Hispanic and non-Hispanic people. Marzio describes the outreach that brought about 150,000 visitors, around thirty percent of them Hispanic, and a Hispanic community committee that stayed with the museum afterwards. Marzio then argues that undercapitalized museums and shrinking federal funds make such exhibitions hard to justify, and that minority artists should hang alongside Old Masters, with context supplied through education rather than labels. Marzio ends by urging mainstream and specialized museums to cooperate.

East and Southeast Asia Marzio mentions one Asian exhibition only: while Hispanic Art was on view, the Museum of Fine Arts also held The Quest for Eternity, a major show of Chinese tomb sculpture from Xian including life-size soldiers and horses, and he credits its crossover visitors with helping attendance.

Museum of Fine Arts, Houston
9Chapter 9: The Chicano Movement/The Movement of Chicano Art: Tomas Ybarra-FraustoTomas Ybarra-Frausto

Ybarra-Frausto traces Chicano art as the cultural side of El Movimiento, the 1960s movement for Chicano self-determination. Ybarra-Frausto divides it into two phases. The first, 1965 to 1975, covers the artists' groups, the farmworkers' newspaper El Malcriado and the student press, and vernacular sources such as almanaques, estampas and altares. He defines rasquachismo, an underdog sensibility of making do, as a key aesthetic stance, and treats posters and murals as the movement's main forms, drawing on Posada and the Mexican muralists. The second phase, 1975 to 1990, he calls one of neutralization: the movement's aims were largely reached, but public art declined, and pluralism and the mainstream market absorbed Chicano work as colorful folklore. He ends by arguing that Chicano art now negotiates between cultures, between defiant otherness and links with other Latino groups, and that no single current dominates.

Part 3: Museum Practices: Steven D. Lavine
10Chapter 10: Locating Authenticity: Fragments of a Dialogue: Spencer R. Crew and James E. SimsSpencer R. Crew and James E. Sims

Crew and Sims argue that authenticity in history exhibitions is a matter of authority rather than factual truth, and that objects cannot speak for themselves. Their cases come from the National Museum of American History: a colonial-revival room whose bare boards misrepresent the merchant who owned it, and the Mullikin-Spragins tenant-farm house, whose exterior was rebuilt wrongly and whose interior walls hold layers of household life. They trace how social history has outrun museum collections, which were built around documented objects of wealthy families and prominent figures, and describe the outreach needed to find ordinary people's belongings for Field to Factory. The authors weigh three options: wait for the right objects, use only what exists, or let historical themes drive the exhibition and use generic objects documented by research. They favor the last, arguing that the team's research database becomes the final authority. The chapter closes by treating the exhibition as a narrative event in which visitors become co-creators of meaning, drawing on Brecht and Aristotle's Poetics.

National Museum of American History
11Chapter 11: Noodling Around with Exhibition Opportunities: Elaine Heumann GurianElaine Heumann Gurian

Gurian argues that exhibitions reveal what their producers think of their visitors, and that many barriers to learning are imposed through unexamined beliefs rather than by content. Gurian sorts museums into establishment, liberal and counterculture types, using the Metropolitan, the New Museum and El Museo del Barrio as examples. Gurian’s central cases are the hands-on exhibitions of Frank Oppenheimer at the Exploratorium and Michael Spock at the Boston Children's Museum, which invited visitors to shape their own learning, and the cluttered, self-directed displays of Charles Eames. Gurian then argues that museum learning is self-paced, nonlinear and visual, and that producers shy away from emotional, playful and theatrical strategies, a reluctance she traces to P. T. Barnum's nineteenth-century museums. Drawing on Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences and on research with novice viewers, she recommends multisensory displays, plain labels and signed, first-person exhibitions. She ends by urging producers to state their assumptions about visitors, since an exhibition also transmits a message about the museum.

ExploratoriumBoston Children's Museum
12Chapter 12: Always True to the Object, in Our Fashion: Susan VogelSusan Vogel

Vogel argues that museums inevitably recontextualize the objects they display, and should say so rather than present curatorial interpretation as neutral. African art, never made to be seen in galleries, is her test case, drawn from her own work at the Center for African Art in New York. She describes three of its exhibitions. The Art of Collecting African Art showed works collectors had rejected as fakes or restorations, with opinionated labels that invited visitors to judge for themselves. Perspectives: Angles on African Art gave ten cocurators, artists and scholars among them, signed comments, and the chapter records their disagreements about form, meaning and whether aesthetics are culture-bound. Art/artifact turned to the museum itself, moving through rooms including a bare white room, a reconstructed 1905 curiosity room and an art-museum case, to show how Western classification has shaped what African objects appear to be. Vogel concludes that museums should admit their subjectivity, since they work as a lens with a particular point of view rather than a frame through which the world's art can be seen.

Center for African Art, New York
13Chapter 13: The Poetic Image and Native American Art: Patrick T. HoulihanPatrick T. Houlihan

Houlihan sets aside the politics of representation to ask what poetic exhibition of Native American art might involve. Houlihan’s starting point is the U'mista Cultural Centre at Alert Bay, British Columbia, which holds potlatch objects confiscated by the Canadian government and returned to the Alert Bay community about sixty years later. Houlihan describes its design, in which masks and regalia sit on platforms around a dance floor so that visitors walk past objects in the spectators' place, reversing the roles of viewer and viewed. Drawing on Bachelard's Poetics of Space, he argues that the poetic image is independent of causality, and so resists the familiar categories of subsistence, religion or primitive art that museums impose. Three examples follow: Pueblo and Navajo turquoise, which means more to its makers than the silver settings collectors value; a Navajo string game that taught star patterns; and one Athabaskan word for a curved form shared by a spoon, a comb and a branch. He concludes that large survey exhibitions need not be repeated in every museum, and that the aim is memorable images that stay with visitors.

U'mista Cultural Centre
14Chapter 14: Four Northwest Coast Museums: Travel Reflections: James CliffordJames Clifford

Clifford's travel reflections on four Northwest Coast museums in British Columbia, visited in 1988, set majority and tribal institutions side by side. The majority side is the University of British Columbia Museum of Anthropology, where a Great Hall treats Bill Reid's carvings as fine art, and the Royal British Columbia Museum, a linear, didactic history from smallpox to land claims. The tribal side is the U'mista Cultural Centre at Alert Bay and the Kwagiulth Museum on Quadra Island, which hold regalia returned after the 1921 Village Island potlatch and surrendered in 1922. U'mista presents the potlatch as a shared Kwakwaka'wakw history, with quotations from Indian agents and elders propped beside the objects, while the Quadra museum shows regalia by family ownership for a local audience. Clifford notes that family accounts of the potlatch differ, and he concludes that no museum can tell the whole story, so majority and tribal institutions should share authority rather than rank one above the other.

University of British Columbia Museum of AnthropologyRoyal British Columbia MuseumU'mista Cultural Centre, Alert BayKwagiulth Museum and Cultural Centre, Cape Mudge Village
15Chapter 15: Why Museums Make Me Sad: James A. BoonJames A. BoonAsia: in part

Boon writes a personal essay on why museums make him sad, and he argues that every museum, from the ethnological to the national, is a place of pillage, fragmentation and captioned display. Boon works through the Renaissance story of a Roman statue's pit-marks, the ethnological shows at the Brighton Aquarium, Peale's Philadelphia museum and the Smithsonian, where he worked in 1969 to 1971. Boon’s main figure is Henry James, whose memoir A Small Boy and Others recalls childhood visits to P. T. Barnum's American Museum and the Crystal Palace. Boon then turns to Venice, which he reads through Ruskin, Proust and James as a city made into a museum and reliquary, and to the Tahitian feather cape collected by British sailors. The chapter ends by claiming that museumgoing mixes mature reflection with childish longing, and it closes by suggesting that the author's own writing on James and Proust is another act of museumlike appropriation.

East and Southeast Asia Boon's one substantial Asian case is Bali, which he treats as part of the Dutch East Indies. Boon notes that Raffles declared Bali an archaeological remnant of pre-Islamic Java around 1817, that Balinese rajas in the 1920s hired Walter Spies to enhance their international reputation, and that Hindu-Balinese make museumy emblems of Dutch, British, Muslim and tourist outsiders and of one another. Javanese temple dancers appear only in a list of Brighton Aquarium attractions.

Brighton AquariumP. T. Barnum's American MuseumSmithsonian InstitutionPeale's MuseumCrystal Palace
Part 4: Festivals: Ivan Karp
16Chapter 16: The Politics of Participation in Folklife Festivals: Richard Bauman and Patricia SawinRichard Bauman and Patricia Sawin

Bauman and Sawin study participation in the 1987 Smithsonian Festival of American Folklife, drawing on fieldwork with about twenty participants from Michigan. Their argument is that participants are not passive display objects. Presenters were charged with explaining the culture on show, but participants had to work out for themselves what they were doing, using frames such as performance, demonstration, instruction, exhibition and work. Demonstration proved the most common and forgiving frame, since it tolerated failure and unfinished products, yet it caused friction for people who saw their work as occupation rather than folklore, such as Great Lakes fishermen and a Michigan cherry grower. The authors trace the strains of the main stage, the talk stages and the staff's show-must-go-on demands, and the ways participants resisted, from private jokes to a staged joke at the folklorists' expense. The chapter ends with the lasting benefits of the festival and a smoother Michigan festival in East Lansing, and it concludes that a fairer politics of festival representation must treat participants as agents.

Smithsonian Festival of American Folklife
17Chapter 17: Cultural Conservation through Representation: Festival of India Folklife Exhibitions at the Smithsonian Institution: Richard KurinRichard Kurin

Kurin asks why museums should mount new exhibitions at all, and he argues that they should help living cultures survive rather than only collect specimens before they vanish. Kurin lists the reasons museums usually give for exhibitions and then sets out his case that museums, through their scholarly authority, can legitimate minority and endangered cultures. The main example is two 1985 Smithsonian exhibitions of Indian culture: Aditi, arranged by the Hindu life cycle in the National Museum of Natural History, and Mela, an outdoor fair on the Mall. Both brought in folk artists from the Shadipur cooperative in Delhi, whose members had been treated as beggars under Indian law. Kurin describes how participants reshaped the displays, with a puja in the museum foyer, a temple built on the Mall, and a bazaar where musicians and craftspeople shared sales profits, as well as the disputes over authenticity and selling. Kurin concludes that exhibitions can serve cultural self-help, because culture must be lived and renewed rather than frozen in a museum.

Aditi: A Celebration of LifeMela! An Indian FairNational Museum of Natural History
18Chapter 18: The World as Marketplace: Commodification of the Exotic at the World’s Columbian Exposition, Chicago, 1893: Curtis M. HinsleyCurtis M. Hinsley

Hinsley examines the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago in 1893 and argues that its displays of non-Western peoples turned them into commodities. Hinsley begins with the industrial expositions of the late nineteenth century and the rise of touring human displays, from Carl Hagenbeck's tours to Barnum's sideshows, and then sets two approaches side by side. One is the serious anthropology of Frederick Ward Putnam and Franz Boas, whose Kwakiutl performers danced in front of a white sheet to recreate a supposedly pristine past. The other is the Midway Plaisance, which Hinsley reads through Julian Ralph's and H. H. Bancroft's descriptions as a stroll through exotic bazaars where every dancer and donkey boy had a price. Photograph albums, captions, fences and the 'Baby Arab' pictures show how viewers kept a safe distance from the people on display. Hinsley concludes that market logic governed both the Midway and the anthropology, producing an early form of touristic consumption. The chapter closes with Boas's retreat from public anthropology after the fair.

World's Columbian Exposition Anthropological BuildingMidway PlaisanceHagenbeck's Arena
19Chapter 19: Festivals and Diplomacy: Ted M. G. TanenAsia: in part

Tanen argues that Americans know too little about other cultures and that a festival, a concentrated presentation of one country's culture, can help. He draws mainly on the Festival of India of 1985-86, with almost eight hundred programs in 140 cities. He recommends agreed goals, quality over size, and exchange programs that outlast the event, and he ends by proposing a festival of the Americas for 1992.

East and Southeast Asia Tanen's Asian material is the planned Festival of Indonesia for 1990-91, organized by the private Yayasan Nusantara Jaya, which includes a training program for museologists hosted by American museums, alongside tourism and business goals. Japan appears as a country with ongoing cultural presentations in the United States, and Thailand and Vietnam only in a list of little-known countries.

Festival of India
Part 5: Other Cultures in Museum Perspective: Ivan Karp
20Chapter 20: Objects of Ethnography: Barbara Kirshenblatt-GimblettBarbara Kirshenblatt-GimblettAsia: in part

Kirshenblatt-Gimblett asks how an ordinary object becomes ethnographic and what exhibitions do to the peoples they show. Kirshenblatt-Gimblett argues that objects are made ethnographic by excision and detachment, so exhibitions present fragments, and she distinguishes in situ displays, such as period rooms, habitat groups and recreated villages, from in context displays that explain through labels and classifications. Kirshenblatt-Gimblett’s history runs from cabinets of curiosities and Peale's Museum through Goode's object lessons to Egyptian Hall, where living Bushmen and Laplanders were displayed as rarities. Kirshenblatt-Gimblett argues that a 'museum effect' turns the everyday into spectacle, whether in slumming or in the panoptic gaze, and she examines festivals, folkloric troupes and the homeland exhibitions for immigrants. Kirshenblatt-Gimblett’s treatment of the Festival of American Folklife and the Festival of India's mela shows how performers are staged as authentic while remaining shaped by tourism and nationalism. Kirshenblatt-Gimblett concludes that all interest is vested, so the conventions of display need as much scrutiny as the objects.

East and Southeast Asia Kirshenblatt-Gimblett discusses Nathan Dunn's Chinese collection, shown at Peale's Museum in 1838 and then in London, with life-size clay figures of mandarins, shopkeepers and servants, and the wax scenes of Chinese daily life at the Oriental and Turkish Museum in 1850s London. Bali recurs as a case of tourist production: Balinese performances developed for the 1930s Paris exposition were brought back to be shown to visitors on the island, and cremations there have grown larger because tourists pay to attend. Chinese and Japanese people appear mainly in lists of displayed peoples.

Egyptian HallSkansenPeale's MuseumPolynesian Cultural CenterOriental and Turkish MuseumFestival of American Folklife
21Chapter 21: Refocusing or Reorientation? The Exhibit or the Populace: Zimbabwe on the Threshold: Dawson MunjeriDawson Munjeri

Munjeri traces how Zimbabwe's national museums served a white minority before independence in 1980. Collections came through white intermediaries, ethnographic material was shown as witchcraft or left in storage, and Africans were discouraged from visiting. He describes the 1979-81 centralization and the exhibitions celebrating Rhodes. He ends by calling for reconciliation, with museums addressing social and cultural issues.

National Museums and Monuments of ZimbabweMutare MuseumBulawayo Museum
22Chapter 22: How Misleading Does an Ethnographical Museum Have to Be?: Kenneth HudsonKenneth Hudson

Hudson, writing as a museum critic rather than a historian, asks how far ethnographical museums mislead their visitors. The chapter starts from Hudson's own book Museums of Influence, which found no ethnographical museum among its thirty-seven pioneers, and then tests that verdict against an exhibition called Hunters of the North at the Museum of Mankind in London. Hudson admires its planning but finds that its displays feed the eye and the mind, not the senses: smells, temperature and sound are missing. The American Museum in Bath is cited as a case, where a New England tavern and bedrooms smell of nothing. Hudson also argues that museums fixate on 'traditional culture', filling rooms with shields, spears and war canoes, which implies that the peoples shown have changed little, and that tourism keeps staged dances alive as bogus culture. The chapter ends by proposing climate and region museums staffed by paid interpreters, and by asking that displays show the modern struggles of the peoples concerned.

Museum of MankindAmerican Museum in Bath
Contributors
Kavanagh, Gaynor (ed.) (1996). Making Histories in Museums. London: Leicester University Press.Asia: slight22 chapter overviews

Overview

Kavanagh's edited volume (1996) asks how museums make history, and argues that museum historians must master material evidence, serve their audiences and face their own political choices, since every museum history includes and excludes. Its 21 chapters, written mostly by curators and museum historians, are organised by subject rather than period or place: medical, rural, women's, family, African American, African Caribbean, work, technology, city, sub-cultural, war, sexual, culturally diverse, religious, archaeological, folklore, curriculum, First Nations and children's histories. Each chapter addresses one subject and the problems of displaying it. Most of the material concerns Britain, with Australia, North America and the Caribbean also represented.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East Asia is discussed only in passing, with one exception. Chapter 16 (O'Neill, Making Histories of Religion) gives Taiwan the most attention: it notes that traditional religious belief has grown there despite rapid economic growth since 1949, and describes the planned World Religions Museum at the Ling-chiu Shan Wu-Sheng Monastery. It also records that Marburg's museum has displays on non-Buddhist religions in China and Japan and on Buddhism in south-east Asia, China, Japan and Tibet, and cites Otto's Far Eastern Buddha figures.

Other references are brief. Chapter 13 (Jones, Making Histories of Wars) and chapter 18 (Rattue, History and Folklore) both concern General Gordon's relics: the embroidered mandarin uniforms and yellow jackets given to him by the Chinese Emperor in 1865, and the canes said to be the ones he carried in China. Chapter 19 (Reeve, Making the History Curriculum) notes that Ancient China and early modern Japan are suggested Key Stage 3 options. Chapter 4 (Buckley) tells an anecdote about a Northern Irish Tai Chi club, and chapter 10 (Fitzgerald, Making Histories of Technology) mentions the Smithsonian's revised Enola Gay exhibition on the bombing of Japan. Chapter 15 (Merriman and Poovaya-Smith) names the Geffrye Museum's 'Chinese Homes' exhibition of 1992, and chapter 11 (Fleming, Making City Histories) lists a Cambodian Association among Philadelphia partners and uses Tokyo and Beijing as examples of very large cities.

Southeast Asia is otherwise absent: there is no treatment of Indonesia, Vietnam or Malaya, of colonial collecting from the region, of Asian objects in Western museums, of museum policy in Asian states, or of restitution. South Asia (Bradford, Leicester, the sub-continent) receives much more attention in chapter 15 and lies outside this question.
