Theoretical approach of this work
Illustrationsp. vii
Contributorsp. ix
Prefacep. xi

Kavanagh's preface introduces a volume on making histories in museums. Kavanagh argues that museum historians must master material evidence, audiences and their own subject, and that every museum history is political because it includes and excludes. Museums, she says, should tell plural, object-rich histories that face uncomfortable matters, such as the social costs of science, rather than hide behind claims that the public wants something else. The book aims to show these practitioners' ideas to readers beyond the profession.

Acknowledgementsp. xv
1Making Histories, Making MemoriesGaynor Kavanaghp. 1

Kavanagh's introduction argues that history museums are places where official histories, presented in exhibitions, meet the personal memories visitors bring with them, and that museums have not yet taken this meeting seriously. Kavanagh draws on Annis's idea of cognitive, social and dream spaces to describe how a visit works. Kavanagh then contrasts professional historians, who work with documents, with curators, who must read objects, using a flat iron that could mean many different things. Memory is treated as a construction that shifts with context and audience, illustrated by a disagreement between two former prisoners over The Great Escape and by the 1994 D-Day family-day plan that veterans rejected. To bridge the two, she suggests organising exhibitions around life stages rather than chronology, and she cites Hull's Old Grammar School, Croydon's interactive displays, Birmingham's Heartlands show and the Museum of the Famine in Roscommon, which offers eight accounts of the famine. The chapter ends by arguing that museums should accept that history and memory collide, and that the emotional response they provoke is worth taking seriously.

People's Story, EdinburghLifetimes, CroydonOld Grammar School, HullMuseum of the Famine, RoscommonBirmingham City Museum and Art Gallery
2Time Heals: Making History in Medical MuseumsKen Arnoldp. 15

Arnold argues that medicine and museums have been entangled since the Renaissance, when physicians formed the first cabinets, and that medical collections were long used for teaching and research. Arnold traces Henry Wellcome's Historical Medical Museum, conceived as a museum of all human history, whose collections were cut back and then lent to the Science Museum. The chapter's main concern is the recent shift from presenting medical science as a story of progress to showing its social and political context. He illustrates this with the Science Museum's 'Health Matters' gallery, which treats machines as nodes of wider change, and with two site-based museums, the Old Operating Theatre in Southwark and the Alexander Fleming Museum at St Mary's Hospital, whose atmosphere is their chief asset. He then turns to exhibitions that bring medicine into art and politics, including Wellcome's 'Picturing the Body' and the 'Birth and Breeding' show on reproduction. Arnold concludes that medical museums can now confront illness and mortality directly, and that the past they present should be remembered rather than forgotten.

Wellcome Historical Medical MuseumScience MuseumThackray Medical MuseumOld Operating Theatre, Museum and Herb GarretAlexander Fleming MuseumMutter MuseumRoyal College of Surgeons (Hunter collection)Parkes Museum of Hygiene
3Making Rural HistoriesJonathan Bellp. 30

Bell asks how rural history museums can present country life when curators and visitors alike carry idealised models of the rural past. Bell sets the 'golden age' of community, promoted by national elites, against the view of peasants as backward, and argues that neither is adequate; the loss older country people feel is best understood through Thompson's 'montage of memories'. Bell traces agricultural museums from nineteenth-century attempts to teach farmers new technology to the folk museums of Scandinavia and Britain and Ireland, which he says tidied rural poverty into a harmonious past. Bell’s central argument concerns objects: a plough does not reveal social relations unaided, since labour recruitment was flexible and changes in women's work depended on processing moving off the farm. Documents, oral history and reconstructions such as an eighteenth-century plough at the Ulster Folk and Transport Museum help curators make the link. He ends by recommending models, film, interactive displays and working farms, while insisting that original artefacts remain the museum's most important resource.

Ulster Folk and Transport MuseumMuseum of English Rural LifeSkansenScience MuseumHighland Folk MuseumWelsh Folk MuseumManx Folk Museum
4Why Not Invent the Past We Display in Museums?Anthony D. Buckleyp. 42

Buckley argues that museums should not invent the past. Buckley begins from the relativism that has become orthodoxy in museums, under which all versions of history are equally valid, and says this view has become a tool of commercial theme parks and of the powerful. Against Kuhn, Feyerabend and others he offers three objections: relativism is self-refuting, people from different cultures can communicate through pointing and shared basic categories, and people's theories must answer to the world when they cross the road. He then argues that truthful history matters because people use the past as models for action and as the basis for rights, property and kinship, and because evidence protects the weak against the strong. Curators, he suggests, look after history for a public that is not very interested in it, much as the 'buffs' of railways and Titanic keep traditions alive. The conclusion is that museums should represent diverse opinions earnestly and in search of truth, and should favour the histories of less powerful groups rather than pandering to what consumers want to see.

East and Southeast Asia Buckley's only reference to East Asia is an anecdote about a small Northern Irish club practising Tai Chi, a Chinese system of exercise. Few members know its history, but their leader, who has studied in China, passes on its stories and parables, and the rest trust him to look after the tradition. Buckley uses the case to argue that popular 'curators' preserve traditions for members who do not care much about them.

5Trying to Be an Honest Woman: Making Women's HistoriesElizabeth Carnegiep. 54

Carnegie argues that women's history cannot simply be added to existing displays; it requires changes to staffing, collecting, buildings and interpretation. Carnegie begins with the male hierarchies that shape exhibitions and with the point that women are not a single category, since class, race and culture divide them. Drawing mainly on Glasgow and Edinburgh, she describes women's growing share of visitors and security staff, and projects such as the Open Museum, which worked with women's groups and oral history. Because many women's products were perishable, curators often have to interpret what is missing, as in the empty pedestals of 'Mining the Museum'. She insists that domestic and working lives must not be split apart, and that subjects such as birth, domestic violence and prostitution need the women concerned to take part. The St Mungo Museum case, where a photograph of female genital mutilation and objections from Islamic elders forced changes to labels and to the display of personal portraits, shows the risks of cultural interpretation. She concludes that every museum should examine its own record on women and adopt a policy that runs through all its activity.

People's Palace, GlasgowSt Mungo Museum of Religious Life and ArtOpen Museum, GlasgowPaisley MuseumBirmingham City Museum and Art GalleryPeace Museum, ChicagoWomen's Museum, Aarhus
6Making Family Histories in the National Portrait Gallery, AustraliaJulia Clarkp. 66

Clark describes the second exhibition of Canberra's National Portrait Gallery, a thematic show on family in Australia, and the reasons for its approach. The team chose a functional definition of family, a group of people who live together and care for one another, which let them include a nun with her orphan pupils and Aboriginal kinship networks. Clark argues that portraits must be read critically: the wealthy Piper and Wentworth families commissioned images that concealed convict ancestry and illegitimacy, while women's public roles rarely appear in domestic portraits. Clark traces the decline of family group portraits after photography and asks whether this reflects changing values. The chapter ends with the diverse families of the late twentieth century, and with visitor reactions that show why curators must state their positions openly.

National Portrait Gallery, Australia
7African Americans, History and Museums: Preserving African American History in the Public ArenaSpencer R. Crewp. 80

Crew traces African American efforts to preserve their own history, from early nineteenth-century literary societies through Carter G. Woodson's Association for the Study of Negro Life and History and Negro History Week. He then turns to the community museums founded from the 1950s, such as the Ebony Museum of Negro Culture and the Anacostia Neighborhood Museum, which saw themselves as agents of empowerment. The chapter's central argument concerns authority: the 1970 protests at the American Association of Museums and criticism of the Metropolitan Museum's 'Harlem on My Mind' pushed larger museums to share interpretive power with communities. Crew describes partnership projects at the Philadelphia Museum of Art, the Smithsonian and the Brooklyn Historical Society, and he cites Colonial Williamsburg's silence on slavery as a failure. Crew concludes that demographic change, social responsibility and African American pressure made the history of African Americans an integral part of museum work.

Ebony Museum of Negro CultureAnacostia Neighborhood MuseumMetropolitan Museum of ArtPhiladelphia Museum of ArtColonial WilliamsburgBrooklyn Historical SocietyValentine MuseumRhode Island Black Heritage Society
8Making Histories of African CaribbeansAlissandra Cumminsp. 92

Cummins argues that for centuries Caribbean history was written as European history, and that museums repeated this by treating African objects as ethnographic relics. Cummins traces colonial historiography in Barbados, citing Poyer's early nineteenth-century defence of racial hierarchy, and shows how early collections were built from private interests and from the spoils of imperial campaigns such as the 1897 expedition to Ashanti. Since the 1960s, historians at the University of the West Indies have made enslaved people and rebels central, and Cummins criticises school textbooks that still portray Africans as passive. Her main case studies are community-based museum projects in Jamaica, Barbados, St Lucia, Belize, the Bahamas and the Cayman Islands, where people contributed objects, memories and interpretation. The chapter ends by arguing that Caribbean communities have a valid claim to their own history and can decide what should be collected, displayed and how it is interpreted.

Barbados MuseumJamaica Peoples Museum of Craft and TechnologyPompey Museum at Vendue HouseNational Museum, BelmopanMelda's Historical Museum
9Cleaning Up the Coal-Face and Doing Out the Kitchen: The Interpretation of Work and Workers in WalesKath Daviesp. 105

Davies argues that museums in Wales present work as machinery and objects while leaving out the people who used them, and she proposes ways to bring workers back into the story. Davies begins with the Welsh Industrial and Maritime Museum in Cardiff, whose 'Hall of Power' treats engines as totemic symbols inspiring awe rather than understanding. Better practice appears at the Welsh Slate Museum at Llanberis, where grubby machines, work clothes and ex-quarrymen convey the whole working world, and at Big Pit in Blaenafon, where ex-miners guide visitors through a preserved mine. By contrast, the staged 'A Shift in Time' at Rhondda Heritage Park is criticised for trivialising mining, and its ex-miner advisers were ignored. Davies then turns to women's domestic and laundry work, arguing that tin baths, mangles and tidy kitchens hide labour, and that collecting policies should record modern service jobs. Davies concludes that the interpretation of work has only just begun.

Welsh Industrial and Maritime MuseumWelsh Slate Museum (Amgueddfa Lechi)Big Pit Mining MuseumRhondda Heritage ParkSwansea Maritime and Industrial MuseumPontypridd Cultural and Historical Centre
10Hard Men, Hard Facts and Heavy Metal: Making Histories of TechnologyLawrence Fitzgeraldp. 116

Fitzgerald argues that technology museums have collected and interpreted technology too narrowly, favouring large, metallic, male-associated machines and presenting technology as neutral and beyond society. Fitzgerald describes an 'internalist' style, object-centred and aimed at male enthusiasts, and a 'celebratory' style that treats machines as icons of progress, citing the Swiss Transport Museum and Snibston Discovery Park. A social historical style, which asks how people used technology, is an improvement, but it still treats technologies as already formed. Fitzgerald therefore proposes an approach drawn from the social construction of technology, which shows how competing social groups shape a technology's form and meaning. Fitzgerald describes a 1993 Manchester exhibition that used a bicycle display, hairdryer cartoons and a kitchen with interactive disability barriers to show this 'interpretative flexibility'. Fitzgerald ends by arguing that curators should consult audiences, use sound and ex-workers as guides, and subject technology exhibitions to critical review.

Swiss Transport MuseumSnibston Discovery ParkMuseum of Technology and Work, MannheimMuseum of Science and Industry, ManchesterNational Air and Space Museum, WashingtonScience Museum, LondonDeutsches Museum
11Making City HistoriesDavid Flemingp. 131

Fleming argues that museums have failed to explain urban life, because their focus on object-based collections has pushed aside people, poverty and the city itself. Fleming sees change coming from a better-educated profession and from local governments that demand social relevance, though these demands may conflict with tourism. Since object collections cannot represent a city, he argues, a city history must draw on archives, memory and the city's own fabric. Istanbul, with more than ten million people, serves as his test case: the new museum there should act as a gateway, signposting historic sites, other museums and heritage attractions, and should work with the commercial heritage sector rather than sneer at it. In the final sections he describes partnership projects in Newcastle, including a homelessness project and a dance project about car crime, and argues that city museums should act as agents of social change.

Istanbul Archaeological MuseumAmsterdam Historisch MuseumRijksmuseumAnne Frank HouseMadame Tussaud's SceneramaMontreal History CentreTyne and Wear Museums
12Travellers' Boots, Body-Moulding, Rubber Fetish Clothes: Making Histories of Sub-culturesAmy de la Hayep. 143

De la Haye describes how the Victoria and Albert Museum came to collect sub-cultural clothing and to display it in 'Streetstyle: From Sidewalk to Catwalk' (1994-95). She first explores sub-cultures, usually youth-based and working-class, whose members use style to signal belonging, and traces their post-war emergence from rising youth affluence, music and the Teds' reworking of Edwardian tailoring. The main argument concerns the difficulty of making a history from clothes kept by enthusiasts: the V&A had almost no streetstyle when the project began, so it relied on specialist advisers, public appeals and replicas where originals could not be found. Outfits were shown on fibreglass 'flatbacks' rather than fashion mannequins, with labels that quoted the wearers, who approved their own text. The exhibition drew 109,000 visitors. De la Haye concludes that museum display risks draining sub-cultures of their defiance, but that museums must face the challenge of collecting the here and now.

Victoria and Albert Museum
13Making Histories of WarsSimon Jonesp. 152

Simon Jones examines how regimental museums of the British Army represent war, and asks whether they can move beyond their purpose of instilling esprit de corps. He traces their origins in trophies, training collections and the 1920s displays of material gathered in officers' and sergeants' messes, and shows how weapons, uniforms, colours, drill and medals carry codes that outsiders find opaque. The chapter argues that the shift from functional to symbolic objects explains much of the ceremony, and that regimental museums have borrowed social history methods such as family-life exhibits, oral history and local links. It then turns to the problem of causation: a social history approach can leave out why wars happened, so Jones suggests showing the everyday commodities, such as tea or cotton, that military power secured for Britain. Focus groups on Merseyside found public ambivalence about the army and about the idea of a true regimental story. The conclusion proposes demystifying the regiment's social organization, especially in battle and in the experience of individual soldiers and their families.

East and Southeast Asia Only one East Asian object figures: the richly embroidered mandarin uniforms that the Chinese Emperor gave General Gordon in 1865. They reached the Royal Engineers with Gordon's relics and were displayed as the relics of a Victorian hero, which Jones cites to show how regimental collections were used to bind a corps to its heroes. Nothing else in the chapter concerns East or Southeast Asia.

Royal Engineers MuseumKing's Regiment museum, MerseysideImperial War Museum
14Making Histories of SexualityMark Liddiardp. 163

Liddiard asks why museums have almost entirely excluded sexuality from their displays, and whether they are likely to take it up. Liddiard first weighs the reasons usually given: a lack of historical objects, which follows from the object-centred habit of museums, although oral history and love letters can partly solve the problem; and the pivotal role of staff, whose professional culture, training and personal views shape which topics reach exhibitions. Drawing on 49 interviews with museum decision-makers and 200 visitor interviews from his doctoral research on warfare exhibitions, he shows how exhibitions result from negotiation between curators, designers and marketing staff. The British Museum's withheld erotica collection and the Imperial War Museum's Forces Sweethearts exhibition serve as the main cases. The chapter argues that commercial pressure, especially on local and independent museums, may bring sexuality in, just as it brought women's history into displays. It ends by warning that if museums keep ignoring the topic, the sex industry, which already runs sex museums in the Netherlands, will take the ground.

British MuseumImperial War Museum
15Making Culturally Diverse HistoriesNick Merriman and Nima Poovaya-Smithp. 176

Merriman and Poovaya-Smith argue that British museums must reflect the country's cultural diversity, both to win over non-visitors from ethnic minority communities and because public funding makes museums accountable to the whole population. They open with surveys showing that white Britons visit museums far more often than Asian and African Caribbean people, and they trace the field's development from grassroots research in the 1970s and 1980s to posts created at Leicester, Bradford and Kirklees. The chapter compares approaches: temporary exhibitions such as Bradford's Warm and Rich and Fearless and the Museum of London's The Peopling of London, community-run museums such as the Jewish museums, and projects that set minority histories within mainstream narratives. It reviews the Geffrye Museum's reinterpretation of its furniture collections for local black and Asian communities, and the Maryland Historical Society's Mining the Museum project. The authors conclude that no single method is correct, and that museums should combine audience research with partnerships shared with communities, while avoiding separatism and the label of the Other.

Museum of LondonGeffrye MuseumBradford Art Galleries and MuseumsMaryland Historical Society
16Making Histories of ReligionMark O'Neillp. 188Asia: in part

O'Neill argues that museums rarely make histories of religion, although most of them hold many objects that once had religious meaning. O'Neill traces this absence to secularization and to the nineteenth-century belief that museums and art galleries would replace religion as civilizing institutions, a view that leaves religious objects treated as art, as evidence of exotic beliefs, or as local history. Museums of religion, mostly Jewish museums in former synagogues, are the main exception. The chapter then weighs the cost of this silence, drawing on George Steiner to argue that museums cannot take their humanist values for granted, and on the sacred meanings that repatriation claims expose. It compares three museums: Marburg's Religionskundliche Sammlung, founded on the collection of Rudolf Otto; Glasgow's St Mungo Museum of Religious Life and Art, which the author describes from the inside; and the Ulster Folk and Transport Museum's reconstructed churches. The conclusion is that museums must acknowledge the dark places of human history and treat objects as part of living experience rather than as scholarly specimens.

East and Southeast Asia Taiwan receives the most attention: the chapter notes that traditional religious belief has continued to grow there despite rapid economic growth since 1949, and it describes the proposed World Religions Museum at the Ling-chiu Shan Wu-Sheng Monastery, whose stated purpose is respect, acceptance and universal compassion. Marburg's museum has displays on non-Buddhist religions in China and Japan and on Buddhism in south-east Asia, China, Japan and Tibet, and Otto's Far Eastern Buddha figures are cited as an example of the sensual appeal of religious portraiture.

Religionskundliche Sammlung, MarburgSt Mungo Museum of Religious Life and ArtMuseum of Christianity, The HagueUlster Folk and Transport MuseumHull City Museum
17Making Histories from ArchaeologyJanet Owenp. 200

Janet Owen argues that archaeological and social history material in museums should be treated alike, since both are past material culture, and that archaeology displays should move beyond safe facts about technology and economy. She draws on contextual archaeology, which reads objects as coded symbols, and on Shanks and Tilley's view that museum narratives reflect their authors' present. Owen sets out three principles: treat objects as expressions of personal and social life, link past societies to present ones, and involve visitors by admitting that the story is only one interpretation. Owen tests these against prehistory galleries at the Museum of London, Colchester Castle Museum and Stoke-on-Trent City Museum. The Museum of London's People Before London gallery comes closest, with questions to visitors, humour and a flint hand-axe displayed beside a Swiss army knife, though its narrative still ignores the bias of the surviving record. The Colchester and Stoke galleries remain didactic and treat symbolism only superficially. Owen concludes that temporary exhibitions offer a low-risk way to test interpretation and to evaluate it with visitors.

Museum of LondonColchester Castle MuseumStoke-on-Trent City Museum and Art GalleryJorvik Viking Centre
18History and FolkloreJames Rattuep. 216

Rattue argues that folklore deserves a place in museums, though historians and curators have kept it at a distance since the later nineteenth century. Rattue blames the separation of folklife from folklore, and the objection that museums collect objects, not stories. Rattue defines folklore as oral-assumptive symbolic behaviour, a definition that links it to objects. Rattue illustrates the point from his own military museum: the flames on the Artillery and Engineers grenades, wartime stories of distant gunfire, and the cult of General Gordon with its relics. Systematic folklore displays are rare, and Bishop's House in Sheffield is the exception he cites. He proposes three approaches: educational role-play, local customs as a source of community identity, and humble oral surveys, since recording folklore alters it. He concludes that folklore reveals the symbols a society uses for its deepest desires and anxieties, so museums that ignore it tell an incomplete history.

East and Southeast Asia Asia enters through General Gordon. The chapter notes the legend that Gordon led the Chinese Emperor's forces against the Taiping rebels armed only with a cane, and that the Royal Engineers Museum holds four canes said to be the one he carried in China. The RUSI eventually displayed three yellow jackets awarded to Gordon by the Emperor, and the Royal Engineers Museum holds four unique jackets.

Royal Engineers MuseumRoyal United Services Institute MuseumBishop's House, SheffieldNordiska Museet, Stockholm
19Making the History CurriculumJohn Reevep. 228

Reeve examines how the National Curriculum, introduced in 1988 and revised in 1995, shaped the history taught in English schools and what that means for museums. Reeve begins with the political argument, from Churchill's and Thatcher's appeals to a national story to the right's campaign against multiculturalism, then shows how English history came to dominate the revised units, with only one non-European option at each stage. Museums responded in several ways. The curriculum's DAPOS model of sources (documents, artefacts, photographs, oral history and sites) boosted school visits, notably to the British Museum, and pushed museum educators into object-based teaching. Reeve documents the Anglo-Saxon 'Making of England' exhibition, its opera project and CD-ROM, and notes that the Museum of Mankind's Paradise show drew few schools, unlike Day of the Dead, because it did not match the curriculum. Reeve concludes that the curriculum gives museums a clearer agenda but also a restraint, and that most museums have no educators at all.

British MuseumMuseum of MankindHorniman Museum
20Shadows and Sacred Geography: First Nations History-Making from an Alberta PerspectiveMichael Ross and Reg Crowshoep. 240

Ross and Crowshoe, one non-Native, one a Piikani (Peigan) elder, examine how Alberta First Nations make history through museum collections, and what that asks of museums. They set out the background: treaties, the Indian Act, the suppression of the Sun Dance, residential schools and the cultural void they left, and the romantic images that shape visitors' expectations. Collections in the Glenbow and Provincial museums carry meanings that differ for Native and non-Native visitors, and sacred objects and medicine bundles need handling protocols and advice from elders. The chapter explores loans, overseas holdings and repatriation, and the controversy over the 1988 exhibition The Spirit Sings, which led to a 1992 task force report. Cases follow: Northwind Dreaming at Fort Chipewyan, a reconstructed Natoas bundle that Crowshoe insists is a new bundle rather than a clone, and a proposed Peigan cultural centre. The authors conclude that First Nations need places in other museums, places of their own, and a seat at the management table.

Glenbow Museum, CalgaryProvincial Museum of Alberta, EdmontonHead-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump Interpretive CentreWhyte Museum of the Canadian Rockies
21Making Children's HistoriesBrian W. Shepherdp. 258

Shepherd asks what a museum of childhood can offer when all history is selective and subjective. Using the Edith Cowan University Museum of Childhood in Perth as his case, he describes three family collections: the toys of the Riley children, whose father was an Anglican bishop; those of Bill Boyd, a post-war boy from rural Victoria; and the improvised toys of Fred Collard, a Nyungar boy. Their juxtaposition prompts visitors to notice gender roles, class and empire. The chapter then argues that visitors bring nostalgic expectations, and that a museum of childhood risks confirming a myth of universal childhood built from toys and christening gowns. Shepherd proposes a dialogue based on the area of mismatch between expectation and display. Shepherd compares thematic galleries at Bethnal Green and the Australian Museum of Childhood in The Rocks, and concludes that any museum offers only a window onto childhood and must be clear about its intentions.

Edith Cowan University Museum of ChildhoodBethnal Green Museum of ChildhoodAustralian Museum of Childhood, Merchant's House, The RocksPowerhouse Museum, SydneyApprentice House, Styal
Indexp. 271
Kirshenblatt-Gimblett, Barbara (1998). Destination Culture: Tourism, Museums, and Heritage. Berkeley: University of California Press.Asia: occasional9 chapter overviews

Overview

Destination Culture (1998) by Barbara Kirshenblatt-Gimblett proposes a political economy of showing: objects gain their meaning at the destination where they are displayed, and museums, world's fairs, festivals, living history sites and tourist attractions produce heritage through display. Its central argument is that heritage is a new mode of cultural production in the present that has recourse to the past, adding value to what is no longer viable and foreclosing what it shows. The essays cover the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, mainly the United States, with cases from France, England, New Zealand and Australia. The book has four parts: the agency of display (ethnographic objects, Jewish participation in world's fairs), a second life as heritage (tourism, Ellis Island, Plimoth Plantation), undoing the ethnographic (the 1990 Los Angeles Festival, an African art exhibition), and circulating value (taste and kitsch).

East and Southeast Asia in this work occasional

East and Southeast Asia are a minor, recurring presence rather than a subject of the book. Chapter 1, Objects of Ethnography, cites Nathan Dunn's life-size clay figures in Chinese costume and settings, shown in Peale's museum in Philadelphia in 1838 and taken to London in 1841, and the wax scenes of Chinese daily life at the Oriental and Turkish Museum in London in the 1850s that followed it. It also notes that Balinese performances made for the 1931 Paris Colonial Exposition were taken back to Bali for tourists. Chapter 2, Exhibiting Jews, mentions Ephraim Benguiat's Damascus Palace at the 1904 St Louis fair, which showed Philippine war loot from the 1898 Spanish-American War and a carved teak Chinese bed. Chapter 3, Destination Museum, cites the Burmese plan to move Padaung women to a model village near Rangoon for Visit Myanmar Year.

The introduction and chapter 3 use Splendid China, the 1993 Florida park reproducing Chinese monuments and minority cultures, as the clearest case of heritage that forecloses what it shows, and mention a planned World-Folklore Theme Park in Guangzhou. Chapters 7 and 8 mention Bunraku and a Peking lion dog only in passing.

Chapter 6, Confusing Pleasures, is the one substantial treatment. The Pacific Rim programme of the 1990 Los Angeles Festival was largely Asian: Balinese children's dance and gamelan, court performers from the Yogyakarta palace, Javanese shadow puppets, Chinese Kun opera, Korean shamans from Chindo Island, Cambodian court dance, and Japanese and Thai artists. The chapter reads the festival's framing as art, and its labels 'multicultural' and 'international', as concealing asymmetries of power, and it recalls Brecht's and Artaud's encounters with Chinese and Balinese theatre. Not covered: museums in East or Southeast Asia, Asian state heritage policy beyond the Burmese and Chinese examples, and Asian collectors, curators or visitors.

ChinaJapanKoreaIndonesiaThailandPhilippinesCambodiaBurma

CONTENTSPDF p. 6

INTRODUCTIONp. 1

Kirshenblatt-Gimblett's introduction asks what it means to show things, arguing that objects gain meaning at their destination and that ethnographic objects are made by the disciplines that detach them. It distinguishes in-context displays, which teach through labels, from in situ displays that immerse visitors in re-created worlds. It then previews essays on world's fairs, heritage sites such as Ellis Island and Plimoth Plantation, the 1990 Los Angeles Festival, and taste. The introduction concludes that heritage is produced through display.

East and Southeast Asia Kirshenblatt-Gimblett cites Splendid China, a 76-acre park opened in 1993 near Orlando, Florida, that reproduces Chinese monuments and palaces and the cultural practices of ethnic minorities, and argues that such sites make heritage by erasing what they show, which drew protests. Kirshenblatt-Gimblett also cites the 'World-Folklore Theme Park' planned in Guangzhou, China. The 1990 Los Angeles Festival, previewed here, presented Korean shamans, Javanese court dance and performers from Thailand and Indonesia as avant-garde art.

Ellis Island Immigration MuseumPlimoth PlantationMuseum for African ArtColonial Williamsburg
Part 1— The Agency Of Displayp. 14
One— Objects of Ethnographyp. 17

Kirshenblatt-Gimblett asks why museums display objects of little visual interest, and answers that ethnographic objects are fragments made by detachment: an object becomes ethnographic when a collector cuts it from its setting and carries it away. The chapter sets two display modes against each other. In situ installations (period rooms, reconstructed villages, live performers) evoke a missing whole, while in context displays use labels, classifications and lectures to treat objects as documents. The evidence runs from Peale's museum in Philadelphia and the British Museum's Ethnographical Gallery to the label-centred exhibits of George Brown Goode at the Smithsonian and Benguiat's jewel-box collection. It then turns to living people exhibited at Bullock's Egyptian Hall, in zoos and at world's fairs, and to the museum effect by which slumming and city streets become exhibits. Festivals and folklife programmes, especially the Smithsonian's Festival of India, close the argument by showing how performance is staged as culture. The conclusion is that all display is interested: the question is how interest is created, not whether an object has visual appeal.

East and Southeast Asia Nathan Dunn's Chinese collection of life-size clay figures in costume, shown with shop and drawing-room settings, was installed in Peale's museum in 1838 and taken to London in 1841, and a diarist called it a perfect picture of Chinese life. Wax scenes of daily life at London's Oriental and Turkish Museum in the 1850s followed Dunn's example. Balinese performances made for the 1931 Paris Colonial Exposition were taken back to Bali for tourists, and Bali cremations now happen more often and on a larger scale because of tourist money.

Peale's MuseumBritish MuseumEgyptian HallSkansenSmithsonian Festival of American FolklifeOriental and Turkish Museum
Two— Exhibiting Jewsp. 79

Kirshenblatt-Gimblett examines how Jews presented themselves at international expositions between 1851 and 1940 in France, England and the United States. Because Jews were a diaspora without a national pavilion, each display had to settle whether they were a religion, a race or a nation, and the chapter argues that exhibition classifications constituted the subjects they showed. The cases run from Isaac Strauss's collection of Jewish ritual art at the 1878 Paris exposition and the Anglo-Jewish Historical Exhibition of 1887 to Cyrus Adler's biblical and religious displays at the U.S. National Museum, and to the Jews who appeared as Turks and portrait types on Chicago's Midway Plaisance in 1893. It then turns to Ephraim Benguiat's Damascus Palace at St Louis in 1904, Boris Bogen's Exposition of the Jews of Many Lands in Cincinnati in 1913, and Meyer Weisgal's Zionist pageants and the Jewish Palestine Pavilion of the 1930s. Each strategy, whether art, science, performance or social work, reflects its sponsors' position in American or European society. The chapter ends by noting that once Israel was founded, its government sponsored Jewish national exhibits at world's fairs.

East and Southeast Asia At the 1904 St Louis fair, Benguiat's Damascus Palace displayed Philippine war loot from the 1898 Spanish-American War as a special attraction, and a carved teak Chinese bed that a correspondent judged finer than anything in the Chinese government exhibit.

U.S. National MuseumH. Ephraim Benguiat MuseumTrocadero PalaceAnglo-Jewish Historical ExhibitionJewish Palestine PavilionExposition of the Jews of Many Lands
Part 2— A Second Life As Heritagep. 129
Three— Destination Museump. 131

Kirshenblatt-Gimblett argues that museums and tourism now feed on each other: places, buildings and ways of life that have lost their function are given a second life as exhibits of themselves, a process she calls heritage. The chapter, which opens Part 2 of the book, sets out seven propositions that organise the argument: heritage produces something new in the present, adds value to assets that are no longer viable, produces the local for export, depends on the instruments that display it, forecloses what it shows, tests the alienability of inalienable possessions, and works through virtuality. Its examples come mostly from New Zealand and Australia, including the Museum of Sydney, Te Papa and the Maori village at Rotorua, and from American sites such as the George Gustav Heye Center, the Museum of Tolerance, Disney's America and Colonial Williamsburg, with the Cluny church ruin and Gettysburg as further cases. The chapter ends by calling tourism a museum of the consciousness industry, where old ideas go to die.

East and Southeast Asia Burmese authorities' plan to move 'long-necked' Padaung women from eastern Burma to a model village near Rangoon, timed for 'Visit Myanmar Year', is cited as a case where exhibition makes what it shows disappear; dissidents call the village an ethnic human zoo. The chapter also notes that the tourist performances on Bali descend from pieces made for Paris expositions in the 1930s.

Museum of SydneyPowerhouse MuseumTe Papa TongarewaAmerican Museum of Natural HistoryGeorge Gustav Heye CenterMuseum of ToleranceCluny church museum
Four— Ellis Islandp. 177

Kirshenblatt-Gimblett treats Ellis Island as a federal immigration station that has been turned into a national shrine. It was once an aperture where the Immigration Service processed steerage passengers, and since 1965 it has been run by the National Park Service as part of a recreational geography of monuments. The chapter analyses the restoration of the Main Building, completed in 1990 with about $158 million from private sponsors such as American Express and AT&T, and the Immigrant Wall of Honor, on which names are inscribed for a fee. The restored Registry Room, the gift shop, the menus and the coloring book turn immigrant history into souvenirs, national identities and a heritage that leaves out most of those who never passed through the island. The list and the grid make every name look alike, and the author concludes that memory here is not reclaimed but produced by those who control the restoration.

Ellis Island Immigration MuseumJewish Museum (New York)
Five— Plimoth Plantationp. 189

Plimoth Plantation is the last case, a living history museum whose Pilgrim Village re-creates 1627 with first-person interpreters beside an exhibit gallery of archaeological finds. Kirshenblatt-Gimblett treats the site as performance rather than reconstruction, and begins with the town itself, which she describes as a museum of heritage performance. Plymouth Rock, a plain rock under a neoclassical portico, is set against the village: the rock is mute, while the village answers the hole left by excavation. Drawing on Snow's study of the site, the chapter traces display traditions including the archaeological fragment, the habitat group and the tourist encounter. It identifies three clocks: a stopped historical moment, a heritage clock that keeps ageing the buildings, and the visitors' own time, in which they test the interpreters and try to make them break character. The chapter concludes by comparing Plimoth with the Ellis Island restoration: both claim inclusiveness, and Ellis Island has absorbed Plimoth, so the Rock becomes just another port of entry.

Plimoth PlantationEllis Island Immigration Museum
Part 3— Undoing The Ethnographicp. 201
Six— Confusing Pleasuresp. 203Asia: in part

Kirshenblatt-Gimblett examines the 1990 Los Angeles Festival, directed by Peter Sellars, and argues that its claim to authenticity lay in audiences' encounters with what they did not understand rather than in the performances themselves. Kirshenblatt-Gimblett traces the festival's origins to the 1984 Olympic Arts Festival and the 1987 Los Angeles Festival, describes its collaborative planning structure and Pacific Rim theme, and sets it against the rejection of 'ethnographic' presentation and of mainstream entertainment. The chapter then places the festival in a genealogy of avant-garde performance, world's fairs, homelands and folk festivals, and modern-art curatorship of 'folk' and 'primitive' art. Her main case is the way performances from Asia, Oceania and the Americas were framed as 'art' and as 'just different', using labels such as 'multicultural' and 'international' that she reads as concealing asymmetries of power. She concludes that the festival's avant-garde reception undoes the ethnographic while depending on it, and that the event was in effect a presentation of Los Angeles as a civilized, multicultural city.

East and Southeast Asia The festival's Pacific Rim programme was largely Asian: Children of Bali, court performers from the Yogyakarta palace in Java, Javanese shadow puppets, Chinese Kun opera, Korean shamans from Chindo Island, Cambodian court dance, and Japanese and Thai performers among the invited artists, with Cambodian and Korean immigrant communities cited as part of the city. The chapter notes that Brecht's encounter with Mei Lanfang's Chinese opera in 1935 and Artaud's glimpse of Balinese theatre in Paris shaped avant-garde taste for these forms.

Museum of Modern ArtCentre PompidouNewark Museum
Seven— Secrets of Encounterp. 249

Kirshenblatt-Gimblett reviews Secrecy: African Art That Conceals and Reveals, the 1993 opening exhibition of the Museum for African Art in its new SoHo home. Kirshenblatt-Gimblett describes its six sections, which ask how art conceals knowledge, marks boundaries, expresses gendered secrets and transmits them, and its choice to show borrowed objects as art in dramatic vitrines. Kirshenblatt-Gimblett’s argument is that the exhibition treats secrecy as a semiotic problem, so that meaning is deferred and visitors take pleasure in not understanding. Kirshenblatt-Gimblett concludes by asking who is preoccupied with secrecy, and points to the secrets kept by dealers, collectors and curators.

Museum for African Art
Part 4— Circulating Valuep. 257
Eight— Disputing Tastep. 259

Kirshenblatt-Gimblett's chapter on taste asks how objects come to be classed as good or bad taste and how that distinction organizes social hierarchy. Kirshenblatt-Gimblett’s case material is The Encyclopedia of Bad Taste and its mirror twin Quintessence: The Quality of Having It, which catalogue commodities, celebrities and bodies in opposing terms. Kirshenblatt-Gimblett argues that bad taste is a category produced by the arbiters of good taste, and that it is unstable: objects move through circuits of exchange, are recoded by subcultures such as punks and low riders, and return as retro goods. Drawing on Greenberg, Adorno, Bakhtin and Elias, she traces the modernist idea of kitsch as a defence of high culture against mass audiences and its class assumptions. The chapter ends by asking whether the erosion of differences between high and low leads to a world of kitsch or to a liberating pluralism, and leaves the question open.

Knell, Simon J.; Aronsson, Peter; Amundsen, Arne Bugge; et al. (eds.) (2011). National Museums: New Studies from Around the World. London: Routledge.Asia: substantial30 chapter overviews

Overview

An edited volume of 29 chapters on national museums (2011), most of them in Europe, grown out of the NaMu research network. Three introductions by Knell, Aronsson and Preziosi set out the theory: national museums perform and imagine the nation through objects, settings and scripts rather than simply reflecting it, and they are negotiated arenas for states, professionals and publics. The case studies cover Britain, France, Sweden, Finland, Poland, Turkey, Taiwan, Korea, China, Hong Kong, Romania, Bulgaria, Belgium, Ireland, Estonia, the Netherlands, Wales and Colombia. The chapters are grouped into origins and ideologies, museology and participation, and ourselves and others, and cover the nineteenth to twenty-first centuries.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

East Asia is one of the volume's strongest threads, concentrated in seven chapters. Chu (ch. 11) traces Taiwan's national museums under Japanese rule, when the Director-General's Museum of 1908 held objects from South East Asia and southern China; under the KMT, whose US-aided National Palace Museum (1962) taught Chinese nationalism; and under the DPP, which mounted Taiwan-focused exhibitions and removed the Chiang and Sun statues in 2004. Choi (ch. 17), Lee (ch. 23) and Scheidhauer (ch. 22) cover the National Museum of Korea in Seoul and the Kaesŏng Koryŏ Museum in North Korea, through colonial collecting, the 1995 demolition of the Governor-General's building and South Korean tourist visits to Kaesŏng. Varutti (ch. 18) covers China's aesthetic displays at the Shanghai Museum and Sanxingdui, Stokes-Rees (ch. 21) The Hong Kong Story, and Barnes (ch. 24) Victorian London's China displays, including the 1851 China Court and the Qianlong throne at the Victoria and Albert Museum.

Knell's chapter 1 mentions Korea, Taiwan and the Edo-Tokyo Museum, and Hughes's chapter 12 mentions China only through the British Museum's First Emperor catalogue.

Southeast Asia is almost absent: it appears only as a source of Japanese colonial collecting in Taiwan, as the US Cold War alliance in South East Asia that Chu notes, and in a Thai contemporary art 'Amity' exhibition staged in Bangkok (Lee, ch. 23). No chapter treats Indonesia, the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia or Singapore.
