Knell, writing for the editors, explains that the book grew out of Making National Museums (NaMu), a European Commission-funded project of 2007-2008 that brought early-career researchers to workshops in Norrkoping, Leicester and Oslo. The chapters, mostly from Old World national museums rather than North America or Australasia, are grouped into themes and framed by three introductions: Knell's theoretical overview, Aronsson's comparative proposal and Preziosi's philosophical essay. The preface also records the editorial process and the follow-on EU-funded Eunamus project, which will compare the origins of European national museums and their uses of history.

Part One: Introductions and reflectionsp. 1
1National Museums And The National ImaginationSimon Knellp. 3Asia: in part

Knell argues that national museums do not simply record nations but perform them, through objects, architecture, scripts and settings that make visitors believe in a particular national story. Drawing on Benedict Anderson and on cases from around the world, he shows how national identity is anchored in memory and folk heritage, how professionals' control of the script clashes with public participation, and how national art museums build canons and project identities abroad. Examples run from Hong Kong's history museum and Bulgaria's communist narratives to Poland's historical paintings and Colombia's multicultural politics. His extended cases are the National Gallery of Art in Washington, where American identity is pressed onto Hopper's paintings and a snapshot display, and the Edo-Tokyo Museum, whose performances continue into the city outside. The chapter closes with a model of the musealised landscape, in which the national imagination passes between museum objects and places such as Malham Cove, and proposes that the nation is performed in the museum as much as it is represented there.

East and Southeast Asia Korea and Taiwan are the main cases. Choi's study of the National Museum of Korea shows national identity performed through art motifs, a positioning Choi comes to see as a legacy of Japanese imposition, and South Korea has sponsored celadon galleries in European and American museums to build its international identity. Taiwan's national museums came to display things 'Taiwanese rather than Chinese' as democracy grew, and the Taiwan Museum of Art shows Ku Ping-Hsing's paintings. Varutti is cited on China's museums, which affirm a single great civilization by forgetting difficult histories. The Edo-Tokyo Museum is described as a musealised city, with Japanese prints used as reconstruction evidence.

National Gallery of Art, WashingtonEdo-Tokyo MuseumNational Museum of KoreaTaiwan Museum of ArtPergamon Museum, BerlinHong Kong Museum of History
2Explaining National MuseumsPeter Aronssonp. 29

Aronsson asks why national museums exist everywhere and why they differ, and proposes a comparative method to test three standard explanations: the spread of the Enlightenment, Napoleonic nationalism and the shaping of subjects into citizens. Aronsson tests these on two groups of cases outside the usual Britain and France: the Mediterranean (Greece, Italy and Turkey) and Scandinavia. In Athens, the Acropolis was cleared of its Ottoman and Christian layers to stage the fifth century BC, and the National History Museum tells a teleological story that omits the Civil War and the junta. In Rome, the Museo della Civilta at EUR and the Risorgimento monument struggle to produce one national narrative, while Istanbul's museums, from the Ottoman-founded Archaeological Museum to Miniaturk, show a more pluralist, privately driven negotiation. In Scandinavia, Denmark's National Museum presents an unbroken national story, while Sweden's prehistory displays avoid the ethnic argument. Aronsson concludes that national museums are arenas where states, elites and publics negotiate, and that comparison should be used to complicate generalisations rather than confirm them.

National Archaeological Museum, AthensNational History Museum, AthensAcropolis Museum, AthensMuseo della Civilta, Rome (EUR)Museum of the Risorgimento, RomeIstanbul Archaeological MuseumMiniaturk, IstanbulNational Museum of Denmark, Copenhagen
3Chapter 3. Myths of nationalityDonald Preziosip. 55

Preziosi asks why national museum narratives work and argues that they rest on an old belief that objects carry fixed meanings and witness the spirit of a people. Preziosi builds the case through the religious and philosophical roots of museum display, from the ancient arts of memory to Christian and Islamic ideas of fulfilment, and treats the museum as a stage on which the past is presented as the cause of the present. Preziosi’s evidence is largely conceptual rather than a set of case studies: he cites Plato's banishment of the arts in the Republic, Byzantine iconoclasm, the 2005 Danish cartoon controversy, and the late nineteenth-century Egyptian policy of destroying or selling objects that did not fit a curator's idea of Pharaonic style. Preziosi concludes that national museums depend on a disingenuous faith in the power of artefacts to testify to a national essence, and that a responsible museology should expose this faith and de-sanctify culture rather than manage it as heritage. The chapter is dense and essayistic, and it suits students already familiar with theory.

Part Two: Origins and ideologiesp. 67
4Chapter 4. Loading guns with patriotic love: Artur Hazelius’s attempts at Skansen to remake Swedish societyMattias Bäckströmp. 69

Bäckström examines Artur Hazelius, founder of the Nordic Museum and its open-air department Skansen in Stockholm, and argues that Hazelius legitimised his museum through an organic Romantic idea of a 'folk community' united by patriotic love rather than through the Swedish state. The chapter draws on Hazelius's letters, memoranda and the museum archive, and centres on the Spring Festivals of the 1890s. It shows how the festival cannonade, church bells and the new Swedish National Day of 6 June staged a harmonious society, and how upper-class women in national costume were presented as its moral embodiment, their genealogies published in the press. Bäckström describes the chaperoning and surveillance that kept festival visitors respectable, the 'Lapp' camp staffed by women who were not Sami, and Hazelius's own angry memoranda about how the festival was run. Hazelius's museum, he concludes, fused Romantic idealism with Darwinian classification, and its feminine emotional community anticipated the later Swedish folkhem. The argument is well documented from the archive.

Nordic MuseumSkansen
5Chapter 5. Narrative and imagination: Remaking national history at the Musée des Monuments français, ParisJennifer Carterp. 88

Carter traces the origins of the narrative history museum to Alexandre Lenoir's Musée des Monuments français, which opened in Paris in 1795 and closed in 1816. Lenoir arranged confiscated royal, noble and church monuments in a former monastery, with one hall for each century of French art and an Elysium garden modelled on the picturesque landscape. Carter's evidence comes mainly from Lenoir's own multi-volume catalogues, the engravings of the halls, and the reactions of visitors such as Michelet, who recalled his childhood impressions. Carter argues that Lenoir fused an eighteenth-century sensibility drawn from garden design with the new public museum, using light, scenography and the parcours to produce emotional experience rather than analytic display. Carter’s central term is the 'fabrique', a composite monument built from fragments, such as the Héloïse and Abélard chapel, which she reads as an 'anti-ruin' that restores a fractured national past rather than mourning it. Carter concludes that the museum was both an art museum and a history museum, and that its poetic narrative placed visitors within the nation's story, even though Lenoir's removal of objects from the provinces contributed to its closure.

Musée des Monuments françaisLouvre
6Chapter 6. National art museum practice as political cartography in nineteenth-century BritainChristopher Whiteheadp. 105

Whitehead argues that the nineteenth-century national museums of London worked as cartographic technologies, mapping the world, society and Britain's place within it through the arrangement and classification of objects. Drawing on cartographic theory, he treats the museum as a kind of map and then examines the British Museum, the National Gallery and the South Kensington Museum, later the V&A. His evidence includes the 1855 Bernal sale, at which the British Museum and South Kensington competed for objects under different collecting criteria, and the letters of curator J. C. Robinson asking for money to buy church treasures from a Spain in revolution. He shows how the National Gallery's old master paintings were presented as morally improving for a new electorate after the 1832 Reform Act, quoting Peel's parliamentary speech, and how Britain was largely absent from the displays until the Gallery of British Art opened at South Kensington in 1857. Whitehead concludes that Britain figured less as a territory on the map than as the cartographer surveying other cultures, and that the weak expression of nationhood in these museums was partly a way of avoiding radical patriotism and social upheaval.

British MuseumNational GallerySouth Kensington Museum
7Chapter 7. Placing Britain in the British Museum: Encompassing the OtherChris Wingfieldp. 123

Wingfield argues that the British Museum has long told a story of 'civilization' rather than a national one, and that the 1866 creation of its Department of British and Medieval Antiquities and Ethnography shifted how the civilized self related to its 'Others' without abandoning that story. Wingfield traces the mid-century 'Ethnographical Room', contemporary complaints that its jumble was unworthy of a national museum, and the campaign for a collection of national antiquities that led to A. W. Franks's appointment in 1851. The chapter's central episode is Franks's use of the Henry Christy bequest in 1865 to secure his position and to bring prehistoric archaeology and ethnography into the Museum. Wingfield also examines the frustrated negotiations over General Pitt Rivers's collection, and Panizzi's earlier wish to clear ethnological material from the galleries to make room for classical antiquities. Wingfield concludes, drawing on Trigger and Dumont, that Victorian anthropology used an 'encompassing' grammar, absorbing the uncivilized past into a global history of civilization with Britain at its culmination.

British MuseumPitt Rivers MuseumNatural History MuseumHenry Christy collection
8Chapter 8. Producing an art history of the nation: The origins of the Finnish National GallerySusanna Petterssonp. 138

Pettersson traces how the collection of the Finnish Art Society became the basis of Finland's first national gallery, the Ateneum, which opened in Helsinki in October 1888. Its leaders, Fredrik Cygnaeus and Carl Gustaf Estlander, wanted a single continuous story of art in the Hegelian manner, but Finland had no royal collections, few private collectors and limited funds, and the early collection simply served the Society's drawing school with copies of European masters and works by Nordic painters. The national character of the collection grew from 1858, when the Society began buying living Finnish artists such as Werner Holmberg and Carl Eneas Sjöstrand. Pettersson draws on the Society's inventories, catalogues and the chairmen's writings to show how the Ateneum then reorganised the works by school and geography, removed historical portraits and weak copies, and shifted from quantity to quality. The chapter concludes that the Society's educational investment in national artists, rather than rivalry with older European collections, gave Finland a collection of national relevance. It leaves open the awkward case of Alexander Lauréus, a Turku-born painter claimed by Sweden, and the question of who counted as a Finnish artist.

AteneumFinnish Art Society collection
9Chapter 9. Reimagining the nation in museums: Poland’s old and new national museumsKaroline Kaluzap. 151

Kaluza examines how Polish national museums have been used to keep a nation alive, from the partitions of 1795 to the boom of new museums after Poland joined the EU in 2004. Kaluza argues that Polish museums have always served national memory, but that the medium has changed: relics and reliquaries in the early 1800s, regional national museums after 1945, and now interactive, testimony-based institutions. Kaluza’s evidence is concrete. Kaluza describes Izabela Czartoryska's museum of relics of the high nobility, Władysław Plater's exile museum at Rapperswil, where Kościuszko's heart was placed in a mausoleum, and the Matejko paintings circulated across partitioned Poland. The Warsaw Uprising Museum, opened in 2004, receives the most attention: it keeps a clock set at 5 p.m., builds its displays on oral testimony and multimedia, and occupies a reconstructed tram power plant. Kaluza concludes that the new museums gather intangible, personal memories and are openly political, backed by European funding, and that the memory of a formerly diverse nation is slowly being recovered.

Czartoryska museum (Puławy)Rapperswil National MuseumWarsaw Uprising MuseumMuseum of the History of Polish JewsMuseum of Modern Art in Warsaw
10Chapter 10. National art museums and the ‘modernization’ of TurkeyAyşe H. Köksalp. 163

Köksal argues that each of Turkey's national art museums was rebuilt to present the nation to outsiders, and that none of the three she examines was ever labelled a national museum. Köksal compares the Imperial Museum, founded in 1869 and reorganised under Osman Hamdi from 1881; the Istanbul Museum of Painting and Sculpture, set up in 1937 in Dolmabahçe Palace on Atatürk's order; and Istanbul Modern, opened in 2004. The Imperial Museum used Helleno-Byzantine and Islamic antiquities to claim Ottoman hegemony over the origins of European civilization, and it excluded Western-style Turkish art. The Istanbul Museum of Painting and Sculpture arranged its galleries chronologically by degree of Western influence, from 'Primitives' to 'Modern', so that Turkish art appeared as an apprentice seeking the West's approval. Her evidence comes from museum regulations, the directors' writings, and visitor figures that fell from 300 to 400 a day in 1937 to about 70 by 2006. Istanbul Modern, funded by the Eczacıbaşı family and opened in the presence of Prime Minister Erdoğan, is presented as a global museum in a global city. Köksal concludes that each museum served the elites seeking Western recognition.

Imperial Museum (Istanbul)Istanbul Museum of Painting and SculptureIstanbul Modern
11Chapter 11. Political change and the national museum in TaiwanChi-Jung Chup. 180Asia: chiefly

Chu traces how three political programmes shaped the national museums of Taiwan: Japanese colonial rule from 1895 to 1945, Kuomintang rule from 1949 to 2000, and the Democratic Progressive Party government after 2000. Chu argues that each regime used museums to tell a different national story. The Director-General's Museum, opened in Taipei in 1908 in Western classical style, showcased colonial power and took on a social education role, and after 1945 it became the Taiwan Provincial Museum with lower status. The National Palace Museum, built in 1962 with United States aid, served the KMT as an instrument for teaching Chinese nationalism through guided tours, bilingual publications and school visits. Chu's evidence includes exhibition lists, annual reports and loan records, and the 2004 removal of the statues of Sun Yat-sen and Chiang Kai-shek from the entrance. Under the DPP the Taiwan Provincial Museum became the National Taiwan Museum in 1999, and new museums were founded to build a Taiwanese identity. Chu concludes that national museums were repeatedly redeployed to imagine the nation, and that the 'provincial' Taiwan was made into a nation.

East and Southeast Asia Japan's Director-General's Museum in Taipei, founded in 1908, held collections of Taiwan's indigenous peoples and objects from South East Asia and southern China, which Chu links to Japan's colonial ambitions. The KMT's National Palace Museum, built in 1962 with US aid, showcased imperial Chinese art and sent treasures abroad, including to Japan's Expo '70 in Osaka and to Seoul in 1973. Chu notes that its exhibitions were used to teach Taiwanese people to be Chinese. Under the DPP, its director Tu Cheng-shen mounted Taiwan-focused exhibitions from 2002 and removed the Chiang and Sun statues in 2004.

Director-General's Museum (Taipei)Taiwan Provincial Museum (National Taiwan Museum)National Palace Museum (Taipei)National Museum of History (Nan-hai cultural cluster)National Museum of Taiwan History
12Chapter 12. The British Museum in print: From national to universal museumSarah A. Hughesp. 193

Hughes examines how the British Museum presents itself as a universal rather than a national museum, using its own printed materials. The chapter applies critical discourse analysis to four British Museum Press books: the Souvenir Guide (2003), Woff's Family Guide (2007), the First Emperor exhibition catalogue and Jenkins's book on the Parthenon sculptures (both 2007, read through their forewords only). It starts from the commercial weight of museum publishing, then shows how the texts describe producers, audiences and the museum itself in generalised terms such as 'humankind' and 'the world', detaching objects from their origins and from ownership claims. Hughes traces a consistent claim to longevity, denies any national origin for the collections and cites the Parthenon sculptures to defend a world museum against local interests. The chapter concludes that these guides carry subtle political messages, presenting the museum as custodian of world culture whose comparisons teach visitors that universalism serves a moral cause.

East and Southeast Asia The chapter says little about East Asia beyond the First Emperor catalogue, whose foreword presents the British Museum's exhibition of Qin terracotta army material as part of exchanges with China. The foreword claims three British Museum exhibitions had toured Chinese museums and treats the museum and the Chinese state as equal partners in cultural exchange. Hughes reads this as a national museum claiming influence beyond its borders.

British Museum
Part Three: Museology and participationp. 205
13Chapter 13. The nation disrobed: Nudity, leisure and class at the PradoEugenia Afinoguénovap. 207

Afinoguénova asks how the Prado, nationalised in 1868, became a national museum in the eyes of its public. The main evidence is the comic sketches, poems and serial fiction that Madrid's satirical press ran from the 1870s to the 1890s, mocking provincial and lower-class visitors shocked by nude paintings and sculptures. The chapter argues these caricatures did not record popular behaviour, since visitor books show no such complaints and literacy was low; they let the literate bourgeoisie claim a civic, playful way of looking against aristocratic and popular habits. It traces the legal transfer of the collection from Crown to state between 1865 and 1873, rising attendance figures, and the museum's place in a 'leisure zone' of cafés and promenades. It also shows the press tying paintings to politics and the stage, through quarrels over large historical canvases. The conclusion is that the nation was produced from below, as middle-class men took possession of the museum through laughter and scandal.

Prado Museum
14Chapter 14. Taking part: Performance, participation and national art museumsStuart Burchp. 225

Burch asks how far national museums genuinely let audiences take part, and argues that participation is always a matter of degree. The examples come from Norway, Sweden and London: the 2009 protest against the relocation of Oslo's Nasjonalgalleriet, the 1968 Modellen exhibition at Stockholm's Moderna Museet, where children played on a foam-block structure, and recent work at the two Tate galleries. Drawing on Pateman's full, partial and pseudo-participation, Burch finds that the rhetoric of engagement often masks control: a critical video was removed from Nationalmuseum, and a Nolde painting with a disputed Nazi-era history stayed on the wall unexplained while its return to the heirs was negotiated. Only the open storage of Moderna Museet's Pontus Hultén Study Gallery comes close to partial participation. The chapter concludes that the decisive question is which obstacles are necessary, and who decides.

NasjonalgallerietModerna MuseetTate ModernTate BritainNationalmuseum
15Chapter 15. Representing Wales at the Museum of Welsh LifeRhiannon Masonp. 247

Mason examines how the Museum of Welsh Life, the open-air branch of National Museum Wales at St Fagans, has represented Welsh national identity. Founded as the Welsh Folk Museum on the Scandinavian open-air model, it was meant to show a 'Wales in miniature' of rural, Welsh-speaking life, and the chapter tests critics' charges that such museums are static and politically amnesiac. It traces how curators from the 1980s began collecting industrial South Wales, beginning with the Rhyd-y-car ironworkers' cottages, and argues that practical pressures shaped this shift as much as ideology: admission charges that cut visitor numbers after 1985, and audience surveys showing most visitors come from the South. The chapter also examines the siting of buildings by social function, the Celtic Village reconstruction, and the confusion of the network's branding. It concludes that the museum is a meeting point for competing ideas of Welshness, and that its planned galleries should prompt visitors to question their own assumptions.

Museum of Welsh LifeSkansen
16Chapter 16. Same exhibitions, different labels? Romanian national museums and the fall of communismSimina Bădicăp. 272

Bădică asks whether Romania's national museums really changed after 1989, or whether the anti-communist exhibitions were 'the same exhibitions with the labels changed'. The chapter compares three pre-1989 communist museums with post-1989 displays at the Romanian Peasant Museum, the Sighet Memorial and the National History Museum. It traces a genealogy from Soviet museology, whose 1957 manual told curators to surround objects with explanatory text, and shows how Romanian exhibitions of the 1970s and 1980s relied on panels, photographs and newspapers, with titles growing ever longer. After 1989 the Peasant Museum's label-free The Plague installation and the prison re-creations at Sighet and Doftana reuse the same techniques, with only the message reversed. The chapter concludes that the object-centred antidote-museum called for by Nicolau remains largely unrealised.

Romanian Peasant MuseumHistory Museum of the Romanian Communist PartyDoftana MuseumSighet MemorialNational History Museum
17Chapter 17. Re-thinking Korean cultural identities at the National Museum of KoreaSunghee Choip. 290Asia: chiefly

Choi uses autoethnography to examine her own visits to the National Museum of Korea in Seoul. Choi finds that its aesthetic, context-free displays steer visitors towards a single account of Korean uniqueness. The chapter traces the idea of Korean art as an essence of 'sorrow', coined by the Japanese critic Yanagi Muneyoshi in 1920 under colonial rule, and argues that Koreans came to define themselves in terms supplied by the colonizer. The core evidence is a talk Choi gave to two American visitors in the fine art gallery, using a Joseon documentary painting to set Korea apart from China and Japan; she then recognises how closely her confidence followed the museum's interpretive approach. Drawing on Hooper-Greenhill, Spivak and Bhabha, she proposes a 'third space' where visitors tell their own stories, and critiques forum-style models that offer only cultural diversity. The chapter concludes that the museum should provide such a space so that visitors can rewrite their identities beyond the path colonialism set.

East and Southeast Asia Korea is the chapter's whole subject: the National Museum of Korea's fine art and archaeology galleries, a Joseon documentary screen of court ceremonies, and the colonial-era idea of Korean art as 'sorrow', which the Japanese critic Yanagi Muneyoshi developed around Joseon white porcelain. Choi also compares Korean documentary painting with Chinese and Japanese neo-Confucian art, and argues that Korean identity was shaped under Japanese colonial rule.

National Museum of Korea
18Chapter 18. The aesthetics and narratives of national museums in ChinaMarzia Varuttip. 302Asia: chiefly

Varutti examines the rise of aesthetic display in China's national museums since the Shanghai Museum opened in 1996, and asks what beliefs such displays manufacture. Based on fieldwork at several museums in Shanghai, Beijing and Sichuan, the chapter argues that beauty-led displays present objects as wonders detached from their histories. It traces the Chinese museum from the Nantong Museum of 1905 and the Palace Museum of 1925, through the Maoist period when objects were 'witnesses of history', to the post-1989 turn to cultural nationalism, which made ancient civilisation a source of political legitimacy. Shang bronzes and Qing calligraphy are shown side by side, with thematic arrangements, sparse labels and dramatic lighting producing a flattened image of a nation defined by longevity and refinement. The chapter concludes that aesthetics is now a mainstream way of staging national pasts, and that in China it works as a 'belief enhancer' which sidesteps contentious questions about national unity.

East and Southeast Asia The whole chapter concerns China: the Shanghai Museum's aesthetic display, Beijing's National History Museum, Military Museum and Capital Museum, the China Millennium Monument's 2004 'Imperial Treasures' show, and the Sanxingdui Museum's presentation of the ancient Shu civilisation of Sichuan. It traces the Nantong Museum of 1905, the Palace Museum of 1925 and revolutionary displays under Mao, and notes that Western museums often file Chinese material under 'Asian Art' or 'Far-East Asian Antiquities'.

Shanghai MuseumNational History Museum (Beijing)Military MuseumCapital MuseumChina Millennium MonumentSanxingdui MuseumNantong MuseumPalace Museum
19Chapter 19. The Dutch National Historical Museum: A national museum for the twenty-first centuryGwenny van Hasseltp. 313

van Hasselt traces the long and contested creation of a National Historical Museum in the Netherlands, starting from debates in the early 1990s over the Rijksmuseum's rebuilding and the loss of its history wing. The chapter follows how a 2006 parliamentary motion turned a schools-oriented canon of Dutch history into a call for a museum, and how fears of nationalism, sharpened by the murders of Fortuyn and van Gogh, shaped the debate. It then explains how Arnhem beat Amsterdam and The Hague as the site in 2007, chosen as a 'watchtower' on regional history beside the Open Air Museum, and how project sessions and a two-man board produced a vision of five thematic 'worlds' with a chronological room. The chapter records disputes over chronology, the canon and global context that followed public debate. It concludes that a national museum in a liberal democracy is produced through the mediation of government, professionals, media and public, rather than through a single settled vision.

RijksmuseumOpen Air Museum (Arnhem)National Historical Museum
20Chapter 20. Who authors the nation? The debate surrounding the building of the new Estonian National MuseumPille Runnel, Taavi Tatsi and Pille Pruulmann-Vengerfeldtp. 325

The authors examine the debate over the new Estonian National Museum, to be rebuilt at Raadi outside Tartu, the site of the old museum and an airfield. They ask who authors the nation: architects, curators, the public or the state. Drawing on participant observation in planning meetings and on media analysis, they show how a competition won by a Paris practice, whose 'Memory Field' design extended an airfield runway into the museum, unsettled a public that expected an ethnographic museum of peasant life. Online commentary was largely hostile, while the jury treated the audience as a vague target group and curators regarded visitors as sources of information. The planning, the authors argue, produced two separate discourses, one popular and essentialist, the other professional and postmodern. They conclude that the museum can become a site of cultural innovation only if it shifts from ethnic toward civic nationalism and opens shared authorship to audiences.

Estonian National Museum
21Chapter 21. Recounting history: Constructing a national narrative in the Hong Kong Museum of HistoryEmily Stokes-Reesp. 339Asia: chiefly

Stokes-Rees asks how the Hong Kong Museum of History builds a national story for a territory returned to China in 1997. Drawing on Bruner's claim that people make sense of themselves through narrative, she reads the permanent exhibition The Hong Kong Story (opened 2001) as a text, attending to its route, dioramas, film and panels. The museum's history is traced from a cluttered temporary display in City Hall in 1962 to the new building. Her main cases are the gallery sequence from geology and the 'rocks at Ping Chau' through the 'tribal' folk culture displays to the high-rise flat model, the Tanka fishing junk diorama, and the multimedia design. She also reports observation of visitors who hurry past most displays, and a Hong Kong visitor's complaint of '50 years of no change'. She concludes that the fixed route and single storyline of transformation from fishing village to metropolis enlist visitors in a rags-to-riches national canon, and that the museum preserves an essentialised Hong Kong identity from before it became China.

East and Southeast Asia Hong Kong is the whole subject: the chapter analyses the Hong Kong Museum of History's The Hong Kong Story, which presents the territory's past as a rise from fishing village to metropolis, and sets it against the 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration and the 1997 return to China. It quotes a Hong Kong visitor calling the exhibition 'dumbing down', and the director of the Hong Kong Heritage Museum, Yim Shui-yen, on the public's need for an 'official history'. The mainland 'motherland' is the foil against which the narrative defines a distinct Hong Kong people.

Hong Kong Museum of History
Part Four: Ourselves and Othersp. 355
22Chapter 22. Kaesŏng Koryŏ Museum: The place of one Korean nation?Ruth Scheidhauerp. 357Asia: chiefly

Scheidhauer asks how one museum can hold the memory of a single Korean nation while serving two rival states. Scheidhauer sets out the 'cultural nation' that both Koreas claim, based on shared blood, language and history, against the ideological nation of each regime. The chapter traces the Kaesŏng Koryŏ Museum from the Kaesŏng Provincial Museum, founded in 1930, through its wartime evacuation and reopening under North Korean authority in 1952, to its move into the Sŏnggyun'gwan academy in 1988. Its main evidence is the displays: Koryŏ celadon, metal movable type, a poster comparing the price of a slave with that of an ox, peasant rebellions, and the dragonheads and inscription linked to Kim Il-sung's visits. Scheidhauer also draws on her 2008 participation in a South Korean tour, where visitors remarked more on the museum's poverty than on its ideology. Scheidhauer concludes that the Koryŏ period serves both states as an idealised shared origin, and that tourism to Kaesŏng briefly eased inter-Korean tension.

East and Southeast Asia The chapter is entirely about Korea, with North and South Korea as its two states. It traces the Imperial Household Museum (opened 1909) and the Chosŏn General Government Museum (1915), the colonial-era museums that shaped Korean collecting, and the Kaesŏng Provincial Museum's collections, which were moved to Seoul and then to Pusan during the Korean War. It also reports the reactions of South Korean tourists to North Korean guides and displays on the Kaesŏng tours of 2005 to 2008, which they found backward yet romantic.

Kaesŏng Koryŏ MuseumKaesŏng Provincial MuseumChosŏn General Government MuseumImperial Household Museum
23Chapter 23. The national museum as palimpsest: Postcolonial politics and the National Museum of KoreaJung Joon Leep. 373Asia: chiefly

Lee examines the National Museum of Korea in Seoul, which reopened in 2005 in a new building on the site of the former Governor-General's building, the seat of Japanese colonial rule. Lee argues that the museum is a palimpsest of colonial and postcolonial politics. The chapter traces the institution from its 1908 Yi royal family museum and 1915 Governor-General's museum, through wartime removal to Busan, to the 1995 demolition of the colonial building under President Kim Young Sam, which Lee reads as a renationalisation campaign. His evidence includes the building's neoclassical design, the claim that its plan spelled the kanji for Japan, and the split reaction of intellectuals who wanted it kept. Lee then sets the state-run National Museum of Contemporary Art, with its 'Amity' exhibitions, against the independent Insa Art Space, which was absorbed into Arts Council Korea in 2009. Lee concludes that the government should step back from making the nation through the arts, and that the small institution revealed national complexity better than the large one.

East and Southeast Asia Korea is the subject throughout. Lee traces the National Museum of Korea from the Yi royal family museum of 1908 and the Joseon Governor-General's Museum of 1915, through wartime removal to Busan, to the Japanese colonial building that Seoul demolished in 1995. Lee shows how colonial power is written into that building, whose architect Ichiro Nomura also designed the Governor-General's building in Taiwan. The chapter also cites a 2008 'Amity' exhibition of Thai contemporary art, staged by the Korean National Museum of Contemporary Art in Bangkok as cultural diplomacy.

National Museum of KoreaJoseon Governor-General's MuseumNational Museum of Contemporary ArtInsa Art Space
24Chapter 24. Exhibiting China in LondonAmy Jane Barnesp. 386Asia: chiefly

Barnes argues that Victorian exhibitions and museums did more than display China: they fixed an image of it as backward and unchanging, and in doing so showed what Britain thought of itself. Barnes’s main case is the Celebrated Chinese Collection, Nathan Dunn's commercial show of Chinese objects at Hyde Park Corner in the 1840s, which she sets against the hostile press coverage of the Opium Wars. Barnes then follows Chinese material through the Great Exhibition of 1851, where the small Chinese court was made up largely of chinoiserie and export wares, and into the South Kensington Museum, whose Asian galleries and taxonomy classed Chinese art as decorative rather than aesthetic. Further evidence comes from the Albert Memorial's figure of China beneath India, and from looted objects such as the Qianlong lacquered throne. Barnes concludes that these institutions made China appear moribund and trivial beside a virile Britain and empire, so that the displays tell us more about Britain than about China.

East and Southeast Asia China is the whole subject. Barnes traces how Opium War coverage, and Nathan Dunn's Celebrated Chinese Collection of the 1840s, presented Chinese things as exotic and degraded, including a human exhibit with bound feet and an opium-smoking display. Barnes examines the Chinese court at the 1851 Great Exhibition, drawn mostly from British holdings and largely export ware, and the South Kensington Museum's Asian galleries, which separated Chinese art from Western art. Barnes also discusses looted objects, including the Qianlong lacquered throne at the Victoria and Albert Museum, taken from the Nan Yuan hunting park in 1901.

Celebrated Chinese CollectionGreat Exhibition of 1851South Kensington MuseumAlbert Memorial
25Chapter 25. Exhibiting the Congo in StockholmLotten Gustafsson Reiniusp. 400

Gustafsson Reinius follows Congolese objects from lower Congo into a Swedish exhibition. She opens with the missionary Svante Flodén's account of a nganga who handed over his drum and staff to missionaries in the late 1890s. She then examines the Ethnographic and Missionary Exhibition held in Stockholm in 1907, which showed about 10,000 objects gathered by missionaries in a single year. Her argument is that the exhibition used the Congo to build a national narrative for a Sweden that had lost Finland and Norway and had no colonies of its own. Her evidence is the display itself: a central nkisi nkondi, varnished minkisi, a leopard skin beneath Swedish and Congo Free State flags, a warning 'Do not touch the objects!', and a diorama of a Congolese village. She reads the village as a vanishing world left behind for the Christian future. She concludes that the exhibition portrayed Swedes as benevolent participants in colonialism, and that Swedish folk magic was kept apart from the colonial objects that resembled it.

Ethnographic and Missionary Exhibition (Stockholm, 1907)
26Chapter 26. After the fall of the Berlin Wall: Nationalism and multiculturalism at the Bulgarian National Ethnographic MuseumRadostina Sharenkovap. 418

Sharenkova examines the Bulgarian National Ethnographic Museum in Sofia after 1989, when the museum had to decide what kind of national institution to become. Sharenkova sets two post-communist options against each other, nationalism and multiculturalism, and argues that the museum's collections already tilted it towards the first. The chapter traces the museum from its 1892 foundation, when it gathered objects from Macedonia, Thrace, Serbia and Dobrudzha and labelled them all 'Bulgarian', through the communist period, when it was placed under the Academy of Sciences and collections from outside Bulgaria were put into a separate store. Her evidence comes from interviews with curators and staff and from the museum's administrative archive. She then follows the 1995 exhibition Gypsies in Times Past and later displays on Jews, Armenians, Karakachans and Aromanians, which divided the country into discrete ethnic communities, and their end under a director who preferred 'Bulgarian' shows. She concludes that the multicultural turn happened without government support and was reversed by risk-averse management, with little visitor research to guide it.

Bulgarian National Ethnographic Museum
27Chapter 27. The IJzertoren Memorial Museum: A Flemish national museum?Karen D. Shelbyp. 429

Shelby asks whether the IJzertoren Memorial Museum at Diksmuide in Belgium can be called a national museum, and answers that it can, but of Flanders rather than Belgium. Shelby places the tower within Flemish nationalism, which grew out of the language conflict with French-speaking Belgium and the wartime experience of Flemish soldiers on the IJzer front. The chapter traces the memorial from the 1919 pilgrimage, through the 1930 tower built partly from recycled heldenhuldes, its destruction in 1946 after wartime collaboration, and the 1965 rebuild, to its reopening as a museum in 1990. Her evidence is the museum's floor-by-floor narrative, the Front Movement's Open Brief, the list of 300 named collaborators, Hendrik Luyten's Golden Painting of Flanders, and the chapel's stained-glass windows. She finds that the curators aim for a moral and peaceful account, but that the building, the painting and a crucifix by a collaborator keep the nationalism visible. She concludes that the memorial is a political actor in its own right, and that the museum's neutral vision is hard to sustain there.

IJzertoren Memorial Museum
28Chapter 28. Postcolonialism, ethnicity and the National Museum of IrelandAlan Kirwanp. 443

Kirwan asks how postcolonial theory applies to national museums in countries where the indigenous population stayed the majority, which he argues was the case in Ireland and India. Kirwan contrasts these non-settler nations with settler nations such as Canada, Australia, New Zealand and the United States, where debate has centred on incorporating indigenous minorities. Kirwan’s main case is the National Museum of Ireland, which began as the Dublin Museum of Science and Arts in 1877 and was designated national in 1908. Kirwan shows how after independence the prehistoric gold and bronze collections, including the Tara Brooch, moved to the centre of the galleries and presented the Irish as heirs of an ancient Celtic culture. Kirwan argues that the new indigenous elite used the museum to affirm a homogeneous national identity, leaving out Anglo-Irish, Jewish and Traveller communities as well as newer Indian-Irish and Chinese-Irish residents. Kirwan compares this with the bicultural approach of Te Papa Tongarewa in New Zealand. Kirwan concludes that postcolonial theory has been surprisingly quiet about such ethnocentric majority museums.

National Museum of IrelandDublin Museum of Science and ArtsTe Papa TongarewaNational Museum of India
29Chapter 29. Facing up to diversity: Conversations at the National Museum of ColombiaCristina Llerasp. 453

Lleras records conversations held in the National Museum of Colombia in Bogotá during and after its 2008 temporary exhibition Velorios y santos vivos, which dealt with Afro-Colombian and other Black, Maroon and Islander communities. Lleras begins with Colombia's 1991 Constitution, which recognised the country's ethnic and cultural diversity, and with the tension between that multicultural mandate and the unity of the nation. Lleras argues that the state's Ministry of Culture presented diversity as cultural assets and essentialised communities, while grassroots practice was more interactive. Lleras’s evidence is 45 interviews with staff and visitors, three focus groups with Afro-Colombians, and a group interview with the museum's exhibitions committee. The conversations divided over whether to tell one inclusive national story or to give communities separate galleries, which staff feared would become ghettos. Visitors and staff agreed that the museum needed community participation, but staff were unsure how far it could show conflict. She concludes that only intercultural dialogue could challenge the museum's old hegemonic narrative, and that temporary exhibitions cannot stand in for lasting change.

National Museum of ColombiaVelorios y santos vivos (temporary exhibition, 2008)
Indexp. 466
Krech, Shepard, III; Hail, Barbara A. (eds.) (1999). Collecting Native America, 1870–1960. Washington: Smithsonian Institution Press.Asia: slight11 chapter overviews

Overview

Krech and Hail's edited volume (1999) studies the private collectors who assembled North American Indian artifacts between about 1870 and 1960 and, in most cases, founded the museums that held them: Sheldon Jackson, David Ross McCord, Charles Lummis, Rudolf Haffenreffer, Phoebe Hearst, Clara Endicott Sears, Ernest Thompson Seton with Mary Cabot Wheelwright, George Heye, and Francis and Mary Crane. Its central argument is that these collectors should be understood in their own time, with their motives taken seriously, rather than judged as presentist or explained by imposed hegemony alone; the authors reconstruct acquisition from printed, manuscript and oral sources. A Foreword by William Sturtevant presents the essays as a model for studying museum histories. The introduction and nine case-study chapters, each by a different author, follow the collectors from the 1870s to the 1950s.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia are barely present. No chapter is about an Asian collection, museum or public, and the Foreword and Introduction do not discuss the region. Asian material appears only in passing. Sheldon Jackson's chance encounter, as a Princeton seminary student, with a missionary collection of artifacts from Thailand (chapter 1, Lee; lines 372, 412) is presented as the origin of his idea that objects could serve Christian ends, and he echoed it in the Princeton cabinet he set up in 1879. In the Southwest Museum's first years (chapter 3, Wilson and Falkenstien-Doyle; lines 1047, 1055) the Caracol Tower was given over to Oriental art, and the building had an 'Asiatic Hall'.

Other mentions are personal or comparative. Phoebe Hearst travelled to Japan and India and wrote of a Japanese princess she met in 1903; Jacknis uses this to show her admiration for elites in foreign cultures (chapter 5; lines 1576-1578), and her art collection included oriental rugs and carved ivories (line 1681), treated as Victorian taste rather than ethnographic material. Mary Cabot Wheelwright's comparative research collection included material 'from Tibet, China, Japan, India, and New Zealand', and in 1940 she travelled to India and Tibet to compare drypaintings with Navajo designs (chapter 7, Parezo and Hoerig; lines 2424-2425). Her interest in Eastern religions is noted at line 2361. Sears's family wealth came from China trade fortunes (chapter 6, Hail; line 1944), but Asia is not treated as a field of collecting.

The volume touches Asia only as background. Morris Jessup's American Museum expeditions explored possible Asian connections to the origins of American Indians (chapter 8, Kidwell; line 2589). Not covered: any East or Southeast Asian collection in a North American museum, Asian visitors, curators or scholars, and restitution claims. The Bering Strait and Arctic objects in Sears's and the Cranes' collections (lines 2035, 3078) are not Asian in this sense.

Contents
ForewordWilliam C. Sturtevant

The foreword introduces a volume on the private collectors who founded North American public museums of American Indian materials between about 1870 and 1960, a largely unstudied subject. Most of them, Sturtevant says, believed they were preserving a romantic record of peoples who were vanishing. He argues that each object's usefulness depends on its earlier history, which museum catalogues rarely record, so the essays draw on printed, manuscript and oral sources. He presents them as a model for studying other museums.

IntroductionShepard Krech III

Krech and Hail set out the aims of the volume: to explain why a group of private collectors of Native American artifacts, active from the 1870s to the 1950s, assembled their collections and, in most cases, built museums. Unlike recent work on looting and repatriation, the editors want to return collectors to their own time and understand their motives without presentist judgement. They introduce about a dozen figures, including Sheldon Jackson, Charles Lummis, David Ross McCord, George Heye, Rudolf Haffenreffer and Phoebe Hearst, and sketch their backgrounds. Their motives varied: McCord and Lummis wanted public museums that taught national or regional history, Heye pursued objects with extraordinary acquisitiveness, and Haffenreffer and the Cranes stressed education. Most shared a belief that Indian cultures were disappearing. The introduction ends with the legacy: the anthropology departments these collections helped establish, the museums that now hold them, and the objects being returned to Native communities.

McCord National MuseumSouthwest MuseumKing Philip MuseumMuseum of the American Indian, Heye FoundationPhoebe Hearst Museum of AnthropologyFruitlands MuseumsMuseum of Navajo Ceremonial ArtSoutheast Museum of the American Indian
11: Zest Or Zeal? Sheldon Jackson and the Commodification of Alaska Native ArtMolly Lee

Lee asks how a Presbyterian missionary who sought to end Native religious practice became one of the most avid collectors of Native artifacts, many of them sacred. The answer, Lee argues, lies in placing missionary collecting within nineteenth-century ideas of science and progress and in the middle-class taste for Native curios. The chapter follows Sheldon Jackson from the 1870s, when he used artifacts as premiums and gifts to raise money for his missions, to his Alaska years, when he wore Eskimo dress on fund-raising tours and used his post as general agent of education to travel on government vessels. The central case is the museum he founded in Sitka, which was stocked with duplicates from his trips north. Lee notes that the Tlingit response survives mainly as a rebuke over a totem pole. The chapter concludes that Jackson's collecting was part of a missionary discourse that set artifacts against Christian civilization, and that the Sitka museum marks the shift from elite cabinets to public museums.

East and Southeast Asia Lee notes only briefly that, as a Princeton seminary student, Jackson saw a missionary collection of artifacts from Thailand, which first suggested to him that objects could serve Christian ends. The chapter's concern is Alaska and the Pacific Northwest, and the Asian material is not discussed further.

Sheldon Jackson MuseumPrinceton University Natural History MuseumField Museum of Natural HistoryPeabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology
22: Rononshonni—The Builder: David Ross McCord’s Ethnographic CollectionMoira T. McCaffrey

McCaffrey examines why David Ross McCord, a Montreal lawyer, built a large ethnographic collection and what place Native objects held in his plan for a national museum of Canadian history. Drawing on the family papers, correspondence and notebooks, the chapter traces his upbringing in a household devoted to natural history and his early contact with Iroquois and Huron communities. It argues that McCord's views were shaped by Romanticism, Canadian nationalism and a Victorian faith in inventory science, and that he saw Native people as noble and vanishing. Most of the collection was built by mail, through dealers, missionaries and intermediaries such as M. E. Roberts in Nova Scotia, and McCaffrey shows how McCord paid high prices, demanded documentation and sometimes accepted dubious provenance. McGill accepted the gift only in 1919, and the McCord National Museum opened in 1921 with rooms arranged by region and type. The chapter ends by arguing that McCord's documentation is now his most valuable legacy.

McCord National MuseumArt Association of Montreal
33: Charles Fletcher Lummis and the Origins of the Southwest MuseumThomas H. Wilson and Cheri Falkenstien-Doyle

Wilson and Falkenstien-Doyle trace the founding of the Southwest Museum in Los Angeles, which they treat as the lasting monument to Charles Fletcher Lummis, a journalist, booster and collector. The chapter follows his early life, his walk from Ohio to California for the Los Angeles Times, and his years in New Mexico and at Isleta Pueblo, where he collected objects, photographed Pueblo life and built El Alisal, a house with a personal museo. It then shows how he recruited Los Angeles's business elite to the Southwest Society, which raised money, sponsored digs such as Hewett's at Puyé and assembled the collections that opened in 1914 in a building Lummis designed around a spiral Caracol Tower. Financial trouble and conflict with the board drove him out of the museum between 1914 and 1919, and he was later reinstated as honorary curator, dying in 1928. The authors conclude that Lummis's broad mission and personal style left the museum with lasting problems of focus, access and use.

Southwest MuseumEl AlisalLos Angeles Museum of History, Science and Art
44: Rudolf F. Haffenreffer and the King Philip MuseumShepard Krech III

Krech examines the private museum that Rudolf Haffenreffer, a Rhode Island brewer and industrialist, built on his Mount Hope farm in Bristol and called, from 1929, the King Philip Museum. Krech traces Haffenreffer's German-American upbringing in Boston, his purchase of Mount Hope and the King Philip associations that came with it, and his western mining trips, from which he returned with trunks of objects. The museum grew from a storage shed into a fireproof building, and the hiring of the archaeologist Foster Saville in 1928 brought documentation, card catalogues and affidavits of provenance. Krech also shows how Haffenreffer drew Boy Scouts into camps and essay contests on Wampanoag history, and how the museum later filled with cigar-store Indians that he used to promote his brewery. The chapter ends with his 1923 speech to the Fall River Historical Society, which took a sympathetic and anti-Puritan view of King Philip and his people, and with the limited evidence about his attitudes to living Native people.

King Philip MuseumMuseum of the American Indian, Heye Foundation
55: Patrons, Potters, and Painters: Phoebe Hearst’s Collections from the American SouthwestIra Jacknis

Jacknis reconstructs how Phoebe Hearst, the Californian philanthropist and first female regent of the University of California, built the Southwestern holdings of the museum of anthropology she founded in 1901. Jacknis argues that these collections were shaped less by a regional policy than by Hearst's network of Eastern anthropologists, chiefly William Pepper, Frederic Putnam, Zelia Nuttall and Alice Fletcher, who steered acquisitions through exchanges with Penn, Harvard and the American Museum of Natural History. The chapter works through the Mesa Verde and Cliff Dweller pottery, the systematic field gatherings of George Pepper, Joseph Peterson and Philip Jones, the Washington Matthews papers, and the paintings of Joseph Sharp and Carl Oscar Borg. It also traces Hearst's personal collecting, bought largely from the Fred Harvey Company, and the clash between donor sentiment and Alfred Kroeber's insistence on disciplinary order over the McLeod baskets. Jacknis concludes that the Southwest holdings reflect the professionalizing aims of a university museum as much as a patron's tastes, and that this process erased the alternative, often oppositional, modes by which the collections were formed.

Phoebe Apperson Hearst Museum of AnthropologyUniversity of Pennsylvania MuseumPeabody Museum, HarvardAmerican Museum of Natural History
66: Museums As Inspiration: Clara Endicott Sears and the Fruitlands MuseumsBarbara A. Hail

Hail examines Clara Endicott Sears, a Boston-raised preservationist who between 1914 and 1945 built a cluster of museums on her estate at Harvard, Massachusetts, among them the Fruitlands Farmhouse, the Shaker House and the American Indian Museum. The chapter argues that Sears used these buildings to promote a spiritual, anti-industrial view of the past, drawing on transcendentalism, Shakerism and her own Brahmin genealogy, and that her Indian Museum (1929) gave priority to spirituality over the material culture of living Native people. Hail describes how Sears assembled nearly two thousand objects, mostly Plains material, with advice from the Peabody Museum at Harvard, Warren K. Moorehead and Colonel Alfred Welch, and how she commissioned re-created Lakota shields and copied an Ojibwa petroglyph floor from Hoffman's 1887 drawings. She presented these re-creations as authentic without labelling them as such, and she set aside Frank Speck's suggestion that present-day New England Native people be included. The chapter concludes that the museum was a didactic monument of real interest, but that its account of Native culture needs critical reading.

Fruitlands Museums (Indian Museum)Peabody Museum, HarvardPeabody Museum of Archaeology, Phillips Academy, Andover
77: Collecting to Educate: Ernest Thompson Seton and Mary Cabot WheelwrightNancy J. Parezo and Karl A. Hoerig

Parezo and Hoerig examine two amateur collectors in Santa Fe who used their collections to educate the public: Ernest Thompson Seton, founder of the Woodcraft Indians, and Mary Cabot Wheelwright, who founded the Museum of Navajo Ceremonial Art. The chapter argues that educational collecting is a form of cultural production, in which the collector first forms an image and then gathers objects to substantiate it. Seton's Seton Village museum held around 1,500 artifacts, mostly Plains and Pueblo material, which were used to model costumes and illustrate his books and so to give youth groups a generalized Indian image. Wheelwright's collection instead documented a single culture: working with the Navajo singer Hosteen Klah from 1927, she recorded more than 400 sandpaintings with their chants, and the museum she opened in 1937 held manuscripts, reproductions and tapestries. The authors show how each collector's image of Native life was shaped by the purpose of teaching, and they conclude that knowledge, rather than the objects, was the critical part of both collections.

Museum of Navajo Ceremonial ArtPhilmont Museum and Seton Memorial LibrarySeton Village museum
88: Every Last Dishcloth: The Prodigious Collecting of George Gustav HeyeClara Sue Kidwell

Kidwell traces the career of George Gustav Heye, a New York businessman's son who from the early 1900s until his death in 1956 built one of the largest private collections of Native American material, roughly a million objects. The chapter argues that Heye's passion was for possession rather than for the lives of living Indian people, and that his collecting was shaped by New York's competitive museum culture, by his early mentors Marshall Saville and George Pepper, and by his rivalry with Franz Boas and the American Museum of Natural History. Kidwell follows the collection through Heye's early purchases, his arrangement with George Gordon at the University Museum in Philadelphia, his 1916 founding of the Museum of the American Indian, and the staff of archaeologists and ethnographers he employed until the 1928 deaths of his main benefactors ended their salaries. Kidwell also examines his expeditions and the contested return of the Hidatsa Water Buster bundle in 1938. The chapter concludes that the collection, transferred to the Smithsonian in 1989, now serves as a living memorial, and that the repatriation mandated with it sits uneasily with Heye's private, elite purposes.

Museum of the American Indian, Heye FoundationUniversity Museum, University of PennsylvaniaAmerican Museum of Natural HistoryNational Museum of the American Indian
99: Grand Amateur Collecting in the Mid-Twentieth Century: The Mary W. A. and Francis V. Crane American Indian CollectionJoyce Herold

Herold tells the story of the Mary W. A. and Francis V. Crane American Indian Collection, assembled by a Massachusetts couple between 1951 and 1968 and later given to the Denver Museum of Natural History. She argues that the Cranes, wealthy amateurs with no formal training in anthropology, built a large systematic collection through a mix of family habits, business sense and a wish for public benefaction, after Francis Crane's heart illness redirected their lives. The chapter describes their search of 335 sources, from Fred Harvey storerooms and small California trading posts to dealers and galleries in several cities, and their shifting rules of selection, which moved from broad coverage to a demand that objects be old, rare and unusual. Herold also covers their bargaining as a nonprofit buyer, their dealings with fakes and Native sellers, and the Southeast Museum in Marathon, Florida, which drew few visitors before it closed in 1968. The Cranes' grand amateur project, she concludes, gathered a varied collection, though one that was late, underfinanced and uneven in its documentation.

Southeast Museum of the North American IndianDenver Museum of Natural History
Contributors
Logan, William; Nic Craith, Máiréad; Kockel, Ullrich (eds.) (2016). A Companion to Heritage Studies. Chichester: Wiley Blackwell.Asia: substantial38 chapter overviews

Overview

A Companion to Heritage Studies, edited by William Logan, Máiréad Nic Craith and Ullrich Kockel, gathers 37 chapters by 44 scholars and practitioners on how heritage and heritage studies have expanded since the Venice Charter of 1964. Its main argument is that heritage conservation is a form of cultural politics, that the field has changed through evolution rather than a Kuhnian paradigm shift, and that heritage should serve communities and human rights. The book has three parts: Expanding Heritage (places, folklore and intangible heritage, intellectual property, documentary heritage, and the Auschwitz memorial); Using and Abusing Heritage (tourism, nationalism, war and memory, destruction in Iraq and Afghanistan, and the Andes); and Recasting Heritage (economics, the World Heritage Convention, law, education, emotion, the Thai-Burma railway, cosmopolitanism and post-conflict reconciliation). Its cases are global, with Europe and the Americas most prominent.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

East and Southeast Asia form a substantial strand, though not an organising one. Five chapters give the region a main case: Akagawa on Japan's role in shaping intangible heritage (ch. 5: the Mingei movement, the 1950 Cultural Properties Law and living national treasures); Yan on China's use of World Heritage for nation-building (ch. 16: the Great Wall, the Grand Canal, Chengde, the Potala Palace, Fujian Tulou and the demolished Old Town of Kashgar); Aygen and Logan on the 'Asian century' (ch. 28: Japan and China, the 1999 timber principles and the 2000 China Principles, colonial heritage in Hanoi, George Town, Malacca and Yangon, and the Preah Vihear dispute); Witcomb on the Thai-Burma railway at Kanchanaburi (ch. 31: the JEATH Museum and the Weary Dunlop Peace Park); and Daly and Chan on post-conflict heritage in Cambodia (ch. 33: the Tuol Sleng Genocide Museum) and in Japan (Yasukuni and Yushukan, the Hiroshima Peace Memorial and the Nagasaki Atomic Bomb Museum).

Other chapters treat the region briefly. Kuutma compares Japanese and Chinese folklore studies (ch. 3). Winter sets Galle against Beijing's District 798, Pingyao, Melaka and Luang Prabang (ch. 13). Vileikis discusses the Chinese sites of the Silk Roads nomination, including Dunhuang and the Mogao Caves (ch. 34). Van Oers covers Preah Khan at Angkor and Manila's Far Eastern University campus programme (ch. 22). Meskell and Swain draw on Thai stupas and Chinese tianxia cosmopolitanism (ch. 32). Museums are seldom the object of study. Asian objects in Western museums, colonial collecting and Asian visitors and curators are not discussed. South Asia (Sri Lanka, Afghanistan) appears only as contrast.

A Companion to Heritage Studies

This unit is front matter rather than a chapter: an extracted e-book navigation list giving the book's full table of contents, followed by the list of tables and figures and the Blackwell Companions to Anthropology series page. It contains no argument or case material. It does show how the book is arranged, in three parts (Expanding Heritage, Using and Abusing Heritage, Recasting Heritage) with chapters 1 to 37.
