Contents

Theoretical approach of this work
List of illustrationsp. xii
Prefacep. xivAsia: chiefly

Lu opens with a Hong Kong taxi driver who thought museums were only for people who read English, and asks who founds, funds and uses museums in mainland China. Lu challenges the ICOM definition, arguing that heritage is chosen by whoever controls the museum, and offers a working definition of a museum as an institution that selects material to serve particular groups. The preface divides Chinese museum history into three phases and previews the eight chapters.

East and Southeast Asia Most of the preface concerns China. Lu sets the book in mainland China and Hong Kong and sketches three phases of Chinese museum history: early museums founded before 1949 by foreign elites, missionaries, Chinese governments or scholars; state-controlled museums from 1949 to the 1980s, when Marxism and Maoism were the only framework; and, from the 1980s, a rise in number and diversity, including ecomuseums and private museums. A 2010 Hong Kong incident opens the preface.

Acknowledgementsp. xviii
List of abbreviationsp. xix
1China between 1840 and 1949p. 1Asia: chiefly

Lu's first chapter sets out the background to China's earliest museums, 1840 to 1949. It describes famine, the opium trade, the Opium Wars and later defeats, rebellions and civil war as an era of humiliation, in which intellectuals such as Kang Youwei, Yan Fu and Zhang Jian pressed for Westernisation and argued that museums should educate the public. Lu identifies the social groups behind the early museums: Chinese intellectuals and political parties, Western secular elites and missionaries. Their clashes with the Qing court and the Western powers are traced through the Rites Controversy and the 1869 letters between the British minister Alcock and London. The evidence is mainly secondary scholarship, supplemented by Qing and British documents and a table of foreign scholars active in China. Lu concludes that the museum came to China as part of Westernisation, foreign influence and nascent nationalism, and so prepares the case studies of missionary and elite museums that follow.

East and Southeast Asia Chapter 1 is chiefly about China, 1840 to 1949: the opium trade, the Opium Wars, the Taiping and other rebellions, the Sino-Japanese wars, the 1911 revolution, Yuan Shikai and the Nationalist and Communist parties. It names Chinese intellectuals such as Kang Youwei, Liang Qichao, Yan Fu and Zhang Jian, who founded a private museum in Nantong in 1905, and Western scholars working in China, including Andersson, Hedin, Karlgren and Weidenreich, whose work underpinned early museums.

Zhang Jian's private museum, Nantong
2Missionaries and early museumsp. 19Asia: chiefly

Lu's second chapter examines the museums founded by Western missionaries in China before 1949. It argues that the Zikawei (Heude) Museum in Shanghai, three Shandong museums and the Hoang Ho Pai Ho Museum in Tianjin were tools of Christian preaching and Western influence, while also feeding natural-history science in Europe. The evidence includes museum histories and pamphlets, visitor figures, the Heude Museum's signature book from 1932 to 1946, and accounts by missionaries and by Hu Shih. Lu shows how the Chefoo museum linked birds and harvests to God, and how Whitewright's Shandong displays contrasted a backward China with a powerful West. The chapter concludes that these museums served religious, scientific and political ends at once, and left a lasting dichotomy between Western knowledge and Chinese tradition.

East and Southeast Asia China is the whole subject: the Zikawei (Heude) Museum in Shanghai, the Chefoo, Tsingchoufu and Guangzhiyuan museums in Shandong, and the Hoang Ho Pai Ho Museum in Tianjin, with their natural history specimens, antiquities and visitors such as Hu Shih. Heude's collecting trips are also said to have reached Cambodia, the Philippines, Indonesia, Vietnam, Thailand and Japan between 1892 and 1902, a list the chapter does not develop.

Zikawei (Heude) Museum, ShanghaiChefoo Museum, ShandongBogutang (Tsingchoufu) Museum, ShandongGuangzhiyuan Museum, JinanHoang Ho Pai Ho Museum, Tianjin
3Social elites and early museumsp. 62Asia: chiefly

Lu studies two early museums in mainland China founded by social elites: the Shanghai Museum, run by the North-China Branch of the Royal Asiatic Society (NCBRAS) in the International Settlement from 1874, and the Nantong Museum, set up by the scholar-official Zhang Jian in 1905. For the Shanghai Museum Lu draws on the society's journal and balance sheets to show its honorary curators, its chronic lack of money and space, and its move into a new building in 1933, when displays were reorganised into anthropology, art and archaeology, and natural history. Visitors were mostly Chinese, yet labels and guidebooks were in English, and Chinese visitors were admitted on set days. The Nantong Museum is treated as one part of Zhang's programme of local self-government, in which factories and schools came first and the museum served them. Zhang funded and controlled it, its collections were partly donations meant to please him, and it declined after his death in 1926. Lu ends by arguing that the Shanghai museum lasted longer because it drew on public and expatriate support, while both museums served only the educated or well-connected.

East and Southeast Asia Both museums are in China and the chapter is about China itself. The Shanghai Museum was a Western-run collection in the foreign concession, built around Chinese natural history specimens, antiquities, art and coins, and by the 1930s it drew mainly Chinese school pupils and students; its displays included Peking Man fossils and Shang bronzes, and its director Sowerby is described as sympathetic to China. The Nantong Museum in Jiangsu held local nature and culture, Buddhist scripts and objects such as a whale skeleton, and Zhang's proposals for a national museum in Beijing followed a Japanese imperial model.

Shanghai MuseumNantong MuseumZikawei Museum
4Museums in modern state formationp. 89Asia: chiefly

Lu traces how the Republic of China's governments used museums to build a modern state in Beijing's Forbidden City. The first part treats the Institute of Antiquity Exhibition, set up in 1913 to keep antiquities from the Chengde and Shenyang palaces and from foreign collectors, and shows it caught between the abdicated Qing court, still living in the Inner Court, and the republican government. Its funding through admission fees and its crowded displays, which the writer Lu Xun likened to an antique shop, are described in detail. The longer part concerns the Palace Museum, opened in October 1925 after Feng Yuxiang forced the last emperor out. Lu covers its board of directors, years of identifying fake works, its twenty-eight themed exhibitions and its magazine. Lu argues that the Palace Museum completed the political task the Institute could not, turning an imperial residence into a national symbol, and compares it with the Louvre. The chapter ends with the Nationalist government's view of museums as tools of social education, by which 53 public and private museums were registered by the mid-1930s.

East and Southeast Asia Almost all of the chapter concerns China. It covers the Qing imperial collection in Beijing, including objects from the Chengde and Shenyang palaces, paintings, bronzes, ceramics, jade and fake works, and the Palace Museum's exhibitions of Qing paintings, snuff bottles and Chinese opera. It names Aurel Stein, Paul Pelliot and Langdon Warner, who took thousands of Chinese antiquities to museums in France, Germany, Japan, Russia, the UK and the USA, and it describes the 1914 export ban. The collection later moved to Shanghai, Nanjing and Chongqing and, from 1965, to Taipei.

Palace MuseumInstitute of Antiquity Exhibition
5Museums under the communist statep. 112Asia: chiefly

Lu examines how the Chinese Communist Party used museums after 1949 to legitimise its rule, and shows the state controlling public museums through ministries, Party secretaries and a fixed ideological framework for exhibitions. The chapter opens with the Party's wartime exhibitions in its Yan'an base, which displayed farm and workshop produce to encourage production and loyalty, and with land-reform displays in Northeast China that set landlords against poor peasants. Lu then traces the rise and fall of museum numbers, from 21 in 1949 to 480 in 1959 and 193 in 1966, and the laws that declared heritage national property. The main cases are the Shanghai Museum, reopened in 1952 as a model national museum of arts and craftsmanship and used for Taiwan propaganda and a 1976 ceramics show, and the National Museum of Revolution in Beijing, opened in 1961 and rewritten several times under senior Party oversight. The chapter ends with the Palace Museum's overseas tours of archaeological finds and with curators and docents whose academic independence was limited. Lu concludes that the political role of museums set up in this period has continued into the present.

East and Southeast Asia Much of the chapter concerns China, with a Taiwan thread. The Shanghai Museum mounted 1950s exhibitions 'Taiwan Must Be Liberated' and one on the Gaoshan people of Taiwan, and the Palace Museum toured a 1955 show against American attempts to steal antiquities in Taiwan. A 1976 Shanghai ceramics exhibition argued that Chinese civilisation was indigenous and that South China Sea islands had been occupied by Chinese since antiquity. The 1973-78 overseas tour of Cultural Revolution archaeological finds visited Japan, the Philippines and Hong Kong among other places, drawing over 6.5 million visitors.

Shanghai MuseumNational Museum of RevolutionNational Museum of HistoryPalace Museum
6Ecomuseums, ethnicity and the management of intangible cultural heritagep. 140Asia: chiefly

Lu examines ecomuseums in Guizhou, a mountainous and ethnically diverse province, and asks what happens when a European model of community heritage is applied there. The chapter begins with the economic gap between eastern and western China, then turns to the Sino-Norwegian ecomuseum projects begun in 1995, two of them public ones in Miao and Dong villages. Lu describes how these ecomuseums were run from above by government and scholars, drew little local participation, and depended on falling funds and small admission fees. The longer case is a private ecomuseum in the Dong village of Tei, founded in 2005 by a Hong Kong businessman, which records village life, teaches Dong songs and sells rice, tea and textiles. Lu reports the villagers' indifference to Dong songs, weaving and ethnic identity, and the curator's doubts that heritage can be preserved. Lu argues that the ecomuseums became tools of poverty relief and tourism, and that by displaying minority culture they hastened its disappearance. The chapter closes by linking this to Han-dominated ideas of modernization and to the discrimination faced by young minority people.

East and Southeast Asia The chapter is about China's southwest. It describes the Guizhou ecomuseums, a Miao village ecomuseum and two Dong village ecomuseums (Dang and Tei), founded from 1995 under a Sino-Norwegian project, and the private Tei Ecomuseum set up in 2005 by a Hong Kong businessman. Lu also compares the economies of Guangdong, Shanghai, Guizhou and Gansu, and notes discrimination against Zhuang people in Guangxi, Naxi people in Lijiang and the Mosuo of Yunnan, with a brief comparison to Tibet and Xinjiang.

Tei EcomuseumDang Village Ecomuseum
7Museums, tourism and local cultural changesp. 168Asia: chiefly

Lu tests whether tourism at a heritage museum always harms local communities, using a case study of a Buddhist grotto site in Gansu province, Northwestern China. The chapter first sets out the region's dry landscape, shrinking land and water, and the state's Great Development of the West strategy, and then the history of the grottoes, from a mid-1940s Nationalist institute to the admission fees charged from the mid-1980s. Fieldwork in three villages, Wei, Qu and Tang, compares their change: Wei has turned to camel-riding and home-stays and grown rich, Qu remains farming with some tourism income, and Tang has lost its land to urban development. Lu shows how the museum's tour routes, short visits and fees shaped tourism, and how most villagers, unable to read the Buddhist art, felt excluded from it except at the yearly Bathing Buddha Festival. Lu concludes that the museum is central to local economic change, and that its effect on community life is mixed rather than simply good or bad, so that site museums need social inclusion to serve local people.

East and Southeast Asia The whole chapter concerns one site in Gansu, north-western China, where the Tsa grottoes are a Buddhist cave complex on the Silk Road. It covers the site's history under the Nationalists, the admission fees from the 1980s, the Bathing Buddha Festival, and three villages (Wei, Qu and Tang) whose economies moved from farming to camel-riding, home-stays and land resumption. It also notes that Buddhism reached Xinjiang and Gansu along the Silk Road, and that foreign explorers took Buddhist art abroad in the early twentieth century.

Grotto Museum
8Museums in a changing Chinap. 196Asia: chiefly

This chapter examines how museums in mainland China have expanded since 1979 and what roles they now serve. It begins with the economic growth and Party cultural policy behind the boom, and with the legal framework: the 2007 Law on the Protection of Cultural Relics and its implementing regulations, which affirm state ownership of heritage, restrict lending and disposal of public collections, and control overseas exhibitions. Lu counts museums province by province, from 263 in 1976 to 2838 in 2012, and shows how site museums, ecomuseums and private collections multiplied. The main case is the Jianchuan Museum Cluster in Sichuan, a privately founded group of nineteen museums whose displays on Kuomintang troops and ordinary people's suffering depart from official history. Lu also covers private museums' legal and financial fragility, grading, the Chinese Museums Association, globalization, admission fees and visitor studies. The chapter concludes that Party ideology and nationalism still dominate museum discourse, that museums serve patriotic education, and that community participation remains weak.

East and Southeast Asia The whole chapter concerns mainland China, so its East Asian material is central. Lu covers the Dunhuang grottoes, whose conservation has been supported by the Getty Institute and the Japanese government since the 1980s, and the Jianchuan Museum Cluster's displays on the Sino-Japanese war, and notes that Chinese museums have organized more than 500 overseas exhibitions since the 1980s.

Jianchuan Museum Cluster
Bibliographyp. 217
Indexp. 234
Lumley, Robert (ed.) (1988). The Museum Time-Machine: Putting Cultures on Display. London: Routledge.Asia: slight14 chapter overviews

Overview

An edited volume of 1988 by Robert Lumley on how British and European museums represent the past. Its argument is that museums, open-air reconstructions and media-influenced displays have become time-machines that sell nostalgia, realism and experience, and that they should instead help visitors orient themselves in a changing world. Chapters by Hoyau, West, Bennett and Durrans examine heritage policy, Ironbridge, Beamish and ethnographic collections; others treat science museums, domestic display, aural culture, the Pompidou Centre and visitor numbers. Lumley's introduction groups the essays into three parts: heritage and the open-air museum, museums in a changing world, and the museum public. Most cases are British, with comparisons to France, Australia, the USA and Canada.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia are almost absent. No chapter treats either region as a main or part subject. The nearest is chapter 11 (Kirby, Policy and politics), which records the 1985 sale of the George Brown Collection of Western Pacific ethnography by Newcastle University to the National Museum of Ethnography in Osaka, Japan, for £600,000, before an export review could act; the British Museum bought four items. The objects come from the Pacific, not from Asia, so the Osaka sale is a Japanese museum acquiring a Western-held collection, mentioned once in passing.

Chapter 13 (Morton, Tomorrow's yesterdays) makes two brief points: Japan is where the latest technologies are developed, which makes a national display of them hard to mount, and British watches are now made in Switzerland, Japan and Hong Kong, which Morton uses to present British watchmaking as a story of decline. The introduction notes that the museum boom is on a larger scale in Japan and the USA than in Britain, France or West Germany. Chapter 18 (Hooper-Greenhill) mentions Leicester's work with Asian and Chinese community groups, which concerns Britain's own population rather than East Asia.

Not covered: museums inside East or Southeast Asia, Asian heritage and museum-building policy, colonial collecting from Asia, and any Southeast Asian collection or country. The volume's comparisons are with Australia, the USA and Canada.

JapanHong Kong

Contents

Theoretical approach of this work
Book CoverPDF p. 2
TitlePDF p. 4
ContentsPDF p. 5
AcknowledgementsPDF p. 8
Notes on the editor and contributorsPDF p. 9
IntroductionRobert Lumleyp. 1

Lumley introduces a collection of essays on how museums represent the past, arguing that the 'renaissance' of museum building in Britain, France, West Germany, Japan and the USA has made the museum a central arena for debate about national history. Lumley explains the book's aim: to provoke, to address non-specialists, and to set contributions from museum professionals beside those of outside researchers. The essays fall into three parts: heritage and the open-air museum, museums in a changing world, and the museum public. Lumley picks out three recurring themes: commercialisation, the pursuit of 'realism' in reconstructions such as Ironbridge and Beamish, and the impact of television and mass reproduction, which he says push museums towards experience. Lumley concludes that the cultural role of the museum lies in helping visitors orient themselves in a world where inherited ideas of time and place are losing their force, rather than in becoming a theme park.

Ironbridge Gorge MuseumBeamish open-air museumPompidou CentreMuseum of the Moving Image
Heritage and 'the conserver society': the French casePhilippe Hoyaup. 25

This unit gives the opening of Philippe Hoyau's chapter on France's 'Heritage Year' of 1980, after the Part 1 title page. Hoyau describes the Ministry of Culture's expanded idea of heritage, which moved from monuments to village wash-houses, factories, patois and oral records, and the Commission for the Ethnological Heritage behind it. Hoyau introduces his argument that this shift is a new discourse of nostalgia rather than neutral preservation. The argument continues in the next unit.

Heritage and 'the conserver society': the French casep. 27

Hoyau develops his critique of the French Heritage Year. He lists its projects, from ecomuseums in Brittany to inventories of cinemas and industrial sites, and argues that 'industrial heritage' restages the labour it once concealed, so that anything historical can count as heritage. He shows the new discipline of ethnohistory absorbing history into the study of unchanging local life, which fixes conflicts and resistance into a timeless past. Quoting the commission's reports and its promoters, Hoyau argues that the policy aims at community identity and political mobilisation, with a 'soft socialism' and decentralisation in view. He concludes that the Ministry's 'cultural mobilisation', through schools, tourism and policing of vandalism, will turn heritage into a dull spectacle, and that the result is a landscape of effective nostalgia.

The making of the English working past: a critical view of the Ironbridge Gorge MuseumBob Westp. 36

West argues that the Ironbridge Gorge Museum, the open-air complex around Abraham Darby's iron bridge in Shropshire, sells a version of the industrial past that hides class struggle and the labour that made it. Drawing on his own visits, including the costumed workers and 'traditional' ale at Blists Hill, he traces the museum's political economy: its origin in a 1967 working party, its funding from industry, government and volunteer Friends, and its reliance on Manpower Services Commission and prison labour. He then describes the 'history business' of shops, guides, image control, awards and royal patronage, and how the museum has reshaped the town of Ironbridge around tourism. Using the Blists Hill sawmill and candle works, he argues that the work displays turn exploitation into spectacle and that the young MSC workers who staff them bear the cost. West concludes that the museum offers the past that worked for capital, though visitors may read it differently, and that he would rather visit a pleasure park.

Ironbridge Gorge MuseumBlists Hill Open Air Museum
Museums and 'the people'Tony Bennettp. 63

Bennett asks whether the post-war turn to the everyday lives of ordinary people in British museums escapes the condescension of the nineteenth-century museum, which either excluded working-class culture or treated it as picturesque. Bennett's main case is the open-air museum at Beamish. Its introductory tape-slide show, narrated first in a BBC voice and then by a fictional Geordie miner, presents the region's people as the dominant culture imagines them. The reassembled buildings, drawn from several sites and set in the grounds of a country house, make industrial change look like a continuation of a harmonious rural order. Bennett traces this 'countryside of the mind' to Skansen and Ford's Greenfield Village. Against Beamish Bennett sets Sydney's Hyde Park Barracks and Glasgow's People's Palace, which tie everyday life to political traditions, though Hyde Park lost its labour display. Bennett concludes that this conservative 'peopling of the past' is not intrinsic to folk museums and can be broken.

Beamish MuseumHyde Park BarracksPeople's PalaceSkansenGreenfield Village
Policy and politics: charges, sponsorship, and biasSue Kirbyp. 87

Kirby opens the chapter by dividing British museums into public and independent sectors and noting that local authorities have only permissive powers to run them. Kirby then shows how funding has fallen: central grants have stalled, purchase budgets have been cut, and the National Gallery's grant has fallen by roughly a fifth in real terms. The Victoria and Albert Museum closed on Fridays and its touring service was shut, while building repairs absorb money meant for new displays.

National GalleryVictoria and Albert MuseumBritish Museum
Policy and politics: charges, sponsorship, and biasSue Kirbyp. 89

Kirby traces how British national and local museums have been pushed to raise money through admission charges, the sale of collections and sponsorship. Kirby reviews the 1974 charges at the national museums, which were abandoned within three weeks at a loss, and their reintroduction after 1984 at the National Maritime Museum, the Victoria and Albert Museum and the British Museum (Natural History), and the falling attendances that followed. The chapter then looks at disposals, including the Trafford sale and the proposed Kirklees sale, the George Brown Collection, and at sponsorship, using the Science Museum's nuclear power gallery to show how sponsors can shape content. The largest concern is bias: Edinburgh's council-directed exhibitions, and the way collecting and funding favour art over social history and labour history. Kirby ends by arguing that the issues should be more widely discussed, since museums need clear policies that serve their public.

East and Southeast Asia Kirby mentions the George Brown Collection of Western Pacific ethnography, which the University of Newcastle upon Tyne sold in 1985 for £600,000 to the National Museum of Ethnography in Osaka, Japan, before the export review could act; the British Museum bought four items. The Osaka buyer is the chapter's only East Asian element, and the objects come from the Pacific, not from Asia.

National Maritime MuseumVictoria and Albert MuseumBritish Museum (Natural History)Science MuseumTrafford collectionGeorge Brown Collection
Putting your house in order: representations of women and domestic lifeGaby Porterp. 102

Porter argues that museum representations of domestic life repeat the sexual division of labour they should be questioning. Museums favour the middle-class Victorian parlour, which survives in quantity, and show women as needleworkers rather than workers, while the material culture of working-class households and servants has largely worn away. The main case is the 1985 display of household appliances at York Castle Museum and the matching gallery at the Science Museum, which take their images and captions from early advertisements and present machines as having liberated the housewife. Porter sets this against time-use studies showing that appliances extended household tasks and moved them onto women. Porter also blames classification systems such as MERL and SHIC, which separate domestic life from working life and so render housework invisible. Porter ends by urging museums to show women's work across home and workplace, to admit the partiality of their records, and to involve people from outside the profession, as the WHAM group has done.

York Castle MuseumScience MuseumBeamish MuseumMuseum of Oxford
Tomorrow's yesterdays: science museums and the futureAlan Mortonp. 128

Morton asks what future science and technology museums have, given that television, shopping malls and theme parks now compete with them. Morton traces their origins to late-nineteenth-century state projects to promote science, and argues that object-centred display foreshortens history, presents progress as a simple sequence and carries nationalist messages. The case is the Science Museum's nuclear power gallery, which stresses Britain's gas-cooled reactor where the Paris museum shows the French design. Morton then links the commodity status of objects to the art market and to museum charges. The remedies are to show human operators and skill, contrast craft with mass production, house art and technology together, and mount small topical displays on the newspaper model. Morton ends by arguing that the real object and the visitor's freedom to browse are museums' strengths, and that history should not be left to advertising.

East and Southeast Asia Morton's Asian references are brief: Japan is cited as a place where the latest technologies are developed, which makes a national display of them hard to mount, and British watches are said to be now made in Switzerland, Japan and Hong Kong, a point used to present British watchmaking as a story of decline. Neither point is developed beyond a sentence or two.

Science MuseumSmithsonian InstitutionDeutsches MuseumPalais de la DécouverteAshmolean Museum
The future of the other: changing cultures on display in ethnographic museumsBrian Durransp. 144

Durrans argues that ethnographic museums, which emerged as adjuncts of European expansion, must rethink how they represent other cultures and what they owe their public. Durrans starts with the time-machine displays that place living peoples on an evolutionary scale, and argues that all surviving societies share the same time-depth. Collections remain valuable documentary evidence, but Durrans holds that how objects are classified and what their provenance is shape the meaning they convey. Durrans considers the colonial origins of the collections, the diplomatic role museums now play, and the repatriation claims they face. Durrans asks museums to show the transactional history of their objects, to present everyday and industrial material as well as art, and to bring visitors and communities into research and display. Durrans concludes that museums should keep a critical distance from both postmodern relativism and the cost-cutting that threatens them.

Museum of MankindBritish MuseumPitt Rivers MuseumHorniman MuseumSmithsonian Institution National Museum of Natural HistoryJorvik Centre
'Astonished and somewhat terrified': the preservation and development of aural cultureJeremy Silverp. 170

Silver argues that museums and sound archives have treated recorded sound as an afterthought, because a 'literal' culture distrusts the spoken voice and sound has no critical vocabulary. Silver opens with Sullivan's 1888 response to the phonograph and then surveys the fragmented collections of recorded sound, from the BBC and National Sound Archive to local oral history projects, which are poorly catalogued and hard to reach. The central figure is the BBC producer Charles Parker, whose Radio Ballads used the speech of ordinary people, and whose dismissal in 1972 the chapter treats as a loss. Silver then examines the audio-visual 'dark rides' at Jorvik and the National Motor Museum's Wheels display, which use studio-made or field-recorded sound and threaten the funding of collecting museums. Silver ends by urging that community recordings, as at the Manchester Jewish Museum, be used in displays, and that museums stop treating sound as background.

Jorvik CentreNational Motor Museum, Beaulieu (Wheels display)Manchester Jewish MuseumVictoria and Albert Museum
The Pompidou Centre and its public: the limits of a Utopian siteNathalie Heinichp. 197

Heinich introduces the Pompidou Centre in Paris as a complex institution, with a public library, a national museum of modern art, an industrial design centre and a research institute, and as a project that a 'right-wing' minister conceived as a democratizing venture. Heinich notes that the building has drawn criticism for its architecture and for its scant avant-garde space, but that its popularity has quieted most of it. The chapter then asks what its publics are.

Pompidou Centre
The Pompidou Centre and its public: the limits of a Utopian siteNathalie Heinichp. 199

Heinich asks who actually uses the Pompidou Centre in Paris a decade after it opened, and whether it has democratized culture. Visitor numbers were almost double the forecasts. Surveys show a young, predominantly male and highly educated public, dominated by students, executives and professionals, with few manual workers, so the middle classes gain most. The chapter shows that visitors divide by activity: most come to the library, others to the gallery or the big exhibitions, and many never visit the rest. Visitors also get lost in the building's unlabelled spaces and acronyms, so they wander or keep to fixed routes. Heinich concludes that the Centre has created new habits of drifting and new needs, but that its Utopian hope of mixing audiences has largely failed.

Pompidou CentreNational Museum of Modern Art (MNAM)Public Information Library (BPI)
Counting visitors or visitors who count?Eilean Hooper-Greenhillp. 213

Hooper-Greenhill argues that museums have measured success by visitor numbers rather than by who visits and what the experience is like. The chapter reviews British visitor surveys, including the English Tourist Board study used to justify charges, and sets them against Canadian and Toledo studies showing that most of a community finds little in museums to merit a visit. It then examines the museum experience itself: the curator's authority, the guarded and surveilled building, the climate control that treats visitors as contamination, and collections inherited from the nineteenth century. Positive cases include the British Museum's touch exhibition 'Human Touch', the Children's Museum in Boston and Leicester's multicultural work. The chapter ends by urging museums to evaluate their displays, plan on their publics' terms and recruit new audiences, or else become 'residual cultural forms'.

British MuseumChildren's Museum of BostonLeicester MuseumMuseum of Art, ToledoNational Portrait Gallery
Indexp. 233
Macdonald, Sharon; Fyfe, Gordon (eds.) (1996). Theorizing Museums: Representing Identity and Diversity in a Changing World. Oxford: Blackwell.Asia: occasional10 chapter overviews

Overview

Theorizing Museums (1996), edited by Sharon Macdonald and Gordon Fyfe, is a collection by anthropologists, sociologists and museum professionals arguing that museums are a rich object for social and cultural theory. The editors' introduction contends that museums are at once contextualizing and contextualized, contestable and contested, and have a content that includes their institutional practice, and that older accounts of museums as instruments of control or distinction are too simple. The chapters cover globalization and the diffusion of museums, time, heritage and memory, the Enola Gay exhibition dispute, ethnographic irony at the Royal Ontario Museum, a feminist reading of displays, visitors and class, Stonehenge as a museum without walls, race and miscegenation at Colonial Williamsburg, and the early Tate and the Chantrey Bequest. Its cases are mostly Anglo-American and European, with wider global history in the first chapter.

East and Southeast Asia in this work occasional

East and Southeast Asia are present but not central. The most sustained treatment is in chapter 6, Zolberg's account of the Enola Gay affair, in which Japan is one of the two parties to the dispute. Zolberg follows Japanese embassy and official responses to the Smithsonian exhibit and to a US postal stamp showing the bombing, which was redesigned after Japanese protests. She notes that Japanese opinion is not uniform, citing the writer Kenzaburo Oe's criticism of his countrymen, and she discusses the internment of Japanese immigrants and Americans in the Second World War as part of American national identity. A passing reference in the same chapter is to a 1994 Guggenheim SoHo display of post-war Japanese art.

The other Asian material is in chapter 3, Prösler's 'Museums and Globalization'. It dates early foundations: Batavia (1778) in the Dutch East Indies, then, from the 1870s, museums in Japan (1871, 1877), Bangkok (1874), China (1905), Korea (1908), Phnom Penh (1917) and Ulan Bator (1921). It notes that new Asian foundations before the 1870s were limited to British India. Its extended case is the National Museum in Colombo, Sri Lanka, which lies outside East and Southeast Asia and is cited as a contrast.

Chapter 7, Riegel, mentions the Royal Ontario Museum's East Asian Gallery only as the neighbour of the Fluffs and Feathers exhibition, and notes that China is displayed on the ground floor. Nothing is said about Southeast Asian collections, colonial collecting in Indochina or the Dutch East Indies, Asian states' heritage policy, or Asian visitors and curators. The volume's theoretical chapters on time, class, gender, Stonehenge and the Tate do not discuss the region.

JapanChinaKoreaThailandCambodiaMongoliaIndonesia

Contents

Theoretical approach of this work
ContentsPDF p. 6
Theorizing museums: an introduction • Sharon MacdonaldSharon MacdonaldPDF p. 8

Macdonald's introduction to the volume Theorizing Museums argues that museums are an under-studied but theoretically rich object for anthropology, sociology and cultural studies. It opens with a paradox: museums are multiplying and diversifying while their authority, audiences and collections come under question, and they increasingly take up controversial subjects and new media. The introduction argues that older accounts, which treat museums only as agencies of social control or as sites of distinction, are too simple, and that a museum should be treated as a process as well as a structure. Museums developed alongside the modern nation-state and share with anthropology and sociology a history of classification and of turning culture into objects. The rest of the piece presents the volume's three parts, on context, contest and content, and summarizes chapters on globalization, the Enola Gay controversy, the Colonial Williamsburg black history exhibit and the Chantrey Bequest at the Tate. It concludes that every museum or exhibition is a statement of position, a theory of the world, and deserves critical scrutiny.

Smithsonian Institution (Enola Gay display)Tate Gallery (Chantrey Bequest)Colonial WilliamsburgNational Museum of Sri Lanka
Part One: Contexts: Spaces and TimesPDF p. 26
Museums and globalization • Martin ProsierMartin PröslerPDF p. 27

Prösler asks how museums spread around the world and came to express the nation. Drawing on world-systems and globalization theory (Wallerstein, Robertson), he argues that the museum is a globally diffused institutional form whose ordering of the world descends from early modern cabinets of curiosity. He faults museology for treating museums as passive reflections of globalization and for developmental measures such as museums per unit of GDP. Turning to history, he charts museum foundations across Europe, the Americas, Asia and Africa, where colonial museums came first. Case studies follow the encyclopedic cabinets of Camillo and the Medici studiolo, the Royal Society's repository, which became a national inventory, and nineteenth-century national museums in Nuremberg, Munich and Warsaw. The chapter ends with the National Museum in Colombo, where Sanni healing masks appear as remnants of a 'traditional' past. Local visitors, he concludes, read such displays in their own ways, so museums link local and global categories without fixing their meaning.

National Museum of Sri Lanka (Colombo)Germanisches Nationalmuseum (Nuremberg)Royal Society repository (London)
How societies remember the past • John UrryJohn UrryPDF p. 51

Urry argues that how societies remember the past should be a central concern of social theory, and that the social sciences have never explained the mechanisms of collective memory. Drawing on Mead's 'philosophy of the present' and on Bergson and Connerton's distinction between incorporating and inscribing practices, he proposes a theory built on time, tradition and memory. He then examines heritage, which he sees as ambiguous: critics such as Hewison and Lowenthal treat it as nostalgic and commodified, but Urry argues that visitors actively perform 'reminiscence' at sites. Evidence comes from Macdonald's study of visitors reading a Science Museum exhibition against its designers' intent, Mellor's work at the Albert Dock in Liverpool, and the Aros heritage centre on Skye, where Gaelic revivalism met commerce. He concludes that museums face fragmented traditions, enthusiast-run sites that contest dominant histories, and a global market that blurs culture and leisure. Museums might still offer 'glacial time' against collective amnesia.

Science Museum (London)Aros heritage centre (Isle of Skye)Albert Dock (Liverpool)
Part Two: Contests: Differences and IdentitiesPDF p. 72
Museums as contested sites of remembrance: the Enola Gay affair • Vera ZolbergVera L. ZolbergPDF p. 73Asia: in part

Zolberg examines the dispute over the National Air and Space Museum's planned exhibition on the end of the Second World War, centred on the Enola Gay. Museums, she argues, help construct national memory, and this dispute shows conflicting interests within the United States and between it and Japan. She narrates the sequence: a curators' script stressing civilian deaths, its revision under pressure from the Smithsonian secretary and veterans, a demand by eighty House members for the director's resignation, and a clash with Japan over a stamp. The Board of Regents finally cut the exhibit to a fuselage section and a plaque. Zolberg then links the case to wider questions of national identity, including Japanese-American internment and a flag display at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. Zolberg concludes that the dispute carries international weight between now-equal nations, and that museums must choose between avoiding controversy, becoming a 'Disneyland', or opening debate.

East and Southeast Asia Japan is one of the two parties to the dispute. Zolberg reconstructs how Japanese officials and the Embassy responded to the exhibit and to a US postal stamp showing the bombing, which was redesigned after Japanese protests. Zolberg discusses Japanese immigrants in the United States and their wartime internment, and notes that Japanese opinion is not uniform, citing the writer Kenzaburo Oe's criticism of his countrymen for not accepting responsibility for the war.

National Air and Space Museum (Smithsonian, Washington)School of the Art Institute of Chicago
Into the heart of irony: ethnographic exhibitions and the politics of difference • Henrietta RiegelHenrietta RiegelPDF p. 87

Riegel examines how irony is used in museum exhibitions that critique the representation of other cultures. Riegel argues that museum display relies on a visual logic which separates viewers from the 'Other' on show, producing an ethnographic distance of the kind anthropology also produces. Two exhibitions at the Royal Ontario Museum illustrate the point. Into the Heart of Africa (1989-90), curated by Jeanne Cannizzo to critique colonial collecting, used verbal irony that many visitors did not read as critique, so it reinforced the distance it sought to undermine. Fluffs and Feathers (1992), a travelling exhibition from the Woodlands Cultural Centre, mixed authentic and popular objects and invited visitors to try on native costume before a mirror, making its irony dialogic. Riegel concludes that irony is a risky strategy, and that it can open shared spaces with publics only when it turns back on the museum's own mode of representation.

Royal Ontario Museum (Toronto)Woodlands Cultural Centre (Brantford, Ontario)
Seeing through solidity: a feminist perspective on museums • Gaby PorterGaby PorterPDF p. 109

Porter applies poststructuralist and feminist theory to museums to trace how gender is represented in their exhibitions, collections and organization. Translating the relation of text, author and reader into exhibition, curator and visitor, she reads displays against the grain. Women are represented as passive, shallow, undeveloped and closed, while men appear active, deep and open, so that women are pushed to the margins of museum narratives. She also discusses the difficulty of theorizing in an empirical museum culture, where solid collections seem to resist critique, and her own dual position as a museum worker and researcher. The final section surveys exhibitions in Britain and northern Europe that work differently: the Geffrye Museum's Putting on the Style, the Women's Museum in Aarhus and the Museum of Work in Norrköping, whose sculptural, sensory and impermanent displays treat visitors as producers of meaning. Their temporary nature, however, leaves them marginal in the record.

Geffrye Museum (London)Women's Museum (Aarhus, Denmark)Museum of Work (Norrköping, Sweden)
Decoding the visitor’s gaze: rethinking museum visiting • Gordon Fyfe and Max RossGordon Fyfe and Max RossPDF p. 131

Fyfe and Ross report preliminary visitor research in Stoke-on-Trent and Newcastle-under-Lyme, based on in-depth household interviews. They argue that class is a cultural process and that museum visiting is a social relationship rather than an attribute of individuals, drawing on Bourdieu, Urry and Douglas's grid and group. The chapter opens with the Antiques Road Show and the 'Ozzy' owl jug, bought at auction by Stoke's City Museum, to show how objects acquire local meanings. Three households follow: the Cartwrights, a local middle-class family who value hands-on engagement with objects; Ms Brown, a newcomer academic who wants new art rather than community history; and the Graingers, working-class residents who find the City Museum's street reconstructions affirming. The authors conclude that visiting is shaped by household, class trajectory and place, and that museums are 'good to think with'.

City Museum and Art Gallery (Hanley, Stoke-on-Trent)Borough Museum (Newcastle-under-Lyme)
Part Three: Contents: Classifications and PracticePDF p. 155
The utopies of social ordering: Stonehenge as a museum without walls • Kevin HetheringtonKevin HetheringtonPDF p. 156

Hetherington takes up Malraux's 'museum without walls' and asks how the space of such a museum can be understood. Drawing on Foucault's heterotopia and Marin's utopies, he argues that the classical museum has always expressed a utopian project of social ordering. The museum without walls is instead heterotopic and contested, with many competing utopias. He illustrates this with Stonehenge, which has been an archaeological monument, a Druidic temple in antiquarian readings, a tourist attraction and the site of New Age Travellers' free festivals from 1974 to 1984. He shows how English Heritage and the National Trust have turned the ruin into a staged authenticity, with a tunnel of English history leading to the stones. He concludes that visitors become would-be curators and interpreters, so the museum without walls invites participation, though not equal participation.

Stonehenge (English Heritage site, as a 'museum without walls')
Maintaining boundaries, or ‘mainstreaming’ black history in a white museum • Eric GableEric GablePDF p. 180

Gable examines how staff at Colonial Williamsburg, the American outdoor living-history museum, handled miscegenation after 'new social historians' tried in the late 1980s and early 1990s to make black history central to every site. Using interviews, taped tours and two evening performances, Gable shows that white guides avoided the topic by insisting on 'just the facts' and treating missing documents as a reason for silence, while black guides on the AAIP Other Half Tour told the story of George Wythe, his freed cook Lydia Broadnax and the mulatto boy Michael Brown. At the Wythe House the documents do not establish paternity. Gable contrasts 'Christmas at the Wythe House', which presents a composite Wythe as the real man, with 'Affairs of the Heart', which is openly framed as fiction. The chapter concludes that white frontline staff treated racial categories as fixed, that historians offered guides little guidance, and that miscegenation stayed marginal to the museum's narrative.

Colonial WilliamsburgWythe HouseWetherburne's Tavern
A Trojan Horse at the Tate: theorizing the museum as agency and structure • Gordon FyfeGordon FyfePDF p. 206

Fyfe argues that sociology lacks an adequate account of museums and proposes that a museum is both an agency of classification and a relationship of cultural interdependence, tied to the uncertainties of modernization. Fyfe draws on Bourdieu's work on symbolic violence and the cultural field, and criticizes Duncan and Wallach, Sherman and Zolberg for treating museums as the creatures of a dominant class or for neglecting their internal conflicts. Fyfe’s case study is the early history of the Tate Gallery, founded in 1897 as the National Gallery of British Art and funded by the Chantrey Bequest, which the Royal Academy administered. Fyfe traces the Chantrey controversy through press campaigns, the Crewe (1904) and Curzon (1911) inquiries, and disputes over board membership and purchases, showing how modern art displaced academy painting. Fyfe concludes that the Tate produced its identity as a museum of modern art through these contradictions, not through the essence of art or the needs of capital.

Tate Gallery
Notes on ContributorsPDF p. 232
IndexPDF p. 235
MacKenzie, John M. (2009). Museums and Empire: Natural History, Human Cultures and Colonial Identities. Manchester: Manchester University Press.Asia: substantial12 chapter overviews

Overview

MacKenzie's Museums and Empire (2009) surveys museums in the British Empire's settler colonies and in Asia, arguing that they expressed a Western conviction in the rational ordering of nature and peoples while slowly stimulating respect for indigenous cultures. The colonial museum is treated as an 'imperial archive', but its claims to scientific and moral benefit are tested against thin funding, few staff and local ambitions. The scope runs from the nineteenth century to the present across Canada, South Africa, Australia, New Zealand and Asia. It is organised geographically, with two chapters for each settler territory and one for Asia, and closes with a five-phase model of colonial museum history.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

Asia is one of the book's geographic units rather than a theme, and its attention is concentrated in two places. Chapter Eight, on the Royal Ontario Museum and the Royal British Columbia Museum, gives the longest East Asian case: the missionary William Charles White shipped several thousand Chinese pieces to Toronto in the 1920s, among them three Yuan dynasty wall paintings taken from a derelict monastery, and MacKenzie reads this, with the Tientsin merchant George Crofts and the curator Currelly, as looting in a time of warlord instability. James Mellon Menzies's refusal to let oracle bones from the Huan River leave China is set against it. Japanese and Korean material in the ROM appears more briefly.

Chapter Fifteen, 'Museums in Asia', covers India and Ceylon, then the Malay peninsula and Singapore, which is the book's main South-East Asian case. The Raffles Library and Museum, with natural history paintings commissioned from Chinese artists and Malay krises, drew 10,500 visitors over Chinese New Year in 1908 and 17,472 in 1918. Its ethnographic and Asian collections moved in 2003 to the Museum of Asian Civilisations in Empress Place, presented as the first pan-Asian museum in the region. The Perak museum at Taiping (1886), the Selangor museum at Kuala Lumpur (1898) and the Sarawak Museum at Kuching (1886) each get a paragraph, and in all three Chinese, Malay and Tamil visitors far outnumbered Europeans. Burma appears only in the introduction, where the Rangoon museum had been shut for over twenty years.

Canadian chapters mention an exhibit from the Normal School Museum that Japan bought after the 1876 Philadelphia Centennial, and Siamese and Japanese donations to the Vancouver museum. Not covered in the passages read are the Dutch East Indies, the Philippines and Indochina, and Hong Kong is named among the areas left out. Asian states' heritage policy appears only through Singapore's post-independence museum reorganisation, and restitution and war memory do not feature.

ChinaJapanKoreaSingaporeMalaya (Perak, Selangor)SarawakBurmaSiam

Theoretical approach of this work
Natural history, human cultures and colonial identitiesPDF p. 1

Front matter for MacKenzie's Museums and Empire (2009), the 'Studies in Imperialism' volume: the general editor's series preface, the list of earlier titles in the series, the title page and the copyright and publishing details. It contains no argument or case study. The series preface states that the series treats imperialism as a cultural phenomenon affecting dominant as well as subordinate societies, and the titles list shows the series' range.

DedicationPDF p. 8
ContentsPDF p. 10
List of illustrationsPDF p. 11
AcknowledgementsPDF p. 12
List of abbreviationsPDF p. 16
Introductionp. 1

The introduction argues that museums in the British Empire expressed a Western conviction in the rational ordering of nature and peoples, at once dispossessing indigenous cultures and, slowly, stimulating respect for them. It traces how the nineteenth-century museum grew out of natural history, world exhibitions such as the 1851 Crystal Palace, railways, telegraphs and the collecting of specimens, artefacts and human remains. The colonial museum is treated as an 'imperial archive' in the sense Benedict Anderson gives to a totalising classificatory grid, but the author warns against claiming too much for it: funding was thin, staff few, and ideals were often unmet. The Miers and Markham surveys of the 1930s, which judged empire's museums by counts of collections, staff and visitors, show the statistical mindset of the age. The book is organised geographically, with two chapters each on Canada, South Africa, Australia and New Zealand and a final chapter on Asia. The introduction closes by describing the study as comparative and critical rather than theoretical, using museums to examine the cultural character of the British World.

East and Southeast Asia The introduction previews the Asian chapter, which covers the region more widely and less deeply than the settler chapters, with only the National Museum of Singapore examined in depth. It notes that Chinese railway building breached tombs whose treasures fed museums in the imperial world, and that the Rangoon museum in Burma had been shut for more than twenty years.

South Kensington MuseumBritish Museum
Canada: the origins of colonial museumsp. 21

The chapter traces the early history of Canadian museums from Quebec seminary collections and Maritime mechanics' institutes to the provincial and university museums of Ontario. It argues that these museums grew out of natural history societies and educational institutions, and were driven by wonder and enterprise, but also by the acquisitive greed of a moneyed class that justified shady collecting by the ends it served. Its evidence is a series of collectors and institutions: Abraham Gesner in New Brunswick, the showman museums of Montreal and Quebec, William Logan's geological survey museum, the Redpath Museum at McGill, the Normal School Museum of Egerton Ryerson, and the Canadian Institute. The longest case is David Boyle, the Elora blacksmith-turned-teacher whose Elora museum and later the Ontario Provincial Museum were built on archaeology and ethnography collected partly through missionaries. The chapter ends by weighing reasons why Canadian museums stayed tentative, among them thin revenues, weak professionalism and a small scientific community, and concludes that patriotic fear of losing collections to American rivals was the catalyst for the Royal Ontario and Royal British Columbia museums.

East and Southeast Asia The Normal School Museum's exhibit at the 1876 Philadelphia Centennial Exhibition was described as the best educational display there, and part of it was bought by Japan to stimulate Meiji educational reforms, the chapter's only substantive reference to East Asia. Collections in Toronto were also built from transfers that moved objects between Ontario, Europe, the Middle East and China.

Royal Ontario MuseumOntario Provincial MuseumRedpath MuseumNormal School Museum
Canada: the Royal Ontario Museum, Toronto and the Royal British Columbia Museum, Victoriap. 44Asia: in part

The chapter traces how the Royal Ontario Museum and the Royal British Columbia Museum took shape in the decades before 1930, one driven by Toronto's wealth and ambition and the other by a frontier province's concern about losing its indigenous heritage. For the ROM, Charles Currelly, a collector with Egyptian excavation experience, won backing from Edmund Walker, Sarah Warren and other financiers to build a museum whose Webb H-plan building opened in 1914. Its Chinese holdings were assembled largely by the missionary William Charles White, who shipped thousands of items from northern China, some looted from graves and a derelict monastery, and the chapter weighs the collectors' justifications against the looting they involved. The second half turns to Victoria, where the provincial museum, founded in 1886 and shaped by Newcombe and Kermode, collected North-West Coast First Nations material in a scramble with American museums. The chapter concludes that the ROM turned to world civilisations while the BC museum presented the province to itself, and that both reflect the competitive acquisitiveness of the imperial era.

East and Southeast Asia The ROM's Chinese collection, among the richest in any museum, was built largely by the missionary bishop William Charles White and the Tientsin fur merchant George Crofts, through shipments gathered from railway-cut tombs, including three Yuan dynasty wall paintings from a derelict monastery. The chapter presents this as looting amid warlord instability, and contrasts it with the sinologist James Mellon Menzies, who refused to let oracle bones from the Huan River near Zhangde leave China. It also notes Japanese prints from Walker and a Korean collection assembled from private sources.

Royal Ontario MuseumRoyal British Columbia MuseumVancouver Museum
South Africa: the South African Museum, Cape Townp. 78

The chapter follows the South African Museum in Cape Town from its uncertain origins in the 1820s, through its refounding in 1855 and the expatriate curators who followed, to its transformation after apartheid. It argues that the museum served white colonial identity, first through economic display and then through racial science. The most disturbing evidence is the life-casts of San and Khoe people made by taxidermist James Drury from 1907, and the trade in skeletons and graves, involving curators and paid agents, that led to the Bushmen Relics Act of 1911. The chapter also reads visitor figures sorted by colour and notes that Africans were never formally excluded yet faced informal barriers, while the staff remained almost entirely white. It ends with the reordering of displays under the Iziko organisation, which now foregrounds the Nguni peoples of the Eastern Cape.

South African MuseumAlbany Museum
South Africa: the Albany Museum, Grahamstownp. 105

The chapter traces the Albany Museum in Grahamstown from its origins in 1855, when a group of mostly military doctors led by William Guybon Atherstone founded a medical society that soon aimed at a general museum. MacKenzie follows its early years in borrowed rooms, its dependence on private donations and a small government grant, and its indiscriminate colonial collecting. The main turn comes with Selmar Schönland, who from 1889 gave the museum a professional scientific profile and made its ethnographic and archaeological collections a central interest, and with the new building of 1900. MacKenzie argues that the museum's claims to economic and moral benefit were largely rhetoric, and that economic growth fuelled museums rather than the reverse. MacKenzie ends with Union-era neglect, the separate settlers' museum of 1965 and the institution's crises around 2000.

East and Southeast Asia Asian material is minor and scattered. Major Orme gave a Chinese crossbow and bolts in the early 1860s, and in 1901 the museum acquired a set of carvings from the imperial palace at Peking, with more Chinese materials added later. John Hewitt, director from 1910 to 1958, had earlier been curator of the Kuching Museum in Sarawak, a fact the chapter gives only in his biography. East and Southeast Asia otherwise figure only in passing.

Albany MuseumSouth African Museum
Australia: museums in Sydney and Melbournep. 120

The chapter compares the Australian Museum in Sydney with the National Museum of Victoria in Melbourne, showing how each was shaped by colonial elites, rival collectors and shifting scientific fashions. In Sydney, MacKenzie follows a museum that began in the 1820s, passed through a string of short-lived curators, and was held back for decades by the Macleay family, who dominated its trustees and kept private collections. The 1873 gold theft and the ruin of curator Gerard Krefft are its dramatic low point. In Melbourne the story turns on Blandowski's failed start, Frederick McCoy's forty years of dominance and his removal of the collections to the university, and the rival Industry and Technology Museum. Walter Baldwin Spencer, honorary director from 1899, rebuilt the National Museum and made its Aboriginal and ethnographic collections central through his fieldwork with F.J. Gillen. MacKenzie argues that the museums' claims to practical and moral benefit were largely rhetoric. The chapter ends with the National Museum's recovery only after the Second World War.

East and Southeast Asia Asia figures only in passing, though the chapter has one substantive point: the Victorian museum drew about 37,000 visitors in 1861, many of them Chinese, a figure that surprised McCoy and that MacKenzie links to the gold rush. The main text says nothing about Chinese, Japanese or Southeast Asian collections, collectors or objects.

Australian MuseumNational Museum of VictoriaMacleay MuseumIndustry and Technology Museum
Australia: the South Australian Museum, Adelaidep. 156

The chapter follows the South Australian Museum in Adelaide from its roots in the 1834 South Australian Literary Association and the Philosophical Society of 1853, through the Institute building opened in 1861, to its transformation after 1883 under Wilhelm Haacke and, above all, Edward Stirling. The early curators Frederick Waterhouse and Haacke built collections but sent duplicates abroad, kept poor records and, in Haacke's case, discarded specimens. MacKenzie argues that the turning point was Stirling's ethnographic collecting, which relied on police, telegraph-station staff and missionaries to gather Aboriginal material from the Northern Territory and along the overland telegraph line, under the belief that Aboriginal people were disappearing. The chapter also covers the north wing of 1895, the collecting of human remains and later export controls. It closes with the appointment of Edgar Waite in 1914 and a reading of the collections through Philip Jones's idea of accommodation rather than domination.

East and Southeast Asia Asia is mentioned only in passing. In 1906 the museum bought two mounted New Zealand moa skeletons in Japan, which MacKenzie cites as evidence of the international trade in specimens. An unusual Oriental rhinoceros entered the collection in 1907, and Chinese and Fijian curiosities were among the items in the 1861 opening display. The chapter says nothing further about East or Southeast Asian collections, collectors or visitors.

South Australian MuseumBritish Museum
New Zealand/Aotearoa: War Memorial Museum, Aucklandp. 184

The chapter traces the Auckland museum from the mechanics' institute and the Auckland Institute of the 1840s and 1850s, through its founding by John Alexander Smith in 1852, to the War Memorial Museum that opened in 1929. MacKenzie argues that New Zealand's cultural institutions were planted almost at once in frontier towns as expressions of colonial and civic identity. It follows the curators Thomas Kirk and Thomas Cheeseman and the local elite whose donations funded the 1876 building. Much of the chapter concerns the large Maori collections, including carvings and meeting houses, whose acquisition he treats as a contested exchange. The carving Pukaki, given to a judge and displayed in Auckland until its return to Rotorua in 1997, and the Waimamaku burial chests, removed after heated debate, illustrate the moral problems of collecting. The chapter ends with Cheeseman's proposal to make the museum a war memorial, which drew in public funds for the neoclassical building and turned the museum into a site of national commemoration.

Auckland War Memorial MuseumColonial Museum, Wellington
New Zealand/Aotearoa: the Canterbury Museum, Christchurchp. 210

The chapter traces the Canterbury Museum in Christchurch, which MacKenzie presents as founded not by an English aristocrat but by the German geologist Julius Haast. Haast became provincial geologist in 1861 and built the collection through exchanges, public subscription and the moa bones that served as his trading currency. The chapter follows the Gothic building of 1870 by Mountfort, its extensions, and Haast's acquisition of a Maori meeting house of no local origin, which MacKenzie reads as an invented tradition. It also covers Haast's destructive exchange of bird skins and his feuds with Hector and McKay over the age of the moa. After Haast's death in 1887 the museum was run by scientists, and the appointment of the ethnologist Roger Duff in 1948, the first ethnologist on the staff, marked a shift toward Maori and Pacific collections. MacKenzie concludes that settler anxieties about extinction shaped the museum, and that its Maori collections came to express a hybrid national identity.

Canterbury MuseumColonial Museum, Wellington
Museums in Asiap. 234Asia: in part

Museums in Asia traces how museums were founded in British India, Ceylon, the Malay peninsula and Singapore. MacKenzie argues that the Asiatic societies of Calcutta, Bombay and Singapore set the pattern: their early museums were literary and historical, and economic justifications were added only later in the nineteenth century. The chapter follows the Indian Museum in Calcutta, the Victoria and Albert Museum in Bombay and the princely museums, where Indian crafts and European art were shown side by side. The second half is a case study of the Raffles Library and Museum in Singapore, from the Singapore Institution of 1823 to the building of 1887. It shows a museum starved of space and staff, damaged by the climate and run by a sequence of curators, which came to be dominated by ethnography and by Asian visitors rather than Europeans. The chapter closes with the museum's later transformation into a national institution.

East and Southeast Asia Singapore is the chapter's main Southeast Asian case: its Raffles Library and Museum, traced from Raffles's and Farquhar's natural history collecting, grew Malay silverware, Chinese porcelain and natural history paintings commissioned from Chinese artists, and drew Chinese New Year crowds of over 10,000 in 1908. The Perak, Selangor and Sarawak museums in the Malay peninsula and Borneo are also described, with Chinese, Malay and Tamil visitors far more numerous than Europeans. Far Eastern ceramics appear in Bombay's Prince of Wales Museum.

Indian Museum, CalcuttaVictoria and Albert Museum, BombayPrince of Wales Museum, BombayColombo MuseumRaffles Library and Museum, SingaporePerak MuseumSelangor MuseumSarawak Museum
Conclusionp. 265Asia: in part

The conclusion draws the book's cases together into a model of five phases in colonial museum history: proto-foundation, pioneering, transitional, pre-modern and modern. MacKenzie argues that colonial museums moved from economic rhetoric and metropolitan models to local and then national identities, but insists that this was not a neat progression and that imperial museums were locally driven yet tied together by networks of exchange. Recent reconstructions are surveyed, among them Kelvingrove in Glasgow, the Walker in Liverpool, the British Museum's move of its anthropology into the main building, the Royal Ontario Museum and the Voortrekker Monument in Pretoria, whose old sculptures could not be reinterpreted. The chapter then turns to museums' vulnerability to looting in Baghdad and Zimbabwe, and to visitor reception, which remains the least documented aspect of colonial museums. It ends with Ruskin's and Huxley's ideas of the museum and with the suggestion that visitors often took from colonial museums messages their creators had not intended.

East and Southeast Asia Singapore returns as the example of a colonial museum turned national: its ethnographic and Asian collections were moved from the National Museum on Stamford Road to the Museum of Asian Civilisations in Empress Place, opened in 2003 as a pan-Asian display. The chapter notes that when large numbers of Chinese, Indian and Malay visitors used South-East Asian museums as an extension of their religious festivals, the museums became places where identity was found. Singapore's museum history is cited as an example of how a colonial museum mutated into a national one.

McClellan, Andrew (1994). Inventing the Louvre: Art, Politics, and the Origins of the Modern Museum in Eighteenth-Century Paris. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.Asia: slight7 chapter overviews

Overview

Inventing the Louvre traces how the modern public art museum took shape in Paris between 1750 and the opening of the Louvre in 1793, and how the state and competing political factions shaped it. It follows the Luxembourg Gallery's comparative, mixed-school hang of royal paintings from 1750, Comte d'Angiviller's unrealised Louvre project of 1774-1789, the Revolutionary Louvre and the Musee central des arts under the Directory and Consulate, and Alexandre Lenoir's Musee des monuments francais, which closed in 1816. McClellan's central argument is that the museum's claims to educate and conserve were political from the start. The book is organised as an introduction, five chapters in chronological order, a conclusion setting the Louvre against Lenoir's museum, appendices on the hangs, and extensive notes.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia are not discussed. Neither the chapters, the introduction, the conclusion nor the appendices name any museum, collection, object, collector, exhibition or person from China, Japan, Korea, Siam, the Philippines, Indonesia, Vietnam or any other country of those regions. The scope is Paris, with Italy, Flanders, Germany and Austria as the sources of comparison and of the war booty that filled the Louvre in 1797-98.

The only non-European references are incidental. The text notes that the Lenormand family, which directed the arts in the 1750s, had its origins in finance and included a director of the Indies company, and a note cites the "Chinese encyclopedia" that opens Foucault's Les mots et les choses as an example of classification. Neither point concerns Asian objects, collections or museums, and South Asia and the Middle East are not discussed either.

Contents

Theoretical approach of this work
List of Illustrationsp. ix
Acknowledgmentsp. xiii
Introductionp. i

McClellan traces how the modern art museum took shape in Paris between 1750 and the Louvre's opening in 1793, and how the state shaped it. Before the Revolution, the Luxembourg Gallery's royal paintings were hung to teach comparison between artists and schools, a break from the dense, decorative princely cabinets at Mannheim. McClellan then follows the change to chronological, school-based display in Düsseldorf and in de Mechel's Vienna gallery, alongside Comte d'Angiviller's unfinished plan for the Louvre. The evidence is the spaces themselves, their printed guides and the reactions of visitors, such as a 1799 account of a village family at the Grand Gallery and the mislabelled busts of Plato and Alexander. McClellan argues that the museum's claims to educate and conserve were political from the start: the Crown tied them to good government, and the Revolution made the Louvre a sign of popular sovereignty and, later, of military conquest. McClellan ends by stressing that museums frame their contents like picture frames, and asks 'Whose museum? Whose art?'

Luxembourg GalleryLouvreMuseum of French MonumentsMannheim Electoral GalleryDüsseldorf GalleryImperial Gallery, Vienna
1The Luxembourg Gallery, 1750-79p. 13

The chapter reconstructs the Luxembourg Gallery, the first public art gallery in France, which opened in the Luxembourg Palace in October 1750 with ninety-nine paintings from the royal collection. McClellan argues that the hang was a pedagogic design rather than a conventional princely display: its juxtapositions invited comparative viewing in the manner of Félibien and de Piles, so that visitors could judge each picture by its performance in the parts of painting. The case is built from the gallery's origins in the circle of Bachaumont and Lenormand, La Font de Saint-Yenne's 1747 attack on the neglect of royal pictures, the restorers Colins and Godefroid, and Picault's celebrated transfer of Raphael's Saint Michael, together with the official catalogue, two visitors' letters, and comparisons with the Crozat and Orléans collections. The chapter ends by linking the gallery to the Ecole royale des élèves protégés, whose students were meant to copy its pictures, and to the 1793 Louvre, whose hang briefly revived the comparative mode before a chronological arrangement replaced it.

Luxembourg GalleryLouvreCrozat collectionPalais Royal (Orléans collection)
2D'Angiviller's Louvre Projectp. 49

The chapter follows the Louvre museum that Comte d'Angiviller planned as director general of royal buildings from 1774 until the Revolution. McClellan traces the long dispute over lighting the Grand Gallery, from the removal of the scale-relief models in 1776-7 through successive committees of architects, to the 1789 trial lantern over the Salon. It shows how d'Angiviller built the collection through dealers such as Paillet, transferred ceiling and wall paintings such as Le Sueur's Saint Bruno cycle, and commissioned history paintings from David and Lagrenée for the walls. The argument is that the planned hang would have been arranged by school and chronology on the model of Vienna's Imperial Gallery, and that the Great Men statues, beginning with Gois's L'Hopital, used royal patronage to shape political opinion during the Parlement crisis. The chapter ends with the 1780s, when commissions grew cautious and the museum passed unfinished to the Revolution.

LouvreImperial Gallery, Vienna
3The Revolutionary Louvrep. 91

The chapter follows the Louvre from the fall of the monarchy in August 1792 to the arrival of Italian war booty in 1798, asking how the Revolution turned the museum into a political sign. McClellan argues that the museum was presented as national property and as a school that would replace the Academy, and shows how the Museum Commission's mixed-school hang, which recalled the Luxembourg, was attacked by David and the Conservatoire, which demanded arrangement by school and chronology. The restoration dispute, in which Picault and Lebrun backed David's charges, and the purification of the gallery, including Rubens's Medici cycle and Flemish genre painting, are further cases. The chapter then turns to the Festival of National Unity of 10 August 1793 and to confiscations in Belgium and Italy, including the 1798 triumphal convoy, which shows the museum becoming a military trophy. It ends by deferring the permanent installation of conquered art to the next chapter.

LouvrePetits-Augustins depot (Museum of French Monuments)
4The Musee Central des Artsp. 124

The chapter covers the Musée central des arts from 1795 to 1803, asking how the Louvre justified its collection once the Italian convoys arrived. McClellan follows the succession of administrations, the closure of the Grand Gallery from 1796 to 1799, and the temporary Salon and drawings exhibitions that filled the gap. The 1797 Marin affair, which charged the administration with neglect and damaging restoration, shows the museum defending its conservation policy. Its central argument concerns the hang: reconstructing the 1799 arrangement by school and chronology, and Vivant-Denon's 1803 redesign of the Raphael bays through Cosway's etchings, McClellan argues that Denon's history of art rejected the cyclical decline of Winckelmann and Quatremère. The chapter ends with the antique sculpture galleries, where the authenticity of the Apollo Belvedere complicated any chronological display.

Musée central des arts (Louvre)Musée spécial de l'école française, VersaillesMuseum of French Monuments
5Alexandre Lenoir and the Museum of French Monumentsp. 155

This chapter reconstructs the Musée des monuments français, the second great Revolutionary museum of Paris, which Alexandre Lenoir built from the depot of confiscated sculpture at the Petits-Augustins. Lenoir became its guardian in 1791, the museum was recognized in 1796 and it closed in 1816. McClellan argues that its contents, mostly medieval and Renaissance French tombs and statuary that few then regarded as art, could only have become a museum under Revolutionary conditions, and that Lenoir shaped them heavily. The chapter follows his rivalry with the Louvre and the Commission des monuments over objects, his catalogues, and his claim to a Republican purpose. It then works through the chronological period rooms, from the thirteenth to the seventeenth century, showing how Lenoir restored or reassembled tombs such as those of Francis I and Louis XII with invented parts, so that French art appears to rise to the sixteenth century and decline under Louis XIV. Later sections cover restitution to churches after 1802, the Empire and Restoration, and the museum's closure.

Musée des monuments françaisLouvreMusée spécial at Versailles
Conclusionp. 198

The conclusion sets the Musée des monuments against the Louvre, which grew under Napoleon into the model of the universal survey museum. McClellan describes the Louvre's expansion under Vivant-Denon after 1804, the crowded rehang of the Grand Gallery recorded in Zix's 1810 drawings, and visitors left dazzled by the walls. It then turns to Quatremère de Quincy's campaign against displacement, which the Bourbon Restoration answered only partly by returning works, and to the Louvre's recovery and the spread of museums across Europe, with Canova's retrievals and the Vatican Pinacoteca as examples. The author argues that Quatremère was right that paintings and monuments lose affective power out of context, but that museums also created a new aura and new historical insight, as Friedrich von Schlegel's reading of the Grand Gallery shows. The chapter closes with Lebrun's Penitent Magdalen, once celebrated and now in storage, as an object orphaned by displacement.
