Meyer, Andrea; Savoy, Bénédicte (eds.) (2014). The Museum Is Open: Towards a Transnational History of Museums 1750–1940. Berlin: De Gruyter.Asia: slight17 chapter overviews

Overview

The Museum Is Open is an edited volume of 23 chapters, built on a 2012 Berlin conference, that rewrites European museum history from 1750 to 1940 as a transnational history. The editors Andrea Meyer and Bénédicte Savoy argue that museums have been read as mirrors of competing nations, while in practice objects, plaster casts, photographs, architectural models, journals and experts moved between capitals and institutions. Case studies run from London, Paris, Berlin, Kassel and Moscow to Turin, Lisbon, Istanbul, New York, Boston, Algiers and La Réunion. The chapters are organised around objects and collections, architecture and display, the actors and their networks, international reform, and the museum as a contested space of national and imperial interests.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia get little attention. The one substantial passage is in chapter 11, Lieske Tibbe’s account of Marius Vachon’s reports on European museums of industrial arts. Vachon praised the Orientalisches Museum in Vienna, housed in the Exchange Building after the 1873 World Fair, whose collections ran from Turkey and Persia to Japan and China and whose labels gave prices, production and sales channels. He wanted France to found a similar agency, drawing on the unused Chinese collection in the Palais de Fontainebleau and the Cernuschi collection, and he bought Japanese swords at the 1889 World’s Fair for his museum at Saint-Étienne. Here Asian goods appear as commercial and educational material for a French industrial museum, not as objects with a history of their own.

Elsewhere the references are passing. The editors’ introduction names recent studies of museums in Turkey, Taiwan and Korea as work on the periphery of the European story, and cites a National Museum in Taiwan study in a note. Christina Kott’s chapter 17 lists China and Japan among the countries that sent delegations to the 1934 Madrid conference of the International Museums Office. Bärbel Küster’s chapter 21 notes that Malaysian, Indian and Chinese immigrants on La Réunion were shut out of the Musée Léon Dierx, without any case study of them. Middle Eastern material in chapter 1 and Ottoman Istanbul in chapter 20 lie outside the region.

No chapter treats a museum in East or Southeast Asia, Asian visitors or curators, or Asian restitution claims. The volume is about Europe, the Atlantic world, North Africa and La Réunion, as its introduction states.

JapanChina

Contents

Theoretical approach of this work
Museums and the Transnational Circuits of Artefactsp. 17
The Ancient Near East in Storage. Assyrian Museum Objects as a Cultural Challenge in Victorian EnglandMirjam Brusiusp. 19

Brusius examines the first British excavations of Assyrian sites in Mesopotamia, chiefly Austen Henry Layard's digs at Nimrud and Nineveh in the 1840s, and what happened to the finds once they reached the British Museum. The article opens with two recent cases: the theft of book pages by Farhad Hakimzadeh in 2009, and the 2010 loan of the Cyrus Cylinder to Tehran, which different nations read in incompatible ways. Layard's expedition was improvised rather than planned, though press accounts made it look purposeful. The sculptures and cuneiform tablets resisted classification, because nobody could read the tablets and the sculptures fitted neither the Greek nor the Egyptian galleries. Biblical expectations made the finds unsettling, since names such as King Pul could not be found and the Deluge on the tablets was not the biblical one. Brusius concludes that the objects were collected for their potential rather than their meaning, and that from the start they unsettled the museum's canon.

British MuseumNational Museum of Iran
Competition, Exchange, Comparison. Nineteenth-Century Cast Museums in Transnational PerspectiveCharlotte Schreiterp. 31

Schreiter asks why nineteenth-century cast museums, collections of plaster reproductions of sculpture, became vehicles of national identity although their casts circulated freely across Europe. The chapter compares London, Berlin and Paris, using the Crystal Palace at Sydenham, which held a large cast collection from 1854, as its central case. It sets this against the British Museum, whose antiquities travellers criticised for their disordered display, and the Neues Museum in Berlin, praised for its chronological order. Schreiter also draws on the Paris Atelier de Moulage, which supplied casts to many institutions and whose moulds dated from the Napoleonic seizure of works of art, and on the South Kensington Museum's Architectural Courts, which were judged against Berlin. Schreiter’s argument is that the trade in casts linked these collections into one network, while the way each was arranged, chronologically or thematically, expressed national claims. The chapter concludes that comparison and competition between institutions, rather than the aesthetic experience of single works, drove the national museum project.

Crystal Palace, SydenhamBritish MuseumNeues Museum, BerlinSouth Kensington MuseumMusee de Sculpture Comparee, TrocaderoLouvreAtelier de Moulage, Paris
Reproduced Art. Early Photographic Campaigns in European CollectionsDorothea Petersp. 45

Peters traces how photographic reproduction of artworks spread through European museums and collections from the 1850s, and how it helped shape the art historical canon. Peters’s main case is Prince Albert's project to photograph Raphael's drawings and paintings, carried out between 1852 and 1862 by photographers from several countries across more than 30 collections; the resulting Raphael Collection at Windsor Castle is treated as a unique assemblage. Peters then follows the commercial photographers who came after: Roger Fenton and Charles Thurston Thompson for the British Museum and South Kensington Museum, Thompson and Charles Marville at the Louvre, and Adolphe Braun, who was refused permission to photograph Louvre paintings in 1866 and turned to drawings and carbon prints. The Photographische Gesellschaft in Berlin, founded in 1862, is the other main firm, photographing paintings in the Berlin Gemaldegalerie, Dresden and the National Gallery in London. Her argument is that these campaigns were transnational, depended on museum staff, and gave art historians unprecedented access, so that the photographs helped to form the canon. The chapter ends by describing this as a shift from connoisseurship of originals to photographic connoisseurship.

Raphael Collection, Windsor CastleBritish MuseumSouth Kensington MuseumLouvreGemaldegalerie, BerlinGemaldegalerie, DresdenNational Gallery, LondonUffizi, Florence
Cross-border Transfers of Architectural Models and Display Principlesp. 59
Top Lighting from Paris in 1750. The Picture Gallery in Kassel and Its Significance for the Emergence of the Modern Museum of ArtStefanie Heraeusp. 61

Heraeus examines the lighting of the Kassel Picture Gallery, built for Landgrave Wilhelm VIII of Hesse-Kassel and opened in 1753, and argues that it marks a turning point in gallery design. Building was halted in 1750, when a visiting Parisian collector, the Marquis de Voyer d'Argenson, suggested the top-lit gallery of the Palais Royal, and the court architect's son Simon Louis du Ry was asked to report on Paris galleries. The Landgrave then redesigned the gallery with a clerestory, and the walls were hung on all four sides, drawing also on the Salzdahlum gallery and earlier top-lit rooms in Florence and Antwerp. Heraeus argues that this allowed symmetrical rows of paintings to face each other, so that viewers could compare them, a move that treated pictures as works of art rather than princely decoration. Heraeus draws on visitors' comments, including praise from the painters Overbeck and Rumohr around 1800, and on the Louvre's later adoption of overhead light. The chapter ends by describing the gallery, confiscated for Paris in 1807, as a product of cross-border exchange in which intermediaries such as Voyer d'Argenson and du Ry played a central role.

Kassel Picture GalleryDresden Picture GalleryLouvrePalais Royal gallery, ParisSalzdahlum picture galleryUffizi Tribuna, FlorenceHotel de Lassay, Paris
A European Museum-Cocktail around 1900. The Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts in MoscowBenedicte Savoy, Sabine Skottp. 77

Savoy and Skott examine the Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts in Moscow, founded by the classical philologist Ivan Tsvetaev and opened in 1912, and argue that it is a synthesis of European models rather than a purely Russian institution. Its cost was met almost entirely by private Russian patrons, above all the industrialist Yury Nechaev-Maltsov, but its design was worked out by correspondence with Georg Treu, director of the Dresden Albertinum, and with the architect Roman Klein. The authors trace room by room how Moscow's galleries copy or combine the Dresden Olympic Gallery, the Louvre's Assyrian rooms, the Munich Glyptothek, the Berlin Neues Museum and the Vienna Egyptian gallery. Courtyards modelled on the Ecole des Beaux-Arts in Paris and the Bargello in Florence hold plaster casts of architecture, and a marble frieze after the Parthenon frieze in the British Museum decorates the facade. The chapter concludes that the building was a product of transnational exchange, used for national affirmation, and that the letters are among the most important recent sources for museum history.

Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts, MoscowAlbertinum, DresdenLouvreGlyptothek, MunichNeues Museum, BerlinKaiser Friedrich Museum (Bode Museum), BerlinBritish MuseumMusee du Trocadero, Paris
The Journal Mouseion as Means of Transnational Culture. Guglielmo Pacchioni and the Dawn of the “Modern Museum” in ItalyAlessandra Galizzi Kroegelp. 89

Galizzi Kroegel challenges the view that Italian museum design became modern only after the Second World War, through Franco Albini and Carlo Scarpa, a view reinforced by Argan's 1952 praise of Genoa's Palazzo Bianco. Her case is Guglielmo Pacchioni, who reorganised the Galleria Sabauda in Turin between 1929 and 1932 and later the municipal collections in Novara and Pesaro. She shows that Pacchioni's 1934 article in the journal Mouseion, published by the League of Nations' International Museums Office, set out a division between public galleries with sparse hanging and study rooms for scholars, and rejected pseudo-historic reconstruction. She traces his ideas to Focillon and Perret, against the conservative Italian contributions in the journal's early issues. Pacchioni's work was better received abroad than at home, where his Novara display was dismantled and he was refused a place in the Italian delegation to the 1934 Madrid conference. The chapter concludes that Mouseion carried the modern museum idea into Italy well before the postwar generation, and that the journal is a neglected means of transnational exchange.

Close Inspections of the “Other.” Commissions and Experts on Tourp. 101
Cultural Excursions. The Transnational Transfer of Museums in the Transatlantic WorldThomas Adamp. 103

Adam examines how museum models travelled across the Atlantic in the late nineteenth century, arguing that the transfer ran in both directions and was driven by wealthy elites. Adam begins with the American visitors who spent months in German cities, above all Dresden, where they gained cultural and social standing. The main case is the founding of the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, promoted by members of the exclusive Union League Club. Its organisers took the membership structure from German art associations, notably Leipzig's, and the nomination procedure from the social clubs. After 1900 transfer became professional: A. B. Meyer's report on American museums found German museums wanting in education and public access, and a Boston commission toured ninety-five European museums before designing its new building. Adam concludes that the German museum-association movement of 1913 was itself modelled on New York and earlier German associations, which Seidlitz overlooked.

Metropolitan Museum of Art, New YorkMuseum of Fine Arts, BostonSouth Kensington Museum, LondonNeues Museum, BerlinLeipzig art museumNew Grand Ducal Museum, Darmstadt
From Model Museum to the Fear of the Uhlan. Museum Relations between France and Germany during the Second EmpireArnaud Bertinetp. 117

Bertinet examines the exchanges between French and German museums under Napoleon III, from the 1850s to the Franco-Prussian War. The Louvre and the imperial museums were treated as models: British and Venetian institutions asked for information on their organisation, and French staff toured Europe, among them Clement de Ris, who in 1860 praised German museum architecture. Exchanges extended to catalogues and plaster casts, while an attempt to swap original paintings with Madrid failed because French collections were inalienable. The central case is 1870, when half the Louvre's most valuable paintings were evacuated to the Brest arsenal and returned only in September 1871. Bertinet argues that this was the first organised attempt to protect French public collections as a whole, and that the war ended these exchanges. Bertinet concludes that the transfer of Strasbourg and other museums to Germany created new French-German exchanges between 1870 and 1914.

Louvre, ParisImperial Museum of Antiquities, Saint-Germain-en-LayeLeipzig museumKarlsruhe museumPrado, MadridRomano-Germanic Central Museum, Mainz
Admiration and Fear. The Reports of Marius Vachon on Museums of Industrial Arts in EuropeLieske Tibbep. 131Asia: in part

Tibbe examines the reports that Marius Vachon, a government-commissioned inspector, wrote between 1881 and 1897 after touring European museums of industrial arts, and his plan for a working museum to rescue French industry. The background is French decline: exports fell as British and German firms produced cheaper imitations, and the Union centrale des arts decoratifs never secured a permanent museum. Vachon judged museums by their educational value, preferring technical collections of series, replicas and libraries to the historical 'Cluny' type of display, and he admired the South Kensington Museum and the museums of Berlin and Vienna. Tibbe links his position to a nationalist and corporatist politics that opposed state direction in favour of local civic initiative. The chapter then describes his attempt to build an industrial art museum in Saint-Etienne in 1889, undermined by the city council after he left. Tibbe concludes that his systematic model lost ground after 1900 as decorative arts museums turned to period rooms and aesthetic display, a shift Vachon denounced.

East and Southeast Asia Vachon praised the Orientalisches Museum in Vienna, housed in the Exchange Building from the 1873 World Fair, as an ideal museum: its collections ranged from Turkey, Persia and India to Japan and China, and each object was labelled with price, means of production and sales channels, linked to an Austrian-Asiatic trade agency. He wanted France to create a similar agency, drawing on the unused Chinese collection at Fontainebleau, the Cernuschi collection and the new colonies. He also bought Japanese swords at the 1889 World's Fair for his museum in Saint-Etienne.

Musee de Cluny, ParisMusee de Sculpture Comparee, TrocaderoSouth Kensington Museum, LondonMuseum fur Kunst und Industrie, ViennaOrientalisches Museum, ViennaKunstgewerbemuseum, BerlinMusee des Arts Decoratifs, ParisMusee d'Art et d'Industrie, Saint-Etienne
Cosmopolitan Scholar, Servant of Art. Transnational Contexts of Igor Grabar in Early Twentieth-Century RussiaRoland Cvetkovskip. 147

Cvetkovski examines the career of the painter and art historian Igor Grabar (1871-1960), arguing that his work in Russian museums cannot be separated from his transnational formation. Cvetkovski spent his early years in Munich as an art critic, absorbing Western art history. Cvetkovski’s 1907 article on Russian art, written after a Paris exhibition of 1906, answered Richard Muther's history of painting, which had treated Russian art as backward, and argued that Russian art had its own autonomous history. After 1913 Grabar reorganised the Tretyakov Gallery in Moscow, removing the crowded hanging left by Pavel Tretyakov and arranging the collection chronologically, so that the rooms worked like the pages of a book on Russian art. From 1918 he headed the restoration workshops, whose work was shown at the 1929 icon exhibition in Berlin and Paris. Cvetkovski concludes that Grabar's nationalism was shaped by European models, and that cross-border exchange was the condition for his museum work.

Reforming the Museum – A Supranational Projectp. 163
Art Beyond the Nation. A European Vision for the National GallerySusanna Avery-Quash, Alan Crookhamp. 165

Avery-Quash and Crookham examine the reconstitution of London's National Gallery in 1855 and argue that German models, above all the Berlin Gemaldegalerie, shaped the reform. The chapter starts with the Gallery's founding in 1824, when its management was unclear and its pictures were hung densely in the manner of private collections, and follows the criticism that followed. Gustav Waagen, director of the Berlin gallery, gave evidence to the parliamentary committees and published his reform proposals in 1853, while William Dyce, who favoured arrangement by school and date, issued a pamphlet; John Morris Moore and William Coningham defended the status quo, Coningham attacking Berlin. The central figure is Charles Eastlake, whose 1845 letter on gallery architecture and 1853 suggestions shaped the Treasury minute of 1855 that made him the first Director. Under him the Gallery introduced object labels and scholarly catalogues and attempted chronological hangs, though lack of space defeated them. The authors conclude that Eastlake's lasting importance lay in making foreign ideas comprehensible and acceptable to a British audience, rather than in originating them.

National Gallery, LondonBritish MuseumGemaldegalerie, BerlinUffizi, FlorenceLouvre, Paris
The Journal Museumskunde – “Another Link between the Museums of the World”Andrea Meyerp. 179

Meyer examines the Berlin journal Museumskunde, founded in 1905 by its editor Karl Koetschau, and argues that it was deliberately transnational and helped shape German museum professionalism. The chapter opens with Bode's first article, on the Kaiser Friedrich Museum, which presented European galleries such as the Louvre, the National Gallery and Munich's Alte Pinakothek as models to copy. Meyer then shows how Koetschau's own reviews praised foreign handbooks and writers, such as Francis Arthur Bather's advice on dividing collections for researchers, students and the public. Meyer describes the journal's English-language articles, its illustrations, and its 'museum chronicle' column, which reported openings and guidebooks worldwide. Foreign contributors such as Hans Dedekam, who criticised German displays from outside, and Bather, who pressed for better annual reports, are examined in detail. The chapter concludes that exchange with foreign museums served German national interests, and that the journal depended on the transnational network it described.

Between Museumsinsel and Manhattan. Wilhelm R. Valentiner, Ambassador and Agent of Wilhelm von Bode at the Metropolitan Museum, 1908–1914Xavier-Pol Tilliettep. 191

Tilliette examines how Wilhelm von Bode, general director of the Berlin museums, and his former assistant Wilhelm Reinhold Valentiner shaped the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York between 1908 and 1914. The chapter sets out the Met's situation under its president J. P. Morgan, who bought famous collections and hired European specialists, and Bode's reform ideas, which grouped works of one period together and encouraged collectors to bequeath to museums. Drawing on Valentiner's unpublished letters to Bode in Berlin, Tilliette shows him acting as Bode's informant and agent in New York: reporting on collectors, trustees and auctions, buying objects, and arranging the Hoentschel galleries on the Kaiser Friedrich Museum model. The chapter also explains why the German curators helped American collectors, citing gifts exchanged with Berlin and the political value of Morgan's ties to Kaiser Wilhelm II. It concludes that this Berlin-New York network was a major channel for transferring German museum ideas to the United States.

Metropolitan Museum of ArtKaiser Friedrich Museum
The German Museum Curators and the International Museums Office, 1926–1937Christina Kottp. 205

Kott asks why German museum curators, who had led European museography before 1914, took only an intermittent part in the International Museums Office (IMO) of the League of Nations, and why no German official attended the 1934 Madrid conference whose handbook drew heavily on German museums. The chapter divides the IMO's history into three phases: 1926 to 1929, when Germans such as Max Friedländer and Richard Graul joined its committees; 1929 to 1933, when cooperation was shadowed by criticism of the IMO's French orientation and language policy; and 1933 to 1937, when the Nazi government ended official participation. Kott draws on UNESCO archive correspondence and the journal Mouseion, and argues that German curators sent museum documents to the conference without attending it. The chapter concludes that the transfer of museographic knowledge through the IMO was real but hard to measure, and that the handbook marks a shift from displayed to stored collections that deserves further study.

Berlin State Museums
Museums as Transnational Sites for National Identitiesp. 219
Building on the London 1881 PretextEmília Ferreirap. 221

Ferreira traces how a national fine arts museum in Lisbon grew out of an 1881 London exhibition of Spanish and Portuguese ornamental art, organised at the South Kensington Museum by John Charles Robinson. The chapter follows the Portuguese commission led by Delfim Guedes, which in April to June 1881 gathered about 160 objects from lenders across Portugal, under strict receipt and insurance procedures. It then shows the commission's campaign to repeat the show in Lisbon, in the Alvor Palace, adapted with skylights, lighting and security. The Lisbon exhibition opened in January 1882 with some 4,000 objects, drew 31,842 paid entries, and was criticised for its crowding and its many religious pieces. Ferreira describes the late catalogue and the accounts, which showed a small profit. The chapter concludes that this success persuaded the government to found the national museum, which opened in 1884 in the same palace.

South Kensington MuseumMuseu Nacional de Arte Antiga
Museum as a Transnational Space for National Identities. A Case Study on the Turkish ExperienceAyse H. Koksalp. 233

Koksal argues that the museum was a transnational form that Ottoman and Republican Turkey adopted to build national identities, and tests this with two case studies. The first is the Ottoman collection of antique weapons and antiquities at Hagia Irene from 1847, which Ahmet Fethi Pasha displayed in a synchronic, spectacle-driven way, and the Imperial Museum opened in 1869 in the Tiled Pavilion of Topkapi, where foreign directors Goold and Dethier and then Osman Hamdi Bey built a collection dominated by Greco-Roman and Helleno-Byzantine antiquities. The second is the Istanbul Museum of Painting and Sculpture, founded in 1937 by Atatürk's order in Dolmabahçe Palace on the Louvre model, whose galleries ran a progressive chronology from primitives to modern art. Koksal shows how this narrative pushed Osman Hamdi and other early painters into the category of primitives. The chapter concludes that Turkish museums borrowed transnational display practices to claim modernity, producing a glocal institution that overwrote distinctly Turkish art history.

Imperial Museum, IstanbulImperial Armory, Hagia IreneIstanbul Museum of Painting and Sculpture
French Art for All! Museum Projects in Africa 1912–1931 between Avant-garde and ColonialismBärbel Küsterp. 245

Küster argues that French museum projects in colonial Africa and on La Réunion were framed as transnational art for universal humanism, yet served colonial nationalism. It opens with the wider history of museums in Africa, from the Musée d'Alger founded in 1838 to colonial natural history collections and ethnographic institutes. It then examines two cases. The first is the Musée Léon Dierx on La Réunion, founded in 1910 to 1913 by the writers Marius-Ary Leblond, who gathered donations of contemporary French art from Paris artists and galleries and built a French historical display that pushed out the island's immigrant and enslaved histories. The second is the National Museum of Fine Arts in Algiers, which became a national museum at the 1930 centenary and concentrated its collection on Orientalist painting. The chapter concludes that the colonial museum's claim to universal art masked nationalism, and that the transnational museum must now be rethought in light of postcolonial demands for restitution and new projects on La Réunion and in Mali.

Musée Léon DierxNational Museum of Fine Arts, Algiers

Miller, Edward (1973). That Noble Cabinet: A History of the British Museum. London: André Deutsch.Asia: occasional16 chapter overviews

Overview

Edward Miller's history of the British Museum, from the founding collections (Cotton, Harley and Sloane, accepted by Parliament in 1753) to the separation of the library in the early 1970s, when the Library Departments were about to become the British Library. Its argument is institutional: the collections grew haphazardly, depended on private gifts and parliamentary grants, and the Museum kept the customs of a private house through successive changes. It is organised chronologically in fourteen chapters that follow the Museum's departments and their Keepers (the Department of Antiquities, Natural History, the Library Departments, the wars), with appendices listing the Principal Librarians, the Keepers and the Reading Room staff. Treasures appear mainly as they relate to the people who secured them.

East and Southeast Asia in this work occasional

East Asia is present but minor: a few episodes in the history of the Oriental departments, not a theme. The earliest is in chapter 8, The Department of Antiquities, 1820-1860: Captain Marryat's gift in 1825 of a colossal figure of a Burmese deity (Gaudma), Masson's 1850 complaint that 'five paltry cases' held the China and Japan antiquities, and the Trustees' refusal in 1836 of a fine collection of oriental antiquities, which shows how little non-classical material was wanted.

The substantial passages are in chapter 11, The Library Departments, 1856-1909, and chapter 13, Two World Wars and After. In chapter 11 R. K. Douglas, formerly in the China consular service, took charge of the Chinese and Japanese books in 1865, catalogued them in 1877 and became first Keeper of the Department of Oriental Printed Books and Manuscripts in 1892; Lionel Giles became its Chinese expert. Colvin's Prints and Drawings bought four Japanese woodcut collections (1902-1909) and the Wegener collection of Chinese paintings (1910), and Binyon's Sub-Department of Oriental Prints and Drawings (1912) became the basis of the later Oriental Antiquities department. In chapter 12 Franks's bequest of 1897 included Japanese ivories and sword guards. In chapter 13 the Eumorfopoulos Chinese collection, from ritual bronzes of about 1122 BC to Qing ceramics, was bought in 1934 for £100,000 jointly with the Victoria and Albert Museum; the Stein manuscripts from a cave in the Gobi, catalogued by Giles, and the Backhouse Chinese books were acquired; a Chinese terrestrial globe of 1623 came in 1961. The 1927-29 Royal Commission's call for a separate Far Eastern department was not adopted when Oriental Antiquities was formed in 1933.

Not covered: Korea, Mongolia and Southeast Asia beyond the Burmese figure; Asian visitors, curators or scholars; how Chinese and Japanese objects left their countries of origin; and restitution claims. Tibetan manuscripts (Bell, 1933) and the Oxus treasure from central Asia are noted but fall outside the question.

Forewordp. 15

John Wolfenden's foreword praises Miller's history of the British Museum as the standard account of the institution. He draws four conclusions: the range of the collections, their haphazard growth, the Museum's debt to private benefactors, and the loyalty of its staff. He then answers the question of who the Museum is for, scholars or the general public, and says it is for both. The foreword ends by noting that the library departments are about to pass to the new British Library.

British MuseumBritish Library
Author’s Notep. 17

Miller explains that he tells the story of the British Museum from its founding collections to the present, when the library is about to be separated from it. Miller stresses continuity, pointing to the Museum's house-like customs such as its housekeepers, house-keys and the Front Hall entrance. Miller notes that treasures are touched on only as they relate to the people who acquired them. Writing at the end of 1972, he reflects on how the staff and the Museum have changed since his first years there.

British MuseumBritish Library
1The Beginningsp. 19

Miller's first chapter traces the collections that were to form the British Museum, from medieval church treasuries and Renaissance cabinets of curiosities to seventeenth- and eighteenth-century English collectors. It argues that England was slow to provide public libraries or museums: the Earl of Arundel's antiquities were scattered and lost, and Tradescant's 'Ark' passed to Ashmole and then to Oxford. The chapter then follows the Cottonian Library, whose gift to the nation in 1700 was followed by decades of neglect, a fire at Ashburnham House in 1731 and the rescue of its volumes under Speaker Onslow. Its climax is the collection of the physician Sir Hans Sloane, built from his Jamaican specimens, antiquities and purchases. Sloane's will offered it to the nation for £20,000, and Parliament accepted it in 1753 alongside the Harleian manuscripts, establishing the institution the rest of the book describes. A brief sketch of a Chelsea coffee-house museum and of earlier calls for a national library rounds out the chapter.

Tradescant's ArkArundel collectionCottonian LibrarySloane collectionDon Saltero's coffee house museum
2The Foundationp. 42

Miller's second chapter covers the founding of the British Museum, from Sloane's death in January 1753 to the opening of Montagu House to visitors on 15 January 1759. Trustees meeting at Chelsea had to petition the King and Parliament, and Parliament accepted Sloane's collection together with the Cottonian and Harleian manuscripts. A public lottery was used to raise the purchase money, and the receiver Peter Leheup's rigging of it caused a scandal. The trustees chose Montagu House in Bloomsbury for £10,000, and repairs cost more than the purchase. The collections were moved in during 1755 to 1757, and the Royal Library, given by the King in 1757, brought valuable copyright deposit rights. The chapter ends with the frugal staff appointments and the strict ticket-only admission rules that limited visitors to a few hours a day.

British MuseumSloane collectionCottonian LibraryHarleian manuscriptsRoyal Library
3The Early Years, 1759-1799p. 64

Miller's third chapter follows the British Museum from its opening in 1759 to the end of the eighteenth century. It begins with the visitors' tour of the house and the cramped Reading Room, whose early readers, regulations and staff quarrels are traced through the Trustees' minutes and the letters of Gray and others. Money is the central theme: Parliament's grants were meagre, the purchase fund was tiny, and the collections grew mostly through gifts such as the Thomason tracts, the Da Costa Hebrew books and material from Cook's voyages. Miller gives the largest share to William Hamilton's Greek vases, bought by Parliament in 1772 for £8,410, and to the scientific and ethnographic work of Solander and Banks. The chapter ends with the Museum still judged inferior to continental collections and still dependent on private benefactors.

British MuseumHamilton vase collectionOtaheiti (South Sea) Room
4A Time of Growth and Changep. 91

Miller's fourth chapter covers the first decades of the nineteenth century, when the Museum began to grow in earnest. It follows the reading room through a series of administrative changes, the struggle to secure new books under the copyright deposit law, and the first parliamentary grants for buying. The main acquisitions are the Egyptian antiquities brought back after the French surrender of 1801, including the Rosetta Stone, the Towneley marbles bought in 1805, and the Portland vase, which Miller traces from Hamilton's hands to the Duke of Portland's loan in 1810. The longest section concerns the Elgin marbles: their removal from Athens, the 1816 Commons committee that debated their value, and their purchase for £35,000. Natural history is treated through Shaw, König and the Greville minerals. The chapter closes with the Burney, Lansdowne and Egerton manuscripts, which began to lift the library towards the standard of the continental national libraries, and with the sculptures still awaiting a proper building.

British MuseumTowneley GalleryElgin Marbles
5A New Era Beginsp. 116

Miller's fifth chapter covers the 1820s and 1830s, when the old Montagu House was failing and the Museum's reputation was under attack. It opens with the decay of the house and the loss of land to the Duke of Bedford, then turns to the theft of prints by the dealer Dighton and the dismissal of Keeper Beloe. The main section concerns George IV's gift of the royal library in 1823, the political struggle over where it should go, and the galleries Smirke built to house it. Miller then follows Henry Ellis's appointment as Principal Librarian in 1827 and the 1835-36 Select Committee, whose hearings on the Printed Books department, the staff and the reading rooms form the chapter's climax. It ends with Panizzi's evidence that the national library needed regular grants and open access, and with his appointment as Keeper of Printed Books in 1837 after a bitter contest with Cary and Madden.

British MuseumKing's Library
6The Making of a National Library, 1837-1847p. 151

Miller's sixth chapter covers the decade in which Panizzi, Keeper of Printed Books, and Madden, Keeper of Manuscripts, fought over the library, its catalogue and its collections. It describes Madden's search through neglected manuscripts, the move into Smirke's new galleries in 1838 and the crowded, hot reading rooms. The central story is the printed catalogue: the Trustees insisted on early publication, the first volume of 1840 appeared full of errors, and Panizzi refused to print until the manuscript was complete, a position the Trustees accepted in 1847. Miller shows how the annual parliamentary grant of £10,000 for books let Panizzi build British, foreign and American holdings. The chapter's climax is Thomas Grenville's bequest of 20,240 volumes, moved through snow in January 1847 into a room too small for it, and the quarrels over who would control the manuscripts and the Clovio volume. The rivalry is left unresolved at the chapter's close.

British MuseumGrenville Library
7Danger from every Sidep. 167

Miller's seventh chapter covers 1848 to 1856, when the Museum faced a Chartist threat, a Royal Commission and a contest for its leadership. It opens with the Chartist rally of 10 April 1848, when Panizzi organised the staff as special constables while Madden grumbled about the defence, and then turns to the Royal Commission of 1847-50. Miller follows its hearings, which examined Forshall's control of the Board, the feuds among the department heads and Panizzi's catalogue and copyright enforcement, and its report of 1850, which vindicated Panizzi and recommended abolishing the posts of Principal Librarian and Secretary. The chapter's main concern is space: Panizzi's plan of 1852 for a domed reading room in the inner quadrangle, approved by the Treasury in 1854 and opened in 1857 at a cost Madden thought extravagant. It ends with Ellis's agreed retirement and Panizzi's appointment as Principal Librarian on 4 March 1856, over Madden's bitter protest.

British Museum
8The Department of Antiquities, 1820-1860p. 191

Miller's chapter follows the Department of Antiquities at the British Museum from 1820 to 1860, when a classical collection grew into one of the largest in the world of Egyptian, Assyrian, medieval and prehistoric material. It argues that the Trustees, raised on classical taste, resisted non-classical antiquities for decades, and that the Keepers, Hawkins above all, had to work around them. Its case studies are the Egyptian sculptures obtained through Salt and Belzoni, the Elgin and Lycian marbles and the dispute between Fellows and Westmacott over their display, the Portland Vase smashed in 1845, and the Assyrian sculptures sent from Nimrud after the Museum took over Layard's excavations from Stratford Canning. The chapter ends with the British and ethnographical collections, long neglected, and with the department overcrowded and eager for change when Hawkins resigned in 1860.

East and Southeast Asia Asia comes up only in passing. Captain Marryat gave the Museum a colossal figure of Gaudma, a Burmese deity, in 1825, and Masson's 1850 guide is quoted complaining that 'five paltry cases' were all that the China and Japan antiquities were given. The rest of the chapter's eastern material is Near Eastern, which does not count here.

British MuseumEgyptian Hall, Piccadilly
9The Natural History Collections, 1812-1880p. 224

Miller follows the natural history collections at the British Museum from 1812 to 1880, years in which the specimens grew steadily while their quarters at Montagu House and then in Smirke's galleries stayed cramped and damp. It argues that the scientific departments were understaffed and poorly paid, and that rivalries among König, Brown and Gray, together with the 1837 split of the department into mineral, zoological and botanical branches, made matters worse. The chapter covers the purchase of the Banksian herbarium, the Zoological Society's transfer of specimens, the Royal Commission's report and the scientists' memorials of 1847, 1859 and 1866 defending the collections. Its central question is whether the collections should leave Bloomsbury, a dispute in which Panizzi and Owen came to favour South Kensington. It ends with the final move of the zoological collections in 1883, which it presents as the close of the Bloomsbury natural history story.

British MuseumZoological Society museum, Leicester SquareHunterian Museum, Lincoln's Inn FieldsNatural History Museum, South Kensington
10The Quiet Years: Consolidation and Retrenchmentp. 245

Miller covers the British Museum's administration from Panizzi's appointment as Principal Librarian in 1856 to Maunde Thompson's succession in 1909, a period the chapter calls quiet though it was marked by quarrels. It argues that the real problems were staff pay, pensions and appointment by examination, which the Treasury resisted for decades, and that Panizzi's campaign on these brought only partial reform. The rivalry between Panizzi and Madden runs through the chapter and ends with Madden's resignation in 1866 on a retiring allowance of £600. Other sections cover the successions of Winter Jones and Bond, the move from gas to electric light, and the extension of opening hours, including Sunday opening in 1896. The chapter ends with the 1900 British Museum Bill, which would have let the Trustees dispose of printed matter and which was withdrawn, and with the new galleries that Thompson secured, completed in 1913 under Kenyon.

British Museum
11The Library Departments, 1856-1909p. 264Asia: in part

Miller covers the library departments of the British Museum from Winter Jones's succession to Panizzi as Keeper of Printed Books in 1856 to the change of Principal Librarian in 1909. The argument is that the library grew faster than its space, staff and funds could manage: the general catalogue outgrew the Reading Room, swinging presses from 1887 stretched the iron library, and Bond's 1879 decision to print the manuscript catalogue produced the British Museum Catalogue. The chapter follows the new Maps department of 1867, the official-publication and newspaper collections (moved to a Hendon repository in 1905), and the Reading Room's readers, from Marx to the staff writers Patmore and Gosse, and it records the staff's complaints about low pay and slow promotion. Its main acquisitions are the Stowe and Newcastle manuscripts and the Malcolm drawings. It closes with the Manuscripts and Prints departments and with Kenyon's succession in 1909.

East and Southeast Asia Douglas, who had served in the China consular service and had charge of the Chinese and Japanese books from 1865, catalogued them in 1877 and became first Keeper of the Department of Oriental Printed Books and Manuscripts in 1892. Giles later became its Chinese expert. Colvin's Prints and Drawings bought four private collections of Japanese woodcuts between 1902 and 1909 and the Wegener collection of Chinese paintings in 1910, and in 1912 a Sub-Department of Oriental Prints and Drawings was set up under Binyon, an authority on China and Japan, which became the basis of the later Oriental Antiquities department.

British MuseumHendon newspaper repository
12The Departments of Antiquities, 1860-1914p. 299

Miller traces the break-up of the old Department of Antiquities after Edward Hawkins's resignation in 1860 into Greek and Roman, Coins and Medals, and Egyptian and Assyrian departments, with British and Medieval Antiquities and Ethnography placed under Franks, who became Keeper of a separate department in 1866. The argument is that the old department had become too large and too mixed for one Keeper, and that its new heads, Newton, Poole, Head, Birch, Franks and Read, built the collections through purchases, bequests and excavations. The case studies are Newton's Halicarnassus sculptures and the Mausoleum Room of 1884, the Blacas and Carlisle collections, the Mesopotamian digging of Rassam and George Smith, which Budge later revived, and the Christy collection, housed in Victoria Street. The chapter closes with Franks's gifts, the Royal Gold Cup and the Treasure of the Oxus, and Read's expansion of ethnography, and it ends with the British and Medieval collections, still crowded and in need of a permanent solution.

British MuseumChristy Collection, 103 Victoria Street
13Two World Wars and Afterp. 321Asia: in part

Miller's thirteenth chapter follows the British Museum from Frederic Kenyon's appointment as Director in 1909 through the two world wars to the early 1970s. It covers the institution's chronic lack of space and the wartime attempts to shut it, including a 1917 Air Board claim on the whole building. The 1927-29 Royal Commission, whose proposals for new stack rooms, a separate ethnographical museum and a Far Eastern department were only partly adopted, frames the interwar years. Miller then describes the rebuilding of the library, the purchase of the Codex Sinaiticus and the Eumorfopoulos Chinese collection, and the evacuation of collections to Aberystwyth, country houses and a tunnel. Bomb damage in 1940 and 1941, including the fire that destroyed the South-West Quadrant of the Iron Library, is set against the Ur and Sutton Hoo excavations. The chapter ends with the post-war reopening, the dispute over a site for a national library and the 1971 White Paper, leaving the Museum's future open.

East and Southeast Asia Miller describes the Eumorfopoulos Chinese collection, bought in 1934 for £100,000 jointly with the Victoria and Albert Museum, which ran from ritual bronze vessels of about 1122 BC through Han jades and Song ceramics to late Qing work. Miller also records the Stein manuscripts from a cave in the Gobi, on the edge of Eastern Turkestan, which Lionel Giles catalogued, the Backhouse collection of Chinese books, and a Chinese terrestrial globe of 1623 acquired in 1961. The 1929 Royal Commission's call for a Far Eastern department is noted.

British MuseumNewspaper Library at ColindaleEumorfopoulos collectionSutton Hoo treasure
14Epilogue: the British Libraryp. 360

The Epilogue traces how the British Museum Library was separated from the Museum to form the British Library. It follows the 1967 government decision to drop the Great Russell Street site, the Dainton Committee's 1969 report, the reversal of 1970, and the 1971 White Paper that set up a new body with reading and reference services at Bloomsbury and lending services at Boston Spa. Miller concludes that much will be lost in the severance but hopes the new body will serve scholars well.

Morse, Nuala (2021). The Museum as a Space of Social Care. London: Routledge.Asia: slight8 chapter overviews

Overview

Morse's book, based on long ethnographic work with the Outreach team of Tyne & Wear Archives & Museums (fieldwork 2011-2013, follow-up 2016-2018), argues that community engagement in museums should be understood through a 'logic of care' rather than the dominant 'logic of contribution', in which communities give something to the museum. It traces the participatory turn and its critical impasse, the institutional life of engagement workers (language, management, 'black lines'), their affective labour in sessions with mental health, dementia, addiction and stroke groups, and curatorial work in the West End Stories exhibition. The final chapter proposes the museum as a space of social care, grounded in an ethics of care, and calls for a 'care-ful museology'. Its scope is one English local museum service and its health partnerships, with wider reference to UK and international museums-in-health work.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia are barely present. The one substantive mention is in Chapter 7 (The Museum as a Space of Social Care), where the closing survey of museums-in-health work lists Japan, alongside Australia, Canada, New Zealand and Belgium, as a place where museums run programmes for people with dementia, stroke survivors and others (lines 8907-8908). Chapter 1 (Introduction) makes the same kind of list in one sentence, naming Japan among the countries with social meet-up activities for older adults and stroke survivors (line 878).

Chapter 6 (Curatorial Work and Care) mentions a Japanese object only in passing. The West End Stories exhibition at the Discovery Museum placed photographs, Roman spoons and other objects next to 'a handwritten note from a Japanese businessman to a military engineering group' (lines 7320-7322). This describes the display; no Japanese collection or its history is analysed.

Otherwise the only East Asian reference is a bibliographic entry, Dudley's essay 'Encountering a Chinese horse' (line 1245). The book does not cover museums in China, Korea or Southeast Asia, Asian collections in Western museums, colonial collecting from the region, or Asian states' heritage policy. Its 'Asian' references concern British communities in the North East (for example line 4525), and Bollywood programmes and Mesopotamia are outside the question.

Morse presents the book as the first considered exploration of 'care thinking' in museums, grounded in the community engagement work of the Outreach team at Tyne & Wear Archives & Museums. Drawing on cultural geography, feminist ethics and practice theory, Morse develops the idea of the museum as a space of social care. The preface traces how a planned study of community engagement turned towards care, and thanks the team, the museum's leadership and academic supervisors and colleagues.

Tyne & Wear Archives & Museums (TWAM)
List of AbbreviationsPDF p. 13
11 Introductionp. 1

The introduction sets out the book's central claim: that the museum can be understood as a space of social care, and that community engagement work should be analysed through a logic of care rather than the dominant logic of contribution. Morse grounds this in ethnographic research carried out with Tyne & Wear Archives & Museums, a local authority service in North East England, in 2011-2013 with follow-on work in 2016-2018, focused on outreach staff who work with mental health, dementia, stroke and addiction groups. The introduction explains the paradox the book addresses: staff say their institution resists a participatory commitment that appears throughout its official language. It places the study within geographies of care, feminist care ethics, debates on the social role of museums and the growing field of museums and health and wellbeing, and it distinguishes community engagement from social work. It closes by outlining the four parts of the book, moving from the participatory turn and institutional life to emotional practice and, finally, a theory of care for the museum.

Tyne & Wear Archives & MuseumsWhitworth Art GalleryManchester MuseumVictoria & Albert Museum of ChildhoodFitzwilliam MuseumMuseum of Modern Art, New York
Part I: The Participatory Turn in Museumsp. 27
22 The Problem of Engagementp. 29

Chapter 2 asks why the critical literature on museum participation has stalled. Morse traces five discourses behind community engagement in UK museums: the representational critique of curatorship, government social inclusion policy after 1997, the economic treatment of visitors as consumers, Nina Simon's participatory museum, and the turn to museum ethics and activism. Each frames communities as sources of contribution that improve the museum, and the newer museums-in-health work follows the same pattern. The chapter then reviews the critiques, including Arnstein's ladder of participation, Simon's typology, Clifford's contact zone and Lynch's charge of 'empowerment-lite' within a welfare model. Drawing on Graham and Bennett, Morse calls the cycle of critique followed by demands for better participation a critical impasse. She names the dominant framework the logic of contribution, in which communities give something to the museum, and introduces the logic of care, drawn from practice-based and participatory action research, as an alternative to be developed in later chapters.

Tyne & Wear Archives & MuseumsManchester MuseumVictoria & Albert MuseumScience Museum
Part II: The Institutional Life of Community Engagement Workersp. 67
33 The Language of Community Engagementp. 69

Chapter 3 asks what community engagement means inside Tyne & Wear Archives & Museums and what the term does there. Morse finds no shared definition, since the museum has no engagement policy, and staff offer examples ranging from a firework display and a Flickr account to a ten-week dementia reminiscence project. Managers link engagement to advocacy, council accountability and value for money; curators treat it as a way of gathering better knowledge and content for social history displays; Outreach staff describe slow relationship-building, a duty of care and support for people to empower themselves. Using Sara Ahmed's idea of the non-performative, Morse argues that the statement 'everything we do is community engagement' lets the museum claim a commitment without changing its practice. The chapter shows how Outreach work is devalued as 'airy-fairy' or 'papier mache', and how team silos and debates over whether engagement is a skill or a disposition reinforce this. It ends by moving from institutional language to the practice of engagement workers.

Tyne & Wear Archives & MuseumsThe People's Gallery
44 Managing Community Engagementp. 94

Chapter 4 examines how community engagement is managed at TWAM, from the policy history of the 1990s to the performance regimes that followed. Morse argues that audit culture, with its priority-group targets, quarterly reports and upbeat evaluations, turned engagement into a matter of counting and produced short, bolt-on projects that Outreach staff call 'scatter-gun' and 'conveyor belt' work. Bureaucracy and organisational silos further isolate the Outreach team, whose People's Gallery was eventually handed back to curators. The chapter then examines four tensions that staff call 'black lines': claims to knowledge and expertise, the policing of quality and public interest, the habit of 'managing expectations', and the discourse of choice and control, which Morse argues closes down engagement by making decisions an end in themselves. Morse shows how staff negotiate between museum and community through institutional work. The chapter closes with the austerity cuts and new health and wellbeing opportunities that drew the team towards long-term partnerships with health and social care providers.

Tyne & Wear Archives & MuseumsThe People's GallerySunderland MuseumTWAM World Cultures gallery
Part III: The Emotional Life of Community Engagement Workersp. 127
55 Community Engagement as Care Workp. 129

Morse examines the emotional life of community engagement workers at Tyne & Wear Archives & Museums (TWAM), asking what they do in sessions and how they describe it. The chapter argues that this work is best understood as care: a proactive interest in participants' wellbeing, put into practice through welcome, safety and inclusion. Morse builds the case from snapshots of sessions in the museum, on a dementia ward, at a drug and alcohol support centre and in a stroke group, together with staff discussions. Its concepts come from geography and the feminist ethics of care (Conradson, Held, Tronto), and from the idea of affective labour. The chapter shows how staff co-produce care with participants, use handling objects and creative materials to make connections, and insist that they are not social workers or therapists. It ends by stressing the emotional toll of this work and the need for support, and it leads on to the next chapter on curatorial work.

Tyne & Wear Archives & Museums (TWAM)Discovery Museum, Newcastle
66 Curatorial Work and Carep. 159

Morse follows the Outreach team's work in Newcastle's West End, where staff 'mapped' local community groups and built long-term links instead of running short projects. The chapter argues that this 'networks of engagement' model, in which the museum is one node among many organisations, changes curatorial work within a logic of care. Its main case is West End Stories, a 2013 exhibition at the Discovery Museum that drew on satellite displays such as Wedding Tales at St James' Heritage Centre, on loaned community objects and films, and on the officer's long contact with local people, while avoiding formal co-production. Morse reads the exhibition as a shared accomplishment and argues that curating is itself a form of caring for people as well as for objects. The chapter ends by setting this work against institutional expectations of quality, choice and control, and by treating the exhibition as one event within a longer process of engagement.

Discovery Museum, NewcastleWest End Stories (exhibition)Tyne & Wear Archives & Museums (TWAM)St James' Heritage Centre (Wedding Tales display)
Part IV: Social Care in the Museump. 183
77 The Museum as a Space of Social Carep. 185

Morse draws the book together by proposing that the museum can be understood as a space of social care. The chapter restates the logic of care against the logic of contribution, which treats community participation as something given to the museum, and applies an ethics of care (Held, Tronto, Fisher) to management, front-of-house and curatorial work. It argues that institutions need a shared purpose, a frank account of power and recognition of affective labour, and it warns that care work is gendered and undervalued. Morse then places the TWAM programmes on wellbeing, recovery, people over 55 and community heritage within austerity and health inequality in England, and within similar museums-in-health work elsewhere. Examples such as food programmes, death cafes and language classes illustrate the wider repair role that museums might take. The chapter ends by proposing 'care-ful museology' as a field for future research.

Muchitsch, Wolfgang (ed.) (2013). Does War Belong in Museums? The Representation of Violence in Exhibitions. Bielefeld: transcript.Asia: slight14 chapter overviews

Overview

A conference volume from the 2011 ICOMAM symposium held at the Universalmuseum Joanneum in Graz, edited by its director Wolfgang Muchitsch. Its title question, whether war belongs in museums and how violence can be shown without glorifying, trivialising or aestheticising it, frames every contribution. Jay Winter's keynote argues that war museums are both museums and memorials and never fully represent 'the war'. The case studies cover German and Austrian military museums, a Swiss armoury, an Oslo exhibition on the beauty of weapons, German city museums' unexploded bombs, Holocaust artefacts, Cypriot war photographs, Styrian memorials, the Minsk Great Patriotic War museum and new panorama museums in Turkey. Its sections are the conference frame and keynote, military museums and social history, war museums and photography, and war museums and national identity.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia are barely present. No chapter treats an Asian museum or collection at length. The one sustained passage is in Per Rekdal's chapter on the beauty of war. He describes his 1995 Oslo exhibition, where Japanese swords and the love poems written about them sat in a section on magical weapons. He sets that beauty against the use of a Japanese sword as a tool of execution, a connection he says museums almost always avoid.

Everything else is passing. Winter's keynote mentions the Hiroshima peace memorial museum, founded in 1955, as a memorial site among the sites of the two world wars. The Dresden Bundeswehr chapter describes an artistic intervention titled 'Hiroshima. Thank You' and sets the Napoleonic era against the Vietnam War. Bounia and Stylianou-Lambert mention a 'Cyprus/Korean' hall in the Istanbul Military Museum that shows the same Cypriot photograph of a murdered woman as the Cypriot museums do. Hacker and Vining's Japanese-American incarceration exhibit in Washington concerns Japanese Americans in the United States, not Asia.

Not covered: no Chinese, Korean or Southeast Asian war museum, no Asian state's heritage or memory policy, no Asian objects in European or American collections and no colonial collecting. The volume is about European and Turkish war museums, with the United States and Belarus as the main outside cases.

Japan

ContentPDF p. 5
Does War Belong in Museums? The Representation of Violence in ExhibitionsWolfgang MuchitschPDF p. 9

Muchitsch, director of the Universalmuseum Joanneum in Graz, reports on the conference held there in 2011 under the title 'Does War Belong in Museums?', part of the Joanneum's bicentenary celebrations. Muchitsch opens with the Landeszeughaus, the seventeenth-century Styrian armoury, whose survival Maria Theresa allowed in 1749 on symbolic grounds. The conference, organised with ICOMAM, was built around a tension that the session summaries return to: war displays oscillate between the fascination of weapons and the didactic urge to explain violence. The rest of the chapter summarises the sessions, starting with Jay Winter's keynote on war museums as sites of contestation and memory. Speakers from the Royal Armouries, the Dresden Bundeswehr museum, the German Tank Museum in Muenster and Vienna's Heeresgeschichtliches Museum described their efforts to move beyond technical display towards human experience, while papers on Cyprus, Minsk and Ankara showed how war museums build national identities. Muchitsch concludes that the conference, like a good exhibition, left visitors with more questions than answers.

Landeszeughaus (Styrian Armoury), GrazRoyal Armouries, LeedsBundeswehr Military History Museum, DresdenGerman Tank Museum, MuensterHeeresgeschichtliches Museum, ViennaUnited States Holocaust Memorial Museum
IntroductionPiet de GrysePDF p. 13

De Gryse, chairman of ICOMAM, gives the welcoming address that opens the thirty-second ICOMAM symposium in Graz. He recalls the association's history from its predecessor IAMAM, founded in 1957, stresses the value of its volunteer-run network for young researchers and small institutions, and places the meeting within the Joanneum's bicentenary of 1811 and the Landeszeughaus, built against Turkish attacks. He introduces the conference theme, 'Does War Belong in Museums?', and recalls a 2002 Delft symposium, 'Presenting the Unpresentable', on renewing object-centred military museums. His central argument is that representing war is ambivalent: aesthetic display can glamorise violence, while a purely technical, engineer's view erases feeling. Drawing on the sociologist Pascal Gielen, he warns that nostalgic displays such as an idealised schoolroom romanticise the past and hide hardship. He ends by introducing the keynote speaker, Jay Winter, and declaring the symposium open.

Universalmuseum Joanneum, GrazLandeszeughaus, GrazLegermuseum, Delft
Does War Belong In Museums?p. 19
Museums and the Representation of WarJay Winterp. 21

Winter, a historian of the First World War, opens with the Auckland War Memorial Museum, designed by disabled veterans after the Armistice, and with a 1920 cartoon that mocked its working title MUSEOMEMORIAL. From this he argues that war museums are semi-sacred sites and capital projects at once, and that they can never represent 'the war', since there was never consensus on what it was. He surveys the museums founded during and after the world wars, including the Imperial War Museum, the Australian War Memorial and Ernst Friedrich's pacifist Anti-War Museum in Berlin, and notes the decorum that Second World War displays kept. Winter then examines the Historial de la Grande Guerre at Peronne, whose horizontal, Holbein-inspired layout resists the thrill-seeking visitor, and the Imperial War Museum's newer First World War and Holocaust galleries. Winter argues that war museums should resist pseudo-realism, show what weapons do to bodies and widen the gender balance of their representations. Winter concludes that they should be sites of interrogation that point visitors towards the battlefields and memorials around them.

Auckland War Memorial MuseumImperial War Museum, LondonHistorial de la Grande Guerre, PeronneAustralian War Memorial, CanberraHeeresgeschichtliches Museum, ViennaBletchley Park
If War Does Belong In Museums: How?p. 39
Military Museums and Social HistoryBarton C. Hacker, Margaret Viningp. 41

Hacker and Vining trace how military museums moved from displaying arms and trophies to telling stories about ordinary soldiers. They identify two ancestries, private armour collections that went public and state arsenals of obsolete weapons, and note that the United States never created a national military museum. The Smithsonian became the closest equivalent, absorbing the material of the 1876 Philadelphia Centennial and the 1893 Chicago fair, while battlefield parks such as Gettysburg were the main American contribution. The chapter then turns to the Imperial War Museum and to how women's uniforms were dismissed as peripheral in London and Washington. The authors argue that the new military history of the 1980s changed exhibitions only slowly. Their main case is the National Museum of American History, whose Japanese-American incarceration exhibit (1987), G.I. (1992) and West Point show (2002) they review, and whose Price of Freedom hall (2004) reverted to chronological displays of weapons. They end by arguing that museums rarely exhibit war itself, only the paraphernalia of the organisations that wage it.

National Museum of American History, SmithsonianImperial War Museum, LondonMetropolitan Museum of Art, New YorkWest Point MuseumMilitary Services Institution museum, Governors Island
Displaying Warp. 61
Contents and Space: New Concept and New Building of the Militärhistorisches Museum of the Bundeswehrp. 63
From Technical Showroom to Full-fledged Museum: The German Tank Museum MunsterRalf Rathsp. 83

Raths, who has worked on the reform since 2008, traces the German Tank Museum in Muenster from its origin as a Bundeswehr study collection that the city and army turned into a public museum in 1983 under a split arrangement in which neither side could act alone. For its first twenty-five years the museum presented tanks as sterile technical showpieces, with war hidden behind the machines, because its staff were largely former soldiers and local politics favoured that view. Concepts of 1985, 1986 and 1999 kept to technical or 'great men' history, and the Waffen-SS was left to the military museum in Dresden. Rising visitor numbers and army reforms prompted a 2004 concept and a post for a historian. Raths explains why visitors resist critical history, chiefly the technical aura of tanks and the myth of a clean Wehrmacht tank corps. The chapter describes the 2011 reorganisation of the Hall of Collections, which will show battle injuries and rank-and-file uniforms. It ends by calling the process slow and contested but necessary.

German Tank Museum, MuensterMilitary History Museum of the Bundeswehr, Dresden
The Museum of Military History/Institute of Military History in Vienna: History, Organisation and SignificanceChristian M. Ortnerp. 99

Ortner traces the Museum of Military History in Vienna from its origins in the Arsenal, built as a defence barracks after 1848. Ortner explains how the building by Theophil Hansen was meant to house the imperial armoury's trophies and historic collections, and how delays over the interiors kept objects in storage until the museum opened in 1891 under Habsburg patronage. The chapter follows the institution through the First World War, when it closed, the loss of objects to successor states, and its use for propaganda after the Anschluss. Air raids and the Battle of Vienna left the buildings in ruins, and a Soviet battalion carried off some 16,000 to 18,000 melee weapons and firearms. In the post-war years the British occupiers rendered historic guns unusable with explosives, and metal from the collections was sold for scrap to help pay for reconstruction. The museum reopened in 1955 as the Museum of Military History, and Ortner ends by setting Austria's military past within social, technological and Central European history.

Museum of Military History (Heeresgeschichtliches Museum), ViennaImperial Artillery Arsenal and Armoury, ViennaMuseum of the Royal and Imperial Navy, Pula
The Beauty Of War And The Attractivity Of Violencep. 105
The Concept for a New Permanent Exhibition at the Museum Altes ZeughausCarol Nater Cartierp. 107

Nater Cartier, appointed in 2009 to head the Museum Altes Zeughaus in Solothurn, describes a 400-year-old armoury whose displays had changed little since the 1970s: cannons on the ground floor, decoratively hung weapons on the first floor, 400 suits of armour on the second and uniforms in a veterans' room on the third. Few texts and little context, yet the museum draws 20,000 to 25,000 visitors a year, while its building needs major repair. A 2008 cantonal strategy proposed a 'war and peace' theme for the museum, which prompted a petition by weapons enthusiasts. Nater Cartier explains the concept that followed: a place for dialogue on conflict that keeps the armour collection and the building's arsenal function. The 2011 design by a Basel firm proposes a 'confrontation zone' with weapons that visitors can handle, four booths on war and representation, art, diplomacy and suffering, a section on the mercenary trade from 1530 to 1792 and a timeline of weapons technology. The concept aims to show weapons without glorifying Swiss battles and to make visitors reflect on their own attitudes.

Museum Altes Zeughaus, Solothurn
About the Beauty of War and the Attractivity of ViolencePer B. Rekdalp. 123

Rekdal, of the Museum of Cultural History at the University of Oslo, describes the temporary exhibition he devised in 1995 on the aesthetics of weapons and war. Staff reacted with anger and disbelief, but he wanted visitors to confront their own fascination rather than be told that war is horrible. The exhibition moved from an old-style weapons display and magical swords to the aesthetics of uniforms and of different kinds of war, shown through a New Guinea documentary, Kurosawa's Ran, Riefenstahl's Triumph of the Will and a computer game. A Norwegian living room, with Gulf War news and a family photograph of a burnt Iraqi soldier, made visitors notice violence in their own surroundings. Rekdal then turns to enemy-making through 1930s cartoons and a film of a Bosnian village, and admits that he avoided the normality of violence, the everyday acceptance of cruelty across history, which he finds the hardest theme. Rekdal ends by urging museums to trust visitors to think, even if they refuse to leave at closing time.

East and Southeast Asia Rekdal's Oslo exhibition displayed Japanese swords together with the love poems written about them, in a section on magical weapons. Rekdal contrasts their aesthetic beauty with the down-to-earth use of a Japanese sword as a tool of execution, a connection he says museums almost always avoid.

Museum of Cultural History, University of Oslo
The Bomb and the City: Presentations of War in German City MuseumsSusanne Hagemannp. 131

Hagemann asks how German city museums display the undetonated bomb, a common object in local exhibitions on the Second World War. Drawing on more than forty history exhibitions she documented for a research project on 1933 to 1945, she distinguishes three ways of presenting it: documentation, with plain labels and the bomb on a plinth; mise en scène, which stages it among ruins, sirens or reconstructed shelters to provoke emotion; and ensemble, which combines the bomb with other objects in a deliberately open or fragmented arrangement. Her examples come from Halle, Weimar, Bremen, Münster, Rostock, Bielefeld, Hamburg and Siegburg. She argues that the bomb becomes either a sacred relic of German civilian suffering or a piece of evidence against the Allies, depending on the text and setting around it. The chapter concludes that war belongs in city museums because it is part of local memory and family biography, but that curators must take a clear position rather than leave visitors with an emotional but empty display.

City Museum Halle (Saale)City Museum Weimar (Bertuchhaus)Focke Museum BremenCity Museum MünsterMuseum Kröpeliner Tor RostockBielefeld Historical MuseumMuseum for Hamburg HistoryCity Museum Siegburg
The Trauma Of War And The Limits Of Mediap. 143
War in Context: Let the Artifacts SpeakRobert M. Ehrenreich, Jane Klingerp. 145

Ehrenreich and Klinger argue that personal objects, properly conserved and set within a narrative, can restore individual humanity to Holocaust victims whose numbers are incomprehensible. They open with the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum's own dilemmas about depicting atrocity without glorifying it or victimising people a second time. Three case studies follow. Rings and jewellery found about ten metres from shooting pits in Busk, Ukraine, are read as deliberate acts of defiance by people who knew they were about to die. A family's photographs, carried from Łacko into hiding and then damaged by later adhesives, show how conservators can strip modern materials while keeping the wartime damage intact. A piece of mica from the Theresienstadt mica factory, which Emma Jonas carried for sixteen years after liberation, is set beside her poems about forced labour. Their conclusion is that such artifacts, with contextual narrative, counter the glorification of war found in displays of weapons and machines.

United States Holocaust Memorial Museum
War Museums and PhotographyAlexandra Bounia, Theopisti Stylianou-Lambertp. 155

Bounia and Stylianou-Lambert examine how photographs work in five war museums in Cyprus, two on the Greek Cypriot side and three in the north. They argue that museums and photographs both pass as objective records, although both involve choices about what to include and exclude. The authors sort the images into documentary proof, portraits of heroes and martyrs, and celebrations of military operations, citing the framed photograph of a murdered Turkish Cypriot woman and her children at the Museum of Barbarism. They then show how captions and panels change meaning: the Struggle Museum in the south and the National Struggle Museum in the north both display the same photograph of a body in a Nicosia street, yet present it as the work of opposite enemies. Using Nora's distinction between memory and history, they conclude that these museums build selective, emotional collective memory, and that an image's meaning depends on captions and on what viewers already know, so the proverb one photo, a thousand words should prompt the question whose thousand words?

Struggle Museum (Nicosia, south)Museum of Barbarism (north Nicosia)National Struggle Museum (north Nicosia)Museum of Peace and Freedom (northern Cyprus)Museum of Commando Fighters of CyprusImperial War Museum North
The Monument is Invisible, the Sign Visible. Monuments in New PerspectivesWerner Fenzp. 173

Fenz surveys recent memorial projects in Styria and Graz that replace the static monument with open, process-based or critical forms. Starting from the title's idea of an invisible monument, he asks whether bodies carved in stone and bronze can still stand for Nazi atrocities after decades of images. He then examines four projects. Helmut and Johanna Kandl's Wächterhaus at a former subcamp of Mauthausen turns a watch house into a guardhouse, with illuminated lettering and updated human-rights information. Jochen Gerz's work on the former Gauleiter Uiberreither runs through a regional newspaper, with readers' choices and parliamentarians' texts. Gerz's sinking lead pillar in Harburg and the flags at the Feliferhof shooting range tie memory to continuing presence and practice. Nasan Tur's Unknown Knight, a bronze figure set in the Graz armoury, questions the myth of the enemy from the South-East. Fenz concludes that memory politics must start from the present, though he finds Tur's project not radical enough.

Landeszeughaus (Provincial Armoury), Graz
Military History, War Museums And National Identityp. 183
Politics of Memory and History in the Museum – The New “Museum of the History of the Great Patriotic War” in Minsk/BelarusKristiane Janekep. 185

Janeke uses the planned new Museum of the History of the Great Patriotic War in Minsk to ask whether war belongs in museums, and what a museum in post-Soviet Belarus can do under a tight political frame. Janeke first sets out Belarus's wartime losses, the destruction of its Jewish population, and how the Soviet narrative of the Great Patriotic War, now used by Lukashenko's government as a founding myth, left out local, national and Jewish experiences. Janeke then compares the existing exhibition with the new concept in four parts: the prologue, occupation and extermination, the partisan movement, and memory of war. Janeke’s criticisms include the absence of introductory texts, the neglect of the Holocaust, and an idealised partisan myth. Janeke also examines the architecture, which copies the Moscow museum, and the education methods, guided tours and dioramas. Janeke concludes that the museum could still become a place of critical discussion through its collection, multilingual information and online access, and she urges European museums to engage with their Belarusian colleagues.

Belarusian State Museum of the History of the Great Patriotic War (Minsk)
Framing the Military-Nation: New War Museums and Changing Representational Practices in Turkey since 2002Patrizia Kernp. 203

Kern examines the wave of new war museums in Turkey since 2002, each devoted to a foundation battle and each using dioramas and 360-degree panoramas instead of the older display of weapons and veterans' belongings. Kern starts with the Atatürk and Independence War Museum in Ankara, opened in 2002 within the Anıtkabir complex, whose Gallipoli and Independence War dioramas were scripted by Turgut Özakman and painted in Moscow under rules requiring Atatürk to appear only in authentic photographs. Kern reads the museum against the 2001 financial crisis, EU pressure and the myth of the 'military-nation'. Kern then turns to two Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality projects: the Miniatürk Panorama Victory Museum, which replaces Atatürk's leadership with a populist, religious and economic nation, and the 1453 Panorama Museum, which presents the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople as a peaceful, tolerant founding moment. Kern concludes that these museums are contested sites in which conservative interests adapt the nationalist founding myth while still reiterating national ideology, and that the panorama has become the standard form for representing war in Turkish museums.

Atatürk and Independence War MuseumMiniatürk Panorama Victory Museum1453 Panorama Museum
Contributorsp. 219
Naquin, Susan (2004). “The Forbidden City Goes Abroad: Qing History and the Foreign Exhibitions of the Palace Museum, 1974–2004”. T’oung Pao, 90 (2004).Asia: central1 chapter overview

Overview

Naquin asks how the Beijing Palace Museum presented itself abroad through the thirty-three exhibitions it sent overseas between 1974 and 2004. Naquin’s argument is that the shows settled on one identity, the Qing court and its palace in the Forbidden City, built from a repeated set of objects, photographs and catalogues. Naquin follows the sequence of exhibitions and their catalogues, sets them against the Taipei, Shanghai and Shenyang museums, and relates them to changing Qing historiography. The article ends by asking whether the museum should keep exporting these packages.

East and Southeast Asia in this work central

East Asia is the central subject of the article. Most of the thirty-three exhibitions went to East Asian venues: the text counts seven shows to Japan and four to Hong Kong, with shows in Macao and Taiwan and a 1992 exhibition in Seoul. Naquin treats the 1974 Tokyo show at the Mitsukoshi department stores and the 1981 Hong Kong show 'Treasures from the Imperial Palace' as the start of the formula, and she sets the Beijing museum against the National Palace Museum in Taipei and the Shanghai Museum as its rivals.

Southeast Asia appears once: the Shenyang Palace Museum's 1989 'Imperial Life in the Qing Dynasty' show in Singapore, which Naquin describes as drawn from the same kinds of court objects as the Beijing shows. Japan and Korea are said to have treated the Qing material as part of 'a vaguely shared East Asian artistic past' rather than as an ongoing exchange.

The article does not discuss the history of imperial objects collected abroad, which Naquin sets aside as beyond its scope, nor restitution, war memory or the heritage policy of the host countries.
