Theoretical approach of this work
The Forbidden City Goes Abroad: Qing History and the Foreign Exhibitions of the Palace Museum, 1974-2004p. 341Asia: chiefly

Naquin asks how the Beijing Palace Museum, the institution housed in the Forbidden City, presented itself to foreign audiences through the 33 exhibitions it sent abroad between 1974 and 2004. Naquin’s argument is that the shows gradually settled on one identity: the custodian of the Qing court and its palace. Naquin traces the sequence from a 1974 department-store show in Japan through the 1981 Hong Kong show, the 1985 Berlin and Vienna exhibition, the 1996-97 Paris exhibition and the 2000-02 Bowers show in California, and she shows how the same set pieces recur: thrones, court robes, armor, clocks, chime-stones and court paintings. The argument then turns to the catalogues, which she treats as the lasting record of each show and as a way of building the palace's aura for readers who could not visit. She places the shows against the National Palace Museum in Taipei, the Shanghai Museum and the Shenyang palace collection, and the changing historiography of the Qing. The essay ends by asking whether the Palace Museum should keep repeating these packages, turn to technological exchange with Europe, or separate the museum from the palace.

East and Southeast Asia Most of the shows went to East Asia: seven to Japan, four to Hong Kong, shows in Macao and Taiwan, and a 1992 exhibition in Seoul. The essay describes the 1974 Tokyo show at the Mitsukoshi stores and the 1981 Hong Kong Treasures of Imperial Palace show as the start of the formula, and it treats Taipei's National Palace Museum as the Beijing museum's rival, with the 2003 Kaohsiung and Taipei shows as an unusual visit to Taiwan. The Shenyang Palace Museum's 1989 Singapore show is the only Southeast Asian case.

Referencesp. 387
Outka, Elizabeth (2009). Consuming Traditions: Modernity, Modernism, and the Commodified Authentic. New York: Oxford University Press.Asia: slight6 chapter overviews

Overview

Elizabeth Outka’s Consuming Traditions (2009) argues that in Britain between the 1880s and 1922, marketers and writers sold goods, homes, towns and shopping as embodiments of noncommercial values: rural England, originality and aesthetic purity. Outka calls this the “commodified authentic” and holds that its commercial origin was central to its appeal, so that the paradox of commerce and authenticity fed the making of British modernism. The book is organised in an introduction, two parts (the countryside and the city) with chapters on model towns, Forster’s Howards End and the Ideal Home Exhibition, Selfridges, and Woolf’s window gazing, and a conclusion on Lawrence, Joyce and Woolf.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia figure only slightly. The one substantive passage is in chapter 4, “The Vanishing Act of Commercialism: Selfridges, Modernity, and the Purified Marketplace.” Outka reads Selfridges’ 1909 article-advertisements in the Times, which said its buyers went “off the high road of commerce” to villages in Japan, Germany and Britain, and which quoted the personality of a “Japanese craftsman” as the mark of distinction. She treats this as an exotic-other version of the cottage-industry pitch, in which the Japanese craftsman stands for a past both primitive and authentic.

The only other Asian reference in the chapter is a list of live craft demonstrations on the store floors, where a Turkish craftsman weaves “Oriental rugs” beside Flemish lace makers and a Scottish crofter. Outka does not discuss these as Asian production or as Asian people; they are part of the store’s staging of craftsmanship.

Nothing is said about Asian objects in British or other Western museums, colonial collecting, museums in Asia, Asian heritage policy, Asian visitors, curators or scholars, or restitution. The Japanese craftsman appears only as an advertising image, not as a producer or a collection that Outka studies. India appears only in passing, as the setting for some of Lutyens’s houses (line 3235), which is outside this question.

Japan

11. Introduction: Selling Authenticityp. 3

Outka's introduction sets out the book's central concept, the 'commodified authentic', which describes goods and places sold as embodiments of noncommercial values such as rural England, originality and aesthetic purity, while their commercial origin is central to their appeal. The author argues that critics who unmask such marketing as fraud miss its attraction and its part in shaping British modernism. Three forms are introduced: commodified nostalgia, seen in model towns, country-style homes and the Ideal Home Exhibition; the originary authentic, the prototype and the limited edition; and commercial aesthetic refinement, exemplified by the Selfridges department store. Outka argues that these forms sustained paradoxes between past and present, and between exclusivity and mass access, which fed the modernist project. The introduction previews the book's two parts, on the countryside and on the city, with chapters on Shaw, Forster, Selfridges, Woolf and the later modernists. It ends by arguing that the same paradox still drives heritage and lifestyle marketing.

Part I: Commodified Nostalgia And The Country Aestheticp. 23
22. The Past Is a Present Country: Model Towns and Commercial Utopiasp. 25

This chapter examines the model industrial communities of Bournville, Port Sunlight and Letchworth, and Ebenezer Howard's Garden City plan, as early instances of what Outka calls the commodified authentic: an invented English countryside built with industrial profit and then sold to buyers. Outka argues that these towns joined nostalgic village imagery to modern commerce, so that a place's authenticity could be manufactured, reproduced and marketed. Cadbury's half-timbered village, its gardens and its paternalist welfare are set beside the Cadbury's Cocoa advertisements that sold the town's purity through the product, and Lever's Port Sunlight, with its reconstructed Thornton Hough and Sunlight Soap copy, shows the same pattern. Letchworth's promotional literature turns the Garden City itself into a commodity. Bernard Shaw's John Bull's Other Island and Major Barbara close the chapter, read as critiques of these schemes, with Major Barbara's divided ending taken as a paradox about paternalism. Outka's closing point is that the towns' real benefits were inseparable from their marketing.

Selly Manor
33. Buying Time: E. M. Forster and the Neo-nostalgic Homep. 68

This chapter uses E. M. Forster's Howards End (1910) as the starting point for what Outka calls neo-nostalgic homes: houses and interiors that combine a rural past with commerce, so that time itself can be bought. Outka sets the cheap London flat of Leonard Bast and the Wilcoxes' Ducie Street home against the failed purchase of a country house at Oniton, then reads Miss Avery's refurnished Howards End as a model of temporal density that Forster ultimately sustains. The chapter then turns to the Domestic Revival, drawing on Hermann Muthesius's account of English building and on Edwin Lutyens's houses, which were artificially weathered and mixed period features for industrial clients, and on the magazine Country Life. Its main case is the Daily Mail Ideal Home Exhibition, whose Tudor village replica, period gardens and cottage-industry stalls offered a democratized country home to the middle class. Outka concludes that Forster both exposes and indulges the wish to purify the home of commerce.

Daily Mail Ideal Home Exhibition
Part Ii: Urban Authenticitiesp. 97
44. The Vanishing Act of Commercialism: Selfridges, Modernity, and the Purified Marketplacep. 99

This chapter examines Selfridges, the department store that opened on Oxford Street in London in 1909, as the fullest urban version of the commodified authentic. Outka sets Henry James's story The Great Good Place, in which a weary writer buys an aesthetic retreat, against H. G. Wells's Tono-Bungay, whose narrator exposes advertising as trickery; James's retreat is read as the model Selfridges copied and Wells as the critic who unmasks it. The evidence is the store's open, classical building, its 1909 newspaper campaign in the Times and the Daily Mail, its staff community and domestic rooms with silver keys, and its Old-time Industry demonstrations of craftsmen at work. Outka argues that the store offered middle-class shoppers the exclusivity of Bond Street, sold by floor from the bargain basement up to the roof garden, while openly admitting that its authenticity was manufactured. The chapter closes by describing Selfridges as offering both the authenticity and the critique that exposes it, which Outka calls a vertical monopoly.

East and Southeast Asia Selfridges' 1909 article-advertisements in the Times claimed its buyers scoured remote villages in Japan, Germany and Britain for handmade goods, and quoted a Japanese craftsman's personality as the mark of distinction. Outka reads this as an exotic-other version of the cottage-industry pitch, set beside the Turkish rug weaver and other craftsmen demonstrated on the store's floors.

55. “Lustrous behind Glass”: Woolf, Window Shopping, and Authentic Displayp. 128

This chapter moves from the department store to the individual shopper's gaze, using Virginia Woolf's Night and Day (1919), set in 1910, and the window displays of London shops around the First World War. Outka distinguishes two kinds of authentic display: the tableau of the authentic dead, such as the relic room in the Hilbery house where a poet's pen, spectacles and slippers are lit as if sacred, and the newer store window, which hides its prices and sells a mood. The chapter follows Ralph Denham's window gazing in the Strand, where Katharine Hilbery seems to materialize as a commodity behind glass, and sets this beside the Selfridges window designs of display men such as Arthur Fraser and Edward Goldsman. Outka then reads Woolf's own dress-buying letter and the blue-dress scene for the same paradox. The final section argues that wartime windows, which stayed full while the rest of London emptied, offered a fantasy of prewar civilization, and that window shopping is a performance of authenticity the viewer knows to be constructed.

Haworth Parsonage
66. Conclusion: Modernist Excursionsp. 155

Outka closes by arguing that the commodified authentic grew over the twentieth century from a marketing technique into a whole marketing climate, and that it helps explain modernism's contradictory pulls toward tradition and novelty and toward commerce and an outside of commerce. Three scenes serve as excursions. In Lawrence's Women in Love, Ursula and Birkin buy an old wooden chair at a jumble market and then disown it, so that modernism becomes restless vacillation. In Joyce's Ulysses, the Ithaca chapter turns the Plumtree's Potted Meat advertisement and a country-house fantasy into a parody that Bloom both mocks and half believes. In Woolf's To the Lighthouse, Lily Briscoe gazes through the window at Mrs Ramsay, a figure of untouchable domestic authenticity. The final pages note that Bournville, Selfridges and the Ideal Home Exhibition still thrive, and define authenticity by personal connection rather than genuineness. The book ends by urging suspicion and attraction together.

Paver, Chloe E. M. (2018). Exhibiting the Nazi Past: Museum Objects Between the Material and the Immaterial. Cham: Palgrave Macmillan.Asia: slight6 chapter overviews

Overview

Paver's book examines how German and Austrian history exhibitions about 1933 to 1945 and their aftermath use material objects. It draws on about 130 exhibitions seen first-hand, excluding art shows, and treats Jewish museums as part of the field. Its main argument is that these exhibitions have made object display routine and use everyday objects, including broken, hidden, stored and recycled ones, to convey a critical, morally framed account of Nazi persecution and of post-war memory. The book builds a conceptual framework of the object as signifier, as conduit for experience and as life cycle, then moves through chronological chapters on 1933 to 1945, 1945 and post-war afterlives, and closes with a conclusion that qualifies the liberal narrative and calls for study of a second democratic generation of exhibitions.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia are almost absent from this book. The full text names China once, in a passing remark in chapter 5 about a modern Hanukkah lamp made in China from red plastic-coated wire, shown in the Fürth Jewish museum, and it names no other Asian country, collection, museum or person. The scope is German and Austrian history exhibitions and their post-war afterlives, and the only comparisons drawn are within Europe.

Contents

Theoretical approach of this work
AcknowledgementsPDF p. 6
ContentsPDF p. 8
List of FiguresPDF p. 10
1Chapter 1 Introductionp. 1

Paver asks why museum objects matter in history exhibitions about 1933 to 1945, a field often thought to rest on documents, testimony and digital media. Opening with anniversary object miscellanies at Hohenems and a Mauthausen visitor centre module, the introduction argues that German and Austrian exhibition-makers already reflect routinely on objects. It answers three objections: that documentation centres are the new norm, that digital display is the cutting edge, and that objects seem trivial beside mass death. Paver shows the field is polarised between object-based museums and object-free documentation centres, some of which have begun collecting objects. Germany's two national history museums report 800,000 and 900,000 objects, though only a fraction relate to the Nazi period. Much of the chapter explains the exhibitionary routine: anniversaries, national, regional and local funding, and institutions staging shows about their own Nazi-era pasts. The study draws on about 130 exhibitions seen first-hand, excluding art shows, and treats Jewish museums as part of the field. It closes by previewing its chronological chapters, in which objects change meaning over time.

Dokumentation ObersalzbergDeutsches Historisches MuseumHaus der GeschichteGedenkstätte Mauthausen
2Chapter 2 Between the Material and the Immaterialp. 24

Paver builds the conceptual framework for the book's case studies, working from a single object: shards of a crystal vase, displayed in 2012 at the Dokumentationszentrum Reichsparteitagsgelände in a Nuremberg exhibition on Aryanization and the November 1938 pogrom. The chapter reads the shards through three models drawn from scholarship: the object as signifier, using the rhetorical figures of synecdoche, metonymy and metaphor; the object as a conduit for experience, emotion and mentality; and the object's life cycle, including the 'rubbish' phase described by Thompson. Paver uses examples from Hohenems, where donated keys raise questions about Aryanization, and from Munich and Buchenwald, where sparse collections are displayed to make absence visible. Paver then reviews work on wartime experience, memory and emotion, which has rarely addressed objects. Confino's argument that post-war German memory must be read against what Germans experienced before 1945 provides a frame. The chapter argues that museums must be read for how they fix an object's meaning through captions, and that post-war object afterlives are central. It closes by pointing forward to chapter 5 and to the mutability of objects.

Dokumentationszentrum ReichsparteitagsgeländeJüdisches Museum HohenemsJüdisches Museum MünchenJüdisches Museum BerlinGedenkstätte Bergen-BelsenGedenkstätte BuchenwaldGedenkstätte und Museum SachsenhausenMAK Vienna
3Chapter 3 Material Experiences, 1933–45p. 64

Paver asks which objects can show the emotions and mentalities of 1933 to 1945 and surveys how German and Austrian exhibitions handle belonging, perpetrators, camps and wartime suffering. The chapter opens with Jewish participation in Heimat culture, such as Tracht, Alpine tourism and local brands, and with the Schnaittach museum, whose Heimatmuseum moved into Jewish buildings and was built on acquisitions by a non-Jewish director who profited from Jewish emigration. Home-made objects, photograph albums and typed remarks are shown to indicate complicity, though they can mislead, as a honey centrifuge inscribed with 'Sieg Heil' shows. Paver then examines how displays at Buchenwald and Ravensbrück present degraded finds and prisoners' creative work, and how Hitler busts and swastikas are deflated by being laid down, pixelated or left packed. The last sections cover wartime suffering at museums in Dresden, Berlin and Hamburg and at Oberammergau, where majority suffering is framed by German responsibility. The chapter concludes that exhibitions rarely draw a forgiving arc from experience to memory.

Jüdisches Museum SchnaittachJüdisches Museum HohenemsGedenkstätte BuchenwaldMahn- und Gedenkstätte RavensbrückDeutsches Historisches MuseumMilitärhistorisches Museum der BundeswehrDeutsch-Russisches MuseumMahnmal St Nikolai
4Chapter 4 Material Collapse, 1945p. 142

This chapter asks how German and Austrian museums use material objects to show the end of Nazi rule in 1945, a date that exhibitions handle with care because 'disengagement from war' was uneven. Paver draws mainly on German and Austrian exhibitions, opening with the Deutsches Historisches Museum's 1945 show, whose objects, such as a smashed pocket watch and a dated lily of the valley, encode unfinished time. The central section argues that objects effaced, buried or recycled in 1945 are displayed to suggest that Germans and Austrians changed their symbols more easily than their minds. Examples include a Hitler portrait scratched out in Cologne, a dyed police uniform and a buried Hitler head at Nuremberg. Paver notes that these readings are often left implicit. The final section turns to Jewish displaced persons, using a belt and a dress from the Munich Jewish Museum to show survivors' continuing relationship with camp belongings. The chapter concludes that exhibitions present 1945 less as a liberation than as a time of counting costs.

Deutsches Historisches MuseumKölnisches StadtmuseumDokumentationszentrum ReichsparteitagsgeländeJüdisches Museum MünchenJüdisches Museum BerlinJüdisches Museum FürthJüdisches Museum WienDeutsch-Russisches Museum
5Chapter 5 Material After-Lives Between the Attic and the Archivep. 171

This chapter follows Nazi-era and Jewish objects after 1945, asking how they were stored, hidden, reused or returned, and how museums now display those afterlives. Paver argues that German and Austrian history exhibitions present the post-war decades as a period of passive forgetting, and they show this by keeping objects in the attics, boxes and bags where they were stored. Early sections look at family donations, such as Nazi badges kept in a chocolate box in Cologne, and show how captions use words like 'erst' ('not until') and 'bis' ('until') to imply a delayed reckoning. The second half turns to Jewish property left in non-Jewish hands, drawing on the Haigerloch synagogue museum, the Jüdisches Museum Hohenems, the travelling 'Legalisierter Raub' exhibition and the Jüdisches Museum München. Paver concludes that the museum is now itself part of each object's life cycle, and that exhibitions leave the critical reading to visitors.

6Chapter 6 Conclusionp. 274

The conclusion gathers the book's argument that German and Austrian history exhibitions use everyday objects to communicate a critical account of the post-war years, and it qualifies that claim. Paver notes that not every museum follows this liberal narrative: the Celle documentation centre plan was abandoned in 2012, and the amateur Celler Garnison-Museum shows Wehrmacht objects with no political context. At the Polizeimuseum Niedersachsen in Nienburg, a dated permanent display sits beside a sharper temporary police exhibition, and a donated uniform of a policeman who died in Soviet internment is treated sympathetically. Paver argues that exhibitions remain committed to moral framing rather than to material culture for its own sake, as in 'Glanz und Grauen' and 'Volk – Heimat – Dorf'. The final pages call for research on a second democratic generation of exhibitions, such as the Jüdisches Museum Berlin and the Cologne NS-Dokumentationszentrum, both due to open in 2019.

Pearce, Susan M. (1992). Museums, Objects, and Collections: A Cultural Study. Leicester: Leicester University Press.Asia: slight13 chapter overviews

Overview

Susan Pearce's Museums, Objects and Collections (1992) is a curator's theoretical study of the museum as a cultural institution. It argues that collections and objects should stay at the centre of museum work and that theory and practice cannot be separated, since every choice of object for display is both. It treats the museum as a modern European institution, traces its origins in Renaissance cabinets and nineteenth-century classification, and then reviews how objects acquire meaning: through the psychology of collecting, function, structure, history, lived experience, power and the market. It ends by proposing that curators work as persuasive interpreters within a critical community. The book is organised as twelve chapters with front and back matter, including an appendix of models for object study. Its examples are mainly British, with some from Scandinavia and North America.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia receive very little attention, and only one passage takes an Asian display as its subject. In Chapter 11 (Problems of Power), Pearce reads the Royal Academy catalogue of The Genius of China (1973-4). Its claim to show Chinese culture through documented, controlled-excavation material is an authoritative stance, the exhibition stops at Marco Polo's arrival in the fourteenth century, and its 'ancient' China and 'masterpieces' carry Western judgements of high civilisation. The same chapter mentions a Japanese insurance company's purchase of a Van Gogh in 1987, which concerns the art market rather than Asian material, and refers to 'Europe and parts of Asia' as the magic circle of high civilisation.

Asian material appears elsewhere only as isolated detail. Freud's collection in Vienna and London included Chinese antiquities and figurines (Chapter 4, lines 3402 and 3427). A Japanese-sword collector is mentioned in passing (Chapter 3, line 2451). A connoisseur who buys Chinese ceramics appears in Chapter 6 (line 5725), and the Japanese netsuke at Blackpool are cited in a Lancashire Museums leaflet in Chapter 9 (line 8660). Chapter 9 also quotes the painter Remington's list of enemies, which includes 'Chinamen' (line 8574).

The introduction cites Clunas (1991, Superfluous Things, on early modern China), Yamaguchi (1991, on the poetics of exhibition in Japanese culture) and Goswamy (1991, on exhibiting Indian art) as evidence that material has been assembled and displayed in other parts of the world, but none of these is discussed. No Southeast Asian place is named. Museums in Asia, Asian states' heritage policy, colonial collecting from Asia, restitution claims and Asian visitors or curators are all absent. The book's concern is European and North American museums.

Prefacep. 12

Pearce's preface argues that collections and objects should stay at the heart of museum work, and that theory and practice are inseparable, since choosing an object for display involves both. The book is aimed at readers inside and outside museums who value museums in European culture. It admits a bias towards human history, drawn from the author's experience, and hopes natural history museums will develop the significance of scientific collections. The preface closes with thanks to colleagues and illustrators.

11. Museums, Objects and Collectionsp. 14

Pearce's introduction sets out the framework for the book, which treats museums, their objects and the collections that brought those objects together as a single 'cultural triangle'. Pearce argues that the museum is a modern European institution, which took shape in Renaissance Italy and spread with European expansion, and that it served the meta-narratives of modernity: science, the study of great men, the market in goods and the idea of progress. Henry Cole's 1857 description of working families visiting what became the Victoria and Albert Museum shows the educational and social purpose the Victorian museum claimed. The chapter then defines 'object', 'thing', 'specimen', 'artefact' and 'goods', using the Apollo 17 moon rock displayed at the National Air and Space Museum to show that selection and display turn a natural item into material culture. Every museum collection is formed twice, first by a collector and then by a museum that accepts it. The chapter ends by placing the book between museum theory and practice and by outlining the chapters that follow.

Pitt Rivers collection, OxfordNational Air and Space MuseumVictoria and Albert Museum
22. Objects Inside and Outside Museumsp. 34

Pearce's second chapter asks what objects are and why they matter in social life. Objects are lumps of the material world whose cultural value comes from selection, and Western thought has long treated material culture as subordinate to mind, a dualism Pearce traces back to Plato and Descartes. Objects also take part in social reproduction, framing our homes and identities in ways that words cannot match. The main case is a broadsword carried by Alistair Macdonald of Keppoch at Culloden in 1746, now in the National Museums of Scotland. Using Saussurean and Barthesian semiotics, Pearce shows the sword as a sign that stays tied to the battle and as a symbol open to new meanings, from the celebrations that followed Culloden to Victorian romance. A stuffed magpie then makes the same point for natural history. The chapter ends by considering how objects are possessed and valued, and how museums turn things into durables.

National Museums of ScotlandLeicestershire Museum Service
33. Collecting: Body and Soulp. 63

Pearce's third chapter asks why people collect, treating collecting as a psychological and social activity rather than a museum one. Every collection rests on selection, which gives each object a real link to its source and a metaphorical meaning as an image of the whole. Drawing on Ellen's cognitive model, Pearce shows how collectors animate objects and treat them as extensions of themselves, and links this to play, competition, rarity and the wish to dominate. Definitions by Durost, Alsop and Belk are weighed, and collecting is separated from accumulating and hoarding. The examples include the Pinto Collection of treen in Birmingham City Museum, Daniel Lambert's belongings at Newarke Houses Museum in Leicester, and a preserved two-headed calf that drew local crowds. The chapter ends with the collector's wish for immortality, which donations and memorial galleries answer.

Birmingham City Museum (Pinto Collection)Newarke Houses Museum, LeicesterCarnegie Museum, Melton MowbrayMouse CottageFire Museum
44. Collecting: Shaping the Worldp. 109

Pearce's fourth chapter sorts collecting into three modes: souvenirs, fetishistic collecting and systematics. Souvenirs, such as trophies and personal memorabilia, carry the past into the present but stay private, and Pearce argues that they serve a romantic view of the self. Fetish collections, illustrated by Freud's antiquities and Joseph Mayer's Liverpool collection, are built from samples that express a possessive self, and they are seldom displayed because they are cut off from social relations. Systematic collecting, classically Pitt Rivers's typological arrangements, selects examples to stand for a class and invites the viewer into a public argument, which is why museums favour it. Using Hegel's idea of objectification, as Miller develops it, Pearce treats the three modes as poles between which real collections move. The chapter also looks at present-day collectables, shown at Walsall and Stevenage, and closes by noting that one object can be a souvenir for one person and a fetish for another.

Pitt Rivers MuseumExeter City MuseumEgyptian Museum, Liverpool (Joseph Mayer)Walsall MuseumStevenage Museum
55. Museums: the Intellectual Rationalep. 138

Pearce's fifth chapter traces how museums became public institutions with an intellectual rationale. Their origins lie in Renaissance princely and private cabinets of curiosities, where objects were arranged to mirror the order of the universe, as in the Ashmolean and Tradescant collections. From the eighteenth century, classificatory schemes such as Neikelius's took over, and royal collections such as the Louvre, the Belvedere and the Hermitage were opened to the public, with pictures hung as a history of art. Natural history acquired its rationale through Linnaean classification, and archaeology through the Three Age System, while Pitt Rivers gave material culture an evolutionary frame. The chapter then examines the neo-Classical building boom, glass-case technology, and the twentieth-century turn to context and community, illustrated by Hazelius's Skansen and Boas's North West Coast Hall. It ends by noting that the social background of collectors and curators shapes the bias of every museum collection.

Ashmolean MuseumBritish MuseumNatural History Museum, South KensingtonLouvreHermitageSkansen (Nordiska Museet)American Museum of Natural HistoryDanish National Museum
66. Making Museum Meaningsp. 180

Pearce's sixth chapter asks how curators make meanings from the collections they inherit. Museum material arrives as an archive shaped by disciplines, chance and patchy documentation, so each object carries several names: a production name, a daily-life name and a collection name. Classification proceeds by binary yes-or-no questions, and the Linnaean, Bronze Age and Welsh Folk Museum schemes differ in how far they mix form with function. Research supplies the cultural content that gives an object meaning, through technical analysis, stylistic study and object biographies, and silver candlesticks serve as the main example. Collection management policies on acquisition and disposal then reinforce the existing system. The chapter closes with exhibitions, which Pearce treats as a form in their own right: their plans, depth and entropy decide whether visitors see knowledge as settled or as open to question, as the two London galleries of the Natural History Museum show.

Natural History Museum, LondonWelsh Folk MuseumRoyal Ontario Museum
77. Meaning as Functionp. 215

Pearce's seventh chapter assesses functionalism, the view that objects are shaped by a society's need to survive and adapt. The approach runs from Malinowski and Radcliffe-Brown to the systems theory of the 1960s and 1970s, and Pearce shows how exhibitions usually take for granted a chain running from environment to strategy, technology and social institution. Two cases illustrate this: a display of the Inuit kayak, shown at Exeter City Museum in 1975, and a George Medal and Bar sold at Christie's in 1990, which Pearce reads as a means of stabilising social roles. Factor analysis of Bronze Age burials and of school uniforms shows function at work, and a systems model of late Roman and post-Roman Somerset is set out as an exhibition brief. The chapter criticises functionalism for treating artefacts as passive and for explaining change poorly, and concludes that material culture both shapes and reflects social activity.

Exeter City Museum
88. Meaning as Structurep. 244

Pearce introduces structuralism and semiotics as a way of reading objects as communication systems. Through worked examples he shows how sets and binary oppositions in clothing, a terraced house, a teapot and a South Devon cattle herd can be plotted into structures, and how Leach's and Miller's analyses reveal the same patterns in material culture. The main museum case is the Abbey Barn display at Glastonbury, organized around the life of a farm labourer as a sequence of paired themes. Pearce then sets out objections: structuralist readings are subjective, since two groups given identical willow-pattern plates produced different binary sets in a 1990 seminar; they reduce objects to form and strip out their particular value; and they cannot explain change. Pearce concludes that structuralism is a useful analytical technique and a reminder that material culture is a communication system in its own right, but that it is ahistorical, and that its implications for museums, the principal holders of material culture, are profound.

Somerset County Museum Service (Abbey Barn, Glastonbury)
99. Meaning in Historyp. 278

Pearce asks how museum objects shape the way we understand the past, and sets out the traditional relation between objects and historical narrative. Pearce traces how antiquarian and Romantic collectors, such as Scott at Abbotsford and Lenoir and du Sommerard in Paris, valued old objects for their age, and how academic historians from Briggs to Thompson have largely treated material goods as illustration rather than cause. From this he distinguishes four museum modes of producing meaning from the past: relics, art and treasure, illustrated narrative, and reconstruction. Each has concrete cases: the Crown Jewels, the Thomas Hardy Collection at Dorset County Museum, the 1991 West as America exhibition at the National Museum of American Art, the Armada 1588-1988 exhibition at the National Maritime Museum, and open-air sites such as Beamish and Greenfield Village. Pearce is critical of the sentimental and commercial side of reconstruction, and of the way Hardy's relics were shaped to fit a myth of the novelist. Pearce concludes that each mode asks the visitor to believe, learn, admire or understand, and that objects are always lifted out of experience.

Dorset County Museum (Thomas Hardy Collection)National Museum of American ArtNational Maritime MuseumTower of London Jewel HouseMusee de ClunyMusee des Monuments FrancaisImperial War MuseumGreenfield Village
1010. Objects in Actionp. 303

Pearce turns from what objects mean to how individuals experience them, and how that experience changes both people and objects. Pearce draws on phenomenology (Husserl, Hegel, Iser), American behaviourist studies of material culture, and the Annales historians, especially Braudel. Pearce’s model sets a fashion-conscious young woman and the clothes of the late 1980s in a cycle of perception and learning, and a viewer and a pair of Chelsea porcelain tureens in the Fitzwilliam Museum in the same kind of interaction. Gravestones studied by Ludwig show how material evidence can revise the written record of New England piety. Pearce then joins this to Giddens's structuration and Braudel's three time-scales of event, conjuncture and long-term structure, illustrating the argument with a Limoges reliquary of about 1200 in the Burrell Collection, Glasgow, whose meaning accumulated through its commission, owners and exhibitions. The chapter ends with two doubts: the model needs real individuals with genuine choices, and it assumes that object meanings are stable rather than radically polysemic. Pearce asks whether such meaning rests on solid ground or shifting sand.

Burrell Collection, Glasgow MuseumsFitzwilliam Museum, CambridgeWalsall Museum
1111. Problems of Powerp. 329

Pearce asks what lies beneath the meanings museums create, and turns to Marxist, Foucauldian and post-structuralist critiques of power and ideology. Museums, on this view, legitimate the capitalist order, knowledge is a form of power, and meaning is groundless. He applies these ideas to museum practice: the art market and the consecrating power of collections, the authentication of fakes, paintings accepted in lieu of tax, and grant funding; collection policies that favour 'good stuff'; and exhibitions. The main cases are The Spirit Sings at the Glenbow Museum in Calgary (1988), sponsored by Shell and opposed by the Lubicon Cree; the Evolution gallery at the Royal Scottish Museum, which presents evolution as self-evident; and the Royal Academy's Age of Chivalry (1987-8) and Egon Schiele (1990) shows. Posters from several British museums are read as reinforcing a romantic, noble-warrior view of the past. Pearce finds the critique powerful but concludes that it drains meaning away, and that curators need conceptual justifications for their work.

East and Southeast Asia The chapter's only passage on East Asia concerns the catalogue of The Genius of China, shown at the Royal Academy in 1973-4. Pearce reads its claim to present Chinese culture through documented, controlled-excavation material as an authoritative stance, notes that the exhibition ends at Marco Polo's arrival in the fourteenth century, and argues that its description of China as 'ancient' and its 'masterpieces' carry Western judgements of high civilization.

Glenbow Museum, CalgaryRoyal Scottish Museum, EdinburghRoyal Academy, LondonMuseum of LondonGeffrye Museum, LondonVictoria and Albert Museum
1212. Projects and Prospectsp. 369

Pearce takes stock of the book and proposes a way forward for curators. Pearce argues that objects are both real things with a concrete link to their contexts and constructed understandings, and that museums are social constructs that produce the past rather than discover it. To escape both the claim of objective authority and the relativism of post-structuralism, he turns to Popper's third world of objective knowledge, Collingwood's coherence and correspondence, and Kuhn's consensus of informed communities. He points to shared human dispositions, such as delight in bright things, material intricacy and the miniature, as a basis for mutual understanding, and cites Gombrich's Night Watch example to argue that some interpretations are better than others. The curator is then described as a persuasive interpreter within a community, making exhibitions that work like art. Examples include The West as America, Still Life at Manchester Museum (1992), the People's Show at Walsall, open storage and identification rooms. The chapter closes by urging honesty about the limits of curatorial authority, and by reminding readers that the museum's past is part of everyone's present.

Pearson, Catherine (2017). Museums in the Second World War: Curators, Culture and Change. London: Routledge.Asia: slight18 chapter overviews

Overview

Pearson argues that the Second World War was not a hiatus in British museum history. Provincial museums stayed open, drew new audiences and built educational services, temporary exhibitions and CEMA-funded programmes, while the Museums Association's long campaign for a central, state-funded national museum service, rooted in the Miers (1928) and Markham (1938) reports, failed in 1949. The scope is British museums and art galleries from 1926 to the early 1960s, national and local, with attention to curators, women's careers, visitors and government dealings with the profession. The book runs in six parts from the inter-war years to reconstruction, covering policy, wartime practice, audiences, memory and staff, then concludes that the profession forgot its wartime achievements.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia are almost absent. The book is about British museums, and no museum, collection, object or curator in East or Southeast Asia is studied. Asia appears only in passing. In chapter 7 (Temples to the arts) a general passage on wartime music cites the POW camps of Singapore and Sumatra (lines 3689-3697), and the curator A L Thorpe's 1942 journal mentions a 'China room' at Derby (line 3859), which the text does not explain. In chapter 11 (Memory and identity) a non-visiting veteran who served in Burma and Sri Lanka is mentioned (lines 5524-5528). In chapter 15 (Towards a regional service) the Korean War is cited as one cause of Treasury cuts from 1950 (lines 6847-6849), and the chronology at the start of Part V records the atomic bombings and Japan's surrender (line 5993).

South Asia (India, Sri Lanka) appears only in the list of figures and in biography, outside the question. The book does not treat Asian museum-building, colonial collecting, restitution or Asian visitors, so the absence is complete rather than partial.

Timeline: major events around the Second World War and the Home Front

A dated chronology of British events from 1919 to 1959, concentrated on the Second World War and the Home Front. It lists air raids, the evacuation of children, rationing, conscription, the call-up of women, and the war's end, alongside a few inter-war and post-war landmarks such as the BBC, the NHS and the Festival of Britain. It is a list of events rather than an argument, and it names no museum or collection.

Introduction: a new perspective

The introduction argues that the Second World War is wrongly treated as a hiatus in museum history: wartime museums were popular, engaged audiences and expanded educational services. It outlines the Museums Association's unsuccessful campaign for central government funding, from the Miers and Markham reports to the Rosse Report of 1963. It then lists the sources, from government records and the Museums Journal to interviews with curators, and closes with biographies of key figures such as Frank Markham and Kenneth Clark.

Luton MuseumGeffrye MuseumYork Castle MuseumColchester Castle MuseumLeeds City Art Gallery
PART I 1918–1939: between the wars
11 Between the wars: museums and cultural politics

The chapter examines how the British museum service was shaped between the wars by education policy, funding and the Carnegie UK Trust. It explains the 1918 Education Act and the Museums Association's 1919 decision to reject transfer to local education committees, a choice that kept museums independent but left them underfunded. Using the Miers Report (1928) and the Markham Report (1938), it documents a fragmented, under-resourced service: nearly two-thirds of museums had budgets under £300 a year, and many learned-society museums were closing. The Royal Commission on National Museums and Galleries (1927-1930) and the Standing Commission of 1931 gave priority to the national museums, which resisted circulating collections for the provinces. Carnegie grants and regional federations produced limited change. The chapter concludes that these developments shaped wartime museums and left a legacy running to the 1960s, while curators' rejection of closer ties with education repeatedly blocked a national service.

Victoria and Albert MuseumBritish MuseumScience MuseumWalker Art GalleryLeicester Museum
22 Charting progress: the Markham Report

The chapter examines the 1938 Markham Report, the second survey of non-national British museums, commissioned by the Carnegie UK Trust in 1936. It places Markham's proposals within the planning reformism of the late 1930s. Markham, an MP and former Museums Association secretary, argued that museums should serve an educated democratic citizenry through exhibitions, loans and cooperation with schools, and that central government should fund a national museum service. The chapter shows that the Museums Association, after rejecting education in 1919, now backed state involvement, but Board of Education officials resisted, and the outbreak of war in September 1939 ended the proposed government inquiry. It argues that wartime conditions in fact pushed museums to set up the education services the reports had recommended. The reform process was overtaken by war.

33 Museums before the war: the context for reform

Pearson examines the reform climate of provincial museums between the Miers (1928) and Markham (1938) reports and the Second World War. The government never adopted the central, state-funded museum service the reports proposed, yet curators called them the 'blueprint of the profession'. Pearson places their recommendations against fears of social control after the General Strike, a Victorian faith in art's educative power and a revival of rural national identity. Evidence comes from the reports, the Museums Journal and curators' recollections. Colchester curator E J Rudsdale's Old English Farm displays, and the National Museum of Wales and Belfast Museum, held up as models, serve as cases, alongside Scandinavian open-air museums and the German Heimatmuseum, whose nationalist turn after 1933 is treated as a warning. The chapter then turns to visual education, poor pay and the absence of qualifications. Women's careers were blocked by the marriage bar, and the Museums Association diploma of 1934 opened new routes. It concludes that these inter-war ideas set the agenda for the wartime museum service.

Colchester Castle MuseumNational Museum of WalesBelfast Museum and Art GallerySkansenHighland Folk MuseumHorniman MuseumLeicester MuseumImperial Institute
PART II 1939–1940: at the start of the war
44 Confronting conflict: collections, closings and openings

Pearson turns to the first months of the Second World War, when museums had to decide whether to protect, close or keep working. The national collections were guarded at the highest level, with the National Gallery's pictures moved to underground stores in North Wales, while provincial museums improvised with basements and bank vaults. Pearson traces the closures, the requisitioning of museum buildings and the bomb damage at Liverpool Public Museum, and the campaign by the Museums Association and the Standing Commission to reopen galleries. Sources are wartime archives, Rudsdale's journals and the Museums Journal. The chapter follows Myra Hess's lunchtime concerts at the National Gallery and the reopened National Museum of Wales, which used unseen objects in new displays. It concludes that most provincial museums stayed open while the national museums stayed largely shut until the war ended, exposing the two-tier structure that Markham had criticised.

National GalleryNational Museum of WalesBritish MuseumVictoria & Albert MuseumLiverpool Public MuseumWalker Art GalleryVictoria Art GalleryColchester Castle Museum
55 As war begins: from propaganda to recognition

Pearson examines how museums were drawn into the Ministry of Information's propaganda campaigns in the first years of war. Markham offered the Museums Association's support in 1939, but curators such as Rudsdale at Colchester, Luton's Anne Buck and Derby's A L Thorpe resisted, stripped out propaganda or simply stood aside, and the Ministry's early 'Britain's Might' displays were withdrawn after Dunkirk. Pearson draws on Ministry files, curators' notes and diaries to show that propaganda in galleries largely failed; a 1942 review judged the sites useless. The chapter then turns to the War Artists' Advisory Committee, founded by Clark at the National Gallery, whose travelling exhibitions brought modern paintings to provincial galleries, and to Mass-Observation surveys recording visitors' reactions to realist art. It concludes that museums kept their audiences by offering cultural escape as well as war subjects, rather than serving as channels for government messages.

Colchester Castle MuseumLuton MuseumDerby Museum & Art GalleryNational GalleryBristol Museum & Art GalleryNorwich Castle Museum
PART III 1940–1944: during wartime
66 State support: the Council for the Encouragement of Music and the Arts (CEMA)

Pearson traces the Council for the Encouragement of Music and the Arts (CEMA), the first state body with formal responsibility for the arts, and asks what it meant for provincial museums. CEMA grew out of a voluntary Art and Entertainment Emergency Council in 1939-40, funded first by the Pilgrim Trust and then by Treasury matching grants. Under Keynes from 1942 it aimed for a permanent footing, and it gave curators practical means to stage exhibitions and concerts that the pre-war reports had urged. Evidence comes from Leicester and Derby museum accounts, which show how small CEMA grants raised outside income, the touring John Farleigh exhibition of 1940, CEMA minutes and curators' contributions to the Museums Journal. Music and drama took most of CEMA's money, so the museum programme is a smaller part of the story, but the chapter shows it drew museums into regional federations and national alliances. It concludes that wartime support laid the groundwork for the Arts Council of 1946 and for the museum service's post-war cooperation.

Leicester MuseumDerby Art GalleryNational GalleryVictoria & Albert MuseumTate GalleryWatts GalleryGeffrye Museum
77 Temples to the arts

Pearson examines how the arts entered British museums during the war, under CEMA's sponsorship and through the National Gallery's example. The chapter argues that the government backed the arts partly to sustain morale, and that concerts, lectures and art exhibitions gave museums new audiences and changed what a museum was for. Its evidence includes the National Gallery's lunchtime concerts from October 1939, the canteen set up for their audiences, museum accounts, visitor reports and the journals of Derby's curator A L Thorpe. The case studies centre on Philip Hendy's Moore-Piper-Sutherland exhibition, first shown at Leeds in 1941 and then toured, and on the National Gallery's Picture of the Month scheme, which spread to local galleries. Pearson also quotes the Walker Art Gallery's director, Frank Lambert, on the museum as a mouseion, a temple of the arts. The chapter concludes that wartime programmes changed curators' views of their work, and that these models of exhibitions and events fed into post-war planning for museums and the arts.

National GalleryLeeds City Art GalleryLeicester Museum & Art GalleryDerby Museum & Art GalleryWalker Art GalleryBristol Museum & Art Gallery
88 Planning for peacetime

Pearson follows the plans for post-war reconstruction that museums drew up between 1940 and 1944. The profession's case for a state-funded service, first made by Markham in 1938, was revived in 1940 and 1942 but failed to win government backing. The sources are Museums Association minutes and memoranda, Treasury and Board of Education files and the papers of Markham and Rothenstein. The Museums Association's 1942 Memorandum on Reconstruction, submitted to the Greenwood Committee and apparently promoted by Jacquetta Hawkes, proposed central grants and community roles for museums. But the Standing Commission declined to speak for provincial museums, and the Treasury gave the national proposals only a cautious reply. Pearson also traces how De La Warr's departure in 1940 removed the museum movement's main ally, how Markham's authority waned after Miers's death in 1942, and how the 1944 Education Act made no provision for museums. The chapter concludes that the profession, having lost unity and momentum, returned to its pre-war emphasis on professional autonomy.

Tate GalleryLiverpool MuseumBristol Museum
PART IV Reflections on wartime practice
99 Community engagement, education and exhibitions

Pearson examines the educational work that museums developed during the war, arguing that wartime experiments carried out the inter-war ideas of visual education and adult learning that the Miers and Markham reports had urged. The evidence comes from museum reports and Museums Journal items, from Molly Harrison's memoir of the Geffrye Museum and from Samuel Thompson's account of Glasgow's schools scheme. Other cases include Leicester's art-appreciation courses for service personnel, the Wells Museum's classes for Isle of Dogs children and the Holidays at Home events. Evacuee schooling, the Army Bureau of Current Affairs and picture loans to RAF messes drove museums into new work, while temporary exhibitions, from Tin through the Ages at the National Museum of Wales to shows on disease and town planning, gave objects new meanings. The chapter concludes that these gains were uncertain. Ronald Adam feared that forces education would be lost after demobilisation, and museum education had yet to secure a place in post-war policy.

Geffrye MuseumGlasgow Art GalleryLeicester Museum & Art GalleryNational Museum of WalesWells MuseumLondon MuseumWollaton Natural History Museum
1010 Audiences in wartime

Pearson asks whether the wartime museum boom that contemporaries celebrated stands up to the evidence. Visitor figures rose in the middle years of the war, but the chapter argues they were distorted by population shifts, travel restrictions and the closure of the national museums, and that head-counts were unreliable and sometimes inflated. The evidence comes from attendance books, annual reports, Museums Journal reports and figures compiled for nine provincial museums, together with curators' letters, Mass-Observation studies and comments from visitors collected by Trevor Thomas at Leicester. Temporary exhibitions, CEMA events and the armed services shows drew the largest audiences, while surveys show that middle-class visitors predominated and that refugees and overseas troops added new audiences. Pearson also reads two wartime films, 'Pimpernel' Smith and A Canterbury Tale, as pictures of the museum moving from dusty mausoleum to a place of dialogue. The chapter concludes that attendance had returned to pre-war levels by 1959, and that the wartime shift towards audiences is what the evidence most clearly shows.

Leicester Museum & Art GalleryDerby Museum & Art GalleryNorwich Castle MuseumCyfarthfa Castle MuseumVictoria Art GalleryNational GalleryNational Museum of WalesYork Castle Museum
1111 Memory and identity

Pearson asks how wartime museums entered visitors' memories and identities. Drawing on Kavanagh's idea of the museum as a dream space, the chapter argues that visitors made their own meanings, often ignoring or subverting the museum's authority. The evidence is reminiscences from people who were mostly under thirty in the war, collected through local groups, together with Mass-Observation records and the journal of York's Violet Rodgers. Pearson sorts the memories into four kinds: of buildings and the visit, of objects, of a new role for the museum and of shared human feeling. Examples include Bert Irvin's memory of the National Gallery's Picture of the Month, a boy's attachment to an Egyptian mummy at Leeds City Museum, and a Colchester visitor who sheltered in the Roman vaults during a raid. Non-visitors, by contrast, kept a traditional view of the museum as elitist. The chapter concludes that wartime experience extended the meanings of objects, so that visitors' recollections, as much as curators' intentions, shaped the museum's past.

National GalleryYork Castle MuseumLeeds City MuseumLiverpool Public MuseumColchester Castle MuseumLeicester Museum & Art GalleryRussell-Cotes Art Gallery & Museum
1212 Museum staff and the war

Pearson examines what the war did to museum staff: who was called up, who stayed on and who gained or lost ground afterwards. The chapter argues that wartime shortages opened posts to women, whose numbers in the Museums Association more than doubled between 1937 and 1942, but that most were demoted or displaced once men returned. Its evidence includes staff records, Museums Journal obituaries, MA membership figures, interviews with women curators and the journals of Violet Rodgers at York and E J Rudsdale at Colchester. Case studies include the dismissal and reinstatement of Iorwerth Peate at the National Museum of Wales, Anne Buck's single-handed running of Luton Museum, and Rudsdale's refusal to reapply for his Colchester post in 1944. The chapter also traces the loss of technical and assistant staff to other careers in the late 1940s. It concludes that the war gave some women a route into curatorship, but that the decline of honorary curators and the loss of experienced staff left a lasting gap in the profession.

National Museum of WalesYork Castle MuseumLuton MuseumColchester Castle MuseumWells MuseumPlatt HallLondon Museum
PART V The aftermath of the war
1313 A national museum service: the final bid

Pearson follows the Museums Association's final bid, from its 1945 report to 1949, for central funding of a national museum service. The MA's proposal for a Museum and Art Gallery Grants Board to replace CEMA was undone by the Treasury, a reluctant Ministry of Education and the post-war economic crisis. Pearson draws on Treasury and Ministry files, Cabinet papers and MA minutes, including officials' dismissive remarks about museums as 'frills'. A 1947 scheme to fund museums through the Ministry of Education was postponed and then abandoned after the 1949 devaluation. Museum professionals were divided, since the MA insisted on a separate grants board while Markham and the Carnegie Trust favoured Ministry funding. The chapter concludes that the MA's intransigence, as much as economics, lost the last chance of a national museum service in 1949.

Colchester Castle MuseumWisbech Museum
1414 The post-war decades: museums in the aftermath of war

Pearson traces what became of the wartime museum after 1945. The chapter argues that provincial museums kept many wartime services until the end of the 1940s, but that austerity, falling local funding and a revived focus on collections gradually reversed them, so that by the mid-1950s curators had turned back towards the past. Its evidence includes Museums Journal reports, annual reports, the Rosse Report of 1963 and E J Rudsdale's journals. Case studies include Birmingham's successful post-war development, the decline of society museums such as York's Yorkshire Museum, and the fate of Trevor Thomas, whose audience-centred plans at Leicester were dropped after he was dismissed in 1946 following a charge in court. The chapter also records the Arts Council's closure of its regional offices in 1956 and the MA's weak campaigning. It concludes that the failure lay with the Museums Association, curators and government alike, rather than with the wartime museum experiment itself.

Birmingham City Museum and Art GalleryLeicester Museum & Art GalleryNorwich Castle MuseumYorkshire MuseumWhitworth Art GalleryVictoria & Albert MuseumWalker Art GalleryLondon Museum
PART VI From austerity to reconstruction
1515 Towards a regional service

Chapter 15 traces the Museums Association's (MA) move from a national museum service to a regional one, 1945 to the mid-1960s. Post-war government neglect comes first: Treasury cuts closed galleries at the British Museum and Tate, and bomb-damaged museums such as Liverpool Museum waited years for rebuilding. The MA's last national bid, a 1955 joint memorandum with the Carnegie UK Trust, the Standing Commission and the Arts Council, was rejected by the Treasury in 1956 during the Suez crisis. Nightingale's 1957 Regional Boards plan replaced it, though the Carnegie Trust and some members resisted. Press campaigns, a threatened closure of the Bowes Museum and the Walker Art Gallery's Rubens purchase brought modest state money. The Rosse Report of 1963 recommended Area Museum Councils, and the 1964 Act gave museums only permissive status. The chapter concludes that wartime lessons were ignored and that Treasury economics, not museum rhetoric, settled the outcome.

British MuseumTate GalleryLiverpool MuseumBowes MuseumWalker Art GalleryNational Gallery
Conclusions: museums forget their past

The concluding chapter argues that historians have wrongly treated the Second World War as wholly damaging to British museums. Wartime museums, with their education programmes, topical and propaganda displays and temporary shows, anticipated many current practices, but the post-war return to collections care erased that record. Evidence comes from Museums Association reports, CEMA-funded collaboration and curators' recollections, with Kenneth Clark's evacuation of National Gallery collections to a slate mine as a key case. Colchester Castle Museum, where US Army Air Force exhibitions challenged the curator's authority, and Bristol City Museum, which mixed reserve objects with surrealist art, show how visitors and outside groups took part in shaping displays. The chapter also notes gains for women curators and provincial museums. It ends by arguing that the profession forgets its past and should recover wartime achievements and its own archives.

Rees Leahy, Helen (2012). Museum Bodies: The Politics and Practices of Visiting and Viewing. Farnham: Ashgate.Asia: slight8 chapter overviews

Overview

Museum Bodies (2012) asks when and how museum visitors acquired the bodily habits of art museum going: how to walk, look, sit, talk, dress and behave, and how to tell when they are doing it correctly. Its central question is when those habits were learned. Leahy argues that the museum is a site of social and corporeal practice, and that visitors are both performers and interpreters of the exhibition script. The book concentrates on English art museums and exhibitions from about 1750 to the present, including the British Museum, the Royal Academy, the 1857 Manchester Art Treasures Exhibition and Tate. It combines documentary, philosophical and fictional sources. It is organised as an introduction, six chapters (on looking, walking, performance, protest and 'disquieting' bodies such as women, children and the working classes) and an epilogue on the British Museum today.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia barely figure in the book. Southeast Asia is not mentioned at all, and East Asia appears in only two chapters, each in a single passage. The introduction, the epilogue, the bibliography and the index contain no reference to the region's museums, collections or visitors.

In Chapter 4, Performing the Museum, the only reference is a hypothetical. Discussing Baxandall's 'period eye', Leahy recalls his example of a fifteenth-century Chinese man, unfamiliar with perspectival painting, who might take the figures in Piero della Francesca's Annunciation to be paying homage to the central column. The Chinese viewer serves as a thought experiment about how cultural expectations shape vision, and is not a case.

In Chapter 5, Bodies of Protest, Japan appears in one episode: the April 1974 attack on the Mona Lisa at the Tokyo National Museum, when a disabled woman sprayed red paint on the painting in protest at the museum's access policy. The episode is set among the Mona Lisa's other attacks. Leahy also remarks in passing that Europeans seem more vulnerable to Stendhal Syndrome than Americans or Japanese. Apart from these, no museum, collection, collector, exhibition or visitor from East or Southeast Asia is discussed, and Asian objects in Western museums and colonial collecting are not covered.

Introductionp. 1

The Introduction opens Museum Bodies with Tino Sehgal's This Progress at the Guggenheim in 2010, in which performers question visitors as they climb the rotunda, to show how visiting a museum depends on learned habits of walking, talking and looking. Leahy argues that the museum must be understood as a site of social and corporeal practice, drawing on Kirshenblatt-Gimblett's idea of a performing museology. The central question is when and how visitors acquired these habits, and the introduction locates the answer in the earliest British public museums and exhibitions, from about 1750 to 1820, where arguments about who should be admitted were fierce. Leahy then introduces the sources: the Penny Magazine's rules for the artisan visitor, Rowlandson's print of the Royal Academy, and Mauss's idea of prestigious imitation, with the Royal Academy and the 1857 Manchester Art Treasures Exhibition as test cases. The chapter closes by setting out the book's scope, which concentrates on English art museums, and its method of combining documentary, philosophical and fictional sources.

Guggenheim MuseumRoyal AcademyManchester Art Treasures ExhibitionBritish Museum
11 Making a Social Bodyp. 19

Leahy asks how a public for art was imagined and physically produced in London between the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, comparing the British Museum with the Royal Academy exhibitions at Somerset House. Two comments by Robert Peel on the National Gallery, made twenty years apart, frame the argument: museums hoped for a cohesive public but met the 'idle and the unwashed'. The British Museum, which admitted visitors only by advance ticket and then on three-hour guided tours, is documented through the accounts of Moritz, Hutton and Silliman, who all found themselves hurried and frustrated; the system was relaxed in 1810. The Royal Academy charged a shilling and let visitors wander its crowded Great Room, a sociable and distracting space recorded in Alken's and the Cruikshanks' caricatures of Tom and Bob. The chapter concludes that the two institutions produced contrasting bodily regimes, one linear and regulated, the other free-ranging and kaleidoscopic.

British MuseumRoyal Academy of ArtsNational Gallery
22 Not Just Lookingp. 45

Leahy asks how museum visitors were meant to look at art and how their attention was managed, moving from the eighteenth-century Royal Academy to the 1857 Manchester Art Treasures Exhibition and then to early twentieth-century museum research. Using the distinction between the attentive gaze and the distracted glance, she argues that museum looking constantly oscillates between the two. The Manchester exhibition, with over 16,000 works, is the central case: its organisers aimed at the 'uneducated eye' through chronological serial hanging, yet visitors were overwhelmed, and Hawthorne, Dickens and dialect writers record their confusion. The chapter then turns to Gilman, Robinson and Melton, whose studies of 'museum fatigue' treated attention as a resource to be managed through layout. It ends by arguing that distraction, from celebrity-spotting to Rogoff's account of a Pollock show, is part of museum looking that the curators' model ignores.

Royal Academy of ArtsManchester Art Treasures ExhibitionNational GalleryMuseum of Fine Arts, BostonPennsylvania Museum of ArtMuseum of Modern Art, New YorkTate Gallery
33 Walking the Museump. 73

Leahy treats walking as a bodily technique that shapes how visitors look at museum displays. Opening with Henry James's Newman, exhausted after a stroll through the Louvre, she draws on the Long Gallery of English country houses, where people walked in step with one another, and on Zola's L'Assommoir, whose wedding party gets lost in the Louvre. The 1857 Manchester Art Treasures Exhibition shows the opposite problem: a vast building that few visitors could walk through with purpose. The chapter then considers how layouts and pace were designed, from the probabilistic and deterministic plans debated in the early twentieth century to Harbison's critique of the Victoria and Albert Museum's confusing floors. It ends with two performances that disrupted walking, Abramovic's Public Drill and Creed's runners at Tate Britain, and with the history of museum seating, which Gilman wanted to support looking without turning galleries into lounges.

LouvreManchester Art Treasures ExhibitionVictoria and Albert MuseumWhitworth Art GalleryTate BritainHamburg Kunsthalle
44 Performing the Museump. 97

Leahy turns from fatigue to performance, asking how visitors act out their roles and how artists and curators unsettle those roles. She draws on Judith Butler's account of performatives to describe the museum's script, then examines Duchamp's surrealist installations of 1938 and 1941 and Robert Morris's 1971 Tate retrospective, which closed after injuries. The Turbine Hall commissions at Tate Modern, from Bourgeois to Eliasson's Weather Project and Salcedo's Shibboleth, show visitors turning a sombre crack into a playground. Reconstructions such as Solkin's Art on the Line at the Courtauld, which recreated the crowded Royal Academy hang, illustrate Baxandall's 'period eye'. Dress adds another layer: Ackermann's fashion plates, tailors' plates set in the Elgin Room, the fustian of the Chartists and Frith's Private View at the Royal Academy (1881). Visitors, the chapter argues, are both performers and interpreters of exhibitions.

Tate ModernTate GalleryCourtauld Institute of ArtGalerie Beaux-Arts, ParisRoyal Academy of ArtsBritish Museum
55 Bodies of Protestp. 127

Leahy examines visitors who protested against the museum through illness, carelessness, damage and violence. She begins with Edward Onslow's scandal at the Royal Academy in 1781 and Mulcahy's 1845 smashing of the Portland Vase in the British Museum, which led to a ban on sticks and umbrellas. The surrender of belongings at the threshold is read through Dickens's 'Please to Leave Your Umbrella' and Valery's account of the Louvre. The chapter then moves to 'museum sickness': Stendhal's palpitations in Florence, the Stendhal Syndrome, Twain's scepticism, and the poor ventilation and missing lavatories that made visitors faint. Vandalism is covered through Gamboni and the 1993 Cordess and Turcan survey, and through attacks on the Mona Lisa, The Night Watch and the Rokeby Venus, which the suffragette Mary Richardson slashed in 1914. The chapter concludes with the 1830 revolution in the Louvre, where crowds destroyed portraits of Charles X, showing the museum as a target of political revolt.

East and Southeast Asia The chapter's only East Asian episode is the 1974 attack on the Mona Lisa while it was on show at the Tokyo National Museum, when a disabled woman sprayed it with red paint in protest at the museum's access policy. Leahy notes in passing that Europeans seem more vulnerable to Stendhal Syndrome than Americans or Japanese.

British MuseumRoyal Academy of ArtsNational GalleryLouvreRijksmuseumTokyo National Museum
66 Disquieting Bodiesp. 153

Leahy turns to the visitors whom nineteenth-century commentators found troubling: women, children and the working classes. Peale's painting The Artist in His Museum (1822) shows an inclusive public whose understanding is ranked by age, gender and class. The chapter examines the 'decent appearance' rule at the British Museum, Trollope's call for a charge at the National Gallery, and the fear that working-class bodies brought dust and 'effluvia' that damaged paintings. At the 1857 Manchester Art Treasures Exhibition, admired factory 'lads of the loom' contrast with middle-class women whom male critics treated as a fashion parade. Degas's and Tissot's images of women at the Louvre are read as ways of seeing women as viewers or as objects, and children, barred from the British Museum under eight even after public holidays opened it, are shown playing in the National Gallery. The chapter concludes that these disquieting bodies were both courted as proof of inclusivity and condemned as a threat to it.

Peale's Museum, PhiladelphiaBritish MuseumNational GalleryRoyal Academy of ArtsManchester Art Treasures ExhibitionLouvre
Epiloguep. 177

The epilogue returns to the British Museum today to ask how the visiting bodies traced in the book compare with present practice. Rees Leahy notes the 5.8 million visitors of 2011, the free admission, and the government-set targets for age, class, ethnicity and disability that now shape the audience. Visitor rules are contrasted with the past, from Bateman's 1916 Punch cartoon of a boy jailed for breathing on a mummy case to the 2011 Treasures of Heaven exhibition, where visitors kissed the showcases. The Great Court, opened in 2000, is read as a space of flows resembling an airport departure lounge, and the chapter moves on to Slow Art Day, gallery rage at the Tate's Gauguin show, and the ticket limits set for the National Gallery's Leonardo exhibition. It closes with E.M. Forster's novel Maurice, whose lovers meet in the museum and are reconciled among its Assyrian sculptures. Rees Leahy concludes that museums can never predict or manage the private encounters that take place inside them.

Sandell, Richard; Nightingale, Eithne (eds.) (2012). Museums, Equality and Social Justice. London: Routledge.Asia: substantial24 chapter overviews

Overview

This edited volume (2012) asks how museums respond to equality, diversity and social justice, and whether these concerns have moved from the margins of practice to its core. Its 21 chapters, by academics, practitioners and artists, fall into three parts. 'Margins to the core?' covers organisational change, staffing, collaboration with community heritage groups, disability access and Fred Wilson's institutional critique. 'Connecting/competing equalities' takes up race, religion, sexuality, gender, autism and intercultural work. 'Museums and the good society' treats human rights, cultural rights, constitutional protest, indigenous representation and African collections. Most cases are British, American or Australian, with chapters on Taiwan and Yemen. The editors argue that museums have untapped potential for a more equal society.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

East Asia is a substantial but minor strand. Marzia Varutti's chapter 17 on Taiwan is the one sustained treatment. It covers the 2-28 Incident museum in Taipei, the white terror memorial on Green Island, the 921 Earthquake Museum in Wufeng and the National Museum of Taiwan History in Tainan. It also examines the indigenous collections of the National Taiwan Museum and the Shung Ye Museum, gathered under Japanese colonial ethnology, and the Big Museum Leads Small Museum programme with Amis and Atayal communities. Its conclusion is that Taiwanese museums are progressive, but indigenous communities are seldom the authors of displays.

Other Asian material appears in chapters 1, 9, 10, 11, 15 and the introduction. Chapter 1 (Nightingale and Mahal) discusses Cedric Yeh's work at the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History on Asian Pacific American objects, including a porcelain figure referring to the 1882 Exclusion Act, and the V&A's Asia department. Chapter 9 (Reeve) presents the Asian Civilisations Museum in Singapore as the regional model for religion displays, criticises the British Museum's 2010-11 Buddhism exhibition as object-centred, and notes Burmese priests blessing the Burmese Buddha. Chapter 15 (Anderson) treats the 2005 Tibet: Treasures from the Roof of the World show at American museums as a case of moral stakes in display. Chapters 10 and 11 mention a Japanese lacquer chest (the Mazarin Chest, linked to Beckford) and a Chinese torture chair at the Wellcome in passing.

Southeast Asia is almost absent beyond Singapore and Burma. The volume's colonial-collecting chapter (21) concerns Africa, and South Asia, Yemen and London's shared-heritage policy fall outside this question.

Title
