Foreword

The foreword argues that museums, reshaped over thirty years by market pressures and critiques of their complicity with power and exclusion, have responded to the human rights revolution that followed the 1948 Universal Declaration. It records museums and staff learning to treat visitors and communities as fully human, a demanding process. Good intentions, the authors add, are not enough without analysis of society. They call the book a clarion call for museums to realise their potential.

Acknowledgements
IntroductionEithne Nightingale and Richard Sandell

The introduction sets out the aims of this edited volume, which examines how equality, diversity and social justice have moved from the margins of museum practice to its core. It concedes that change is uneven and may be stalling, and argues for examining how museums both reflect and shape ideas of fairness and power. The editors define equality, diversity and social justice as the book uses them, and note contributors from academia, art, activism and practice. The chapters fall into three parts. Margins to the core? covers organisational change through cases such as Fred Wilson's work and disability access. Connecting/competing equalities covers particular strands, including religion, sexuality and autism, and Younge's argument that identity categories are necessary but flawed. Museums and the good society takes up rights claims, including those at Taiwanese museums and the Museum of Australian Democracy. The editors end by calling for museums to realise their untapped potential for a more equal society.

East and Southeast Asia Varutti's chapter, summarised here, looks at Taiwan's national, local and newly created museums since the end of military rule in 1987, and at how they have been drawn into indigenous rights movements and into efforts to recognise rather than suppress difference. It is a single paragraph of the introduction.

Victoria and Albert MuseumTate BritainMuseum of Australian DemocracyNational Museum of African American History and Culture
PART I Margins to the core?
11 The heart of the matter: Integrating equality and diversity into the policy and practice of museums and galleriesEithne Nightingale and Chandan MahalAsia: in part

Chapter 1 asks how far UK and US museums have built equality and diversity into their policy, leadership, staffing, partnerships and collections. Nightingale and Mahal, both with equality roles in London museums, draw on interviews with staff at the Museum of London, the V&A, Birmingham and several Smithsonian museums. They find that policy alone does not produce change: committees can lack influence, equality impact assessments can be bureaucratic, and the Horniman grew its black, Asian and minority ethnic audience with little formal policy. They argue for measurable objectives, diversified staff, shared leadership and partners with real influence. Most examples concern race and ethnicity, and the authors see socio-economic class as the most neglected strand. The chapter ends with a picture of an equitable museum that is measurable, collaborative and ready to take risks.

East and Southeast Asia Cedric Yeh's work at the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History (NMAH) is the main Asia case: he found Asian Pacific American objects catalogued as 'machinery' or 'fabrics', and the first object displayed was a porcelain figure of a white man pushing a Chinese labourer out of a nest, referring to the 1882 Exclusion Act. The chapter also notes the V&A's long work with South Asian and Chinese communities through its Asia department, a Chinese New Year festival and a Chinese Watercolours exhibition, and the Chinese Museum in New York.

Museum of LondonVictoria and Albert MuseumBirmingham Museums and Art GalleryHorniman MuseumNational Museum of American HistoryNational Museum of African American History and CultureNational Museum of the American IndianBrooklyn Museum
22 Museologically speaking: An interview with Fred WilsonJanet Marstine

In this interview Janet Marstine questions the artist Fred Wilson about how museums can become more socially just, drawing on his experience as an outsider and as a trustee. Wilson argues that American museums now see inclusion as necessary, and that boards discuss diversity, but that large institutions still follow rather than lead, and change is slow because of money and differing trustee views. Embedding diversity means hiring across all departments and backing words with systemic action. He values culturally specific museums such as the National Museum of the American Indian for challenging mainstream assumptions, and warns that activism can become a brand. He credits 1960s to 1980s artist agitation with changing museum practice. He ends with the Pulitzer Foundation's decision to hire ex-offenders as gallery guards, which, he says, showed curators how much they could learn from new staff.

National Museum of the American IndianPulitzer Foundation for the ArtsMetropolitan Museum of ArtMuseum of Modern ArtSmithsonian Institution
33 Moving beyond the mainstream: Insight into the relationship between community-based heritage organizations and the museumKimberly F. Keith

Keith examines collaborations between community-based heritage organisations and mainstream museums, asking whether they can advance social justice by challenging the museum's authority over its narrative. Drawing on a discussion among four practitioners, including Singh of the Anglo-Sikh Heritage Trail and Anand of the Institute of Jainology, the chapter shows how curators are hard to reach and how staff turnover breaks relationships. Anand's work as a V&A education officer and later JAINpedia partner illustrates an insider-outsider position that can shift interpretation, but the practitioners see many projects as tokenistic. Temporary funding, short-term contracts for minority staff and unpaid 'budget of love' expertise leave partners feeling used. Keith describes the Staying Power project with the V&A and Black Cultural Archives as consultative rather than reciprocal. The chapter concludes that lasting change needs shared values, permanent posts and funders who understand minority communities, and that partnerships should be judged by whether they endure.

Victoria and Albert MuseumBlack Cultural ArchivesRoyal Geographical Society
44 Beyond compliance? Museums, disability and the lawHeather J. L. Smith, Barry Ginley and Hannah Goodwin

Smith, Ginley and Goodwin, practitioners at the V&A, the National Trust and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, ask whether anti-discrimination law can make museums accessible to disabled people. They trace how disability activism in the US and UK produced the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 and the Disability Discrimination Act of 1995, and argue that the law's reliance on 'reasonable adjustment' lets organisations settle for the minimum. Using Majewski and Bunch's three tiers, they review progress on the physical environment, on content such as captions and audio description, and on the representation of disabled people, which they see as almost ignored. Their main evidence is how specialist access posts at each organisation drove change. The authors conclude that legal compliance is not enough and that co-creative work with disabled people is needed for lasting change in museum culture.

Victoria and Albert MuseumMuseum of Fine Arts, BostonNational Trust
55 Museums for social justice: Managing organisational changeDavid Fleming

Fleming, who directed Tyne and Wear Museums and then National Museums Liverpool, sets out how a museum can manage for social justice, drawing on twenty years in two deprived regions of England. Fleming argues that leadership, mission and values, governance, organisational culture, staff structures, budgets, programming and promotion must all change together. Concrete cases include the Laing Art Gallery's children's gallery, the Walker's Big Art for Little Artists area and the International Slavery Museum, which led to the Federation of International Human Rights Museums. Fleming records the struggles with councillors and trustees, and staff exercises that described the organisation as bureaucratic and risk averse before a 2011 revisit found it changed. Fleming’s main claim is that the social role must be embedded in corporate commitment and sustained over years, not left to one-off projects. Fleming ends by pointing to international networks such as INTERCOM and FIHRM.

Tyne and Wear MuseumsNational Museums LiverpoolLaing Art GalleryWalker Art GalleryInternational Slavery MuseumMuseum of Liverpool
66 Fred Wilson, good work and the phenomenon of Freud’s mystic writing padJanet Marstine

Janet Marstine examines how the artist Fred Wilson's interventions in two American museums, The Museum: Mixed Metaphors at the Seattle Art Museum (1993) and SO MUCH TROUBLE IN THE WORLD at the Hood Museum of Art, Dartmouth (2005), affected the staff who worked with him. Drawing on interviews with curators, guards, registrars and preparators, Marstine applies the GoodWork Project's model of ethics, which depends on individual values, professional domain and wider social rewards being aligned, to argue that Wilson's compassionate institutional critique helped museums act on social inclusion. The evidence covers new mission statements and strategic plans, acquisition and deaccession decisions, the 2007 rehanging of the Seattle galleries, educational tours, and new roles for security staff and preparators. The central case is the Hood's Webster portraits set against the busts of The Races of Man, which Wilson presented as individuals rather than types. Marstine concludes that Wilson is one driver of change among many, but that his process has left a lasting model of reflexive practice in museum memory.

Seattle Art MuseumHood Museum of Art
PART II Connecting/competing equalities
77 The margins and the mainstreamGary Younge

Gary Younge's essay is not about museums; it is a general reflection on identity, race and diversity that the book includes. He opens with two white-born women, Sandra Laing, reclassified as coloured under South African apartheid, and Bliss Broyard, who learned that her father had been passing as white. From these cases he sets out four points: the margins define the core, categories such as race and religion are porous and contested, the boundary is set by power rather than by numbers, and the relation between the two is constantly changing. Evidence includes Israel's 2008 disqualification of some 40,000 conversions, the French headscarf ban, Caster Semenya's gender testing and the question of how Barack Obama should be classified. Younge criticises complaints about political correctness and arguments against gay marriage that treat tradition as a fixed fact. Younge concludes that the tension between margins and core is productive but must not be ignored, and that identity is a sound place to start but a poor place to finish.

88 Cultural diversity: Politics, policy and practices. The case of Tate EncountersAndrew Dewdney, David Dibosa and Victoria Walsh

Dewdney, Dibosa and Walsh, reporting the Tate Encounters research project, examine how New Labour's cultural diversity policy was turned into practice at Tate Britain. They trace a shift from the 1980s politics of visibility, associated with artists such as Lubaina Himid and her exhibition The Thin Black Line (1985), to policies that counted and targeted BAME audiences. The evidence comes from an organisational study of Tate staff, a survey of over 200 students, and a video, Whirlwind at Millbank, made with student co-researchers. The authors argue that targeting and market segmentation reduced difference to skin colour, and that diversity work was managed as a risk to the museum's core values and confined to education departments. Students' responses, which resisted identities based on race and ethnicity, suggest that visitors were more interested in the museum's control of viewing than in racial identity. The chapter concludes that Tate should give more weight to everyday knowledge and open its networks to publics it has not yet counted.

Tate BritainInstitute of Contemporary Arts, London
99 A question of faith: The museum as a spiritual or secular spaceJohn ReeveAsia: in part

John Reeve asks why museums have been so reluctant to present religion and what practice has worked. He starts from the view that major museums have long behaved as secular temples, and that religion is now a matter of public controversy that curators find hard to handle. Using Mark O'Neill's four questions as a framework, he reviews cases including the St Mungo Museum in Glasgow, the V&A's Jameel Gallery of Islamic art and its faith advisory groups, the British Museum's Islamic gallery, the British Library's Sacred exhibition and Norwich's The Art of Faith. The evidence comes from faith advisers such as Atul Shah and Irna Qureshi, from exhibition websites, and from the author's own work at the British Museum. Reeve argues that curators should consult living faith communities, present objects in their religious contexts and use multiple voices, rather than retreat to aesthetic or neutral display. Reeve concludes that museums should be braver in engaging faith, while accepting that they cannot satisfy every group.

East and Southeast Asia Reeve draws on Karen Chin's account of the Asian Civilisations Museum in Singapore, which he calls the first museum in the region to present religions holistically, describing its pilgrimage displays, the way students respond to its galleries, and its aim to show religion as an ecosystem of ideas linked by trade. Reeve also discusses the British Museum's 2010-11 exhibition Images and Sacred Texts: Buddhism across Asia, which he judges object-centred and without context. Reeve notes that Burmese priests blessed the Burmese Buddha in the British Museum's Asian gallery, and that the main Asia gallery has almost no material after 1900.

Victoria and Albert MuseumBritish MuseumSt Mungo Museum of Religious Life and ArtAsian Civilisations MuseumHorniman MuseumNorwich Castle Museum
1010 A book with its pages always open?Oliver Winchester

Oliver Winchester asks how a museum can present same-sex desire and LGBTQ histories without reducing them to a story of gradual liberation. He starts from the tension in gay liberation between ending discrimination and affirming difference, and warns that discovered hidden histories can become retrospective outing. He describes the V&A's LGBTQ Network, founded in 2006, and its public programmes and the Sexing the Collections roundtable. The cases are Gran Fury's poster Kissing Doesn't Kill, whose political urgency is lost once it moves from street to gallery, and William Beckford, whose scrapbooks and collecting show a queer interest that biography alone cannot explain. The V&A's plaster cast of Michelangelo's David, with its fig leaf and later gay reappropriations, shows that meaning depends on the visitor's context. Winchester concludes that the museum should be a book with its pages always open, where exclusions are deliberate and visible rather than arbitrary.

East and Southeast Asia Winchester notes one East Asian object: the Mazarin Chest, a Japanese export lacquer piece of about 1640 that William Beckford acquired in 1800 and that is now in the V&A's collection. It is cited as one of the most significant objects linked to Beckford, whose collecting the chapter reads as a queer activity. No other East or Southeast Asian material is discussed.

Victoria and Albert Museum
1111 Unpacking gender: Creating complex models for gender inclusivity in museumsAmy K. Levin

Amy K. Levin asks how far museums have become gender inclusive, both by showing more women and by moving beyond the male-female binary. Levin traces the museum's gendered origins, from the nobleman's picture gallery to the exclusion of women from curatorship, and sets out feminist and queer theory as frameworks. Levin’s evidence is three London exhibitions of 2010: Identity: 8 Rooms, 9 Lives and Medicine Man at the Wellcome Collection, The Empire Strikes Back at the Saatchi Gallery, and Where Three Dreams Cross at the Whitechapel Art Gallery. Levin finds that the Wellcome's display of male scientists beside crowded rooms for April Ashley and Claude Cahun reinforced binaries, while the South Asian shows offered more varied gender expressions, though these stayed narrow in places. Levin concludes that the task of queering the museum is far from accomplished, since local gender schemas and colonial norms still resist inclusion.

East and Southeast Asia Levin mentions one East Asian object: a Chinese torture chair in the permanent Medicine Man display at the Wellcome Collection, which curators placed close to a birthing seat and a dentist's chair to jar visitors' expectations. Levin’s other exhibitions are South Asian (India, Pakistan and Bangladesh) and do not count here.

Wellcome CollectionSaatchi GalleryWhitechapel Art GalleryLeather Museum & Archives
1212 Museums and autism: Creating an inclusive community for learningSusan Davis Baldino

Susan Davis Baldino argues that museums can offer autistic learners a more inclusive education than the segregated classroom, drawing on social learning theory. She sets out Bruner's critique of one-way teaching, Lave and Wenger's communities of practice, and the constructivist museum theorists Hein, Hooper-Greenhill and Falk and Dierking. The chapter then reviews the rise in autism diagnoses, the limits of behaviourist interventions, and the SCERTS model as an alternative. Its main evidence is the Museum Learners Club, which Baldino set up in 2006 with six pupils, three of them on the autism spectrum, who spent a school day a week visiting museums and building a project for their class. She reports greater participation, leadership, social confidence and friendships among the autistic members, though the evidence rests on her own participant observation. She concludes that inclusion benefits all learners and that museums can affirm the abilities of autistic learners and others who have faced discrimination.

1313 Museums as intercultural spacesSimona Bodo

Simona Bodo argues that museums founded to validate national or group identities can become intercultural spaces that foster dialogue between communities. She contrasts an essentialist view of heritage, in which curators transmit fixed objects to passive visitors, with a dialogical view in which heritage is continually renegotiated, and notes that European policy has mostly favoured the first. Targeted and culturally specific programmes, she finds, often reinforce stereotypes and treat dialogue as a goal rather than a process. Her evidence is three Italian experiments: Tongue to Tongue at the Turin museum of anthropology, where migrant mediators created autobiographical displays; Plural Stories at the Guatelli Museum, a theatre project with women of different origins; and City Telling, a photography and video project with young immigrants run by a Turin foundation. Bodo concludes that intercultural work must be built into the core functions of museums, since education and outreach remain marginal to curatorship.

Museum of Anthropology and Ethnography, University of TurinGuatelli Museum
PART III Museums and the good society
1414 Museums and the human rights frameRichard Sandell

This chapter asks how museums, usually wary of controversy, have come to use human rights as a frame for exhibitions and public debate, and what follows when they do. Sandell combines social anthropology, social movement studies and museum studies, and works through one case: sh[OUT], the 2009 programme at Glasgow's Gallery of Modern Art (GoMA) on lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex rights. The chapter traces how staff and advisory group members negotiated which identities to include and whether to stress difference or shared humanity, and how Mapplethorpe prints and a community display of LGBT people of faith provoked a long press storm. It then analyses more than 1,300 comment cards and interviews, sorting visitor responses into confirmatory, oppositional, negotiated and questioning categories, and considers how transgender activists used the gallery. Sandell concludes that controversy is a necessary part of museum human rights work, and that museums seeking more progressive norms should adopt cosmopolitan understandings of rights and accept the controversy this invites.

Gallery of Modern Art, Glasgow
1515 Creativity, learning and cultural rightsDavid AndersonAsia: in part

Anderson argues that cultural rights, though affirmed in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, are rarely discussed in plural democracies, where debate narrows to the freedom of high-profile artists such as Ai Weiwei. Drawing on Henry Shue's theory of basic rights and on creativity research, the chapter rejects three standard classifications of culture (as capital, as creativity and as a whole way of life) because each treats citizens as passive consumers. Anderson proposes instead that citizens have rights to cultural identity, engagement with other cultures, participation, creativity and freedom of expression. The 2005 controversy over the Tibet exhibition in American museums illustrates how display carries moral stakes. The chapter argues that museums should prioritise public learning, treat their resources as a commons that unequal barriers currently protect, and keep gallery space open rather than ceding it to faith groups. It concludes that cultural rights could give museums an organising purpose, and that this obligation extends to their international work.

East and Southeast Asia Tibet is the chapter's main Asian case. The 2005 exhibition Tibet: Treasures from the Roof of the World, curated by Tibet's Bureau of Cultural Relics and staff of three Lhasa institutions, was shown at the Bowers Museum, the Houston Museum of Natural Science and the Rubin Museum of Art, and critics accused the venues of complicity in the occupation of Tibet. The Dalai Lama welcomed the show as evidence that Tibetan art had survived. The chapter also opens with the 2011 arrest of the Chinese artist Ai Weiwei, but only as an example of a narrow view of cultural rights.

Bowers MuseumHouston Museum of Natural ScienceRubin Museum of Art
1616 Exceeding the limits of representation? Petitioning for constitutional change at the Museum of Australian DemocracyKylie Message

Message asks whether a museum can exceed the limits of representation by treating protest as a force that acts on law, using the Museum of Australian Democracy (MoAD) in Canberra as a test case. MoAD occupies Old Parliament House, where the 1963 Yirrkala Bark Petitions were displayed and where the Aboriginal Tent Embassy has stood since 1972. Drawing on critical legal studies and the new museology, the chapter separates constituent power (protest from outside the constitutional order) from constituted power (government) and traces the building's history from its 1927 opening through the 1992 occupation. The petitions and the Embassy, Message argues, challenged the nation's founding documents rather than only seeking reform. MoAD's Living Democracy exhibition mentions the Embassy on its front lawn without interpreting it. By contrast, the National Museum of Australia's exhibitions, and its 2001 yingapungapu ceremony, gave Yolngu people a national platform for land claims. The chapter concludes that MoAD could make the limits of the Constitution its subject by engaging with the Embassy and its residents, though its reliance on government makes this hard.

Museum of Australian DemocracyNational Museum of Australia
1717 Towards social inclusion in Taiwan: Museums, equality and indigenous groupsMarzia VaruttiAsia: chiefly

Varutti asks what it takes for museums in Taiwan to pursue social equality, and whether their growing attention to social issues extends to the way indigenous groups are represented. Drawing on fieldwork, the chapter sets Taiwanese museum practice against the political shift after martial law was lifted in 1987, when a 'four ethnic groups' model and a multicultural 'new Taiwanese' identity came to shape national museums. It surveys memorials to disaster, the 2-28 Incident and the white terror, then turns to indigenous representation, tracing how Japanese colonial ethnology framed indigenous peoples as inferior and how collaborative programmes such as Big Museum Leads Small Museum now involve indigenous communities. The National Museum of Taiwan History's reinterpretation of national history is a central case. Varutti concludes that Taiwanese museums are becoming more progressive, but that social concerns are mostly confined to temporary exhibitions, that indigenous curators and communities are seldom the authors of displays, and that unilaterally conceived representations risk reproducing inequality, so indigenous perspectives must enter institutional decision-making.

East and Southeast Asia Almost the whole chapter concerns Taiwan: museums commemorating the 2-28 Incident in Taipei and the white terror on Green Island, the 921 Earthquake Museum in Wufeng, and the National Museum of Taiwan History in Tainan, which presents Taiwanese history as multicultural. It details the indigenous collections of the National Taiwan Museum and the Shung Ye Museum, the Japanese colonial ethnology that gathered them, and the Big Museum Leads Small Museum programme with Amis and Atayal communities. It also notes exhibitions on migrant workers and Hakka museums.

National Museum of Taiwan HistoryNational Taiwan MuseumShung Ye Museum of Formosan Aborigines921 Earthquake Museum of TaiwanTaipei 228 Memorial MuseumMuseum of Ethnology, Academia Sinica
1818 Social justice and community participation in non-Western contexts: The Marib Museum Project in YemenSusan Kamel and Christine Gerbich

Kamel and Gerbich ask how a museum in a non-Western setting can pursue social justice and inclusion, using the planned Marib Museum in Yemen as their case. The museum is a development project of the Social Fund for Development, with exhibitions designed by the German Archaeological Institute, and was meant to draw tourists, create jobs and strengthen local self-esteem in one of the poorest regions. The authors set out the new museology and what they call appropriate museology, and ask whether these ideas can travel to Arab countries, where museums were often imperial showcases. Their evidence comes from a survey of nearly 500 visitors at Sana'a National Museum, where most Yemenis had never visited a museum, plus consultations with blind people, disabled women, teachers and guides. Yemenis preferred folklore dioramas to archaeological displays, and women's access was limited by literacy and family patterns. Insecurity and tribal authority in Marib restricted access to the communities the museum was meant to serve. The chapter concludes that inclusive planning depends on diplomacy and local networks as much as on expertise.

Marib MuseumSana'a National MuseumNubia Museum, Aswan
1919 Embedding shared heritage: Human rights discourse and the London Mayor’s Commission on African and Asian HeritageJanice Cheddie

Cheddie asks how human rights language can push London's museums and heritage institutions to represent African and Asian histories more fully. The chapter examines the Mayor's Commission on African and Asian Heritage (2003–2009) and its reports Delivering Shared Heritage (2005) and Embedding Shared Heritage (2009). Drawing on post-structuralist theory, Cheddie argues that the Commission used human rights and equality frameworks, including its 'six cases for diversity', to move debate beyond the visibility of people of colour towards structural inequality and cultural democracy. The Commission is read as an interpretive community, and Iris Marion Young's account of structural inequality frames the analysis. The chapter also describes the Revisiting Collections project, which asked London's collections to address the city's imperial past. It closes by weighing post-2010 funding cuts, growing multiple heritage populations and persistent inequality, and concludes that human rights discourse can sustain the dialogue needed to make heritage shared.

2020 Social media towards social change: Potential and challenges for museumsAmelia Wong

Wong asks whether social media can advance equality, diversity and social justice in museums, or merely extend their existing reach. Drawing on international examples and on outreach at the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, the chapter defines social media as a culture of openness, participation and collaboration, shaped by ideas of networked collective intelligence. On equality, social media can widen access and make museums feel everyday, as with museum profiles on Flickr and Facebook and the Indianapolis Museum of Art's Art Babble. On diversity, they can share authority through projects such as the Virtual Shtetl, Flickr Commons and folksonomic tagging, which replace rigid classification with varied public description. On social justice, museums use blogs, Twitter and personal story archives to make invisible histories visible, as the Lower East Side Tenement Museum and the Canadian Museum for Human Rights do. Problems include persistent digital divides, polarised online discussion and corporate profit from free participation. Wong concludes that museums should use social media with explicit goals, evaluation, ethical standards and staff from across the institution, and should work as networked partners.

United States Holocaust Memorial MuseumIndianapolis Museum of ArtBrooklyn MuseumLower East Side Tenement MuseumCanadian Museum for Human RightsMuseum of the History of Polish Jews
2121 Museums, African collections and social justiceHelen Mears and Wayne Modest

Mears and Modest ask how African collections in British museums can serve social justice, given that most were gathered by colonial collectors rather than by African people and displayed through racialised narratives. The chapter traces how displays moved from imperial spectacle and 'fetish' stereotypes to New Labour-era social inclusion policy, and draws on Iris Marion Young's distinction between cultural and positional difference to test three curatorial strategies. The Horniman Museum's African Worlds gallery (1999), developed with curators from Africa and its diaspora, is read as a dialogic model. The Museum of London and the V&A's African Diaspora Research Project, which located more than 4,000 relevant objects, are read as 'hidden histories' models that stay marginal to core practice. The Geffrye Museum's The West Indian Front Room (2005–06) addressed a Caribbean community for which no collection existed. The authors conclude that naming difference is easier than dismantling the structures that produce inequality, and urge museums to undo colonial categories rather than target communities by origin.

Sellers, Charles Coleman (1980). Mr. Peale’s Museum: Charles Willson Peale and the First Popular Museum of Natural Science and Art. New York: W. W. Norton.Asia: occasional10 chapter overviews

Overview

Sellers's 1980 history of the Philadelphia museum that Charles Willson Peale founded in 1784, from its beginnings in his studio through its move to the State House and Philosophical Hall to its dispersal between 1845 and 1854. The argument is that Peale's museum was a new kind of popular science institution, combining scientific order with 'rational amusement' for a broad public, that it shaped American natural history, and that commercial imitators such as Barnum undermined its model. The book is arranged chronologically in nine chapters, each covering a phase of the museum's life and collections, and it draws on the Peale papers, museum records and sale catalogues, with a colour portfolio and notes.

East and Southeast Asia in this work occasional

East and Southeast Asia are present throughout the book, but mostly as passing material, with one substantial episode. Chapter 8, Titian and Franklin (1827-1845), gives the most space to China. Nathan Dunn, a Quaker merchant who had spent about thirteen years trading in Canton, brought a large collection of Chinese life to the Museum: life-size clay figures of mandarins, shopkeepers, priests and servants, with furniture, tools, boats and a pagoda. James Silk Buckingham and the diarist Sydney Fisher admired it. Dunn took it to London in 1841, where it earned over $50,000 a year. The same chapter notes William Wood's purchases in China and the East Indies, butterflies from China and Japan, and an Argus pheasant from Malacca.

Elsewhere the Asian material is mainly in gifts and lists. Chapter 2, Small Beginnings (1784-1790), covers Lafayette's Chinese golden pheasants, a mandarin cap, boots and a Chinese lady's shoe given by Mrs Morris, and a cargo from Sumatra. Chapter 5, Foundations: The Public (1795-1801), describes a Chinese laborer and a Chinese mandarin among the racial wax figures of 1797, whose faces were probably cast from servants brought from Canton by Van Braam Houckgeest, who also lent Chinese clothing and utensils. Chapter 6, High Tide, mentions Chinese and East Indian objects in the Antique Room. Chapter 9, Full Stage and Final Curtain (1845-1854), lists Chinese curiosities, a war junk, a boat and a pagoda in the 1848 sale catalogue, and a pair of Chinese boots given by William Burke Wood.

Japan appears only in a fake mermaid made by McGuigan and advertised as Japanese work, and in the butterflies. Southeast Asia is touched only through the Sumatra cargo, the Malacca pheasant and the East Indian figures, and no other East or Southeast Asian place figures in the passages read. The book does not examine how the Canton trade shaped these collections, beyond noting that Dunn refused to join the opium traffic.

Contents

Theoretical approach of this work
Forewordp. vii

Sellers's foreword explains how the book came about. Edgar P. Richardson urged in 1970 that a history of Peale's Museum be written, and the work began in 1973 with support from the Barra Foundation, alongside the editing of the Peale Papers by Lillian B. Miller. Sellers thanks the Philadelphia institutions that held Peale material, the many institutions and individuals who answered requests, and those who advised on style.

Peale's Museum
List of Illustrationsp. xi
1A New Science for a New Erap. 1

Sellers's opening chapter places Peale's Museum in Philadelphia within the intellectual world that made it possible. Charles Willson Peale, a portrait painter and Revolutionary politician, opened it in 1784 in a skylit gallery at his studio, and the chapter traces how it grew out of his painting and his 'moving pictures', a painted spectacle first shown in 1785. It then examines the scientific ideas behind the venture: Linnaean classification, Enlightenment faith in a natural order, Rousseau's educational theory and the dispute with Buffon over American degeneracy. Sellers works through the advice Peale received from Ramsay, Rittenhouse and Patterson, and the models he drew on, including the Ashmolean, the British Museum and the Leverian Museum in London. The chapter closes with Peale's innovations in display, such as habitat groups and the mounting of skins, and with his hope for a national institution, a hope that commercial imitators, Barnum among them, undermined.

Peale's MuseumAshmolean MuseumBritish MuseumLeverian Museum
2“With Harmony Small Beginnings Effect Great Things” (1784-1790)p. 21

Sellers traces the first six years of Peale's Museum in Philadelphia, from its opening in the family house at Third and Lombard Streets to Rachel Peale's death in 1790. The chapter follows the crowded household and the growth of the menagerie and collection as Peale preserved birds and animals and displayed them in landscaped cases. Gifts arrived from sea captains, diplomats, politicians and naturalists, and the public's taste for oddities, such as a five-legged cow and a murderer's trigger finger, pushed against Peale's plan for scientific order. Sellers also describes the newspaper appeals, the beginnings of a catalogue and Peale's painting tours in Maryland, which helped fund the enterprise. The chapter closes with Peale's February 1790 address calling for a national museum, which drew only a lukewarm response, and with Rachel's death that April.

East and Southeast Asia Chinese objects reach the Museum mainly as gifts. Lafayette's Chinese golden pheasants, sent from the Royal Aviary in Paris to Washington and then passed to Peale, are the chapter's main case, and Peale's letter about them remarks on Chinese paintings of such birds. Mrs Morris gave a mandarin cap, boots and a Chinese lady's shoe, and George Harrison, who had sailed to China, contributed Pacific material. These appear in lists, so the East Asian presence is slight.

Peale's Museum
3Foundations for a National Museum: The Elite (1790-1795)p. 49

Sellers's chapter covers 1790 to 1795, when Peale's Museum sought public support and found a new home. It follows Rachel Peale's death, Peale's second marriage to Betsy DePeyster, and the New York American Museum, a Tammany Society venture that pointed him toward a board of trustees. The board of visitors he assembled in 1792, with Jefferson as president and a constitution drafted by Nicholas Collin, is described alongside the scientific aims in minerals, fossils and exchanges with Stockholm, London and Paris. Sellers then shows how the 1793 yellow fever epidemic and a legislative petition that stalled disrupted the work. The chapter ends with the lease of Philosophical Hall from the American Philosophical Society, a move that promised a permanent site beside the State House, and with the parade of animals that carried the collection there.

Peale's MuseumLeverian MuseumMuséum national d'Histoire naturelle, ParisAmerican Museum, New York
4Foundations: The Public (1795-1801)p. 87

Sellers covers 1795 to 1801, when Peale's Museum, now housed in Philosophical Hall, struggled for public money and lost his son Titian to a relapse of yellow fever in 1798. The chapter describes the catalogue planned with the botanist Beauvois, the exchanges opened with the Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle in Paris, and the rattlesnake hunts and Indian visits that brought new material. It then examines the forty lectures Peale gave from 1799 to 1802, which Sellers describes as the most comprehensive American summary of mammals and birds at the time, and the moral and religious ideas that ran through them. Sellers also covers the wax figures of the races of mankind, which Federalist critics ridiculed, and Peale's 1800 petitions to the Pennsylvania Assembly. The chapter ends in June 1801 with Peale leaving for New York in search of a complete skeleton of the Incognitum, a bold bid for the national attention he had long wanted.

East and Southeast Asia Asia appears mainly in the racial wax figures. The eight figures completed in August 1797 include a Chinese laborer and a Chinese mandarin, whose faces were probably cast from servants who came from Canton in the retinue of the Dutch traveller Van Braam Houckgeest in 1796. The Dutch traveller also lent Chinese clothing and utensils for the figures.

Peale's MuseumMuséum national d'Histoire naturelle, ParisAmerican Museum, New York
A Color Portfoliop. 115
5The Great American Incognitum (1801-1804)p. 123

Sellers follows Peale's 1801 journey to New York and the Hudson valley to recover a complete skeleton of the Incognitum, the huge animal whose bones had turned up in marl pits in Ulster and Orange counties. The chapter describes the excavation at John Masten's farm, the wheel and bucket chain that drained the swamp, and the later digs that produced a nearly complete skeleton. It then covers the reconstruction in the Hall, with carved replacements and a red line marking where fact ended and conjecture began, and the public excitement that followed, with a separate room and admission charge. Sellers examines Peale's appeals for state support, Latrobe's designs for a building and Jefferson's reply that Congress lacked the power to fund a museum. The chapter ends with Rembrandt and Rubens's trip to England and Betsy Peale's death in childbirth in 1804.

Peale's MuseumBritish Museum
6High Tide (1804-1810)p. 159

High Tide covers 1804 to 1810, when Charles Willson Peale's Philadelphia museum was at its most admired. Sellers opens with the visit of Alexander von Humboldt in 1804, who toured the State House collections and endorsed Peale's plan for a national museum, then walks through the arrangement of the rooms: quadrupeds, birds, insects, minerals and the Marine Room. The chapter follows the Lewis and Clark material that Jefferson sent to Peale, including skins, skeletons, costumes and the peace pipe from Cameahwait, which Peale used in a wax figure of Lewis. It then traces the hopes for a national institution, from Joel Barlow's plan and the Museum's lottery schemes to the Assembly's favourable report of March 1810 and the bill's defeat by six votes in 1811. Sellers ends with Peale at sixty-eight, still painting gallery portraits and promoting the Museum's moral value, while his son Rubens runs its daily management.

Peale's Museum
7Rubens and Rembrandt (1810-1827)p. 215

Rubens and Rembrandt covers 1810 to 1827, from Rubens's takeover of the State House museum to Charles Willson Peale's death. Sellers follows Rubens as he turns the Museum into a fashionable lounge with gaslight, evening lectures, music, novelties and popular exhibits, and follows Rembrandt, who opens his own Peale Museum in Baltimore in 1814. The city councils refuse Peale's proposals to take over the collection, and the chapter traces the failed bids for public ownership, the 1816 gaslight controversy, the Redheffer perpetual-motion exposure, and the Wilson and Bonaparte bird work. It covers the 1821 incorporation as the Philadelphia Museum Company, the failed faculty of lecturers, and Titian's return from the Long expedition with mounted animals and birds. The chapter ends with the 1826 purchase of a disputed Indian collection from traders and with Charles Willson Peale's death on February 22, 1827.

Peale's MuseumPeale Museum (Baltimore)Peale's New York MuseumWestern Museum Society (Cincinnati)Washington Museum (Philadelphia)
8Titian and Franklin (1827-1845)p. 255Asia: in part

Titian and Franklin covers 1827 to 1845, from the founder's death to the collapse of the Philadelphia Museum Company. Sellers follows the move into John Haviland's Arcade and then the costly new building at Ninth and George Streets, opened in 1838 with a great saloon, lectures and popular entertainments. Titian, the naturalist, runs the collections and their publications, while Franklin, the manager, pursues mechanical displays. Much of the chapter concerns Nathan Dunn, the Quaker merchant whose Chinese collection drew praise from James Silk Buckingham and whose departure to London in 1841 left the company with debts. Titian's service on the Wilkes exploring expedition and the government's decision to send its collections to Washington follow, along with the dispute over private specimens. The chapter ends with the 1843 sale of the building and Edmund Peale's 1845 offer to buy the collections, which the directors left unresolved.

East and Southeast Asia Nathan Dunn, a Quaker merchant who had spent about thirteen years trading in Canton, brought a large Chinese collection to the Museum: life-size clay figures of mandarins, shopkeepers, priests and servants in costume, with furniture, tools, boats and a pagoda, which James Silk Buckingham and the diarist Sydney Fisher both admired. In 1841 Dunn took the collection to London, where it earned over $50,000 a year. The chapter also notes William Wood's purchases in China and the East Indies for the Museum, and butterflies from China and Japan, and an Argus pheasant from Malacca.

Philadelphia Museum (Peale's Museum)Chinese Museum of Nathan DunnAmerican Museum (New York)Boston Museum
9Full Stage and Final Curtain (1845-1854)p. 307

Full Stage and Final Curtain covers 1845 to 1854, the years in which the Peale collections were broken up. Edmund Peale buys the Museum at a sheriff's sale and reopens it in Masonic Hall with a theatre in the saloon, competing with Barnum, who acquires much of the collection after 1849 and runs it in the Swaim Building until a fire destroys much of it at the end of 1851. Sellers reconstructs the 1848 sale catalogue item by item and then traces what survived: objects that went to Kimball's Boston Museum, the Dickeson auction, and the Harvard Peabody Museum and Museum of Comparative Zoology. The portrait gallery goes to Cincinnati, returns to Philadelphia, and is sold at auction in 1854. The chapter closes by arguing that Peale's model of popular, scientific display was lost in America and revived through Bickmore's American Museum of Natural History and the British New Museum Idea.

East and Southeast Asia Sellers notes the Asian material in the 1848 sale catalogue: three cases of Chinese curiosities, a Chinese war junk and boat, a pagoda, twelve fans and umbrellas, and 98 East India figures, the model junk probably sent by William Wood in the 1830s. A Carbondale collector's 1858 list includes forty-four cases of Chinese insects, which Sellers links to Wood's 1831 shipment, and a pair of Chinese boots came from William Burke Wood. A fake Japanese mermaid made by McGuigan is also described.

Shapiro, Michael Steven (ed.); Kemp, Louis Ward (1990). The Museum: A Reference Guide. New York: Greenwood Press.Asia: slight12 chapter overviews

Overview

The Museum: A Reference Guide, edited by Michael Steven Shapiro and Louis Ward Kemp (1990), is a bibliographic survey of the literature on American museums, written for general readers, museum studies students and beginning professionals. Each of its twelve chapters, by a different contributor, takes one kind of museum or one aspect of museum work (natural history, art, science and technology, history, folk, collections, education, exhibition, the public, biography, professionalism) and pairs a historical narrative with a critical survey of sources and a bibliographic checklist. The introduction argues that the literature has been neglected and disorganised. Appendixes list museum directories, archives and periodicals, and an index follows.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia receive slight attention, almost all of it in passing. Asia appears in the chapters' historical asides and survey sources, not in any extended account of museums in Asia. Asian objects surface in Western collections: Chinese porcelain in European cabinets of curiosities and China-trade goods in Peale's early Philadelphia museum, including Chinese pheasants that Peale obtained from George Washington (chapter 1, lines 391-393, 469-470 and 834-835); Oriental curiosities in Peale's museum (chapter 10, Kemp, lines 12900-12901); and Fenollosa's introduction of Charles Lang Freer to Japanese art, which Freer built into a collection of Oriental paintings (chapter 10, lines 13361-13362 and 13859).

Asian museums come up only as citations. The science and technology chapter cites a 1979 study of children and the science museum in Bangkok, a 1974 article on the Singapore Science Centre and a 1980 workshop on science museums in Asian countries (chapter 3, lines 3307-3308 and 3505-3508). The natural history survey cites a 1976 study of anthropology museums in East, South and Southeast Asia (chapter 1, lines 904-905). The one substantive remark on Asia is in the professionalism chapter (chapter 11, Teather, lines 14916-14923): Japan requires a four-year museology programme at one of sixty-seven approved universities and a national examination for the rank of professional curator, which is contrasted with voluntary training in North America. None of the passages read names a Korean, Taiwanese or Philippine museum, and the volume does not treat colonial collecting, restitution or Asian national heritage policy. The Japanese-American internment exhibit discussed in the history chapter (chapter 4, lines 4679-4682) concerns the United States, not Asia.

Theoretical approach of this work
Acknowledgmentsp. ix
Introductionp. xi

This introduction to a reference guide on American museums argues that the literature has been neglected: books about museums were written mostly by directors and insiders for a small readership, and the field is disorganized and unevaluated. Each chapter pairs a historical narrative with a survey of sources and a bibliographic checklist. It previews chapters on natural history, art, science and technology, history and folk museums, education, exhibitions, audiences, collections management, biographies and professionalism. Appendixes list directories, archives and periodicals.

1The Natural History MuseumCharlotte M. Porterp. 1

Porter traces how natural history museums in the United States grew out of eighteenth-century cabinets of curiosities. Charles Willson Peale's Philadelphia museum is the starting point: its mounted birds, reconstructed mastodon and painted habitats set a model that later institutions copied. Porter then follows rival institutions, among them the Academy of Natural Sciences in Philadelphia, Agassiz's Museum of Comparative Zoology, the Smithsonian's National Museum, the American Museum of Natural History and the Carnegie and Field museums, whose dinosaur hunts and habitat groups were paid for by wealthy patrons. A later section turns to ethnographic collections, including the Jesup North Pacific Expedition and the clash between Franz Boas and Henry Fairfield Osborn over how museums should present non-European peoples. Porter argues that federal constitutional limits, private philanthropy and the fossil feuds of Marsh and Cope shaped these institutions more than any coherent scientific plan. Porter closes by noting that collection policy is now being reassessed in light of habitat loss and conservation.

East and Southeast Asia European cabinets of curiosities held Chinese porcelain, and the China trade supplied some of Peale's early clothing, weapons and utensils. Chinese pheasants that Peale obtained from George Washington are still on display at Harvard's Museum of Comparative Zoology. These are passing mentions only.

Peale's Museum, PhiladelphiaAcademy of Natural Sciences of PhiladelphiaMuseum of Comparative Zoology, HarvardAmerican Museum of Natural HistoryU.S. National Museum (Smithsonian)Peabody Museum, YaleCarnegie Museum, PittsburghField Museum, Chicago
2The Art MuseumEdith A. Tonellip. 31

Tonelli traces the Western art museum, and mainly the American one, as an institution split between preserving precious objects and educating the public. Tonelli starts with the Greek setting-aside of objects for contemplation and the royal collections that opened to the public in Europe, then turns to the first American museums, which mixed art with historical and natural objects. The bulk of the chapter covers the 1870s founding of the great urban museums and the clash between Gilman's aesthetic position in Boston and John Cotton Dana's democratic one at the Newark Museum, along with New Deal and postwar debates. Its most detailed section covers the 1960s and 1970s, when Hoving's 'Harlem on My Mind' show, museum strikes and the Pasadena takeover of the Norton Simon collection exposed the tension between elite standards and social relevance. A long survey of the literature follows, sorting chronological histories from partisan essays. Tonelli ends by arguing that the art museum must keep its treasure-house role while serving diverse publics in an interdependent world.

Metropolitan Museum of ArtMuseum of Fine Arts, BostonNewark MuseumMuseum of Modern ArtPasadena Museum of Modern Art (later Norton Simon Museum)National Gallery of ArtGuggenheim MuseumBrooklyn Museum
3The Museum of Science and TechnologyBernard S. Finnp. 59

Finn traces museums of science and technology from Renaissance cabinets of curiosities and nineteenth-century industrial fairs to large historical collections such as London's Science Museum, the Deutsches Museum in Munich and Chicago's Museum of Science and Industry. Finn sets these against science centers, beginning with the Palais de la Decouverte in Paris (1931), which taught principles with few original objects and multiplied after Sputnik. Finn shows how social history, large-format film, microcomputers and the cost of storing big machines have shaped recent exhibits. Much of the chapter is a critical survey of the literature on museum origins, visitor evaluation and exhibit reviews. It records critics such as Basalla and Learner, who faulted displays of technological progress for lacking social context and for corporate promotion. The chapter closes by describing the field's literature as small and recent.

East and Southeast Asia Finn reviews literature on science museums in developing countries, citing a 1979 study of children and the science museum in Bangkok, a 1974 article on the Singapore Science Centre, and a 1980 workshop on science museums in Asian countries whose participants wanted to keep elements of the past. These are citations in the survey of sources rather than discussion of Asian museums by the chapter itself.

Science Museum, LondonDeutsches Museum, MunichMuseum of Science and Industry, ChicagoPalais de la Decouverte, ParisSmithsonian Museum of History and TechnologyNational Air and Space MuseumExploratorium, San FranciscoFranklin Institute, Philadelphia
4The History MuseumScott T. Swankp. 85

Swank argues that history museums are central to collective memory, the selected version of the past that families, groups and nations use to form their identities. Swank starts with early American ambivalence about history and with the historical societies of Massachusetts, New York and Pennsylvania, which functioned more as libraries than museums, and with the 1876 centennial, which prompted federal collecting. The chapter then follows the antiquarians, whose historic houses and period rooms, from the Essex Institute to the Metropolitan's American Wing, promoted a colonial ideal of taste. It traces the split between academic historians, who professionalized after 1884, and museum workers, then the federal entry into the field during the Depression and the creation of the Museum of History and Technology in 1960. Swank shows postwar and bicentennial museums moving from commemoration toward interpretation and social history. Swank ends by urging museums to confront the people and events they have ignored, since memory is a selective principle.

National Museum of American History (Museum of History and Technology)Metropolitan Museum of Art (American Wing)Colonial WilliamsburgEssex Institute, SalemGreenfield Village
5The Folk MuseumElizabeth M. Adlerp. 115

Adler traces the folk museum from eighteenth-century European rustic fantasies, such as Marie Antoinette's Petit Trianon, to the open-air museums begun by Artur Hazelius, whose Skansen in Stockholm (1891) set the pattern. Adler shows how Scandinavian founders collected peasant life before industrialization erased it, and how folklife research gave these museums a theory of studying a whole culture. The chapter then covers Britain, where open-air museums came later and mostly through individuals, and the United States, where Old Sturbridge Village, the Farmers' Museum and Colonial Williamsburg followed the Scandinavian model while newer sites such as Old World Wisconsin stressed ethnic history and visitor involvement. The long survey of sources reviews guides and theory and sets out disputes over reconstruction versus preservation in situ and over whether folk museums simplify the past. Adler ends by listing unresolved professional problems, among them the dilution of reality and inadequate funding.

Skansen (Nordiska Museet), StockholmFrilandsmuseet, CopenhagenMaihaugen, NorwayOld Sturbridge VillageFarmers' Museum, CooperstownColonial WilliamsburgOld World WisconsinPlimoth Plantation
6Museum CollectionsKatherine Spiess and Philip Spiessp. 141

Spiess and Spiess explain how museum collections are formed and managed. They begin with the motives of collectors, from the Renaissance cabinet of curiosities to the private gifts that became public museums in the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. The chapter then argues that public museums have a dual duty to preserve and interpret what they hold, and it traces how that duty was learned through damage and loss: the deterioration of excavated objects, the Wilkes Expedition specimens destroyed at the National Institute, and the scientific conservation that followed the excavation of Tutankhamen's tomb. It then turns to the 1970s, when press attacks on the Metropolitan Museum's sales and claims for sacred objects forced museums to document their holdings and write collections policies. The concluding survey guides students to works on collecting, law, conservation and computer documentation. The chapter ends by noting that collections management is now a formal set of duties rather than a secondary task.

Metropolitan Museum of ArtPeale's Museum, PhiladelphiaNational Gallery, LondonNational Institute for the Promotion of Science, Washington
7Museum EducationKenneth A. Yellisp. 167

Yellis begins with a puzzle: museums are popular, yet most Americans visit rarely and find the museum code foreign. Yellis traces the debate over museum education from George Brown Goode's labels-and-specimens model and Gilman's view that art must be enjoyed, not taught, through Dana and Kent's populism, to Low's postwar call for museums to serve the public. Yellis argues that this debate produced rival ideologies rather than tested theory. The more productive body of work is visitor research, from Edward Robinson's studies of fatigue and orientation in the 1920s to cold-war studies of attitude change and the Milwaukee exhibit surveys. The strongest recent line is Marilyn Hood's model of frequent visitors, occasional visitors and non-visitors, which treats museum-going as a learned behavior shaped by family and schooling. The chapter ends by urging museum leaders to put visitor needs first, though it notes that the field still lacks a theory to guide them. The survey of sources is a critical review of this literature.

Metropolitan Museum of ArtMuseum of Fine Arts, BostonNewark MuseumMilwaukee Public MuseumRoyal Ontario Museum
8Museum ExhibitionWilcomb E. Washburnp. 199

Washburn traces how museum exhibition developed from the private cabinets of early collectors into the designer-led displays of the late twentieth century. The chapter begins with the relic cases of medieval churches and the Renaissance galleries of Italian princes, then turns to America, where Charles Willson Peale's habitat groups and P. T. Barnum's hoaxes shaped a style aimed at a mass audience. It follows the nineteenth-century world's fairs, the separation of public exhibits from research collections, and the Kensington case. The main body concerns post-war modernization: designers brought in from outside, Frank Oppenheimer's Exploratorium, Thomas Hoving's Metropolitan, the Eames show attacked by Hilton Kramer, and the controversy over the British Museum (Natural History). It also surveys visitor-behavior research and the slow start of exhibition reviews in scholarly journals. Washburn concludes that whether exhibits teach better than objects remains unanswered, and that the case for design rests on evidence not yet gathered.

Peale's MuseumBritish MuseumAmerican Museum (Barnum)Milwaukee Public MuseumExploratoriumMetropolitan Museum of ArtVictoria and Albert MuseumPompidou Center
9The Public and the MuseumMichael S. Shapirop. 231

Shapiro challenges the traditional story of the museum and the public, which runs from crowds of gawking commoners through Enlightenment optimism to a modern ideology of public service. Shapiro argues that eighteenth- and early nineteenth-century museums were restricted, that the bourgeoisie had not yet adopted the habit of museum-going, and that public-service ideals emerged gradually. Shapiro’s evidence includes the British Museum's ticket system, the Louvre's limited opening days, Henry Cole's evening lighting at the South Kensington Museum, and the international exhibitions. Later sections cover the 1920s fight against museum fatigue at Boston's Museum of Fine Arts, Depression-era branch museums, postwar talk of an informal liberal arts college, the crowds for the Mona Lisa at the National Gallery, and Thomas Hoving's efforts at the Metropolitan. Shapiro concludes that 1970s visitor surveys showed an audience that was young, educated and affluent, and that working-class and minority Americans remained underrepresented.

British MuseumLouvreSouth Kensington MuseumMetropolitan Museum of ArtMuseum of Fine Arts, BostonNational GalleryMuseum of Modern ArtNewark Museum
10Biography and the MuseumLouis W. Kempp. 263

Kemp argues that each museum reflects the interaction of a forceful personality, its local community and prevailing intellectual trends, and tests this across a long run of cases. The chapter begins with the London of Hans Sloane and the coffeehouse of Don Saltero, which show elite and popular museum styles side by side, then follows Charles Willson Peale in Philadelphia, Daniel Drake's Western Museum in Cincinnati and P. T. Barnum's New York museum. Louis Agassiz's Harvard museum and the Smithsonian's divided aims under Joseph Henry and Spencer Baird come next, followed by the British Museum, Henry Cole at South Kensington and the industrialists who founded museums in Pittsburgh and New York. It ends with Dana's Newark Museum, Andrew Mellon's National Gallery and the directors recruited by trustees, and Thomas Hoving's Metropolitan in the 1960s. Kemp concludes that Hoving's effort to combine scholarly and popular styles collapsed under his own flaws, leaving the task to later museum people.

East and Southeast Asia Kemp touches on Asian objects only briefly. Peale's Philadelphia museum displayed Oriental curiosities that reflected the city's role in the China trade, and Ernest Fenollosa introduced Charles Lang Freer to Japanese art, which Freer later built into a collection of Oriental paintings.

Peale's MuseumWestern Museum of CincinnatiAmerican Museum (Barnum)Museum of Comparative ZoologyBritish MuseumVictoria and Albert MuseumMetropolitan Museum of ArtAmerican Museum of Natural History
11Professionalism and the MuseumJ. Lynne Teatherp. 299

Teather asks whether museum work is a profession and concludes that it is at best a semi-profession. The chapter explains that museum staff have come by many routes, as amateurs, technicians, artists and scholars, and have divided between an object-centred ideology of research and a public-oriented one of education, a split that weakened professional claims. The chapter follows the founding of the Museums Association in 1889 and the American Association of Museums in 1906, the spread of training courses from Iowa to Leicester and Manchester, and the 1930s debate between Alexander Ruthven, who denied that museum work had any basis of its own, and Laurence Coleman, who did not. Later sections cover postwar accreditation, codes of ethics and the 1971 strike at the Museum of Modern Art. Teather finds that North American training remains voluntary, that no single body of knowledge has emerged, and that museology is still an emerging field. It ends by arguing that its future depends on developing theory within the occupation's social structure.

East and Southeast Asia Teather notes that Japan has the most closely controlled system of museum preparation: every museum worker must complete a four-year museology programme at one of sixty-seven approved universities and pass a national examination before becoming a professional curator. Japan's position contrasts with North American museums, where training remains voluntary.

Sherman, Daniel J.; Rogoff, Irit (eds.) (1994). Museum Culture: Histories, Discourses, Spectacles. Minneapolis: University of Minnesota Press.Asia: occasional14 chapter overviews

Overview

Sherman and Rogoff's edited volume Museum Culture (1994) gathers nineteen essays on how museums shape the objects, contexts, publics and reception they present, and on the exhibition culture that lies behind display. The editors' introduction sets out four structuring concepts, object, context, public and reception, and draws on Foucault, Benjamin, Adorno and critical artists. The essays are grouped into Histories (Hoffmann on the German art museum, Koven on the Whitechapel picture exhibitions, Zolberg on audiences, Poulot on the French ecomuseum, Azoulay on Israeli museums), Discourses (Georgel, Sherman, Groys, Grasskamp) and Spectacles (Bohrer, Rogoff, Higonnet, Wallis). The scope is mainly nineteenth- and twentieth-century Europe and North America, with one chapter on Israel.

East and Southeast Asia in this work occasional

East and Southeast Asia are barely present. The one sustained treatment is Brian Wallis's chapter 17, 'Selling Nations: International Exhibitions and Cultural Diplomacy', which gives a substantial case study to the Festival of Indonesia (1990-92). Wallis shows that its exhibitions of classical sculpture and court arts ignored Indonesia's Muslims, who make up 90 percent of the population, until an ethnographic show, Beyond the Java Sea, was added. He also describes the oil-company sponsors (Mobil put up $1.3 million for The Sculpture of Indonesia), a Ford Foundation grant for lectures on East Timor and deforestation, and a wall label praising 'Indonesian grace' beside a sculpture of Vishnu.

Elsewhere the coverage is passing. Five Thousand Years of Korean Art (1979) appears in a list of blockbuster exhibitions, and Thailand and Vietnam appear only as future festival candidates in Ted Tanen's list. Zolberg's chapter 7 mentions that the Los Angeles museum printed educational materials in Chinese, Japanese and Korean. Azoulay's chapter 9 refers to Oriental Jews only within Israel. Bohrer's chapter 14 on exoticism concerns Egypt and the Near East, not East Asia.

Not covered: China, Japan, the Philippines, Burma, Cambodia and the other Southeast Asian states, and any Asian museum-building, collecting, restitution or war memory. The Asian festivals that the volume does treat sit beside an India exhibition at the Met (1985-86) and Turkey, which are discussed as parallel cases of cultural diplomacy outside the scope of this question.
