Introduction: Frameworks for Critical AnalysisDaniel J. Sherman and Irit RogoffPDF p. 10

Sherman and Rogoff introduce the collection by setting out a framework for studying museums as more than sites. They distinguish exhibited culture, what museums show, from exhibition culture, the ideas and values that shape showing, and argue that every museum rests on four linked concepts: object, context, public and reception. Museums classify objects and give them a national, local or period context, claim to serve a public, and then shape how that public receives them. The authors draw on Foucault for classification, on Adorno and Benjamin for collecting, and on artists such as Buren, Broodthaers and Haacke who expose museums' ideological work. They cite recent histories by Coombes, Poulot, Sherman and Zolberg, and feminist work by the Guerrilla Girls and Frenkel on the absence of women. The essays are grouped into histories, discourses and spectacle. The introduction ends by saying that these questions reach well beyond the museum and are a prerequisite for changing the culture they describe.

The German Art Museum and the History of the NationDetlef Hoffmannp. 3

Hoffmann traces how the German art museum came apart from the national past. Hoffmann starts with the post-Napoleonic sense of the Holy Roman Empire as a dead father whose treasures had to be kept, and with the Boisserée collection that became the nucleus of the Alte Pinakothek in Munich. Wackenroder's call for galleries as temples and Goethe's treatment of the Boisserée pictures as art history split art from history. The Germanic National Museum in Nuremberg, founded in 1852, was a collection of historical objects, while Louis-Philippe's history museum at Versailles and Kugler's proposal for a German equivalent joined history to painting. Hoffmann argues that the nineteenth-century museum divided art from history, so that its gaps, such as the absence of the working class and of women, went unnoticed until after 1968. Hoffmann then turns to the Nazi use of art, the 1992 Berlin exhibition on degenerate art and the German Historical Museum project. Hoffmann ends by proposing contemporary commissions and an aesthetic biography built from personal pictures, so that the art museum can show how national myths are made.

Germanisches Nationalmuseum (Nuremberg)Alte Pinakothek (Munich)Versailles history museumMuseum of German History (Zeughaus, East Berlin)German Historical Museum (Berlin)Altes Museum (Berlin)
The Whitechapel Picture Exhibitions and the Politics of SeeingSeth Kovenp. 22

Koven examines the picture exhibitions held at St Jude's parish school in Whitechapel from 1881, organised by Samuel and Henrietta Barnett of Toynbee Hall to bring art to the East End poor, and their successor, the Whitechapel Free Art Gallery of 1898. Koven sets the Barnetts' aims beside Ruskin's view that seeing is moral and religious, and beside Ruskin's own museum at Walkley near Sheffield, which the Barnetts adapted by opening on Sundays with a cheap catalogue. The catalogues, which quoted Ruskin and Watts, told visitors how to read pictures morally, and they ignored form and colour, since Samuel Barnett was colour-blind. Koven argues that the public used the exhibitions for its own ends: visitors voted for narrative pictures, read gold frames as signs of wealth and linked a painting of a convent child to their own guilt and poverty. Attendance reached 73,271 in 1892, and a docker who saw Crane's The Bridge of Life found his own house more squalid afterwards. Koven concludes that the exhibitions were both instruments of social control and sincere attempts at cross-class exchange, and that the settlers' cultural philanthropy was later rejected by William Beveridge.

Whitechapel Fine Art Loan Exhibition (St Jude's)Whitechapel Free Art GalleryRuskin's Walkley Museum (Sheffield)National GalleryBritish Museum
~An Elite Experience for Everyone~: Art Museums, the Public, and Cultural LiteracyVera L. Zolbergp. 49

Zolberg asks whether art museums can serve a broad public without giving up the standards of high art, taking Joshua Taylor's phrase an elite experience for everyone as her title. Zolberg separates the museum's public into self-selected visitors and those the museum might seek out. Drawing on DiMaggio, Useem and Brown's review of more than three hundred audience studies, she finds that art museums draw better-educated, wealthier and older visitors than history or science museums, and that many American museum people have rejected an educational role since Gilman in 1915. Museum educators are a devalued profession, outranked by curators. Bourdieu's 1960s studies in several countries found that a visit depended on education and habitus, so the least educated felt intimidated by solemn halls and unclear labels, while the highly educated came prepared. Zolberg then describes the Centre Pompidou, whose audiences proved as narrow as any French museum's, and American programmes such as the Brooklyn Museum's partnerships and the Los Angeles museum's multilingual materials. Zolberg ends that the elite experience can be widened by treating art education as a social right, and that the museum's authority over standards is already shared with critics and artists.

Centre PompidouBrooklyn MuseumLos Angeles Museum of Contemporary ArtNew Museum of Contemporary Art
Identity as Self-Discovery: The Ecomuseum in FranceDominique Poulotp. 66

Poulot examines the French ecomuseum, which appeared in the 1970s as part of the wider 'new museology' and was given its classic definition by Georges-Henri Rivière, who co-founded the Musée de l'Homme and the National Museum of Popular Arts and Traditions. The ecomuseum, he argues, rejected the classical museum's claim to hold a national heritage in favour of a community's own territory, memory and participation, and its roots lie in French ruralist geography, interwar ethnography and the folklore museums of the Vichy years. Two cases anchor the discussion: the Le Creusot-Montceau-les-Mines ecomuseum of 1974, whose four fields of activity he sets out, and the Nord-Dauphiné ecomuseum, whose 1980s exhibitions on local wine, photographs, military service and truck drivers he examines. Poulot shows the form drifting toward industrial conversion and nostalgia during economic crisis, and balancing self-recognition against presenting a community to outsiders. Poulot concludes that the ecomuseum aims to reveal the meaning of everyday practice in the present, a mirror held up to its community.

Musée de l'HommeNational Museum of Popular Arts and Traditions (ATP)Ecomuseum of Le Creusot-Montceau-les-MinesEcomuseum of the Nord-DauphinéPaper Museum at Ambert
With Open Doors: Museums and Historical Narratives in Israel's Public SpaceAriella Azoulayp. 85

Azoulay examines how Israeli history museums build a public image of the past that supports the Zionist claim to the land. Through the Tower of David Museum of the History of Jerusalem, Bezalel, the Shrine of Art at Ein Harod and Yad Vashem, she shows four procedures: universalized preservation, which presents national claims as neutral scholarship; art enlisted for ideology; the enthusiastic amateur founder; and fabricated exhibits set among authentic objects. The Jerusalem museum omits the Jordanian period and Palestinian claims, and Yad Vashem sends memorial certificates into private homes. After 1977, when Likud came to power, roughly eighty new museums opened for previously marginal groups. Azoulay argues that most of them, including the Jewish Diaspora Museum and the Museum for the Heritage of Babylonian Jewry, absorbed their subjects into the established Zionist narrative. Palestinian commemoration survives only in temporary forms such as Land Day and graffiti. The chapter concludes that the new openness of recent decades has been absorbed by dominant culture rather than changing the image of the past.

Tower of David Museum of the History of JerusalemBezalel museumShrine of Art at Ein HarodYad VashemTel Aviv Art MuseumJabotinsky HouseJewish Diaspora MuseumMuseum for the Heritage of Babylonian Jewry
The Museum as Metaphor in Nineteenth-Century FranceChantal Georgelp. 113

Georgel examines the nineteenth-century French museum as a metaphor, arguing that the illustrated press of the period borrowed the museum's name, aims and layout, so that the 'printed museum' became a model of encyclopedic knowledge available to all. Georgel surveys more than seventy periodicals with 'museum' in their titles, from the Musée des familles of 1833 to the archaeological and hunting journals of later decades, and shows how their editors promised readers collections of reproductions, complete coverage of human knowledge, and moral instruction through family portraits and anecdotes. Georgel then links these publications to the Louvre and to the department store, both of which used display, glass cases and shop vocabulary, and argues that the press, the museum and the store were complementary machines of consumption and accumulation. Visitors and magazines alike treated works of art as costly commodities. The chapter ends by asking whether the crowds at major museums today still seek this symbolic possession, which the catalogue now partly carries on.

LouvreMuseum of Natural History (Paris)Calais museum
Quatremre/Benjamin/Marx: Art Museums, Aura, and Commodity FetishismDaniel J. Shermanp. 123

Sherman examines the critique of art museums as commodity fetishism, arguing that it began not with Adorno or Marx but with Antoine-Chrysostome Quatremère de Quincy, the leading art theorist of the Revolution and later secretary of the Académie des Beaux-Arts. Sherman reads Quatremère's 1796 Lettres à Miranda and 1815 Considérations morales against the background of the Louvre's creation, where the Revolutionary commission rejected the dealer Lebrun as too close to the marketplace. Quatremère's objection, Sherman argues, is that museums remove works from their original context and so strip them of moral purpose, turning them into objects of price, a 'picture shop' in his phrase. Sherman then sets Quatremère beside Marx, Adorno and especially Walter Benjamin, whose 'aura' and exhibition value parallel Quatremère's loss of utility. The chapter concludes with the Belgian artist Marcel Broodthaers, whose 1972 Documenta 5 'museum fiction', a black square on the floor marked 'Private Property', is presented as a modernist version of Quatremère's critique.

LouvreMusée des Monuments Français (Lenoir's museum)Musée d'Art Moderne, Département des Aigles (Broodthaers, Documenta 5)
The Struggle against the Museum; or, The Display of Art in Totalitarian SpaceBoris Groysp. 144

Groys examines the Russian avant-garde's assault on the museum after 1917 and the Stalinist culture that followed. Groys argues that the museum, a place set apart for pure contemplation, was intolerable to totalitarian projects that wanted art and daily life to coincide. Malevich's essay 'On the Museum' urged that old art be left to ruin or burnt, and Tarabukin wanted the museum abolished in favour of production, yet both still viewed the world from a museum perspective. The Soviet state requisitioned imperial and private collections and recast their art as folk culture stolen by the ruling classes, drawing on Lenin's 'two cultures in one' to justify this. Socialist realism then filled public space with works modelled on museum art, and the Artists' Union, not curators, controlled purchases and exhibitions. The chapter concludes that the attempt to merge art and life produced a glut of serial, interchangeable works that devalued art for the museum and the market alike.

~Degenerate Art~ and Documenta I: Modernism Ostracized and DisarmedWalter Grasskampp. 163

Grasskamp examines the first Documenta, held in Kassel in 1955, as an answer to the Nazi exhibition Degenerate Art of 1937, which he argues it answered only partly. The founders rehabilitated modernism with a sweeping, universal account of art, placing archaic and 'primitive' works on the lobby photo wall while suppressing the sources the Nazis had attacked: art by the mentally ill, colonial sculpture and children's drawings. Photographs of respectable artists in suits and the Lehmbruck Kneeler at the entrance answered the charges of degeneracy. Grasskamp also shows that the Documenta depoliticized art, excluded Weimar political artists and German-Jewish artists, and sidelined design and photography. The reduction of modernism to an 'ism' prepared the ground for later postmodernism, he argues, and only Documenta 5 in 1972, under Szeemann's 'Individual Mythologies', openly took up the buried history.

Degenerate Art exhibition (Munich, 1937)Documenta I (Kassel, 1955)Documenta 5 (Kassel, 1972)Museum Fridericianum (Documenta venue)
The Times and Spaces of History: Representation, Assyria, and the British MuseumFrederick N. Bohrerp. 197

Bohrer examines how the Assyrian sculptures excavated by Layard and Botta in the 1840s were displayed and read at the British Museum and in the popular press. Bohrer argues that the Assyrian objects sat uneasily between antiquities and art, and that the trustees, one of whom called them 'a parcel of rubbish', housed them first in a corridor-like Antiquities Gallery and then in a basement room before rooms were built for them in 1853. Public pressure, visible in the Boxing Day 1846 crowd turned away at the gate, shaped the decision to place the great winged bulls in the entrance hall. The Illustrated London News, Layard's best-selling Nineveh and Its Remains, a panorama and Charles Kean's staging of Byron's Sardanapalus each recast Assyria from a temporal, antiquarian object into a spatial, visual spectacle. Bohrer concludes that the museum's primacy was never really threatened, since these popular versions confirmed its authority while carrying the objects beyond its walls.

British Museum
From Ruins to Debris: The Feminization of Fascism in German-History MuseumsIrit Rogoffp. 223

Rogoff asks how German history museums display National Socialism and argues that they have 'feminized' it, filling exhibitions with women, domestic objects and the culture of survival rather than with the state, the military and the regime's own aesthetic. Rogoff opens with a 1946 Vogue article on German women and with a 1930s lingerie mannequin she saw in the City Museum in Osnabrück, reading both through Freud's idea of the fetish. Rogoff’s wider frame is the Historikerstreit and the Alltagsgeschichte school, which she thinks encouraged displays of debris over coherent narrative. Rogoff’s main cases are the Topography of Terror in Berlin, left as unreconstructed Gestapo cellars, the Berlin, Berlin exhibition of 1987 and the opening show of the Deutsches Historisches Museum in 1989. Helke Sander's film on the mass rapes of 1945 shows how women's experience was excluded from official narratives. Rogoff concludes that casting visitors as victims produces empathy rather than critical understanding, so that the national past is never mastered.

Topography of TerrorBerlin, Berlin exhibition (Martin Gropius Bau)City Museum, OsnabrückDeutsches Historisches Museum
A New Center: The National Museum of Women in the ArtsAnne Higonnetp. 250

Higonnet examines the National Museum of Women in the Arts (NMWA) in Washington, D.C., which opened in 1987, and argues that the controversy around it was less about women's art than about feminism's entry into the economics of the art museum. Critics on the right objected to mixing politics with culture, and critics on the left felt it did not mix them enough, while others objected to its separate status. Higonnet follows the founder, Wilhelmina Holladay, whose fund-raising, corporate sponsorship and amateur administration were set against professional museum norms. Higonnet’s evidence includes the $8 million refurbishment of a former Masonic temple, whose ground floor is given over to a lobby, a gift shop and rentable halls, and a membership drive that reached more than 80,000 people by 1988. Higonnet sets this beside the Boston Museum of Fine Arts, whose galleries and volunteer docents rely on women's labour and gala fund-raising. Higonnet concludes that the NMWA is effective, compromising feminism, which exposes the class and commercial assumptions of the art museum and gives many women a voice, while making plain the gap between feminist ideals and what can be done.

National Museum of Women in the ArtsBoston Museum of Fine Arts
Selling Nations: International Exhibitions and Cultural DiplomacyBrian Wallisp. 265Asia: in part

Wallis treats national cultural festivals, such as Mexico: A Work of Art (1990) and Turkey: The Continuing Magnificence (1987-88), as public relations for nations, and asks how the art exhibitions at their centre construct a national identity for American audiences. Wallis argues that the festivals are designed and funded largely by American organizers, advertisers and corporate sponsors, and that they replace negative stereotypes with chosen images of past glory. Wallis’s case studies are The Age of Sultan Suleyman the Magnificent at the National Gallery of Art, Mexico: Splendors of Thirty Centuries at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, and the Metropolitan's India! Art and Culture show of 1985-86. He reads catalogues and wall labels closely: the Mexico show moves from Aztec art to the Spanish conquest and modern painting without explaining the conquest, while the Turkish show presents an elite court culture, which Wallis calls self-Orientalizing. He ends by linking festivals to tourism, trade and corporate sponsorship, and by arguing that such exhibitions leave out contemporary politics and turn museums into a form of promotion.

East and Southeast Asia Wallis gives a substantial case study to the Festival of Indonesia (1990-92), whose exhibitions focused on classical sculpture and court arts and ignored Muslims, who make up 90 percent of the population, until an ethnographic show was added. Wallis describes oil-company sponsorship, Ford Foundation lectures on East Timor and deforestation, and a wall label praising 'Indonesian grace' beside a Vishnu. Five Thousand Years of Korean Art, and Thailand and Vietnam as future festival candidates, appear only in passing.

Siegel, Jonah (ed.) (2008). The Emergence of the Modern Museum: An Anthology of Nineteenth-Century Sources. New York: Oxford University Press.Asia: slight48 chapter overviews

Overview

An anthology of nineteenth-century writings on the museum in Britain, drawn from parliamentary committees and debates, periodical articles, catalogues and testimony, with a long introduction and a headnote to each section by the editor. Its argument is that the public museum emerged as a compromise between preservation, study, display and instruction, and that its meaning was never settled: objects reach the museum after losses, and visitors see things their collectors did not intend. The selections concern London's British Museum, National Gallery, Elgin Marbles, South Kensington Museum and India Museum, with provincial collections and natural history. The book runs in two parts, 'From Collection to Museum' and 'Rationalizing the National Collections', the second including pedagogy, reform, anthropology and archaeology, and India.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia appear only in passing. No chapter is marked as main or part, and the mentions in about a dozen selections are catalogue items, comparisons and remarks on taste. In William Bullock's 1810 catalogue (chapter 6), a Chinese lady's shoe, sixteen hollow ivory balls cut 'by the Chinese' and a mother-of-pearl Chinese pagoda sit among curiosities. The 1836 Penny Magazine history of the British Museum (chapter 18) lists a gilt figure of Gaudma, a Burmese idol, presented by Captain Marryat. The 1859 Leisure Hour tour of the South Kensington Museum (chapter 39) describes a Siamese state chair, canopy and gold vestments given to Queen Victoria by two Siamese kings, a sword sent by the King of Siam to Palmerston, and Chinese and Japanese porcelain, lacquer and bronzes in the Structure Gallery. Bicknell's 1847 tour (chapter 32) places idols and figures from China and Japan in the Ethnographical Room.

Later selections use the region mainly as comparison. The 1853 testimony on the national collections (chapter 28) asks whether 'more barbarous specimens, such as the Chinese' harm taste, and the answer is that artists should look at such objects less. Pitt-Rivers's 1874 Bethnal Green catalogue (chapter 48) includes a Chinese skull among its cast skulls. Jevons's 1883 essay (chapter 44) praises a loan of Japanese art shown at Nottingham Castle, lists Japanese idols as a possible curator's hobby collection, and gives a cork model of a Chinese temple as one of the odd objects in a county museum.

Southeast Asia is represented only by Siam and Burma, and no Asian museum, collector, curator or visitor is discussed. The large non-European topic is India (chapters 49 to 52), which is South Asia and outside this question; the Indian collection was divided between South Kensington and the British Museum in 1879 and 1880. The chronology lists Calcutta's Oriental Museum (1814) and the Tokyo National Museum, but the book does not treat them. The Preface regrets the lack of sustained treatment of imperial museums. Nothing is said about how Asian objects reached Britain beyond these passing items, about restitution, or about museum building by Asian states.

Contents

Theoretical approach of this work
PrefacePDF p. 11

Siegel introduces an anthology of nineteenth-century writings on the museum in Britain, which had become recognisably modern by 1914, when over 400 museums existed in Great Britain. Siegel explains that public museums are compromises between conservation, study, display and instruction, and that the texts, arranged thematically, mix essays and journalism with parliamentary testimony. Siegel also lists what is left out, including libraries, zoos and the Crystal Palace, and sets out his editorial conventions.

South Kensington Museum
AcknowledgmentsPDF p. 15
Chronologyp. xvi

A dated list of museum foundations and openings, mostly in London and elsewhere in Britain, from the Ashmolean (1683) and the British Museum (1753) to the Queen Elizabeth II Great Court and Tate Modern (2000), with a few continental entries in italics. It marks milestones such as the arrival of the Elgin Marbles in 1816, the Museums Act of 1845, the Great Exhibition, the South Kensington Museum (1857) and the wartime closure of all public galleries in 1916.

IntroductionJonah Siegelp. 3

Siegel's introduction argues that the nineteenth century was the age of the museum, when public institutions took shape in response to revolution, empire and a growing mass public. Siegel presents the museum as a compromise: it gathers objects usually torn from their original settings, so each museum rests on loss and dislocation. Siegel traces how Napoleonic plunder and the Elgin Marbles, bought for the British Museum in 1816, made display a symbol of political power, and how the British Museum grew from Sloane's collection into a repository that outgrew its premises. Siegel then shows how institutions were justified by claims about taste, design and social order, from Robert Peel's hope that museums would ease class division to the South Kensington Museum's design instruction. Siegel ends by arguing that objects rarely teach what their collectors intended, so the meaning of the modern museum remains unresolved.

British MuseumSouth Kensington MuseumLouvreNational GalleryAshmolean MuseumDulwich Picture Gallery
OneFrom Collection to Museump. 11
IPrivate CollectionsJonah Siegelp. 13

Siegel argues that English museums grew from private enterprise and a fragile public consensus rather than state direction, so private collections had to exist first. Siegel illustrates this with William Bullock's commercial display at the Egyptian Hall in Piccadilly, a mix of natural history, curiosities and paintings. Siegel then turns to Waagen's survey of British private holdings and to Hazlitt's sketches of picture galleries, which show art seen only sporadically through sales and visits to stately homes.

Bullock's Museum (Egyptian Hall)Leverian MuseumSir John Soane's MuseumBritish Museum
A Companion to Mr. Bullock's Museum (1810)William Bullockp. 15

Bullock's 1810 'Companion' is the catalogue for his Piccadilly museum, arranged case by case so that the visitor can follow a fixed route from the first case on the left. The opening cases hold Pacific material from Cook's voyages, including feather cloaks and helmets from the Sandwich Islands, a war club, and a fly-flap whose handle was made from a chief's arm bone, which Bullock obtained in exchange for a Queen's-ware wash basin. The catalogue then moves to a staircase case of fishing tackle, a shoe worn by the Polish dwarf Count Borulaski, wax and rice-paste figures, ivory carvings of Windsor and Geneva, and a long run of curiosities. The 'Natural History' section lists a baboon that let its wounds be dressed, a boa constrictor, a rhinoceros, a panther and a polar bear, set among artificial trees in a tropical forest. The last pages offer fossil bones from North America and Cheshire, Egyptian mummies, and hornbill heads. The entries combine exact description with showman's anecdote, so the text works both as an inventory and as an advertisement.

East and Southeast Asia The catalogue describes two Chinese objects: a set of sixteen hollow ivory balls, cut one inside another from a single piece 'by the Chinese', and a model of a Chinese pagoda in mother-of-pearl, carved and gilded. A Chinese lady's shoe is listed by name only.

Bullock's Museum (Egyptian Hall)Leverian Museum
Collecting in EnglandGustav Friedrich Waagenp. 26

Waagen traces the English taste for pictures from Henry VIII and Charles I, whose gallery the Parliamentary sale of 1649-53 scattered, through the country-house collections of the eighteenth century, to the purchases made after the French Revolution. Waagen finds the typical eighteenth-century gallery rich in Carracci, Guido and Poussin but thin in early Netherlandish and German masters, and singles out Earl Cowper's Panshanger as an honourable exception. The main case study is the Orleans Gallery, sold off in 1792 and bought by Bryan's syndicate of Bridgewater, Gower and Carlisle for far less than its value, followed by the Calonne sale of 1795. Waagen notes that Revolutionary upheaval brought the best Continental altarpieces and palace pictures to England, which had the money and buyers to take them. The excerpt ends with pictures consigned to England in large numbers.

Orleans GalleryPanshanger (Earl Cowper's collection)Walpole collection at Houghton HallCalonne collection
Blenheim PalaceGustav Friedrich Waagenp. 30

Waagen's short account of Blenheim Palace, the Marlborough seat near Oxford, calls its paintings one of the most considerable galleries in England. The chief interest is the Rubens collection, mostly of his earlier and middle periods, with admirable Van Dyck portraits. He describes the rooms in order, and says he was allowed to study the pictures alone for as long as he wished.

Blenheim Palace
Sir John Soane's MuseumGustav Friedrich Waagenp. 32

Waagen describes Sir John Soane's house-museum in Lincoln's Inn Fields as one of London's most remarkable curiosities, crowded with architectural casts, sculpture and pictures. Waagen singles out the Egyptian alabaster sarcophagus that Belzoni found in 1816 and Soane bought in 1824, and the Hogarth and Canaletto pictures hung on screens. Waagen judges the whole a feverish mixture of objects, though a splendid example of English eccentricity.

Sir John Soane's MuseumBritish Museum
Panshanger, Seat of Earl CowperGustav Friedrich Waagenp. 33

Waagen visited Earl Cowper's seat at Panshanger in Hertfordshire in 1835 and praises its mostly Italian collection, largely bought by the earl's grandfather while ambassador at Florence. Waagen admires the drawing-room, lit by skylights and hung with crimson silk, and the English habit of hanging art in rooms people use daily. The piece is chiefly a record of six hours alone with the pictures, interrupted only by bees and a housekeeper's keys.

Mr. Angerstein's CollectionWilliam Hazlittp. 34

Hazlitt's 1824 essay on John Angerstein's London collection praises it as perhaps the finest gallery of its size in the world, where a few first-rate pictures hold the eye. Hazlitt argues that seeing originals is like a pilgrimage, while prints only hint at what the painter achieved. The essay returns to Ludovico Carracci's Susannah and the Elders, which Hazlitt first saw years earlier in the Orleans collection.

2Toward a Public Art CollectionJonah Siegelp. 37

Siegel's section introduction argues that the move from private collection to public museum was contested from the start. Siegel shows how the 1816 Elgin Marbles report and debate raised questions of taste, cost and the morality of the marbles' acquisition, and how the National Gallery, founded on Angerstein's collection, was justified by Robert Peel's hope of easing class tensions. Siegel ends with Anna Jameson's 1842 handbook, which voiced art lovers' frustration with the gallery.

British MuseumNational Gallery
Report from the Select Committee on the Earl of Elgin's Collection (1816)House of Commonsp. 39

The 1816 Select Committee report records testimony from artists and connoisseurs on whether Lord Elgin's marbles from the Parthenon should become public property and what they are worth. The sculptors Nollekens and Flaxman praise the marbles as the finest works ever brought to England, and Flaxman argues that the Apollo Belvedere is a copy, giving detailed reasons. The questioning turns on whether the Theseus and Apollo are originals, and whether the Parthenon sculptures date from Pericles' time or were added under Hadrian. Richard Payne Knight, who places most of them in a second rank, values the collection at £25,000 by comparing it with prices Townley and Lansdowne paid to Roman dealers, while conceding that it would fetch under half that if sold piecemeal. Knight argues that the marbles' worth lies in their use as a school for artists, and that Elgin deserves national gratitude. The report closes by asking whether a national collection would improve British art, and Knight answers that a general museum would be valuable, while denying that sculpture has yet advanced.

British MuseumTownley collectionMuseo Pio-Clementino, Vatican
Parliamentary Debate on Purchasing the Elgin Marbles (1816)House of Commonsp. 50

This 1816 Commons debate records the argument over Bankes's motion to grant £35,000 for the Elgin Marbles. Bankes stresses the marbles' quality, their value compared with the Townley purchase, and the claim that the sum did not exceed Elgin's outlay. Curwen opposes the grant on grounds of public economy, and Hammersley on grounds of dishonesty, since the firman gave only limited rights and Elgin acted as ambassador. Croker defends Elgin at length, describing the ruin already suffered by the Parthenon, and calls the proposal to return the marbles to Turkey absurd. Long, Ward and Grant support the purchase as an opportunity that will not recur, while Best and Newport reject it on grounds of justice. Brougham doubts that the country can afford the purchase and a building to house it. The House divides and the motion is carried by 82 votes to 30.

Parliamentary Debate on Building the National Gallery (April 1832)House of Commonsp. 60

Peel asks for a definite sum, about £30,000, for a plain, well-lit gallery, noting that the National Gallery drew over 100,000 visitors a year. He argues that the fine arts matter to manufacturers, whose designs lag behind their machinery. Lord Althorp agrees a place is needed but will not spend on architecture, while Warburton and Lord Ashley back a plain building, the latter because it would draw artisans from alehouses.

National Gallery
Parliamentary Debate on Building the National Gallery (July 1832)House of Commonsp. 62

Spring Rice moves a first grant of £15,000 towards a National Gallery building costing £50,000 and made wholly of stone, with the Royal Academy's rooms at Somerset House exchanged for public offices. Peel welcomes the vote and argues that about £10,000 of the sum would secure the public records. He links the gallery to easing class tensions, since working people cannot hope for private pictures. Colborne predicts that donors will give works once there is a building.

The British Museum [History and Description] (1836)Anonymousp. 64

This anonymous 1836 Penny Magazine series, in four parts, traces the British Museum from its origins. Part I surveys the collections that preceded it, from Tradescant's 'Ark' and the Cotton and Sloane collections, to the lottery that funded their purchase in 1753, and visitor numbers rising from 33,074 in 1814 to 289,104 in 1835. Part II describes the Museum's departments and its official Synopsis, and suggests a cheaper, improved guide. Part III reports that most visitors skip the Gallery of Antiquities, and Part IV argues that taste is acquired through knowledge and that the Egyptian antiquities reveal daily life. The series ends by treating the collections as historical documents that show what humanity has been.

The National Gallery (1842)Anna Jamesonp. 72

Jameson's 1842 introduction to the National Gallery argues that England let the great collections of Charles I and the Italian nobility pass abroad, and was slow to found a public gallery. Jameson traces the purchase of Angerstein's collection in 1823, pushed through by Agar Ellis and Sir George Beaumont, and the gifts that followed, including Beaumont's own pictures in 1826. Jameson’s main complaint is the collection's gaps: few early Italian masters, scarcely any Spanish or Dutch painters, and almost no Van Dyck. Jameson describes the cramped rooms, the cellar where unshown pictures are kept, and the lack of arrangement, and argues that a gallery aimed at instruction must show the history of painting in order. Jameson compares it with Berlin, Munich, the Louvre and Florence, and ends by hoping that public enthusiasm will grow, since knowledge comes after love.

3The Public in the MuseumJonah Siegelp. 79

Siegel's section introduction argues that the public, more than the collection, shaped the nineteenth-century museum, and that fears of vandalism, dirt and the working classes drove debate. Siegel ties these fears to the weakness of British design against foreign competitors, and to the Penny Magazine and the 1836 and 1841 parliamentary reports. Siegel ends with a 1914 Punch cartoon of a boy breathing on glass in the British Museum, which shows the anxieties surviving into the twentieth century.

British MuseumNational Gallery
The British Museum (1832)Anonymousp. 82

An anonymous Penny Magazine piece of 1832 answers the charge that the English public is prone to mischief, arguing that people should be admitted freely to parks and galleries. It takes an artisan family through a visit to the British Museum, describing the free entry, the Elgin Marbles, and three rules: touch nothing, do not talk loudly, and do not be obtrusive. It ends by advising repeated visits.

British MuseumElgin Marbles (British Museum)
Report of the Select Committee on Arts and Their Connexion with Manufactures (1836)House of Commonsp. 85

The 1836 Select Committee on Arts and Manufactures concludes that British art has received little encouragement, and that the nation's weakness in design, compared with France and Prussia, comes from the expense and inaccessibility of art. The report argues that a manufacturing nation must encourage art in its higher forms, since good design raises humble industry, and points to free public galleries and cheap casts in Paris as models. It praises the Prussian design books of M. Beuth and the cheap magazines that spread images to working families, and it condemns the fees charged at Westminster Abbey and St Paul's. Its practical recommendations cover catalogues naming schools and painters, opening the galleries in the evening in summer, a room for British art and the Cartoons, and professional experts on the purchasing committees of the National Gallery. It ends by hoping that the inquiry will raise the status of the artist.

National GalleryBerlin GalleryMunich Gallery
Report of the Select Committee on National Monuments and Works of Art (1841)House of Commonsp. 90

This extract from the 1841 Select Committee on National Monuments and Works of Art gathers the Committee's comments on public admission to the British Museum and the National Gallery, with evidence from their officers. The Report praises the Museum's holiday openings, which drew up to 32,000 visitors in a day, and the Gallery's free access four days a week, whose numbers passed 500,000 a year. Most of the chapter is testimony. Gallery secretary Thwaites and attendant John Peter Wildsmith discuss crowding, catalogues and the case for Sunday opening, while the British Museum's Sir Henry Ellis, Edward Hawkins and John Edward Gray discuss the rule excluding children under eight, the closed King's Library, seating, cloakrooms and the dust that visitors bring in. Gray's comparisons with Paris, Munich and Vienna, where guards and fees restricted visitors, make the strongest case for open access. The chapter closes with his proposals for a ladies' cloakroom, dust gratings at the entrance and cheaper guides.

British MuseumNational GalleryLouvre
Report of the Select Committee on the National Gallery (1850)House of Commonsp. 124

This unit is testimony to the 1850 Select Committee on the National Gallery, given by the Keeper, Thomas Uwins, and by the secretary, Colonel Thwaites, under questions from members including Disraeli and Baring Wall. It turns on crowding, the condition of the pictures and the artists who copy in the Gallery. Uwins accepts that the atmosphere harms the paintings and blames visitors who eat, drink and let children run about in the rooms. He thinks admitting young children is injudicious, though Lord Liverpool wanted it, and explains the limits on students: two days a week are reserved for artists, about seventy may be admitted in each monthly period, and copying for sale is condemned, although he cannot say the Royal Academy students avoid it. He compares the Louvre, open to the public only on Sundays, with London's free access. The chapter ends with Uwins's answer that the Gallery has no room for a large donation.

4Art and the National GalleryJonah Siegelp. 137

Siegel introduces the second part of the book, on the rationalising of the national collections in London in the 1850s. Siegel sets the National Gallery's small, cramped holdings against the British Museum's sprawling collection, which includes the Elgin Marbles, and asks whether objects should be grouped by artistic value or by historical interest. The Great Exhibition and the Assyrian sculptures found by Layard frame the debate. The chapter ends with Waagen's 1853 essay on gallery design.

British MuseumNational Gallery
Testimony Before the Select Committee on the National Gallery (1853)House of Commonsp. 141

Witness testimony to the 1853 Select Committee on the National Gallery, from Charles Eastlake, the British Museum's antiquities curator Edmund Oldfield and the sculptor Richard Westmacott. The question is whether the national collections should be combined in one building, and where. Eastlake would divide the British Museum into books, fine art, mechanical art and natural history, with an art library and engravings beside the pictures, but concedes that inscriptions and drawings cannot be cleanly separated from the objects they explain. Oldfield argues that the Museum is chiefly a collection of historical antiquities and sketches a long museum on an open site, preferably Hyde Park, clear of smoke. Westmacott wants pictures and sculpture together so that painters learn form from casts and marbles, and says the Nineveh sculptures would not dull taste for the Elgin Marbles. The unit ends with his view that the medals must move as a whole and that the Etruscan vases belong with the sculpture.

British MuseumNational GalleryMuseum of Practical Art, Marlborough House
Testimony Before the National Gallery Site Commission (1857)House of Commonsp. 160

This long extract from the 1857 National Gallery Site Commission gathers evidence from five witnesses on whether the British Museum's antiquities should move, and whether they belong with the National Gallery's paintings. Panizzi, the principal librarian, defends the library as essential to the study of the marbles and wants the Natural History collections moved to free space. Hawkins, keeper of antiquities, favours a new museum in the middle of Hyde Park, clear of London smoke, and describes the marbles' discolouration and the soap-and-water cleaning. Oldfield, curator of sculpture, is more cautious and says that dust and smoke, rather than damp, do the harm. Westmacott favours a union of art in principle but will not see the Museum's sculpture divided. Ruskin, in the longest testimony, wants chronological galleries, with a popular gallery in the city and the precious works kept in a safer building. The unit closes with his views on glass, copies and restoration, which he would replace with perfect copies.

British MuseumNational GalleryMuseum of Practical Art, Marlborough HouseCrystal PalaceLouvre
Thoughts on the New Building to Be Erected for the National Gallery of England (1853)Gustav Friedrich Waagenp. 200

Waagen, the German art historian who had arranged the Berlin picture gallery, sets out his advice for the new National Gallery building, which the Government was funding from the surplus of the Great Exhibition. The site must lie beyond London's smoke yet stay close enough for public access, and the building needs far more wall space than the existing gallery, which he judges well below the Louvre. He treats lighting, the control of the architect by a commission, and damp, dust and crowding as threats to the pictures, and wants infants and persons in dirty clothes kept out. He compares Dresden, the Tribune in Florence and the Salon Carre in the Louvre to show how mixing schools diminishes masterpieces, and recommends arranging pictures chronologically by school and period. He ends with the case for an annual purchase grant of at least 30,000 pounds and for filling the gaps in the highest styles of the sixteenth century.

5Natural History and the British MuseumJonah Siegelp. 213

Siegel introduces Chapter Five, on natural history and the British Museum. The museum's mix of antiquities and natural specimens drew criticism at mid-century, notably from Elizabeth Eastlake, who argued for a separate natural history institution, and from the paleontologist Richard Owen, whose 1862 prospectus for it is excerpted. The chapter ends with an 1893 guide to the museum.

British MuseumNatural History Museum
The British Museum (1847)W. I. Bicknellp. 214

Bicknell's 1847 tour of the British Museum, printed in his illustrated survey of London, describes how the institution had recently opened up from a closed curiosity shop to a place where ordinary visitors, families and working people among them, could walk through the galleries. Much of the piece is practical: the days the public was admitted, how the reading rooms worked (readers wrote out their requests on slips and handed back their books before leaving), and which collections were restricted to special permission. The tour then moves through the rooms in turn: the Ethnographical Room with its Pacific, Arctic and American material, the natural history galleries of animals, shells, minerals and fossils, and the sculpture galleries, where Greek works from the Townley and Elgin collections are praised as models that modern British architecture and sculpture fail to match. The piece ends with the Egyptian Saloon, whose objects Bicknell links to Napoleon's expedition and the British capture of Alexandria. Its tone is patriotic and admiring rather than analytical.

British Museum
The British Museum (1858)Elizabeth Eastlakep. 220

Eastlake's 1858 review, drawing on parliamentary reports from 1835 to 1858, addresses the lack of space at the British Museum and the proposal to remove its natural history collections. The article argues for separation on four grounds: no single site can house departments that all grow at once; one building becomes too large to supervise; no director can command antiquities, natural history and literature together; and trustees vote on subjects they do not know. Answering a memorial from leading naturalists, the review contends that Parliament, not Sloane, founded the Museum, cites the loss of specimens in its early decades, and doubts that natural history draws most visitors. Kensington Gore or Burlington House are proposed as sites. The sharpest criticism falls on the superintendent's duties, which tie Richard Owen to routine office work and to lectures held at Jermyn Street, and the review ends that each collection hinders the others and only removal will help.

British Museum
The British Museum. Committee Moved For (1859)House of Commonsp. 226

A Commons debate of 1859 in which Gregory moved for a Select Committee to inquire into the reorganisation of the British Museum, a motion the Chancellor of the Exchequer had already agreed to grant. Gregory's case rests on congestion: natural history specimens are inaccessible and at risk, prints and drawings are poorly displayed, and antiquities lie in cellars or behind glass conservatories. Gregory cites reports by Gray and Panizzi from 1854 and 1857, recalls Lord Elcho's plan to split natural history among Jermyn Street, Kew and learned societies, and notes that a protest by 114 scientists, including Owen, opposed it. Regent's Park is proposed as an alternative to the Government's plan for Brompton. Gregory then turns to smaller matters: the Act restricting how surplus objects may be disposed of, the links between department heads and trustees, and the scarcity of scientists on the board. The speech closes by urging popular lectures for the middle and working classes, since foreign opinion will judge the reorganisation.

British Museum
On the Extent and Aims of a National Museum of Natural History (1862)Richard Owenp. 231

Owen's 1862 essay sets out what a national museum of natural history should contain and how much space it needs, at a time when the natural history departments of the British Museum were short of room. It begins by arguing that collections, prepared and arranged for comparison, are indispensable to natural knowledge alongside fieldwork, and traces how Aristotle, the Romans and later collectors used or lost their specimens. Owen then describes the four planned departments of zoology, geology, botany and mineralogy and explains which animal groups can be shown only in spirit or as coloured models. Three purposes for a museum are distinguished (public amusement, elementary teaching and scholarly study), and a fourth, a metropolitan display giving every class proportionate representation, is argued for. Once such a display is complete, growth in the number of specimens will need far less new space, and the objection that the public wants only birds and shells is rejected. The essay closes by presenting England as a model for national natural history museums.

British MuseumJardin des Plantes
Topographical Description of the Museum and Its Contents, British Museum (Natural History) (1893)William Henry Flowerp. 239

Flower's 1893 guide walks visitors through the Central Hall of the British Museum (Natural History), beginning with a fifty-foot sperm whale skeleton, presented in 1863 after the animal was stranded near Thurso. Flower uses it to show that a whale's flipper contains the same bones as a human arm and that vestigial hind-limb bones remain. The floor cases around it illustrate general principles of variation and adaptation: pigeon breeds derived from the rock dove, the seasonal plumage of the ruff, the winter camouflage of hares, stoats and grouse, and crows and goldfinches that grade into one another, blurring the idea of a species. The alcoves round the hall hold an introductory morphological collection, nicknamed the 'Index Museum', which is described as a general introduction to the systematic galleries. Its labelled skeletons of a monkey, bat, sloth, baboon, antelope and porpoise show how limbs are adapted to different ways of life. The guide is instructional rather than argumentative, designed to prepare the untrained visitor for the systematic displays beyond.

British Museum (Natural History)
6Pedagogy: South Kensington and the ProvincesJonah Siegelp. 244

Siegel's headnote introduces the pedagogic side of museum building. The South Kensington Museum, founded from Great Exhibition funds, was driven by teaching aims but soon became as heterogeneous as the older national collections. The section then turns to provincial museums, which a Chambers's Journal article of 1866 wanted reorganised around regional natural history, and to the national loan circulation from South Kensington that linked them to London.

South Kensington Museum
Extracts from an Introductory Address on the Functions of the Science and Art Department (1857)Henry Colep. 245

Cole's 1857 address defends the South Kensington collections as heterogeneous but useful, since the objects had lain unseen in cellars. The address argues that the temporary iron building must give way to permanent homes for patents, animal products, architecture and art, and that labels should let ordinary visitors understand what they see without buying a catalogue. It stresses evening opening for working people, free student access, and the museum as a central store that lends objects to provinces on request.

South Kensington MuseumArchitectural MuseumPatent Museum
The South Kensington Museum (1859)Anonymousp. 247

The anonymous author of this four-part series in the Leisure Hour (1859) gives a discursive tour of the South Kensington Museum. Its origins lie in the surplus from the Great Exhibition of 1851, and its buildings remain temporary iron sheds and galleries, while the Science and Art Department supplies provincial schools of art. The second article covers the Educational Museum, with its books, school models and object lessons, quoting the official guide at length. The third turns to the Museum of Animal Products and Food, where barley, starch, beer and wool are explained, and then to the Museum of Ornamental Art and the Architectural Museum, with its casts and plaster of Michelangelo's David. The fourth article covers the Patent Museum, with its glass pump, screw propellers and meat kept fresh with sulphurous acid. The writing is affectionate and anecdotal rather than argued, and it moves from one collection to the next without a single thesis.

East and Southeast Asia The author describes Siamese objects with some enthusiasm: two Siamese kings recently gave the Queen a state chair, a golden canopy and vestments of gold tissue made only in Siam, which are shown in the museum, and a sword sent by the King of Siam to Lord Palmerston was later given to the museum. Chinese and Japanese porcelain, lacquer and bronzes appear in a list of oriental art in the Structure Gallery.

South Kensington MuseumMuseum of Ornamental ArtArchitectural MuseumPatent MuseumEducational Museum
Provincial Museums (1866)Anonymousp. 259

This 1866 article in Chambers's Journal argues that provincial towns need museums of purely local specimens. Its anonymous author opens with a long quotation from Edward Forbes, who found English provincial museums to be heaps of curiosities from far away, labelled only with donors' names, and notes some improvement since. Local collections matter, the author argues, because a geologist can learn more from one good local museum than from a fortnight of travel, and because railway cuttings and quarries yield fossils that vanish once the works are finished. Antiquities such as coins, weapons and seals might otherwise end up in the British Museum or on a drawing-room chimney-piece. The article then sets practical rules: accept only specimens from a radius of ten to fifteen miles, mark the boundary on an Ordnance Survey map, and either separate local material into its own cases or mark it with a distinctive label. It offers two models, a Bern cabinet that marks Swiss specimens with a red cross and the Ferdinandeum at Innsbruck, where Tyrolean material has its own rooms.

British MuseumFerdinandeum (Innsbruck)Bern Museum
Report on the System of Circulation of Art Objects on Loan from the South Kensington Museum (1881)F.R. Sandfordp. 263

Sandford's 1881 report for the Science and Art Department traces how objects from South Kensington were lent to provincial schools of art and museums. It starts with the Museum of Ornamental Art at Marlborough House and its move to Brompton in 1857, then the first travelling collection, shown at Birmingham in 1855 and taken round the country with its own cases, truck and officer. Sandford sets out the conditions attached to loans, such as free admission for students, a penny fee on evenings and the division of surplus funds, and the later changes: the 1864 minute allowing any exhibited object to be lent, and the 1880 extension to corporation museums. Statistics for 1880 show thousands of objects sent out for about fifty-one days each. Demand was met by splitting pairs, drawing objects from the cases and making electrotype and fictile-ivory copies. The report ends with safe transport by railway van, locked cases, fire precautions and official handbooks, and presents South Kensington as a national store-house for the whole kingdom.

South Kensington MuseumMuseum of Ornamental Art
7Reform and the Psychology of Museum AttendanceJonah Siegelp. 277

Siegel's short headnote to the chapter on reform introduces two critical reflections on museum building: Ruskin's 1867 lecture on the national gallery and Jevons's 1883 essay on the psychology of attendance. Both writers, Siegel argues, recognise that displays compete for individual attention, and that expansion calls for clearer distinctions between kinds of museum and between their aims.

On the Present State of Modern Art, with Reference to the Advisable Arrangement of a National Gallery (1867)John Ruskinp. 278

Ruskin's 1867 lecture argues that educational collections must be kept distinct from both places of amusement and national museums. The lecture opens with a passage from Ruskin's own 1866 Times letter describing the British Museum as neither a parish school nor a circulating library, and proposes three kinds of public collection for teaching: libraries, natural history museums and art museums. Libraries should hold only rare books, with access to the British Museum reading room made a privilege, while a small selected series of casts, engravings and photographs should form a museum beside each library. Natural history collections should be arranged to reward inquiry and include duplicates that students may handle. Art is different: bad examples mislead, and a student learns best from one first-rate piece studied for a long time, so the Kensington collection must be purged of inferior work. The lecture ends with a sketch of the National Gallery as a stately, extensible palace of art built in three storeys, which Ruskin concedes will never be built.

British MuseumNational GallerySouth Kensington Museum
The Use and Abuse of Museums (1883)W. Stanley Jevonsp. 283

Jevons's 1883 essay argues that the purposes of public museums are poorly understood and that many visitors gain little from them. It opens by noting the lack of any systematic treatment of museum management and by distinguishing the very different benefits a visitor may take, from idle strolling to real study. Much of the essay criticises the South Kensington Museum, whose turnstiles count visitors but not learning, and the crowding of long galleries that confuse children and casual visitors. Jevons prefers unified displays such as the Thorvaldsen Museum at Copenhagen and the Museum of Economic Geology in Jermyn Street, and holds that the best museum is the private collection a student builds at home. Duplicates and near-duplicates are, Jevons insists, essential evidence, so the British Museum's stores should not be broken up for the provinces. Jevons proposes a six-part classification of museums, a four-branch local museum (archaeology, natural history, a curator's hobby and a space for loans), and a Museum Association so that curators can act for themselves.

East and Southeast Asia Jevons calls the loan collection of Japanese art shown at Nottingham Castle beyond praise, and credits the castle museum partly to South Kensington. Japanese idols appear in his list of what a curator's hobby collection might hold, and a cork model of a Chinese temple is one of the odd objects that clutter a county museum.

British MuseumSouth Kensington MuseumThorvaldsen MuseumMuseum of Economic GeologyBethnal Green MuseumTower MuseumParkes Museum of HygieneNottingham Castle Museum
8From Wonders to Signs: Anthropology and ArcheologyJonah Siegelp. 300

Siegel's headnote introduces the move from curiosity cabinets to scientific archaeology and anthropology. It sets Murray's account of specialised museums beside the Ashmolean, where John Henry Parker sought a systematic archaeology supported by photographs, and the early Pitt-Rivers catalogue, which reads skulls and native implements through a developmental, Darwinian frame.

The Modern Museum (1904)David Murrayp. 301

Murray's 1904 excerpt argues that the modern museum is defined by specialisation and careful classification, with archaeology as the clearest case. Thomsen's three-age system, applied in the Copenhagen museum, is presented as creating the science of archaeology, and the Germanic National Museum at Nuremberg is praised for arranging its material chapter by chapter to tell the German past. The excerpt insists that separating national from foreign objects, and comparing the arts of living peoples with prehistoric ones, put archaeology on a sound basis.

Copenhagen National MuseumGermanic National Museum (Nuremberg)British Museum
The Ashmolean Museum: Present State and Prospects (1870)John Henry Parkerp. 304

Parker's 1870 lecture to the Oxford Architectural and Historical Society sets out how the Ashmolean should become a museum of archaeology alone, with paintings left to the picture galleries. Archaeology, the lecture argues, is history taught by the eye, and objects stay in the memory better than what is read. Because the building is small, Parker proposes to illustrate architectural history with photographs made in Rome, following the chronological plan of Seroux d'Agincourt, whose engravings are judged too poor to rely on. The lecture describes some two thousand photographs with a printed catalogue and index, covering Roman remains, statues and busts, carved ivories, mosaics and frescoes down to about 1000, and medieval material with dated inscriptions. It admits that buildings of Egypt, Palestine, Greece and Ravenna must wait for another season, and that some sets depend on Arundel Society casts and chromolithographs.

Ashmolean Museum
Catalogue of the Anthropological Collection Lent by Colonel Lane for Exhibition in the Bethnal Green Museum (1874)Augustus Henry Lane Fox (Pitt-Rivers)p. 308

Pitt-Rivers's 1874 catalogue of his anthropological loan to the Bethnal Green Museum opens with a preface on how the objects are arranged. Ethnological specimens, the preface argues, should be sorted by form, to show ideas passing from simple to complex, rather than by geographical origin as in the Christy Collection. Anthropology, it explains, covers human constitution and culture, and culture is the field of sociology, studied through objects. Living 'savages' are presented as a traditional portrait of primeval man, their arts preserving forms from earlier stages, while prehistoric archaeology supplies the missing links. The note describes the layout of the South Basement, and Part I opens with skulls: the cephalic index, the long-headed and round-headed types, and the phrenologists' claims, which the catalogue sets aside. A numbered list of casts and actual skulls then runs from a Neanderthal cast to Australian, Ethiopian, Patagonian, Anglo-Saxon and Irish examples, with findspots and indices noted for each.

Bethnal Green MuseumChristy Collection
9Exhibiting IndiaJonah Siegelp. 314

Siegel's headnote places the India collection in its imperial setting. The East India Museum passed from the Company to the India Office, moved through makeshift quarters at Fife House, and was divided between South Kensington and the British Museum in 1879 and 1880. The headnote reads the 1861 Illustrated London News piece, Watson's 1874 reform plan and Hendley's 1913 article as showing the contradictions of an imperial museum: who its audience is, what it should show, and who should pay.

India MuseumSouth Kensington MuseumBritish Museum
The India Museum, Whitehall (1861)Anonymousp. 315

The 1861 Illustrated London News piece describes the India Museum's move from the India House to Fife House, Whitehall, where silks, jewels, stuffed birds and Buddhist marbles from Amaravati were crowded into rooms ill-suited to display. It is a room-by-room catalogue rather than an argument, with praise for the Elliot marbles and a note that the British Museum took most of the natural history specimens. The museum is open three days a week.

India MuseumBritish Museum
On the Measures Required for the Efficient Working of the India Museum and Library (1874)J. Forbes Watsonp. 318

Watson's 1874 paper, the first part of a plan to reorganise the India Museum and Library, argues that the collections have been left in makeshift quarters since the East India Company's house was given up. Its history runs from the Company's museum of 1798, through Wilkins and the 1851 Exhibition, to the move to Fife House in 1860 and then the new India Office. Watson says the store has become so inaccessible that scholars and the public cannot use it. The paper proposes arranging the museum as a machine for specific purposes: specialised groups for merchants, manufacturers, scientists and artists, each arranged for its class of visitor, with literary information beside the specimens. The model is the textile trade collection, identical sets reproduced for distribution to commercial centres in England and India. Trade museums, educational needs and public apathy about India are offered as justifications, since the scheme would give Parliament and the public the knowledge that underlies political judgement.

India Museum
The Future Treatment of the Indian Collection at the Old South Kensington Museum (1909)Lord Curzon et al.p. 331

This 1909 record of a deputation asks the Board of Education not to disperse the Indian Collection at South Kensington. Curzon, speaking for the British Empire League and Oxford University, recounts how the collection, begun at East India House, was split in 1879 among Jermyn Street, Kew, the British Museum and South Kensington, though the India Office never gave up its ownership. The case rests on four arguments: political (India should be visibly present in London), the needs of foreign and Indian visitors, artistic (Indian art is best seen whole) and scientific and educational value. Curzon proposes a new Indian museum on a new site under the Board's control, and suggests gifts from Indian patrons. Bhownaggree and Rees support the case. Runciman, replying for the Board, agrees that India should be brought together, but defends placing Indian art alongside Western material categories in the Victoria and Albert Museum, and promises to consider the matter with the India Office.

Siegel, Jonah (2020). Material Inspirations: The Interests of the Art Object in the Nineteenth Century and After. Oxford: Oxford University Press.Asia: slight14 chapter overviews

Overview

Material Inspirations (2020) studies how nineteenth-century writers on art used appeals to matter, the physical object and its material conditions, to ground or halt their arguments. Its central claim is that matter and idea were never settled in the period: the century kept returning to art to think about things, while museums, reproductions and the disciplines of art history and archaeology kept changing. The book has three parts. 'Interesting' treats Raphael's Transfiguration, desire and death in images of artists, and Ruskin's Turner. 'Remains' treats classical antiquities, Blake's Laocoön, Vatican display, and Benjamin's allegory. 'Things, Personally' treats Ruskin on mass reproduction and Pater on the museum. The scope is European art, mainly British, French and Italian, its canon, collections and museums, c. 1800 to 1900.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East Asia is touched only in passing, and only in Chapter 4 (Matter, Form, Abstraction), on Flaxman's 'Sculpture' article for Rees's Cyclopaedia. Beside Egyptian, Persian and Etruscan pieces, Flaxman's plates include 'more exotic pieces, from India and China', which Blake engraved. Siegel reads them as one sign that the classical canon was challenged by alternative traditions. Siegel discusses no Chinese object further and names no East Asian collector, museum or visitor.

The only other East Asian reference is in the Introduction (p. 2), where Siegel mentions 'the old but still forceful Chinese insult' of asking a person 'What kind of thing are you?', a rhetorical aside on reification. The index lists China (pp. 2, 148) and India (p. 148).

Southeast Asia is absent: there is no Siamese, Indonesian, Indochinese, Malayan or Philippine material, no colonial collecting and no Asian museum or heritage policy. The 'Asiatic Patriarchs' and Asia of Blake's visions belong to a mythical Near East, and the book's museums are the British Museum, the National Gallery and the Vatican.
