Stewart, Susan (1984). On Longing: Narratives of the Miniature, the Gigantic, the Souvenir, the Collection. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press.Asia: slight8 chapter overviews

Overview

On Longing (1984; 1993 edition) asks how narrative, exaggeration and scale produce the objects that stand for longing in Western culture. Stewart reads the miniature (miniature books, toys, the dollhouse, the 1948 Museum of Art in Miniature) as a figure for the enclosed bourgeois interior self, and the gigantic (giant legends, Gulliver's Brobdingnag, earth art, the tall tale) as a figure for the collective authority of the state. Freak shows, the souvenir and the collection are treated as objects of desire that distance and possess the world, and nostalgia is named as the disease of narrative. The book has a preface, a prologue, four chapters (on description and the book, the miniature, the gigantic, the imaginary body), two parts on the souvenir and the collection, a short conclusion, notes, bibliography and index. Its scope is limited to a Western tradition from the eighteenth century onward.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia receive very little attention. The preface sets them aside: the study is limited to 'a Western tradition', and the author leaves out 'the rich non-Western tradition of experiments with scale and the fantastic', naming the Japanese netsuke, Persian and Indian miniatures and Indonesian and Chinese giants as forms that could not be discussed without violence to their context.

Asian material appears only in passing, and no chapter is about Asia. In chapter 2 (The Miniature), the Metropolitan Museum reduced to stamps in the 1948 Museum of Art in Miniature includes Chinese works among its categories. In chapter 3 (The Gigantic), an Aragonese procession of figures is trailed by 'a Chinese man', and the temples of Angkor appear as a simile for the scale of a shell. In chapter 4 (The Imaginary Body), the Siamese twins Chang and Eng are discussed among freak-show performers, and the text notes that they were the children of Chinese parents living in Siam. A racial theory deriving the Irish from Asia Minor is cited in the same chapter, and a collecting handbook's advice in chapter 5 (Objects of Desire) ends with 'some Java wine-jars' in an eclectic room. Colonial collecting, Asian museums, Asian heritage policy, Asian visitors and restitution are not discussed; the nearest point is the general remark in chapter 5 that treasures of one culture are stored and displayed in the museums of another.

ChinaSiam (Thailand)Indonesia (Java)

Contents

Theoretical approach of this work
Preface/Hyperbolep. ix

Stewart's preface sets out the book's method: it examines how narrative relates to its objects through the metaphors of history and stasis, inside and outside, and partiality and transcendence. Narrative is treated as a structure of desire that invents and distances its object, and nostalgia is named as its social disease. The preface glosses the title through three meanings of longing (yearning, pregnancy cravings and belongings) and introduces the miniature and the gigantic as figures for the bourgeois self and the state. It ends by limiting the study to a Western tradition.

Prologuep. 1

The prologue offers three short landscapes, suburbs, countryside and city, each a site where vision and distance fail. Stewart reads the suburbs as a negation of the present and the countryside as a space of childhood and death. The city is a place of partial vision and class, where the state's language turns monumental and silent. It closes with the three landscapes left unjoined, like the paragraphs of a text.

1On Description And The Bookp. 3

Stewart's first chapter asks how description and the book produce a sense of the real, arguing that realistic fiction, printed texts and everyday speech all depend on a gap between signifier and signified. Stewart traces how the eighteenth-century novel turned the reader from a seeker of moral signs in allegory into a character reading for signs, with exactness replacing closure as the value that matters. Robinson Crusoe is read as a parable of possession and social time, and Tom Jones as a case of manipulated narrative speeds. Stewart then moves through Lumiere's early film, bluegrass, television and a Rolex advertisement, claiming that mechanical reproduction erases its makers and their labor. Narrative closure, he argues, is ideological, and ordinary language is itself a deviation from standardness. The chapter concludes that nostalgia, a sadness without an object, is the characteristic emotion of narrative, and it ends with the book as object, from bibliophiles' bindings to a skin-bound volume.

2The Miniaturep. 37

Stewart's second chapter treats the miniature (miniature books, micrographia, toys and the dollhouse) as a figure for the interior self of the bourgeois subject. Its evidence runs from fifteenth-century miniature books and Hooke's Micrographia to children's books, Gulliver's Lilliput, pastoral poems by Jonson and Marvell, and Roussel's word games. Stewart argues that the miniature offers a spatially closed, transcendent world that arrests time, so that toys and models become emblems of stopped life and private time. Case studies include the flea circus, miniature railways, H. G. Wells's floor games, the Queen's dolls' house and the 1948 Museum of Art in Miniature, which reduced the Metropolitan Museum's holdings to stamps that could be pasted into an album. The chapter concludes that the miniature is nostalgic for preindustrial craft and is both sanctuary and prison for the subject, and it closes by promising a move from transcendence to partiality.

Museum of Art in Miniature (Book-of-the-Month Club, 1948)Metropolitan Museum of ArtQueen Mary's Dolls' House
3THE GIGANTICp. 70

Stewart's third chapter sets the gigantic against the miniature: where the miniature is closed, interior and domestic, the gigantic is exterior, public and natural. Stewart reads giant legends of landscape, from Cerne Abbas and the White Horse of Uffington to Gargantua's Paris and the London Guildhall giants Gog and Magog, as claims made on the land, in which giants move from nature into the marketplace and the state. Gulliver's Brobdingnag is treated as a world of consuming bodies and threatened vision, and the sublime and the picturesque are set against each other as styles of exaggeration. Stewart then links earth art, Warhol and pop, the tall tale from Rabelais to Hurston, and American frontier heroes to commodity advertising, from the Jolly Green Giant to Disney. The chapter argues that exaggeration depends on genre and social function, and that the body is the still center against which both the miniature and the gigantic are measured.

4The Imaginary Bodyp. 104

Stewart's chapter asks how the body becomes an object of imaginary desire, moving from the grotesque body of carnival to the spectacle of the side show. Carnival's grotesque exposes orifices and blurs the body with the world, while the freak show distances the viewer and turns the body into a stilled, perfect or aberrant image. Stewart draws on eighteenth-century handbills for dwarfs and giants, Gulliver's fate in Brobdingnag, Fiedler's history of the freak, and the Siamese twins Chang and Eng. The miniature is then followed through fairy lore, Victorian fairy-child photographs such as the Cottingley pictures, Joyce's tableaux in Ulysses, and Tom Thumb weddings, which Stewart reads as parodies or models of bourgeois marriage. Lockets and limnings show how a face could be possessed at a distance. The chapter closes with microcosmic thought, from Plato and the Cabala to Fechner, which projects the body onto the universe and back, leaving the body both a subject of knowing and an image through which the self is constituted.

5Objects Of Desirep. 132

Stewart's second chapter argues that the souvenir and the collection are two ways of turning the world into private possession. The souvenir is a partial sample of a lost experience, made meaningful only by a narrative of its owner, such as the giant's lucky ring or Gulliver's relics from Brobdingnag. The collection is a finite, classified series that replaces history with order. Stewart traces antiquarianism from Camden and Aubrey to the Romantics, who turned rural and folk life into nostalgic objects, and the tourist market that miniaturizes native arts for Western buyers, with African carvings and Eskimo soapstone as examples. Pepys's arrangement of his library, Tiffany postal scales and the hoarder's coins illustrate collecting. The chapter concludes with the museum as the central metaphor of the collection, and with kitsch and camp, which it reads as metaconsumption that erases labour and makes the consumer's acquisitions appear magical and given.

Part IThe Souvenirp. 132
Part IIThe Collection, Paradise of Consumptionp. 151
Conclusion/Litotesp. 171

Stewart's short conclusion gathers the book's arguments. The miniature gives the subject an illusion of mastery, turning time into space, while the giant binds the self into a collective ideology. Stewart defends studying the childish, the feminine, the mad and the senile as marginal forms that expose the rhetoric of the sign system. Each sign is figured as a postcard from the land of the dead, its referent always deferred.

Notesp. 174
Selected Bibliographyp. 193
Indexp. 205
Stocking, George W., Jr. (ed.) (1985). Objects and Others: Essays on Museums and Material Culture. Madison: University of Wisconsin Press.Asia: slight10 chapter overviews

Overview

George Stocking's edited volume (1985) collects essays on the history of anthropological museums and asks what the museum does to the objects of 'others'. Stocking's introduction treats the museum as an archive of three-dimensional material objects that are historically displaced and entangled in power, wealth and aesthetic value, and reads the two halves of the title as overlapping projects. The essays cover the Peabody Museum at Harvard, Pitt Rivers's typological collection, Boas's exhibits at the American Museum of Natural History, Rockefeller funding of anthropology, the Trocadero in Paris, the Southwest Indian art market, Quebec's heritage law and the historiography of archaeology. Clifford's afterword reads Western collecting as the building of a possessive self. The scope is mainly American, British and French institutions from the 1830s to the 1980s.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia appear only in passing, in five of the eleven parts, and no chapter takes them as its subject. The introduction notes that the Siebold collection opened to the public at Leiden in 1837 focused on Japan, and that the Renaissance cabinet of curiosities took in objects from the New World and the East. Chapman (ch. 2) shows Pitt Rivers using Siebold's work on Japanese arms as a reference when he began his own Japanese pieces, and buying Chinese vases as fine art for his home rather than as ethnographic material. Stocking (ch. 5) notes Boas's appeal to railroad owners for Far Eastern research after the Spanish-American War, and the Rockefeller Foundation's support for Davidson Black at the Peking Union Medical College, whose work led to the discovery of Peking Man in 1926, with almost $300,000 to Black and his successor over the following decade.

Williams (ch. 6) mentions the 1900 Paris Exposition's replica of a Khmer temple, popular despite criticism in the Gazette des Beaux-Arts, and notes that French interest in exotica later turned toward the colonies, including Southeast Asia. Jacknis (ch. 4) records that Jesup gave $250,000 for an expedition to the north Pacific coasts of Asia and America, and that a Siberia hall stood beside the Eskimo halls. Clifford's afterword (ch. 10) mentions the Hall of Asian Peoples at the American Museum of Natural History only as an example of boutique-style display, and Wade (ch. 7) notes Chinese turquoise sold to Pueblo craftsmen, a trade matter in the American Southwest.

Not covered: there is no study of Asian collections in Western museums, of colonial collecting in Java, Indochina or the Philippines, or of museums in China, Japan or Korea. Asian objects appear only as examples in comparisons of European and American display.

JapanChinaCambodia

Contents

Theoretical approach of this work
ContentsPDF p. 8
Essays on Museums and Material Culturep. 3

Stocking's introduction frames the volume, which studies the history of anthropological museums and asks what the museum does to the objects of others. Stocking reads the two parts of the title, Objects and Others and Museums and Material Culture, as overlapping projects, the first philosophical and the second institutional. Stocking defines the museum as an archive of material objects that are three-dimensional, historical and entangled in power, wealth and aesthetic valuation. The essay then traces museum anthropology from the cabinet of curiosities and the British Museum through the Danish National Museum, Leiden, the Peabody and the Pitt Rivers collections, using Sturtevant's 1969 survey and Lurie's 1981 Museumland Revisited as benchmarks. It shows the decline of museum anthropology in the mid-twentieth century and a revival of interest in exhibition, along with repatriation disputes since the 1970 UNESCO convention, including the Albany and Onondaga wampum case. The essay ends by listing topics the volume leaves unexplored, such as repatriation, world's fairs and the radical critique, and presents the essays as an opening for discussion.

East and Southeast Asia Stocking notes that the Siebold collection given to the Leiden museum, opened to the public in 1837, focused on Japan, and that the cabinet of curiosities took in artificial and natural curiosities from the New World and the East from the time of Cortes. These are brief remarks, and the essay is chiefly about Europe and North America.

British MuseumAshmolean MuseumNational Museum of DenmarkRijksmuseum voor Volkenkunde, LeidenPeabody Museum of Archaeology and EthnologyMilwaukee Public MuseumNew York State MuseumSeneca-Iroquois National Museum
Arranging Ethnology: A. H. L. F. Pitt Rivers and the Typological TraditionWilliam Ryan Chapmanp. 15

Chapman examines how A. H. L. F. Pitt Rivers came to arrange his ethnographic and archaeological collection by typological form, and why that arrangement was contested. He traces the collection from the 1850s, when Pitt Rivers gathered weapons and boomerangs while serving as a soldier and in the United Service Institution, through his conversion to Darwinian evolutionism and his engagement with the Ethnological and Anthropological Societies. Chapman sets Pitt Rivers's principle of continuity against the geographical system of Leiden, against the schemes of Jomard and Klemm, and against Christy's collection. Chapman then follows the move to South Kensington, the negotiations that failed, and the transfer to the University of Oxford in 1882-84, where Tylor and Balfour managed it. The chapter ends with Pitt Rivers's Primitive Warfare lectures, his plan for a concentric anthropological rotunda and later attempts to realise it, which show how pragmatic display and audience interest pushed museums toward geographical arrangements.

East and Southeast Asia Chapman notes that Siebold's well-known work on Japanese arms was an important reference when Pitt Rivers began his own collection of Japanese pieces. Chapman also records that Pitt Rivers later bought Chinese vases, but as fine art for his home rather than as ethnographic material. These references are brief, and the chapter's Asian material is marginal to its concerns.

Pitt Rivers MuseumBethnal Green MuseumSouth Kensington MuseumBritish MuseumRijksmuseum voor Volkenkunde, LeidenFarnham Museum
From Shell-Heaps to Stelae: Early Anthropology at the Peabody MuseumCurtis M. Hinsleyp. 49

Hinsley traces the early history of the Peabody Museum at Harvard, founded in 1866 with George Peabody's endowment, and asks why anthropology struggled for support there. Hinsley argues that the museum's first decades were shaped by its rivalry with Agassiz, by a Boston elite that valued classical antiquities for moral education, and by a thin financial base that left curators such as Frederic Ward Putnam dependent on donors. The case of Charles C. Abbott, the Trenton amateur whose claims of palaeolithic man in New Jersey Putnam supported but could not defend, shows how fragile both reputations and institutional standing were. Hinsley then describes how the Peabody turned to Maya archaeology, especially the Copan expeditions funded by Charles P. Bowditch from 1891, which drew elite money and produced the first academically certified archaeologists. The chapter concludes that the museum's later success depended on finding a worthy subject and a professional structure, and that the move from shell-heaps to stelae made museum anthropology respectable in Boston.

Peabody Museum of American Archaeology and EthnologyMuseum of Comparative ZoologyEssex InstitutePeabody Academy of ScienceUniversity of Pennsylvania MuseumMuseum of Fine Arts, Boston
Franz Boas and Exhibits: On the Limitations of the Museum Method of AnthropologyIra Jacknisp. 75

Jacknis examines how Franz Boas, the founder of professional American anthropology, ran exhibits at the American Museum of Natural History between 1896 and 1905. Jacknis begins with Boas's 1887 quarrel with Otis Mason of the U.S. National Museum over whether artifacts should be grouped by typology or by tribe, which shows Boas's view that objects make sense only in their cultural setting. The chapter then sets out the constraints on his work: trustees and President Jesup, a director who sided against him, cramped storage, poor lighting, and the competing needs of popular, school and scholarly visitors. Its main case is the Northwest Coast Hall, arranged by tribe after 1901, with its synoptic series, life groups and labels. Jacknis shows how the life groups and the labelling dispute exposed the limits of realistic display. Boas resigned in 1905 over authority and exhibition style, and the chapter concludes that this break marked the end of the museum era in American anthropology.

American Museum of Natural HistoryUnited States National MuseumField Columbian Museum
Philanthropoids and Vanishing Cultures: Rockefeller Funding and the End of the Museum Era in Anglo-American AnthropologyGeorge W. Stocking, Jr.p. 112

Stocking argues that Rockefeller philanthropy, more than any colonial demand, moved Anglo-American anthropology away from object-centred museum work toward field-based studies of behaviour and culture. Stocking starts with the museum as the chief employer of interwar anthropologists and the object as the currency of their funding. Stocking then traces Rockefeller grants: racialist psychobiology in Peking, Hawaii and Australia that was reshaped into cultural determinism, the backing of Malinowski's functionalism through the African Institute, and Radcliffe-Brown's proposal for a worldwide salvage programme. The 1932 American Anthropological Association plan and Outhwaite's survey were both overtaken when the depression led the Foundation to end its anthropology programme. Stocking weighs the charge of colonial complicity against the Kirchoff affair and finds it secondary. Stocking concludes that Rockefeller money, by financing field work through universities rather than museums, helped bring the museum era to an end.

East and Southeast Asia Stocking notes that after the Spanish-American War Boas sought Far Eastern research money from railroad interests. The Rockefeller Foundation funded Davidson Black, who held the chair in embryology and neurology at the Peking Union Medical College from 1918; his work led to the discovery of Peking Man in 1926, and Foundation support for Black and his successor reached almost $300,000 over the following decade.

Bernice P. Bishop MuseumAmerican Museum of Natural History
Art and Artifact at the Trocadero: Ars Americana and the Primitivist RevolutionElizabeth A. Williamsp. 146

Williams asks why pre-Columbian objects long counted as ethnographic specimens rather than art in France. Williams opens with the 1928 Louvre exhibition of pre-Columbian art, whose catalogue introduction hesitated over whether aesthetics belonged to the show at all. The chapter then traces American collections from the Louvre's 1850 display of Longperier's artifacts to the founding of the Trocadero museum in 1878, after Charles Wiener's Peruvian exhibit. Its central contrast is between Soldi, who argued in 1881 that materials shaped art and that American work deserved new museums, and Hamy, the Trocadero's director until 1908, who treated the collections only as scholarly and pedagogic material. Williams shows how state-funded missions and diplomats supplied the collections while the museum remained underfunded and crowded. Williams concludes that avant-garde primitivism and surrealist visitors changed the status of these objects, but the tension between aesthetic and instructive display remains unresolved.

East and Southeast Asia Williams notes that the 1900 Paris Exposition included a giant replica of a Khmer temple, which drew crowds despite criticism in the Gazette des Beaux-Arts for its false detail, and that public interest in exotica later turned to France's colonies, where Southeast Asia figured. Williams does not treat either region at length.

Trocadero Museum (Musée d'Ethnographie du Trocadero)Louvre
The Ethnic Art Market in the American Southwest, 1880–1980Edwin L. Wadep. 167

Wade traces the Southwest Indian art market from 1880 to 1980 as a contest among traders, collectors, scholars and philanthropists over what Native arts should become. Wade begins with the railways, whose tourist trade pushed potters toward smaller, saleable wares. Museum buying from dealers such as Thomas Kearn, whose demand encouraged the Sikyatki revival associated with Nampeyo, and the pothunting of the Wetherill brothers at Mesa Verde show how collecting created the market. The longest section covers the 1920s and 1930s, when patrons, the Gallup Ceremonial, Santa Fe's Indian Market and the Museum of Northern Arizona tried to save traditional craft by insisting on vegetable dyes and old forms, which Wade judges often subjective and unsuccessful. He ends with the 1970s Individualists, who broke from ethnic expectations, leaving contemporary artists to choose between a folk-craft niche and mainstream fine art.

Museum of Northern ArizonaPeabody Museum, Harvard University
On Having a Culture: Nationalism and the Preservation of Quebec’s PatrimoineRichard Handlerp. 192

Handler examines the idea of cultural property as it appears in Quebec's heritage laws and in the museums that hold heritage objects. Handler begins with Boas's 1907 essay, which doubted that museum specimens could convey cultural relations, and notes that repatriation claims now treat museums as plunderers. The chapter then reviews Quebec legislation from 1922 to the Cultural Property Act of 1972, from the 1920s inventories of churches and old houses, which tied heritage to French Catholic origins, to a law that extended protection to archaeology, ordinary life and whole neighbourhoods. Its main case is the Place Royale restoration in Quebec City, where government specialists rebuilt French-Regime buildings, and critics objected that this turned a living district into an artificial museum. Handler argues that nationalists and their critics alike treat culture as a bounded possession, and he offers a typology of ownership disputes. Handler ends by observing that objects have become the symbol of culture itself.

LouvreBritish Museum
Writing the History of Archeology: A Survey of TrendsBruce G. Triggerp. 218

Trigger surveys how the history of archeology has been written, moving from nineteenth-century popular accounts of exploration to the intellectual histories of Casson, Daniel and Laming-Emperaire, and then to the positivist and social histories of the 1970s and 1980s. Trigger shows how national traditions in Britain, France, the United States, Scandinavia and Central Europe each shaped their discipline, and he argues that the New Archeology's claim to a cumulative, science-driven past rests on a selective reading of earlier work. Trigger’s evidence is a set of published histories and case studies, among them Willey and Sabloff on American archeology, Klindt-Jensen on Scandinavia, Sklenar on Central Europe, Bernal on Mexico, and McKusick and Meltzer on American debates about the antiquity of man. Trigger holds that social and political conditions influence archeological interpretation, and that archeologists need the history of their discipline to recognise their own biases. Trigger ends by urging work on two fronts, with archeologists tracing how data and methods developed and historians examining the funding, institutions and ideologies behind them.

Objects and Selves—An AfterwordJames Cliffordp. 236

Clifford's afterword reads James Fenton's poem on the Pitt Rivers Museum as a way into the fascination of ethnographic collections, which can be a place of desire and personal obsession as much as of instruction. Setting this against Macpherson's possessive individualism and Handler's study of Quebec's cultural patrimoine, he argues that Western collecting builds a possessive self, culture and authenticity, with rules of taste that separate the good collector from the fetishist. Drawing on Susan Stewart, Baudrillard and Fabian, he traces how non-Western objects were reclassified over time, moving between the Trocadero, the Louvre and modern art museums, and how the New York tribal-art exhibitions of 1984-85 blurred the line between art and artifact. Clifford ends by proposing three ways of intervening: seeing objects again as fetishes, keeping the power relations of collection in view, and displaying the history of collecting itself. The afterword leads into the volume's essays, which he presents as steps in that direction.

Musée du TrocaderoMusée de l'HommeMuseum of Modern ArtMetropolitan Museum of ArtAmerican Museum of Natural HistoryMuseum of the American Indian
Tseng, Alice Y. (2008). The Imperial Museums of Meiji Japan: Architecture and the Art of the Nation. Seattle: University of Washington Press.Asia: central8 chapter overviews

Overview

Alice Tseng's study of the three Imperial Museums that the Meiji state founded in 1889 in Tokyo (Ueno Park), Kyoto and Nara, together with the Hyokeikan art museum of 1908 in Ueno Park. Her argument is that the architecture and the collections were designed as one project to present a constructed image of the nation: Western models were used, yet the museums show Japan as distinct from the West. The chapters follow the Meiji envoys' first understanding of the museum and the coinage of hakubutsukan and bijutsu, Josiah Conder's facade for the Ueno museum, the Kyoto and Nara museums by Katayama Tokuma, the Hyokeikan, and a conclusion that answers Valéry and Malraux. Scope: Meiji Japan, its state museums and national expositions, set against world's fairs and Western museum theory.

East and Southeast Asia in this work central

East Asia is the whole subject, and Japan is its only place of study: the three Imperial Museums in Tokyo, Kyoto and Nara, the Hyokeikan, the Japanese displays at the 1873 Vienna and 1893 Chicago fairs, and the temple and shrine treasures of Kyoto and Nara. The attention is concentrated in chapter 2 (the Museum in Ueno Park), chapter 4 (the Imperial Kyoto Museum), chapter 5 (the Imperial Nara Museum) and chapter 6 (the Hyokeikan), with chapters 1 and 3 on the envoys' writings and the reorganisation of the 1880s. The Kyoto chapter compares the museum with the Hōōden national pavilion at the 1893 Chicago exposition, and the Nara chapter follows the Hōryūji and Nara icons from Edo-period temple airings into the museum.

Other East Asian places appear only in passing. Chapter 3 records Fenollosa's outline proposing that Japan survey and collect art in China, Korea and Mongolia, as German and French museums had done for Greece and Egypt, and his judgment of Chinese ceramics at Philadelphia in 1876. Chapter 6 notes that the 1908 Hyokeikan committee planned to show Chinese, Korean and Indian art beside Japanese painting. Chapter 4 mentions the Taiwan Government-General Museum (1915), built by Japan as an imperial institution in its colony, as a use of Western classicism for imperial authority. The conclusion answers Valéry and Malraux, who said China and the Far East lacked the museum idea, by pointing to late-Edo temple airings and painting gatherings as earlier public display.

South Asia is not discussed, and no Southeast Asian place is named in the argument. Chinese, Korean and Southeast Asian collections are not studied as collections; Asia appears as a foil for Japan's Meiji self-presentation.

Introductionp. 3Asia: chiefly

Tseng introduces the Imperial Museums of Meiji Japan, the three state museums founded in Tokyo, Kyoto and Nara in 1889, and argues that they were built to project a constructed image of the nation. Tseng sets out the forces that shaped them: Japan's opening to the West after 1853, a new sense of a break with the feudal past, and a shift of art from elite to national ownership. Tseng’s central claim is that the museums' architecture and collections drew on Western models while being designed to show Japan as distinct from the West. Tseng then reviews the historiography, noting that the institutional histories written by the three successor National Museums treat the museums as separate stories and hide their joint design. Tseng places the study within work on world's fairs, Western museum theory and Meiji art history, and she previews the chapters: the prehistory in Ueno Park, the Kyoto and Nara museums, and the Hyokeikan in Tokyo. The introduction ends by arguing that the buildings should be read together with their collections, since contemporaries praised the architecture but were harder on the objects.

East and Southeast Asia The whole Introduction concerns Japan, so East Asia is its subject. It describes the Imperial Museums at Tokyo (Ueno Park), Kyoto and Nara and the Hyokeikan in Tokyo, along with Okakura Kakuzo's 1888 plan for a triad of museums in which the Tokyo museum would specialize in Tokugawa art and the artifacts of Asia. It also uses Japan's Hodden pavilion at the 1893 Chicago World's Columbian Exposition as a parallel national display. No other East or Southeast Asian place is discussed.

Tokyo Imperial MuseumKyoto Imperial MuseumNara Imperial MuseumHyokeikan
1Encounters and Translations: The Origins of Hakubutsukan and Bijutsup. 18Asia: chiefly

Tseng traces how the Japanese envoys who visited the West in the 1860s and 1870s first understood the museum, and how they named it. Tseng argues that hakubutsukan, the term for museum, was a translation that meant a hall of diverse objects, and that it stressed the scope of collections and their use for popular enlightenment rather than the Greek Muses. Three texts carry the argument: Fukuzawa Yukichi's Conditions in the West, which defines the museum through scientific specimens; Kume Kunitake's True Account of the Iwakura mission, which describes London's British Museum and South Kensington Museum and reads the displays as a sequence of national progress; and Sano Tsunetami's 1875 report on the Vienna exposition, which proposes a South Kensington-style museum for Ueno Park in Tokyo. Tseng then turns to bijutsu, the term for fine art, coined for Japan's entry to the 1873 Vienna exposition, and shows that fine art was an unstable category at international fairs from London in 1851 onward. The chapter concludes that the museum and the fine arts were initially separate concerns that merged only later, when the Imperial Museums adopted art as a collecting category.

East and Southeast Asia Japan is the chapter's subject. Fukuzawa, Kume and Sano are Japanese officials and writers, and the chapter follows the Tokugawa envoys' missions of 1860 and 1862 and the Meiji government's 1873 display at the Vienna exposition, where Japan showed its products and a national pavilion. Sano's 1875 proposal envisions a composite museum for Ueno Park in Tokyo. No Chinese, Korean or Southeast Asian collections are discussed.

British MuseumSouth Kensington MuseumLouvreUffizi GalleryGreat Exhibition, London (1851)Weltausstellung, Vienna (1873)
2The Museum in Ueno Park: Styling the Nationp. 39Asia: chiefly

Tseng studies the Museum in Ueno Park, the permanent building that opened in Tokyo in 1882 and was designed by the English architect Josiah Conder. Tseng’s main argument is that the facade was meant to express a Japanese national identity that Conder could not define: he called the style pseudo-Saracenic, borrowing Islamic arches and domes from British and Indian models rather than Japanese forms. Tseng traces the rivalry between the Home and Education ministries over the Ueno site, the brick-construction debates of Meiji Japan, and Conder's training under William Burges and at South Kensington. Comparisons with the South Kensington Museum and with American and British museum buildings of the 1870s set out the building's sources. Tseng also shows that its display rooms were criticized for poor light and too little space, and that the Japanese press largely ignored it. Tseng ends by arguing that Conder's facade set the model of monumental national museum architecture, even though his later statements show ambivalence about the design.

East and Southeast Asia Japan is the whole subject of the chapter. It covers the 1877 Art Gallery at the First National Industrial Exhibition in Ueno Park, built by the Japanese builder Hayashi Tadahiro, and the Japanese woodblock prints of the 1877 and 1881 exhibitions. The Japanese statesmen who fought over the Ueno site, Conder's Japanese students, and Baron Hamao Arata, who praised the building's Eastern taste at a 1920 ceremony, all appear. The Saracenic forms are read as an unstable sign for a generalized East, and the Jaipur building is used only as a comparison.

Museum in Ueno Park, Tokyo (1882)South Kensington Museum, LondonMuseum of Fine Arts, BostonMetropolitan Museum of Art, New YorkAlbert Hall Museum, Jaipur
3The Age of the Imperial Museump. 82Asia: chiefly

Tseng follows the Ueno museum from 1881 to 1889, when it moved between government ministries and was renamed the Imperial Museum, with satellite museums in Kyoto and Nara. The reorganization is usually told as a shift from science and industry to fine art, and she argues that this shift is too neat, since the new museums kept their interest in international exhibitions and state economic goals. The chapter looks at the administrators who led the change, Kuki Ryuichi, Yamataka Nobutsura, Ernest Fenollosa and Okakura Kakuzo, and argues that their work grew out of the exhibition activity of the 1870s and 1880s rather than a reaction against Westernization. Preparations came from the Fine Arts Commission, which toured Western museums in 1886-87, and from a survey of temple and shrine treasures from 1888 to 1897, which made Kyoto and Nara the repositories for temple objects. The chapter ends by treating art as the link between old and new Japan, with national pride sought through Western appreciation.

East and Southeast Asia The chapter is mainly about Japan: the temple and shrine treasures of Kyoto and Nara, the Tokyo School of Fine Arts, the journal Kokka, and Okakura and Fenollosa's buying trips in the Kyoto and Nara regions. Fenollosa's outline proposes that Japan survey and collect art in China, Korea and Mongolia, as German and French museums did for Greece and Egypt. He also judged the Chinese ceramics and wood carvings at Philadelphia in 1876 and criticized Japanese and Chinese export ware as a sign of decline.

Imperial Museum, TokyoImperial Kyoto MuseumImperial Nara MuseumMuseum of Fine Arts, Boston
4The Imperial Kyoto Museum: Locating the Past within the Presentp. 93Asia: chiefly

Tseng asks how the Imperial Kyoto Museum, completed in 1895, fitted the Meiji government's plan to make Kyoto the sacred, historical counterpart of modern Tokyo. Tseng shows that the site, on the edge of the temple district around Hōkōji and Sanjūsangendō, and the Western Neo-classical design by Katayama Tokuma both reflected that symbolic role. The building is studied in detail: its mansard domes, Composite portico, sculpted pediment of Japanese deities, and rooms planned by object type, a plan the curators did not follow. Debates over masonry in earthquakes, between Fenollosa and Conder, and the critic Mamizu Hideo's objections to the museum's style and character frame the argument. The chapter then compares it with the Hōōden pavilion at the 1893 Chicago fair, which recreated historical Japanese interiors, and concludes that the Kyoto museum presented Japanese art as isolated objects in a Western building, a stance that made Kyoto a cultural capital of the modern nation.

East and Southeast Asia Japan is the whole subject. Tseng presents the Imperial Kyoto Museum as a Meiji state project that made Kyoto the historical and sacred counterpart to Tokyo, and he compares it with the Japanese national pavilion (Hōōden) at the 1893 Chicago fair, whose period interiors contrast with the Kyoto galleries that classified objects by medium and type. Its architect Katayama Tokuma drew on European and American models, and the chapter notes the Taiwan Government-General Museum (1915), built by Japan as an imperial institution in its colony.

Imperial Kyoto MuseumImperial Museum in Ueno Park
5The Imperial Nara Museum: Administering History and Religionp. 137Asia: chiefly

Tseng turns to the Imperial Nara Museum, opened in 1895 to hold the Buddhist and other treasures of the Nara region. The chapter argues that moving icons from temple to museum changed their meaning, and it sets this against Edo-period practices of temple unveilings, airings and sideshows, which had already displayed sacred objects to the public. It then reviews the Meiji policies that separated Shinto from Buddhism, the anti-Buddhist destruction that followed, and the national surveys by Fenollosa's Temporary National Treasures Investigation Bureau. Tseng sets Fenollosa's memorandum for a plain, top-lit brick building against Katayama Tokuma's thick-walled design with a raised skylight and thirteen rooms, where the curators grouped objects by medium rather than the architect's intended order. The chapter concludes that the museum made icons visible as national art while keeping them close to their Nara origins through loans and compensation rules.

East and Southeast Asia Japan's Nara region is the whole subject: icons from Hōryūji, the Shōsōin and Nara temples are followed from Edo-period unveilings and airings into the Imperial Nara Museum. Tseng covers the early-Meiji separation of Shinto from Buddhism and the attacks on temples, the 1875 Nara Exhibition, and the Hōryūji treasures sent to Ueno Park in Tokyo, which he presents as a transfer of Buddhist art to a secular national collection. Fenollosa's proposal for a museum in Nara and the regulations paying temples for their loans are examined in detail.

Imperial Nara MuseumImperial Kyoto MuseumImperial Museum in Ueno ParkNara Exhibition of 1875
6The Hyokeikan Art Museum: Debating the Permanent Place of Artp. 171Asia: chiefly

Tseng examines the Hyokeikan, Japan's first permanent, purpose-built art museum, completed in Ueno Park in 1908 with money raised in Tokyo to celebrate the crown prince's marriage. Tseng argues that the building was defined less by a clear idea of art than by its attachment to the Tokyo Imperial Household Museum and to the crown prince's Akasaka palace, which Katayama Tokuma designed at the same time. Tseng traces the terms bijutsu and kogei through the Meiji expositions and the 1893 Chicago fair, where Japanese works were admitted to a fine arts category by exception, and then sets out the rival museum models proposed by Masaki Naohiko, Hayashi Tadamasa and Taki Seiichi. The chapter also examines the 1909 reviews by the critic Nipporijin, who attacked the glass cases, the labels and the inclusion of lacquer. It concludes that the Hyokeikan made older painting visible as art, though it never became the independent museum that critics wanted.

East and Southeast Asia Japanese art is the subject, set against the Western standards of Japan's Meiji diplomacy. Japanese works were admitted to the Palace of Fine Arts at the 1893 Chicago fair as an exception, and the 1908 committee planned to show Chinese, Korean and Indian art beside Japanese painting and sculpture. Tseng notes that Japan had recently defeated China and was soon to defeat Russia, and he cites Natsume Sōseki's novel The Wayfarer, in which a son first admires Japanese painting in the Hyokeikan.

Hyokeikan Art MuseumTokyo Imperial Household MuseumMetropolitan Museum of ArtMuseum of Fine Arts, Boston
Conclusionp. 210Asia: chiefly

Tseng's conclusion answers Paul Valéry and André Malraux, who treated Asia as lacking the museum idea. It argues that the museum was no more natural to Europeans than to Asians, and that the Imperial Museums in Tokyo, Kyoto and Nara arose from specific Meiji aims of national display and public education. It notes late-Edo temple airings and painting gatherings as earlier public displays, and says the museum's Western architecture made its constructed nature plain. It ends by calling the Imperial Museums a microcosm of how modern states display national identity.

East and Southeast Asia Japan is the subject here. Tseng answers Valéry and Malraux, who said that China and the Far East lacked the museum, by pointing to late-Edo temple airings and painting gatherings as earlier public display, and to the Imperial Museums' role in educating foreign tourists as well as Japanese visitors about the nation's art lineage.

Veldkamp, Elmer (2014). “Keeping It Real: The Exhibition of Artifact Replicas in National Museums of Korea”. Acta Koreana, 17.2 (December 2014): 557-581.Asia: central1 chapter overview

Overview

Veldkamp asks what it means for a Korean national museum to show replicas of its most important heritage objects, and what copies do to a visitor's sense of the real. Veldkamp argues that authenticity depends on perception and purpose as much as on material originals. Veldkamp’s evidence is the National Museum of Korea's replica of a Paekche incense burner, the reconstructed tomb of King Muryŏng at the Kongju National Museum, the dispute over lending the Pensive Bodhisattva, and a certified replica of a celadon burner in Leiden. Veldkamp concludes that replicas have real value for a general public.

East and Southeast Asia in this work central

Korea is the whole subject, so East Asia is central and Southeast Asia does not appear. The article looks at the National Museum of Korea's replica of the Paekche gilt-bronze incense burner, labelled as a replica while the original is in Buyeo, and at the reconstructed royal tomb of King Muryŏng at the Kongju National Museum, set beside a model tomb hall. It also treats the Cultural Heritage Administration's programme of certified replicas, the 2012 lifting of the travel ban on the Pensive Bodhisattva, its proposed loan to the Metropolitan Museum of Art in 2013-14, and a Korean celadon incense burner replica held in Leiden.

The Korean institutional background is covered briefly: the National Museum's origins in the Imperial Household Museum of 1909, its years as the Chosŏn Government-General Museum under Japanese occupation (1915-1945), its move to the present site in 2005, and the thirteen national museums whose regional displays repeat the treasures of Paekche and Silla. Japan appears only as a comparison, through the Ise Shrine's periodic rebuilding at the 1994 Nara Conference and a footnote on a Buddha room in Leiden.

Korean replicas also circulate through logos and signs, such as the Heavenly Horse Tomb motif in Kyŏngju and the Paekche gold crown in Kongju. No South Asian, Southeast Asian or war-memory material appears; the wider comparisons are Holtorf, Benjamin and Smith.

Keeping It Real: The Exhibition of Artifact Replicas in National Museums of Koreap. 556Asia: chiefly

Veldkamp asks why Korean national museums display replicas of their most important heritage objects, and what copies do to a visitor's sense of the real. Veldkamp argues that authenticity depends on perception and purpose as much as on material originals: a good replica can give a casual visitor what Holtorf calls 'pastness', while specialists need the original. The evidence is his own observation in the National Museum of Korea, where a Paekche incense burner was on show only as a replica, and in the reconstructed tomb of King Muryŏng at the Kongju National Museum, which differs in small details from a model tomb hall beside it. He also discusses the controversy over lending the Pensive Bodhisattva to New York, the state programme of certified replicas for loans, and a celadon replica in Leiden that the Cultural Heritage Administration authorised. The article traces how icons of Korean heritage spread through logos, souvenirs and museum social media. Veldkamp concludes that replicas have real value and that copies may serve a general public's need for a shared national past.

East and Southeast Asia Korea is the whole subject. The article looks at the National Museum of Korea's replica of the Paekche gilt-bronze incense burner, which is labelled as a replica while the original is in Buyeo, and at the reconstructed tomb of King Muryŏng at the Kongju National Museum. It discusses the Cultural Heritage Administration's programme of certified replicas and the dispute over lending the Pensive Bodhisattva to the Metropolitan Museum, and it notes a Korean celadon incense-burner replica held by the National Museum of Ethnology in Leiden.

Vergo, Peter (ed.) (1989). The New Museology. London: Reaktion Books.Asia: slight9 chapter overviews

Overview

The New Museology (1989), edited by Peter Vergo, is a collection of nine essays by British museum staff and scholars, prefaced by the editor's introduction. Its central argument is that the 'old' museology concentrated on museum methods and too little on what museums are for, and that the questions museums raise about meaning, value, knowledge, pleasure, memory and power should form a critical 'new' museology. The essays cover the meanings objects acquire inside museums, the claim that museums teach through looking, exhibition making, theme parks, the nineteenth-century international exhibitions, museum visiting, and the law of cultural property. The scope is mainly Britain from the eighteenth century onward, with some attention to the United States and Australia, and it leaves out administration, conservation and sponsorship.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia receive very little attention. The fullest mention is in Greenhalgh's chapter 5 on the international exhibitions, where the 1910 Japan-British Exhibition at White City is counted among eleven major events of the first order, and where the 1896 'India, Ceylon, Borneo and Burma Show' at Earls Court appears in a list of exhibition titles. Greenhalgh also mentions the series of thirty-nine houses by Charles Garnier shown at a Paris exhibition, which included Japanese and Chinese houses. These references are descriptive; the chapter is concerned with spectacle, Empire and entertainment rather than with Asian objects or peoples.

Palmer's chapter 9 on cultural property has one Asian case: in Winkworth v Christie Manson & Woods, Japanese works of art stolen from an Oxfordshire house were resold in Italy, and the English court applied Italian law (the lex situs rule), so that the Italian buyer's title prevailed. Palmer uses the case only to illustrate the rule. Philip Wright's chapter 7 on art museums has brief passages: Sherman Lee's rearrangement of Far Eastern arts at the Cleveland Museum of Art, old Chinese art placed in archaeology museums rather than art museums, and Japanese haiku and Indonesian ikat offered as possible settings for modern works.

Not covered: any museum in Asia, Asian states' heritage policy, colonial collecting from Asia, Asian visitors or scholars, and restitution claims. The India and Ceylon shows in the exhibition titles fall in South Asia, outside this question.

IntroductionPeter Vergop. 1

Vergo's introduction defines the 'new' museology as dissatisfaction with the 'old', which concentrates on museum methods and too little on what museums are for. Vergo warns that British museums risk becoming 'living fossils' unless they re-examine their role beyond visitor numbers. The volume omits administration, conservation and sponsorship, and is written mainly from a British standpoint. Its essays were chosen for the authors' passion rather than for representativeness.

1Museums, Artefacts, and MeaningsCharles Saumarez Smithp. 6

Saumarez Smith argues that museums remove artefacts from private ownership and use and give them a new meaning, one that is supposed to be non-arbitrary and open to the public. He traces this from Tradescant's personal 'Ark' to Ashmole's Oxford foundation and to the British Museum, which took Sloane's private collection and became a museum once it was public and perpetual. Nineteenth-century idealism, exemplified by Henry Cole's South Kensington Museum and Moncure Conway's 1882 account of it, treated objects as comparative evidence. Against the idea of neutral museum space, he works through three Victoria and Albert case studies: the Saxon statue Thuner, the Mark Lane archway and the Clifford's Inn panelled room. Each shows an object's meaning shifting inside the museum, and he uses them to argue for mixed display styles, awareness of artifice and more reflexive museum scholarship.

Ashmolean MuseumBritish MuseumSouth Kensington MuseumVictoria and Albert Museum
2Objects of Knowledge: A Historical Perspective on MuseumsLudmilla Jordanovap. 22

Jordanova asks how looking at museum objects produces knowledge, a link she says museums assume through their architecture, arrangement and labels. Jordanova distinguishes three levels of classification: the institution's category, the arrangement of its interior, and the label on each object, which confers value. Jordanova’s main cases are the Jorvik Viking Centre in York and the Bethnal Green Museum of Childhood in London, whose claims to recreate the past and childhood she calls illusory, since no object can embody an abstraction. Jordanova then examines scientific and colonial trophies, Donna Haraway's study of the American Museum of Natural History's primate hall, wax models in Florence and Madame Tussaud's, and the fetish, linked to Marx and Freud. Jordanova concludes that museums cannot teach abstract ideas, and that the belief in knowing through looking needs historical scrutiny.

Jorvik Viking CentreBethnal Green Museum of ChildhoodAmerican Museum of Natural HistoryLa SpecolaMadame Tussaud's
3The Reticent ObjectPeter Vergop. 41

Vergo argues that exhibition-making is curiously unreflective, since the criteria that choose objects, loans and programmes rest on an unspoken sense of purpose. Vergo divides approaches into 'aesthetic' shows, which let objects speak for themselves, and 'contextual' shows, which use objects as tokens of a culture and surround them with text. Vergo rejects the aesthetic view through a Scandinavian painting show at the Hayward Gallery that had no captions or map, and the over-documented display, illustrated by an imagined medieval prayer book buried in explanation. Good exhibitions, he proposes, need knowledge of their audience and non-verbal means such as an Austrian family tree or a costume beside paintings, with designers involved from the outset. He uses the Nazi 'Degenerate Art' exhibition of 1937-8 in Munich to show how hanging and captions can make an argument. He concludes that makers must articulate their educational aims, since the Victorian balance of instruction and diversion has been lost.

Hayward GalleryTate GalleryImperial War MuseumMuseum of Mankind
4Theme Parks and Time MachinesColin Sorensenp. 60

Sorensen, Keeper of the Modern Department at the Museum of London, argues that the popular appetite for re-entering the past shapes both entertainment and museums. Sorensen traces historic theme parks back to the hermits placed in eighteenth-century estate grottoes, and sorts them into restored real places, such as Colonial Williamsburg and Ironbridge, and wholly artificial parks, such as Henry Ford's Greenfield Village and Beamish in County Durham. Sorensen argues that such parks deny the passage of time, so that then and now look alike, and that they tell us more about ourselves than about the past. Sorensen describes the small Scottish Museum of Fisheries at Anstruther, where visitors leave flowers for drowned fishermen. Sorensen then argues that museums should record living context on film, illustrated by Sam Hanna's craft films and Arthur Elton's Housing Problems, rather than only piling up objects. Sorensen ends by suggesting that today's yesteryear parks will be read in the future as symbols of this age.

Colonial WilliamsburgIronbridgeGreenfield VillageBeamishScottish Museum of FisheriesDisneyland
55 Education, Entertainment and Politics: Lessons from the Great International ExhibitionsPaul Greenhalghp. 74

Greenhalgh asks what the great international exhibitions of 1851 to 1914 can teach British museums that now also need crowds and sponsors. Comparing English shows with the Paris Expositions Universelles, he traces three phases: the Crystal Palace and the 1862 South Kensington show, which treated education and commerce as one mission; the serial and specialist shows of 1871-91, including the Earls Court series; and the White City exhibitions of 1908-14, which mixed galleries with rides and stadia. He argues that English organisers separated education from entertainment, a division rooted in the ethic of work in Mill, Ruskin and Morris, whereas Paris, from Le Play's 1867 show onwards, made pleasure part of instruction through full-scale reconstructions. He stresses that the exhibitions were openly political, above all about Empire, and that museum neutrality is a fiction. He closes by setting a 1980 Dali show in Paris beside its London counterpart, where the English version kept pleasure at bay.

66 On Living in a New CountryStephen Bannp. 99

Bann opens with a letter handed to him at a Perth bus stop by a man researching his family history, and sets beside it John Bargrave's seventeenth-century cabinet of curiosities, made after his family died out in the Civil War, and Victor Hugo's medieval family myth. These show that the individual's relation to the past is always mediated by collective forms. He rejects Donald Horne's contrast between an Australia without history and a Europe turned into 'The Great Museum'. In Adelaide he examines the Migration and Settlement Museum, with its diorama of an emigrant street and computer terminals, and the South Australian Maritime Museum, whose recreated immigrant hold makes the visitor hear the ship's timbers. He then sets Littlecote, a Berkshire house where costumed displays dilute Macaulay's account of the Glorious Revolution into sentimental domesticity. He concludes that a museum in a 'New Country' cannot escape the political debates over its national past.

Migration and Settlement MuseumSouth Australian Maritime MuseumLittlecote House (The Land of Littlecote)Carrick HillMusee de Cluny
88 Museum Visiting as a Cultural PhenomenonNick Merrimanp. 149

Merriman reports a national survey of attitudes to heritage in Britain, carried out in 1985, to explain why some people visit museums and others never do. Visiting is common: between 40 and 58 per cent of adults visit in a year, and 82 per cent say they have visited at some time. He divides the public into five groups, from frequent visitors to non-visitors, and compares them by age, status, education, reasons for going and images of the museum. Interest in the past is the first condition for visiting, followed by attitudes to the museum's experience, its image and the visitor's age. Merriman tests two accounts of this pattern: the psychological theory of leisure choice advanced by Hood and Prince, and Bourdieu's theory of cultural capital and distinction, which he finds too narrow because it rests on French art galleries. Merriman proposes a synthesis based on Kelly's idea of leisure opportunity and argues that museums both divide society and widen participation as schooling and affluence spread. The chapter concludes that the greatest hurdle is the initial opportunity to visit, and that a substantial group will probably never visit museums.

99 Museums and Cultural PropertyNorman Palmerp. 172

Palmer surveys the English law that governs how museums acquire, keep and dispose of cultural objects, and argues that it is haphazard and cannot be relied on to protect national heritage. Palmer begins with voluntary codes such as the Museums Association's and the 1970 UNESCO Convention, which the UK has not ratified, and then turns to the general law of title: a museum that buys an object with defective title commits conversion even if it acted in good faith, so provenance must be checked with care. Treasure trove and the civil law of finders, which decide ownership of discovered antiquities, are shown to be defective, with the Overton coin case and the Derrynaflan hoard in Ireland as examples. Foreign sales and the lex situs rule can cut off an owner's title, as the Stowlangtoft panels and the Maori door in Ortiz show. Palmer then examines the bailee's strict duty of care for loans and the special duties of national museums to exhibit and to dispose of their objects. The chapter ends by warning that proposed wider disposal powers could threaten bequests, and that the debate has reached a Consultative Paper with uncertain safeguards.

East and Southeast Asia Palmer's example of the lex situs rule is Winkworth v Christie Manson & Woods, in which Japanese works of art stolen from Winkworth's Oxfordshire home were resold in Italy, where the buyer obtained good title. Slade J applied Italian law and dismissed the owner's claim. Apart from this one case, the chapter says nothing of East or Southeast Asia.

Yallop, Jacqueline (2011). Magpies, Squirrels and Thieves: How the Victorians Collected the World. London: Atlantic Books.Asia: substantial22 chapter overviews

Overview

Yallop's study of Victorian collecting follows five collectors whose archives survive: John Charles Robinson of South Kensington, Charlotte Schreiber, the dealer Murray Marks, the Liverpool jeweller Joseph Mayer and the doctor Stephen Wootton Bushell. Its argument is that private collecting and dealing in the nineteenth century laid the foundations of today's public museums, and that none of these collections survives intact. The book opens with the 1862 loan exhibition at South Kensington and moves through the Museums Acts, the rivalry between the British Museum and South Kensington, the European buying trips, the blue-and-white and Peacock Room episodes, the forgery trade and Bushell's collecting in Peking, ending with an epilogue on what became of the collections. It is organised in twenty numbered chapters with unnumbered interludes, and covers Britain, France, Italy, the Netherlands and China.

East and Southeast Asia in this work substantial

East Asia is substantial but concentrated in the last three chapters. Chapters 18 to 20 (The Route to Peking, The Promise of the East, Collecting Without Boundaries) follow Bushell, a doctor at the British Legation in Peking from 1868 to 1899, who collected Chinese bronzes, mirrors, ceramics, ivory, jade and lacquer from palaces, private houses and the markets near the Wu Men gate. He sent consignments to South Kensington from 1874 and bought on the museum's behalf from 1882, and he worked for William Thompson Walters (Oriental Ceramic Art, 1896) and Heber Bishop (jade). Chapter 19 also covers Japan: the opening after sakoku, the Japonisme vogue, royal gifts of Japanese arms to South Kensington, and Franks's purchase in 1881 of over 3,000 Japanese paintings for the British Museum. Chapter 20 describes the looting of the Summer Palace in 1860.

Elsewhere East Asia is secondary. Chapters 15 and 16 concern Chinese blue-and-white supplied by Murray Marks, treated as display and sale rather than as makers or origins. Chapter 5 mentions Franks's Japanese netsuke and Chinese bronzes, chapter 9 the Japanese porcelain of the seventeenth-century craze, and chapter 13 a Guanyin bronze taken from Putuo in the First Opium War. Southeast Asia is almost absent: the only mention is Raffles's Java collection in chapter 18. Siam, the Dutch East Indies and Vietnam are not discussed. India, by contrast, is treated at length in chapter 19.
