Preface

The preface presents Victorian collecting as a subject worth close study, since nineteenth-century collectors laid the foundations of today's private collecting and public museums. Yallop explains that the book follows five collectors, whose archives show what a collection is, what drives collectors and how private holdings relate to public museums. The author stresses that none of the five is well known and none of their collections survives intact.

East and Southeast Asia The preface notes that Stephen Wootton Bushell, one of the five collectors, was sent to China as doctor to the British delegation and became a pioneering expert on Chinese art.

South Kensington Museum
Catching the Collecting Bug
11. Exhibition Road, London, 1862

Yallop opens in June 1862 at South Kensington, where the London International Exhibition of Industry and Art, housed in Francis Fowke's glass-domed building, drew over six million visitors in six months. The chapter's real subject is the Special Exhibition of Works of Art on loan at the South Kensington Museum: more than 9,000 medieval, Renaissance and later objects lent by over 500 owners, from the Queen and aristocratic families to livery companies and public schools. Yallop describes the crowded, unarranged galleries and the press response to a taste for medieval and Renaissance art that was then little studied. The show was the work of John Charles Robinson, the museum's Librarian-Curator, whose network of collectors, built through the Fine Arts Club, turned a modest loan display into a national event that drew over a million visitors. The chapter argues that the exhibition revealed for the first time how many Victorian collectors there were and how far collecting shaped homes, municipal identities and a commodified culture.

London International Exhibition of 1862Special Exhibition of Works of Art (South Kensington, 1862)South Kensington Museum
22. The Useful and the Beautiful

This chapter places the 1862 exhibition in the aftermath of the Great Exhibition of 1851 and of the design-reform campaign that Henry Cole ran from South Kensington. Yallop argues that the 1851 show, meant to restore British manufacturing, quickly took on competing aims, from free trade and imperial display to the Church's concerns, so that its meaning was disputed from the start. The author traces Cole's career from civil servant and Penny Postage planner to reformer of the government Schools of Design and first director of the South Kensington Museum, where he wanted objects to educate public taste. Robinson, the museum's leading curator, did not share Cole's view of art as a tool of manufacture and clashed with him repeatedly. The chapter then sets out the mid-century argument between utility and beauty, citing Ruskin's attack on the museum and Arnold's essays. It concludes that Robinson's loan show, with its stress on refined and historic objects, made a deliberate case for collecting for pleasure against Cole's commercial rationale.

South Kensington MuseumGreat Exhibition of 1851International Exhibition of 1862
33. A Public Duty and a Private Preoccupation

Yallop turns from the 1862 exhibition to the Victorian boom in collecting, arguing that the break-up of aristocratic collections and the rise of middle-class buyers made collecting a public as well as a private activity. The chapter traces the sale of old holdings such as the Orléans paintings and the Stowe sale of 1848, and the Settled Land Act of 1882, which let families sell their treasures. Ralph Bernal's 1855 sale, which raised over three times his outlay, shows the appeal of cheaper decorative objects. Yallop shows how provincial towns competed to found museums under the Museums Acts, many grown out of Mechanics' Institutes and literary societies, and how their collections depended on private loans. The author argues that museums were also meant to instruct and steer the working classes, as in Ruskin's Sheffield museum, whose visitor book records a broad local audience. The chapter ends with London, where restrictive access at the British Museum, the National Gallery and the Royal Academy left the provinces ahead of the capital.

British MuseumNational GalleryRoyal AcademyRuskin's Sheffield museum
Making Museums: Collecting as a Career
44. On the Banks of the Seine

This chapter follows John Charles Robinson from his Nottingham childhood to his appointment at the South Kensington Museum in 1853, arguing that his formation as a collector was built in Paris and Italy rather than in Britain. Yallop describes his years in the Paris ateliers, where afternoons in the Louvre gave him a lasting taste for Italian Renaissance art. The author contrasts the Louvre's public, chronologically arranged galleries with the closed private collections of Britain, and presents the Hôtel de Cluny and Sauvageot's crowded apartment as models of connoisseurship. Robinson's collecting in Paris ended in 1846 when his money ran out, and he returned to Nottingham and then to the Hanley School of Design. The second half covers his 1851 journey through Italy, where he found a spiritual home in Venetian and Renaissance art, and the political turmoil that opened objects to collectors. It closes with his promotion and move to London, where Henry Cole took notice of him.

LouvreMusée de Cluny (Hôtel de Cluny)National Gallery
55. The Battle of South KensingtonAsia: in part

Yallop follows John Charles Robinson through his battles with Henry Cole at South Kensington, arguing that the quarrel was over what a museum was for: Robinson wanted rare and beautiful objects for connoisseurs, Cole practical examples for design education. The chapter covers the move from Marlborough House to the new site, Robinson's buying trips to Italy and his failed bid for objects from the Campana collection in Rome in 1859, which the board refused to fund. Yallop shows how his personal debts, his close ties to the Fine Arts Club and his habit of buying on his own account blurred public and private collecting, and how Cole's demands for records led to Robinson's demotion and dismissal in 1868. The chapter ends by setting Robinson beside Augustus Franks at the British Museum, whose similar private collecting was tolerated because of his class and generosity to the museum.

East and Southeast Asia At the British Museum Augustus Franks, a collector as well as curator, bought Japanese porcelain instead of classical pottery and bequeathed some 1,500 netsuke, Japanese miniature sculptures, to the museum. Yallop also notes that he invested in Chinese bronzes, and that in 1885 he swapped a painted Japanese figure from the collection for a finer wooden one of his own.

South Kensington MuseumMarlborough House museumBritish Museum
66. The Tricks of the Trade

This chapter follows John Charles Robinson out of the museum and into the art trade after his dismissal in 1868, arguing that his dealing career depended on blurring the line between gentleman collector and tradesman. Yallop shows how Robinson bought and resold works for clients, among them John Malcolm of Poltalloch, Sir Francis Cook and Princess Vicky, and how his house at Newton Manor in Dorset worked as a showroom that disguised commerce as country-house collecting. Account-book entries show sharp mark-ups, and the author argues that Robinson was among the first to combine dealing with his own collecting, a path later followed by Joseph Duveen. The chapter then returns to South Kensington, where the museum bought a lot of over 300 of his loaned objects for £6,800 around 1880, after advice from Franks and Poynter. It ends with Robinson's late campaign against the museum's management, in which he presents himself as both a public-minded critic and a man with a commercial stake in the collections.

South Kensington MuseumNational GalleryBritish MuseumBowes Museum
77. Changing Times

This chapter covers Robinson's later career, from his appointment as Surveyor of the Queen's Pictures in 1882 to his death in 1913, and the dispersal of his collection. Yallop shows a collector acquiring Renaissance medals, British paintings and decorative objects, rewarded with honours and with a post that required little acquisition. The chapter then traces the sale of about 1,000 textiles to the Whitworth Institute in Manchester in 1891 for £3,570, and a display of 73 of his objects at South Kensington in 1901, where Assistant Director Arthur Banks Skinner questioned Robinson's labels and a compromise was reached. Yallop places this clash within the emergence of art history as a scholarly discipline, drawing on Waagen, the Vienna school and Wölfflin. The chapter ends with the sales of the 1890s and 1902, Robinson's death and the scattering of his collection, and argues that a collection, unlike its individual objects, does not last.

Whitworth InstituteSouth Kensington MuseumNational Gallery
Ransacking and Revolution: The European Crusade
88. Mrs Schreiber’s Big Red Bag

This chapter gives the biography of Charlotte Schreiber, the wealthy collector whose journals are the chapter's source, and explains how she came to collect late in life. Yallop opens with the Schreibers' journey from Bordeaux to Paris in 1871, with their red velvet bag, arriving after the Paris Commune, when Charlotte went at once in search of dealers and bought a Chelsea china set from the one surviving dealer she could find. The author then goes back to Charlotte's youth as Lady Charlotte Bertie, her marriage to the Welsh ironmaster John Guest, her work at the Dowlais ironworks, her schools and her translation of The Mabinogion. Yallop shows how the 1851 Great Exhibition, her cousin Austen Henry Layard's excavations, Guest's death in 1852 and her second marriage to Charles Schreiber in 1855 prepared her for collecting in the 1860s. The chapter's point is that collecting was a conscious choice, one that her journals record in detail.

Great Exhibition of 1851Nineveh Porch at Canford
99. Pushing and Panting and Pinching their Way

This chapter follows Charlotte and Charles Schreiber on their buying trips through the Netherlands, Belgium and France in 1873, where dealers and rival collectors repeatedly beat them to objects. Yallop uses the rivalry with the dealer Joseph Joel Duveen, who out-bid Charlotte for a porcelain hoard in a remote Dutch village, to make competition the defining feature of mid-century collecting. Yallop then turns to the rivalry between the British Museum and South Kensington Museum, which divided the Bernal collection in 1855 and later fought over long-term loans and a proposed merger. The chapter's main argument concerns gender: women were largely excluded from clubs, learned societies and museum hierarchies, and married women could not legally own what they bought until 1870. Women therefore gravitated to cheap, undervalued fields such as china, which Charlotte exploited, and she became a respected dealer and runner, even for the London firm Mortlocks. Yallop ends by noting how few of her peers matched her travel and dealing.

East and Southeast Asia Yallop's only Asian material is historical background on the European porcelain craze: Queen Mary II's seventeenth-century collection of oriental porcelain, Japanese ceramic imports that peaked in the early seventeenth century before cheaper Chinese pieces flooded the European market, and Macaulay's scorn for the mottled green 'baubles' of the period. Charlotte herself collected European and English china, so the two regions enter only as origin stories.

South Kensington MuseumBritish Museum
1010. The Gourd-shaped Bottle Gourd-shaped

Yallop follows Charlotte Schreiber's collecting across Europe in the 1870s and 1880s, using the story of a gourd-shaped faience bottle as its main case. Charlotte and Charles bought the bottle in Rotterdam in 1873, sold it after a friend dismissed it as cheap German ware, and then saw identical bottles given pride of place in the Rouen Museum in 1874. They recovered their own bottle in a Brussels shop, and Yallop reads the episode as a turning point in her scholarship. Her growing expertise shows in a Wedgwood mark she found under a false Boselly signature in Genoa, a Bristol figure she spotted in Amsterdam and a Spanish figurine she identified against a dealer's view. The chapter then covers her turn to playing cards and fans, which she pursued as a serious scholar without the professional standing open to men. It ends with Charles's illness, his death at Lisbon in 1884 and Charlotte's gift of her English porcelain to South Kensington Museum, and of her fans and cards to the British Museum, which made her one of the most respected collectors of her time.

Rouen MuseumSouth Kensington MuseumBritish Museum
Pride, Passion and Loss: Collecting for Love
1111. Waiting for the Rain to Stop

Yallop follows Joseph Mayer, a Liverpool silversmith and collector, from a portrait of about 1840 that shows him among antiquities to his career of buying whole collections. The chapter first places Mayer in the vogue for antiquarian collecting, using Walter Scott's fictional study and Abbotsford as reference points. It then argues that Mayer, unlike Robinson, lacked scholarly confidence and relied on friends, chiefly Joseph Clarke and Charles Roach Smith, to find objects in London and Kent. The central case is his purchase in 1853 of the Faussett collection of Anglo-Saxon grave goods, which the British Museum had refused, followed by the Fejerváry ivories and the Rolfe collection. Yallop reads these purchases as a compulsive, Victorian urge to possess, and shows the cost: the failed Bram Hertz consortium left Mayer with heavy losses. The chapter ends with his luck in finding the Wedgwood archive in a Birmingham scrap dealer's loft in 1848, which made his Wedgwood holdings among the most important in private hands.

Joseph Mayer collection (Liverpool)British Museum
1212. Mummies, Crocodiles and Shoes for a Queen

Yallop follows Joseph Mayer's move from private collector to museum founder. In 1852 Mayer opened the Egyptian Museum at Colquitt Street in Liverpool, with a shilling admission fee and a full-time curator. The name was a marketing choice, borrowed from Bullock's Egyptian Hall and the fashion for Egyptian antiquities after Napoleon's invasion, and Yallop places Mayer's displays within the Egyptian collecting boom. Agents clearing sites in Egypt, the Rosetta Stone, the Magdala Treasure from Abyssinia and Layard's excavations show a culture of looting that Gladstone's 1871 remarks only began to question. Mayer's museum is presented as a hybrid of public and private: it mixed Egyptian sculpture and a mummy room with Napoleonic relics, Wedgwood, Italian majolica and a stuffed crocodile, in the tradition of cabinets of curiosities such as Tradescant's. Yallop concludes that Mayer's luck and enthusiasm, rather than scholarship, made the museum successful, and that its appeal lay in entertainment as much as in education.

Egyptian Museum (Liverpool)British MuseumEgyptian Hall (Bullock's museum)
1313. The Treasures of the North

Yallop describes the Manchester Art Treasures Exhibition of 1857, a show built on private collections and the setting for Mayer's public success as a collector. The chapter explains how the committee bought the Soulages collection of medieval and Renaissance decorative arts after the government refused to fund it, and how Prince Albert urged a chronological arrangement that set northern and southern European schools side by side. Yallop shows how this method was later admired by curators, including George Scharf at the National Portrait Gallery. The exhibition drew over a million visitors, many of them brought by railway excursions, and the Duke of Devonshire dismissed it as an absurd venture for a cotton town. Mayer's objects were widely praised there, and in 1867 he offered his collection of some 14,000 pieces to Liverpool, where a neo-classical museum had opened in 1860. Yallop concludes that Mayer's gift made the Egyptian pieces the core of a public museum that the town could claim as its own.

East and Southeast Asia Yallop's Asian material is a single episode: a nearly life-size bronze of the Buddhist goddess Guanyin, made in the fifteenth century, which Major William Edie took from the pilgrimage island of Putuo near Ningbo during the First Opium War. Mayer bought it with four other Putuo statues in the Bram Hertz collection and displayed it at Manchester while the Sotheby's sale was pending.

Art Treasures Exhibition (Manchester, 1857)Liverpool MuseumEgyptian Museum (Colquitt Street, Liverpool)
1414. A Larger World

Yallop follows Mayer's later life, from his move in the late 1850s to Pennant House at Bebington on the Wirral until his death. Against the Victorian image of the collector as a lonely, obsessive figure, Yallop sets Mayer's emotional life: his long relationship with Peggy Harrison, commemorated in a marble bust by the sculptor Giovanni Fontana, his brief friendship with the writer Elizabeth Meteyard, and an engagement in 1863 that never led to marriage. The chapter then turns to novels by Henry James and George Meredith and to Punch cartoons, which portrayed collectors as weak or comic, and shows how Mayer's second collection of autographs, gems and theatre papers expressed his private life. Its main case is Mayer's philanthropy in Bebington, where he founded a volunteer company, sports clubs, a village library of 20,000 volumes and a public garden, turning the village into a model. The chapter ends with his plan to sell the Pennant House objects after his death to fund those projects, while the Liverpool museum kept the core of his collection.

Liverpool MuseumPennant House collection (Bebington)
Fashion, Fine Dining and Forgeries: Dealing in Society
1515. Rossetti’s PeacockAsia: in part

Yallop follows the London dealer Murray Marks, whose first visit to the Cheyne Walk house of the painter Dante Gabriel Rossetti, with its menagerie and jumbled interiors, opens the chapter. Yallop argues that Marks was a new kind of dealer, educated and cultured, who linked artists, collectors and fashion. Yallop’s friendship with Rossetti, whose erratic demands he managed, is set beside the careers of Joseph Joel Duveen and Asher Wertheimer, all three born into Jewish emigre families outside the social circles of museums and clubs. Yallop then shows how Marks's expertise in blue-and-white china, drawn largely from unfashionable Chinese wares in Dutch homes, made him wealthy. The chapter follows his Sloane Street showroom of the 1860s and his Oxford Street premises, rebuilt by Richard Norman Shaw in the 1870s to set a new standard of display for the trade. Its last image is the business card Marks commissioned from Rossetti, Whistler and William Morris, showing a blue-and-white jar with peacock feathers.

East and Southeast Asia Blue-and-white is the chapter's main Asian thread. Yallop traces Chinese blue-and-white from the Yuan period (1271-1368) and the K'ang-hsi wares of the late seventeenth century, shipped by the Dutch East India Company, to the Chinese export services ordered with European coats of arms. Marks's supply came largely from seventeenth-century Chinese blue-and-white still on Dutch farmhouse dressers in the 1860s, which he bought up before prices rose and direct import from China became cheaper. Yallop also notes that Marks was interested in Chinese art from childhood and wanted to travel to the Far East, though his father refused.

1616. A Notorious SquabbleAsia: in part

Yallop continues the story of the London dealer Murray Marks into the 1870s and 1880s, when his showroom became a fashionable meeting place. The chapter describes the market depression of those decades, Marks's marketing of dinners served on blue-and-white china, and his 1878 exhibition of the collection he assembled for the surgeon Sir Henry Thompson, whose china was sold at Christie's two years later. Yallop then turns to the American collectors who relied on dealers, above all J. Pierpont Morgan, for whom Marks found Renaissance bronzes and a twelfth-century triptych from Stavelot. The longest case is the Peacock Room at 49 Princes Gate, built for the shipowner Frederick Leyland, in which Marks supplied the blue-and-white and Whistler painted over the leather after a dispute over payment. Yallop argues that the quarrel has overshadowed Marks's role as designer and supplier. The chapter closes with Duveen's later decorating commissions, which show that dealers had come to shape the display of collections as much as the collectors who paid for them.

East and Southeast Asia Blue-and-white from China and the Far East runs through the chapter: Marks assembled Sir Henry Thompson's collection from contacts in Paris, Holland and the Far East, and it was shown in 1878 with a supper served on blue-and-white dishes. Marks also supplied the Chinese blue-and-white that Frederick Leyland displayed on the shelves of the dining room now known as the Peacock Room. The chapter's Asian material concerns display and sale rather than the objects' makers or origins.

Peacock Room (49 Princes Gate, London)Sir Henry Thompson blue-and-white exhibition (1878)Pierpont Morgan collection
1717. The Fake Flora

The central case is the 'Flora affair' of 1909-10. Murray Marks sold a wax bust, which Wilhelm von Bode had declared a work by Leonardo da Vinci, to the Kaiser-Friedrich Museum in Berlin, and then faced a press dispute when it was claimed to be the work of the Victorian sculptor Richard Cockle Lucas. Chemical tests in the 1980s, which found synthetic stearin, settled it as a fake. Yallop widens the frame to the Victorian forgery trade: Bastianini's Renaissance busts, a quartz skull in the British Museum and Robinson's costly purchase of a Palissy dish that was a copy by Georges Pull. Yallop argues that connoisseurs such as Franks, Robinson and Bode relied on the 'eye' long after science could test objects, and that dealers profited from the uncertainty. The most troubling case is the Vasters drawings, which Marks owned and which documented Vasters's forgeries, and a reliquary cross Marks sold after acquiring it in 1881, despite its probable links to a Viennese forgery scheme. The chapter ends with his association with South Kensington Museum and the Bacchus bronze, now thought modern.

Kaiser-Friedrich Museum (Berlin)South Kensington MuseumBritish Museum
Collecting the Empire: In Pursuit of the Exotic
1818. The Route to PekingAsia: chiefly

Yallop follows Stephen Wootton Bushell, a doctor raised on a Kent farm, who sailed for China in 1868 as medical attendant at the British Legation in Peking. The chapter opens with the Victorian taste for souvenirs and exotic objects, then uses Bushell's career to show how a European in China could become a serious collector. Yallop describes the cramped legation enclave, and Bushell's decision to use it as a base: he learned Chinese, read Chinese history and moved freely through the city, where his free medicine for local patients won him a reputation. Yallop’s collection grew from markets, palaces and private houses, and from a journey in 1872 with Thomas Grosvenor to Shangdu, the summer capital of Kublai Khan. Yallop argues that his consignments to South Kensington Museum, and his work for Augustus Franks at the British Museum, made him a pioneer of Western study of Chinese art. The chapter ends with his marriage, his return to Peking with his new wife and his arrangement with the museum in 1880 to send a steady flow of carefully chosen objects.

East and Southeast Asia Bushell, a doctor at the British Legation in Peking from 1868, collected Chinese objects from palaces, private houses and the markets near the Wu Men gate, and in 1872 visited Shangdu, the Yuan summer capital in Inner Mongolia, with Thomas Grosvenor. From 1874 he sent consignments of Chinese bronzes, mirrors and weapons to South Kensington, and by 1880 he was building a collection with the museum in mind.

South Kensington Museum
1919. The Promise of the EastAsia: chiefly

Yallop widens the frame from Bushell to the Victorian museum's view of the wider world. The chapter explains the dilemma of whether ethnographic objects were art, the display models that grouped them by evolution or by geography, and how Darwinian ideas shaped the way they were shown. It then turns to empire: the Colonial and Indian Exhibition of 1886 at South Kensington, and the East India Company's Indian Museum at Leadenhall Street, dispersed in 1879, whose Tippoo's Tiger became a symbol of British power. Japan's opening and the Japonisme craze are followed through royal gifts and Franks's purchases. Bushell's story runs through the second half, with his Peking collecting, his agency for the museum and his stories behind each object. Yallop argues that Bushell, though a respectable doctor, changed attitudes by treating Chinese objects as cultural evidence, a position Franks shared, while the museum's writing about China remained shaped by contempt. The chapter ends with Bushell's Chinese Art, which closes on a white agate vase carved with a fable of scholarly perseverance.

East and Southeast Asia The chapter surveys East Asian collecting from the 1860s to the 1880s: Japan's opening after sakoku and the Japonisme vogue for netsuke and tsuba, royal gifts of Japanese arms to South Kensington, and Franks's purchase of over 3,000 Japanese paintings for the British Museum in 1881. China comes through Bushell's Peking collecting, his bronzes, Ming porcelain and plain Chinese bangles, and the 1872 South Kensington catalogue's description of the Chinese as an 'effeminate race'. Franks and Bushell, Yallop shows, tried to replace that contempt with an understanding of the objects.

South Kensington MuseumBritish MuseumEast India Company Museum (Leadenhall Street)
2020. Collecting Without BoundariesAsia: chiefly

Yallop follows the British doctor Stephen Wootton Bushell through his thirty years in Peking to show how collecting had become international by the late nineteenth century. The chapter opens with Bushell's fascination with Chinese bronze mirrors and his close study of ceramics, ivory, jade and lacquer, and his explorations of imperial architecture such as the Ming tombs and the Summer Palace. It then turns to the British and French looting of the Summer Palace in 1860, which sent relics into more than 2,000 museums in forty-seven countries. The main case is Bushell's work for the American collector William Thompson Walters, whose catalogue, Oriental Ceramic Art (1896), took Bushell to Baltimore and became a pioneering study of Chinese, Japanese and Korean art. Yallop also describes Bushell's jade catalogue for Heber Bishop and his decision to trade in Chinese porcelain for London clients, a venture that brought him money but compromised his scholarly standing. The chapter closes with Bushell's retirement and with the Boxer Rebellion, which made such collecting far harder.

East and Southeast Asia Almost all of the chapter concerns China. Bushell spent thirty years in Peking, studying and buying Chinese bronzes, ceramics, ivory, jade and lacquer, and the imperial architecture of the Ming Tombs and the Summer Palace. Yallop describes the 1860 burning of the Summer Palace by British and French troops and the looting that followed, which scattered relics across more than 2,000 museums. Bushell's catalogue of Walters's porcelain, Oriental Ceramic Art (1896), and his jade purchases for Bishop, both made in Peking, are also described, as is his sale of Chinese bronzes to South Kensington Museum.

South Kensington MuseumBritish MuseumWalters collection, Baltimore
Epilogue

Yallop's epilogue asks what became of the Victorian collections studied in the book. Ruskin's phrase 'stay what is fleeting' frames it: collectors believed that gifts to public museums would keep their collections intact. They did not. Schreiber's collection was dispersed after her death, Mayer's was broken up and much of it destroyed in the 1941 bombing of Liverpool Museum, and Marks and Robinson are largely forgotten. The epilogue closes by noting that these collections still shape today's museums.

East and Southeast Asia Bushell's Chinese objects are mentioned only briefly. Few remain on public display, and their labels carry only a '1883' prefix rather than his name. Yallop recommends his Chinese Art (1904, 1906) as the best guide to his collecting and research.

Yanni, Carla (1999). Nature’s Museums: Victorian Science and the Architecture of Display. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press.Asia: slight9 chapter overviews

Overview

Nature’s Museums (Athlone and Johns Hopkins, 1999; paperback 2005) is an architectural history of natural history museums in Victorian Britain. Its argument is that the buildings helped legitimize the knowledge displayed in them, and that Victorians never settled on one building type because naturalists disagreed about what nature was. The core is six case studies from the 1830s to 1881: the Hunterian Museum, the Cambridge University Library museum rooms, the Museum of Practical Geology, the Oxford University Museum, the Edinburgh Museum of Science and Art and the Natural History Museum in London. Chapters on cabinets of curiosities and on the museum today frame them, and an epilogue sets two American institutions side by side.

East and Southeast Asia in this work slight

East and Southeast Asia are barely present. The book names no museum, collection, collector, visitor or state heritage policy in either region. Asia appears only in passing references in Chapter 1, ‘Museum Vision’: Foucault’s ‘certain Chinese encyclopedia’, quoted from Borges, is a classification text rather than a Chinese museum (lines 1098–1103); Greenwood’s description of Bullock’s Egyptian Hall lists ‘curiosities from America, Africa, and Asia’ (line 1618); a musician’s ‘Chinese bells’ appear in a show at Peale’s Philadelphia museum (line 1732); and early twentieth-century anthropologists are said to have called ‘sometimes Asians’ primitive (line 1136).

The one extended mention is in Chapter 6, ‘Still Life’ (lines 6546–6550). Henry A. Ward’s taxidermy group of two male orangutans fighting over a female in the Bornean forest, shown in 1879, is cited as an example of narrative display, and the American Museum of Natural History bought a similar tableau that year. The chapter describes no Asian museum or visitor. The imperial collections of the Museum of Practical Geology and the Edinburgh museum are discussed in terms of British and colonial resources without any Asian material being named. Nothing in the book is concerned with how Asian objects reached Western museums, or with Asian states’ own museum building.

Introductionp. 1

Yanni opens with a dead rhinoceros at London's Regent's Park zoo in 1849 to show how natural knowledge was once made in gentlemen's houses, and how much the later purpose-built natural history museum depended on new institutions. The book argues that the architecture of these museums helped legitimize the knowledge displayed in them, and that Victorian Britain never settled on one building type because naturalists disagreed about what nature was and how it should be shown. Its core is six case studies: the Hunterian Museum of the Royal College of Surgeons, the Cambridge University Library, the Museum of Practical Geology, the Oxford University Museum, the Edinburgh Museum of Science and Art and the Natural History Museum in London, framed by chapters on eighteenth-century collecting and twentieth-century contexts. Yanni places the work between architectural history and the sociology of science, takes issue with Foucauldian readings of museums, and stresses lighting, iron and glass, patronage and public access. The introduction ends by setting out the range of meanings of nature, from divine creation to natural resource, that the buildings expressed, and states that the book is a historical argument rather than a call for preservation.

Hunterian MuseumCambridge University LibraryMuseum of Practical GeologyOxford University MuseumEdinburgh Museum of Science and ArtNatural History Museum, London
Museum Visionp. 14

Yanni traces how natural history displays moved from the cabinets of curiosities of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, which gathered the strange and monstrous, to the nineteenth-century museum, which arranged typical specimens for close visual scrutiny. Yanni attributes the change to natural theology, which wanted nature shown as evidence of God's order, and to the rise of science as a profession, which needed purpose-built, naturally lit rooms. The argument is set against Foucault's reading of classification and against the claim that cabinets were the origin of museums. The evidence runs through Imperato's cabinet in Naples and Worm's collection, the Tradescant Ark and the Ashmolean Museum at Oxford, Hans Sloane's collection at Montagu House, Bullock's Egyptian Hall in London and Peale's Museum in Philadelphia. Agassiz's pickled-fish lesson at Harvard illustrates the Victorian faith in looking. The chapter concludes that object-based knowledge was the founding principle of the Victorian museum, which replaced the cryptic cabinet with rational, purpose-built rooms for a wide public.

Ashmolean MuseumBritish MuseumBullock's MuseumPeale's MuseumMuseum of Comparative Zoology
Displays of Natural Knowledge in the 1830s and 1840sp. 33

Yanni compares three 1830s and 1840s buildings: the natural history displays planned within the Cambridge University Library, the renovated Hunterian Museum of the Royal College of Surgeons, and the government-funded Museum of Practical Geology. Yanni argues against a simple move from gentlemanly amateur to professional scientist, showing how natural theology and the Paris Jardin des Plantes shaped what British patrons wanted. The Cambridge section follows three competitions from 1829 to 1836, in which Cockerell's classical plan beat Rickman's Gothic one, and shows the natural history displays subordinated to a library and only partly built, with lighting a persistent problem. The Hunterian section follows Owen's remodelling of Dance's building by Barry, where skeletons of giant extinct animals near the entrance pushed the museum beyond medicine. The Museum of Practical Geology is read as nature turned into economic resource and tied to empire, through its built-in stone portal, stratigraphic galleries and evening lectures for working men. The chapter concludes that these buildings express a range of meanings of nature, from capitalist resource to God's second book.

Cambridge University LibraryHunterian MuseumMuseum of Practical GeologyMuséum d'Histoire Naturelle, Paris
Nature as Creationp. 62

Yanni argues that the Oxford University Museum, built from 1855 to 1860 by Deane and Woodward, was commissioned by clients who were natural theologians and saw no conflict between science and religion. The chapter sets out the Oxford context, including the 1853 delegacy report that required skylit museum rooms modelled on the Hunterian and the Museum of Practical Geology. It then recounts the 1854 competition, in which Barry's classical design lost to the Gothic Nisi Dominus, and the debates among clients such as Acland, Johnson, Burgon and Phillips, who did not divide neatly into Gothic and classical camps. The building is described as an iron and glass cloister with carved capitals copying plants, column shafts of British and Irish stone labelled for teaching, and a portal relief of Adam and Eve by Pollen. Ruskin's influence and the engineering of the roof are weighed against the clients' own aims. Yanni ends with the 1860 Huxley and Wilberforce exchange held in the building, which he reads as a home for Wilberforce's science, and concludes that no single architectural response carried one meaning for every visitor.

Oxford University MuseumHunterian MuseumMuseum of Practical GeologyAshmolean Museum
Nature as Natural Resourcep. 91

Yanni turns to the Edinburgh Museum of Science and Art, planned from the 1850s and built from 1861 to 1889 by Francis Fowke, to argue that nature there meant raw material for commerce rather than God's second book. The chapter places the museum within Scottish nationalism and an education system geared to industry, and shows how the Board of Trade and the Department of Science and Art shaped its programme. The museum descended from the Museum of Practical Geology and was shaped by the Great Exhibition of 1851 and the Sydenham Crystal Palace, which Yanni treats as a model of spectacle and commodity display. Fowke's career, from the Royal Engineers to the South Kensington galleries, explains his preoccupation with glare and lighting. Budget cuts removed the facade's geological polychromy, while the iron and glass Great Hall recalls the Crystal Palace. Yanni compares the hall with department stores and the Bethnal Green Museum, and argues that the building set natural history beside art and industry rather than devaluing it. The conclusion uses Prince Albert's cornerstone speech to show that the meaning of nature was local and commercial.

Edinburgh Museum of Science and ArtMuseum of Practical GeologyCrystal Palace, SydenhamBethnal Green Museum
Nature in Conflictp. 111

Yanni tells the story of the Natural History Museum in London, from Owen's 1850s plans for an encyclopedic museum of the national collection to its opening in 1881. The chapter treats the building as a site of conflict: Owen wanted every specimen shown as evidence of imperial and divine order, while Huxley wanted a small didactic display with research collections behind it. It traces the move from Bloomsbury, the 1862 Exhibition Building and the proposed Thames Embankment site, and sets Fowke's winning competition design, which Kerr attacked as a 'bazaar' like the Crystal Palace, beside Alfred Waterhouse's terracotta Romanesque building. Waterhouse's ornament of extinct and living animals, Hawkins's dinosaurs and the statue of Adam on the gable drew praise from the press and criticism from Nature, which found the building unsuited to science. Yanni concludes that Owen's encyclopedic plan and its division of living from extinct species were already out of date by 1881, so the museum expressed a range of meanings of nature, from creation to secular science.

Natural History Museum, LondonBritish MuseumCrystal Palace, SydenhamSouth Kensington Museum
Still Lifep. 147

Yanni asks what nineteenth-century museums mean for today's natural history museums, which face commercial pressure, spectacle and changing science. Yanni argues that buildings fixed in stone cannot easily follow shifts in knowledge, and that the Victorian interiors were too inflexible for later curators and too close to fairs. Moving through taxidermy, dioramas and the animal groups of Hornaday and Ward, he traces the tension between spectacle and science, linking it to Haraway's critique of the American Museum's Africa Hall and to the Field Museum's 'Man-eaters of Tsavo' merchandise. Victorian object lessons are contrasted with today's audiophones and interactive screens, drawing on Gould's defence of crowded cabinets and Secord's view of dinomania. Yanni shows how the Oxford, Hunterian and London buildings now carry meanings their builders did not intend, and how environmentalism has replaced earlier ideas of nature. The chapter ends with the lottery-funded earthquake gallery in London, which he treats as the same identity problem, to entertain or to educate, that Victorian museums faced.

East and Southeast Asia Ward's taxidermy group of two orangutans fighting in the Bornean forest, shown in 1879 and bought by the American Museum of Natural History that year, is cited as an example of narrative display. The chapter mentions it only in passing and describes no Asian museum, collector or visitor.

Natural History Museum, LondonAmerican Museum of Natural HistoryField Museum, ChicagoDublin Museum of Natural HistoryHunterian MuseumOxford University Museum
Conclusionp. 159

Yanni closes by arguing that museums present their knowledge as neutral when they in fact help define science, and that Victorian architecture made its claims openly. The conclusion restates that nature meant different things to different audiences: natural theology at Oxford, useful resource in London and Edinburgh. The museums, Yanni argues, should be preserved as historical records.

Oxford University MuseumHunterian MuseumMuseum of Practical GeologyEdinburgh Museum of Science and ArtNatural History Museum, London
Two More Arks – The Museum of Creation and the Museum of Jurassic Technologyp. 162

This epilogue to Yanni's book sets two contrasting institutions side by side: the Museum of Creation and Earth History near San Diego, a creationist display that borrows the methods of mainstream natural history museums to claim scientific truth, and the Museum of Jurassic Technology in Los Angeles, an ironic institution that copies the founding myth of the Ashmolean. Yanni walks the visitor through the choreographed rooms of the creationist museum, from Babel and the Neanderthal skulls to a nineteenth-century passage that sets creationist worthies against evolutionist villains, and then to its claim that Darwinism produced Nazi racism. The Jurassic Technology museum, by contrast, blurs belief and disbelief, using the bat that flies through lead as its example. Both museums expose the same premise: displays legitimize knowledge. The chapter concludes that the natural history museum cannot escape its inheritance from Noah's Ark, the first vessel to house the whole natural world.

Museum of Creation and Earth HistoryMuseum of Jurassic TechnologyAshmolean Museum

Yoshida, Takashi (2014). From Cultures of War to Cultures of Peace: War and Peace Museums in Japan, China, and South Korea. Portland, ME: MerwinAsia.Asia: central9 chapter overviews

Overview

Yoshida asks whether Japanese society has in fact forgotten its imperial past. Yoshida argues that after 1945 a 'victimizer consciousness' took hold, as the Occupation's War Guilt Information Program repeatedly publicised Japan's atrocities. The book traces war and peace museums in Japan from the 1850s to the present: prewar military museums and the Yushukan at Yasukuni, the postwar peace museums of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and the smaller museums that show Japanese aggression, kamikaze and Self-Defense Forces museums, the 1990s and 2000s disputes over exhibits, and six museums for peace in China and South Korea. An introduction and seven chapters are followed by a conclusion that asks whether patriotism can promote peace.

East and Southeast Asia in this work central

East Asia is the main subject. Japan dominates, but China and South Korea are treated at length in Chapter 7 (Peace Museums in China and South Korea) and in the conclusion, which compares the Nanjing Massacre Memorial Museum, Beijing's Memorial Museum of the Chinese People's War of Resistance, Shenyang's September 18 Historical Museum, Seoul's Independence Hall of Korea and Seodaemun Prison History Hall. Chapter 3 (Expansion of Peace Museums) concentrates on museums of Japanese aggression in China, Korea, Taiwan, Manchuria and Southeast Asia, among them the Okuno Island Poison Gas Museum and the Korea Museum and Women's Active Museum in Tokyo, which trace sex stations in China and Burma and the testimonies of Korean women such as Pak Yongsim. Chapter 6 (History Wars) is also largely about Asia: Nagasaki's Nanjing and chemical-warfare displays, and Peace Osaka's China and Korea corners.

Colonial and imperial museums appear in Chapter 1 (The Rise and Fall of War Museums in Imperial Japan): the Imperial Museum in Ueno and the imperial museums in Nara and Kyoto collected the empire's treasures, and the Museum of the Governor-General of Taiwan is noted. Chapter 2 (The Rise of Multi-layered Pacifism) covers China as victim: the Maruki panels toured China in 1956, and the return of 551 Chinese laborers' remains from Hanaoka in 1953. Chapters 4 and 5 treat Asia mostly through absence, as at Chiran and the Yamato Museum, which omit Korean and Chinese workers.

Southeast Asia is marginal. Burma appears through a sex station, and a Thai-Burma railroad locomotive at the Yushukan omits the forced labour and deaths behind it. Peace Osaka has a 'Southeast Asian Nations' corner, the Sakai museum's 1994 corner has photographs from the Philippines and Thailand, and the 1940 invasion of northern Indochina is cited. Indonesia, Malaya and Borneo are not discussed, and the passages read give no account of Asian collections in Western museums or of restitution claims.

Contents

Theoretical approach of this work
Acknowledgmentsp. ix
Introductionp. xiiiAsia: chiefly

Yoshida challenges the assumption that Japanese society has united in forgetting its imperial past. Yoshida argues that a 'victimizer consciousness' took hold after 1945, when the Allied Occupation's War Guilt Information Program repeatedly publicized Japan's wartime atrocities, and that many Japanese came to repudiate the wartime culture that had glorified sacrifice. The book then traces war and peace museums in Japan from the 1850s to the present. Its chapters cover the rise and fall of prewar war museums, the origins of pacifist movements focused on Hiroshima and Nagasaki and on foreign victims, a survey of nineteen peace museums, kamikaze museums that present pilots as heroes, revived war museums, disputes over exhibits since the mid-1990s, and six museums for peace in China and South Korea. Yoshida also discusses how to define a peace museum, setting Johan Galtung's narrow definition against Anzai Ikuro's broader one, which includes structural violence and Japanese destruction abroad.

East and Southeast Asia Yoshida's focus is Japan, with museums in the People's Republic of China and the Republic of Korea as a second concern. Yoshida discusses the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum and the Nagasaki Atomic Bomb Museum, both opened in 1955, and the Battleship Mikasa museum, whose renovation in the Cold War was supported by American fleet admiral Chester Nimitz. Yoshida notes that six museums in China and South Korea use large photographs and wax figures to show Japanese atrocities, and that Japanese disputes over memory shape how they do so.

Hiroshima Peace Memorial MuseumNagasaki Atomic Bomb MuseumBattleship Mikasa Memorial MuseumYushukan
1The Rise and Fall of War Museums in Imperial Japanp. 1Asia: chiefly

Yoshida traces Japan's war museums from the Tokugawa exhibitions and the Meiji government's first museums to the end of the Occupation, arguing that they rose with militarism and collapsed with it. Yoshida describes how Japanese envoys visited the Smithsonian and the Tower of London armory, and how Fukuzawa Yukichi introduced the Western museum to ordinary readers. The chapter's centre is the Yushukan, a military museum opened in 1882 on the grounds of the Yasukuni Shrine. Enlarged in 1908 and rebuilt in 1931, it drew 1.89 million visitors in 1940, and the adjacent National Defense Hall let children fire modified rifles and sit in a bomber cockpit. Yoshida shows that the exhibits presented a sanitized, united nation and omitted the police repression of dissenters and Japanese atrocities. Yoshida then examines the War Guilt Information Program, which publicized Nanjing and Manila through newspapers, films and the Tokyo trial, and how the shrine's priests reshaped the Yushukan to survive. The museum did not reopen as a museum until the mid-1980s, by which time peace museums had taken its place.

East and Southeast Asia Japanese museums are the subject, with Taiwan and Korea as colonial sites. The Imperial Museum in Ueno and imperial museums in Nara and Kyoto collected the treasures of the empire, and a Memorial Museum of the Battle of Port Arthur opened in 1906. A zoo and botanical garden were built in Keijo (Seoul) in 1909 to facilitate imperial worship, and Yoshida notes that the handbook of the Museum of the Governor-General of Taiwan stressed peace and humanitarianism, although the imperial government had abandoned its cooperation policy by the mid-1930s and invaded northern Indochina in 1940.

YushukanBattleship Mikasa Memorial MuseumImperial Museum (Ueno)Memorial Museum of the Battle of Port ArthurNational Defense HallNavy MuseumMuseum of the Governor-General of Taiwan
2The Rise of Multi-layered Pacifism and Early Peace Museums in Postwar Japanp. 20Asia: in part

Yoshida traces how a pacifist current in postwar Japan produced peace museums, beginning with the Occupation's democratization of museums and then Hiroshima's campaign to become a city of world peace under Mayor Hamai, whose festivals and appeals to foreign cities led to the Peace Memorial City Construction Law of 1949. The Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum, opened in 1955, is the central case, and the chapter follows its history through a 1970s remodel with wax figures. A second case is the Maruki Art Gallery, where the painters Iri and Toshi produced the Hiroshima Panels, exhibited them abroad, and later painted Japanese perpetrator atrocities such as the Nanjing Massacre. Yoshida then examines a pacifism that confronted Japanese war crimes: the repatriation of Chinese laborers' remains from Hanaoka and the confessions of former soldiers held in Fushun and Taiyuan. The chapter ends with history teachers and the historian Ienaga Saburo's textbook lawsuits, arguing that these movements explain why later museums began to show Japanese atrocities.

East and Southeast Asia Most of the Asian content concerns China and Korea as victims. The Maruki panels toured China in 1956, where a one-legged woman in Beijing told the artists the panels helped her understand Japanese suffering. The chapter describes the 1953 return of 551 Chinese laborers' remains from Hanaoka in Akita to Tianjin, and the Fushun and Taiyuan confessions of atrocities in China. Korean victims of the atomic bomb and the Crows panel on Korean survivors are also discussed.

Hiroshima Peace Memorial MuseumMaruki Art Gallery
3Expansion of Peace Museums: Acknowledging Japanese Aggressionp. 48Asia: chiefly

Yoshida surveys the peace museums that spread through Japan from the 1980s and 1990s, arguing that they carry forward postwar self-critical pacifism into displays of Japanese aggression and colonial rule. The chapter moves through small and mid-sized institutions: the Osaka Human Rights Museum, the Okuno Island Poison Gas Museum, the Grassroots House Peace Museum in Kochi, the Museum for Bamboo-Bush Grave Markers in Hokkaido, and the Kyoto Museum for World Peace at Ritsumeikan University. For each it shows how local activists or curators shaped the displays and how the institution was contested, for example when city officials forced out the Okuno Island director after he raised Japan's chemical warfare in China. It then covers the Textbook Museum in Sakai, founded by a retired teacher after the city's own peace museum removed material on Japanese atrocities, and the Korea Museum and Women's Active Museum in Tokyo, which address colonial and wartime sexual violence. The chapter ends by noting that these museums face sustained political pressure and offer perspectives that patriotic narratives exclude.

East and Southeast Asia Most of the chapter concerns Japan's aggression in China, Korea, Taiwan and Southeast Asia. Okuno Island's director Murakami tells visitors of the more than 80,000 Chinese killed or wounded by Japanese chemical weapons, and the Kyoto museum displays atrocities in Taiwan, Korea, Manchuria, China and Southeast Asia. The Korea Museum in Tokyo covers Prince Shotoku's Korean tutors, the 1923 killing of Koreans after the Kanto earthquake, and the Hainan Island labor camps, along with a Taiwanese woman's memoir of a sex station. The Women's Active Museum traces sex stations in China and Burma and the testimonies of Korean women such as Pak Yongsim.

Osaka Human Rights MuseumOkuno Island Poison Gas MuseumGrassroots House Peace MuseumMuseum for Bamboo-Bush Grave MarkersKyoto Museum for World PeaceTextbook MuseumKorea MuseumWomen's Active Museum on War and Peace
4Bringing Peace to War Deadp. 112Asia: in part

Yoshida asks what peace means for museums that commemorate the war dead rather than document Japanese aggression. The chapter examines three peace museums without such artifacts: the Himeyuri Peace Museum on Okinawa, built on the cave where student nurses died in 1945; the Voiceless Museum in Nagano, a gallery of paintings by young artists killed in the war; and the Center on the Tokyo Raids and War Damages, which was founded after a Tokyo assembly froze funding for a proposed museum. It then turns to kamikaze museums at Chiran, Tachiarai, Bansei, the Navy Practice Pilots Museum and the Yamato Museum in Kure, which honor suicide pilots and sailors with little criticism of the state. Yoshida reads the letters on display and the visitor comments, and reports the textbook dispute over mass suicides on Okinawa. The chapter concludes that the kamikaze museums honor sacrifice without questioning the policies behind it, whereas the Himeyuri and Voiceless museums, though not about aggression, are incompatible with patriotic narratives.

East and Southeast Asia The chapter says little about Asia except through absence. Chiran's displays include eleven pilots born on the Korean peninsula, and Tachiarai's exhibits include Korean pilots, yet no trace appears of the Korean laborers who expanded the air base. The Yamato Museum omits the Korean and Chinese workers who built Kure's underground tunnels, and the Tokyo center's symposia address Japan's bombing of Chongqing. A Chinese student visiting Himeyuri urged the museum to show Japanese aggression in China and Korea.

Himeyuri Peace MuseumVoiceless MuseumCenter on the Tokyo Raids and War DamagesChiran-Town Peace Museum for Kamikaze PilotsTachiarai Peace MuseumNavy Practice Pilots MuseumBansei Peace Memorial Museum for the Special Attack ForceYamato Museum
5The Revival of War Museums in Postwar Japanp. 144Asia: in part

Yoshida argues that war museums revived in Japan from the 1960s, even though postwar society is officially defined by peace. The chapter starts with the Battleship Mikasa Memorial Museum, restored in 1961 with support from Admiral Nimitz, conservative politicians and the American Navy, who saw it as a way to rebuild national pride. It then examines the Yushukan, the war museum of Yasukuni Shrine, reopened in 1986 and renovated in 2002 to present the 'true' history of modern Japan. Its panels on the Zero fighter and a Thai-Burma railroad locomotive omit the forced labor and deaths behind them, and its displayed quotation from the Indian judge Radhabinod Pal and monument inscription are inaccurate. The last section surveys about forty Self-Defense Forces museums on bases, with close readings of the Kakishoshukan at Fukuchiyama, which omits the Nanjing massacre, and the Kanoya Air Base Museum. The chapter concludes that these museums never connect wartime loyalty to the suicide missions they honor, and that they are part of a continuing political contest over the war's history.

East and Southeast Asia Its Asian content concerns how the Yushukan and SDF museums treat Japan's conduct abroad. The Zero panel cites a 1940 battle over Chongqing, and the locomotive display omits the roughly quarter-million forced laborers who built the Thai-Burma railroad, around 40,000 of whom died. The Yushukan honors Taiwanese and Korean colonial soldiers but no foreigner beyond Pal. The Kakishoshukan's panels omit the 20th Infantry Regiment's role in the 1937 Nanjing killings, documented in a corporal's diary, and the Kanoya museum leaves out some 500 Korean laborers who fortified the air base.

Battleship Mikasa Memorial MuseumYushukanKakishoshukanKanoya Air Base Museum
6History Wars: Responding to Pressures from Different Interest Groupsp. 162Asia: in part

Yoshida examines the 'history wars' of the 1990s and 2000s, when public museums that showed Japanese aggression were attacked by revisionist politicians and groups. Four cases form the core. The Nagasaki Atomic Bomb Museum kept its displays on the Sino-Japanese and Pacific Wars, but after LDP pressure two photographs were swapped, and a citizens' committee then revised other captions and removed wartime propaganda films. Peace Osaka faced years of complaints about its photographs and in 2000 stopped leasing its auditorium to civic groups. The Peace Museum of Saitama renamed its Nanjing Massacre entry 'capture of Nanjing' in 2006 after prefectural criticism, including the governor's remarks. Against these, the national Showa Hall and two other government museums in Tokyo show only Japanese suffering, and were shaped by compromises with bereaved families. Yoshida concludes that the disputes mark a shift from seeing Japanese people as innocent victims to recognizing their responsibility, and that denial of atrocities helped drive the growth of museums that display them.

East and Southeast Asia Most of the disputes concern how Asia is shown. Nagasaki's display of the Nanjing Massacre and Japanese chemical and biological warfare in China was altered under LDP pressure. Peace Osaka's China and Korea corners, covering the Three-All Operation, Unit 731 and the March First Movement of 1919, drew attacks, and Saitama's references to Korean forced labor at Yoshimi were criticized as too thin. The three national Tokyo museums show only Japanese suffering, and a Japanese repatriate's childhood in Pyongyang is their sole link to Korea.

Nagasaki Atomic Bomb MuseumPeace Osaka (Osaka International Peace Center)Peace Museum of SaitamaShowa HallExhibition and Reference Library for Peace and ConsolationHistorical Materials Hall for Sick and Wounded Soldiers
7Peace Museums in China and South Koreap. 199Asia: chiefly

Yoshida surveys the peace museums of China and South Korea, where, unlike in Japan, museums that condemn wartime atrocities often also promote patriotism and national identity. The chapter opens with three Chinese sites: the Nanjing Massacre Memorial Museum, the Memorial Museum of the Chinese People's War of Resistance against Japan in Beijing, and the September 18 Historical Museum in Shenyang. Their graphic displays of Japanese atrocities are paired with heroic accounts of Chinese resistance and calls for national unity. Yoshida then turns to South Korea, where the Independence Hall of Korea and the Seodaemun Prison History Hall recast colonial rule as a simple contest between innocent Koreans and evil Japanese, and omit the abuses of later South Korean governments. The privately funded History Museum of Sexual Slavery by the Japanese Military is described as more international in outlook, and the micro Center for Peace Museum in Seoul is presented as a pacifist counterpoint. The chapter ends with the struggle to build a War and Women's Human Rights Museum, opposed by veterans' groups, and asks whether patriotism can contribute to peace in Northeast Asia.

East and Southeast Asia Yoshida discusses China and South Korea at length, and treats their museums as nationalist. The Nanjing Massacre Memorial Museum, opened in 1985 and rebuilt in 2007, honours Japanese such as Honda Katsuichi and in 2010 hosted the cartoonists' exhibition 'My August 15'. Beijing's Memorial Museum of the Chinese People's War of Resistance against Japan and Shenyang's September 18 Historical Museum are described as patriotic education bases. South Korea's Independence Hall of Korea (1987) and Seodaemun Prison History Hall (1998) present Korean martyrs against Japanese colonial rule, and the latter's torture experience rooms, staged for visitors, are described; the chapter says Korean governments' postwar abuses are not shown there.

Nanjing Massacre Memorial MuseumMemorial Museum of the Chinese People's War of Resistance against JapanSeptember 18 Historical MuseumIndependence Hall of KoreaSeodaemun Prison History HallHistory Museum of Sexual Slavery by the Japanese MilitaryCenter for Peace Museum
Conclusion: Patriotism vs. Peacep. 232Asia: chiefly

The conclusion returns to the book's central question, whether patriotism promotes peace. Yoshida traces Japan's postwar culture of peace, in which peace museums such as Hiroshima and Nagasaki gained public favour while war museums lost theirs, and contrasts the Yushikan war museum, which calls the Pacific War a just war of liberation, with the Chiran kamikaze museum and the Kyoto Museum for World Peace. The Kyoto museum, Yoshida argues, gives victims of Japanese aggression as much place as the kamikaze pilots, and the Women's Active Museum deplores sexual violence regardless of nationality. Peace museums need not show Japanese atrocities, Yoshida holds, but on no account should they glorify aggression. Yoshida then judges that museums in China and South Korea foster an 'innocent-us' and 'savage-them' nationalism, and calls for peace museums to be depoliticised and focused on human suffering. It ends with a plea that Japan's postwar denunciation of war violence continue and spread to other countries.

East and Southeast Asia Japan, China and South Korea are compared throughout. Yoshida contrasts Japanese museums such as the Kyoto museum, which covers victims of Japanese aggression and of the wartime state, with museums in China and South Korea that display vivid images of Japanese atrocities, legitimise just wars and foster 'innocent-us' nationalism. Yoshida wants those Chinese and South Korean museums to show citizens working with Japanese for reconciliation. Nosaka Sanzo, who founded an anti-war alliance in Yan'an, and the journalist Honda Katsuichi are cited as Japanese who challenged their own government.
